As much of the hype went about with this remastered prequel.  It's lived up to that hype.  However its still not the best RE game out there.  Probably this is the weakest and hardest out of the main canon due to some interesting mechanics introduced into a game keeping the genre fresh back in 2003.
Positives:
Both Characters have nice variations about them,  Health, physical strengthl, weapon handling.
No more item boxes - (if you know the optimal route after your playthroughs getting the S Rank feels less of a chore)
Items can be swapped and dropped on the ground.  This feature is excellent to be honest.
Co-Op (Single Player) Now you can team up fighting the horde that awaits you!
Breaking the norm from the previous 3 titles at the time.
Requires actual thought to play the game.  No hand holding like the negative reviews.
Wesker Mode - Nice to go about murdering everything with an overpowered character!
Leech Hunter - Skillful minigame to unlock extra goodies.
Additional Costumes which the original only had 1 for Billy and Rebecca.
Negatives:
Weakest story in the series.
Inventory system will annoy newcomers but thats what its supposed to do otherwise it wouldnt be fun if it takes less than 2 hours to complete.
Huge arsenal of weapons
Lurker (Frog) can ruin a no save game near the end!
Hard Mode Final boss can be an absolute bullet sponge if you dont take enough ammo with you which will result you to replay an early save just so you have enough ammo to kill it.
Mediocre final boss.
Extremely narrow corrodors compared to RE1HDR - Difficult to do a knife run.
Knife is absolute pants in the game due to character animations - alot of speedrunners complain about this.
Requires some knowledge of RE franchise as theres alot of spoilers in the game.  Its Reccommended you play this game after completing RE1,2,3.
Team AI can be stupid during combat.  Shoots when you fire first. No initative to assist if grabbed.
Overall Capcom did an excellent job optimising this game.  Not perfect but still alot of fun.

If you have any interest in Visual Novels you may be pleased with this game. You take up the role of Elodie, a soon to be queen who must prepare herself for her future queenhood (is that even a word?). The game plays out a little hasty as you must decide what skills to train up and what to do in order to change/maintain your mood. All of these effect how you dialogue and actions go with other characters. Ultimately, if you don't study enough in a particular area at times you will be presented with an event that results in your death and oh boy is there a lot of that.
Verdict? Get this game if you like the art style/visual novel playstyle. It's got a semi-decent story (enough to keep me playing at least) and amusing outcomes to situations depending on the things you study. Replayabilty is semi high, considering it's short length as well.

The final installment of the Street Fighter 4 series. The legendary fighting game's latest edition.
This new version is more than a simple tweak pack  - it adds four characters returning from previous games, a new "Version Select" similar to the "isms" or "grooves" from previous Capcom fighters, a handful of stages from SFxT, and Decapre.
Yes, Decapre. As in Masked Russian Cammy Clone Bison Doll. And honestly, I have to say that as uncreative as she is, she is definately a character to at least try. But's that's not the point of this review.
The point of this review is whether Ultra Street Fighter 4 lives up to expectations. Which honestly, I have to say it does.
Gameplay: It's Street Fighter. Almost always solid, and Ultra is no exception. Of course, you do run into the occasional Hadoken-spammer or button masher, but that's to be expected. Unfortunately, Arcade Mode Seth is STILL in this game. 9/10, High Priority
Visuals: They're not super-realistic, but why would that be necessary? Street Fighter has always had this slightly stylized art design. The game looks very smooth, which unlike other graphical niceties is actually important in the fighting game genre. It's also pretty visually appealing. 9/10, Medium Priority
Story: N/A. Doesn't Apply. Fighting games don't do stories, or at most they have excuse plots. No rating, Minimal Proirity
Soundtrack: Very well mastered. Sounds great on a Logitec 5.1 surround system. There are a few songs I don't necessarily like, but that's personal preference. 9/10, Medium Priority
Innovation: I can't say the Street Fighter series has changed much on these terms, at least since Vanilla SF4. I wouldn't go looking for new innovations in what is essentially an expansion pack. 3/10, Low Priority
Reliability: I can't give it a 10/10. I can't give it a 9/10. I can't even give it an 8/10 in this category. Training Mode and Only have a tendency to drop frames. The Netcode isn't exactly the most reliable - you can get a 4-bar connection that feels like 1-bar on the PS3, and you can get a 1-bar connection that feels like you're fighting over wired LAN or the new Wireless 802.11AC protocol used by corporate-grade wireless routers. However, the game is VERY playable otherwise. 7/10, High Priority
Street fighter has always been a great series (with a few exceptions that were forgettable), and Ultra Street Fighter 4 delivers. There are a few things that need to be worked out, but they're all technical issues that can be fixed with updates.
Recommended for: Fighting Game Fans, Competitive Gamers, Fighting Game Beginners
Stay Away: Bro Gamers, UB3R L33T Gamzorz (people who play games based on trends), People who can't take losing (The game isn't hard in and of itself, but you WILL get wrecked online for the first few weeks, if not months. Also, Arcade Mode Seth.)

Cavern Escape is a small indie title created by the devolper White Dog. It is a tough platform puzzle title.
You guide a little blue torch with eyes to the end of the level while collecting gems to open up a second mode with more levels. The game is severely lacking any kind of narative that would explain why this torch needs to get to the very end of each level while risking his life dodging spikes littered around each stage. The stages are very linear and get even more rigid the further you get into the game. The game has a world map where you go along unlocking stages until you reach the very end. The game gets crazy hard by level 15 of the first mode, you need some crazy speed to get past the game.
The graphics are very basic. They're clean, you can tell the spikes hurt you. There are torches with a little flame animation on them. There are pillars that move into place when you first enter a stage. There are also balls and blocks with spikes that will move around in a pattern that act as a obstacle for the little blue torch. The game is very purple in mode 1, and green in mode 2. I was hoping for a little more variety but I couldn't get further to find out if there was a third color later in the game.
The game has sounds, and there is a musical score that plays in the background. There is even a soundtrack available if you enjoy what you hear. I don't remember one bit of it even now that I just got done playing the game less than 30 minutes ago. I'll just say it's very forgettable.
Overall I think this game needs to be avoided even if you can get it on sale. There are cards you can collect. If that is your thing, just idle it. Even then the electrical costs, computer depreciation, time, etc will probably not make it worth it to get the cards.

Perhaps the game that embodies modern rogue-lites aside from Spelunky, Binding of Isaac is a game I have struggled to accept its demands of skill as well as luck for nearly five years, and it cemented my distaste for the genre with its emphasis on difficulty. As a result of my history, you can imagine my surprise when after years of a hiatus I had given Rebirth a try and I beat the game on my very first attempt within under 30 mins of beating Isaac’s mother. Only then after beating the game several times to unlock the next phase of progression with Mom’s heart did I learn to appreciate the merits of BOI as something more than a luck-based game with so many factors to influence your skill.
This is perhaps the reality of the situation with rogue-lites/likes; it’s difficult to enjoy, much less judge, an experience that can be as soul-crunchingly insurmountable as well as a test of the player’s attrition in situations of distress. Some people will relish in overcoming the odds while others like myself will become frustrated at being stone-walled by the same challenge and the replaying of old content that begins to lose its luster with every restart. BOI:R, however, does enough under the hood of its mechanics of the original as well as adding a sense of progression to the game that makes its frustrations more bearable without demanding the player to be the greatest player or have the best build to succeed. This alone makes the Rebirth an outstanding game, let alone the successor to one of the most influence games within its genre.
If anything was responsible for my ability to succeed upon years of failures, the addition of proper controller support without the limitations of Joy2Key was the beginning of the refinement of the original. BOI:R has initially balanced its difficulty curve by adding a progression system of smaller victories that unlock more dire challenges in future playthroughs as you also build a greater collection of items to influence your chances of success. There are also more health, item and new pick-up buffs and items dropped within the default difficulty that requires the player not to be too careless as they play but also are allowed more screw-ups as they learn to improve.
All these changes, when combined with the different level-tiers, new bosses and enemies, various room-sizes, and overall satisfaction of replaying the game in runs that begin in 20 to 30 mins that take up almost an hour to complete once you have proven your competency, are all the differences from a frustrating game that has less barriers of progression and lower rates of success that forces the player to become more adept at the game. Learning from failure can only carry a game so far before the the inability to succeed instills the player with hopelessness in every run.
SoulsBorne games get a lot of bad rep for adding any means of accessibility to their games, and roguelites/roguelikes have also carried that stigma with them since their inception. It’s finally nice to see that even the greatest games within this genre has made their game more accessible without compromising the original’s merits by having a harder mode similar to the original as well as rewarding players more in that mode with newer items that cannot be unlocked on the default difficulty.
Having said all these benefits of the game, there are still issues centered around the design of BOI, perhaps even more so in Rebirth than the original, that are worth noting. Many of which are the result of the game having RNG in its DNA as a game rather than being all hand-crafted.
As a result of the varied room designs, especially with bosses, some of the cramped quarters bring into question the idea that every randomly-designed room is possible without taking damage that the original boasted. Enemies that leave trails that cause damage are often the culprits of these unavoidable hits that cannot really be overcome unless you are quick to kill them or fortunate to have the enemy AI behave in a way for your benefit. Sometimes luck is really an overriding factor on the success of the player if the items given are not helpful in every floor or if the player takes damage, and that is something all rogue-likes/lites suffer in their conception.
Another commonly accepted mechanic with these games is the idea of obfuscation of mechanics which results in players fumbling around in the dark for success or having a fan-wiki open on another screen to give details the game refuses to tell you. This is a trope I’ve never feel comfortable with because it promotes failure for players who do enjoy the discovery as well as going outside the game for support, which is never a great idea. It wouldn’t be so bad in BOI:R if the game allowed you to see what the items do that you have unlocked in the basement to give the player some in-game means of a refresher rather than forcing the player to memorizes hundreds, upwards to 500 now with all the expansions, of effects and combinations. Even the messages and recipes of Sword in the Stars: The Pit allowed players some permeant means of cataloguing all the experimentation they unlocked with every defeat, and eventually will let players stay in-game rather than rely on failure or a wiki.
Even the storytelling and themes addressed in this adapation of the Biblical story has rather the potential to capitalize its usage of child-abuse, paranoia born from zealouts, and  theself-reflection of these two sources of conflict are something the game could focus on in greater detail rather than adding tons of spoof and shock endings along with a lot of poop to the game. As much as I want to enjoy the narrative hidden in the details, it's ultimately not what the game was about, which is a shame since more games should explore these dark themes.
Regardless of these blights, everything else about the game from its mechanics, bosses, items and traps are so finely polished and so varied of challenges that the randomization and unpredictability is a quality in its favor than being a source of annoyance, but I think these two aspects are still blunders of a genre accepted for its own sake rather than having reasons for its existence. As there are generations of gamers who grew up on these randomized luck-based games of success, perhaps reexamining the purposes behind these games is needed to innovate them


In spite of these issues and the overall barrier of entry for rogue-lites, the Rebirth edition of BOI is so finely polished in its gameplay beyond its appeal of endless variety that these complaints are rather blisters of a genre in its puberty. Perhaps advances in dynamic difficulty that take the player’s skill into consideration or further tweaking of the probabilities behind these games are areas for the genre’s growth, or perhaps something even not even considered yet will be born from all these games taking aspects of Rogue in a new direction. Whatever the result, the plethora of rogue-lites/rogue-likes available on Steam perhaps needs the firm hand of direction from their creators to stay the hand of blind faith to redeem these aged-old conventions from sacrificing their descendants.

In today's Steam Review collection, people base their purchasing decisions on trailers and blurbs, and get upset that the game they imagined might exist is not in fact the game that does. People get pissy about how they backed something that they didn't realize was a survival simulation game despite the publically available and linked to original Ludum Dare concept game being a survival simulation game. And, a personal favorite, people hate hard games for being hard.
To understand if you'll like Gods Will Be Watching, you need to play Gods Will Be Watching. The original game, I mean:
If you enjoyed that, you'll enjoy the full release. If you didn't enjoy that, and felt it was too much micromanagement, or you were incapable of recognizing the animation cues, or understanding the systems in play surrounding 'chance', or if you felt it was too hard and unforgiving by not letting you succeed and forcing you to sometimes start over because of a combination of bad luck and bad management...Well, it's not for you, then. Don't purchase, and move on. It's a very love it or hate it game, but at least be informed what you're getting into.

I have to say, I see where the negative reviews are coming from. Original mode is balls-out hard; pure and simple. It is harsh, brutal, and unforgiving; an apt description of the game at large as well. However, it is very thoughtful and stressful, every decision having consequences both immediate and delayed. I feel that maybe people were offput, thinking it a similar game to Superbrothers' Sword and Sworcery (another phenomenal game I highly recommend), but it is not a simple game like that was; you must manage everything on screen, or failure WILL occur. Once again, I feel this is actually a strong plus, going in the vein that your choices ultimately culminate, for ill or good. Another thing I can see rubbing people the wrong way is that the game gives you zero insight into what to do. It does not tell you what to do with hostages, how they're doing, etc. You have to watch their demeanor, their way of speaking and tone of voice, etc. Once again, this is not an easy game by any means, but It does make you think if you are making the correct decisions, and whether you could have done something different. Granted, I have only passed the first chapter as of this writing (after changing it to easy, admittedly), but so far I am eager to see what else happens.

I cannot recommend this game strongly enough. What initially strikes as just a "bad decision" simulator develops over time into a strange but thought provoking game with a fantastic aesthetic, killer soundtrack and deliciously somber tone. Parts of it can seem unfair or tedious, but in the you'll come to understand why it needs to be that way.

This game does what it sets out ot do extremely well.
What it sets out to do is present a series of resource-management challenges that encourage thinking and - in a pinch - creativity.  The levels are extremely challenging; those with flimsy patience should steer clear, as Gods Will Be Watching takes a very old-school approach when it comes to your success.  Your success in this game will be earned, my friend, or you won't get to taste it at all.  Believe me, though, success in this game tastes delicious.  Delicious.
Rewards for advancing through the levels include experiencing more of the very-well-done story, pieces of concept art, and alternate music for the stages.  I found (and am still finding) that just seeing what happens next is reason enough to keep driving forward.  Feeling like an absolute boss when clearing a stage helps as well.
There are some parts within the scenarios where choosing the wisest course of action comes with a percentage of success.  In all cases but one, this percentage can be boosted up to 100 before being used, if one is playing well enough.  One fibbly gripe I have with the game is the one situation I've encountered where you can't perfectly ensure success (there is a 1 in 7 chance of failure at best), and I was unlucky twice in a row.  Pretty mean trick there, but honestly, playing the level 12 times instead of 10 or 11 isn't the end of the world.
Engaging story, a mighty fine soundtrack, and the game is very pretty - these things add to the fantastic feeling of accomplishment when you beat something, and the interesting story rounds out a fun, unique video game.  Just be sure to bring your man pants; this game will beat you worse than you'll beat your hostages.

Dead Effect's a strange beast. It's a F2P Android game reworked into a paid Steam release, which usually sends up nothing but red flags. Mercifully, your $5 purchase is actually put to decent use. The developers have included 3 levels with this release and a whole bevy of weaponry to outfit your arsenal. Strong enemies will also drop weapon upgrades and unlocks for free so you have to grind less. Gold bars are dropped as well, which is crucial given they pay the way for your revives. The gameplay is considerably slower than most FPS's and ammo management is somewhat more pressing than your average shooter affair. The game isn't survival horror by any stretch of the imagination but does do a decent job building a gory, creepy environment.
Enemies are your standard fair for a zombie survival shooter. You have slow walkers, runners, hurlers, chainsaw guys, one or two bosses and a few odds and ends. It's nothing special but the game throws enough zeds your way that you'll be happy variety is limited. Headshots are as important as ever and will help you survive the most dangerous of opponents. Level 3 is a tad unfair in that it throws a billion zombies at you without offering terribly many places to go. This is a DOOM-like corridor shooter, minus the faster and more responsive movement.
Your enjoyment of Dead Effect is dependent on what you expect from a $5 mobile port. The game is decent and offers some playability but in its early state, has a small amount of content. It's a short experience with multiplayer and more levels potentially inbound. If you're looking to splatter some more undead brains on the wall, turn your own brain off and pick this up. If you're looking for a deep, nuanced zed-hunting experience, look elsewhere.

One of the weakest of the best is still good, right? Resident Evil 0 is a rather mediocre entry among the absolute best classic Resident Evil titles, which means, it's still way above a lot of classic survival horror wannabes. And in its HD Remake version the game got better. Not just visually, like it mostly was with REmaster (not like it was a bad thing, mind you) - RE0 HD is actually more fun to play than the original GC (and later Wii) release.
Resident Evil 0 itself is a game with a long history of development. Prequel idea started being R&D'ed before RE1 was even released, game was finally shown in some playable state on N64 in 2000, but it seems like a lot of post-train story and gameplay was still not 100% set. After that the development was completely restarted for GC alongside REmake with slight story adjustments for both for continuity. And I think for a lot of people the concept of the "Resident Evil on a train" was something that stuck with them - it sounded interesting and new. And it actually is. Sadly, the Train is only about 1/5 of the entire game.
The game has a lot of intersting concepts - two playable characters at once, change from item boxes to "put item on the ground anywhere", a bit more emphasis on unique abilities of playable characters - something RE1 introduced and since hasn't really been used again in the series. But it's the implementation that makes it all go average instead of great. Playing as two characters is not as fun as it could be, item management is more forced and boring and unique abilities of characters apart from gameplay differences (Billy deals with recoil better and gets hurt less), are very rarely used despite the possibilities. Even the ideas from other games in the series up to that point, are either unused or underused - zombies travel across rooms only once, Crimson Heads are not here, there's no dodging or self-defence items, no creepy pursuing enemies (just an annoying, but often easily skippable, leech-monster), no real scenario variety.
But the main downer is the levels and the overall feel of the game. Story is all over the place, never sticking to any particular tone, with jRPG fabulous-looking evil guy being the main bad, game opening with documentary style narration (but never going back to it), character suddenly referencing the future (because it's prequel, you see?). And yes, it's storytelling in Resident Evil, who cares, right? Well, thing is - no matter how silly a lot of RE stories went, they usually did it with style and in a memorable cool way. RE0 is just "eh, it happened, I guess". And the levels are just... boring. So are the bosses. They all feel like a collection of discarded classic RE ideas put together in one game. It also cannot really choose between the more colorful and stylish look of classic PS1-era REs and the "creepy old" look of REmake, something that was improved a lot in the HD Remaster (original was very gray/yellow-ish), but still feels not as good as other games.
But HD Remaster fixes not just visual issues and makes the game look very good. In addition, it adds several welcome changes in the controls (realtime reload button is a cool thing), most notable of which is the alternative control scheme. Now it was also present in REmaster, however REmake worked perfectly fine with classic tank controls - all the animations felt right, moving and shooting and evading was fun to master and use. In RE0 original tank controls have a slight delay due to additional animation frames for a lot of actions which are simply removed in alt. control scheme, making it a much better option, especially when controlling the partner character, even despite few places, where camera changes to screw up your movement. In addition to that, game also gets a silly and fun to play Wesker mode, where Billy is changed into RE5-style Wesker, who can run at super speed and explode enemies with his aura at will. It's a ridiculous mode, that gets even sillier when you complete it once, as sadly there is no Wesker Leech Hunter, but all the rewards in the game are just unlocked for the second playthrough. It's funny, it's fun, it's a nice way to relax after Leech Hunter or hard mode playthrough, and it's always fun to explode zombie heads with your thoughts.
So, is it a good game to get? Well, if you like classic survival horror and this is the game you've missed before - definitely. If you're a fan of RE series - yep. If you want to get into classic survival horrors - only after you try out better options. REmaster is a better option, but I would've suggested checking RE Director's Cut (just not dual shock ver., if you value your ears), 2 and 3 as well, if possible. And same goes for people who are just checking this out without knowledge of the genre and the series - this is a rather good way, but there are better options to start with.

Disclaimer: Disregard my hours played as of this review (almost three). I played this extensively on GameCube, finished it on all difficulties, and even went through again using just the rocket launcher. As the gameplay itself hasn’t really changed, this should not be an issue in terms of time spent in-game.
Resident Evil 0 is both good and bad in so many ways, and some of them aren’t even related to this HD remaster. I’m a Resident Evil junkie, and I have been since I got hooked on the PSX original back in 1996, after reading a review of it in Game Informer, one of those things called magazines that you had to buy at stores or wait for it to arrive by mail.
Resident Evil 0 was the last “real” Resident Evil, a slow and methodical game, before Capcom decided the non-stop action and set pieces were the way to go. Not a knock against Resident Evil 4, though. RE4 was a terrific game, it just wasn’t a terrific Resident Evil game.
That said, Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster is a fantastic remaster. It shines on PC. The enhanced graphics bring the backgrounds to life, you can read signs and notices that were blurry on the GameCube version, the story (while not the best in the series) does an excellent job of providing more background on Umbrella, and while it introduced a couple of new things to the series (character switching, ability to drop items), it also removed some (such as item boxes).
It’s Resident Evil, you either love it or hate it. It’s great because it’s the slow paced explorative gameplay that Resident Evil was, but it’s sad because it truly is the last of its kind (Resident Evil 4, 5, 6, forthcoming Umbrella Chronicles, etc).
Regardless of your view on the game, it’s well worth the time. It is a great revisit for old fogies like me, and it’s a great survival horror game for newcomers. As long as you don’t compare this to the current crop of horror games, you’ll enjoy yourself.

Despite its appearance, Long Live the Queen is not a Japanese dating sim. Instead, it's a surprisingly compelling RPG. You develop your character's skills over the course of the game and these skills determine the outcome of the game's many events. In turn, these outcomes create branches that affect how you progress through the game's narrative. Possible branches include civil wars, foreign invasions, forest adventures and chocolate-induced fatalities. If you survive until your coronation, the game's many endings explain the long-term consequences of your actions (Fallout style). As a result, there's a ton of replayability if you  want to find every possible permutation of the game's story.
Don't let its look deceive you; Long Live The Queen is a game worth playing for anyone who enjoys story-driven RPGs.

In Long Live The Queen you play as Princes Elodie, the incoming Queen. It is up to you to ensure that the Princess lives to be crowned Queen.
The game works on a weekly cycle. At the start of every week you will be required to choose two classes in which Elodie will participate. These classes will determine which skills are increased. It is important to note the Elodie's mood, as her mood will determine the bonus or penalty to learning skills. For example, if Elodie is depressed, she will not be very fond of attending a class on court manners, hence, that skill will receive a penalty, and spending time on it will not result in any meaningful increases.
On the weekend, you are given the choice of a weekend activity, which will determine changes to Elodie's mood.
Interspersed are events that require Elodie's skills to be of a certain level in order to be successful, and if not, a negative outcome results. These events give life to the story, and illuminate the intrigue of Nova and its people: noble, commoners, and criminals alike.
The gameplay can be rather formulaic, however, the beauty and tactical reasoning arises when determining the combinations of skills that will keep you alive, and keep your realm and people safe.
The magic of the game is found in honing one's skills of forecasting and strategy. Seems like tensions in the realm are rising? Do I prepare for war or hope for the best? These are some of the questions that may need answers as you play, knowing that the wrong decision could very well prove fatal.
It is a perfect Groundhog Day scenario to experiment with choices and their ramifications.
Visually, it has an anime-esque appeal, but one wishes for a greater variety of scenes and backgrounds. The outfits, which are unlocked by increasing skills in the same branch, are very well designed and emphasise Elodie's demeanour and personality.
I highly recommend Long Live The Queen for players interested in a strategy game with flair.

I haven't beaten the game yet, so this will be going off what I have experienced thus far.
Night in the Woods is a game I was interested in since I first heard about sometime back in November. At first it simply drew me in because of the art style, there was an article that mentioned it I believe, and it posted a few screenshots. Once I saw its release date, and that it was up for pre-prder on Humble Bundle, I just HAD to get it.
The story is easily the best part of this game. It's the main focus as well, revolving around 3 specific characters, one of which you play as, and a few characters attached to them. Each has their own struggles, their own worries, wants and fears. It starts off simple enough, your character returns home after dropping out of college. But from there, the game delivers a multitude of amazing moments, be they hard hitting, depressing, or a pretty good laugh. And from what I've seen so far, the game only becomes increasingly more "real", targetting themes I've never seen a game take head-on. And yet, it does it in a way you don't really get the full impact of what you just experienced right away.
As I said, the art style is originally what drew me in. It's colorful, evem with it's somewhat limited palette, but it doesn't hinder the game as it takes place during the fall. The art only adds to the soul of the game, though it is also where my biggest gripe is so far, and it's more of a nitpick than a flaw. The game is on a 2D plane, with backdrops in the distance. As such, the characters do not move their heads, and the eyes are what help you keep track of who each character in the game is interacting with (even the random people you see walking around will follow you with their eyes). This, to me, detracts from some of the more heartfelt scenes, as I feel giving the characters the ability to look at the ground, or blink, or any other number of nuances would have them immensely more hard hitting. Though, this may be intentional to help kind of displace the importance of what the game is discussing.
The game uses very simple animations, with a simple run cycle, a jump cycle, birds flying, cars driving by, etc. This game is not an action game, by any stretch of the word. You do some crimes here and there, but you don't go from fight to fight, grinding or progressing like you do in a lot of other games. The sole focus is the characters, their relations to one another, and how the passage of time affects everything around them.
I love this game, hands down, and without a doubt recommend it wholeheartedly. Each character, even the supporting ones, are well written and feel like they have their own lives. It covers themes I think everybody needs to face up to at some point in their lives, yet does it in a way that it doesn't force you into a total feelstrip.
(As an added caveat, Greggory, one of the three main characters, is gay).

Night in the Woods is a very strange game. It's not quite a visual novel, but it's also not quite a "game" in the conventional sense either. It is one thing though, at least in my personal opinion;
It's griping, and a lot more emotionally engaging than you may assume at first.
You play as the character Mae, a 20 year old college dropout who returns home to their small town with no plans for the future. The game initially follows her attempts to reconnect with her old friends and grasp on to the past, and does so with a great sense of meaninglessness, until the tone begins to shift when it becomes evident that something mysterious is going on in town.
Positives:
+ Great story that manages to speak out about real-world issues without sounding pretentious or forced.
+ Fantastic writing. All the characters feel human, both in the way they talk, and the way what you say effects them. They all have unique personalities with suitable depth.
+ Beatiful, clean art style and fluid animation.
+ Amazing soundtrack that fits each moment of the game perfectly.
+ Replayable. The game is split into different chapters with set amounts of days, and you are given the choice of which character you want to spend time with during each day. You can spend one playthough committing petty crimes with Gregg, or rebuilding your friendship with Bea, to give two examples. While the overarching "mystery" doesn't change, what does is the experience leading up to and following it.
+ I encountered no bugs throughout my playthrough.
+ Mae's laptop has a 10 level long roguelike game called "Demon Tower" that you can play, extending the game's l. Game-ception, if you will.
Negatives:
- The game initially doesn't provide you with much choice, although this changes around a third of the way through as I said in the positives section.
- Little conventional "gameplay". While the story got me hooked, the gameplay consists mostly of tied together minigames and platforming segments. Neither feel out of place. The minigames are how you interact with the world and help make the game feel more engaging whereas the platforming comes naturally. However, if you are seeking something with more meat to the actual gameplay, it's worth noting.
- The ending is somewhat sudden. While the plot of the "mystery" side of the game is left open-ended and can be resolved with a little thought, when it comes to the stories of the individual characters it ends on a bit of a cliffhanger.

The game is flawless and i truly believe that. A+. Any gripes i have with this game do not lie in its actual design but rather the various things involved IN fighting games, especially those with online play. From a strictly gaming review standpoint, it is worth the investment BUT there is a catch, which i will get to now.
First and foremost if you are a first time fighting game player (like myself), be prepared for a lot of losses and depending on the type of gamer you are, some rage aswell. Fighitng games are infinetely complex. On the surface, it seems simple. Light - High punches and kicks, some commands & chargers, jumping attacks, thats it right? WRONG! I learned this the hard way. There are techniques which the game is not so forthcoming with that will have you confused. Know what linking is? FADC? Canceling? Plinking? Ever heard of a man named Daigo? Know what a fightstick is? CONFUSED? I sure was. There is a great deal of information you have to discover yourself in order to truly enjoy this game, or any other fighting games for that matter, but once you do, learning one is perhaps on of the most enjoyable gaming endeavors you can undertake. There lies the catch. The game itself is great but to justify investing in purchasing this game, you have to be willing to also invest time in learning it.
I imagine for most people, including me, it went something like this:
1. Bought USF4
2. Spent a couple days playing around with the CPU, most in arcade mode, and exploring the character roster
3. Found a character you liked
4. Spent more time with that character
5. Went online for some multiplayer
6. Got♥♥♥♥♥♥♥br>7. Uninstalled (well i didn't but you get my point)
One thing i will say is that they seemed to have fixed matchmaking in this game. In SSF4 (which i purchased not too long before the USF4 upgrade came to steam) when you asked for an opponent of your same skill, it was a gamble. Rarely would you actually get an opponent you could handle. I once faced a Zangief that was ranked 3 in my region, while i was still figuring out how to dragon punch.
TL;DR: The game itself is a gem, but there is work to be put in if you want to become proficient in playing it. Playing with friends only? go for it, but if you plan to play online, be ready to work a bit harder.
P.S. You do not need a fightstick to play fighting games. Is it recommended? Yes but if you research you will find may professional players who using a gamepad. Have you ever wanted to step into the boots of a stone cold bounty hunter bringing in criminals and making piles of cash? Then this might just be the game for you. Oh and it takes place on an alien world where everything is crazy too.
This game is great fun; it starts off a little slow but once it gets rolling you will have a hard time putting it down. Set in oddworld you know it’s going to be crazy. Every mission and town you go through has its own little narrative and everything seems to be an adventure all culminating in an epic tale of vengeance and surgery…..yes.
I loved the bounty system, it’s one of my favourite things in any game and in this one it’s great. Take people in alive and get paid more money, even bosses can be brought in alive. It just adds another layer of challenge to the title. Something about collecting them all drove me to obsession.
The story and world are obviously fantastic, neither are expanded on greatly but they add a sense that there is a lot more going on in the world around you and you are just carving your way through a very tiny part of it. The character you portray is a man of few words and that just adds to the mystery of who he is and what he wants.
Now we talk about the weapon, you only get one but with the HUGE amount of ammo (living critters you catch and shoot at bad guys) you will not be disappointed. It is one of the most unique weapons I have used in any game and with all the upgrades you can get throughout the adventure it always seems new and fresh.
The combat is fast paced and seamlessly switches from third person fighter to first person shooter. Both have their place and neither feels tacked on. There are tons of environments to explore and fight in and so many enemies to kill or capture each with their own personality. And the difficulty could be pretty brutal in places.
I would recommend this game if you have a few hours to spare and want to get taken into a world that’s more crazy and odd than most. The npc’s are huge chickens for gods sake. On sale you have to have this.

Out of alle the Oddworld games, Strangers Wrath was always the one I overlooked. Didn't have an original Xbox back in the day and when they released the HD version it was riddled with hella bugs. But now I finally gave it a whirl!
Strangers Wrath is a unique blend of 3rd person platforming and 1st person shooting. Most of the game evolves around bountyhunting outlaws, those little bossfights give you room for lethal and even nonlethal approaches which you'll want to do to earn more moolah. True to the universe, the world is hella ...odd, one cool aspect is that the ammo for your gun are living critters which you need to hunt to restock constantly. There are almost a dozen different critters to use to give room for the own preferred playstyle. The game never got boring, allthough the first half until a certain reveal might overstay its welcome a little bit. But what happens leading up to the games end is ridiculous and definitely worth seeing.
As expected and reported numerously, Strangers Wrath HD comes with some hefty technical shortcomings. This is as barebones as a PC port can get, I had to fiddle with graphical settings for almost half an hour until I had no strange FPS problems or weird bugs like my character not being able to move forward (Tip: turn vsync on!). There is controller support but it's not good, the game lets you rebind all the buttons but prompts show up as JOY1, JOY2. Fortunately the keyboard+mouse controls are totally fine and give benefits when aiming in first person mode.
Strangers Wrath is a really really cool game which combines 3rd person and 1st person action unlike anything I've seen before and ultimately -considering it's over 10 years old at this point- left me very impressed. The world and its characters are exactly what you expect when Lorne Lanning gets to work his magic. Speaking of which, he really should make a new game!

Let me start by saying I generally love all things Resident Evil. I cannot, however, endorse this port. The very little I've played of it has given me a headache. Yeah, it's pretty, and it's got a whole new control option, but the new option actually manages to be worse than the classic controls. Yeah, you can turn around and move a bitfaster and don't have to continually hold down a run button, which occasionally comes in handy, but moving in a straight line is awkward and when the camera shifts it completely screws up your orientation. You also automatically go through doors, whether you want to or not. It's the original Resident Evil Zero with some new polish. But faces some new challenges.
First of all, Let's make this clear. This is the exact same game from 2002. Only with 60FPS gameplay, New controls and higher resolution Textures. If you was expecting a "Remake". That's not what this is, this is a more modern version of the already amazingly beautiful, crisp and solid GameCube game from 2002 (And Wii during the later years). So you should treat it as such.
Somehow, Capcom managed to make this game look even better than Resident Evil 1 HD. I can't place my finger on it but it overall looks crisper. Almost as if they've done more effort than before. The details in the environments make the GameCube version, even though it's still a spectacular visual experience, look way outdated.
There is a problem however, the game looks so good, that the CG Movie clips looks outrageously bad. It's ripped straight from the GameCube and you can see this clearly in the credits as it uses the old Logo. The CG Videos looks extremely compressed and honestly worse than the actual game. Some moving objects in the background seems to be running at a lower FPS than the rest of the game, which is fine but may look odd in some situations. Yet the intro movie when you start up the game is done very well for some reason. Odd.
Interestingly enough, This game doesn't include any strange "Remixed" or "Remastered" sound tracks like in Resident Evil 1 HD. Even more strange it doesn't include the Soundtrack. Pre-order bonus or not. Not a huge deal just a tad odd.
It definitely shows that Capcom put in some more effort into this one. There's actual DLC Costume packs, which while Resident Evil 1 HD does add 1 extra outfit for Chris and Jill. Here you have 5 Packs for Bill and Rebecca. Plus a new game mode to boot. What gives Capcom? Give RE1HD the same treatment!
Since it's the same game as the 2002 Gamecube original. It suffers from the same problems. It's a very slow, sometimes very tedious Survival Horror game. With fixed Camera angles and even though it has a more modern "Better" control Scheme. The long animations of the characters make the action extremely slow paced and sometimes frustrating. However, That's how Resident Evil was loved before. That's how we remember it. And it's a love or hate argument. Simply put, if you only play Resident Evil 4 and above. Stay away from this one or any of the classic ones unless you're ready for a much slower game.
Now for this versions biggest flaw. Controls. Firstly, the Inventory and Sprint keys for the tank controllers are flipped. None of the Control options can change this. At all, you can't even map manual actions like in RE1HD. How did Capcom screw this up is beyond me.
It may not seem like an issue. But oh goodness is it a problem. The "Y" button on a X360 controller switches characters. You can see how that is already a problem. If you played RE1HD a lot. That same button should be inventory. Instead, it's the "X" button, Which should be Run if you're playing in Tank control mode. This is unacceptable. Even in the GameCube version and I dare say the Wii. The Control buttons made sense. Here it's setup in some absorb rubbish. I don't care if it's "Japanese" style or whatever. It doesn't change the fact that in the first game it was set to it's normal controls. And this is the PC version, which is Internationally the same with a simple Language change.
That doesn't seem like a horrible issue. But it's quite the annoyance, especially since it got me killed a few times.
All in all. This is a fantastic Remaster. And I'm happy, because this is one of my favorite Resident Evil games. If the Controls could be mapped, the CG Videos redone in a higher resolution and less compression. Possibly add the soundtrack for consistency? Then I'd say this is a perfect remaster. And it still is a great ride.

The Disciples series is one of the most beautiful underrated franchise in gaming strategy. It is the same genre as the classic Heroes of Might and Magic, and it has become a sort of "cult classic"ever since the massive success of Disciples II.
This third entry follows that tradition, by keeping a beautiful, dark, artwork, combined with unforgiving mechanics and an enticing world/factions. However, Disciples 3 was a complete wreck at launch, laden with game breaking bugs and suffering with inferior mechanics to it's predecessor.
The "Reincarnation" version of the game, the one I'm reviewing, is definitely a more polished version of Disciples 3 "Gold" (the vanilla + ressurection expansion). This, sadly, does not mean the game was completely overhauled in it's faults, but simply that all of it's game breaking bugs were fixed and some balancing issues were addressed.
Overrall, Disciples 3: Reincarnation is a good game which follows a strong tradition laid by the classic Disciples II. However, it is still, at it's best, an unpolished gem, very rough in the edges. That means people with low tolerance to lack of polish will not enjoy this game, and people new to the series fare better to begin their immersion in the Disciples world with the predecessors games. However, if you are a fan of the HOMM-like strategy genre, you will definitely like this game, which is by itself worth your money in any sale, as unpolished as it may be.

Full disclosure: I haven't played any previous Disciples games. Also, I am only in the first campaign so far and am playing on easy level since I'm not exactly the most skilled gamer. Disciples III: Reincarnation is a mix of strategy and RPG with turn-based combat. There are four campaigns each featuring a different faction: Empire (human), Legion (demons), Alliance (elves) and Horde (undead). Each campaign is made up of multiple missions each with its own map. Each campaign also has you playing a main hero, although you can also hire others.
When heroes level you get points to spend in a skill grid which can be used to increase their attributes or gain other abilities and perks (e.g. increasing your leadership to allow more units in your party or gaining resistence to a certain element).
Regular units also level but you cannot choose their skills; instead, they progress along a skill "line". However, at the cost of gold and stone you can build structures in your base that allow units to upgrade to a higher tier which provides increased damage/healing and health and sometimes additional benefits. For example, the Empire's archer can be upgraded to a marksman who shoots fire arrows and then can be upgraded again to an assassin who throws daggers which add a poison debuff. Each unit also has a toggle that prevent upgrades if you want. Using the previous example, you might not want one of your marksman to upgrade because they have longer range and can hit physically immune monsters. Upgrade paths may be mutually exclusive so once you choose a path the others are locked. For example, Empire healers have two path choices: single target high value heals or area of effect lower value heals.
Combat takes place on a hex grid which may contain melee, ranged or magical power spots. Placing your character on these spots will increase your damage or healing. Combat is turned based with an initiative system that is not entirely intuitive. If a unit has a very high initiative compared to others, it will not only go first but may act again in the same round.

If you were expecting a narrative based experience as advertised, don't bother with this game; this is a survival resource management game, story is not this games focus. But still on the merits of such is it a good game? No, as it is so brutally and (more importantly) unfairly difficult, that it makes Dark Souls look tame.
I can only give you my impressions so far at this point in writing, but after many attempts I have now progressed to the 5th of 7th chapter on easy difficulty, due to the bone crushing nature of the normal mode, and the game suffers from, I feel, 3 key issues:
Lack of checkpoints
Luck based gameplay
Trial and error situations
If you fail a chapter at any point, you must restart the whole thing again; and these are not short levels at all, they can be up to 30 mins or more.
What makes this all the more infuriating is the unfair nature of the situations you are thrown in. Some personal highlights of frustration:
-Erratic and unreliable behaviour indicators on hostages, along with dice roll elements for progression in chapter 1
-Russian roulette in chapter 2, where if the RNG decides you just go back to the start of the level.
-Trial and error elements are also at play in the same chapter, where the pattern of torture is easy to circumvent if you know in advance what is coming but you'd only know that through hindsight and past failures.
-Chapter 3 has shifting goalposts - devised a plan around what you were told at the start of the mission? Too bad chump! We've got more work to do! Again, only hindsight would allow you to plan for the "real" goalposts.
-Chapter 5 is purely luck! Find a hidden base, that is in a randomised location each time!
And it's at this point that I just wonder if there is any point in continuing this arduous slog. High difficulty has its appeals, the popularity of Souls series and Roguelikes are proof enough but they at least are fair.
This is closer to a frustrating dice roll simulator than a survival game. Don't waste your time.

Dark Souls quickly became one of my favorite games of all time. There are so many things that work together to create one of the best gaming experiences I've ever had. There are many things that it does right that no other game has done effectively. It is the pinacle of game world design and has an extremely solid combat system on top of that. Dark Souls is deffinately worth the time it takes to play through it.
So what does it do right? The world design is the best I've ever seen in a video game. Many of the different areas you will travel to are all interconnected. This means its possible to walk from one area to the next without breaking the immersion. While many games do this well, Dark Souls takes it to a whole new level. It appears to take you way off in a direction, but when you finish the area you are looped back to where you started. This means getting back to the Bonfire can be quick and can provide a sense of relief right after a difficult challenge. This provided me with one of the most memorable experiences ever in a game; where everything just clicked in about where I was. After an elevator ride, I instantly knew where I was and had my mind blown. This was because of how effortless the game made it seem. The first half of the game flows together perfectly like this for many of the areas.
Level design and world design are two different things, and Dark Souls has some varried quality when it comes to the levels. The world flows together extremely well, but some of the levels are far from perfect. The best levels are the ones that loop back around on themselves. This allows them to use one Bonfire efficiently. New shortcuts and ways to approach a problem are oppened up. New items can be discovered and navigating the level can be a great challenge your first time through. Some of the most fun I had in the game was just learning the layout of a new area, not knowing what danger would be next. Unfortunatly, not every level is perfect. The later levels in the game feel rushed from a development standpoint and are not as detailed as the earlier levels. Getting lost in the early levels was entertaining because you knew you would end up in the right place, but later levels become enfuriating. Those levels allow you to get lost with no clear direction to get to next. There are some areas where there is constant damage applied to the player; this made me rush through the level. I never fully explored those level and don't really remember the layout very well. They switch from intricate pathways stacked on top of each other to open planes with no clear direction opened up. While this did make the levels less fun to play through, they are still a solid challenge to be met.
Combat is the backbone of Dark Souls. World exploration made the game solid, but its obvious the combat was the focus. Everything is extremely lethal. Every enemy can deal out massive damage if you aren't careful. The player can also deal out massive damage in return. This turns every combat encounter into a test of skill. Every attack has a swing time, meaning that you don't do damage as soon as a button is pressed. You and your enemy have a chance to react to the incoming attack by dodging or blocking an attack. Skilled play is about seeing what attack is coming and accounting for when it is going to hit. From there you can roll out of the way, or take the hit on a shield. There are also other moves for advanced play that keep the combat varried and the skill cap high. The one massive downside to this system is dealing with multiple enemys. Attacks stack on top of eachother and enemy's can attack through eachother. If you aren't careful a group on enemy's can kill you quicker than you can react or block. Learning to deal with multiple enemy's is not taught very well in the game and if you can, attack only one enemy at a time.
There are a lot of subtlety's in the game that I won't cover, many of them would spoild the expereince. However, between the world design and fantastic combat this game is well worth playing. Those two features carry it to one of my favorite games of all time. I would strongly recommend this game to anyone even remotely interested. Don't let its advertising and high difficulty get in the way of a great game.

I played this on xbox 360 completed it 1 1/2 times and just bought it on pc recently it took me 20 hours to 96% the game (couldn't be bothered finishing the hunting challenges but other than that I found every single collectible and completed every single mission +bonuses).
Pros:
+Assasin's Creed combat but with more variety
+Easy 20 hours of gameplay
+Very smooth
+Decent storyline
+Orcs were interesting
+DLC's were entertaining enough to keep me playing
+Good movement
Cons:
-Combat gets repetive after 20 hours
-Hard to give up your progress and powers so you can replay
-Small glitches (not game breaking but not entertaining, just annoying and breaks immersion)
-Doesn't have an aesthetic or a personality
-Annoying camera
Conclusion:
This game got 80% of things right for me e.g. Orcs: diferent personalities, entertaining, funny interactions, feels like a community but are too badly programmed to put up a challenge and new interesting combat mechanisms are shoved in your face rather than staying subtle. Talion/Celebrimbor: Good contrast between morals, not too tryhard but is still cool to play as, not an annoying personality but some cringy dialougue can really ruin their relationship. Orc Hierarchy:  gives the game an edge over games like assasin's creed, you can form genuine likes and dislikes for certain uruk, good personalities, interactions between uruk are smooth 80% of the time but very messy and stiff to try and configure and takes a long time to organise your army. I have killed so many of my favourite uruk with a simple misclick.

Are you a Tolkien fan that erupts into a foaming rage when someone misspells the name of your favourite elf? Do you enthusiastically throw around death threats upon witnessing the slightest of mistakes made in the lore of Silmarillion? Did you felt personally violated when the Lord of the Ring movies deviated from the books?
If any of the above apply to you, I suggest you avoid this game.
Otherwise, it's a great experience that I recommend to anyone who has an interest in the genre. Plenty of collectibles, a nice, open world to roam (although don't expect anything grandiouse), several upgrades and runes to choose from.
The story is okay (nothing to write home about in my honest opinion) but the gameplay makes up for it.
The combat is the meat of the game, that's what you will be doing most of the time. Being Arkham-style it's not very challenging and right from the get-go you will be nigh impossible to defeat if you pay close attention to what buttons to press to counter incoming attacks. There are some occasions when a particular combination of orc captains will give you a hard time but those are seldom and choosing a different tactic based on their wekanesses will surely solve your problem. Later on with runes and upgrades you will even grow stronger and ultimately become an unstoppable killing machine with insane mobility and power.
Although the combat is not particularly challenging, I must note that this is one of the most cinematic and fluid implementations of this combat system I have seen so far that makes up for the lack of difficulty for me. Even when I was done with the game I launched it again just to fight orcs randomly for no other reason but to marvel at the combat. It's a joy to watch and I applaud the developers for delivering such smooth, seamless animations.
While I think the game is great I must note that there are some flaws as well. First of all the DLCs aren't much to write home about: The Bright Lord is okay-ish but you are essentially doing the same thing as in the main campaign with slighty different combat and some added story.
The Lord of the Hunt DLC would be fine if not for the only weakness of the game which is beast-handling. Riding and fighting with mounted beasts often felt clunky to a level where I became downright frustrated. I can not help but think this part was an afterthought as it is just not as polished as the other aspects of the game (for example, riding through the land with your graug looks pretty ridiculous). However, this isn't the most prominent part and I think the positives greatly outweigh this one negative.
All in all, a fairly enjoyable title and the GOTY edition well worths the asking price (DO NOT buy the base version, they are both sold for the same price while the GOTY edition contains all the DLCs and skins).

I'm not a huge player of RPGs (the last I've played are the Dragon Age 1&2, Divinity Orginal Sin, and Skyrim), but I can honestly say that this game went straight to my heart. The dialogue is great and there are so many options that immediately after completing it I felt the urge to play it again with a different character with a different personality. I came to this game more the paradox than the obsidian side as I'm a huge fan of strategic games. This game obviously doesn't play like an RTS but there are still some strategic sources - but dont buy this game expecting a fantasy CK2 or EU4, it isn't that.
That being said, the game does have some pretty blatant flaws. The main one is the wealth of statistics and numbers that the game throws at you from the second you launch it. There are stats that effect stats that affect stats that actually affect something that matter. I can sense the Paradox influence here of sometimes confusing making these more complicated rather than making them intricate or interesting. The way stacking sometimes works and sometimes doesn't adds to this. That said, as a casual player you can ignore the precise numbers and go along with what sounds good. Other problems involve the dull and uninspiring way crafting/enchanting/unique weapons are handled and pretty bad AI in path finding.
But these are relatively minor flaws in an otherwise excellent game. Highly recommended for anyone with even a passing interesting in RPGs.

A good port, good HD Remaster, but Resident Evil 0 was not that great to begin with.
Sure, It's an oldschool-style Resident Evil just like the first three games but I find this one boring. It's similar to the first Resident Evil game where you solve puzzles in a huge building, this time it's a facility instead of a mansion. It's good to have two characters that following each other everywhere and solve puzzles together but it's not a new feature for people who played modern titles like RE5 and RE6.
AI of the other character is VERY VERY DUMB. You cannot rely on your partner at all when it comes to combat. They aren't even smart enough to use a gun in their hands. They might help you shoot at enemies once in awhile though.
Unlike RE1-4, there's no storage chest in this game. Really? Yes! the game forces to to throw away items to the floor. You have 6 item slots on each character and most of the heavy weapons required 2 slots to carry, so... another slot for bullets and you have one free slot to carry something else. Have fun running back and forth to pick up items.
The good thing is, it's a very good port. No problem at all on my system, with highest settings. Maybe you'll have a little trouble with the control schemes because the game doesn't allow you to remap buttons manually. It has 5-6 types of control for you to choose but none of them are close to the PS1 version of RE1-3 so if you prefer to control the characters like those games you'll be disappointed. Of course you can solve this issue by using some 3rd party controller mapper.
Should you buy this game? If you like RE1-3, you'll like it, but if you hate RE1-3, you'll hate it.
I give it a 6/10. It's worth playing to complete the story of the Resident Evil series but if you're not a hardcore RE fan it doesn't really mean anything.

I tried to play this game on few occasions, and it always makes me regret it. It's a barely playable mess. Reincarnation is a transformation of original Disciples 3, that tries so hard to be like Disciples 2, that it makes you wonder: why play this, when you have an excellent Disciples 2? Akella made the same game THRICE, and while Disciples 2 is an improvement to 1, Reincarnation is not even close to being equally good as either of the previous entries. They changed this game into a bad version of Disciples 2, worse in almost every aspects (if not literally every).
I can stand the unintuitive UI and sluggish controls, but I can't - for the love of all that is holy - bear the combat and that is my main issue with this game.
First, we have a leader that is completely useless. I don't even know if he will become a force to be reckoned with later on, he is useless at the beginning and dies from one or two hits, while dealing 1/3 as much damage as normal units. Then we have the overall balance of combat; it's INCREDIBLY hard. I don't understand how am I supposed to defeat even one group of enemies that have some overpowered units with hundreads of health and AoE attacks that two-shots my mages and heroes. It's not like they are not standing right in front of my base, guarding basic resources...
Is this a game about exploration and looking for that one, specific group of enemies that will allow me to level up? Or is this a game about taking that one-and-only useful hero and a very specific combination of units? Neither of these appeal to me, and neither of these was mandatory in Disciples 2.
Hotseats (that can be played with AI) feels just unplayable. Campaign is barely more bearable, but equally not fun with the clunky, slow and random combat. I felt like they lowered hit chance to around the same, idiotic values as in Disciples 1 or even lower and one, just ONE miss can completely ruin whole encounter.
Mind you, I don't take into account the artstyle and music. It's good, art is even great, but a hit or miss sometimes. It can be gorgeous at times and it can be ugly on another asset or picture, but the overall design is what you would expect from the series: unique and very atmospheric.

After a lot of thought (which is what this game engenders), I've had to change my review. I still maintain that this is more interactive fiction than modern game. This isn't something that you're intended to powergame, it's something you're meant to experience. It's about a lot of things, but among the overarching themes is how twisted ethics become when dealing with things like slavery, decadence, and violent retaliation. The game is a meditation on right and wrong, and yet, there is no right or wrong here. I still don't know what the right decision is, after having beaten the game.
I think the game may actually be too smart for a bulk of its audience. The biggest reason I changed my review was because I feel the game could not exist in any other medium. I think what Devolver has done with gaming is what I have always wanted to see done with gaming: Instead of a math simulator where you're min/maxing your orc warrior princess from a distance, you're actively drawn in through various clever hooks, both mechanical and plot-driven. This game overclocks the medium, showing off gaming's unique immersive ability. It is something rarely done in gaming.
For everyone who is frustrated: Get past the first episode and the game opens up. This is one of those games that needs a little bit of time to turn on. Remember how Fallout 2 was terrible for the first 15 minutes? Remember how Fallout 2 was the best Fallout in the series?
This game is worth your 10 dollars if you're looking for an immersive, important, and expertly crafted story. If you're just looking for some mindless fun to burn some time, however, this isn't it.
This isn't a fun game. This is a game that will get under your skin. It's uncomfortable, but the discomfort, you'll realize, is necessary for it to tell its story.
GWBW has one of the better stories you'll run across in gaming. It's actually pretty rare to run across a story this good. It completely gets away from the typical binary of good and bad and right and wrong. It's not an ethics puzzle game as advertised, however. The game falls short in the gameplay. It essentially boils down to a resource management game that punishes the player for a misstep in the same way that an old Sierra adventure game might (I'm looking at you, Space Quest 4). Remember those old platformers from the early 90's where you had to play a level like 100 times over to figure out how to beat it? That's what this is like, except instead of jumping puzzles you're clicking through dialog and making people eat or sleep.
Having to restart from scratch and waste 15 minutes of playtime is annoying, and however well this mechanic is worked into the story (no spoilers), it just ends up being an obvious method of extending the game's length. This is another problem: While there is some replayability, the game is extremely short, and your choices end up having little impact on the end. Yes, your choices impact the story as it's going along, but ultimately the ending is a self-contained minigame that ends up being really boring. I'm not sure how I feel about this. Something makes me want more closure regarding the choices I made with my team. You do get some impactful moments based on your decisions that are written into the story, depending on how you behaved, but again, no spoilers.
The game aims to make your choices harder and more meaningful, and to put stress on the player as if the player were right there with the characters. I can respect this. The problem is that this turns into a horrible grindfest devoid of all fun. If they had included a checkpoint system or shortened the vignettes by about half, they would have made an excellent game. As it stands, it's just extremely frustrating to play, and if they had shortened the grindier parts, the game would have taken like four hours to beat.
I wanted to like this game. In fact, I DO like this game. I want to say that I love this game, but I don't love it as a game. I love it as an interactive story. I wish steam had more than a yes or no voting system, because if you're looking for a really amazing short story with beautiful graphics and music, you must buy this. If, however, you're looking for a game with fun mechanics, you need to pass this up. The grinding just absolutely kills it.
Wait for a sale. I think it's worth 10 dollars, but then I found the story really meaningful.

A delightful take on a rarely-seen genre, Long Live the Queen falls into the "raising sim" category of  life-simulators, and appears to take inspiration from one of the more famous game series within that uncommon genre, Princess Maker.
The essence of the game is relatively simple: it is played in a series of weeks, during each of which you must pick two topics of study - skills - for Elodie, and an activity for free time.  As the game progresses, events occur which provide pass/fail test for said skills, either individually, multiples totaled, or sequentially, and the results of passing or failing can lead to everything from getting or missing a bit of information all the way to...well, let's just say it's not called "Long Live the Queen" for nothing.
There is a *very* wide selection of skills available to choose from, and unlike other sims of a similar nature (or "monster trainer" games), you don't have to deal with certain skills being decreased when you train others.  Rather, the mood system provides a similar hazard; based on Elodie's mood, certain skills get a bonus to their training, while others suffer a penalty.  And to mention in advance, no mood is good for studying Economics, so don't bother searching for one.
Beyond that, the characters (while all anime-esque) are varied in personality, motivation, and likability, and Elodie herself is sympathetic and adorable, the sort of character that inspires protective instincts - and which evokes a certain pride when she becomes more capable, ideal for a game like this.
The game is all-around a delight to play; depending on how you raise her, Elodie can be naive or savvy, powerful or frail, elegant or tomboyish, or all these things together.  There is plenty of replay value to the game, since there is no single "perfect" path, and your decisions (and training) have a large effect on what happens.  Will your nobles rise up against you?  Will you withstand assassination attempts?  Will you make peace or war with neighboring countries?  Who will you marry, if you live that long?  While the game doesn't have quite as diverse a set of endings as certain others in the genre - after all, Elodie is to be crowned Queen - there remains abundant variety in how you get to that end goal (or die trying), and what happens after.

Just bought the game during the summer sale 2014 for $5 ($10 right now) and I got to say, this game completely surprise me. Its one of those games you come along that you don't expect much out of it since there is little fanfare about and its done by a small studio that you might not ever heard of. Mostly, you wonder if you just wasted money buying it and having it sit in your library reminding you of that horrible purchase. Well, you can put your fears to rest, this game is definitely worth buying and very addictive. To give a rough idea what type of game it is, if you were to put all the good things from dead island, the walking dead, skyrim, thief and the sims in a blender and mix it real good. The end result would be this game. Plus this is the first time I play a game that after I logged out of the game to go do things in real life the game doesn't pause and start where you left off when you logged back on. Its continues on without you and you might not like the results when you get back. I found that out the hard way after not playing for a two days. In my case, I came back to find the base morale at 25%, two characters had died from their wounds and several infestations had shown up close to base while I was logged out of the game. So now, everytime I logged out, I start wondering if my base is secure, hoping no one dies, and so on. But definitely gets you wondering what's going on while you away. There is still some things that still need to polish like minor clipping, some more options on customizing the graphics of the game (Ultra setting the game looks awesome, but the blur bugs me a little bit when I move around real fast in 3rd person), maybe having a first person setting and having some basic tutorial levels to play around before diving into the game. Other than that, I definitely recommend playing this game especially if you want to play zombie bashing game. I give it a 8.5/10.

You are going to die before the end of the year, when you are to be coronated as queen. Many times, and in many different ways. The whole learning to become a good queen is your secondary objective in this game. The true objective? Survive.
Manage to survive, and you'll be treated with an ending that is not informing you of your untimely demise. This game will be difficult. This game will frustrate you. This game will make you curse your lack of foresight, lack of obvious hints about what is going on, and most importantly, all those times you forgot to save, making you have to backtrack through the autosaves or your even older ones to completely re-tune your skills just to survive. The upside of this? You will love doing it, if only because even if your army is ruined by the end, your kingdom's people are in riots, and you end up having to marry someone out of political motives, you survived. You took everything this game threw at you, and, even if by just the skin of your teeth, you lived to see another day past the coronation.
This is why you will play this game. The princess is dead (many times over), Long Live The Queen!

Cavern Escape is your
mediocre platformer/puzzle game on steam, that does not have either terms tagged as a category for the product. Hmm.
At a first glance, the game looks as basic as an amateur high school project. Sadly, this is the case. To start off, we have no plot or story whatsoever, and there is no tutorial for how to play. There isn’t even an Options available on the menu!
The gameplay only gets worse. Your only control is your mouse, which makes this game NOT controller supported at all. Moving our character proves also to be difficult, because without good precision or control of your only tool, your character can go spiraling off the course. I’m not sure why the developers would implement such a horrendous control method, instead of the classic arrow keys, or the “AWSD” keys. Whether it is a mistake, or to add as a challenge for players, I have no idea. I was done playing at level 6.
But, to give a benefit to the doubt, I will say that the BGM was not bad. The harp and low chord string instruments really adds to the tension of the environment we are in, trying to overcome the obstacles in each level. But this is the only audio existent in the game. The music goes in a loop, making it repetitive. There’s no mute button available as well.
The graphics of the game are simple and flat by nature. Each set of levels appear to have a specific colour theme:  The first 15 levels has purple. Nearly everything from the BG, flooring and walls to the pillar torches are coated in this colour. The 2nd set (Unlocked by 50 collectables) is green instead. It makes some distinction between the sets of level, since the green levels (supposedly) indicates more hard levels. This topic is probably the only aspect of the game where I feel neutral about, instead of repulsion.
To wrap things up, this game is not a good choice if you are looking for a decent platformer/puzzle game. Cavern escape gets a thumbs down from me.

I find Shadow of Mordor's battle system to be much more enjoyable than the Arkham games; although they are obviously very similar. It can be very repetitive, but it remains fun as long as you enjoy the setting, the fighting, and manipulating uruks with the nemesis system.

Oddly enough, early game is much more difficult than late game thanks to the numerous abilities and power ups you attain. So make note of that.
There exist some stealth elements, which are often recommended rather than charging in and raising alarms, but you are free to tackle a situation however you like as long as you aren't being instructed on specific actions through an active quest at the time.
Well worth the money, especially on its often cheap sales.
