Mmm... this would be in the "meh" pile if steam ever gets around to adding one. But here we are...
Long story short, it's not worth the money. That's my biggest gripe. $20 is too much for this game. $15, maybe.  I only have so much playtime because 1. I left it idling for probably an hour or two over the course of my playtime and 2. Replaying for achievements, but even doing as much as you can I don't see you squeezing much more than 10 hours in the game with a single playthrough.
And that'd be fine if it was a worthwhile 10 hours, but... it's so padded out with filler. All the dream sequences could be cut and the game wouldn't change a bit. They get tiresome quickly and there's no "challenge" to them, they're just tedious. As well, exploring the entire world every day to make sure you're not missing something before going to the two or three points where you can actually move the game forward also ends up feeling repetitive, especially by the third act where the game world gets pretty large. This probably has about 6 hours of interesting content in it total.
Also you have the demontower minigame which... I don't like. I don't like roguelikes, and I don't like how this game controls much, and I especially don't like the decreasing health system, nor the procedural generation which can really screw you over on later levels. Also those bloody dagger-throwing enemies can just go die, forever.
Anyways. What DO I like about this game then? The writing. It's pretty good. And Bea. She's reeeeally good. Really great character there. Lori's pretty great too. Germ has his moments. Gregg and Angus can be alright too. Angus feels underutilized, you get like, 2-3 decent-sized scenes with him max.
I don't really like Mae though. She's self-aware at times but it's not enough and she's kind of a horrible jerk to people without it ever feeling justified. Bleh. And she's the protagonist so I'm kind of stuck with her. She's not awful though, just not that good either.
The main story is... okay but it reeeally takes a while to start existing. Really it doesn't start until the end of act 2 and then tries to cram a game's worth of story into the last third of the game. The climax is pretty satisfying and I don't really feel the ending is abrupt, but that's mostly because the pacing is so out of wack and wrong to begin with.
Graphically the game is pretty good, the only thing I don't really like is the big eyes which can be a bit creepy at times. Mae's animations are pretty fluid but most of the other characters get little to no animation at all most of the time.
And the soundtrack is great, no complaints on that front.
On the whole this is like. A very slight positive because I like the writing enough, it's witty and charming and funny when it needs to be. It's a bit rough around the edges though and I would not recommend it for full price, but, on sale, maybe check it out, yeah.

Would highly recommend this, especially for those about 18 to about mid twenties. The story is top notch and really hits home on more than one occassion. If you are after a simple but in depth story telling game I would highly recommend going for it.

Well, of course no one can recommend this game. No one can, because it is like a little child trying to show you a fun little trick he learnt, but fails three times in a row and ends up kneeling and crying. Before asking ourselves the question what kind of game it is, if it does its job right and if it is worth the price, we have to ask ourselves if the game is functional. And it's simply not.
I don't want to be angry about this game, partly because I got it for 10 cts and because it's not offensive how it fails. It feels more like the first work of a little developper that was so proud of what he could achieve so far that he decided the game was fine as it is and released it on Steam. You can be proud of your work, but when money comes into the balance, things get serious. What baffles me is how this game got accepted. You know what, sod it, I am angry after all.
Right, so we will begin with how the program in itself behaves; it starts off without any settings availalbe, you are taken to the main menu with only two options, play or close the window (if alt+f4 wasn't enough for your majesty). What flabbergasts me is that this game doesn't even have fullscreen support, which is just weak, seriously; most libraries you can use to code have this essential feature available by default, and even if you use something like GameMaker, fullscreen support so basic I don't even know why I am writing so many words for it. It just has to be there.
Secondly, interactions between Operating Systems, peripherals and programs aren't my strongest point but the way it behaves, it looks like the game doesn't actually take mouse acceleration into account. So what you have is you use your mouse pointer to move your character (we will talk about this in a moment), but very quickly (in a matter of seconds), the mouse cursor's position and your character's get desynchronized. It is disturbing and an amateur's work.
About the game in itself: it is some kind of puzzle game, where you have an isometric view of a room. The game starts without any tutorial or any indication whatsoever; you click on the first level, you are presented said level, and you have to guess what is what: the little head is your character, the spikes kill you, you have to collect the diamonds and there is a finish line somewhere. You even have to GUESS what is your objective.
Once (and if) you figure out how to entertain yourself with this nice little game you have bought, you could start to count the glitches and bugs you will encounter during every minute of this wonderful time you will be having. For example, when you pick a level, the game will blackscreen as if loading it, but will get you back to the level select screen, but acting as if you just unlocked the level you just selected, so you can basically skip steps. What is more, sometimes up to two levels can be unlocked after finishing one and you can tell it's not intended, because they are presented in a linear string; the character get stuck in walls and you can get out of bounds.
On another note, some annoyances can not be labelled as glitches but are more than questionable "game design" choices. For example, you have a music loop that starts when you are playing a level; this music loop STOPS when you die, followed by the "You are dead" music, and then re-starts when you press "Restart". And you die a lot, very quickly in this game, because the rooms are small, and the challenges many, so it gets very frustrating to hear the same first notes over and over again. Another rock in the shoe is the fact that walls kill you. You touch a wall, it kills you. This is an isometric game, mind you, and your character CLIPS through some textures, so you will die a lot without even seeing it coming, trust me. And that "game mechanic" isn't consistent: some walls kill you, some act as walls and some are holes you can out-of-bounds of.
To sum it up, Cavern Escape is an unchallenging game (because you can see the solution just by looking at the room) that will frustrate you, even for a very short time, by its glitches, bugs, stupid design choices and very likely lack of QA testing undergone by someone else that the developer's mom. Flee from this, although I have heard it is useful to buy it because of the cards, if just like me you have a massive -90% sale ticket.

Whilst I have recommended this game, I do so because I feel it has potential rather than being a game that I can solidly invest a lot of time in.
The mechanics, graphics, style and atmosphere in Stranded Deep are VERY addictive. I find myself getting lost in the world and trying to do lots of things to improve the life for my character who wakes up with almost nothing and needs your skill and planning to survive.
The issue I have at the moment is that too much of the game is 'missing' or still 'in development'. I realise this is an early access game and that is the point, which is why I have given the game a thumbs up - for now. It seems there was a change in the way the game was being developed and a lot of things, most notably the crafting system, which is the absolute core of the game, have been taken back to the drawing board.
As such, after about an hour of gametime, where you survive, learn to feed yourself and make a bed, there is very little in the game to actually do. Sure you can row your liferaft around to other places to explore and pick things up, but you can't currently DO anything with those things. You can look at them, but can't make a power boat or a raft of your own or anything other than the basic constructions afforded to you in the construction menu.
My biggest concern with the game is - what happens then? If the devs add back in the crafting to make these things... what am I going to do? It's fun learning to survive for an hour or so, but then what? There seems to be a farming thing in development, but I can't see myself coming back to Stranded Deep unless there's more to do. It's a sandbox game, but at the moment the walls of the box are too restricted.
Based on the work that's gone into it so far, I'm encouraged by the dev team and what they are doing. Hopefully my concerns will be allayed and the game will be improved in the new year. It's a great start, but be wary, it's very much 'EARLY' in the early access.

I've been palying this game at my friend's house for a long time and descided to buy it for myself.
Why? Because I fell in love with the survival concept of the movie "Cast away" and this game follows that idea.
You can craft, hunt, explore, gather materials to build a house or anything else you can come up with your imagination.
There's a watch on your wrist that keeps track of time, days of survival, temperature, hunger, thirst and health.
The graphics look great, you really get the impression that you are on your own in a world that has no zombies or such, but just basis survival elements.
Chop down trees, climb into palmtrees to grab coconuts, use a spear to catch crabs or fish. Swim in the ocean to reach a sunken boat and explore it to find helpful items... but keep a eye out for the dangers lurking in the deep blue sea.
You can get sick, hungry, thirsty or even fall out of tree and break something. Help isn't coming, only you can help yourself.
The devs are very acitve and they try out new stuff. They are also very helpful: I had a problem with my water bottle... Fixed. Lost my boat and hoped for the raft to return... Fixed. Return of weather... Fixed.
Just talk to them normally and they will listen.
Got bugs? Use the bug report, they will try to fix things. Don't forget, they are a small team so things might take time.
I love to see what the future brings for this game.

For a game that bills itself as a game about choice and tension, I've found Gods Will Be Watching to be more about trial and error than anything else.
I liked the original Gods Will Be Watching mostly because one playthrough felt like that was enough to understand the game. I was sure that there was some way to win, but I felt like accepting the inevitability of failure was enough.
The basic conceit of paying $10 for this game is that I want more of the same. What I don't think the developers understood, though, is that I didn't care about winning in the original.
I cared more about choosing how I lost, and realizing that my efforts weren't enough to solve the problem.
Here's where things get tricky with this game:
I haven't played this game very much, but I already understand the basics of how this will work. I'm going to have to discern how people are feeling based on the animations of their sprites.
As a result of my inability to discern what the sprite animations are trying to tell me, I've lost the first level a bunch of times. The problem is, though, that I don't really care about losing.
I didn't spend $10 on this game to figure out the correct way to solve a problem. I paid $10 to spend 15-20 minutes each in various high-tension situations.
I don't want to feel bad for playing on easy, I want to feel bad for letting a hostage bleed out and not think about how to optimize the bleed-out time to better release a fake video game virus.
I like the idea of this game, I like the art, but the execution is shockingly bad. Really.

First and foremost, this game certainly isn't for everybody.
As far as I can tell, the experience heavily relies on your capacity to become immersed in the story and to emphatize with the other characters (so, to put it a bit differently, I imagine it is better suited for passionate readers rather than hardcore gamers).
In most of the cases, the negative reviews complain about the difficulty of the game, and yes, Gods be good, this game won't forgive you nothing. But that's part of its beauty.
At first, I too had the impression that the HEAVY emphasis on difficulty and the amount of focus on succeeding unecessarily distracts you from actually questioning the morality of your actions, but after a while I begin to realize that this is EXACTLY the point;
the game is hard and cruel and unforgiving, and it is up to you whether you will lose your cool and become a ruthless, abusive monster driven by nothing than your wish to beat the game, or whether you will maintain your solidarity and humanity even against such impossible odds.
And it IS possible to win and yet do things right, never doubt it!
So that's the biggest, greatest plus of Gods Will Be Watching - to sum it up in different words, the game will put ridiculous pressure on you, and the real beauty of it is not so much in beating each chapter as rather in HOW you beat each chapter, how hard you will try find the right balance between being effective and being self-destructively kind and naive.
It is fair to say that the main strenght of the game is not so much in what happens on the screen as in what happens within you while you struggle with frustration. (though, to be fair, not once have I gotten frustrated to the point of being angry at the game, despite having to repeat each level good three to eight times)
The second thing that I feel I must praise is the incredible diversity.
Every chapter has entirely different setting, mood and atmosphere, and that is rare to say at least. Thanks to this, the game never gets boring or repetetive - I mean, DAMN! Just when I thought I had a pretty good idea about what I am into, after resorting to terrorist actions for nonetheless decent cause, through surviving in extremely hostile enviroment and withstanding torture, BAM! I find myself stranded in the middle of the desert in hopeless battle against both the enemy forces and the never-ceasing heat.
I can't really find the words to describe this aspect of the game, so let me just call it what I feel it is: MAGIC! DONWRIGHT MAGIC!
Finally, the writting is excellent. The plot is grown-up and doesn't resort to dividing characters into good guys and bad guys, the characters you meet are all unique, believable and relatable (not to mention likeable - Liam! You magnificent ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!),
and quite soon you will find yourself caring for them.
Brazillion outta ten; I am happy beyond words to see a game such as this, and wish to see many more in the future.
This is where gaming meets art. This is where gaming becomes an instrument that further encourages exploration of the human nature and nudges you towards unsettling and unusual questions about yourself and the world around you, rather than being just means of entertainment.

Having played this game a ton already, I feel I can write a good review of the game now. In the review, I'll cover what I like about the game, what I don't, what can be improved on, and what I think should be added in the long run of the game.
-------
Some things I really liked about the game is that it's difficult at first. You're thrown into an appocalyptic world with nothing other than a flashlight and your wits. The struggle to find food, drink, and gear is really immersive, having you look in every crack and crevice to find even the most common of items. The scenery and overall atmosphere of the game is really well done as well, especially when playing at night with headphones. If you're playing alone, the feeling of isolation and hopelessness really sets a great mood while playing this game. A survival game like this shouldn't make the player have the feeling of power and strength right away, which was well done in my opinion. If you're looking for a more happy go lucky survival game however, I recommend unturned, the free to play sort of silly survival game.
-------
There wasn't much I didn't like about the game, but some things I didn't like is that it's attacking system is a little strange to me. I understand the game is in alpha right now, but when you hit a mutant with a melee attack, it doesn't feel like you hit them at all until they go down. I think this could be improved on by adding a little more knock back with certain melee attacks to add the feeling of a good hit. Another thing I think can be improved on is the inventory system. I say this because there are time when I need to move things out of an article of clothing to change that clothing, but the items will not move, even when there is ample space available. To me, both of these things I think can be improved on at some point. These issues don't really take away from the game at all though. The game itself is still very enjoyable.
-------
Something I really think should be added in the long run of development is a good character creator. Seeing as every time you die, your character changes in ethnicity and clothing, I don't think a character creator would be that difficult of a request. Another thing I'd like to see added would be graphics settings to help make the game run a little smoother on lower quality pc's such as mine. The game is still playable, but the game doesn't exactly run as smooth as I'd like it too. A final addition I'd like to see in the game is the ability to easily make and host your own private servers for you and your friends to enjoy. In my opinion, being able to play with your friend alone without fear of another player coming and killing you both and seperating you would be a fantastic addition.
-------
All in all, I totally recommend this game to anyone that enjoys more slow paced survival games like this. Also with the devs still active and working to keep adding content to this game, I see a ton of potential for it to rise in popularity. I really like what the devs are doing and I plan to continue playing this game for a long time.
-------

Saga MMORTS Review
This game Is one I would truly enjoy being able to love. Sadly its not possible. The premise of the game is pretty simple actually. You start out choosing a faction, get a simple base, some starter units that are generic and nonfaction, then go out and start doing quests. The quests can be interesting to completely boring. There gameplay is similar to older style games in that most of your units are blocks of guys controlled all at once as opposed to singles.
Your basic premise is building up your land, upgrading, leveling units and getting gear from quests. To get more units..well you need to buy booster packs really. Yeah there is tournaments you can do but it takes along time, and each card is only one guy..where most units need 8-25 of the same card to become a full unit. There are a few quests that give you a few special units but far and few between. This makes it really less free to play, but also doesnt make it pay2win either.
The fighting, the meat of the game, is pretty  basic. You have a few simple stances, some units may have a special ability or not and you have a few spells that can help during battles as buff, debuff, heal or direct damage/DoTs. Even for its age I still enjoy the look and feel of most of the units.
The game is old, and even back before it came to steam..the game code had flaws, and still does after all these years. Alot of random bugs, and really not much has changed outside a new rogue faction you need to pay to get boosters for and a new quest or two centered around them.
So I guess my point
What makes this game really worth it? My answer is..i dont know really. The original developers care more about indie films than they do the game. I think only one is still left working on it..It had great potential to sadly.I guess in the end Ill wait for total war: warhammer for my fix of this type of strategy game.

A SAGA. A game that died in 2012 after a kickstarter for an expansion failed. The forums are as dead as they ever were, and nothing was mentioned. Then it popped up here and I expected several changes.
A worthless game through and through. Back in 2009 I liked this game a lot. It had interesting aspects of any RTS: Home building (as limited as it may be) and unit building. Oh. Did I say unit building? You can forget that.
Back then I got what I thought was just the starter army: Several human units, a behemoth, two spells, and a battering ram. I would've thought this sufficint until I could purchase some new units. Guess what, unless you shell over real cash for a slot machine, you aren't getting any new units. Why do I call it a slot machine? Well, you aren't guaranteed to get what you want unless you purchase specific packs which cost more money than the basic packs.
What's that you say? You don't want to waste your money in Vegas? Good then! Once you've built a few mines, you just have ato wait a few years to get enough gold to buy a single, powerful unit from the in-game store! It's not enough that you have to spend thousands of gold on a single unit. Nah. You think you're good? Unless it's a dragon it needs a unit, and guess what that entails. That's right! More gold that you don't have and never will have!
"But there are world map quests! Surely I can get gold from those."
Right you are, Timmy, but you're still an idiot. Go sit in the corner!
Wanna know how much gold you can get per quest? Almost none, and that's from looting the chests decimated squads drop. You can make your own squads with a limited number, and while that might seem great, it's not. You're limited to about two or three full squads per battle moment. You have units in reserve, thus. The problem? You face hundreds of powerful enemy units that field full armies while you have a handfull of troops that can't face every situation but of the extreme limits your head is being perpetually punched into and grinded like a blunt blade.
Don't expect to win any quests after level six without shelling out lots of cash, and don't expect to field a single squad of what may seem like a powerful unit to you. It'll be smashed in milliseconds and the enemy squad will have no damage. I mean, sure. The squads level up and you can get equipment from loot and the market, but a spoon can only get you so far when cutting meat.
Oh, did I mention the tournament? Why, yes. There is a tournament mode. You join it, sometimes for free, then you wait about an hour to get the necessary amount of people. Then you get random cards, then you get obliterated. I won't delve into this. It's pvp. Suffice to say, participating in it isn't enough. No. You need to win. As such, you get no tokens. Ever. You win the first branch? You get a single token. You need at least eighteen to buy a tournament booster pack, and considering that a match can last more than half an hour, you can see how annoying this is. Money money money money money money money money money, dollah dollah. Dollah dollah.
Now let's go into the ressources. As any base building RTS would require, you start with a keep and must build housing for your peasants (which you don't see) and task a certain number of them to a variety of jobs, such as building/repairing, farming (for when you make farms), mining (stone and gold), and lumbering.
The system itself is good as you have to watch your peasants, the amount of food they have, their happiness...basically the poor man's Stronghold. If you don't keep them happy they riot. Nothing happens except for a few damaged buildings. Nothing notable. However, the amount of ressources you get with each station and the amount you need are two different things.
Despite having tons of spots to build stone quarries and gold miness, you can only build a limited number of each station as well as housing. You need more? Go do the quest where you assault an extremely fortified enemy stronghold full of dozens of units plus towers that shoot at you when you get too close. Aw
You can only field two units? Boohoo cry sniff.
Once you conquer one, you get a new zone to build on (that also has sharp limits). Now for the ressources, as I mentioned, what you need and what you get are two different things. I have around five gold mines, plus taxing, plus the 'research' that boosts mining. I get about three hundred gold per day. That's right. It's not per hour. IT'S PER DAY. Which means twenty-four hours. You need around 10k in ressources to upgrade your university to reach the next level university? Gotta wait a while. You want gold to buy a unit? Gotta wait a looooooooooong time. You need more to make a squad? I hope you enjoyed your nintieth birthday.

Read other reviews for story and playability, this is more of a technical complaint on control scheme.
The only reason this game does not get a max score on my review is because the control schemes were frustrating.
I played the RE 0 and 1 on the Gamecube and learned to play with that controller.  For the RE-1 remastered on Steam I used the "Type B" control scheme since it emulated best the old GC controller.
What is frustrating to me is that Type B on tank (original) controls you ran with X and inventory was with B.  In RE-0 the functions of X and B flip and confuse me to no end.
Also, Type B had you aiming with RT (right trigger) and firing with A, which is sort of the staple for the default one on this game (except on RE0 Type A you aim with RB).  Type A on RE1 had aiming with LT and firing with RT (as far as I can remember)
I really wish CAPCOM included a little bit of controller consistency on these two titles, they did so well in with the GC versions.
Other than that no complaints  9.3/10

Capcom one again brings a classic title to Steam in full HD Glory, an overlooked gem from 2002. They completely remastered every background this time because they had access to the original game files so that's a plus. Everything from the original is carried over along with a few extras made exclusively for the remaster itself.
- Wesker Mode (Beat the game once on any difficulty to unlock)
- Full HD Backgrounds
- Gallery Mode (Includes all the game FMV's, Unlocked from the start and progresses as you do)
- 60 fps (PC Exclusive) consoles are locked to 30, variable frame rate is included.
- New control scheme similar to the action games, various layouts to choose from
- Exclusives costumes, were shown as in game but are actually paid DLC which is typical Capcom
- 5 fan made t-shirts for free if you voted during the campaign
Already played through the entire campaign and Leech Mode and I had no issues with the gameplay itself. Mechanic/story wise nothing was changed from the original 2002 release which isn't a bad thing. Capcom attempted to bring co-op to the game but it didn't work, pretty obvious why it wouldn't work.
is very different from other RE games, this one elimates the need for Item Boxes completely from the start. Newcomers will probably hate the constant backtracking to find items they dropped but old school players will feel right at home. If you are having issues locating items go into your Map and turn on the UI, for some reason reviewers didn't mention this and people are having issues finding it.
are pretty much the game as Remake Remastered from last year, according to most people the backgrounds are locked to 1440 resolution again. Running the game on max settings I was able to play through the entire game without slowdown except the area where you meet your first leech, I think there's a bug here with the flame effects. Other than that I had a constant 60fps experience, also tried variable which for some reason locked the game to 45 fps, tried 30fps for the hell of it and it was too slow for me lol.
Overall, if you're a hardcore RE fan from the early days you should pick it up. If you're newcomer and have patience I'd reccommend trying the game out, just don't expect an action experience this one is a bit slower than the original game but it offers solid gameplay if you give it a chance. Only thing I feel needs work is the control scheme, I dunno who's idea it was to map the run button to X but that needs to be changed. They should have just given the option of using the original gamecube layout.

The port is trash. Thankfully, the PC community stepped up and fixed the game. Ive been using DSfix from the start, but I was always afraid to unlock 60fps because of glitches it can cause. I decided to give it a go recently, just to see what it felt like. As soon as the game loaded, I almost cried; the improvement was obvious. Its hard to describe, but its not just smoother; it also drastically changes the way the game looks. Ive not seen such a massive difference in other games when comparing 30 and 60fps. As soon as I beheld the holy land, I knew there was no going back; I was gonna have to live with the side effects.
Tested over 80 hours and numerous playthroughs: Im happy to report that I had no major issues with 60fps. I slid down every ladder, never fell through the world, and I never got stuck at a bonfire. Should it happen to you, both of those glitches can be fixed by reloading the game. Weapons do degrade faster, but durability is so high in DS1 that it doesnt matter. At 30fps you might never need to repair your weapons. At 60fps youll need to repair a couple times; no big deal. 60fps does affect jump distance, but I didnt have any issues.
One serious thing I ran across was difficulty walking up slopes. At 60fps you can end up hitting invisible walls on certain slopes. Sometimes, you can take a couple steps back, and it wont be there when you go forward again. Other times, that wont help at all, and youll need to switch to 30fps. Thankfully, you can do that with a simple press of a button; the default key in DSfix is Backspace. Tip: switch to 30fps for The Great Hollow.
If your PC can handle it: be sure to get the HD texture pack mod and sweetfx. They make the game look nearly as good  as DS3. Both can be found at
Beyond that, theres not much I can say that hasnt been said already. I dont think DS1 is old enough to call a timeless classic, but it will eventually be regarded as such. This is a top 3 all-time game for me.
Buy it, mod/fix it, and love it forever.

Ok, I need to write a review about this game. Are you a Disciples fan? Have you found yourself lost in the previous versions for hours on end? Then buy this game. Its better than all the other new "R" incarnations I can't spell (Renaisance, Resurecction, whatev) since it takes the best from all of them and leaves the rest out. I read some of the negative reviews on here and like a fool I let it delay me from having the best Disciples experience since Sacred Lands Gold. This is polished, flowing, and builds on the previous games while adding modern mechanics and TONS of new artwork. People giving negative reviews can be listened to but their complaints are mostly about Disciples in general. Is it hard? Not nearly as hard as the first Disciples was. Is it tedious? Not nearly as much as Disciples 2 was. The magic is very specific, as in certain spells may sound all-powerful (and be bloody expensive) but there are many times they will be useless in battle. You have to be careful and cherish everything you find. There's lots... LOTS to explore and discover. It will take you a long time to develop powerful characters that can face anything (as in, multiple levels and countless hours), but yeah that's Disciples for you. The game is all about power-matching and countering, like any good magic fantasy, but Disciples was always famous for ramping things up and this version is no different. You will be forever out-matched, that's the point! Courage and charge on! Also, get good at healing and using powerups. Again, if you liked the original Sacred Lands with all its glitchy headaches and miserable gameplay (ie. always being outgunned), then you will like this game. Also, you can now carry forward two heroes with 9 items each to new campaign levels (!!!)  Oh and when you resurrect a unit, they retain their experience from the previous battles and will level up upon returning to life if they can! Yay improvements! The art is fantasic, worth it just for that imo, and also if you're obsessive compulsive like me and love a good, complex, interesting and ultimately satisfying game (your souls are MINE you damn dirty elves!)
Hints if you've never played before or its been a while;
- When upgrading your leader skills, you should ALWAYS been gunning for the extra leadership point. Adding another member to your team is the best possible thing you can do.
- Set difficulty to easy and leave it there.
- Legion was always unfairly powerful, its the same this time, so play as them I guess if you're having trouble. Invest in Fiends and have them do the dirty work.
- Pretty everything you do should be geared toward upgrading two good, balanced teams. When a member dies you gotta go back and resurrect/heal, yes every time. Pump all experience into the same 8-10 units. Spend all extra cash on leveling up dudes in training camps.
- The easy enemies in the beginning are very valuable. Save them as easy pickings for your newest recruits.
- Turn the music off or you're going to drive yourself insane! (My last level was 140 turns!!)

I love Terraria. Starbound is kind of like Terraria, except with Terraria the game itself is highly polished, but limited in its scope of environments. Starbound isn't as highly polished as Terraria, but makes up for it with MASSIVE amounts of content. Not necessarily main quest type content, but the universe in Starbound is so vast that I believe it would be impossible to traverse and explore every world in it. With the added mod support Starbound has it makes the game almost overwhelming. You have to be able to focus on a single task at a time, because there is so much going on to distract from your primary mission.
If you are a builder, then you can build in an insane amount of ways, the circuit system in Starbound is a lot of fun to play with. You can try and make a smart home in ways that I have seen people even make elevators with buttons for each floor of their complexes. The main quest is fun, but semi repetitive. The side quests are again repetitive, but quirky and can be fun to mess around with. The differences in difficulty in different worlds is interesting. Overall I really enjoy Starbound. It is fun, diverse, and if this style of game ever got a AAA release with the refinement, polish, and possibly a dedicated server listing or player finding features, then I would be sold on it all over again.
Cons
- Not the best optimized game and it isn't uncommon to be able to create an environment where your FPS drop. This usually happens to me when I create a small city of NPCs. This happened even before I modded the game, but I play a modded version of it now.
-Some QoL mods that are available through the steam workshop should be a vanilla part of the game.
-Steamworkshop is a nightmare to navigate. No categories or real way of finding specific types of mods, or the up-to-date mods.
Pros
-The game is fun
-Great music
-Even at ~50 hours in the game I probably have only experienced about half of the different types of worlds out there in this massive Starbound universe.
-So much of this game just works.
-The game is apparently easy to mod, and you can find a mod to almost anything if you look hard enough.
-Just derp around and have some fun! It isn't AAA game priced, but can easily eat more hours than a standard AAA game.

This game was a true disappointment for a free to play user. If you do not want to end up paying real money or being extremely disappointed, do not download this game.
Here's how my experience went: I downloaded the game, created my nation, started doing tutorials and learning stuff, and it was pretty great! I was thinkin I may actually keep this game for quite a long time. I start to gain more peasants, build more buildings for my city, continue to quest, etc. Later on I find out how to do quests with my friend, which was cool as well. However, I couldn't find out how to gain new troops.
So once I got offline, my friend continued to play and looked more into it, built a University in his town and all that, and informed me that the game was extremely disappointing. He found out that the way you gain new troops is.... you guessed it. Booster packs! You may or may not have guessed those exact words, but basically the only way to get booster packs is through credits (the game's "real money" currency), or something called Play to Win tokens. We don't quite understand too much about the Play to Win tokens (feel free to enlighten me if you please) but from what I understand, one of the ways you can earn them is through PvP (Player vs Player, for those who dont know) battles. My friend also explained to me later on that you can earn booster packs through PvP as well. OR you could also buy new troops on the marketplace with the cheapest troop selling at 1000 gold, which isn't too easy to get, as far as I can tell (I played to level 8 before I quit).
Basically what I'm saying is that you either pay real money, fight other people tooth and nail, or grind quests for gold in order to buy new troops, which was the most disappointing thing ever to discover about this game. They sure know how to make Free to Play look like slavery! Everything else about the game was great though! The base building, the combat, everything. I enjoyed the game quite a bit during my short time of playing it. However, the thing about how to get new troops was quite disappointing. I don't want to be grinding using my basic newbie troops: the human cavalry, human archers, behemoth, etc. I want to use some mother♥♥♥♥in nature elves!
Pay to Win crap. Not recommended. 4/10 stars

Saga combines several genres into one game: MMO, Nation Building, and Collectable card games with a generous sprinkling of pvp and non pvp game content.

Saga takes skill to win, you don't win by default just because you spent an insane amount of money on the game.  The prices also do not continuously scale up from their original price.  Booster packs cost the same.  Quests available in game allow players to get cards without paying, as does participation in the tournaments and farming gold lets you buy units as well.  Expecting to be able to access mid and end game content a few hours/levels into a game is unrealistic. It may not be for everyone, but I highly recommend it.

Ever since I got this game it has swallowed my life up.
There's so much content it's ridiculous, tons of items to unlock and mess around with, a bunch of characters all suited to differing playstyles, many different floor layouts, and lots of fun and creative bosses.
This game doesn't get stale after a few hours, you can play it for days and days and weeks and weeks and never get tired of it because every run is different. You can combine items to create amazing synergies. For example, you can combine the Tech X upgrade, which replaces your attack with a charge-up laser ring, and the Brimstone upgrade, which replaces your attack with a charge-up giant laser beam of death to create giant laser Brimstone rings of death. Or the combination of Dr. Fetus (bomb shots), Pyromaniac (explosion immunity) and Mutant Spider (quad shot) which allows you to shoot four bombs in one shot at enemies without taking any damage from your own explosions.
It also has an amazing dynamic soundtrack, this means that the music gets more intense depending on how many enemies are in a room. For example, the Flooded Caves theme is a slow, atmospheric song. But if you enter a room with a lot of powerful enemies, an awesome guitar solo kicks in which really gets you pumped.

And if there isn't enough content for you, you can mod the game easily with the Steam Workshop for many creative community-made items.

At first glance, this game seems to be a girly and cozy game without any real gaming involved. This turns out to be quite the opposite, as shortly after you begin playing you will die.

This game is fun and different then others, as well as addicting. Every time you die you find yourself thinking of different skills you could study, different scenarios you could choose. You come back with a thirst for victory, and when you achieve it, it is all the more glorious.
It is also a game that once you are done, you aren't actually done. You can go back and play different story lines, and try to unlock deaths you missed or even how your kingdom does after you are crowned Queen.
Overall, this is a game you can keep coming back to without it feeling old and stale. Despite the girly feel, the game is quite serious, so be prepared to spend hours trying to overcome the dreaded skill-checks to achieve your ultimate victory.

At first the game looked like a decent "Do not Touch the Wall" Maze Game which I was excited to see the developers take on this. However, it soon became apparent that it was nothing more than a glitchy "Do not Touch the Wall" Maze Game and here’s why:
Pros:
♦ Concept is like a "Do not Touch the Wall" Maze Game
♦ Graphics are decent (For what they are)
♦ Music is decent (To an extent)
♦ Has Steam Trading Cards (However, the game is too small to collect them all)
♦ Okay past time if you are really bored
Cons:
♦ No Steam Achievements (Not really much room to add too many achievements, but a game made in 2017 on Steam that doesn't have achievements or make full use of Steam features just seems to be lacking. Plus adding achievements gives people a further reason to play/replay the game to unlock and collect all the achievements)
♦ The game description on their store page is wrong (It says it’s a platform puzzle game, when it’s a click and drag maze game. There is no platform or puzzle elements in the game)
♦ Store Page classes the Full Version as the “Ultimate Casual Brain Teaser, Almost Impossible to Beat and Over 40 Challenging Levels” (There is no brain teasing about the game, you just dodge some obstacles, which is about timing and collect some crystals. Plus, this game isn’t challenging or a puzzle as there are no actual puzzles in the game (Dodging obstacles isn’t a puzzle). So, the game isn’t almost impossible and if the Full Version only has 40 levels and ATM the EA game has 20 levels which I completed in 20minutes… that means the game will only be 40minutes in length)
♦ Hardly any sound effects (Only one is when you die)
♦ Controls are dodgy (Only able to use Mouse)
♦ No Options Menu (No way to change graphics, volume levels, mute the game or even change resolution)
♦ Music is way too loud and no way to turn it down or off in game (Annoying as the music is almost double in volume to what any other game I play is)
♦ Music is a 10 second sound wave and you can hear the pause before it starts over again (Shouldn’t be able to hear the music stopping and starting over, that is lazy implementation in my opion)
♦ Clicked to do world 1, level 3 and level 4 unlocked (I didn't even have to play level 3. Levels shouldn’t randomly unlock when trying to play previous levels)
♦ No way to put it in Fullscreen as there is no options menu or the ability to change resolution (Even Alt+Enter did nothing)
♦ Clicking world 1 level 6 unlocked world 1, level 7 and 10 (I didn't have to do world 1, level 6 or 7 or 8 or 9, I could just skip to 10)
♦ World 1 after unlocking Level 7, every world 1, level 1-10 says I have 3 Crystals to start with (This is weird as I hadn't collected anything)
♦ Doing the same level over gives you more total crystals (This allows you to do easier levels twice to gain more crystals to unlock the next world)
♦ World 1, level 7 is very glitchy (Going outside the map to avoid the moving spikes is very glitchy and half the time it says I die on the way out)
♦ Unlocked World 2 and level 7 is already unlocked (This is shouldn’t be the case as I’ve just unlocked the world)
♦ World 2 I start with 6 crystals a level (This is broken because I shouldn't start with any)
♦ World 2, level 1 glitched and wouldn't let me finish the level, I had to die and restart to finish (Annoying because I had collected everything and couldn't finish)
♦ Finishing world 2, level 7 unlocked world 2 level 8, 9 and 10 (This shouldn't be the case as I should have to finish a level to unlock the next)
♦ World 2 is easier than World 1 (This is because world 1, level 7 seems glitched making it almost impossible)
♦ No way to exit a level once in it without winning (Annoying if you click the wrong level)
♦ Beat the game in under 20minutes, that's almost 1minute a level (Way too short)
♦ No storyline or cinematics (When you finish the 2nd world all it says is "The End, Tap to Continue" in big letters)
♦ No Replayability (There is nothing to incentives playing a level or even the again)
♦ Has a "More Games" button on the Main Menu which does nothing (When clicked it does nothing and this button overlaps the exit button slightly. Really poor to have a button that does nothing on a menu)
As of 28/3/17:
♦ More levels were added to world 1. (More levels are good, however the developer shouldn't be adding more levels when there are still major glitches, bugs and features missing)
♦ New levels 11-15 in world 1 seem rushed, untested and poorly made (This is bad as it seems as though the developer wanted to get more levels out as quickly as possible without actually taking the time to make them properly and well)
♦ Developer claimed to fix bugs but added more (Didn't really fix any and added more bugs)
♦ Trying to monetize off the soundtrack (Chargin 0.49 USD and trying to profit off of the soundtrack, that is poorly edited looping tracks that you can even hear when the song loops is an outrage. Also at this moment, there is hardly any songs/soundtracks in the game to warrant having a buyable soundtrack)
Overall, I know everyone must start out somewhere when making games. However, there are way too many cons and basic glitches that cause me not to be able to recommend the game as the cons and glitches break core game fundamentals.

Cavern Escape is an indie "platformer/puzzler". Your goal is to make it across a series of obstacles in order to get to the finish line.
In the "About this Game" portion of the Steam store page, the Developer has written "drag the small cute character". I'm sorry, did I miss something? There was no "cute" character in the game. Your character is a horrendous.. thing... with hair made of fire. The levels themselves look decent but there are probably a total of 10 textures in the whole game, with everything being reused constantly. The second "world" in the game features the same sprites in a different colour.
There soundtrack of "Cavern Escape" consists of looping tracks with slightly altered pitches. The first and second world have almost the same tracks with slight changes in the pitch. The game over music is a looping 6 second track that gets irritating VERY quickly.
From what I could tell, non existant. Very disappointed that the developers couldn't make, well, ANYTHING to explain the world of Cavern Escape.
The game flaunts it's difficulty as a feature, but, in all honesty, I think it's because of the developer's inability to program proper hit boxes. You will die quite frequently due to insanely messed up hitboxes, but other times you will be able to walk through certain obstacles because they're hitboxes aren't properly calibrated to the sprite. Also, the brick walls can kill you. Spikes I can understand. Falling into the empty void I can understand. But walking into a brick & mortar wall? Oh the horror. I'm sure millions of people are killed worldwide due to walking into a plain wall.
The controls in Cavern Escape are also horribly done as well. Don't bother with WASD or the Arrow keys. You're using your mouse on this one, and the developer couldn't even get that part right. The mouse control just feels off. When you play a game that requires precision in order to complete the levels that are already difficult due to the horrible hit boxes, you'd want at least semi-precise mouse movement. Well, the precise mouse movement I was talking about is not present in this game. Everything feels so off and confusing, and you'll be quite frustrated due to the fact that the movement and hitboxes are so out of whack.
I was able to nearly complete the game and experience everything there is to be experienced in the short amount of time that I have played. I have a small personal rule when it comes to reviewing; Play ~an hour and get a grasp on every main aspect on the game and find it's weakest links. There were no specific "weak links" in Cavern Escape. The whole game was the "weakest link". I was able to fully experience the game in less than 30 minutes which is insanely disappointing for what resembles a terrible mobile port. Unless the developer is able to fix the hitboxes, create a story, and re-do the controls, then I cannot possibly recommend this game to anyone.

State of Decay is one of those games where you've decided only a few hours in you've already decided that you want a sequal, but have found the game only decently enjoyable. The premise is solid, survive the zombie apocolypse by creating a fortress from which you search for survivors, savenge supplies, and build defenses. Many actions, such as resource depletion and base upgrades, happen in real time, meaning if you queue up a hefty infirmary upgrade, you can leave the game and when you come back it will be closer to depletion. In addition, resources like food and mdicine slowly drain over time, requiring more careful managemnent. The real-time aspect is reminiscent of those free to play mobile games, except not a mind numbing cash cow. Some players have complained that mechanic unfairly punishes players that don't play often, but the develpors claim that not playing for a week or even a year will have only neglible negative impact on your game. Personally, I have not owned the game long enough to comment on this.
While these core functions are mostly well implemented and enjoyable, the game is marred by poor and sometimes baffling develpoment decisions and details. The game allows the player to switch between any character they have become friends with as currently used players become tired or injured, but for no apparant reason there is no way to swap items between them except by selling them to the shop and buying them back at an increased price. Many of the missions are incredibly poorly designed, the most notable of which are the "besieged" side missions. These missions task the player with "defending the perimeter" of another groups house, but the awkward camera angles and inabily to melee through windows make the battles far drawn out than they need to be. In fact, the game seems to reward doing the opposite of your mission and letting them in to fight them inside the house. The other side missions all revolve around the same few mission types, none of which are much better than this one. The game also does a poor job informing the player of even basic game mechanics like adding recruiting survivors, something which would have required minimal briefing in game.
Despite it's flaws, the game is still enjoyable. The combat is fluid and satisfying (though occaisonally the mouse and keyboard controls leave something ro be desired). The graphics look great for the most part, except when faced with long draw distances the ground textures are tiny and ugly. The voice acting is mostly solid, but repeated background dialogue gets annoying after a while. All in all This is a solid game, definitly worth a buy if the premise sounds intereting to you, or during a decent sale

I must admit, the game I got is not exactly what I was expecting. When I first glimpsed and pre-ordered this, I understood a point and click narrative story with moral choices and consequences like it was an episodic Telltale game. However, what I got is a trial and error puzzle that probably has a really deep story. I couldn't even finish the first level on easy mode. I can see where there are moral choices (shooting your hostages, smacking them around, letting them run off or shooting them down), but that really loses it's effect when you have to do that 10 times in a row because all the hostages died or you do something else game over-worthy
I know that Devolver is known for their trial and error games (Hotline Miami, Luftrausers), but this should Not be one of those trial and errors. I think that this game can be so much better if the trial and error part was taken out. This could be a great game with episodic Telltale game-esque choices and consequences and a deep story, but for now the experience is muddled by the trial and error elements that are apparent in several of Devolver's other games.
Despite all that, I still like this game and I really hope something is done about this.

Extremely punishing trial and error simulator, make one mistake and the last 10 minutes of your time are down the drain. The thing about trial and error is, you must first error to then learn and do better the next time. You are virtually guaranteed to lose multiple times per level wasting a huge amount of your time since there are 0 checkpoints. It's like theres some excel sheet in the background you're entering numbers into, and if you ♥♥♥♥ up you have to start from the beginning again. The fact that theres a lot of dice rolls built into the game makes it feel extremely unfair and punishing.
In a certain level if you do a certain action 4 times, you instantly lose and have to restart (15+ mins of your time) If you do it 3 or less you're fine. However, the alternative to that action is an RNG dice roll. Whether or not the last 15+ mins of your time were wasted is often dependent on such dice rolls.

Gameplay:
I have been playing this game for a while now, and I have to say that I am enjoying it quite a bit. It is a VERY interesting approach to point and click. Let me start off by saying that the game is very hard. Usually, it is not to the point that it gets too frustrating, but it actually encourages you to try something different or improve on what has worked until you beat the stage. Although the game does base a lot of its mechanics on luck, there is a certain amount of thrill to some of the gambling aspects in the game. In fact, I do not quite understand why this surprises so many people: luck has always been involved in almost all turn based games. Yet what is much more important than raw luck, is logic and time management, and using your resources in the best way possible. Besides, I always felt like I needed skills and tactics to proceed, with each failure I improved at the game and got a bit further, until I eventually beat the chapter that I was stuck on. Each stage plays very different to the last, which is important, because after failing a few times (which you will, trust me), each stage can get pretty repetetive and variety is desperatly needed. Sometimes it feels like you are just fullfilling a bunch of chores, rather than doing some ethical decision making, and the "ethical dlimena" aspect of the game slightly drowns in the mix. I think that this is also the reason that a lot of people are disliking the game: They were expecting a "Telltale Games" type of product (me included, as I should add), yet this game is actually challenging and requires more thinking than people wanted it to. The idea of loosing in a point and click discouraged a lot of people, but I find it very refreshing and something new. Personally, I would like to see more adventures that challenge and put pressure on the player.
Misc. Aspects:
The asthetic works in my opinion, the art style works, but obviously its not something mind blowing. The sounds are very good, the soundtrack is nice but can get a bit repetetive after replaying the same level severall times, the dialogue is well written. At the end of every stage, you get to see your decisions compared to other people's, which is a good addition.
Conclusion:
Overall, I can recommend the game, although it is deffinatly not for everyone. Especially casuals will have a hard time and might rage after the first few failed attempts and give up.

I love Terraria. Starbound is kind of like Terraria, except with Terraria the game itself is highly polished, but limited in its scope of environments. Starbound isn't as highly polished as Terraria, but makes up for it with MASSIVE amounts of content. Not necessarily main quest type content, but the universe in Starbound is so vast that I believe it would be impossible to traverse and explore every world in it. With the added mod support Starbound has it makes the game almost overwhelming. You have to be able to focus on a single task at a time, because there is so much going on to distract from your primary mission.
If you are a builder, then you can build in an insane amount of ways, the circuit system in Starbound is a lot of fun to play with. You can try and make a smart home in ways that I have seen people even make elevators with buttons for each floor of their complexes. The main quest is fun, but semi repetitive. The side quests are again repetitive, but quirky and can be fun to mess around with. The differences in difficulty in different worlds is interesting. Overall I really enjoy Starbound. It is fun, diverse, and if this style of game ever got a AAA release with the refinement, polish, and possibly a dedicated server listing or player finding features, then I would be sold on it all over again.
Cons
- Not the best optimized game and it isn't uncommon to be able to create an environment where your FPS drop. This usually happens to me when I create a small city of NPCs. This happened even before I modded the game, but I play a modded version of it now.
-Some QoL mods that are available through the steam workshop should be a vanilla part of the game.
-Steamworkshop is a nightmare to navigate. No categories or real way of finding specific types of mods, or the up-to-date mods.
Pros
-The game is fun
-Great music
-Even at ~50 hours in the game I probably have only experienced about half of the different types of worlds out there in this massive Starbound universe.
-So much of this game just works.
-The game is apparently easy to mod, and you can find a mod to almost anything if you look hard enough.
-Just derp around and have some fun! It isn't AAA game priced, but can easily eat more hours than a standard AAA game.

The original Binding of Isaac was a good, solid rogue-like; and Rebirth is an improvement in every aspect, perfecting an already great game. Firstly, the visuals in Rebirth are gorgeous, the vividness of colours on certain floors, as well as the number of ambient particles truly make the game astounding to look at, and provide a great environment for the player. The audio is terrific, re-mastering sounds from the original game, as well as adding numerous songs to create an overall epic OST. The various characters are diverse, and relatively balanced, and unlocking them does truly represent the player improving their play and gradually getting better at the game. Enemies are varied, and provide a good challenging slope as you descend further into the dungeon, with unique abilities and behaviors. The previous statement also extends to the bosses, they're diverse, and a player really does need to invest time to perfectly learn their moveset and behavioral patterns to excel in the future. The game runs great, and doesn't require a very beefy computer to reach a nice 60 FPS. Overall, The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is what I'd call the perfect rogue-like, and will definitely serve as an inspiration for future entries into the genre. 10/10

Counter-Strike: Condition Zero is a game that I am quite fond of. Considering that I purchased CS:GO at the same time and played it for almost 2 hours while I have 12 hours on CZ. Can't hate it, and it is quite classic.

Counter Strike: Condition Zero comes with two games:
1. Condition Zero
2. Condition Zero: Deleted Scenes
1. Condition Zero
Basically Counter Strike 1.6 but with improved graphics and the addition of bots. The bots are amazing considering when this game was released (they're still inferior to human players). In addition, the bots are a great way for beginners to learn about the game in a more relaxed environment. There is also a singleplayer Tour of Duty, which is basically regular counter strike missions against bots, but with additional challenges (example: kill 3 enemies with a sniper rifle). Sadly, the Tour of Duty missions are Counter-Terrorist only. There are no Terrorist missions.
2. Condition Zero: Deleted Scenes
This is a singleplayer game. It uses the same weapons and game mechanics as Condition Zero, but with some additions, including the awsome fiber optic camera. Level design is one of Deleted Scenes' greatest strengths. The AI is passable. The story is where it fails, in that each mission is its own self-contained story with practically no connecting elements. I suspect you don't even play as the same person in each mission. Immersion takes a serious hit because of this. It helps to pretend you are playing as the same person. I recommend Adrian Shephard before Black Mesa.
I had a lot of fun playing Condition Zero and Deleted Scenes. I highly recommend these games as well as any other Counter Strike game (or any game by Valve for that matter). By the way, check out the first screenshot on the store page. Really take a close look at the plane...

I am not new to games that require multiple tries and may cause frustration (I'm looking at you, Binding of Isaac, Papers Please). I am not new to games that try to teach you things through long trial and error and difficult decisions (Always Sometimes Monsters, anyone?). I really looked forward to this game as an awesome mesh of possibilities, going down many different paths to many different endings, all based on your moral standing.
That is, sadly, not what I got. Maybe it's just me, but I could not get into the moral portion of this game. For one thing, your decisions don't seem to offer you much of a moral choice. I probably haven't explored the game enough, but the other thing is, there's nothing that makes me really want to. Sure the dark humor is great, and sure the characters are pretty memorable, but they're also kind of...bland. Not really as deep as I had hoped.
And the gameplaay itself. Not the path traveling and searching I had hoped for. More of a trial and error (as above descibed) micromanagement game, which is not bad in and of itself, but really disappointed me. The micromanagement is annoying as heck to get around, and usually requires a few trial and error. The game ends up being very dedication-based; as long as you keep hitting it with your forehead, you'll get to the end, and never mind how many bodies and limbs you have to leave in your path.
Every game I've got, even the ones I ended up not playing very much, even the ones I can't run on my computer because I don't have the graphics card (♥♥♥♥ you, Mortal Kombat), have left me with some sort of satisfaction or resolution. A sort of resignation, even, but at least a satisfied close. Maybe I'm a shopaholic on Steam, but anyways, this game just didn't do it for me. I was left staring at it, wanting something...tangible, damn it. I found myself frustrated, annoyed by the game.
Perhaps I am to blame, but I have never wanted ten dollars back so badly.

I recently bought State of Decay from Steam’s summer sale for around 4€ and I don’t think I’ve ever been happier with a game purchase. I’ve heard/read people saying it’s a good game but didn’t realise it was SO addicting too.
Let’s start by explaining what the whole game is about, without spoilers of course. It’s zombie apocalypse time and you are one of the survivors. You aid other survivors, build a community, search for supplies like food, gas, ammunition and weapons to survive.
You have the freedom to move around the open world how you like, set up a base (home) in various locations, choose what kind of services your base has (medical room, library to study, mechanics to fix cars & gear etc.)
You can build watch tower in your base, order men to practice shooting, extend the safe zone around your map by sniping everyone around your base, train other neighbouring survivors in your camp in exchange of goods.
You can take over empty buildings like gas stations, cafeterias etc. and build outposts there. Outpost have a ‘safe zone’ around them, where zombies will not spawn so it’s a good place to have a breather. Outpost also grant you access to your base supplies, so you can quickly switch weapons and other gear there.
Your base has a radio that helps you keeping in contact with other survivors and NPCs in the world. This is also how you will get most of your quests, distress calls etc. You can contact your base via radio and ask them to track specific supplies for you - or you can just scavenge around and search houses and buildings for everything usefull.
You can load stuff you find in your backbag and in trunk of a car. When you can’t carry more, you can ask base to send runners who will make their way to your location and loot the place. You can wait for the runner and aid him in returning the goods back home, or go your merry way and let them do it without you. They are usually quite handy with their weapons, though it all depends on what gear you are giving to your community.
Sometimes they chew more than they can handle and might end up surrounded by zombies, trapped in house etc. If you like your buddies, you go and help ‘em - or let them struggle alone. If you don’t offer any help, that has an impact in your own reputation within the group. So basically, don’t ♥♥♥♥ around and help your own men. Also helping neighbours and other communities has it’s benefits.
The more people you have living in your base, the more rations they take up per day. The more people you have, the more security you have. The more people you have, the more inner problems you have. People will occasionally get mad at each other, have sleeping problems, fear the outside world. Quite often you can solve these issues - but there’s bound to happen something nasty eventually.
You start the game by controlling one person. After a while you gain more friends and allies and you can then control them too. Once a person is too badly wounded or too tired, you can then switch to another person and keep doing the tasks required to survive, while others rest and keep up the base. (Guard the perimeter, cook food, hunt for supplies, fix broken equipment, manufacture traps, silencers, bullets etc.)
The world inside State of Decay goes on, even when you are offline. The event gradually slow down, the more time you are away from game and in three (3) days the time will be almost at stand still. So, if you have a real life too and log in the game next day, be prepared. Something might have happened to your community while you were away.

This game has quite a lot going for it and after putting in a few days I can say I am relatively impressed. There are a wide variety of features that I find to be quite fulfilling especially in this era where true rts experiences are pretty rare. The MMO aspect of this game makes it appreciatably more fun with a vast variety of repeatable mission that can all be played in 2 person co-op. That being said the game is certainly beggining to show its age and could do with a bit of a modernizing makeover. Also, while its does provide the means to grind out progression a player should expect to spend many months in order to gain a faction based army considering that cards are relatively expensive to acquire. There are some roadblocks to progression that i feel could be reworked in the coming months to make this game much more accessible to a wider gaming audience, which might include a re-thinking about some of the basic faction troop card prices, and a visual update.
Pros-
Deep strategy elements - formations, unit abilities, building capture, and a wide variety of units overall
Base building mechanic- based on real-world building times which allow a player to set it and forget it
Resource gathering- based on using peasents effectively and building new resource gathering structure
Research- Tech tree for giving nation wide bonuses
PVP- 1-4 player pvp standar matches, Tournaments for winning currency to purchase booster packs
PVE- massive set of co-op friendly quests and quest chains for many hours of fun gameplay
Guilds- Joining guilds provides extra resources for new players trying to get on their feet
Cons-
Still too grindy- Expect to spend a good deal of time building infrastructure before purchasing some cool units
Chat- Chat is confined to a single general window which will be unsuffiicient if the game grows beyond a small playerbase
Auction House- Its a bit confusing at first and doesnt really allow a lot of flexibility
Graphics and sound effects- Phew this game was made a long time ago and it shows
Performance- Stange performance issues still arise on certain machine configurations
Honestly, I would love to see this game grow after its hiatus. There really aren't many things out there like it and it still provides a lot of unique ideas 7-8 years after being released. With a little bit of tuning to the free-to-play model I could see this becoming popular once again.

This is a game that I really wanted to play ever since it came out on consoles. I have just finished the game and I can say that it was fun to play. This review will be broken up into several parts
controls: controls can make or break a game. When I started this game the controls were all over the place. The shoot/punch button was start capturing was R3 and other weird crap. Weather the game didn't detect my 360 controller layout or what I don't know. It took me a good hour to configure everything correctly but after that no issues were had. The controls are a bit stiff but that is a small gripe and I think its due to it being an older title and being a hybrid game. The controls weren't bad by any means but they did get in the way several times. The camera was so so most of the time it cooperated but occasionally it did not. Overall the controls weren't too bad but were a weak point in my experience of the product.
Story: About a 7 out of 10 the story had a lot of personality and spunk although the npcs could get a little annoying and the main character was really bland due to his slow speaking drawl. There was the occasional where do I go or what do I do but by process of elimination or asking npcs you found your way quickly enough. It however did lack any suspense. There's quite a few occasions where you can see whats about to happen an hour or two in advance but it doesn't get in the way too much and the stories entertaining enough to keep you entertained.
Voice/sound: Both are done quite well it might be part of the HD remake but everything sounded crisp and nice. There were however npcs that would repeat things like a broken record and during fire fights or another conversation it could annoy the crap out of you. Almost everyone has a voice in this game and even though they all sound the same and say the same thing except for main story line characters the world seems lively.
Visuals: Being and HD remake I didn't expect too much I never played the original game so I had nothing to compare it to however the game looked nice and played smooth there were no draw distance issues and the characters all seemed well represented. However there are still some blocky textures and areas that look very similar to each other but being a game from the early 2ks you should be expecting that much. Overall with the overhaul the game looks and feels good. I did however have to change my resolution from 1440X900 to 1200X900 the game just seemed too stretched out and the visuals washed  when on my full resolution settings.
Gameplay: The meat and potatoes if the game is not fun to play whats the point right? This game even with some challenging controls happens to be a joy to play. Your character stranger doesn't use guns instead uses a crossbow with “Live Ammo” living animals as his weapons. Each one is unique and each one is useful unlike some games where you will use a weapon or gun once and never touch it again this game makes every ammo useful to some degree. There are ammos that you will prefer to another but other than that the mechanic is very well done. You are a bounty hunter and throughout the better half of the game you collect bounties which are basically you doing boss runs. The game is a bit linear in this manner go for a bounty collect it go for another one repeat. However this is not the full story for this game and the gameplay switches up after you collect the last guy. You can collect your bounties one of two ways dead or alive. Dead nets you less reward but is easier alive nets you more but is harder. Some bosses are almost forcing your hand to collect them dead as they will not go down easily. And speaking of that this game is surprisingly challenging. Even on normal I found myself struggling in some areas. There are clear difficulty spikes during boss battles and in some other areas. However this game can still be beaten no matter which way you play and for the most part (spoiler) it doesn't matter in the end how you bag them I had troves of money left and I bought all of the upgrades too and never needed to buy ammo. The game doesn't change (far as I know) depending on how you play the game. Overall the game is fun to play with very few flaws.
This game was fun to play and I suggest it to anyone who thinks they might like this game!

I was interested in this game for a long time, and was surprised to see it on Steam. I was immediately turned off by the boost pack system, but at least now, they promise more units will become available for gold.
That is the issue now. When you start the game, gold is incredibly tedious to farm. The starting units they give you don't particularly excell at anything, other than the Light Human Cavalry, which will swiftly become your staple, "anti-d00dz" unit, and the Covered Ram, which is only good for destroying buildings or capturing defensive structures.
Your choices for farming are very limited, as quests will become more difficult the second and third time you play them, and there is no way to decrease the difficulty. Even if you amass what seems like a decent starting sum of resources, the game wants you to make a thousand, tiny f***ing houses for your constant stream of peasants, or bad things may or may not happen. Each house houses five peasants, and there is absolutely no upgrade for them, or better option. You finally get enough gold to buy your first "F2P" unit. Nice! You now have a troop of 1/1 of that unit. Yes, you actually need 24 more just to rival your freebie h00minz.
So assuming you're farming the Lv.4 quest, "Treasure Valley," which gives on average 235-250 Gold per run on gold difficulty, and you need ~50,000 Gold to get one troop of your MOST BASIC units of your faction, you'll be at it a while. The difficulty curve is extreme, to the point of some, to most quests being totally impossible with your starter units, solo.  Cruel tricks occur all the time, where you try to be agressive, or even defensive, when suddenly, a dragon! You lose. Too bad. Hope you had your units flee before they died, or you'll have to pay an unknowable amount of gold to ressurect them. (Is it PER unit, or per squad? I have no idea.)
Even if you were to sink some money into this game, the way card packs work, you're only guaranteed rares and some uncommons of your faction. This means to even start from commons, you could potentially pay $1,000 and never get a full squad; you'll have to trade for them. Even if you were able to solo most of the quests, there is no hope toward progression; the university (your "tech upgrade" building) offers nothing of real importance or interest, at least to me. Some resource accrual rate boosts, defensive upgrades, faster bulding/repairing. Really, you'd just go for gold, because the standard 5 peasants per mine is literally not worth it, as you would get well less than 100 gold per day, at some arbitrary time. The whole point of the game is getting gold, to buy units that are not necessarily better, but different.
If I could compare this game to any other, I would compare it to the late BattleForge. There is a F2P aspect, you do buy card packs, and you lead an army that appears out of nowhere to capture and wreck stuff. That's where it ends. In BattleForge, you could buy any card on the auction house with your daily premium currency rewards, whereas no one would EVER want to sell any cards for any F2P currency in SAGA. It just makes no sense to move premium value to F2P. In BattleForge, it was fun to create decks, and use strategies (especially really bad ones) to "grind" quests for their rewards. Jumping into random 4-player adventures was fun and entertaining every time. In SAGA, even doing the same quest of the exact same difficulty with the exact same units and strategies, you might fail miserably, for no clearly visible reason. There is no incentive to farm anything for me, and thus, none to play the game.
Bear in mind, I scoured the internet for guides on how to start off as a F2P player. Problem is? The name. Google does not do case-sensitive searches, and "SAGA" becomes, well, LITERALLY every single "Saga" game there is. Candy Crush, Eternal and Romancing (I love those games though), Eternal, Banner, F***boyYOLOSwaggitySwagLookAtMeIDesignedAFlashGameForTheInternet. All of it. They even wiped the forums due to failure to defend against spam. You'll have to ask people in-game how to do things, and with some redesigns between its original release and wherever it is now, some things are just unknowable. Maybe as they work on the game in a modern market, they'll adress some of these issues, but ultimately, this game can't change very much, or it would have long ago.
TL;DR: "What am I even doing right now?"
Longer TL;DR: "How can I exploit this game's mechanics to get any form of advantage I possibly can to have fun?" Nobody knows. Possibly impossible.
If you noticed my grammar is atrocious in this review, it's because I'm profoundly nonplussed.
