The Great Wobo Escape:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

We must be desperate for resources lately.  We have created an automated mining factory in space for goodness sake, where cute, little white robots are mining. How do we know they are mining the right stuff for us? No-one knows really. All we‘ve been told is that there are big, red robots with zapping devices that supervise the colony. What do we call them? Oh yes, the watchers. Well, everything was peachy until one of these robots, named Wobo, decided to make a run for freedom.
The Great Wobo Escape is a side-scrolling adventure game combined with a touch of stealth where you control a white robot named Wobo.
The game offers eight stages and three levels: Normal (where you can save your progress by using scanners along the way), Hardcore (you can’t save your progress at all; if you die, you’ll spawn back to the start of the stage), and Time trial (in this mode of difficulty, you must finish the stage by a specific time).
The first stage is really a tutorial and will show you how to control Wobo either by using your keyboard or gamepad. One of the aspects I really like about this game is that anyone of any age can play it due to the fact that there is no violence at all. It is simple and fun to play. Nonetheless, you need to be careful not to be caught by these big, red robots with electric shock guns. If you are caught, Wobo will be zapped into pieces. As you progress through the game, you will notice faint images of Wobo in between structures here and there. There are locations where your robot can hide and avoid these nasty red robots. You also have obstacles to worry about, such as pressure smoke coming out of pipes, damaged electric cables, moving platforms and more. There are levers and terminals to activate which can open doors to new areas as well as cutting off the electricity and pressure in pipes, which will resolve the issue with the pressure smoke. You also have to free other woblings (small robots) within each of the stages and you’ll be rewarded with extra points at the end of each level.
You also have puzzles or mini games to complete; they are pretty obvious and give this game a bit more to its overall content.
Graphically, the game looks very good and runs well. In terms of the controls they are responsive, whether you’re using the keyboard or the gamepad. It terms of the length of the game, you’ll be finishing your first walkthrough in about two and a half hours on the normal difficulty. The Great Wobo Escape side-scrolling casual game with light stealth elements, its a game that feels aimed at a younger gamer.
You can find a about 15 minutes of gameplay with commentary here:

You play as Wobo - a newly made robot on a remote mining station, a station controlled by robots. Your goal is to escape the station, as Wobo soon learns that staying will result in his destruction. The story is light, but there are 2 cut scenes that try to explain why Wobo and the station exists.
Movement is left and right on the controller or keyboard, with a jump, an interact button and a sneak. Game mechanics are clearly explained by billboards when something new is encountered. It is not an overly technical game though, which lends it towards a younger gamer or someone who has no (or very little) experience with side scrolling or platform gaming.
The game involves no overt violence, when Wobo is captured or falls from a height, his arms, legs and head pop off and the game reloads from the last save point. This is another thing that I feel makes it a good game for a younger gamer, there was nothing in the game that would make me not want to let my own children have a turn.
There are 3 difficulty levels, an Easy level when you can use the MANY save points littered throughout a stage. A Hardcore setting that puts you back to the start of a stage if you die and a Time Attack mode where you can try to beat a defined counter per stage. All stages have the optional mission of saving other robots - "Woblings" - which provide a points bonus to your score.
Game length will vary depending on your own abilities, but on the hardcore mode it took me about 2 hours to complete the 8 stages. The price is about right with the current discount and am happy to recommend it, I feel a younger gamer will get a lot of value from this title.

Background: I've played Starbound since early access (around 2013). I've seen my fair share of updates that I've liked and disliked. I stopped playing early access after Upbeat Giraffe, simply because I lost interest. Coming back to 1.0, I can say I'm really impressed with how the game was changed.
What I liked:
-Planet exploration is really fun. The way they divide up the difficulties is also really cool (unlike the sectors in the early beta).
-The different planet types are also really cool to explore. My personal favorites are the volcanic planets, midnight planets, and ocean planets.
-I like most of the changes to combat. Secondary abilities to weapons are very useful and have saved my life plenty of times.
-They removed the massive difficulty spikes. Back then, if you found a weapon that was super powerful on one planet, it would be useless on another because it was in a different sector or something. Now, I don't feel like I have to throw away my weapons on a new planet.
What I didn't like:
-I know I just talked about the combat, but it goes both ways for me. What I don't like about the combat is how the enemies can just consistantly do damage to you by touching you. This made it so that 3+ enemies would corner♥♥♥♥♥♥you and you would die practically instantly. I remember they removed this feature in the beta, but it seems they brought it back for the final release.
-Finding guns seems too easy. I remember in the beta when finding a gun was a challenge, but it was rewarding. Now, they're giving it out left and right. I know finding some guns are harder than others, but if I could find 3 rocket launchers ON THE SAME PLANET, you have a bit of a problem.
Story: A lot of people complain about the story. But TBH, I didn't mind it. The story isn't a big part of the game so its not like it "ruined" Starbound as many people would say. Does the game force you to do the story...kinda. But it's really just the first two missions which could be done in 15 minutes. Bottom line, I thought it was okay.
Final rating (TL;DR) 8/10: For the most part, I love this game. I agree with most of the changes, though some could either be tweaked are reverted. One more thing, for maximum enjoyment, have your friends all download the same mods and play together. It makes the experience that more enjoyable.

I see a lot of people complaining about the lack of moral choices in the game. These are my two cents about this issue.
First of all, I'll have to say that I backed Gods will Be Watching campaing on Indiegogo, and I did it after playing the web browser demo Deconstructeam developed for Ludum Dare. I really fell in love with the game. Loved the art style, the atmosphere, and the combination of resource management and moral choices (not in narrative terms, as the Telltalle interactive dramas, but in terms of survival simulation).
And last but not least, I really enjoyed how DIFFICULT it was.
What was I expecting of the complete game? More or less, the same interactive experience I really enjoyed in the Ludum Dare version.
What I wasn't expecting? A deep, intrincate narrative experience, full of plot-twists, dialogs, and Renegade/Paragon choices. And, honestly, I've would've been dissapointed if they had changed the game I backed into some sort of interactive drama. Don't get me wrong, I love Telltalle Games, but this is not what GWBW is.
Survival Simulation + Resource Management + Sci-fi + Opressive atmosphere + Retro pixel art = Gods Will Be Watching. And I knew it beforehand because, as I've said before, I played the Ludum Dare version months ago. I liked it. I backed it. I wanted to see GBWB become a full game. And after a few hours playing, that's what I've got.
I know that the trailer might lead to make people believe this game is an interactive drama, but it really amazes me that nowadays someone would buy a game just for what he/she sees in a trailer. Even more if there's a demo to try the game and see if you like it or not.
My advice? Go here:
. Play it. You liked it? Buy the game, it won't dissapoint you.
I really think the work of Deconstructeam speaks for itself.

The port is trash. Thankfully, the PC community stepped up and fixed the game. Ive been using DSfix from the start, but I was always afraid to unlock 60fps because of glitches it can cause. I decided to give it a go recently, just to see what it felt like. As soon as the game loaded, I almost cried; the improvement was obvious. Its hard to describe, but its not just smoother; it also drastically changes the way the game looks. Ive not seen such a massive difference in other games when comparing 30 and 60fps. As soon as I beheld the holy land, I knew there was no going back; I was gonna have to live with the side effects.
Tested over 80 hours and numerous playthroughs: Im happy to report that I had no major issues with 60fps. I slid down every ladder, never fell through the world, and I never got stuck at a bonfire. Should it happen to you, both of those glitches can be fixed by reloading the game. Weapons do degrade faster, but durability is so high in DS1 that it doesnt matter. At 30fps you might never need to repair your weapons. At 60fps youll need to repair a couple times; no big deal. 60fps does affect jump distance, but I didnt have any issues.
One serious thing I ran across was difficulty walking up slopes. At 60fps you can end up hitting invisible walls on certain slopes. Sometimes, you can take a couple steps back, and it wont be there when you go forward again. Other times, that wont help at all, and youll need to switch to 30fps. Thankfully, you can do that with a simple press of a button; the default key in DSfix is Backspace. Tip: switch to 30fps for The Great Hollow.
If your PC can handle it: be sure to get the HD texture pack mod and sweetfx. They make the game look nearly as good  as DS3. Both can be found at
Beyond that, theres not much I can say that hasnt been said already. I dont think DS1 is old enough to call a timeless classic, but it will eventually be regarded as such. This is a top 3 all-time game for me.
Buy it, mod/fix it, and love it forever.

I'm here to briefly (and straight to the point) tell you about the quality of the Remaster itself. Spoiler-free.
The entire game is one huge eyecandy, every background has been re-rendered, they're at way more higher resolution and do not have obvious compression artifacts. Moving parts of the backgrounds, lighting, shadows, item icons, some 3D objects and bloom were drastically improved along with some character model and font tweaks. The only semi-original things that are left in are the FMV cutscenes which were also cropped accordingly. Just like in RE1HD you can rebind KB&M controls to your liking (with the exception of mouse, it seems, as it's used for aiming and shooting by default).
The game itself is mostly left unchanged, but it has a couple of extra bonuses added like the Wesker mode where you use RE5 Wesker's special abilities to battle BOWs. This mode is unlocked when you finish the game at least once. There are also extra purchasable DLC costumes if you're into that sorta thing. Worth mentioning that this game supports achievements some of which are rather creative.
As for port itself it's the superior version among the platforms offering you variable framerate refresh rate, 4K resolution, but for whatever reason lacks DoF (blur in distance) which is currently present on PS4. For some with weak/machines with compatibility issues the game might run in slow motion (if you had this issue with RE4UHD, RE1HD then you'll likely have it here). Also currently there's bug with doors stuttering a bit when opened, likely a cache issue (not present on newer graphics cards).
If you care about Survival Horror in this industry and/or oldschool RE then you should pick this up.
Let me know in the comments if I missed something or something needs a correction.

Until the day of writing this, Resident Evil: 0 was the one Resident Evil title I'd never played. After delving into this blind, I can safely give off several first impressions. To preface this, however, if you love survival horror or the Resident Evil series, then buy this right away. That said, to add more incentive here are the following pros:
+Better item management than the entire series. This game does away with item boxes and allows you to leave items in a location, handily marked on your map, and retrieve it at any time. There's also your partner's inventory, which you can trade items with back and forth at your leisure.
+Bosses. Within the first ten minutes the game will have thrown its first boss at you. My opponent was a giant scorpion made of leeches, and due to my blind foray into the game, I had no weapons on me. What followed was a breathtaking, heart-pumping fight for survival where my knife held me through adversity. A feeling I haven't felt since the original 2002 release of last year's Resident Evil: REmake.
+Characters. Billy Coen, hands down is the best male protagonist in the Resident Evil series. His past a mystery, the true nature of his placement as a prisoner on the ecliptic express reveals a backstory of melancholy and betrayal. Capcom nailed it with his motivations, and his portrayal. Rebecca is a much loved character from Resident Evil 1, and if you loved her in that, her stepping into the spotlight in this game will satisfy you.
+Enemy design. With a much more diverse sideshow of enemies to battle and run from than its predecessor game, Zero offfers an abundance of grisly and challenging foes that are sure to plague your nightmares. Giant scorpions, leech men, to the cerberus that's become iconic in itself. Each room offers a challenge and an opportunity to encounter only the most fearsome of Umbrella's dark experiments.
+Controls. The initial control system was rather iffy, but only because it was different to REmake. To my joy, there are three control configurations as well as the default, and control type D plays just like last year's REmake remaster. This game has done away with tank controls, and it feels good.
+Set pieces. Can't go into detail much, but if you ever thought you wouldn't have a countdown to an explosion early into an RE game, this game changes everything.
Cons:
- Same audio as the original release: It's quite jarring that in such a pretty, upscaled and retouched environment the sounds are still as weathered and old as the game's age itself. This is particularly telling in monster cutscenes, where a door being smacked off of its hinges sounds like several boxes falling off of a shelf.
- Cutscenes haven't been remade. Due to their FMV nature, it's understandable they couldn't be edited. That said, Capcom could at least have upscaled them from 4:3 to 16:9/10 for the sake of visual consistency. Seeing two black boxes at the sides is quite the immersion killer.
Overall, this game gets a 9/10 from me. It's almost as good as REmake, although I will forever maintain that REmake and Resident Evil 3 are the kings of the series. If you're hungry for more Resident Evil, or want a particularly challenging horror game with mechanics ahead of its time, then this is for you.

After I finished my first playthrough ever of this game (Never played RE0 on GCN), I think it's time for a review.
This is a great game, I'm a long time Resident Evil fan and this game didn't disappoint me at all. While I think it did most things really well, there were some others that I didn't like as much, but I'll get to that later.
Let's start off with the technical stuff. Oh man, this game is a wonderful remaster. The graphics are unbelieveable good, considering that this is originally a game from 2002. The backgrounds, although pre-rendered, have never been so dynamic, it's often hard to distinguish between pre-rendered and actual rendered models because they are both so detailed, pre-rendered backgrounds have never looked so good.
Force Feedback/Controller vibration is also a thing, even during the cutscenes, and it underlines some intense moments very well.
The controls also received an overhaul. In my review of the HD REmaster I complained about the new control scheme, feeling out of place by making character movement look unnatural and that you need to adjust your stick when the camera changes. While the latter problem presists, the movement feels much more natural now. Definitely an improvement.
You can now also set the refresh rate to up to 144 Hz, while the HD REmaster only allowed 60 Hz.
Next up is the game itself. The gameplay is solid, it might feel strange controlling 2 characters at first, but you'll get used to it. You can switch between the characters almost anytime, and they both have different strenghts and weaknesses.
A weaker point of the game is, in my opinion, the plot. While I love the RE storyline, this one had a few elements that I didn't like. Don't get me wrong, I know Resident Evil isn't know for it's perfect writing, but this one seemed a bit weaker compared to the other games. First off, Marcus in his young/leech/whatever form. The way he looks is just ridiculous, and that chorus like singing...just no. Another point I didn't like so much was Billy's backstory. The guerilla village thing just seemed too forced and didn't fit into the story at all. The message "war is bad" dosen't fit into Resident Evil, we have other game series like Metal Gear for that.
Where this game really shines is level design. It's so good I could talk about it the whole day, but I'll try to keep it short.
First off is are the settings. The train is awesome, the atmosphere of it driving during rain, all the moving objects on the tables...just perfect. The training facility is probably the longest part of the game. One might say it's basically a cheap version of the mansion from RE1, but I would have to disagree. My favoriten part however is the factory. In this part you are seperated from Billy, so you are alone and can only play as Rebecca. Here you will revisit some places from Resident Evil 2, and I would have to lie to say that it didn't make me feel a bit nostalgic.
Then there are also the treatment facility and laboratory, which also have great level design. The way you have to interact with your partner over different rooms is just amazingly thought through, no argument there.
+amazing level design and atmosphere
+slow paced gameplay, with an overall good character switch system
+excellent soundtrack
-plot has it's weakpoints
While this REmaster is better from a technical standpoint, I just prefer the core game of the remake/first REmaster.

Overall, the game is fun, but largely incomplete and buggy (as to be expected from a game still under development). By buggy, I mean you really have to make the habit of saving every few minutes otherwise your game will eventually freeze up (often when opening up menus or using steam in-game).
It doesn't really feel challenging enough to fall under a "Survival" category, especially since all you need to do to survive is find food, of which there are plenty of fish to catch. Maybe I haven't played it long enough, but it is hard to do so, seeing as my game crashes or freezes regularly. I found it more fun screwing around doing things like building or making a mountain out of sticks. It is strangely satisfying.
Building is a whole lot of fun. It's a shame that a lot of the times I can't place things down where I want even when it seems like nothing is blocking the way (e.g sometimes can't place down a foundation next to another foundation).
Exploring seems to be quite tedious. I'm not bored of it yet, but it feels like Wind Waker v2; a whole lot of rowing in one direction.
Since the islands are bigger now, I think it's a good idea to implement new island features, like maybe ancient ruins or abandoned island villages. There needs to be more land threats/features if it is to be much of a survival game. Also, something really has to be done about inventory management... seems to be a problem with a lot of games nowadays. I come home with an inventory full of sticks and it turns out I can only build about 6 wood platforms..
There are other nitpicky issues I have with the game, but mostly are insignificant, seeing as this game is in alpha. I hope the developers are able to continue seeing which direction the game should go and what mechanics should take place to really polish up the game.

Ever since I got this game it has swallowed my life up.
There's so much content it's ridiculous, tons of items to unlock and mess around with, a bunch of characters all suited to differing playstyles, many different floor layouts, and lots of fun and creative bosses.
This game doesn't get stale after a few hours, you can play it for days and days and weeks and weeks and never get tired of it because every run is different. You can combine items to create amazing synergies. For example, you can combine the Tech X upgrade, which replaces your attack with a charge-up laser ring, and the Brimstone upgrade, which replaces your attack with a charge-up giant laser beam of death to create giant laser Brimstone rings of death. Or the combination of Dr. Fetus (bomb shots), Pyromaniac (explosion immunity) and Mutant Spider (quad shot) which allows you to shoot four bombs in one shot at enemies without taking any damage from your own explosions.
It also has an amazing dynamic soundtrack, this means that the music gets more intense depending on how many enemies are in a room. For example, the Flooded Caves theme is a slow, atmospheric song. But if you enter a room with a lot of powerful enemies, an awesome guitar solo kicks in which really gets you pumped.

And if there isn't enough content for you, you can mod the game easily with the Steam Workshop for many creative community-made items.

I haven't played tons of VNs, but I've enjoyed the few I have played, and so it's nice to see some leaking into major English markets like Steam. The biggest issues with getting quality VNs put up is that most of them are Eroge (which is to say adult only) games, followed with the issue that the VN genre is rather wide, ranging from literally a book you make minor decisions in, to lots of gameplay coupled with long visual still scenes and text. LLTQ pulls off a nice balace of gameplay and story text, with a fun pace that won't bore you. This makes it a great entry level game of you are new to the VN genre and want to see what it can offer.
LLTQ is not very long for the price tag, and the art isn't anything amazing (in fact it comes off as rather generic). However, LLTQ makes up for this with interesting gameplay and plenty of replayability. Half the fun of this game is taking different paths and trying new things to see how it ends up for Princess Elodie, and the game pulls this off with a lot of grace. While not a strict VN, the game doesn't have much action. If you're looking for something akin to Kamidori or Sengoku Rance, you're barking up the wrong tree. However, if you enjoy VNs in general and like some quirky and strategy based gameplay tossed in, LLTQ should make you a happy camper.

Oddworld: Stranger's Whrath HD is a first/third person game. You are a bounty hunter who works his way up from capturing and turning in wanted criminals for Moolah. You play a character simply called Stranger who uses like ammo to trap his enemies which is the only way you can turn them in.

It's worth noting Saga is an old MMORTS that originally used a hybrid pay to win concept by allowing you to buy and scan physical cards to unlock new units. These boosters are now wholly virtual, though in theory an old phys booster may still work. The only mechanic to get boosters for free is through the tournament system using random assortments of units. It's semi balanced but it's always possible to get hard countered to all hell.
1. The graphics have not aged well, they were already old fashioned on release but now you could look at any other RTS and have a prettier thing to look at. If you can look past this great, but it's hard imagining spending money on a game when you can just buy a better looking one on steam
2. Behold a Total War ripoff that makes no effort to act like a total war ripoff. Your units are made up of up to 35 cards of the same type, depending on type. Units have absolutely no weight to them, happily pass through enemy units, and be kited easily. Unit's don't engage, they get as close as they can and start attacking. So if you are focusing on one unit the enemy can pull the unit back so that your units just chase them (Kiting) where this would never happen in any other game in this genre; likewise there are no wargame systems like flanking or such going on. All fighting is on a 1v1 basis that makes no goddamn sense. You CANNOT go into this game expecting a tactical wargame, you'll just get dissapointed. Even that Fantasy War battles thing had more realistic unit fighting, and that game also suffered from overpowered micro.
3. Units are gained through the market or boosters. Boosters must be gained from tournaments or money, and the amount of gold needed to buy from the market makes it impossible to get any units until you already have enough units to progress, You are caught in a catch 22 where you can't progress without new units but you need to progress heavily in order to start being able to afford units. Thus you have to play tournaments, which can take hours to complete for no real payoff. You will frequently run into a longtime player that cheats you by playing the game like a starcraftian RTS where there's no real skill involved besides micromanaging (Which some argue is a talent, but I really don't agree.) Even when you get the points to buy a booster there is no real chance of being able to field a unit since each unit is made up of several cards. The exception being the few and far between solo units
4. Base building falls into the same Catch-22 as above. Resources are most plentiful through fighting, and after awhile you won't have a good enough army to fight for resources until you get a few boosters. The game won't tell you but it's wise to build as many lumber mills as you can and man them, coming back each day to do a few more fights until you can start building other structures. The resource gathering rate is pitiful, you only get a few hundred per day when you can easily get a few hundred from each fight.
Most of these problems could be fixed by simply devoting time and effort into development and balancing. But having played in a few alphas for these developers I know that time and effort is the last thing they are going to invest in. Balacing the resource rates, making it possible to field your factions units without spending a week grinding tournaments , and fixing the weightless combat system are just the tip of the iceburg. What Saga really needs is to die and become Saga 2 with a new engine and motivated dev team.

Night in the Woods isn't exactly what I expected, yet fights it's way back with unique style, shockingly relatable writing and good execution.
You might stumble upon the title name Aquaria when searching about NiTW or one of the creators: Alec Holowka. His previous work, released nearly ten years ago is a precious favorite of mine, which I hold dearly near my gaming heart. This alone made my initial Kickstarter impressions gone skyrocket, but fortunately I managed to go into the game with the open mind, toning my expectations down a bit before release.
Game suprised me that it ultimately ended up as 3/4th a friend-hanging-out simulator and only 1/4th atmospheric, paranormal story. Emphasis of the game is mostly centered on the main character, her small circle of friends and the forgotten by the world town they live in. Game is separated into acts and those are further divided in game "days" where you explore the neighborhood, talk to townsfolk and finally decide on the main activity for the day. Parties, preparing dinner, petty crimes or garage band training sessions... those are mostly used to drive various characters with their own story arcs. Interactions between protagonist and her friends are varied, interesting and often times touching difficult subjects what young people may face. While this focus comes with the sacrifice that will be mentioned later, I was really impressed with the work done here to flesh out characters and their interactions in the surprisingly realistic way. While I couldn't relate to all of the story presented, at several points in the game dialogue went so deep in the "so true" territory that it felt uncanny. This is undoubtedly a one of the game's strongest points, even if I didn't expect game to be as much pushed in the this, seemingly "mundane" direction.
Unfortunately, as I said before, game suffers a little bit because of this aim and makes the paranormal sections feel a bit forgotten or not developed enough for my liking. People tend to criticize the last act of the game because it abruptly switches gears to the spooky mode on the whim. In my opinion, people are barking at the wrong tree, because that last act is incredible with its tense action and atmosphere. I just couldn't move my eyes away from the game until it was done. The problem is that this sudden shift would work better with the bigger build-up and game lacks it in the earlier chapters. While living day-by-day is a unique concept, it would definitely benefit from more frequent breaks for the spooks than it was ultimately delivered. Both aspects of the game would seem as stronger by this.
I won't write too much about the gameplay mechanics, because they don't contribute that much and are made at decently enough only to warrant a passing mention. You have a bit of platforming, which is fine, some easy puzzles and nothing much else. It's a bare minimum, but fortunately it isn't that much noticeable when dialogue takes the main role. More mechanics would be nice, but they are not necessary.
While I praised the writing, I need to point out that there are points, where it becomes too "hip" for its own good and ends out as condescending or pretentious instead of clever and touching. Game art, backgrounds, characters and places are also generally amazing, but there are some noticeable blind spots that look not as great as the rest of the game. As for music, I can say that I would struggle to find a fault in it, even if somebody would hold me on the gunpoint. Soundtrack is the place where you can hear most of the Aquaria's influences and I thank greatly for that. I won't however forget about the load times that are atrocious for the reasonably simple game. They were really close to break the immersion of the game.
While ultimately NiTW isn't as wallbreakingingly great as Aquaria was, it's still an excellent title for those interested in narrative games with surprisingly human stories that ring familliar tune to young adults looking for their place in the world. I can recommend it on the uniqueness lone, since I would struggle to find the game with similar artstyle, story and gameplay structure. While I wouldn't scream
at top of my lungs, I still consider Night in the Woods as enjoyable time spent worth the money and multiple playthoughs, which are pretty much required to see it all.

Trailers are typically the most effective way to convey to gamers how this game looks, feels and what kind of actions you as a gamer will be able to undertake.
The trailer was my sole reason to buy this game. Once playing this game however, I find it is not heavily based on story or choice but resource management. Resource management is not the same thing as story based based moral choices.

A fascinating idea ruined by tedious micromanaging. What interesting moral dilemmas the player might face are rendered insignificant by gameplay mechanics that rely too hard on percent chance and the "Game Over, try again?" screen. The extreme difficulty and lengthy dialogue clash awkwardly: You'll have to repeat "levels" over and over again, meaning you'll have to read the same dialogue over and over again. This repetition lessens whatever effect the situations may have on you, and forces you to focus instead on micromanaging character statuses. This undermines the moral dilemmas the game tries to put the player in, forcing them to rewatch the same grisly violence over and over again and rendering its effect meaningless.
For a game that relies so heavily on character statuses, it does a poor job of informing the player of those statuses. Art can be vague, and characters don't react consistently. This would be fine if the game's failstates didn't rely so heavily on the actions of these characters.
Not fun. Not effective. Not recommended.

I was very excited when I first saw the gameplay trailer for Gods Will Be Watching. It looked like someone took all those extreme "would-you-rather" or "what-if" nightmare scenarios that friends sometimes play and mashed it with the heavy moral weight ala Telltale's The Walking Dead. What will you do to survive? Will you sacrifice your humanity?
Sadly, this all falls flat in the execution. First off, this game is VERY difficult (which is not necessarily a bad thing). However, each  failure feels like a punishment as the game makes you start over from the very beginning of the chapter. This would not be an issue if each chapter weren't so long (it tooke me at least an hour and a half to complete the first chapter). Adding to this, the options available to you for each scenario is fairly limited. Add that to the frequent deaths going back to square one and each chapter can feel like a real drag. Whereas The Walking Dead made each decision have a real weight to it that would really affect your environment, this game makes each decision feel significantly less important. This is due to the fact that after a while you start to realize that you are going to be repeating that same decision every time you have to restart the chapter. The final episode of Telltale's the Walking Dead would have had a lot less emotional punch if you kept on having to
Finally, it seems as though every scenario has a very narrow set of sequential actions that will allow you to move on to the next chapter. This results in each chapter feeling more like a guessing game rather than an actual scenario where each decision feels wholly your own. Ultimately, this was what really drove my decison to give this game a thumbs down. Stick with  Telltale's the Walking Dead if you want a game with weighty moral dilemmas.

Gods Will Be Watching is an interesting concept for an adventure game marred heavily by some really dumb design decisions.
The premise is you are Sgt. Burden (no♥♥♥♥♥♥, leader of men in a bleak far future where you have to make tough utilitarian choices to survive. Beyond this interesting idea though there isn't a whole lot worth paying for.
The game is too difficult in the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t of manners. At the outset you have a choice between "easy" or "original" difficulties, with original being devoid of any hints or help and said to be how the devs want you to play. I chose original because I enjoy challenging games, but this is another level. For a game that consists of fairly long scenarios where you are sent back to the start if you die, far too many outcomes are based on chance. For example, the 2nd scenario you have to survive torture for several days and one method used on you is Russian Roulette. I had gotten to this part before, had a plan and went to execute it, however on my second turn I got my head blown off because there was a 1 in 6 chance of it happenening. At this point I looked to the sky and said "Thank you Jesus for bestowing me with these hard-hitting, quality independently developed games". This wouldn't be such a big deal if it wasn't for the fact you have to run through scenarios several times till you know what is happening.
The torture scenario, again, I had to play several times till I eventually had no choice but to write down the order torture methods were used in order to succeed. It was actually clever and there was logic to it but it didn't become apparent until over an hour or so of experimenting and dealing with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t RNG deaths, which made the cleverness substantially less impressive. The manner in which you have to repeat these scenarios is also detrimental to the game's core theme. Any tension that exists as part of making these choices is dulled by frustration and rigmorale. You get to a point where you don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥how many puppies you have to kick, you just want to see the next screen. Considering this was "playing the game the way the developer intended", I wonder if they played it themselves because it is not enjoyable.
In general the game could use more polish. There's plenty of typos and graphical errors like sprites shooting 180 degrees behind them without turning around. Speaking of graphics, the backgrounds look great but the character sprites and animations could use more effort. In a game where caring about the characters is a big deal, maybe giving them actual faces would have helped. This could be more of a personal gripe though because I think games that do this (Superbrothers etc.) are downright ♥♥♥♥ing lazy. All that time spent on background and yet no one could be bothered to draw just two dots and a line on some faces. Some people will say this is "minimalism" as the game was a Ludum Dare game with that very theme, but you could ask someone to make a Ludum Dare game about cheeses at this point and they will just make whatever the ♥♥♥♥ they want and relate it back somehow.
Overall, super disappointing. Do not buy for less than five bucks.
EDIT: I do have to give this game credit though for having consequences that carry over between scenarios and actually have an impact on your situation. In that sense it's better than what Telltale has been doing. Just a shame it's so damn frustrating.

Okay so I've played through for almost an hour and a half. It's really really cool. The game is reeeally intense and unforgiving.
Initially I was overwhelmed by what was going on in the first situation and to really get an idea of what to do. And like they warn you when you choose regular difficulty, I failed a lot! You would think this would become frustrating. But it hasn’t it just made the more nerveracking.  Playing this game is like navigating a minefield, making one wrong step means disaster. One too many mistakes at any point spells complete failure, in some situations I found that you can only afford a single error and that you're dead if your ♥♥♥♥ up again. Decisions that mean the difference between life and death and just success or failure in making it to the next decision are relentless. Not only that, you also must pay attention to multiple situations in a given scenario, you can't neglect any of them. It's delicate balancing act. I can barely comprehend success in this game being possible on regular difficulty. After failing the first chapter at least 5 times or so I went back and put it on easy and made it to the second situation. Even on easy difficulty I was having a hard time not repeatedly failing and having to start the chapter again from the start. After a few attempts I made it to like the third day and was stunned to be told I need to keep my characters who are undergoing torture alive without giving away too much intelligence for 20 days! I made it to the part where the protagonist is strapped to the torture wall. But I pushed it just one little bit too far and he was instantly dismembered.
The game looks very good. The sound and music is well done. The suspense, horror and the brutality of the situations is conveyed really well. The developers weren't afraid to illustrate extreme brutality. For instance a hot iron shoved into your character crotch. You will be in contant fear of some really nasty things happening to your characters and bad situation going beyond critical. I grimaced when my character was taking a hammer to the knee and I gasped when he was suddenly ripped in half. I haven't gotten to the part where you have characters sitting around in the wilderness eating steaks. But I have a bad feeling about where that meat comes from!
So, yes I recommend this game. Initially intitially I had a feeling that because there are only 6 chapter it would be short title. I haven't completed it yet. But just getting to end of a chapter is long and arduous. I'm pretty sure the challenge can keep you occupied for quite some time and it's really exciting to play pretty much the whole time.

A very tentative recommendation. Do not play if:
- You are heavily discouraged by poor unit balance
- The stupid physical immunes from Disciples II were your bane
- You expect the enemy AI to actually do anything on the overworld map
- You expect experience proportionate to challenge
- You expect the highest point in the challenge curve to be late-game rather than right at the beginning
That last point is the real issue. Early-game heroes are weak as day-old kittens - no more being the equivalent of a tier 2 from the start! - and the neutral units seem heavily biased toward a fast hero with high accuracy. Meanwhile, at the end of a campaign you'll stomp through the highest tier enemies like they weren't even there. Which is very cathartic.
All of the elements of a good Disciples game are here - the gothic setting, the glorious art, the sudden but inevitable betrayals. I'd say it's worth playing for those times when the balance sits just right.

Now, Ive played this game A LOT. At the time of writing this it's 260 hours. I've played this game sense the closed alpha, and I can say i'm not dissipointed in how this game has changed over the years. Let's start from the beginning.
Closed Alpha:
The base content we all know was in the game, and there were 2 tiers of planets in the first (and only) sector: Forest(Lush) and Desert. Food was in the game via a bar in the top right screen, and temperature was a mechanic. standing near a fire gave you heat, while standing in water cooled you down. I recall clothes gave you warmth. There was no weather, and ships used wood for fuel. The only structure I ever found was an very early avian village and some gear trap. Oh, and one handed weapons were actually viable.
Beta:
It's hard to list the beta in one review because of how long it went on. From early 2012 to mid 2016, the amount of content added was immense. Food and tempurature were replaced with a new mechanic, Protection Packs. There was a weapon overhaul, moons were added, and there were 10 sectors. One of the biggest changes was the "Space stations" a new feature that was a big city on a ship in the brand new astroid biome.  This changed into the outpost that we know today. You accessed it by going to a monolith which is where you open vaults today. Novakids were added from their kickstarter stretch goal. Quests were added and were very different. The erchious mining facility stayed pretty simular as it is today, though it was much more challenging than now. The floran temple was actually a floran ambush, and there was no nuru. Dreadwing and shockhopper were fought on planets, then moved to quests given by a penguin. Pets were added, farming was completely redone, they added nanotechs and replaced Protection packs, planets were removed from sectors in favor of a new solar system ideolagy, lore was added and then... progress stopped. A few bug fixes were added, but nothing substantial. for about 6 months people waited for an update...
1.0 and beyond:
Out of nowhere unstable stopped having nightly builds. Starbound 1.0 unstable had been released. I first was upset to find they removed many features. nanotechs and drawables. Modding was essentially reworked, forcing modders to completely remake their mods. But looking back the features they added compensate for this. thousands of items, biomes, settlements, quests, animals, planets, cutscenes, and mechanics were introduced. The whole story was redone and EPPs (Protection packs) were back. Most of you reading already know 1.0's features, so I won't bore you with them.
This is currently where we are today, the 1.2 update. I'm an active modder and done almost everything. I talk with the community and have played a little over a child's lifetime.
Thank you starbound for bringing endless fun to people through games. Stardew valley is getting it's big update now, and im planning on playing and modding that a ton as well.

This game is a refreshing iteration of the zombie genre. You are not a one man army fighting the zombie horde, instead you are part of a group of survivors. Scavenge the infested town for food, medicine, guns/ammo, and building materials to sustain yourselves. Overall, very fun game but it does get a bit repetitive towards the end when you run out of "story" missions.
It would have been nice to have impromptu moments in the game, such as: random survivors running across the map that you can save and have join your crew, surprise invasions from zombie hordes to add more excitement to the home base, and being attacked by other survivors for your resources. If there will be a sequel to this game with such additions, I will undoubtedly buy it.
Oh yeah. The AI for survivors can be atrocious at times. For example, if you're trying to meet someone for a mission and zombies attack you, that person will stand there and not help you at all. Also, survivors have a tendency to keep kicking the zomie endlessly until you kill the zombie. I would really like to see these issues fixed, but I won't hold my breath.

Resident Evil 0 was the ninth game in the titanically influential series and arguably the last to showcase a style that modern gaming was fast leaving behind. The pre-drawn environments, the fixed camera angles, the creaky door cinematics that covered the loading times between areas, having to stand in exactly the right bloody spot to pick up an item... they would all disappear quickly after Zero, leaving the radically different masterpiece that was Resident Evil 4 to pick up the pieces.
Even so, Capcom had already begun to change their gameplan here, introducing a buddy system in which the player freely shared control of the game's two main characters: S.T.A.R.S medic Rebecca Chambers (who you might remember from RE1 as the mostly useless pianist who rescued Chris Redfield's cack-fingered attempts to play Moonlight Sonata) and convicted ex-soldier Billy Coen. Although control of multiple characters was nothing new in the franchise, here it was the centerpiece of the game as most of the puzzles and combat scenarios are engineered to require each character's strengths and to prey on their weaknesses.
I played Resident Evil 0 to death when it originally made its appearance on the Gamecube back in 2002 and, although it did truly rock some ingenuous design, the controls were an absolute horror show especially in any combat scenario. If you've spent any time with the original version, you'll immediately notice how far improved they are in this remaster along with some truly stunning visuals. I'm a sucker for the pre-drawn background art style and it has never looked better than it does here. Also added for a bonus playthrough is Wesker Mode which really does what it says on the tin: blaze through the game as Johnny Bravo's evil twin, sneering and shadow-punching zombies into twitching mulch.
Remaining unchanged, however, is the game's notorious inventory system which truly is the most unforgiving in the entire series. You will often find yourself having to leave useful items behind for sheer lack of carrying space which can mostly be blamed on the Hookshot; a vital piece of equipment that has to be dragged through much of the game while occupying a gluttonous two squares of inventory room. The sheer amount of micromanagement between characters, especially with only Rebecca being able to create healing items, was a pain in♥♥♥♥♥♥then and it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥now.
With that said, whatever faults Resident Evil 0 might suffer are relatively minor. It's one of the weaker titles in the franchise but it's certainly far better than the catastrophe that was
and when you consider that it's only really weak in comparison to the mighty original trilogy, the excellent Code Veronica and REMake and the near-flawless Resident Evil 4, well... that's barely a criticism at all really.

Resident Evil 0 is probably the most polarizing game in the series, only beating out 6 because it's harder to find a person who genuinely enjoys 6 as a Resident Evil game than it is to find Wesker without sunglasses. Some people will tell you it's the worst non-6 game in the main series, others will tell you it's one of their favorites. I had never played it until now, so I had no idea what to think going in, but I was pleasantly surprised.
First off, for those who are just here to see the port changes, it's pretty well-done overall. The HD Remaster of REmake was put down a bit due to the developers not having original sources for most of the backdrops, so a lot of scenes looked grainy or artifacted, especially if you were playing in HD, and it made 3D geometry like items or puzzle objects stand out awkwardly. In RE0 HD this has been completely fixed, and whether you choose to play in widescreen or in the original aspect ratio everything except the cutscenes looks fantastic. The game still has the same problem with mouse and keyboard play as REmake HD did in that the cursor never goes off screen, so I did play it with a gamepad, but if you can ignore the cursor it controls fine either way. The main new addition aside from the DLC costumes is Wesker Mode, which is an amusing little extra mode where you replay the game replacing Billy with Wesker, complete with a couple of superpowered attacks.
As far as the game in general, I thought it was great. The new mechanic introduced lets you swap between two different characters, which is mainly used to add some spice to the classic Resident Evil puzzles. This means you have a larger combined inventory, but this is offset by what seems to be the most polarizing change - unlike most RE games, there is no magical transporting item box in RE0. Anything you can't carry with you has to be left on the ground somewhere, encouraging you to make caches in certain rooms. Some people will hate this change, and I can understand that, but I thought it added a lot of pressure to manage your inventory and choose carefully what to keep and what to leave behind. Any items that you've interacted with show up on your map, so it isn't a hassle to figure out where you've left something. The game is somewhat faster paced in that you start facing BOWs and acquiring weapons (though not necessarily ammo) to fight them earlier than you probably would in REmake on your first try, but it's still a more resource-scarce and survival-like game than others like Code Veronica. It is shorter than REmake by nature of only having one campaign instead of two like RE1 had, but I found 0's campaign to be a little longer than one of 1's campaigns and on your first playthrough it should serve you a fair amount of time.
In many ways it feels similar to REmake, and some locations will definitely feel familiar, but it keeps things fresh enough to feel more like an encore than a retread. My only real complaint about it is that the train portion of the game is actually fairly short and only makes up a small portion of the game, which disappointed me because I loved the look and atmosphere of it. But overall, if you're a fan of REmake, I can't see any reason not to try this as well, assuming you already haven't in the past decade or so.

For a six-year old game, the core SF4 experience holds up well. You pick one or more characters to master, then either fight with your buddies face-to-face, search for rivals in the arcades, challenge the world online (if you have a good Internet connection), or fight the best of the best by signing up for tournaments.
As for the USF4 changes:
(01) Having access to 5 new characters (Elena, Hugo, Rolento, Poison, and Decapre) is great, but for some reason Capcom did not include rival cutscenes for them, even though they only use the game engine.
(02) The voice acting for the new characters (excepting Decapre) is a bit uneven (sometimes it's tolerable, sometimes it grates on the ears). I like Hugo's best.
(03) The anime cutscenes are the prettiest the series have had yet (compare these to the ones Vanilla SF4 had, which were pretty low-budget).
(04) No trials for the new characters, and still no new trials for Arcade Edition additions Evil Ryu, Oni, Yun, and Yang.
(05) I like the fresh Training Mode ideas (like how you can spend time in Training Mode while waiting for a challenger, and how you can simulate lag so you can formulate lag-proof combos). I wish there was an option to turn on hitbox and hurtbox viewing, though.
(06) They still haven't brought back the Gallery Mode. Bizarre.
(07) The story's as disjointed and nonsensical as ever. I think Capcom should've included both SF4 OAVs as unlockables at least.
Is it worth the upgrade price? For serious fighting fans, there really is no choice in the matter. For casuals, it won't matter much unless they've taken a fancy to one of the 5 new characters.

Night in the Woods isn't exactly what I expected, yet fights it's way back with unique style, shockingly relatable writing and good execution.
You might stumble upon the title name Aquaria when searching about NiTW or one of the creators: Alec Holowka. His previous work, released nearly ten years ago is a precious favorite of mine, which I hold dearly near my gaming heart. This alone made my initial Kickstarter impressions gone skyrocket, but fortunately I managed to go into the game with the open mind, toning my expectations down a bit before release.
Game suprised me that it ultimately ended up as 3/4th a friend-hanging-out simulator and only 1/4th atmospheric, paranormal story. Emphasis of the game is mostly centered on the main character, her small circle of friends and the forgotten by the world town they live in. Game is separated into acts and those are further divided in game "days" where you explore the neighborhood, talk to townsfolk and finally decide on the main activity for the day. Parties, preparing dinner, petty crimes or garage band training sessions... those are mostly used to drive various characters with their own story arcs. Interactions between protagonist and her friends are varied, interesting and often times touching difficult subjects what young people may face. While this focus comes with the sacrifice that will be mentioned later, I was really impressed with the work done here to flesh out characters and their interactions in the surprisingly realistic way. While I couldn't relate to all of the story presented, at several points in the game dialogue went so deep in the "so true" territory that it felt uncanny. This is undoubtedly a one of the game's strongest points, even if I didn't expect game to be as much pushed in the this, seemingly "mundane" direction.
Unfortunately, as I said before, game suffers a little bit because of this aim and makes the paranormal sections feel a bit forgotten or not developed enough for my liking. People tend to criticize the last act of the game because it abruptly switches gears to the spooky mode on the whim. In my opinion, people are barking at the wrong tree, because that last act is incredible with its tense action and atmosphere. I just couldn't move my eyes away from the game until it was done. The problem is that this sudden shift would work better with the bigger build-up and game lacks it in the earlier chapters. While living day-by-day is a unique concept, it would definitely benefit from more frequent breaks for the spooks than it was ultimately delivered. Both aspects of the game would seem as stronger by this.
I won't write too much about the gameplay mechanics, because they don't contribute that much and are made at decently enough only to warrant a passing mention. You have a bit of platforming, which is fine, some easy puzzles and nothing much else. It's a bare minimum, but fortunately it isn't that much noticeable when dialogue takes the main role. More mechanics would be nice, but they are not necessary.
While I praised the writing, I need to point out that there are points, where it becomes too "hip" for its own good and ends out as condescending or pretentious instead of clever and touching. Game art, backgrounds, characters and places are also generally amazing, but there are some noticeable blind spots that look not as great as the rest of the game. As for music, I can say that I would struggle to find a fault in it, even if somebody would hold me on the gunpoint. Soundtrack is the place where you can hear most of the Aquaria's influences and I thank greatly for that. I won't however forget about the load times that are atrocious for the reasonably simple game. They were really close to break the immersion of the game.
While ultimately NiTW isn't as wallbreakingingly great as Aquaria was, it's still an excellent title for those interested in narrative games with surprisingly human stories that ring familliar tune to young adults looking for their place in the world. I can recommend it on the uniqueness lone, since I would struggle to find the game with similar artstyle, story and gameplay structure. While I wouldn't scream
at top of my lungs, I still consider Night in the Woods as enjoyable time spent worth the money and multiple playthoughs, which are pretty much required to see it all.

With the steam release, I thought it would be fun to venture back into SAGA. I played this game a ton after it came out a long time ago. I've hundreds of hours of play logged back then, but it has been many years since my last login. But since it's on steam...
Anyhow, I digress...
What is SAGA. It's a mmorts, though you can play it mostly single player, or coop, or PVP, or do tournaments or whatever. You basically build up a city, build an army, train your troops, get epic loot, trade for new troops, join guilds, etc. All the standard MMO stuff, but with your "character" being a city and armies. Each player has their own plot of land on some nebulous world (you can't see who is adjacent to you or anything) and you can expand your land over time. The game is mostly about building up your own little empire, but with a heavy focus on your creating and outfitting the perfect army. There are 6 nations to choose from, and each is very unique in how it functions.
GRAPHICS
The game is old. It shows. The graphics aren't super great, but they weren't amazing when it released back in 2008 or so either. They are adequate. Not much can be said. An overhaul of the graphics would make a huge difference, but I'm not sure if that's something that could be done with a game this old.
SOUND
Both good and bad here. The music is amazing. When I started up and was greeted with the old tunes it was like meeting an old friend. I LOVE the music in SAGA. The composer was fantastic, but I haven't followed him since the old days. His name is Panu Aaltio, I think. So the music is fantastic, but the sound effects are kind of not great. It's not that they are super bad, but the mixing and when they happen isn't great. I wish they could remix how they are being done. Some are really great, but others are just kind of glaring in your ears. If you hit charge like 10 times fast you'll see what I mean.
UI
The UI is serviceable, much like the graphics. There's actually quite a few buttons, but they aren't super invasive. There are little tricks and hidden things too, like lots of hotkeys and toggles for various bits and ends.
GAMEPLAY
Ok, this game is more comlex than it seems. At first it seems pretty simple, but by the time you figure in all the items, abilities, formations, and other little bits, there's a ton of number crunching and theorycrafting to be had. You can see that the game has some roots in collectible card games, so the standard realities of that sort of game apply. You can theory craft for days and still not come up with all the best builds. Back in the day there were things that seemed over powered, but there was almost always a counter. Be aware, though, that you're going to probably be a bit confused when you start playing. Thankfully there is a help chat and usually somewhere there to help you out when you're confused.
So basically, there's city building, battling (RTS style - sort of like the total war games), questing, coop questing, loot gathering, tournaments, PVP, and a few other things.
CONTENT
There are a megaton of quests in the game as well. Some are really good, and others can fill like filler at times. There is also PVP (which can be brutal if you go up against someone who knows the game really well, but there is a ton of gameplay and fun to be had in the PVP). There is also just the city building aspect, which is kind of like sim city super-lite. Building takes time, so you can tinker a little each day, do a few quests to gather resources, and then just put SAGA down until the next day.
My favorite part about the content is playing COOP. Almost any game I play these days needs to have COOP (except RPGS) and SAGA allows it for all the quests, which is cool.
There is also some advanced stuff like raiding of other players outskirt territories and stuff, though I know there were some changes with espionage and that sort of thing and I haven't played for a long time so I'm not sure how that is functioning currently. There were some safeguards to prevent players from ransacking your territories to death, but again, you'd have to check on the forums or ask around for more updated info.
STORY
There is quite a bit of story and history hidden away in SAGA, but it's definitely not the strong point You aren't going to see an amazing plotline unfold with great characters and whatnot.
OTHER THOUGHTS
Will you like it? That depends. There is a lot to try out and enjoy in SAGA, but it's old, and parts of it feel really old. As I mentioned before, I'd LOVE to see an overhaul to the engine that focused on graphics, smoothness of animations (I didn't mention those...they aren't great), and an overhaul to how sounds work. But even with how old it is, there's a lot to enjoy. You can spend countless hours developing your empire, questing with your friends, and just having a lot of fun figuring out new strategies and running PVP or tournaments. If you don't want to play with other people, just turn off chat and treat it like a single player game. There's not a great story, so don't be expecting that. If you like card games, RTS, total war-styled battles, simple city building, trading, theory crafting, and things like that, then you may like SAGA. I guess it's free now, and it looks like a legit F2P game, so there's not much risk.
I like it. I'm not sure if I'll get into it like I did almost a decade ago, but I'm enjoying tinkering and reminiscing. Grab a friend. Laugh at how clunky some of the games of the past were, and give it a go. I'd recommend at least an hour or two before bailing on it, but there's a billion great games out there. To each his or her own, right?

Now, Ive played this game A LOT. At the time of writing this it's 260 hours. I've played this game sense the closed alpha, and I can say i'm not dissipointed in how this game has changed over the years. Let's start from the beginning.
Closed Alpha:
The base content we all know was in the game, and there were 2 tiers of planets in the first (and only) sector: Forest(Lush) and Desert. Food was in the game via a bar in the top right screen, and temperature was a mechanic. standing near a fire gave you heat, while standing in water cooled you down. I recall clothes gave you warmth. There was no weather, and ships used wood for fuel. The only structure I ever found was an very early avian village and some gear trap. Oh, and one handed weapons were actually viable.
Beta:
It's hard to list the beta in one review because of how long it went on. From early 2012 to mid 2016, the amount of content added was immense. Food and tempurature were replaced with a new mechanic, Protection Packs. There was a weapon overhaul, moons were added, and there were 10 sectors. One of the biggest changes was the "Space stations" a new feature that was a big city on a ship in the brand new astroid biome.  This changed into the outpost that we know today. You accessed it by going to a monolith which is where you open vaults today. Novakids were added from their kickstarter stretch goal. Quests were added and were very different. The erchious mining facility stayed pretty simular as it is today, though it was much more challenging than now. The floran temple was actually a floran ambush, and there was no nuru. Dreadwing and shockhopper were fought on planets, then moved to quests given by a penguin. Pets were added, farming was completely redone, they added nanotechs and replaced Protection packs, planets were removed from sectors in favor of a new solar system ideolagy, lore was added and then... progress stopped. A few bug fixes were added, but nothing substantial. for about 6 months people waited for an update...
1.0 and beyond:
Out of nowhere unstable stopped having nightly builds. Starbound 1.0 unstable had been released. I first was upset to find they removed many features. nanotechs and drawables. Modding was essentially reworked, forcing modders to completely remake their mods. But looking back the features they added compensate for this. thousands of items, biomes, settlements, quests, animals, planets, cutscenes, and mechanics were introduced. The whole story was redone and EPPs (Protection packs) were back. Most of you reading already know 1.0's features, so I won't bore you with them.
This is currently where we are today, the 1.2 update. I'm an active modder and done almost everything. I talk with the community and have played a little over a child's lifetime.
Thank you starbound for bringing endless fun to people through games. Stardew valley is getting it's big update now, and im planning on playing and modding that a ton as well.

I used three common emitter amplifiers for my design. I started by designing the last stage of the amplifier first, and then worked backward. First, I set Rc of stage three equal to the load resistor of 47Ω, however, during optimization, I found that by raising the value of Rc to 62Ω the gain of the circuit increased causing improved performance. Then I picked an RE value that was much smaller than Rc to create a large gain. After looking at the resistor values we have in the lab, I arbitrarily chose a 5Ω resistor. At first, I placed an emitter capacitor in parallel with RE, but this caused my circuit to oscillate, so I removed the capacitor in my final design. I used the value of RE to pick my RB by using the parameter RB=10%*β*RE, where β was assumed to be 170 for the third stage transistor, because that was the measured value of the transistor I picked out in lab for that section. However, this value did skew my PSpice estimates, because PSpice used different values. The different stages of the amplifier were showing transistors with β values ranging from 172 to 104, which needs to be addressed in my final design.

Of all the newer crop of cRPGs, PoE is probably the closest to the old Infinity Engine games, which is great because BG 2 one of my favorite games of all time.
While it certainly has the look and feel of BG and IWD, there are some tweaks here and there, like the old min/max character creation strategy doesn't really work great here. For instance, might affects virtually all damage types, not just melee damage. This means it is important for all characters rather than just your front line tank-y types. Some people complained about this, but I like it. It makes different character builds more viable and doesn’t really punish you as much for not dumping every possible point into a particular stat.
The expansion packs add some good content, I especially like the soul-bound weapons which get more powerful as you reach certain requirements.
The only thing I can complain a about is the performance, honestly this game doesn’t run well at all. On an i7-6700K and GTX780 with 16 GB RAM I can usually get 60FPS, but the framerate can drop into single digits with a lot of spell effects on the screen. Oy vey...
It sounds like there will be a PoE 2 at some point, it would cool if they tuned it into a franchise like the Elder Scrolls. I just hope they improve the performance next time!

I've watched let's look at, let's plays, and other videos of this game and I have to admit I was pretty intrigued. It seemed challenging and it does have an interesting story with some neat and amusing characters so I thought for the price it might be a decent pick up to tide myself over for some big name releases.
Upon playing I found that there are only sound options, and nothing for windowed mode; how I tend to plamost if not ALL of y PC games. So I went into the directory to see if there were any files that might allow me to fix this.
And low and behold, I find something astounding; Every chapter has its own seperate folder out in the open with all the data it relies on completely present and, get this, editable by the user. I don't know much, heck, I don't know ANYTHING about programming but I can recognize numbers and quantities when I see them.
You see, each folder has a 'control' file, for instance chapter 3's is labeled 'p3_control'. Go into this file and you can edit various factors about the mission. In doing so I could make any mission so hilariously easy it doesn't warrant the challenge. Now, this isn't me saying that this how you beat the game.
But this is incredibly exploitable and easy to do.
So why am I saying this in a review? Because I wanted it to be known that trial and error can be fun, and in games like Dark Souls and Monster Hunter learning how to handle situations is exciting. In this game you sit and try again and again as what worked once seemingly fails to consistently get the same results. Things changing a bit is nice, but I don't think such inconsistency in methods that seemingly work is a good thing.
Is the story worth the price? Maybe.
Is the game worth a look? Definitely.
Are the mechanics reliable? I can't say for certain.

I recommend it even if you don't normally enjoy the extremes of the dress-up simulator/spreadsheet game genre spectrum. It's a happy medium that should appeal to a wide audience.

The developers successfully crowded-funded the game by promising to bring us a new Baldur's Gate-style game, and they succeeded. If you liked Baldur's Gate or Icewind Dale, this is a great game. The worldbuilding is excellent and it's always fun to see how your character's specific background, stats and actions shape their options in dialogue. There are times when it feels like I am playing with the world's longest-suffering DM, as I sneak my thief protagonist about and raid every single container available even in a poor residential area. I can imagine this DM rubbing their forehead and sighing, then announcing, "Fine, you find some cheese. No, there are no more boxes to open."
Strategy is important. Mechanics are balanced, to a point that I generally have a difficult time judging if any particular item is better or worse than any other -- this set of armor has better damage reduction, but it slows down the character's actions; this weapon has better damage rolls, but it takes longer to use so maybe it's better to hit an enemy multiple times with a smaller-damage weapon. Some of it turns out to simply be about knowing the types of enemies you'll be fighting in an area, as this ghost is immune to piercing damage but that creature is well-armored and you should go in with armor-bypassing weapons. So on.
The single-player of this game is excellent and the AI is actually quite good. I enjoy source's multiplayer more but this game still has an edge on it in a few respects.

Background: The game takes place on the podium next to Resident Evil 1 as "Resident Evil Origins" a package with 2 sets (even 0 came much later, but chronologically speaking) who started the franchise start Capcom Games Horror / Survival Horror. The game is set in 1998, hours before Alpha Team (where Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield in the first Resident Evil) reached the Arklay mountains, in this case took control Rebecca Chambers, a rookie in STARS and member of the team Bravo, who is sent to investigate a series of mysterious murders in the suburbs of Raccoon City, during the arrival to the forest the helicopter suffered a breakdown and is forced to an emergency landing, Rebecca and his companions then divide to search track on a fugitive Billy Cohen and the game begins when Rebecca arrives at Heliptic Express, a mysterious train nearby and investigate what happened and get hints of what is happening.
Core of the game: The game mechanics is similar to its version SD, ie have the original controls Gamecube (remapped to new controls such as the Xbox) or other controls pc and alternative controls that are designed to give more dynamic movement (which is a hassle for veterans as our character and the terrible management of cameras can be very annoying during the course of the game), we have the implementation of Widescreen (16: 9) and classic Letterbox (4: 3 ), the basic mechanics remains intact, the game allows us to save a limited amount of time as in the original version (even easy) and we must do in the game determines points for this purpose (using ink ribbon MACHINES write), the handling of the camera is isometric (perspective is on the player in angular format, from above and focus on cinematic angles) which gives an excellent experience for a horror game but quickly becomes annoying when running (eg when you are short bullets and you must escape the zombies). In this case most of the time we control both characters (Billy and Rebecca) by pressing a button and both need to use throughout the game to solve puzzles and fight our way to travez of the different stages of the game.
Graphics: It's really remarkable the upgrade graphics that the game had, with a precedent excellent as was playing Resident Evil 1 HD, the textures, shadows, lighting effects, particles etc, was enhanced to a much definitido appearance and lived to play, while maintaining its constant 60 fps (with option for 30 pc's oldest) always bringing the same game with a much more clear and warm to the eye, this question receives a 10/10 game on my part, they knew polish the details, keep the fps and play compatibility while maintaining the fps. The video options are few but enough to play the game at the highest quality, auque older computers have the option of receiving something a bit smaller for not sacrificing performance.
Conclusion: Despite having played this game on GameCube in his time, I have finished and I have enjoyed it a lot, the Steam version brings a refreshing touch to the sequel that deviated from the path after RE 6 opting for action and leaving side roots of the genre, RE 0 recalls those early games of the franchise were so funny and made us more frightening when we were kids, in my experience I had high expectations for this game were met and was very pleased with what Capcom did I hope to continue making games like this.

CS just like 1.6 but... with small map changes and... same♥♥♥♥♥♥all over again...
EXCEPT: great awesome singleplayer campaign
These 80 hours i played this game was 95% spent on single player campaign, which gives unique experience of small missions besides the match. There are 18 maps to play on those campaign (classics like dusts or aztec but also forgotten maps like chateau). Games are pretty much about getting better score, just like in any other CS with some changes:
- Teammates Selection - Before the match starts, you get an option to choose up to 5 teammates. Each teammate costs points, which you get for winning the maps. Each bot is prefering different weapon, has different skill level, differently play as team, different bravery. So if you are playing map like aztec, you should get some snipers and on office get some guys with higher teamplay skills.
- Mini-Objectives - While you play the match, you have usually 3 main mini-missions to finish during the match. Easier ones are like to get few kills with specific weapon, harder are to kill flash-blinded enemy. Sometimes you will have to kill two guys with pistol and survive the round, one of the hardest is even to kill an enemy with knife. To win the match, you have to finish all those objectives and be 2 wins ahead of terrorists. However, if you let them be 2 wins ahead, you loose and you can start all objectives over.
Campaign is only playable as Counter-Terrorists, but there are a lot of downloadable campaigns, you can even easily make your own with your own bots and custom maps.
+++ Single Player Campaign - you wont find anything like this in any other CS
+- Its pretty old game, so graphics is just fine.
- Forget multiplayer, i guess its not alive in this game

One of the best games for the original XBox, yet it was never advertised as it was intended, and that kinda killed the game's chances on the public market. Quite a shame what shady business can do for an amazing game such as this.

A gripping storyline and absolutely unique mechanics that I found myself coming back to after almost a decade, wondering if Steam had this gem. And thanks to JAW, it is here on Steam, and it's one of my favorites to play through. Not much replay value, but DEFINITELY worth the once through, or if you're feeling an itch to relive the glorious gameplay and laugh at the cheesy boss names (Jo Momma and Eugene Ius come to mind).
A strong 8/10, and I would recommend it, even to people who don't like shooters.
P.S. Oddbox is only like ten dollars and you get this with three other games that are all pretty damn good. Pick it up, it's DEFINITELY worth the price!
