I'll keep this short as you have better things to do i'm sure :)
I'll start with the cons because i like to end on a positive note :)
First of all, they recently upped the server count from 36 to 50. this may not sound like a big deal but for my money, the map is a bit too small for this number, 36 was near perfect but now you'll find yourself in the south side of the island with 30 - 40+ other players within a 5 mile radius which makes it feel cramped and the chances of surving more than an hour on your own is slim at best,
It can also get quite tedious in places, all the towns with the exception of the big city to the north, look about the same, its a fun game to explore, but don't expect the towns to be vastly diffent from one and other.
There isnt much choice in terms of clothing and food for survival although this will most likely change with future develpment. at the moment you rely on canned foods and water canteens for survival
Theres no "prone" postion yet. so the only chance you have of hiding from people is by hiding in the bushes or staying far away from the busy areas.
The base building can be fun but 90% of people are exploting the "floating base" glitch so no point raiding them as you can't get to where they hide the booty
The zomies are dim witted and easy to kill at the moment so they pose little challenge, with that being said there is a behmouth monster that is near impossible to kill unless you are fully geared up with rifles and plenty of ammo, they need to scale the difficulty for sure.
Vehicles are in the game but there is little varitety to them at the moment, you get a car, bus, truck, tractor ( no idea why) and a bike. parts for these are common but the chances of you being able to survive long enough to collect them all and fix up a vehicle is very slim.
Now for the pros :)
The sever selection is vast and caters to all needs, you can one with 24h day with lots of loot scattered around, or if youre a more hardcore person who wants to full on experince with a day/ night cycle and little loot, or anything inbetween. youre bound to find a sever you like
The crafting is simple and easy to do, they are tinkering with the speeds and weights of crafting materials with evey update
Speaking of updates, this game is updated reguarly, usually once every couple of weeks. and with the updates comes new parts of the map, new attachments for weapons, and new clothing options
The game looks good, it might be too cartoony for some but most agree it looks diamond compared to other games of the genre
Its a very simple game to get used to, there isnt many factors that go into if you die or not, you can get poisned, or die of thirst or hunger. but theres no chance of breaking your legs or fracturing your arm etc etc, this may in all likely hood chance with the updates but for the moment at least, its simple and i like simple
The city in the north is fantastic, theres sky scrapers to expolore, city flats and housing to loot and the hotels and shops to loot as well. if you survive long enough to get there, its worth it.
The weather effects are increadible, they range from clear sunny days to heavy thunder storms with fog as thick as the sexual tention between you and that girl you liked when you were in collage and you knew she liked you too but nothing ever happend.
My summery:
If you want a dayz like game thats a bit more simple and not as brutal (yet) then this is a must for you. its one of the better early access games on the market and is well worth the small investment :)

One of the greatest RPGs to date. Dark Souls separates itself from it peers by offering immersive depth, rich level design, amazing story (although, obfuscated and perhaps not easily accessible), and above all unparalled combat.
This last feature is what has spawned a culture of "git gud." That culture is a true disservice to the greater gaming community. What Dark Souls offers is punishing combat. Meaning if you make a mistake, you will be punished. But it also gives you a plethora of options to not make the mistake. I would often spam roll or turtle block when a newcomer to the series, and would subsequently die and feel cheated. The path to salvation was simply learning to remain calm in a fight, and trying to different methods of attack. Maybe I buff my weapon, maybe I try a different weapon, maybe I try a shield, maybe I try different gear, and maybe I try summoning if nothing else works.
Dark Souls is not your typical game. You would not expect to beat portal without some amount of thought, and Dark Souls should be treated the same way.
As for the other attributes I mentioned, let me touch on them briefly. When I say the game is immersive, I mean the depth is outstanding. Much like the monster hunter series, simply playing with a new weapon can chane your entire experience. There are just so many build, and build varieties that once you are comfortable with the game, there is a lot of game to explore. As for world design, for many this is a selling feature. Personally, I think it is cool, but what I like more is that every area you go to is memorable and distinct. It is definitely one of those games where every corner is distinct in your mind. And as for the story, it is a masterpiece. It is presented, mainly indirectly through character interactions and short descriptions of items. With a dilligent enough eye, you can eventually piece together the story. The overall affect though is that you learn of events and people the same way you would learn about legends. In this way, the people you fight really become legend. It is truly effective.
Before concluding, the games two major faults must be addressed. There is little direction at the start. And it is frustrating. Be aware of this, you will feel lost and directionless at the beginning of the game. While this is probably the emotion they wanted to produce, they do not capitalize on it well. If you want to overcome this without seeking outside help, I would suggest making detailed notes of what the NPCs say to you. What seem like extremely minor statements are  actually vital keys. Second, the interface on steam is especially wonky. There are outside methods of fixing these problems, that will also increase the resolution. I would suggest looking into these.  I would also suggest playing with a controller.
So, in conclusion, this game is amazing. If you put in the time, and are pre-disposed to action rpgs, you will eventually absolutely love this game. To the point where other games are no longer important. Umbasa.

This is a decent game. It has some design flaws, but also a couple of good ideas. I did enjoy playing, but I doubt I will revisit it anytime soon.
First the flaws. The constant spawning of time-sensitive missions at first help create a sense of desperation (hunt down a special zombie, survivor in need, survivor creating morale problem at home, etc.). But these become tedious and irritating, as when you are out trying to scavenge a particular resource, you often won't have time for everything. These missions repeat often, eliciting a "what, again already?!" response from me. I would like to see longer, more involved missions that result in greater resource benefit, possibly even special benefits for the home base (finding a Special Forces Medical Handbook, an ammunition reloading kit, or food preservation equipment).
There needs to be more character interaction in this game. The character interactions are extremely limited - I can't recall a single character name, and I played it a couple of weeks ago. Story drives a game more than any other aspect, and in a zombie survival game, story must center around characters - people need each other to survive more than at any other time!  Longer missions could also help support this need.
While melee and firearm detail are satisfactory, details of medicine, food, contruction materials and other possible survival resources could be better. What are they? What about imaginative uses for these resources? Creativity is a must in a survival scenario with few resources, and even fewer renewable resources. Also, contruction materials would be the MOST COMMON, but I found that to be the limiting factor during my play. Imagine scavenging materials from your immediate vicinity, and you get what I mean.
Now for the good ideas. Allowing a choice of home base location is a good idea, and creating upgrades is great. Good way to create an interesting choice (close to scavenge vs. better protection). I'd like to see this expanded. The upgrades that allow trading with the survivor community at large is excellent as well.
Survivors have skills, some useful, some not - good idea, as it is realistic. It's a good point from which to expand the playability of this game as backgrounds will create stories. I also like the ability to improve combat skills. Surviving an encounter with zombies is the best teacher.
I did like the dead-is-dead for characters in the game, and a lack of a manual save feature. No do-overs in a real survival scenario, and why this is closer to a simulation than anything else. It's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥when learning the game, as I started over a couple of times, but once I had the mechanics figured out, you need to be extra careful with you best characters (some are more useful than others).
All in all, buy this game on sale. I believe this is just the first of a good series of games, and I hope the developer will improve on all aspects.

This game is pretty well done. I had high hopes and I was not disappointed. There are a few flaws but nothing game breaking or insurmountable.
Pros:
-Large open exploration world
-Fast travel in the form of vehicles
-Large selection of weapons and types
-Several "Bases" to choose from
-The ability to upgrade your characters
-Suits several play styles from run and gun to stealth
-Loads of gore (good in a zombie game)
-Good levels of realism without overdoing it (IE Stamina for actions good, no gas needed for cars better)
-Lots of quests/missions to keep you entertained
-Over 200+ hours of game play if you take your time
-Well worth the price especially on sale
-DLC fixes some of the flaws
I could go on, but that's the major stuff.
Cons:
-Missions come too fast or inconvenient at times
-Your group can easily get into trouble without you especially at first
-A scripted section with a character at your first base is very hard to avoid a bad outcome
-Once you've cleared out an area you'll have to move on or you die (kind of good/bad)
-Ammo counts reset every day regardless of supply
-The game continues when you turn it off (biggest gripe)
-this means your characters can die when you are not even playing
-they also use supplies and gather some others, but it seems to be diminishing returns
-If your base was strong when you quit, it may survive till you get back, maybe
Anyway I don't claim to be an expert, but I do know I really got my monies worth out of this title. Good luck to all of you.

WARNING: If you don't know what to expect of this game, do yourself a favor and play the free flash version at
first!
Not only does it explain background and core gameplay mechanics, but it also give an indication as to what exactly this game is about. Based on that, you may or may not disagree with my assessment as this is NOT A BAD GAME, simply not what was advertised.
ACTUAL REVIEW:
If you want a story-based experience of tough choices: do yourself a favor and play Unrest instead.
I bought Gods Will Be Watching assuming it to capture at least some of the hard human decision-making that made games like Always Sometimes Monsters, The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, Mass Effect and others so unique and brilliant. Unfortunately, Gods Will be Watching had none of this.
Straight away, the game throws the player into a situation that may seem morally interesting at first, but is soon realized to be nothing other than a simple (as in: not complicated, but still very hard) time management game. It is at this point where it dawned on me that this was, in fact, competing not with the games mentioned above but with Cook, Serve, Delicious and the like - only that it was doing so badly.
As the player never really learns about their character or has any chance to immerse themselves in the setting, the "moral choices" one has to make are appropriately bland and meaningless. Even worse, some decisions turn out to actually have no effect - for example, in at least one instance, a dead crew member comes back to life in the level after they were killed without a mention and sticks around to provide dialogue. Decision-making is limited to the aforementioned time management and resource exchanges (shooting a hostage earns more time, but costs a hostage). Moral dilemmas? Not really.
What the game has going for it are its beautiful pixel graphics and its soundtrack. If you are looking for a challenging time-management puzzle game, Gods Will Be Watching can be an interesting distraction. I, personally, was disappointed by its lack of character and narrative.

Now, Ive played this game A LOT. At the time of writing this it's 260 hours. I've played this game sense the closed alpha, and I can say i'm not dissipointed in how this game has changed over the years. Let's start from the beginning.
Closed Alpha:
The base content we all know was in the game, and there were 2 tiers of planets in the first (and only) sector: Forest(Lush) and Desert. Food was in the game via a bar in the top right screen, and temperature was a mechanic. standing near a fire gave you heat, while standing in water cooled you down. I recall clothes gave you warmth. There was no weather, and ships used wood for fuel. The only structure I ever found was an very early avian village and some gear trap. Oh, and one handed weapons were actually viable.
Beta:
It's hard to list the beta in one review because of how long it went on. From early 2012 to mid 2016, the amount of content added was immense. Food and tempurature were replaced with a new mechanic, Protection Packs. There was a weapon overhaul, moons were added, and there were 10 sectors. One of the biggest changes was the "Space stations" a new feature that was a big city on a ship in the brand new astroid biome.  This changed into the outpost that we know today. You accessed it by going to a monolith which is where you open vaults today. Novakids were added from their kickstarter stretch goal. Quests were added and were very different. The erchious mining facility stayed pretty simular as it is today, though it was much more challenging than now. The floran temple was actually a floran ambush, and there was no nuru. Dreadwing and shockhopper were fought on planets, then moved to quests given by a penguin. Pets were added, farming was completely redone, they added nanotechs and replaced Protection packs, planets were removed from sectors in favor of a new solar system ideolagy, lore was added and then... progress stopped. A few bug fixes were added, but nothing substantial. for about 6 months people waited for an update...
1.0 and beyond:
Out of nowhere unstable stopped having nightly builds. Starbound 1.0 unstable had been released. I first was upset to find they removed many features. nanotechs and drawables. Modding was essentially reworked, forcing modders to completely remake their mods. But looking back the features they added compensate for this. thousands of items, biomes, settlements, quests, animals, planets, cutscenes, and mechanics were introduced. The whole story was redone and EPPs (Protection packs) were back. Most of you reading already know 1.0's features, so I won't bore you with them.
This is currently where we are today, the 1.2 update. I'm an active modder and done almost everything. I talk with the community and have played a little over a child's lifetime.
Thank you starbound for bringing endless fun to people through games. Stardew valley is getting it's big update now, and im planning on playing and modding that a ton as well.

I'm mixed about this game.
I've been polaying it for quite a while, but somehow I can't seem to either love it nor hate it.
First of, I love this style of game. You control a hero and a small party, and you walk on a fogged map discovering locations, enemies and quests. I've had a lot of fun with a similar one (Expeditions: Conquistador) and so I thought I'd try this one out.
You start with a kind of cliche history about demons, the end of the world and all that. Since I'm not a native english speaker, I felt like they could've added sulbtitles so I wouldn't get so lost and disconnected about the history. After the intro, you get a nice tutorial, which explains pretty much all the basics of the game (altough the different factions and units are not explained at all, so each one you play with you'll have to see it for yourself what suits you better by trial and error). After that, you're all set to play the campaign.
First of, I think the narrator did a very nice job. All of them read pretty nicely the texts that open each act from each faction. Problem is, that's al lthe voice acting you get. The rest is just at the beggining or after battles and it's the same sound over and over again. The history is presented to you at the beggining of the acts and while playing them, by non spoken dialogue.
For me the game started fun (on hard mode), I would walk and take my time to kill every monster and discover every part of the map (which is what the developers wanted, I guess). But some monsters are impossible to beat on any given map on the early stages of the game, even with a full party with max lvl soldiers.
The graphics are neither top notch nor bad, they fit decently into the game's theme. Only visual problem I had was with some long dialogues being cut by the "continue" buttom you must press after each characther has spoken. So you kind of miss some information. Couldn't the devs have made a scroll bar or just have the person say something in two dialogues instead of one?
Anyways, the fun I've had in the previous 30 hours gave place to a feeling of boredom. I mean, after all you just go from map to map doing the same thing over and over, there are two or three secondary quests tops and the only thing keeping you forward is a little piece of history given to you before each act. And there are a lot of acts from all the factions. So you play each act for about 5 hours or more (if you kill every guy like me) and then there is 5 more lines of history and then 5 more hours doing the same thing. It gets boring pretty fast, especially if you don't like this kind of game.
What keeps it better is that you can kind of "auto-resolve" a battle to make the game run faster, but the AI is so stupid that even aganist the weakest enemies you can lose one or two soldiers because the AI chooses to advance with only one guy aganist 7, even though you have 5 guys to attack (Idk why its so stupid since the AI of the enemy computer, altough not very bright, isn't that stupid).
My veredict is that, if you like this kind of strategy games, give this one a try, especially if on sale. I'll be fun for quite a while. But be warned that you'll be bored before knowing how the history ends. If you're going to go all the way to the end is up to you. I, myself, don't know if I will.

There is a lot of good things in Reincarnation, but the AI and map progression issues have not been resolved from the previous versions.
In general:
The Good:
-Fun races, lots of units, nice strategic approach.
-Nice Music.
-Graphically appealing, while not being demanding. Well Optimized. (Not last gen tough).
-Good Campaign Storyline.
-Almost no bugs or glitches (so far).
-Leveling system is addictive and dynamic. Can have different builds.
The Bad:
-Horrible AI. Seriosuly.
-Strategic approach is fine, execution is terrible. Weird and unfair issues with CPU enemies.
-Extremely slow paced gameplay.
-Difficulty is based 100% in the raw power of the enemy armies and it scales poorly as the game goes on.
-Once behind it's almost impossible to recover.
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Now, explaining with more detail:
1.- Disciples is a franchise that relies heavily into the management of the encounters you have. The main strategy of the matches rely heavily in how you develop your troops WITHOUT DYING, mainly because the game punishes you hard if you loose a leveled squad. In the past, this kind of difficulty was appealing, but by today standards, it's just not well implemented.
The game is more about choosing the right targets to level up and not about the strategic combat. This means that the difficulty is developed by the way you approach the leveling and not about the challenge of battling or developing the resources.
2.- The AI is just broken.
During the map phase, all the enemy armies just clean the mobs and level up in a certain rate, making few mistakes, while you need to see your way trough the random neutral troops that can range from easy to impossible. While the idea of having a linear leveling experience is boring, making you roam the map searching for the right mobs seems hardly an improvement. This is worsened by the fact that you can't afford to loose a single troop from the squad, so you will be repeating certain battles just for the sake of keeping the squad alive and not loose time in healing (wich, too, can be punishing in certain situations). And you can add to this the fact that while you loose time choosing targets, the AI already knew the right path so now it's 3 levels abobe you and still power-clearing camps.
In combat is worse. Melees will approach to engage, ranged will target the nearest high priority target (weakest).
No much variation there. All the difficulty relies in you having to clear the lesser troops because usually the neutral enemies will have an outstanding threat that you need to carefully engage if you don't want to get one-shotted. And that is all. It's an easy clean or a fight you will have to repeat until the mobs behave the way you needed or until certain platforms that give you power spawn in better positions for you (wich ends up being the only strategy that the field of battle provides and that is completely random. The AI will rarely use them well).
-While fun and useful when you level and clear the map, spells are rather secondary. They can be extremely necesary in certain maps that have incredible neutral camps difficulties; and be just a fun thing to do in other scenarios.
Don't get me wrong with this review. Reincarnation is still a good game. It pretty much is a revamp of disciples 2 with a new combat system that is not really that cool. But i can hardly recommend it with all the issues it haves. Gaming has gone a long way from the games that had broken gameplay and weird AI issues. D3 should have been the improvement in those departments and not just the downfall because they not only couldn't fix them but maked them worse.
There were other minor issues, but i settled with the most important in my opinion. To do this review i waited to play enough time, but now I felt like I was ready to give an honest, objective opinion about the game.
Cheers!

I'm re-reviewing this game because my last review(s) were in January, and after the news of the future update I figured a fresh overview would provide more insight.
Let me start off by saying that Starbound is without a doubt the greatest example of a successful early access game that I have ever been part of, and is one of - if not the only - game I can ever truly say utilized the early access funding. As you can see by the overwhelming positive reviews, this is by far one of the greatest games to hit steam in general, and clearly deserves the positive remarks. If you have ever played terraria, you without a doubt need to try this. If your friends are looking for a game to drown hours into, you need to try this. If you enjoy space exploration or sandbox games, you need to try this.
Starbound is an open world survival / building sandbox, similar to terraria, however it supports multiple planets, diverse biomes, mobs, and in the next couple of months - total space exploration. However what truly differs starbound from other games of it's sort - it has a story. A legitimate story, you meet NPCs, follow the quests, and beat the game. And it PERFECTLY goes in sync with your development in the sandbox aspects of the game (albeit your items may outscale the campaign slightly - but that's not a problem). All of this can be done, while still progressing with your friends and proceeding to horde items, build too many chests to store them in, and die hilariously.
The bosses and monsters feel adventourous and challenging. You actually gain a sense of accomplishment when you beat them (they are kind of layered in tiers based on planet level, to go with the campaign. There are bonus bosses too like the penguin ones). Each fight is enjoyable, and you always want to try to beat it or find the next best weapon if you can't.
For a survival game like this with progression-based scaling, never once had the game felt grindy. I never felt like I was getting no where, I was never bored, I never ran out of items to collect or monsters to kill, I never left the game early because the repetition was too overbearing (which is common in a lot of sandbox games), all while the game balanced itself at the perfect level of difficulty.
The map and world is what really pulls you in though. From arcade machines to old statues, every planet has it's loot - and all of that loot can be brought on your ship. I have upgraded my ship to look like a crazy arcade club, while my friends have gone for medieval styles. The possibilities were endless. Every environment was lootable. You find an underground scientific lair that you like? Loot it. A broken building on the surface with rustic furniture? It's yours now. An underwater futuristic city full of machines and fun? Who's stopping you (maybe the AI, but that's why we have guns.) The fact that every where I went, I was always on the look for new items to collect, and I never felt like I ran out was what really kept me going. The same goes for weapons. Tons of tons of different weapons, with different styles, stats, elements, sizes, shapes, everything. I never stuck to the same weapon until towards the very end, and I never felt like one was greatly overpowering another. There was always a sense of balance between them, and it was fun to try new ones out.
I can't really put to words how exciting it is to go back to this game every now and then, and the only reason why I leave such gaps between gameplays is because the game leaves such an impact on my mind and is so enjoyable, that I almost have to let myself forget about it just so I can enjoy it all over again. That and the fact that chucklefish is an amazing development team, and they have constantly been updating it since. They added procedural dungeons to account for extra endgame fun, and by the end of the month - we're getting the space exploration and mechs we always wanted. They truly know how to appeal to a fanbase. I honestly respect them as developers greatly because they listened and improved. And all through development, release and unstable, I felt like the game was always being polished. Even now they throw updates and bugfixes here and there, and let everyone test them out before they push them for the release version.
So my advice to anyone looking at this game is to buy it. Tell your friends to buy it. Play it alone, or with friends. Just enjoy the experience - because it is one of, if not the best, steam games you will ever play. It is a 2D sandbox game and it outshines so many AAA games out there. Try it, give it a shot. It's worth it.

I wanted very, very badly to like Disciples 3.  The art is as stunning as Disciples 2, perhaps even more so.  However, the balance is all off - XP gain is not proportional to threats, combat is a slow and frustrating affair (unless you're losing, at which point it will end in two rounds), and even after battles that I've won I had to make a trip back to my capital every single time to resurrect people.  And then, if I'm unlucky, sit and mash "END TURN" until I have the money to afford them.
The fact that I can only claim land in specific points also adds to the tedium, as I have to watch my territory ponderously expand toward resource cites that I've cleared out for dozens of turns before they are claimed.
Of course, the quest dialogue and voice-overs are terrible.  Fortunately there's an easy way to turn unit voices off.
There were plenty of improvements between Disciples 2 and Disciples 3, by the way.  Combat is now on a tactical grid a la Heroes of Might & Magic.  Each grid has randomly-determined sites that can increase the effectiveness of one unit type, and leveraging these effectively can make a moderate battle into an easy one (although they still don't make difficult battles into reasonable threats).  Some overworld spells can be cast into runes, which can then be used to cast a scaled-down version of the spell during a battle.  Heroes have something not unlike a very toned-down version of the Sphere Grid from Final Fantasy X, or the leveling system in Final Fantasy 12 - basically a grid in which each square has some sort of bonus, and you can claim any square adjacent to an already-claimed square when leveling up.
But ultimately I'd give this one a skip, even as a fan of the genre.

I'm late to the hype train, but better late than never.  I've seen people play these From Software games on Twitch, but not enough to actually spoil much or ruin things.  I knew what I was in for by watching the pain and anguish of other players this way.  Even so, on my first play through it took a good while to learn how to not have my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me.
01. Punched the 1st Undead Asylum boss in the butt until I got sat on about 100 times.
02. Aggro'd the Crestfallen Warrior at the Firelink Shrine thinking I could lulz and reload.
03. Bought new armor from Mr. Giggles petting an invisible cat only to find I could no longer move while wearing it.
04. Learned I could zoom in with the bow but not until after I got the Drake Sword with it in 3rd person.
05. Read a message on a cliff that said "TRY JUMPING" and listened only to reap the rewards.
06. Poked a black knight in the butt with just the tip to see if he liked it.  He didn't.
07. Went onto a bridge with full knowledge of the Drake guarding it and died in a horrible fire anyway.
08. Said "Oh, they're just stupid rats, same as every RPG, what harm could they do?" and learned how long poison lasts.
09. Turned human for all of 10 minutes until I was invaded by a red twink with H4X.
10. Used my mouse to click focus back into the Dark Souls window from checking Twitter only to realize left click attacks and attacking while standing in front of the blacksmith may not be the best choice to make at this juncture in the game since I haven't purchased the Crest of Artorias yet and the Priest wants 20,000 souls to patch things up.
It's an extremely difficult game, and very unforgiving if you let it take advantage of you.  Zelda this game is not.  You won't be able to take multiple hits to the face to learn a boss' moves like you can in Ocarina of Time, which can be off-putting for newer players, but if you stick with it and allow yourself to learn the nuances of what the game expects it won't disappoint you.  The only disappointing thing is just how awful this PC port is.  720p at a cap of 30fps?  Give me a break!
Just to let you know what you're in for:
First, you want the mod DSFix.  If you never use any other mod for the game, let this be the one.  This mod allows you to fix the resolution and framerate which are both completely terrible bone stock.  As for myself, I also had to add the game's .EXE to a list of exceptions in Data Execution Prevention, because for some reason the game was only giving me 23fps.  After DSFix I'm running at a stable 1080p @60fps with no problems and gosh it's pretty.
Second, I use an Xbox One controller and it works perfectly.  Mouse and Keyboard are totally broken and should be avoided if at all possible.  There are fixes, but I haven't messed with them.
Yes, it sucks when a Steam game requires tinkering just to get it to work, especially when it's some old dollar piece of junk from 1993 you got on a sale, but this game is worth the tinkering.  The community has some great stickies you need to read and they'll help immensely.  Trying to parry at 10fps is impossible, so it was nice to realize it wasn't totally my fault once DSFix was running.
10/10 would give a black knight just the tip again.

don't let its feminine anime charm fool you; this is a dark as hell game with a surprising amount of depth. despite it looking and somewhat playing like a visual novel, Long Live the Queen is instead a twisted quasi-strategy game - in which one slight misstep in your princess's teachings can result in an unexpected death. a fun little jaunt, if somewhat stretched a little thin.

Long Live The Queen is a graphical text adventure game where you play a princess who'll one day become the queen,... if you can survive until the coronation, that is. The princess will have to take daily classes (one in the morning, one in the evening) and that way level up her skills. It's up to you how you invest those skills. Want her to study court manners and impress your friends or relatives ? Or study naval strategies ? You decide how you want to do make her the best queen she can be.
There are many things to take into consideration, like bonuses and penalties, and things that have yet to happen. And do you want to level up a few skills completely, or do you want to level up a bit of everything.
One thing's for sure; there's no right way to properly finish this game, because it involves a lot of luck and a certain bit of skill and there are many, many different outcomes.
I enjoyed it quite a bit. It's different than many of the other games I usually play, and that's saying something.
[Rating: 75/100]

This one is tricky.
As Zero is not my favorite [old] RE game, that will forever fall on RE2, I find myself loving and then ... not so much at times. I haven't played this particular game since 2003 or so, so the old RE play style takes some getting used to again. It's survival horror / puzzle / jump scare / etc and thats what made me love the older RE titles. That is intact, and upgraded, and the modern control scheme makes on hell of a difference. Though all of the old gripes are still there. As an 'HD Remaster' it looks fatastic, even if the cut sceens are just upscaled versions of the original, the game itself is pretty as pie. It doesnt feel like a cheap reskin like a lot of other 'HD' re-releases.
Being that most of the puzzles after the first 10 minutes require you to switch back and forth between the two main characters, is not only frustrating at times, but utimately begs for a mutiplayer / co-op mechanic. There is none, there never was. Thankfully there is no real need for partner AI, other than 'Don't waste all the damn ammo' which you have control over. Another annoying, though expected of the series, some of the puzzles are not nearly as self explainitory as you would think. Sometimes they require you to be literally in two places at once, and after learning that you have to backtrack a character.
The inventory in this particular game, is well, horid. You have 6 slots for each character, 12 in total, and at minimum 2 from each are for a weapon, and applicable ammo. To say nothing of health items and puzzle items, which you will be endlessly juggling back and forth when you absolutely need all of the things, then backtrack to pick up whatever you had to leave behind. Old gripe, but could have used some tweaking.
Technically speaking, the game need a little work. My machine meets / exceeds the recommended specs, and there are some sections, mainly around smokey / foggy areas, where it slows to a crawl. I dropped the resoltion to 1280, and the visuals to medium to compensate. Which still looks good, but is NOT why I re-bought a game that I owned over a decade ago.
All things considered, I still favor this entry to the series over literally ANY of the later games, as they have long forgotten there survival-horror roots, which is ltteraly the only reason I liked the older games to begin with. Omg ... 5 was f**king terrible. I am happy that they are making a return in these 'Remake' versions, and I look forward to playing RE1:HD after I complete this one. And RE2:HD if it's not just a rumor (fingers crossed).
If your an old fan of the series, I'd say buy it. Even if it isn't as great as the others, it's still a solid pass. If you like the later, more 'action-y' entries, this probably isn't for you.

Pros:
-The old school RE feel.
-Sound and music are great.
-Pre-rendered backgrounds look fantastic.
-Decent story, not the greatest ever, but it's cool nonetheless.
Cons
-There are NO ITEM BOXES. None. This is because you can drop any item in your inventory, whenever, wherever. Don't worry, it'll be marked on your map. The only reason I put this in the 'cons' is because, well, I liked item boxes. It kept things more organized.
-Several lame boss battles.
-Voice acting is forgettable, but in reality, none of the games in this series have had decent voice acting.
8.75/10  Solid entry in the series.

Instead what we have here is a series of scenarios you play through in order - tried to play through the first in the recommended difficulty and I just repeatedly failed, it did not seem to matter what I chose and the biggest issue was the lack of visual clues of how well you were doing and how the hostages were responding. One minute all seems to go well and in a second later the hostages run one by one and you can either let them go free or shoot them - all winding up wth you having no hostages and failing soon after. Alternately you concentrate on the hostages and the guards take you out.
What looked like a game where I could play out these scenes with some experimentation end enjoy different narrative outcomes is in fact a linear experience - someone will no doubt post a guide up that you have to follow to get a win for each scenario - but where is the real fun in that? The game is a lesson in frustration and nothing more. Its nowhere near as exciting or as adventurous in its approach as it would have you believe from the trailer video in its current form.
Its a micro-management game with poor visual clues, limited choices and also looks like it will have little replayability to it. Looks like you either have to complete a scenario one way or not at all. Its like a McPixel with more choices but less humour.
BEWARE FOR ANY MAC USERS. This game runs terribly on OSX 10.9. It's nearly unplayable. Until this issue is resolved I wouldn't recommend it to any MAC users. I cannot speak for Windows.

While Gods Will Be Watching has a unique and appealing artstyle and promises, 'narrative puzzles and moral dilemmas that will affect both the lives of your team and the people you’re are sworn to protect.' The game however is unfortunately based on resource management and a laughable amount of RNG based choices; also the promise of moral dilemmas seems to impact very little on the game itself.
Whilst the intriguing story and beautiful sountrack create an immersive experience, it is unfortunately ruined by many of the in-game choice being determined solely on 'Lady Luck' which many perceive as simply a high level of difficulty which is simply not the case.
To conclude I would not recommend this title due to the game; mostly relying soley on luck which overall detracts significantly on what could have been an immersive and enjoyable experience.

There are currently a number of issues with the game that force me to be unable to recommend a purchase at this time.

This is, for many people (read the forums), considered a bug that needs fixing before the first level is adequately enjoyable or even completable without simple luck.
Further issues have been raised regarding the second stage, and a transitional story/immersion breaking incident between the second and third stages.
I am fully aware that the game is supposed to be difficult, but there's difficult and near impossible - even on the advertised 'easy' mode.
The developers need to read the forums and answer the concerns raised, dealing with the perceived issues in urgently-needed patches. Once these issues have been resolved, I expect to be able to change my recommendation accordingly.

(RPS REVIEW POINT: It’s beautiful, no doubt. The pixel art is wonderful, and the soundtrack is splendid. Looking at just the screenshots, I’d be reaching for my wallet. But the core game is just so tedious. By the fifth chapter, you’re literally wandering through near-identical scenes of desert, and at this point I’m honestly wondering if maybe this is the point? Maybe it’s some arch commentary on gaming, on our repeating tasks because we’re told to, for meaningless rewards? There’s certainly enough meta-stuff going on along the way to imply this is where it’s heading, but dear me, if so, then the smugness would burst the walls. I really cannot find the will to keep putting myself through it to find out if the point was how much I’m wasting my time putting myself through it. During my fifth go the game announced it was out of memory, and closed itself, and yeah, that will do.
I’m really gutted about this. I’ve been interested in the project since the first screenshots, and there’s unquestionably a huge amount of potential for someone to try to combine long-term survival with resource management in this form. But this is a tiresomely repetitive affair, and snarky with it. Perhaps the big reveal that lies at the end would astonish me, but there’s been nothing to earn the persistence I already put in, let alone any more. Let the gods judge me for that.)

The developers successfully crowded-funded the game by promising to bring us a new Baldur's Gate-style game, and they succeeded. If you liked Baldur's Gate or Icewind Dale, this is a great game. The worldbuilding is excellent and it's always fun to see how your character's specific background, stats and actions shape their options in dialogue. There are times when it feels like I am playing with the world's longest-suffering DM, as I sneak my thief protagonist about and raid every single container available even in a poor residential area. I can imagine this DM rubbing their forehead and sighing, then announcing, "Fine, you find some cheese. No, there are no more boxes to open."
Strategy is important. Mechanics are balanced, to a point that I generally have a difficult time judging if any particular item is better or worse than any other -- this set of armor has better damage reduction, but it slows down the character's actions; this weapon has better damage rolls, but it takes longer to use so maybe it's better to hit an enemy multiple times with a smaller-damage weapon. Some of it turns out to simply be about knowing the types of enemies you'll be fighting in an area, as this ghost is immune to piercing damage but that creature is well-armored and you should go in with armor-bypassing weapons. So on.

Now I know that's more than I probably needed but I liked taking the long route with everything. This is a game that puts you in the character's shoes and has you run a marathon, and I mean that in a good way. You start to feel for Mae, for Bea, for Angus, for Gregg, for Casey, and for everyone else. You choose what you say to them, choose where you go and how, and you form your own path in this sense. I can't speak for everyone as there's probably someone who claims to have predicted everything and got it right, but this game caused me to expect different outcomes from each interactions, and then took nearly of them and gave me something I never would have thought of.
I fully intend to play through the game again, choosing different paths, and I think anyone else who has played this game will agree with me when I say, you'll want to as well.

I already own 2 copies of Renaissance - one purchased at Amazon to get the non-updated, non-broken version so I could finish the thing - and 1 of Resurrection - which I've never finished because of all the bugginess and the way the Undead Hordes are so underpowered and handicapped it isn't even funny. Even so, I went ahead and purchased this based on the positive reviews that indicated a lot of the issues have been resolved.
I expected simply a better working, better balanced version of the original but I'm happy to say that this is an entirely different game all the way around. Not sure I'm happy with the new battle mechanics, though, but I suppose I'll get used to it. I can already tell that the balance for the Empire army has drastically changed - not nearly as overpowered as it was, which gives me hope that perhaps the balance of the Legions and the Undead Hordes has improved so that they aren't so weak. On the other hand, I will probably not use auto-combat in this one as much as I did in the others. My army tends to get decimated if I'm not in control.
Another hope is that I won't experience as many crashes as before, although the game did freeze up after one battle. Once I got the game to minimize, there was a low memory warning on the screen that doesn't make sense since my computer is built to be a gaming computer with as much gaming power as HP could give it.
Also have to mention the opening, which is phenomenal. Much better than the original. The storyline seems much improved as well. Kind of makes me wish I could read Russian so I could read the book that was written based on the game.
Despite the nerfed battle system (only my opnion, though), I believe this is going to be $30 well spent and I do recommend the game.

There are threads and threads of bad press about this game in its past forms. Gods Will be Watching first came into being for Ludum Dare 26, at the end of April 2013. The demo is freely available, and was interesting, if bleak-- I never beat it. The demo places you in the role of a Sergeant Burden, stranded with his crew on a hostile planet. It's a game of multi-tasking; you need to keep you and the crew warm, fed, free of disease, keep morale up, repair the radio so you can send out a distress signal, and fend off the local wildlife.
If that sounds like a lot, it is. Like I said, I never beat the damn thing. I kept focusing so hard on staying on top of things and doing my best to save everyone. I inevitably spread myself too thin, so I would consistently end up saving no one at all. But the demo handled this well, very well, even. Nothing happens all at once-- instead things slowly start going to hell around you, and as you try and patch up one problem, another crops up. By the time you realize things have gotten out of hand, it's too late.
It's a fascinating approach to handling choice in the storytelling, because it's based so much on knowing how people are going to play the game. It's never posing binary options to you: it asks you to prioritize, and it will actively use perfectionist tendencies against you.
The full version of Gods Will be Watching steps up the game. Where the demo had no real urgency to it, the first gameplay sequence is a tense hostage situation. The atmosphere very much encourages you to rush, though the game is largly turn-based: time only advances when you make a choice.
If you rush, you will die. You'll die a lot in general, actually. The game is broken up into multiple discrete scenarios, and until you learn to manage the unique needs of each scenario, you will die repeatedly, even on easy mode. With this comes one of my few quibbles with the game-- there's no quicksave or way to save within a scenario. When you die, you have to start over from the beginning, no matter how far you've gotten. While this plays well into the game's ethos of outright forcing you to sacrifice something, after a few tries it gets really frustrating to have to go through ten or twenty minutes of gameplay over and over again. I would really appreciate being able to drop a save at a mid-scenario checkpoint.
The art style is that skinny-legged highly-pixelated look that Sword and Sworcery popularized. I'm not a fan of the style but it's skillfully done, and reducing faces to a pixely blur actually helps the mood of the game. It looks good, and the game covers subject matter where it needs to be careful to walk a line between showing too much detail and not enough.
This is because the game throws you into a torture sequence as its second scenario. It doesn't pull any punches. I was nervous going into this sequence, given you can beat, maim, or kill hostages in the first one. You don't ever really have to, but the option remains open and visible, and I kept wondering if I would have to. In a few failed attempts, I did. But I'm avoiding talking about the torture scenario. It's brutally portrayed-- the heavy pixelation of the graphics is both a relief for being so vague and a horror for leaving enough open to the imagination. It's explicitly not torture porn, because pornography is intended to be pleasurable.
Which, if anything is, the central flaw of the game. It's not pleasurable: it's a harrowing experience. It's compelling, it's fascinating, but it's not something that will ever make you feel good. I don't think it's important that a game be pleasurable experience, however. It's not something necessary to any other sort of fiction-- most books, movies, and TV will be fun, to be sure, but by no means do any of them need to be fun to be good. But it's definitely something worth noting; you're going to need to hug a pet or loved one after playing.
Going as far in the game as I have (as I said, it's very difficult; I'm still working on it), it's still in question to me if how you play each scenario affects anything at all about later ones. The game does track, say, if anyone at all dies, but dead characters seem to still appear in the following chapter. Something seems strange about it, though-- I'm not entirely certain if those returning characters are real or some sort of hallucination. I'm not entirely sure if it matters either way, for two distinct reasons.
First, the choices you make in the gameplay are the gameplay. It's never really telling you that it's doing it; it's never giving you prompts of "be good person y/n". But every action you take is at the expense of a different action, with its own risks. It's certainly possible to try and go for a 'perfect' run-through or a 'villain' game but without a guide in hand you'll have to take your chances, and only you the player-- the titular, metaphorical 'god'-- will be judging the actions. The game follows through on the notion that it's not assigning a meaning of right or wrong to your actions in a way that few do. The only goal you are given is to survive to the end of the scenario. Anything else along the way is optional, and you're not even informed of what all your options could have been until the end of the chapter. (At the end of each, you're given data on how your actions match up to how others have played the same scenario, something I'm glad to see in wider usage than just Telltale games. This is the closest the game comes to judging you: your overall approach will be characterized with a single word. My attempts to dribble out miniscule amounts of information in order to space out beatings were inevitably characterized as 'suicidal'. The assessment appears to have no impact on play.)
Second is that GWBW tells a reasonably compelling story. Enough so that I've been fairly circumspect about saying anything at all about it. There's an evil space empire and a rebel group you've infiltrated and an apparently-neutral third party that you work for. Biological weapons and the question of where the line between freedom-fighting and terrorism actually is, and how being personally affected will change where you see those lines. It's heavy stuff, and I don't see the game answering any of those questions for you. But there's a character story in here, too, or more specifically a story about relationships. Donald and Sarah are married, Jack loves the dog that comes along, Burden and Jack go through hell together... and then there's the relationship between Burden and Liam, head of the rebel group Xenolifer. It's strangely intimate, the way Burden speaks about him, hangs so much of his sympathy for the Xenolifer cause on Liam
himself. It stands out starkly amidst the stilted phrasing and outright gameness that forces you to keep the game at arm's length.
Gods Will be Watching is not an immersive game, but that's okay. It's a game that works best at a distance, when you're treating it as a game to be beaten, a puzzle to be solved, because that's where the failure cascades the game thrives upon come from. If you throw yourself into the place of Sergeant Burden, if you decide in advance what constitutes acceptable losses, you're not going to be feeling that rising dread, and it won't change to panic just before everything goes all to hell.
The game is by no means flawless; the text of the game is, even where it's grammatically correct, written in stilted, unnatural English. Given Deconstructeam is based out of Spain, I'm neither surprised nor hugely bothered by this lack of conversational mastery, and they know how to use it to create atmosphere. But a more thorough edit is a level of polish that I think would make for a better game.

Gods Will Be Watching is point & click game that's all about making the right - and sometimes moral - choices in order to survive. Take your time, the decision-making is basically turn-based so keep your wits about you!

3 and a half hours in, and I'm done.
The good: the hand-drawn artwork is unique. The story is interesting and creative.
The bad: voiceovers are awful and really detract. Dialogue is, I think, meant to be humorous but comes off as childish and unpolished. Repeated translation wonkiness from German -- count how many times you see the word phantasm used wrong! Cutscenes are animated but the quality here is pretty poor compared to the rest of the game.
As an adventure game, there are quite a number of wonky puzzles you have to solve through "creative" logic. Some make sense, others are the usual adventure-game nonsense, like grabbing tree resin that you can only get in one very specific way in spite of having a bunch of decent objects in your inventory that can be used by any sane person.
Confession: I had to use a walkthrough to get out of the first area as I couldn't for the life of me figure out what the game wanted. Things got a little better after that, but then the nonsense logic puzzles returned. I lack the patience to make another go at figuring out the logic in the designer's mind.
The engine itself reminds one of a 90's LucasArts game, with colored text appearing above each speaking character. The text is typically various shades of brown, so it has a tendency to blend into the backgrounds at times, making things harder to read. Why games still model themselves from 90's LucasArts in this regard is a mystery: word balloons would make a world of difference. Easier to mimic what once worked, I guess.
I also had some difficulty clicking on items. Sometimes I had to hold the mouse button down longer, sometimes I had to click real fast. I couldn't really figure out a system that worked consistently.
I'm not really cut out for adventure games, honestly, so in the end it's not a surprise this didn't click for me. If you like the adventure game genre, maybe this will work for you.
Not recommended: 2.5 out of 5.

The Whispered World is not a point and click adventure (PCA) for the faint hearted. The game is suited to someone who enjoyed the challenge of games like Discworld back in 1995 or someone who is a fans of a story driven PCA with puzzles to solve and mystery to unravel.
I fear this game will be quickly passed over by many due to two factors: They will dislike the voice acting for the protagonist and or the PCA/puzzles will be too frustrating to figure out.
My advice is try not to scorn the character based on the voice but rather try to have some empathy for the character, he is after all; on first impression, a rather woeful Milquetoast, with an underlying pensive sadness disguised with apathetic sarcasm. The true irony however is that he is in fact a melancholic clown and even the poignancy of his humour is so that the juxtaposition of this character leaves you curious for what more it has to offer and I can tell you the answer is a lot more.
Due to the availability of information on the Internet, we no longer need to spend weeks trying to figure out a single puzzle or wait for the game guide to be released at the local PC store. If you are stuck, to the point of thinking about giving up on the game, I implore you to seek assistance in overcoming your particular challenge and continue on, this game, I feel, can only really be appreciated to its full extent if played to the end.

-To start off, DaS1 was my first played in the series with well over 1k+ hours on the PS3. From there I branched out to Demon's, DaS3, and finally DaS2 (SotFS), in that order. I've never played an ounce of gameplay from Bloodborne (hopefully that'll change soon) but I've watched extensive amounts of it.-
So what can there be said that hasn't been said already? This game is truly a classic and a masterpiece of its time.
The most important feature of a game should be its gameplay, and the designers of the combat system knew exactly this. While fairly simple on the surface, it's incredibly flexible and deep, while at the same time feeling satisfying and rewarding with the main limit being your own choices. Your options constantly expand as you gain knowledge about the game's mechanics and enemies, and you yourself only improve which breeds a healthy sense of accomplishment.
It cannot be ignored that this game has received a notorious reputation for being extremely hard and difficult. While I don't disagree, I believe the simple notion of being challenging was widely overblown (and massively over-advertised). But don't let that turn you away from this game. It is a game of learning, requiring a slower, analytical approach to the obstacles you face, and then formulating an effective strategy to overcome them. All this finally ending in a test of your own skill and execution. There is a solution to every hurdle you encounter, multiple in fact, so it's just a matter of finding you own.
Outside the core gameplay, all the other aspects of the game hold up just as well and only serve as icing on the cake.
The world design is superb, with gigantic, sprawling, and diverse areas that brilliantly exude the atmosphere of a dark and lonely journey. It's a shining example of how a metroidvania (if you acknowledge that term) should be transitioned into 3d. A darker themed Zelda would suffice as a moderate comparison I believe.
Music, mainly restricted to boss fights, is absolutely top notch, often fitting with their intimidating looks and/or with the environment you fight in, as well as just being exciting battle fanfare.
The Story is rather interesting and can branch out to multiple scenarios, which can also include your own made-up one like a good ol' rpg. What makes that last case possible is what I think is the story's greatest strength, which is staying in the background, allowing you to be involved in it as much or as little as you desire.
There really is so much I've left untouched with this review, but I've gone over what I believe are the most pertinent aspects this game has to offer and why it has appealed to and garnered the hearts of so many people. This is a game unquestionably worth your money, whether it be 20$ or the common sale for 5$ (regardless, it already comes with the DLC!)
Final mentions
-Controller is an absolute must though (if you didn't read the disclaimer near the top) unless you want to suffer more than already will on a first playthrough.
-Look into the DSFix mod for 60fps if your eyes cannot stand the game's normal 30.
-Look into the DSCM app/mod for increased online activity.

This game will be great, but needs further development. It freezes sometime. I'm playing on a Mac, so here are some protips for Mac users:
• The crouch command is set to left control initially. That doesn't apply to every Mac user, so I reassigned it to 'K' for kneel.
• Anticipate it freezing up often. The best way to deal with this is to save constantly, & when it freezes up type ⌘+option+esc simultaneously (the Mac equivalent to ctrl+alt+delete) & then enter twice to exit the application. This will keep you from having to restart your computer for the sake of the game.
• The game does not respond well to being out of full screen mode. I tried that for a while, so that I could type ⌘+shift+tab simultaneously to go to the Finder & regain control of the mouse. Ultimately I don’t recommend it. It freezes up within 5 minutes of starting the game this way.
Otherwise the game is quite enjoyable. Strategically gathering & allocating your resources while figuring out the pretty straight forward controls & character capabilities is great! If you were a fan of Minecraft, Starbound, or other simulation games, then you will enjoy Stranded Deep, & since it's still early access there's so many dynamic possibilities for the game!

Counter-Strike: Condition Zero is the first official sequel to mod Counter-Strike, released in retail in 2004. It was pretty much same Counter-Strike on same engine and minimal changes when it comes to multiplayer experience, but it had more to often to solo players, with addition of bots and "Deleted Scenes" pack of single-player missions.
Now, for multiplayer community... Is as good as ever. While it's not on the level of Counter-Strike 1.6, you will still be able to find few almost-full servers, whetever it's yet another De_Dust2 map or some server that actually rotates maps. Just more smaller tighter community. BUT it's kinda way too high-skilled by now for newbies to be able to enter in easily.
So, when it comes to the main, expected, multiplayer part of the game, it didn't recieve many changes. Explosive grenades are stronger. Hostages are a bit more realistical. The end.
Oh, and you will ntoice that graphics got a small boost, as far as HL1 engine goes ("GldSrc"). Models got more detail to them. Few tweaks here and there. Maps are much interesting as far as graphical design goes. If you are going to play de_dust2 non-stop then better do it at the less bland one.
And yes, I don't really like Counter-Strike realistical gameplay much here either.
Now, for single-player, you finally get some bots to play with. Which are less frustating for new people than online play and helps to hone aiming skills as well better. Though, while they navigate through default maps quite nicely, they don't always make best decision. As a protip, always send them a voice command to stick together, team. They also try not to steal your fun of defusing bomb, waiting for commander to do it, even if said commander is in opposite end of map. Yes, it's a flaw.
And like Quake 3 Arena and UT, CZ single player consist of repeated matches with bots, as you will progress through trio of maps, being able to pick less and less stupid teammates over time, always being on side of Counter-Terrorists. And on each map, you have to have more than 2 wins over score of Terrorist team and have to complete each of three objectives, which go like "rescue <x> hostages", "kill <x> amount of Terrorists yourself", "finish some round in <x> time" and "kill <x> terrorists with <y> weapon".  So, fun for a while, but more of "just so something was there".
And now for Deleted Scenes. This is what Counter-Strike: Condition Zero was supposed to be at some point, a full-blown single-player campaign. It was "cancelled" once Valve saw magazines giving it low ratings to preview, just to have it put along as bonus into final game. All just to get low ratings once again due to being "more of same". Deleted Scenes had 12 missions in retail release, with Steam version adding 6 more that you can select anytime from World Map.
Now, Deleted Scene is a mix of good and bad. The excellent level design and repetive core gameplay.
First, good things. Level design is quite good one. You will have to take control of unnamed heroes of counter-terrorist operations all over the world, with missions having great variety, with enough lenght to keep you playing, having to stop terrorists from taking over nuke in snowy part of Russia, defending yourself in Arabain town or fighting your way through the jungles. Seriously, some of the missions just have a bit of that scripted hollywood love that would make them worthy of being in Call of Duty and alikes, quite epic! Levels themselves are also build with knowledge of pacing and a bit of exploration, albeit linear.
And it really tries to push GldSrc engine! In order to make it look like it's capable of more than expected, developers made a lot of animations of death for terrorists as well as destruction animations. Hell, I was amazed to see a stack of boxes getting squeezed by a door in the third mission, it's all quite joy to look at even if it's scripted. And well, it does hurt occasionally when it comes to enemies deaths. Like, when you shot with pistol at melee enemy into knee and he suddenly teleported half-meter away to the door, swirled and fell toward the door, just to get it open.
But core gameplay of Counter-Strike doesn't translate well at all into linear levels of single-player. What you bassicly will do, is to shoot few bullets into heads, while taking some hitscan bullets back. Repeat it on every enemy. Until the end of the game. It really is repetive and boring. Weapons don't matter much, all of them are good enough for bursting enemy again and again. Grenades aren't given often and flashbang don't seem to be as useful as in multiplayer. Smoke grenade is more offensive there though, making enemies cough instead sometimes. There is little enemy variety as well, you just got whatever hitscan stupid enemy, stationary snipers with laser, whatever melee enemy that rushes you and terrorist with freaking bazooka that is pain to avoid too! So, burst headshot, and burst headshot, repeat repeat repeat.
It also finally get to have some music there. For once. So, something definitely good.
Counter-Strike Condition Zero is better offer than Counter-Strike 1.6 and has more value for solo players, but it's still not good enough to get me much interested in such twitchy realistical shooter. I still wouldn't recommend new people, especially with newer CS titles out there, only those who already play Counter-Strike should check out this one.

To all the fans of Baulder's Gate: you need this game in your life.
Incredibly deep and wonderfully immersive, Pillars of Eternity is absolutely stuffed to the brim with so much lore that you'll wonder which has more - this, or Skyrim. With tons of races, classes, and choices of playstyle, you're guaranteed to find the perfect fit.
As someone who has no patience for turn-based combat, I'm rather fond of the fact that I can just let my party go at it with enemies on auto-pilot. Very often I'll find they've decimated the opposition so quickly that some summoning spells have just been cast and now I have to wait that extra second or two for the summoned allies to disappear before I can loot all those corpses. Other times, I'll find my party absolutely destroyed because I've run headfirst into a difficult fight that really shouldn't be attempted without using the turn-based combat system properly, or else over-leveling by a lot.
One of the most intensely satisfying things about Pillars of Eternity is the vast number of choices in dialogue and how different choices affect your story in different ways. This is not the game to go about "exhausting all the dialogue options" - often, if you try to, you'll find that you've♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥someone important off, or doomed a character's fate, or swayed a faction's views in the opposite direction from your intention.
So! Do yourself the favor: Buy this game. Play it. Immerse yourself. And don't look back.

The graphics are kind of weak, the story is a boring cliche, the music is practically nonexistent, and the gameplay is repetitive, but despite that I still love State of Decay! That's because as far as zombie survival games go, State of Decay actually is about survival. You have to find a group of other survivors to join because you won't last long alone. You have to defend whichever safehouse you have chosen from roaming zombies and hordes. You have to scavange other places for suplies such as weapons, food, fuel, construction materials, and medical suplies. You have to create outposts with traps in strategic locations (up to you to decide what's strategic) to keep the hordes from owerwhelming your safehouse. You have to find and take care of vehicles as damage to them can be permanent. You have to manage your inventory when searching for supplies, along with managing your safehouse construction projects, and whatever group problems that might arise. You have to take care of infestetions and some special zombies, otherwise they'll do some serious damage if they get into the safehous area. You have to do some side missions for other survivor groups and rescue strangers if you want to expand your own group. And once you've done all that and practically looted the whole town, you can pack up and move to a different safehouse.
There are some issues with the game though: the animations are kind of buggy - sometimes zombies will attach to you while you swing an axe at them or jump over a fence, or in the midst of a roll dodge animation; vehicle physics are some of the worst in all of games I've ever played; mouse & keyboard controls suck; aiming is extremely hard with a controller as the camera sensitivity is too high when aiming a gun; and lastly, Lilly doesn't seem to know the concept of not talking! Although there is a mod that fixes the last problem.
I'd recommend getting the Breakdown DLC, even though it should've been included in the original game. It's the proper sandbox zombie survival mode.

This game isn't as good as the REmaster from a year ago, but it's still great if you're looking for some more classic Resident Evil. Controlling two characters can put a damper on the game for some, but to me it just increases the tension. Another character to look out for means another weapon to keep loaded and another person to keep healthy.
Item management is a bigger thing here, and there are no item boxes. However you can drop items wherever you like and use some items when picking them up, even if your inventory is full. Both characters have their own item slots (making 12 slots in total), however there are items and weapons that take up more than one slot. Not going to lie, item management can get a little sloppy at times.
Graphical enhancements are the same as what you would expect after playing the first REmaster, with some character models and pictures being redone. I have run into a couple hiccups with the audio during cutscenes, but it's not even for a second, so it isn't really that bad. 1080p, 60fps goodness is here as well. No 4k resolution support that I am aware of.
Controls, like the first REmaster, are completely customizable for keyboard and mouse, while controller gets five different preset controls. I recommended keyboard and mouse for the first REmaster, but I may have to recommend a controller this time. Main reason being is that you can control the other character with the other stick without having to switch to the other character. You can still control the other character with the arrow keys (or whatever keys you wish to bind them as). Also, you cannot control one character with the new control scheme (non-tank controls) and then control the other character with classic tank controls. You have to control both characters with the same control scheme.
The game still keeps the non-hand holding and throwing you into a maze type of game, well if you can really call being on a train a maze. If the game doesn't do it for you right away, get past the train at least. The game pick ups after that and gets a lot better. The environment will feel a lot more "Resident Evil" then. Plus leech men are probably the freakiest thing you'll encounter.

Let me start off by saying that, in my opinion, this is the BEST ccg out there.  As you can tell by my hours logged in, I obviously love it.  A lot of time has actually been played via my browser too so I probably have close to an additional 400hrs.
With all that aside, this isn't your typical Pay to win model.  You can purchase ANY card in this game without having to pay real money.  Is there a grind?  Yes.  I'd be lying if I said there wasn't.  However, you can earn gold rather quickly through several ways.  One way is the campaign.  They now did away with the energy bar so you can play as much of the campaign as you'd like.  Once you defeat the campaign, the energy bar is implemented if you want to replay any of the "Nodes".  Another way to earn gold is through Guild Wars.  You can gain gold if you win your certain matches then bonus gold if your guild wins that war.  It can build up quickly. Also, there are daily rewards for logging (Which can also reward you with cards, or gems).  You can also purchase any hero for Gold.  There are currently 27 heroes, 6 or 7 of which you earn through completing the campaign.  You can also gain gems through playing in the arena.  2 per day and a bonus of a minimum of 20 at the end of the war if you play something like 20 PvP matches.  On top of that, if you log in 20 times during the month, you're awarded an addiitonal 20 gems.
My favorite part of the game is the variety.  There are 6 Kingdoms along with a 7th neutral kingdom if you will (Unaligned).  There are heroes for each, with their own special abilities which gain charges each turn.  Each hero truly feels different and all have their own benefits to play to a certain playstyle and deck build.   There are numerous types of cards to play:  Creatures, Gear such as weapons and armor/shields, Spells, Runes (Which take effect each turn and benefits or hurts each side).  Like I said, a lot of variety.  It should also be noted that creatures also have abilities.  And there are A LOT of abilities.  However, with all of this being said, the learning curve is very short.  There is a lot you can do but its easy to learn but difficult to master type of thing.
I can also say that the player base is overall very friendly and helpful.  Someone is always around in the chat to offer guidance and advice with new players.  There are also 4 tiers for Guild Wars, which is pretty easy to find someone to take you in to "Show you the ropes)  =)
Update*  Just purchased my 2nd Legendary card in the past 3 months.  Both with gold earned from Guild Wars and the Arena.  Also during that time, I purchased 2 boxes (20 packs) worth 149 gems each without having to pay a dime of my real money...  For ppl who say this is a P2W game, you may need to revise your strategy =)

-To start off, DaS1 was my first played in the series with well over 1k+ hours on the PS3. From there I branched out to Demon's, DaS3, and finally DaS2 (SotFS), in that order. I've never played an ounce of gameplay from Bloodborne (hopefully that'll change soon) but I've watched extensive amounts of it.-
So what can there be said that hasn't been said already? This game is truly a classic and a masterpiece of its time.
The most important feature of a game should be its gameplay, and the designers of the combat system knew exactly this. While fairly simple on the surface, it's incredibly flexible and deep, while at the same time feeling satisfying and rewarding with the main limit being your own choices. Your options constantly expand as you gain knowledge about the game's mechanics and enemies, and you yourself only improve which breeds a healthy sense of accomplishment.
It cannot be ignored that this game has received a notorious reputation for being extremely hard and difficult. While I don't disagree, I believe the simple notion of being challenging was widely overblown (and massively over-advertised). But don't let that turn you away from this game. It is a game of learning, requiring a slower, analytical approach to the obstacles you face, and then formulating an effective strategy to overcome them. All this finally ending in a test of your own skill and execution. There is a solution to every hurdle you encounter, multiple in fact, so it's just a matter of finding you own.
Outside the core gameplay, all the other aspects of the game hold up just as well and only serve as icing on the cake.
The world design is superb, with gigantic, sprawling, and diverse areas that brilliantly exude the atmosphere of a dark and lonely journey. It's a shining example of how a metroidvania (if you acknowledge that term) should be transitioned into 3d. A darker themed Zelda would suffice as a moderate comparison I believe.
Music, mainly restricted to boss fights, is absolutely top notch, often fitting with their intimidating looks and/or with the environment you fight in, as well as just being exciting battle fanfare.
The Story is rather interesting and can branch out to multiple scenarios, which can also include your own made-up one like a good ol' rpg. What makes that last case possible is what I think is the story's greatest strength, which is staying in the background, allowing you to be involved in it as much or as little as you desire.
There really is so much I've left untouched with this review, but I've gone over what I believe are the most pertinent aspects this game has to offer and why it has appealed to and garnered the hearts of so many people. This is a game unquestionably worth your money, whether it be 20$ or the common sale for 5$ (regardless, it already comes with the DLC!)
Final mentions
-Controller is an absolute must though (if you didn't read the disclaimer near the top) unless you want to suffer more than already will on a first playthrough.
-Look into the DSFix mod for 60fps if your eyes cannot stand the game's normal 30.
-Look into the DSCM app/mod for increased online activity.
