Today we have released a number of fixes and adjustments based on community feedback.
Tournaments
All Paid Tournaments (those with a Ticket Entry cost) will now award Light Ascending packs as prizes.
For our many new players, we are currently working on a new special prize pack for tournaments that will include all of the cards from our first three expansions, Eve, Rise and Tribes. When ready, we'll add this to the tournament rotation. We're also reviewing the overall tournament schedule to make it more fun for new players, including reintroducing the Pauper and Kingdoms formats. We'll have more on this in a later update.
Tribes
Tribes packs have been reduced in Gem price and are now available for Gold at a price of 20,000 per pack.
Rare Prices
The prices of rare singles in Eve, Rise and Tribes have been reduced overall.
Raise the Guard
Due to an unexpected interaction between Indestructible and self-sacrificing creatures (they don't die when Indestructible) we have removed the granting of Indestructible from Raise the Guard. We will be working to fix this interaction in an upcoming release, and at that time may reintroduce Indestructible to the card.
Note that yes, you can still achieve this using Belnir's 4 charge ability, but as this can't happen on turn 1 and takes effort to set up, we're leaving this as is.
Bug Fixes
Inverted Hourglass will no longer cause Out of Sync errors while being used in PVP.
AI Defending has been given an overhaul. It will no longer set creatures to defend improperly, and will be more likely to defend properly. Creatures with 1 Health and Armor will also no longer set themselves to Defend while Bleed is in play.
Realm Crusher will no longer count creatures with Indestructible as having been destroyed when setting its ATK/Health
Steam users can now use the Password Reset feature.

Kingdoms CCG looks simple on the surface but rates high in strategy. It is simple to learn and a good deal of fun, but a good strategy will take time to develop (or you could just youtube it) and the right cards to pull off. This is where a lot of players might be iffy on the game, as getting those cards freely isn't easy. The game has a huge campaign (huge for trading card games) that has daily and hourly rewards, gives lots of nice cards, and is very challenging towards the end. By the time you finish it you should have a decent core deck and be working on the expansions. The expansion cards themselves are not more powerful than the core cards, they simply open up more and different strategies, so the power creep isn't as bad here as it is in other TCG games and new players will only be behind in terms of the options they will have immediately availble to them (a still considerable amount in my opinion)
Alot of the negative reveiws for this game stem from the P2W argument and the FB Game style energy requirement. As for the P2W argument, I simply don't understand where its coming from, and I've played a lot of actual P2W games. The latest expansions do require premium currency (diamonds) instead of gold, but premium currencty can be aquried each day through daily events. As with most F2P games, almost every card in the library (and there are a lot) can be aquried with time, patience, and a bit of grinding. If you don't like grinding (understandable) there are also free tournaments and guild play, both of which have coin rewards and the tournaments reward free tickets, which allow you access into the tournaments that give cards and diamonds for rewards. As for the cards that can't be aquired this way, they are usually event and tournament rewards. There is VIP system in place if you do wish to spend money, but none of the cards they give are more "instant game winners" than many of the combinations and cards you can easily set up and aquire for free.
As for the energy issue, upon writing this the devs have already stated it will be removed for campaign progression. It is also not neccessary AT ALL for arena, tournaments, and guild based play. The only place it will still be required is picking up the freebies and crafting items that reset daily on the campaign map and for griding old campaign nodes if you don't want to play for gold in guilds or the arena.
Thus far the development team has been very active, and the prospects look fairly bright for a 2yr old card game. Should anything change drastically I will update this review, but if you like TCG and have some time to kill, this game is definitly worth taking a look at.
EDIT: After half a year things have only gotten MUCH BETTER for this game. Those marking it down arn't really giving it a chance at all. Many of the old arena and guild systems that caused some issue are being revamped. GANZ has released 2 new, game changing sets (with a third on it's way shortly). Older cards have actually been rebalanced to make them either playable, or to reign in some of the OP nonsense that pushed many newer players away. And deck building is going to be revamped to encourage more balanced and tactically based decks, dealing with the no.1 complaint of some competitive decks being nothing but a mash up of the highest curved cards. Some issues remain from the time ANTIC ran this game, but everything is looking up and it should definitely be given a fair chance.

Okay, I played the game through once and collected all artifacts etc.
So how do I feel about the game?
Short version:
It is a crude, very repetitive, button mashing game.
Longer version:
At first it feels like an actually good game, but after an hour or two you will see just how repetitive it gets.
There's only a few types of enemies that you beat over and over again, just like in a Dynasty Warriors game.
At first the combat system feels well done, that is when you fight a few enemies at a time. However, most of the time you will be swarmed with 20-30 orcs at the same time and it becomes a simple button masher which gets boring very, very fast.
While the story is ok, the game is artificially extended through stupid collecting of artifacts which are not interesting at all. You found a bag of weed. Yay. You can now rotate it around and look at it. Not to mention the only "quest" besides the main story you get is "Rescue the Slaves".
You have to do the "Rescue the Slaves" quest 24 times during the game. It's the same quest always, and the Slaves are carbon copies of each other. They all wear the same clothes, they all look exactly the same. So you're basically just saving clones. Boring...
Now, the game gives you the illusion you can make a difference, such as killing orc captains to weaken Saurons army. But no, you won't make a difference, it's simply a never-ending cycle. You kill a captain, and it will be replaced soon. You can keep killing them, and they come back.
It would be more fun if you actually could kill them permanently and significantly reduce the number of enemies by doing it, but no.
So okay, I did finish the game, and I didn't like it much. Sure, it looks quite pretty, runs smooth and the voice actors are good. But the rest of the game is just boring button masher, with annoying quick-time events.
Maybe I'm just getting too old for these button mashers, and kids like this stuff.
Anyway, If you want to try this, get it on sale. Maybe you'll like it, maybe you won't.

Maybe the best all around Avernum on steam (or at least until Avernum 2 and 3 show up in some form).  If you've never played an Avernum it might be best to start with "Escape From the Pit," but Avernum 6 is probably a stronger game overall.  Like EFTP it's very open world (although a few areas are closed off at the start), but it's biggest advantage is in its stat system, which uses the older skill based system that EFTP abandons in favor of a more simplistic skill tree model.  Plus, unlike Avernums 4 and 5 (which had trouble justifying their existences plot wise), the writing is great, setting the game in a sprawling kingdom in decline and exploring some darker themes like drug addiction, famine, and terrorism.
A great end to the series.

A+, a must play game. Amazing gameplay and graphics, even a couple years out from release. Keyboard-and-mouse controls are largely very intuitive, though I did find myself accidentally jumping off caragaths when sneaking unexpectedly transitioned to open combat.
Transition between moves is incredibly fluid given the sheer number of things you might do at any one time, and characters and environments look photorealistic; the acting (both vocal and on character faces) is excellent. Gameplay is a blast - the first half of the main story has play somewhat like Far Cry 4 (and apparently several other games I haven't played), and then halfway through you pick up some truly innovative tactical abilities.
The nemesis system - individually named orc captains who have varying personal abilities and remember your prior encounters! - is simply astonishing and brilliant. Combined with the effects of your growing legend, it feels like you're really having an effect on the world. It's also occasionally hilarious: the results of the "fear of X" mechanic, and the orcs' bragging about their lack of said fears, can be very funny. And then there's the orc captains' names... I ran into one with the epithet "Runny-bowels", and some of their actual names are impossible to listen to the wraith's delivery of without laughing, nevermind the Ominous Chanting that accompanies a warchief arriving.
Story is very strong, with interesting moral implications for the main character.
About the only complaint I have is that it's impossible to hear the voices in the loading screens (which apparently reveal bits of backstory) when volume is set reasonably for the rest of the game, and they aren't subtitled even with that option on.

This isn't just another zombie game, state of decay takes a unique take in allowing you to manage and swap between a group of survivors who are all stationed at one home base. This game focuses on the ability to build trust and and relationships between other survivors in order to lean them towards joining your group. You can also maintain and build up your home base. From tons of places to break into and rob blind, and endless hours of zombie killing fun, coming from someone who just beat this game and is now depressed, I definitely recommend it.

Death is permanent. You must recruit survivors. Maintain your base. Scavenge and find weapons, guns, medicine, and food.
Deal with your "friends" and their emotions; deal with them by killing zombies. Stay on good terms with survivors not yet in your community and they might just join you. Collect cars, and keep them working, because if they blow up or stop working they won't spawn again. Endure the night time, where hope is drained almost as fast as the bullets leave your rifle. Run from hordes, or if you are brave enough, and stupid enough, then take them on. Encounter dangerous special infected, ones so dangerous they can literally rip you in two. Set up outposts and make your area zed-free. Your fellow survivors will go on dangerous scavenging runs for you, fight for you, and die for you. Learn their stories, get to know them, and fight with them. You are a survivor. You are a KILLER. You are a savior. There is only one objective: Escape the valley.
This is how the game basically goes. I reccomend it 100% because it is amazing. Sure it suffers from some technical issues and such, but its still good.

Rest in peace, Marcus.
After establishing a strong settlement and successfully relocating them to the Snyder Trucking Co. Marcus lost his life. On night number 8, while trying to save 2 survivors.
He had already completed his initial mission, of hunting a Juggernaut, but the survivors showed up on his drive home. In desperate, and immediate need of help. Marcus was low on ammo and tired, this neighborhood was still dense with zeds and it was after dark... but he had to act.
Besieged by a horde with a feral, Marcus knew they couldn't make it. He had to act, I mean these were two fine honeys and the community needed more fine honeys!
Marcus dove from the pickup truck, leaving it hurtling towards a propane tank, which wiped out half of the horde. That should make up for the lack of ammo from the previous mission.  But, alas, the explosion attracted the attention of a nest of nearby screamers, AND failed to kill the feral.
Bravely, Marcus and the Honeys fought the remaining horde and the new zombies pouring out from the nearby infestation to their last breath. All was going well, when Marcus's trusty metal oar broke.
"6 slugs in my 44, a screamer, one feral and a whole passle of zombies... You got dis!" Marcus said to himself. Bam! Bam! Bam! Bam! Bam! 3 zombies and a screamer down. One shot left to take out the feral. The honeys can handle the half a dozen zeds. BAM! MISS!
"This ain't good, Marcus! You gotta come up with something. You gots ta save these honeys!" Marcus doubled back, he remembered seeing a Trans Am down the street, he could run the freak down. He hops in the whip, and power slides around the corner. Bearing down on the freak. It dodges. Marcus cranks the wheel hard and hits the hand brake. The TA was going to fast! He slides into a rock, rolling the car.
Marcus ejects, but he can't struggle to his feet fast enough. The freak is on top of him. Clawing and biting at his neck, he struggles free, and takes an exhausted and futile kick towards the freak, as three zeds are surrounding him. The honeys are engrossed in one on one battles for their own lives. They can't help him. He's on his own.
"COME AT ME, BRO!" Screams Marcus. The feral freak lunges. Marcus dives out of it's path. Scrambling to his feet, he kicks one zed against a picket fence and drives it's skull onto the wooden stake. He's grabbed from behind by another zed as he turns to strike at the freak. The freak latches onto to Marcus' legs, as the zed is biting into the back of his shoulder. Marcus struggles to get free, but in vain. The freak clamps down and tears Marcus in half, as he screams out into the night.
Your deeds will live on in the community you built. Farewell, Marcus. We will never forget The Black Knight.

What separates a cheap gimmick from a solid game mechanic is that a gimmick is a cute trick that's shown once, easily implemented, and then forgotten about. In "Forced", you're introduced to a variety of simple mechanics - but after learning them, you actually have to plan out your approach, and then you have to execute those mechanics under evolving conditions.
As a gladiator, you can equip one of four weapons, all of which are made available to you at the start and can be swapped out whenever you're not in a combat arena. What's impressive is that each one feels distinctly unique yet  equally effective. There is no "right" answer, but you need to familiarize yourself with whatever skillset you choose. Want to detonate kamikaze creeps at a distance with the Bow and Arrow? You'll have to position yourself so your line of sight isn't blocked by other enemies or obstacles. Or would you rather stand fast and absorb their explosions with the Shield? You'll need to make sure that your Blocking ability hasn't been triggered by other creeps by the time they connect. Or would you prefer setting them off with the invincibility frame of the Dagger's dash? You'd best double-check that you aren't dashing into an even worse position. "Forced" also uses my favorite kind of customization system, the kind that rewards good performance and encourages experimentation: outside of combat, you're free to mix and match any three active and three passive abilities that you've unlocked. This isn't a game for grinding - if you want to mindlessly farm loot for better gear and levels, search elsewhere. "Forced" is looking for players to go in, die, figure out what else they could try or how they could better execute their plan, and then go in again.
And on that note, you will definitely die, frequently with a curse on your lips. You will curse the fixed camera angle. You will curse the melee aiming controls. You will curse the occasionally dodgy hitbox. And then you'll put all of that aside and stubbornly head back into the same arena, and tackle the same enemies with a bit more insight and a touch more finesse, and then, suddenly, you'll have completed the Challenge and beaten the Time Limit and shout in triumph as you finally relax and soak in the feeling of a victory well earned.
The majority of my game time has been spent playing solo, which can be satisfying if you're the masochistic type; the game definitely wants to be played with friends. The framing device is another nice little touch. While it's nothing deep - just some light set dressing - the setting is plausible and manages to set itself apart from the typical "heroic journey to kill the ancient evil and seize forbidden treasure" cliche. Each of the major bosses has enough style to differentiate himself from the others, and Balfus has enough dialogue variety that he never becomes an annoyance.
"Forced" is by no means a perfect game (refer to the aforementioned sources of cursing) but it definitely carves out a memorable niche for itself. This is the proving grounds for gamers to test their timing, planning and patience. If you're the sort who's willing to go after tricky challenge objectives and you feel like beating down a small horde of monsters along the way, then grab some buddies and arm up: this arena could take a while.

Okay so when I initially heard of this game I was dubious, was it going to be like classic rpg's a la Neverwinter nights or would it be a pale update of the old games. But I was so very pleasantly surprised at how awesome this game really is. My main strategy in games like this is to avoid the main plotline for as long as possible so I can savor every nuance of the game so even though I've logged a bunch of hours I haven't even hit the end yet. So here's what I think of the game in a nutshell:
Pro:
-beautiful 2-d graphics polished so the environment still has depth and realism while still paying homage to the old school RPG's
-The choice dynamics and alliances in the game are so nuanced you actually feel like your decisions carry weight, I have to seriously think about my decisions and what it could mean for how I want to end the game
-in depth story, characters, and lore make this feel like a complex and deep world where nothing is simply black and white and where people have real faults and real motivations behind them
-there is certainly no shortage of quests or side quests to do to get you out from the beaten path and discover the dark corners of this world.
Cons:
-the combat is...not forgiving (It's not a bad thing it just gets frustrating) at a certain point the enemies become leveled so you have to employ a bit of strategy and while I don't have a problem doing that occasionally some battles would require you to pause every couple of seconds and take a breath or otherwise death is imminent
-food mechanic is a little useless, you can make food that will give you long term bonuses outside of combat but I find myself with a ton of materials for making meals and rarely use them (probably operator error more than anything else but anyway)
On a side note some mention that the constant reading is boring and sluggish to get through but being a visual person myself I personally love it, while it does get tiring after playing a long time I can immerse myself in what's going on and that's endearing to me personally.
Overall anyone looking for a great RPG like Neverwinter Nights or the like should look no further than this game, it will keep you occupied for a very, very, very long time.

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Gameplay: This was not my first time playing this game; in fact, this is my sixth time playing through the game, counting the five playthroughs I had of the Xbox version (also the game really can't do the "Only on Xbox" claim anymore, so that's kinda funny). I took a couple of years off from this game, since it was one of my yearly playthrough games, and coming back to it with both a new perspective and a new control scheme, this game is still as fresh as ever. It's a blend of FPS, stealth, and platforming that just works when it honestly shouldn't.
The FPS elements can be very tactical in nature, with your main weapon being a crossbow that can hold two of nine available ammo types; each one having their own specific uses. You'll soon find the three or four that work for you and forget the rest, but again, that's not to say that they're useless. There does seem to be mouse smoothing and auto-aiming in this game, which can be distracting for some, but I never found it to be that big of a deal. They can be disabled, as far as I know. This game does have replenishing health, but it's different from how a Call of Duty game does it. You have a health and a stamina gague; the stamina gauge is replenished by either taking in enemies or standing still. Sprinting doesn't drain stamina, but it doesn't replenish it, either. You also use stamina to heal yourself, with a full stamina bar often recovering about 75% of your total health. There's a great deal of tactics to healing, with the choice oftentimes being made between ducking behind a wall or stunning everyone guns-a-blazing.
Of course, another option is to stealth your way around areas, especially if there happens to be a very dense crowd of enemies. It's still recommended that you bag enemies, though, and it's all your choice how you tackle the areas. Your punch, if you've been upgrading it through the store, will most often knock out enemies in one hit. Goons and bosses have their own health and stamina gagues as well. Obviously, an alive baddie is worth more than a dead baddie, so do try to take 'em in alive. It is possible to take in every boss alive (some are pretty hard to do, though) with the exception of very late game bosses, but the stakes have changed at that point, and that's all I'll say on that.
All in all, I didn't really have any issues with any of the areas, with the possible exception of the last bit before the final boss fight being one helluva difficulty spike. It's something that I can guarantee is different from anything you've played before, and even after six playthroughs, the game still feels fresh and juicy as ever. 10/10.
Story: Man, this game has some great dialogue. It's easy to spend a while in towns just listening to what the Clakkerz have to say. The Grubs have some pretty great lines as well. Basically, there's a lot of lines in this game that'll almost assuredly get a laugh out of you if you even have a remotely crude sense of humor. The surprising bit is that the storyline actually gets good about 2/3 of the way through. That's not to say that the first 2/3 of the story are worth losing; it's just that the stakes become that much higher at that point. The ending is unexpectedly dramatic and actually really good. For a lot of great laughs and a surprisingly well-written story, I give the story a 9/10.
Graphics: As expected from an HD port, the game looks great. One thing that I'm glad to have seen toned down from the Xbox version is the utterly absurd amount of bloom. Seriously, the amount of bloom in the Xbox version far surpassed any premise of artistic direction. Speaking of, the art direction of this game is absolutely fantastic; as to be expected from an Oddworld Inhabitants game. It's an excellent mix of high-tech gadgets and old-timey western aesthetics. The characters, enemies, ammo, areas... just everything looks fantastic. The technical aspects... aren't so fantastic. For starters, the game uses SSAA, which is HORRENDOUSLY inefficient. The game itself isn't too demanding, but the really weird part is that the game prefers my Integrated Graphics on my i5-3470. I could only really run it on 4x SSAA because of this (and yes, I did try and go through NVIDIA Control Panel; it didn't change anything). Even despite the not-so-great technical side of this game, the game still looks fantastic enough for me to give this game a 4/5 for graphics.
Sound: Well, the music is pretty good. I always make the note as to whether or not I'd bring this along with me on my MP3 player, and I wouldn't really do that for this soundtrack, but there are some very good songs in there that fit the "odd" vibe this game is trying to pull. Voiceacting is great, with a lot of the humor coming from just the inflections that the voiceactors use. Again, it's hilarious how the Grubs seem to be speaking in all-caps. A rather disappointing aspect of the voiceacting, however, is that the voice clips are rather low-fidelity. I don't have the greatest audio equipment in the world (a Gamecom 777 headset into the included USB sound card) and I can hear the compression on the voice clips. It makes me sad. Surely they could've sourced some uncompressed master audio files or something? Because of this, I can't give the audio portion of the game a perfect, but I still feel alright giving it a 4/5.
Overall scores are 10/9/4/4; 9.0/10. Despite not being the best coded port of all time, the gameplay is still very much worth your time and money.

The Whispered World is a tricky point & click adventure of a sad joister called Sadwick. He is accompanied by his pet catapillar Spot and tries to save the world, while the prophecy says he will destroy it instead.
The story is quite simple at the start and gets a bit more tricky a the end, but nothing too serious though. Every quest in this game is connected to progressing the story, so you basically gather all the needed items, combine them and place them on the right spots to progress in the game. Some side quests are more intersting to fulfill, while others feel a bit repetative especially when you have to get to one place, just to get an item that you needed in your first place anyway. The end has a sweet touch to it, to actually bring some sence into the game, but nothing you shuld be shedding a tear about.
There is no real combat in this game, whole process is made only by either using and combining items, or solving puzzles, of which you will find enough in this game. I rarely play point & click adventures, so the puzzles encountered in this game were quite tricky. Some of them took some minutes thinking, others took some time figuring out by try & error principle, but in both cases were not too long and still enjoyable. It made the game besides walking between places far more fun and challenging.
The graphics in this game are lovely and received a lot of detail from the developers. Every scenery has a nice touch to it and both the characters and landscapes fit really well together. The colours are nice to watch for the eyes and between the chapter transitions you will see nicely animated cut scenes. The interface is simple and immersive, the bag could have been slightly bigger so you dont have to scroll for items in longer chapters.
The progress in The Whispered World sometimes feel nice and quick, especially when you have challenges that you immerse yourself into, while some chapters feel insanely slow because you have to walk a lot (and the character is not the quickest) and try tons of possible items on possible solutions. The progress gets nice and quick though if you get a walkthrough or a guide, that would help you figure out steps you've been spending too much time on.
I really enjoyed the music and the sounds in this game. Even though some sound effects feel a bit kinky or kiddy, it kind of fits the game, so it only supported the immersion created by the graphic and the story. The music was chosen well for this game, sometimes its more a classical tune, other times it sounds more gipsy-like, but is definetely supporting the game well.
The Whispered World is a nice point and click adventure, that you will quickly get through, but if you enjoy figuring out some puzzles and dont mind having a bit clumsy and kiddy progatonist, you will surely enjoy solving the puzzles and figuring out items the game provided.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.
~ForestWolf

Not a bad game. Game usually ends within 7 turns. The objective is the same as any other Collectible Card Game. You can see a lot of similarities with Hearthstone.
1. Reduce your opponent's life points to zero before you do.
2. Cast Spells/Summon creatures with mana, creature have damage and hit points
3. Attack or defend
4. Add a Rune Word, Gear
4. Rinse, repeat
I'll recommend it because you ought to see what they have created. It's a good effort but the buying of expansion booster packs with cash isn't something I want to do. It will be extremely hard to make me want to come back and play repeatedly.
PROS
1. Heroes
The hero art is amazing. Unlike Hearthstone, each hero is unique. Their health points, mana gain and abilities are different. 14-16 health points, 1-3 mana gain per turn and up to 3 abilities. These abilities don't cost mana but use charges.
Something similar to the heroes from World of Warcraft The Card Game, the card game that died.
2. Campaign
The map is intriguing, You feel like you are exploring.
3. Rune Words
They work like Global Enchantments. Both players are affected by it but they expire after X number of turns. Interesting concept but there are similar ideas in Might and Magic : Duel of Champions.
4. Gear
You attach them to your hero and they have an effect. They are permanent and are pretty good to use. E.g. Longsword. Deal 1 damage to enemy hero per turn.
CONS
1. Creature Slots
Limited to 3 (1 top, 1 mid, 1 bottom)
2. Art
The map looks like a kid drew it but it is somewhat interesting. Especially when you reach the capital city. You will feel like you are exploring some thing interesting.
3. Repetition
It's the same few boring matchups. You see the same cards over and over again. E.g. Beggar/Vagrant, Traitor.
4. Crafting
Doesn't seem exciting at all. You put a core, sprinkle some essence (up to the hundreds of essence, you start with 10) and you "gachapon" a potential rare card.
5. Pay-To-Win

Let me start out by saying that I did finish this game and it wasn't horrible by any stretch, but it really wasn't good either. I guess I'll start with the bad and go from there. I like point and click adventure games but I like them to make sense also. It happens enough times in this game that once figuring the next step out by randomly trying stuff or looking it up I can honestly say that I never would have thought of that. Also the game mechanics are not in any way standard for a point and click game, which, isn't horrible in and of itself but after the entire game it still wasn't feeling "natural" or anything like that. I still had to remind myself to hold and choose what action I wanted to use on the object of interest. Again, not a deal breaker, just kind of annoying. I ended up having to restart my game after starting it because they released an update that seemingly "broke" my game not allowing me to skip minigames, which is required to get all the achievements, and even after that after finishing the game I had to look up how to get the last acheivement due to another glitch needing to turn the commentary off in order for it to register with the game! Again, I honestly could've dealt with any of these issues fine I think but overall the game quality was not enough to wow me into giving it a positive recommendation.
Now for the positive: It is a fairly unique storyline and atmosphere. I did enjoy that although it did get to be silly at times. Having your caterpillar friend who can learn new forms and change shapes for you to help you in your uest was also a very unique feature that added another dimension to the game, and was fairly intuitive to use so they did that aspect well. The twist at the end of the game, to me was completely unexpected and really kinda tied the entire story together to me and I did really like the ending.

Not by a lot, and I still wish steam would add in another choice for these reviews because I do try to write reviews on my games but knowing what I know of this game I would say no. Maybe get it on sale if you're really interested or watch some gameplay videos online but just know that it's not great. Overall I'd give this game about 4.5 out of 10 for a score.

One of the worst FPS games I've ever played. Weapons feel terrible and behave very differently compared to the multi-player versions of those exact same weapons. AI is horrible. Visuals are decent for a game running on top of the goldsrc engine but at the same time visuals are not very optimised causing slowdowns now and then. Sounds and music are low quality stuff. Voice acting is ridiculously bad. There are plenty of issues to talk about. But all this is mostly forgivable stuff.
Why you might ask? It's because of the mess that is the development history of this game. It was originally conceived in 2000. It was announced in 2001 at E3. However the studio that started the development, Rogue Entertainment, went defunct later that year. The development was then handed over to Gearbox Software but they were not allowed to complete this game after missing out the 2002 deadline. Then the bits and pieces were sticked together in a rush by Ritual Entertainment in 2003 but that work was for naught. It's a miracle that CS:CZ was even released at all. The fourth studio to work with this game, the newly founded Turtle Rock Studios, abandoned the whole single-player campaign to make their own thing. CS:CZ was eventually released in 2004 as a multi-player focused training game with bots.
CS:CZ:DS offers a curious peek into the future of what could have been. More refined version of CS:CZ:DS is what the grand single-player Counter-Strike game should have been. Instead we got a campaign about series of matches against bots with challenges in CS:CZ. That's all fine and dandy but that isn't very interesting. What's interesting about CS:CZ:DS is that here we have a game, that's more of a precursor to Call of Duty, and a game that has a lot in common with the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare games, and other "Modern Military Shooters" in-general.
CS:CZ:DS is a long pipe FPS, that features series of disconnected missions, extremely heavy scripting, NPC interaction similar to the Call of Duty, similarly boring repetitive gunplay, vehicle battles against Hind helicopter, explosions, terrorists launching nukes from old Soviet missile silos, and all the other stuff except the high quality craftsmanship that goes into the Call of Duty games.
I bought the game when it was originally released in 2004 and it was pretty bad even then. I just installed CS:CZ to replay it since it was release for Linux in 2013 and I'm mostly spending my time in Linux thesedays. The CS:CZ:DS can be an interesting precursor for the modern military shooters if you're interested in playing that kind of stuff but in-generally people should avoid this game for what it is. It's an unfinished single-player Counter-Strike game that features normal Counter-Strike multi-player mode with slightly updated graphics and bots.

Resident Evil Zero is a interesting game for the series as it tries new ideas with its dual character gameplay. On one hand its commendable that it stands out from any other Resident Evil game, but on the other, the execution could have been better handled. There are some neat puzzle solving moments using the two separate characters, but overall the game feels a bit underwhelming despite some great promise early on. There’s perhaps too much of an over-familiar feeling due to a reliance on similar locations from the original game. That said, the increased resolution and 60 frames per second make for smooth gameplay experience which is most welcome. So whilst this is perhaps one of the weaker games in the series it’s still worth picking up to play considering its low price point. If you’re a Resident Evil enthusiast who doesn’t want to dust off the old Gamecube then this is a neat game to play for an afternoon and relive some memories in HD. If you’ve never played before then there’s much to like even if there’s vague and fiddly elements to contend with alongside the zombies.

FORCED is one of those games that just happened to be an add on in a humble bundle pack, so I figured why not give it a go? Turns out it's actually a really solid game. It plays similar to a Diablo-esque game, where you control a character with one of 4 unique weapon types, get new skills and passives through completing levels, challenges, and time trials, and get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked to hell and back over the course of 25 levels that take a handful of mechanics and throw the kitchen sink at you with them.
A big point is the difficulty in the missions, which is definitely there but mitigated (in a good way) with a 30 second revive system that will still allow you to reasonably complete missions, though it locks out bonus crystals. All of the weapon styles are well balanced once you get a good number of crystals for good loadouts, there is a good stable of enemies, both environmental and biological, that will keep you on your toes, and you even have a little bobbing orb that can activate buffs, bombs, and other fun things while never shutting up.
It's a good game, if you can get it in a package like humble bundle then fantastic! You should give it a go. I think it's worth the ~$4 sale price tag, so definitely pick it up if you like the combat sense of diablo more so than all of that loot and exploration. There weren't any game breaking bugs that I noticed, but rolling the dice with online multiplayer probably won't result in finding anybody, thankfully the game is good in a single player setting.

State of Decay is a fairly unique case. On one hand, it is somewhat unstable and rather buggy, while on the other it is a fantastic open world zombie survival game! Although it tends to recycle voiceovers or character models, there is sitll something rather fun about these particular survivors as you level up their skills and grow personally attached to them. Very much like in XCOM: Enemy Unknown! The dark zombie infested world that these survivors live in is rendered fairly lovely, despite a few lackluster low res textures on the characters, and the ridiculous amount of bright color filters will put strain on the eyes of some players. As for the sound and music, it has a few standout tracks especially during combat with hordes of zombies! The gorey sound effects are also quite satisfying and fun for an appropiately gorey game.
State of Decay is good, and made even better by the DLC it has. The Breakdown DLC is by far the most hardcore and difficult zombie survival game mode of all time, and you WILL get wrecked if you aren't staying on your toes scavenging for resources or killing rampant zombie hordes! It, in particular, is an "endless mode" version of the normal campaign. I played Lifeline pretty extensively, and it has a military perspective with an entirely new map! It's pretty good, but it's very difficult and quite rough with wave based zombie sieges that occur between helicopter extractions (you extract high value people and rescued civilians).
That's the thing about State of Decay. It feels very much like an early access game with the numerous bugs and stability issues, but yet I keep coming back for more! I'd say that that this game is the Grand Theft Auto 5 of zombie games, and you will hardly run out of things to do in this robust open world game! Just make sure you bring your patience, because your allies and other survivors are constantly asking for your help. Grab that crowbar, reload that pistol, and get your zombie survival on!

State of Decay is a good game. I often hunt for just one game in each genre that I like and this one may scratch an ich. Establishing/maintaining outposts is fun and the tone of the game is pretty good (scary, apocalypsee, that sort of thing). You may find yourself attached to characters that you build up, only to watch them get torn apart in a blaze of glory (which by the way, unlocks an award!). Aside from the occasional glitch, it more or less delivers what it promises. For now, this as close to a "Walking Dead" action game as you can get besides of course, the Telltale graphic adventure, based on the comics. Which, if you're a fan of the show and comics, is definitely worth the look but an etirely different game (less gameplay, more plot). Anyhoo, hope you enjoy it like I did.

The content you can access gets greater as you progress with things. Balance Elodie's mood with various activities and events so that you can better raise her skills is an important, and at time, difficult skill to master, but it make sures you always have a goal and can push towards growing your skills almost regardless of the situation. The costumes . . . Could have been left out, admittedly, but they do add skills to supplement things. The one thing I would have liked to see is more art, more than just the portraits during the conversations and maybe some backgrounds to represent what was going on in the events, but that is a minor gripe to a great game. It's engaging, fun, and held my attention which so few games actually manage to do nowadays. If you THINK you might like it, you probably will.

While the game can be admittedly pricey. I'd go so far as to say is Kingdoms is the best online only CCG I've ever played. I've played the other ones on here, Solforge, Infinity Wars, Might And Magic, Bloodrealm Battlegrounds. And after awhile it just feels like your just banging cards together and playing a slightly more advanced variation of war. Kingdoms has so much more variety with what you could do with your decks. Aggro, control, mid-range, burn, tons of combo decks that play totally differently. The "Heroes" you can choose to play your deck with are really diverse, each one feels really different and has a huge effect on the game. The creatures, gears and spells you can play can do so much interesting stuff.
More so than any other online CCG, I'd say that this game is closer to the complexity and diversity of Magic: The Gathering. And if you've played M:TG, you'll be able to pick this up in like 5 minutes. It's got the same basic concept of mana, things cost mana, kill your opponent by attacking with guys and using spells. And It's nice that mana isn't some randomly inserted cards in your deck that you might not draw and have to lose a game for kind of a stupid reason. You just always get 2 mana a turn unless something is changing that.
There's a decent amount of different formats and different ways you can play. A format for players with more stuff that has almost no restrictions on what you can run. A format with limitations on how many of the rares cards you can use that's more quickly accessible to new players. You can play against AI if you're not ready to play real players and still earn the in game currency. There's a guild system that really helps you to earn gold and get a better idea about deck building with tiers that range from people just starting to top level competitive stuff. And there's a really active chat right on the side of the game and people are generally pretty chill and willing to help with questions and the best stuff to do when you're getting started.
This is the CCG I've stuck with for 2 and a half years (on a different site, not Steam. Hence the not having a lot of time on the game here) and still actively play. No other online CCG ever kept my interest like that.

You are a panther.
+++PROS+++
The Story
I liked that Splinter Cell had a very grounded protagonist; I thought Sam Fisher's emotional role as a father made his story uniquely about him over all the grand political schemes of other stealth games. The story in this game has returned to a simple Terrorist vs America fight, but it is very well done.
This story is well done for several reasons. We learn to love the team because through plenty of cinematics and dialogue with great direction. They also affect our gameplay; not directly while we're in the field, but we buy upgrades from them. Thanks Charlie!
The enemy is very well done. Cutscenes show us how smart and dangerous they are; we see how the team, the president, and the news reacts to them. We see them in action, operating and executing. The brutality is kept to a necessary minimum; it does not try to shock us with how bad they are with violence and gore; it presents, through the reactions of the world, the significance of their attacks. In addition, the enemy is given a face, the leader. This leader is as well made as the rest of the characters, and, like a good antagonist, attacks the team and gets in very close. We meet this enemy early on, and are fighting them throughout. I think another reason this game's story worked so well was because there was emphasis on the enemy being the whole organization, not just one man. That way, I'm fighting the enemy throughout, not just fighting fodder to get to one man.
The twists and turns of the chase provide a thrilling hunt, and joining the team in the close up shots around the SMI table make you feel like you're part of the team. You follow lead on lead in a game of chess against the enemy, trying to figure out how to catch this elusive enemy; it's not a situation of let's investigate, never encountering the enemy until we have proof to take them down at the end.
I would have liked a new character, as Sam Fisher is getting a bit old. I think the game tries to squeeze in a few years by giving a younger sounding voice actor. I miss the stone edge of Ironside, but this new voice is still gruff enough, though not with the same extreme of Ironside. The voice acting is still wonderful though, subtly threatening and suitably expressive.
Gameplay
A lot of stealth games try to allow for varying styles of play; they do this because they couldn't make enough ability to evade pursuers. This game truly has room for varying styles of play. Ghost, Panther, and Assault are all viable and flexible, and players can switch between them; they can go as stealthily as is natural for them. The only things that encourage a player to keep reloading files is frequent checkpoints, the reward system, and a player's own perfectionist compulsion. For my own edification, the flexibility is done through making enough design decisions to accommodate all playstyles, including level design, player customization, multiple methods of execution, and pros and cons of each method.
The levels are a nice maze. There are plenty of corners, covers, lights and shadows, hidden spaces, and vertical spaces. This is what allows players to evade and ambush so well.
I like the enemies, more in terms of their gameplay than their visual design, and their audio dialogues help. Their designs inherently garner a different attitude from the player. The grunt riflemen are fearful fodder that a player hopes for many of. The helmeted ones are annoying, but still easy enough. The amoured ones are brutes to be feared, and the snipers worrisome. The AI itself are tough enough, eventually grouping up back to back, and each class has a different behavior style.
VISUAL/AUDIO
The animations are great. Sam moves smoothly, and his poses are appropriately stylized. His crouch is like a panther's, his kills are artful, varied, impactful, and emotionless; you can feel his weight, quietly pouncing. The audio is well suited; most of the sounds are very quiet and minimal, but the necessary sounds of the sharp ticking spotter and voices of the enemies are very clear; you can hear what state the enemies are in.
GAME FEEL
Here's a vague dynamic element for a topic. I liked that upon a first playthrough, a player can play very patiently, smartly surveying the area. As they become familiar with what they can get away with, mostly Sam's ability to kill from the front, they start rushing. Thus, they become swift plagues, brazenly speedrunning. This practiced mastery and the reward and upgrade system add considerable replay value to the game.
---CONS---
I don't like that the weapons have straight upgrades, one loadout that is clearly better than all the rest.
The replay value is there. Nicely done!

Legend of Zelda with gambling and Satan.
Nothing in the game is predictable. What items and weapons you get, what enemies and bosses show up, what the level maps will be like. Every aspect of the game is a complete gamble.
At first, it feels overwhelming, arbitrary and unfair.
However, as time goes on, you learn to manipulate luck. You get to know what items synergize well and what combinations have the potency to ruin the run, you'll train your gut feeling to find secret rooms with just a couple of bombs, you'll know how much blood you can afford donating without being ripped to shreds in the next room and how much money to spend on the arcades and where.
Some item combinations are extremely weak, some are overpowered, some are just too gimmicky to care about anything else.
The developers managed to catch the very essence of gambling and distilled it into a Zeldaesque top-down roguelike. It infuriates, it teases you with unrealistic hopes for a great streak of luck that never happens, it captivates, and it sucks hours upon hours of time without you even noticing it.
PS
The visuals are gross. They're only funny if you've been lucky or young enough to not have had your loved ones suffer and die from cancer before your eyes. However, the stellar gameplay makes it worth to try and overlook the teen edginess of the designs and the story.
PPS
Once you beat Mom, don't feel too ashamed to look up item descriptions in the wiki. Many of those I would never have figured out myself, and even more I would have kept forgetting every run.

You have the endurance to master grim, gladiatorial combat; either solo or with a tightly-knit team of friends who are willing to die a lot.
Forced is a very polished game, both in its concept and execution. You play as 1-4
,
,
...
subject to arenas spanning a superb mix of combat, puzzles and planning. The ability to align yourself to 1 of 4 weapons is also pretty fun - particularly mixing and matching different abilities and passive bonuses. Just be aware that, in my experience, some builds (or even weapons) tend to favour certain levels more than others - so be prepared to alter your build to beat each level, as opposed to finding a single, favourite combo to play the whole game with.
The levels are delightfully varied and have their own unique twist. The 3 challenges (and rewards) for each level are also a great touch: 1 for just winning, 1 for beating the time limit and 1 for overcoming a special condition. As such, there's a lot to do and a lot to master.
But therein lies the catch, it's gladiatorial in more ways than one... it's bloody difficult. After the first level or 2, the ante quickly ramps up and you need to be quick on your feet, well-coordinated and honed to a fine edge. So expect to die a fair bit and understand that completing all the challenges will require a fair bit of practice (or outright stubbornness).
This, too, applies to co-op; this is most definitely a cooperative game... not a party game. The game scales the number of enemies, time challenges and even puzzles with the more players you have, so the difficulty is always there. Unfortunately this means that your team will all equally need to be sharp and willing to put in the time and communication to master the levels. The game will unceremoniously prune weaker players, leaving a harder level for everyone else - which can quickly kill the fun for casual gamers. As such, single player is considerably more enjoyable than playing with an uncoordinated team, so bear this in mind if you're looking for multiplayer games to share with your gaming buddies.
The final catch is that (annoyingly) the network connections between players can be a little inconsistent (though this was a few years ago). I could easily create a party of 2 players - but would always have trouble getting the 3rd on board. A bit frustrating for a game specialised for co-op.
But playing solo, I've find this to be a very enjoyable and varied challenge... if a little intense at times. It's unforgiving but equally rewarding when you nail it. One to dip into when you really fancy a tough gaming wall to climb.

Just finished this charming point-and-click adventure & I loved it!! I finished it in 2 nights and just under 12 hours, and did not have any issues clicking with the cursor to start my adventure. That bug seems to be fixed. :)
What I loved:
- The art style is gorgeous, and I loved the retro style animated cutscenes! I see that for some players this was a drawback, but not for me!! It gives the whole game a nostalgic storybook fantasy feel, which is a huge plus in my opinion. The music is also lovely, and suits the game perfectly!
- I played this game with the English audio, and aside from some odd clipping in some early dialogue, I thought it was great! I see that many players are complaining that Sadwick's voice is annoying, & they suggest playing it with the German audio & English subtitles. I personally didn't find his voice irritating at all, and found all of the game's English voice work to be very quirky and reminiscent of all my favorite vintage cartoon shows. I think it is important to understand the spirit of the game (which seems to be a kind of homage to all of my favorite dated fantasy things) in order to appreciate the English audio's charm. But it is wonderful that the German language audio is an option, of course. :)
- The puzzles are pretty challenging! I am usually complaining that puzzles in adventure games are a bit too easy, but this is not so in The Whispered World! The puzzle solutions are often not obvious at all, & *most* of the time I enjoyed the challenge. (will explain further below.)
- The world is very quirky & charming, with lots of oddball characters who have lots of personality & provide some very strange tasks to complete! The Neverending Story/Labyrinth vibe is STRONG in this game, so if you like puzzle point-and-click adventure games and also loved those movies then you will probably love the Whispered World! :)
- The story & characters were compelling. Not that I expected anything less from a Daedalic adventure, but still! :D  I was in a rush to get through the puzzles so I could see what happened next!
- The ending. I did not expect the ending AT ALL. It was a pleasant surprise, and unexpectedly moving. I totally cried because I am a big softie.
- I really loved the game's sense of humor as well. I laughed a lot playing this game.
There is one aspect of The Whispered World however that was very irritating to me, and that is....
SADWICK WALKS VERY SLOWLY!! Yes, you can double click to skip to the next area, but only as long as you can see the exit node, and many canvases were very big!! So before I could skip to the next location I would still have to wait for Sadwick to sloooowly plod along. This is especially frustrating when dealing with a challenging puzzle that has objectives all over the place. I ended up having to consult a guide a few times, which I *hate* doing, just to save me time walking from point A to point B over and over again trying to work a puzzle out so I could get on to enjoying the story!
Overall though, I really enjoyed playing this game, & I absolutely recommend it! I'm playing its sequel 'Silence' next, & I can't wait!

TL;DR at the bottom.
The Whispered World is an interesting game.
FIRST THINGS FIRST:
I played this game completely in German with English subtitles. This is because the game is originally in German, so German voice acting is stellar. The English dub has strange audio clipping and is much worse. It also makes the Protagonist almost unbearable to listen to. To anyone interested in playing this game, I would HIGHLY ADVISE PLAYING IT IN GERMAN (with English subs if you don’t speak German).

Secondly, I didn’t have any problems with clicking or graphics. The game worked for me from the get-go.
THE ACTUAL REVIEW:
The Whispered World is a decent point and click with only a small handful of “What the heck am I supposed to do?” moments. The art style is amazing and really feels like you’re inside of an artist’s drawing book. The characters are interesting and the dialogue is often very funny. The music is PHENOMENAL. It puts you straight into the world. The story is interesting and easy to follow, nothing too convoluted. I would all-in-all recommend this game, despite its few flaws.
TL;DR: I liked it. Play it in German with English subs.

I think anyone around the age of 20-30 will greatly appreciate the cast and find at least one person they can relate with. Every character basically can fit into the category of "I was this person, or I knew this person". The game is masterful at giving you feels when you get into a fight.
It's still early in the year but this could easily could be my pick for GOTY. I can only genuinely think of 3 complaints I have (at least that I felt on my first playthrough).
1. The dream sequences can be annoying. The platforming isn't difficult, and while the music is great, I don't find them genuinely interesting enough for how long they take with the backtracking.
2. The ending is perhaps a little too open. Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed the ending, even the semi-cliche twist towards the end, but I would have liked to see a bit more revealed before credits rolled.
3. I would have liked to do everything on the first playthrough. I get that the game wanted me to make some choices, but after seeing my friend show me some clips of the game I really wish I had gotten to experience the same stuff as him. You're not able to do every minigame/interaction. I'm sure I'll replay the game to see more, but even just as an epilogue it would have been nice to have full access.
Despite these fairly minor issues, I'd 100% reccomend the game to anyone who feels even slightly interested. And I'd also reccomend the 2 free companion games to go along with.

An absolutely wonderful character-driven playable story, it's easy to get immersed into this slice of Mae's life. Even incidental characters feel to me like actual people instead of simply "characters" (or worse, "props"). Life in Possum Springs is complicated, as it is anywhere, and nobody has all the answers (or indeed necessarily any answers). Sometimes despite your best intentions, you screw up and make people mad at you. Or maybe they're just mad at themselves. But that's okay, life still goes on. Part of being friends or family is being able to forgive and standing by each other, no matter what happens. Without each other, we have nothing....
There's plenty of people to interact with and various activities to engage in, some of which involve simple minigames or platforming. And then there's the dungeon-crawler "Flash game" on Mae's laptop, a game-within-a-game to play which is pretty fun (and can be a bit challenging).
As someone who loves a good story, this was absolutely worth the price of admission. And the animation and the way all sorts of emotions are conveyed is wonderful. I wasn't completely in love with the art style up front from screenshots, but it's beautiful to see in motion from Mae's somewhat noodly limbs when jumping to the way her mouth scrunches up when she's upset.
The only real complaint I have (and it's minor) is that sometimes when talking to someone you'll be presented with an option to do something with them (which will take the rest of the evening, dropping you at home when it's over) and there won't necessarily be a "maybe later" option. Sometimes there is, which is nice, but other times it's a choice between turning them down flat or going with them immediately. Obviously it may be less of an issue on subsequent playthroughs, but it's something to note if you're like me and want to be sociable (as much as people want to talk to Mae given any sort of history they have with her).

The idea behind this game is rather simple.  You're the princess of a country and you have to prepare for your coronation so you can become the queen.  The problem is that some people don't want you as queen.  Some people would rather be the ruler themselves.  Some people might not have a problem with ending your life so that this could happen.
So what do you do?  Well, basically you go to school every day and learn stuff in hopes of raising skills to a point where you can fend off these attacks.  The problem is, you can't expect to learn everything easily.  Your mood affects which skills you can learn and how fast you can learn them.
So how do you fix that?  Well, you have a choice of activities that can affect your mood in several ways.  Some activities open up for a very short time, some open up as the result of other skills being learned.  Other activities have desired and less desired effects (you have to take the good with the bad).
If you used to like those "Choose your own adventure" books, this has a similar feel to it, except the plot can go a bunch of different ways depending on how you worked on your skills.  You won't just be able to say "oh, I need to choose this so I can get the good ending" because you have to manage your mood AND study the right courses to get to a point where that option is even available.
A nice bonus for studying extensively in a certain set of courses is that you unlock a costume that boosts your skills...so now you have the added benefit of choosing an outfit to help you through a tough portion of the game.  For example, if you know that military skills are needed for an upcoming section, you can change into your military outfit and you'll stand a chance of doing better than you would otherwise.
There's no stress or time limits to how you choose to play the game, and you are free to plot out how to get the best possible endings...in fact the game lets you save pretty much the entire game to a text file so you can study the choices you made and figure out what went wrong.   If you're the careful planning and analytical type, you'll probably enjoy this.
If you are the type to spin the wheel and/or flip a coin when presented with a choice, you won't last long, or if you do, you'll have no idea what it is you did to get there.  This game isn't easy...but it isn't frustrating really.  The game gives you the option of seeing which skills failed and which ones passed as the story goes along, so if you die you can see what it was you needed to prevent it from happening.
If you're hardcore, you'll turn this option off and just try to use logic, though sometimes your idea of logic will differ from the game's idea...keep in mind that this is a 14 year old girl and not you... YOU know not to eat strange food shipped to you from weird addresses, but Elodie doesn't (unless you teach her the right things)

I would really like to recommend this game as it feels like a spiritual successor to Yars' Revenge. Like Yars, defeating the enemies requires a two step process: clear a vertical line in the grid and then shoot the boss though the gap you created. The only way to get a shot is to gather three globs of a single color without touching another color. So the core of the game is deciding which color to gather and deciding when to shoot the canon.
Meanwhile, the enemy occationally drops a black glob, which will end the game if it reaches the floor. The canon can destroy the glob, but it can take a while to collect more colors for another shot. A made shot can move the player to the next screen and a missed shot can doom the player to destruction. This is very much the same sort of tension you feel in Yars when preparing to make the final shot. It's a good design and more challenging that it first looks.
Radical Spectrum: Volume 1 isn't quite as compeling as Yars' Revenge, however. (For a glipse into that game's design, read
.) It's just too slow and repeative. But for the price, it's worth trying out if you enjoy thinking about action game mechanics.

What is special about this game?
This Oldschool-Horror Survival Game comes first time with 2 Characters that you can control. (Yes, Resident 5 and so on had also multiple characters). The special thing about these two characters is both of them have their special skills. Rebecca can't take a lot of damage, but she can mix herbs, which can be very useful. Billy got a lighter, which can be helpful for some things. In addition he can take a lot more damage before he will die. In the most time you are playing together, while you can decide with whom you move. You can also decide if your partner will support you in the fight or if he will even follow you or rather stay on his position. This gameplay with both characters CAN make you feel a bit more safe, but don't lean back that much because there will be several situations where you both are lost and on your own, trying to find each other of you. In this case you will feel very lost and desperate. This makes this game so special. You have to keep an eye on both characters, make them survive this game. If one of your characters dies, the game is over.
How good is the new HD graphic?
While the original Resident Evil Zero on Gamecube was very old fashioned and mushy, this new remastered version comes with some new effects. The game overall looks way better than the old version but you can still see some ugly details which doesn't look that great. Just dont expect too much. It looks just fine, but there is nothing sensational about it. It can be kinda compared with Resident Evil 1 Remastered.
My final words:
This lets me conclude that this game is really good and it is a REAL Resident Evil. Its not a shooter like the newer games. This game is hard, can be frustrating and brings a lot of fun. You will feel like you felt in Resident Evil 1-3, i will guarantee you. If you never played Resident Evil, but you're a fan of horror-games, then i can also recommend this game for you. For people who want a modern game with a GREAT graphics and a lot of shooting, i really can't recommend this to you, because you might be disapppointed.

If you check the Wikipedia and Wikia articles of CS:CZ, you will find out loong story of the development of the game; it was a disaster... Valve ordered the game to Rogue Entertainment in 2000, however the departure of the producer of the studio to Sony led the company defunct. After that failed startup, Valve gave the project to Gearbox Software which made a remarkable progress however failed to meet the deadline. Therefore,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Valve took the project from them and gave it to Ritual Entertainment. The "clever" people in Ritual decided to remake the game instead of developing well designed job of Gearbox. Then, ta taaaa; the gold version the game was boring, dull, unpolished and even clunky. The critiques were so bad that Valve decided to pull the game back and ask Turtle Rock Studios to complete the job. Turtle Rock restarted the work of Gearbox and completed the game that we have now as CS:CZ which is quite nice. But how about "Deleted Scenes"? Well, that single player game was released as a free addon to actual CS:CZ with the name of Deleted Scenes.
Yeah, that was the story of the development. But, is it worth to play Deleted Scenes? Not at all!
All 19 missions are totally uninspired and dull. The game shamelessly respawns enemies to the locations that you have already cleared. Worst, you killed a guy in the corner, you want to take that corner as a cover, right? Na na na na naaa; a new enemy is likely to be respawned right back of you. The developers did not even bother to respawn those enemies to a fairly distant location. If you are annoyed with the instant back spawning of Arch-Vile in Doom 3, you will be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in this game which is not even a fantastic horror FPS...
Deleted Scenes has one of the most linear level progress ever; it can even compete nowaday's modern shooters such as COD in the case of linear level progress... I can understand the need for linearity in order to have scripted events which are pretty much the curse of nowadays' shooters. However, the game does not let you backtrack most of the times. It is not like "hey, you fell down from that roof which is not reachable right now" scenario; you pass a door and after a short loading, that door is now cannot be openned in the very same level! You are simply caged between the loading points. I do not play nowadays' noob shooters, thus I have few information about their level progress but that does sound even foolish for those games. Gold key seeking in the mazes of Doom 1 is way more innovative even for "today"...
Conclusion;
I cannot say "do not buy" Deleted Scenes; it is bundles with Counter-Strike and Counter-Strike: Condition Zero. But I can easily say that do not bother to play that game. If you are too bored and looking for something to kill you time, grab one of the F2P games... The only reason that I played and even finished all the levels of this game is my current computer is so crappy that it can handle very few games; that is one of them. That is it...

Counter-Strike: Condition Zero is a first-person shooter game from Valve. It is the next installment of the Counter-Strike series. Counter-Strike: Condition Zero is basically a slightly improved version of the original Counter-Strike, but with many addition to the game, it can also be considered as standalone expansion pack.
Counter-Strike: Condition Zero gameplay is 100% the same with original Counter-Strike. But Counter-Strike: Condition Zero has new Tour of Duty mode, more maps and the new singleplayer campaign named Counter-Strike: Condition Zero Deleted Scenes. Tour of Duty is a singleplayer mode game that is basically has the same game mode, but has some challenges objective that needs to be completed to win the map. Counter-Strike: Condition Zero also introduce offline multiplayer bots, where you can play against AI controlled player in offline game.
Counter-Strike: Condition Zero graphics is also basically the same as Counter-Strike, only has some improved models, textures and maps, but older maps are still included in the game.
Counter-Strike: Condition Zero is a good improvements to Counter-Strike. I recommend this.

The most important thing about this game is that it has a very specific moral hidden in the gameplay mechanics:
Dark Souls teached me that the game is never over, unless you give up. It's parallel to our own life. If you refuse to give up, everything is possible: you can cheat death, you can find true love, you can become the greatest writer in this world. Everything is possible as long as you don't give up.
If you give up your dreams and goals, you are dead. You'll become a corpse moving without will, a Hollow and your life will become meaningless.
Well, after all the fun - by fun I mean burning the "YOU DIED" text into my LCD screen - I had with this game, I realized a couple of things, some expected, some that noone was talking about and something that was more than just what people were talking about.
What I did expect was death, people were already talking about how hard this game is and be honest, it kinda is before you learn how to play it. Even afterwards, the devs found ways to deal with even the most prepared players.
What noone was talking about is how dark the game actually is. Your own death is a thing you can get used to, but the others in the world die permanently.
What made this game a masterpiece is however, that people have dark backstories, their life and death is hopeless, everyone is stuck in a metaphorical cage made entirely of their own sorrow. The whole setting is as dark as you can imagine it.
The narration, which is pretty much almost non-existent makes the whole experience full. It's unlike your generic RPG where people are crying all over the place for that how awful their life is. The people of Dark Souls already gave up, most of them are already beyond help and they are not trying to burden their own problems on the player's shoulder. They can't pay you, they can't give you anything and they don't expect you to even care as you have your own problems already. They understand that you have far more important things than their life.
As such, the NPCs of Dark Souls are real heroes themselves in some understanding. They are real and it feels much more of a loss to see one of them go...
As you can already understand, the Dark Souls is not just a game, it makes you more after experiencing it. Not just technically, like it really improves your reflexes and your ability to tap into the future, but in more than one way. You'll experience loss, you'll experience victories. This game became a part of me. The experience I got from this game made my life better by teaching me how to deal with loss.

I went into this questioning whether or not I would enjoy it. This is NOT becuase I am not a splinter cell fan. I have played through literally all the splinter cell series. My favorite one of the series has always been Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory. I was underwhelmed by double agent, although I did enjoy that game. I thought conviction was terrible.... It abandoned a lot of the stealth features of previous games and instead focused on a more action-based experience that, in my opinion, is not the point of the Splinter Cell series.... I am EXTREMELY happy to say that I think that splinter cell has returned to the classic stealth-based gameplay. I view this as the real successor to Chaos Theory and really the next evolution of the series. This game has a nice mix of action and stealth. On harder difficulty settings, it is not easy to just go into a room and take out 5+ guys... This is how I want my stealth games. Fun, tense, hiding in the shadows and taking out targets one at a time. If you liked classic Splinter Cell, you probably will like this game. If you did not like classic Splinter Cell and only liked the more action-based gameplay of Conviction.... There are plenty of action games out there. Go have fun. This is a more classic-style stealth game that has been lacking in recent years. The graphics are also extremely good... 10/10. Would highly recommend to fans of the series.

Forced is a interestingly unique Gauntlet Legends style top down game, with a lot of puzzle-esque elements and battles to attend to at the same time. You play as one of 4 unique characters each with their own strengths and weaknesses.
It's heavily intended to be played with co-op, with each additional player a scaling difficulty setting. And much like Magicka, the ways in which each player dies is more hilarious than the last. Me and my buddies have had way too many laughs at the expense of our lesser game inclined friends, throwing them into the game with a basic knowledge base of the games mechanics and watching them try their hardest to no avail.
Pros:
+ Up to 4 player Co-Op fun
+ Hilarious gameplay
+ Puzzle Mechanics incorporated into the battle system
+ Unique characters that suits each playstyle
Cons:
- Some challanges are extremely difficult and potentially unencouraging if you're an achievement hunter
TL;DR:
9/10 Top down Gauntlet Style Co-Op game with puzzle mechanics

The idea behind this game is rather simple.  You're the princess of a country and you have to prepare for your coronation so you can become the queen.  The problem is that some people don't want you as queen.  Some people would rather be the ruler themselves.  Some people might not have a problem with ending your life so that this could happen.
So what do you do?  Well, basically you go to school every day and learn stuff in hopes of raising skills to a point where you can fend off these attacks.  The problem is, you can't expect to learn everything easily.  Your mood affects which skills you can learn and how fast you can learn them.
So how do you fix that?  Well, you have a choice of activities that can affect your mood in several ways.  Some activities open up for a very short time, some open up as the result of other skills being learned.  Other activities have desired and less desired effects (you have to take the good with the bad).
If you used to like those "Choose your own adventure" books, this has a similar feel to it, except the plot can go a bunch of different ways depending on how you worked on your skills.  You won't just be able to say "oh, I need to choose this so I can get the good ending" because you have to manage your mood AND study the right courses to get to a point where that option is even available.
A nice bonus for studying extensively in a certain set of courses is that you unlock a costume that boosts your skills...so now you have the added benefit of choosing an outfit to help you through a tough portion of the game.  For example, if you know that military skills are needed for an upcoming section, you can change into your military outfit and you'll stand a chance of doing better than you would otherwise.
There's no stress or time limits to how you choose to play the game, and you are free to plot out how to get the best possible endings...in fact the game lets you save pretty much the entire game to a text file so you can study the choices you made and figure out what went wrong.   If you're the careful planning and analytical type, you'll probably enjoy this.
If you are the type to spin the wheel and/or flip a coin when presented with a choice, you won't last long, or if you do, you'll have no idea what it is you did to get there.  This game isn't easy...but it isn't frustrating really.  The game gives you the option of seeing which skills failed and which ones passed as the story goes along, so if you die you can see what it was you needed to prevent it from happening.
If you're hardcore, you'll turn this option off and just try to use logic, though sometimes your idea of logic will differ from the game's idea...keep in mind that this is a 14 year old girl and not you... YOU know not to eat strange food shipped to you from weird addresses, but Elodie doesn't (unless you teach her the right things)
This is going to be the game I play when I'm in the mood to kick back and think instead of worrying about reaction times or aiming skill.   I just added +15 to my judgement abilities.
