Yikes.  This game just goes to show how unfit a queen I would be if the role were forced upon me.
Cutthroat politics, aristocratic relationships, exciting celebrations, brutal war, and even magic come into play when you're on the road to queendom.
This game plays sort of like a visual novel.  Playing as princess Elodie, you take weekly "classes" that improve her various skills, such as court manners, public speaking, dance, swordsmanship, falcon handling, history, internal affairs, divination, and more.  Elodie also has a mood meter of 4 attributes: angry/fearful, cheerful/depressed, willful/yielding, and pressured/lonely.  Depending on what her mood is for each skill category you potentially increase can be affected by a bonus/penalty that influences the rate of learning for that particular skillset.  Each skill you improve will ultimately decide Elodie's fate- there is a failure/partial success/success rating that ensues when an event occurs and depending on what you get, the outcome of the game will be based on these failures or successes.  Be warned!  You *will* die at least once in this game, but don't worry- you can start over from an earlier time or from the beginning, ensuring you have the right knowledge/skills to get through a major event.
You also get the opportunity to dress the princess up in various outfits when you improve categorized skills to a certain extent.  Examples include a tutu, catsuit, military regalia, and even magical girl.  Totally adorbs.
Music's decent.  It is fitting for the subject matter.

I paid for early access as soon as a working demo was released years ago. Over the years, they added and promised a lot of exciting features. I saw a lot of potential in this game, and I still do. This game is very feature and content rich, and the art is great quality. Unfortunately, a lot of the features are pretty disappointing, and a lot of things that were promised were never added or just not executed very well. Some survival features can be completely negated, such as heat, cold, and breathable air, all that's left is the hunger mechanic which is not balanced well in my opinion. Despite all of this, I would still recommend the game, because it's very fun with friends.
However, this game is very poorly optomized. I believe it's the pathfinding of enemies and NPCs that cause severe FPS drops in crowded areas of the game. Weather also drops FPS, making me think it's the way ponds appear during rain. Nothing can be done about this. I'm confident that the graphics are not causing the low FPS, a beefy GPU won't help. It requires good CPU, which is not typical for most games. It runs poorly on my desktop with a 4.2MHz processor, and it causes my laptop to overheat and shut down. This makes the game completely unplayable in some cases.

After promises that were unfulfilled and a sold PS4 and moving back to the world of PC (*-*) in late 2016 due to circunstances in life, I had a lot of sci-fy games in my wishlist.
Then after some time I realized i just needed two sci-fy games to fulfill my desires for space exploration with interesting things to do: Starbound and Elite Dangerous.
With Starbound I got a massive procedural game with side quests, main quest, planets to explore, a lot of deaths, a lot of different biomes and some mixture of Terraria with space exploration.
Starbound in short is minecraft 2D in space, with quests, bosses, secrets to find (most of them underground), nice cave systems, really deep cave system, big enough planets for a 2D game, houses to build and rent, machines to build and make things, from cloth to weapons and a lot of weapons and secrets to find and customizations not only for your character but for your ship too.
And this review is writen before I even figure out how to survive in hazardous planets, which makes my so many hours played until now more worth than ever. There are a lot for me to find and I will hit the 100h mark easily without even finishing the main story, from the way I like to play slow and enjoying stuff.
TL,DR: I recommend this game for any space explorer that like to build houses, rent it for money, explore deep cave systems and do a lot more.

Ok.  At first, I wasn't a fan of this game because of the interface.  It was clearly designed with a controller in mind, and if you know me, you know I HATE PC ports of games that don't consider things that PC gamers EXPECT to have as norms:  PC keyboard and mouse control (done well), and SAVE ANYWHERE.   Checkpoint systems, for the most part, are dated concepts tied to systems with insufficient resources to implement proper saves.
That said, you can turn down the mouse sensitivity to the point it's fairly playable, and even though you can't "save anywhere", the biggest detraction I've seen isn't saving per se, it's LOADING.   You can't load after a mistake...and I have to say, for a survival horror game, that works for me.   Shortly into my first game (a couple hours), my main character died...and the game went on.   I went and looted his corpse and he was gone, leaving the rest of "us" to continue to try and make it in the world.
Gameplay is for the most part very similar to Dead Island, except the game world is quite open and bases may be relocated and upgraded.  It's mission driven, but there's some story elements that keep it going.   I'd prefer a little more storyline and character developement, instead of the "build a base" options, but for the most part it works...I keep coming back to play more.   We'll see if after my first play through I go back, but it was a steal during the summer sale, and it has already paid itself off.

, this is perhaps due to the fact that it is essentially an updated and carefully expanded version of Street Fighter 2 – the game that in many respects defined the genre.
The motions and inputs required to perform moves are often daunting to players unfamiliar with fighting games and accustomed to the streamlined, immersive control schemes of today's FPS games and platformers, where pressing the 'right buttons' isn't really a factor you have to worry about. This may be in part the reason why Street fighter has a smaller (but no less passionate) following than the big MOBA, RTS and FPS games despite being such
. Because to access that part of the game where you need to consider timing, reading, predicting, matchups etc
But at the same time this is what makes Street fighter so great. The controller motions and inputs and the special attacks they yield have a sense of logic to them. 'Shoto' characters launch most of their special moves by timing an attack at the end of a quarter circle movement with the joystick. 'Charge' characters achieve their special moves by momentarily holding the joystick in one direction and then pressing an attack as they move it in the opposite. Grappling characters launch devastating throws and slams by doing entire loops with the joystick just before they attack, and Special and Ultra moves are done by pulling off really quick 'double movements' and by pressing down three buttons at once.
On top of that Street Fighter boasts some of the most iconic video game characters of all time who are conceptually inseparable from their signature special moves. In summary,
This is great!!

RPG Maker, in all of its forms, is an excellent tool for novice and experienced programmers.
RPG Maker 2003 will allow you to envision any kind of 2D game that you can imagine. Don't be fooled by all of the typical tools presented to you—database, chipset map, battle system—with perseverance and ingenuity, you can ignore these completely, and have a surprising amount of flexibility in realizing the type of game you want to design.
You really can design anything. RPG Maker 2003 makes it easy, as there's no type-it-in-yourself programming required. Even very experienced programmers might find RPG Maker 2003 useful, for rapid prototyping. (One of the most important aspects of game design, is to make sure your game is fun as you actually play it... It's important to get in there and figure that out first, before you spend a ton of time on all of the stuff surrounding the game, like graphics, sound, etc...)
It's a must-buy for aspiring game developers who do not quite know how to program yet. The programming "language" used, consisting of event commands, has plenty of options, but its lack of fine tuning will nurture problem solving and abstract thinking, incredibly important skills for when you do make the jump to a programming language that you have to type out in notepad.
As someone who is casually into game devleopment, RPG Maker 2003 is a great, easy place to start. Easy to learn, tons of content to use online.

is a point & click adventure game made by Daedalic Entertainment. What most likely seemed like a good game on paper (a medieval fantasy setting and a basic mystery to build a story around, decent graphics, nice music and sound effects) turned out to be a sub par game due to its meager story, its lack of interesting characters, its awful voice acting and the fact that too many situations will have you searching for a walkthrough to look up the far-fetched or completely illogical solution.
You play as Sadwick, a child clown from a small family of travelling circus artists. Sadwick is plagued by ominous nightmares and he wants to find out more about them. So he's off to find an oracle who supposedly lives in the forest where the circus happened to make camp.
Sadwick is a whiner. Plain and simple. In every conversation he will talk about how he feels sad and worthless, and complain that nobody likes him. Even after statements that don't call for whining, he does it anyway. For example, when clicking on a statue and he says "The statue won't move", he adds "Pretty much like everything else in my life". Even after basic statements to tell the player "I can't do that" he sometimes adds things like "I'm too stupid/clumsy/weak/worthless". This gets old very soon.
The story and the dialogue aren't very captivating. Most of the conversations are repetitive and long-winded with little content. It didn't take long before I found myself skipping through most of it and just glimpsing the gist of the conversation from the subtitles that raced past.
A second reason to skip through the dialogue is the terrible voice acting. Sadwick's voice is forced and annoying. Most of the other character's voices are annoying, too. The remaining voice acting is mediocre at best.
The humour isn't funny at all. A senile grandpa who says 'compost' when he means 'compass'. Hilarious. Your character who misunderstands the messenger when he says 'the whispering stone' and repeats 'the blistering bone?' Side-splitting. If childish wordplay isn't your thing, don't worry. They included gags that require visualizing, too, for example:"That stone looks like a cow's behind"!
Not far into the game things seem to take a turn for the better when an interesting and mysterious element is added to the story when
But Sadwick says, and I quote: "I've decided to just ignore them" and that's that. You can't talk to the other characters about them and you can't examine them further. Seriously? This is the equivalent of looking out the window into your backyard, seeing a space ship landing there and thinking to yourself: "Ah well, I'll close the curtains and have a look what's on TV tonight".
The ending is predictable and actually makes little sense when you think about it. But it's clear the developers didn't give the story a lot of thought so we shouldn't either, I guess.
The gameplay is a bit strange for a point & click game. A minor gripe is that you have to target stuff with the
of a large mouse pointer. Even though it doesn't take long to get used to this, it keeps feeling clumsy throughout the whole game. More importantly, they turned
into a 'point &
game': a regular short mouse click only makes your character walk to an object, but to interact with it you need to hold the mouse button down for a second. The whole thing just feels counter-intuitive.
You can press SPACE to highlight all the objects you can interact with. I read that a lot of people find this game hard because some of the puzzles are rather far-fetched, so I used this function a lot. I wanted to avoid 'pixel hunting' and getting stuck because I missed some small item in a corner somewhere. Sounds like a plan, right? Well, the first time I got stuck and looked up a walkthrough, it turned out I missed an item anyway. This item was hidden somewhere, in a corner so to speak, and it did not show when pressing SPACE. *Sigh* So use the highlight function, but don't count on it being foolproof.
And, by the way, those people were right: at least a dozen of the solutions to problems in this game are far-fetched or just don't make any sense. After a few of those moments I pretty much gave up on playing this game without a walkthrough next to me. Which is a shame, because that takes a lot of the fun out of playing an adventure game.
When you execute one of those impossible-to-guess solutions, Sadwick litterally says: "That's so crazy... I don't even know why I try." Seriously. No kidding.
The developers even created an achievement for using a walkthrough! You get an achievement called '
' for solving a puzzle without performing any wrong action, which is indeed only possible if you're following a walkthrough to the letter. There's another achievement that requires you to do a whole segment of the game perfectly, without making any error, so that's pretty much the same thing.
The graphics are decent enough. The decors of this medieval fantasy world aren't breathtaking but they are easy on the eye. What I don't understand is why a 'special edition' release from the year 2014 has no widescreen support. Besides, the game was originally released in 2009 so it wasn't ancient to begin with. But unless you still have a 4:3 monitor, you will see a broad black bar on the left and right side of your screen. This isn't a matter of settings. Take a look at the screen shots on the store page: they have the black bars, too.
Often, you hear no music at all. But when there is music playing, it's quite beautiful and atmospheric. I especially liked the music in the second chapter. The sound effects and the ambient sounds are very nice, too.
There are a few minor bugs in the game. Sometimes you hear or read a completely different line than intended. A few objects still have their German names. Like I said: minor bugs but signs of sloppiness nevertheless. I also experienced a couple of CTD's (crash to desktop) so save regularly.
has 7 trading cards. You'll get 4 while running the game.
The Steam Achievements are uninspired. First, you have your classic, unmissable story-related achievements. Then there are a few missable achievements. I already talked about the two achievements that reward people who use a step-by-step walkthrough or at least a 100% achievement guide. Well, there is also an achievement for skipping all of the game's minigame puzzles. That's about the equivalent of giving a medal to wartime deserters, isn't it?
The other missable achievements usually boil down to 'perform an optional action 10 times'. Each of those 10 times you'll have to sit through an animation or even an entire cutscene, so they're pretty boring achievements that you'll only get when you use an achievements guide.
And then there is an achievement called '
', which you get for clicking a few hundred times on some ingame buttons. Again. They already did the same thing in
with its '
' and '
' achievements.
Steam Achievements can be a great thing when they add optional extra 'quests', challenges and depth to a game. I'm seriously starting to have my doubts about Daedalic Entertainment. Apparently they are convinced that 'click some buttons 500 times' is a challenge that adds more fun to playing a game, and that people should be rewarded for using a walkthrough and for skipping puzzles. I still have a few more games from the 'Daedalic Bundle' to go, so wish me better luck on my next pick...

Starbound is a game that went to my wishlist after the sci-fy bug of 2013-16. Mainly after the release fiasco of NMS in 2016.
After promises that were unfulfilled and a sold PS4 and moving back to the world of PC (*-*) in late 2016 due to circunstances in life, I had a lot of sci-fy games in my wishlist.
Then after some time I realized i just needed two sci-fy games to fulfill my desires for space exploration with interesting things to do: Starbound and Elite Dangerous.
With Starbound I got a massive procedural game with side quests, main quest, planets to explore, a lot of deaths, a lot of different biomes and some mixture of Terraria with space exploration.
Starbound in short is minecraft 2D in space, with quests, bosses, secrets to find (most of them underground), nice cave systems, really deep cave system, big enough planets for a 2D game, houses to build and rent, machines to build and make things, from cloth to weapons and a lot of weapons and secrets to find and customizations not only for your character but for your ship too.
And this review is writen before I even figure out how to survive in hazardous planets, which makes my so many hours played until now more worth than ever. There are a lot for me to find and I will hit the 100h mark easily without even finishing the main story, from the way I like to play slow and enjoying stuff.
TL,DR: I recommend this game for any space explorer that like to build houses, rent it for money, explore deep cave systems and do a lot more.

Here is a story about a young princess on her road to be queen. Along the way you'll carefully teach her to become a truly regal benevolent queen... and then promptly watch her die by accident, stupidity, assassination, explosion, or gruesome murder in front of a crowd of cheering onlookers.
Scratch whatever I started with.
Here is a story about a naive young girl thrust into a world of cutthroat politics, scheming nobles, and capricious acquaintances. Teach her to trust no one, suspect everything, and approach all situations with borderline paranoia as she manages to cram just enough information into her tiny teenage brain to survive her final year of adolescence.
Make no mistake. You will die. The world does not care that you are a cutesy 14 year old princess dressed in pink and pretty outfits.
I recommend playing through without saves (saves ruin the thrill of survival). A successful playthrough will take about an hour or so once you've played a few times so death doesn't set you back all that much. As fair warning, it might take 4-5+ playthroughs just to figure out a way to beat the game utilizing your desired approach, only to realize that there are multiple approaches that require the same amount of care and "learning" (and by learning, I mean dying) as your first. This isn't a deterrent; however, as it adds addictive replayability when you ask yourself "I wonder if I could survive with 'X' type build or what would happen if I ensured that 'Y' situation ended differently."
If you like mashing buttons and melting faces with combos then this game is not for you. If you have OCD and like to track stat bonuses and every piece of random information coming your way just so that you can click the correct word bubble then this is a game for you.

I found Shellshock Live after watching the Derp Crew screw around for a bit, and since then have found it sliiiightly difficult to let go of myself. It plays tribute to a lot of the older flash games, but remains current due to the one-man dev constantly updating the game with additional content that challenges hardcore and new players alike. The graphics are simple but bright and compelling, and the game offers hours of gameplay whether alone or with a group of friends.

An important aspect of this game that really entices me is the ability to upgrade everything. As you progress through 100 levels, tanks can be upgraded with new skills or parts, and new weapons can be unlocked. These weapons which are constantly being introduced can also be upgraded further to cause a outrageous amount of damage. Furthermore, the in-game store also offers a chance to purchase speciality themed weapons with "gears" that are earned throughout game-play.  There are no micro-transactions which make this game stand out even further. Once you've brought the game, you own everything, which means people with a rich daddy can't get an advantage over you this way.
There are currently 8 game-modes available which respective challenges to keep people active on the servers. The aiming system is consistent and easy to get the grasp of, but new players can dive into the campaign levels to help level their tanks quicker and understand the mechanics before diving into multiplayer if they so choose.
Like all games, theres always going to be a group of party-poopers that tend to ruin the game for you. However due to such a large playerbase, you're likely going to meet some pretty rad players too, and you'll be able find more chill groups to play with. The in-game mute button also helps cease the cancer that might be pestering the current game, but you can use it as a tool to identify players before you allow them into your lobby for the next game. Rage-quitters and "Ruler" cheaters are always going to exist, so it would be nice in the future for more penalties to exist to combat this issue. Overall though, you're going to make friends whether you like it or not, because most people are pretty chill.
Shellshock Live is constantly changing for the better. Theres always new content, a great xp system, and overall fun people play with. I got it super cheap, but I'd be happy to pay a little more for the amount of fun I've gotten out of it.

Absolutley fantastic. Easily one of the best games I've played in months.
The game is 95% story and 5% platforming and minigames. Personally I didn't care for the minigames because I wasn't very good at them, but even though I failed every single one, the game didn't stop and I didn't miss any perfect ending because I screwed up the bass solo on a song at band practice. The platforming is alright, though. It's mostly for exploration, there are very very *very* few spots where platforming is compulsory in any way, but I'd encourage everyone to really explore. I would have missed out on an entire pretty damn good character arc if I didn't decide to jump and climb my way to a rooftop. There are also quite a few scenes you don't get if you don't talk to everyone every day, and while that can sound or feel like a chore, it's really worth it because you feel like you're actually building relationships with the characters.
Just remember that Mae isn't you, you may be able to influence her decisions and dialogue at points, but she is very much her own character and will take the lead in the story plenty of times. Your choices do matter, however, as most days you have to choose whether you want to go with one friend or another and you get entirely different scenes. Your relationships with the characters you don't pick don't exactly suffer, but they don't grow either. I'll be playing this one a few times to find all the secrets and see all the different scenes, because there's plenty to see.
The story was, for me, extremely relatable since I live in the sort of small town it takes place in. I also have close friends that the characters in the game are extremely reminiscent of. It made me really think about the world around me in a new way. At some point in the game, it dawned on me that I'd have to either stay in the town i know and watch it change into something different, something that wou;dn't be my town anymore, or leave and miss the hell out of home. It depressed me for a while, but the game also gave me hope. Whatever happens, things have to work out in the end. Nothing gold can stay, people grow up and move on, and things change, but that doesn't have to be a bad thing.
Of course, not everyone will feel as strongly as I did about the story, but that said, I would highly recommend it to anyone and everyone. If you're thinking about buying it, you really can't go wrong.

State of Decay is an interesting mix of zombie survival and storyline.  The game has strong emphasis on survival, guiding you to gather various types of materials (building, weapon, food, medication, etc).  However, you take the role of different characters (between which you can, and many times must, switch).  The game is semi-realistic, in that, people fatigue, weapons break, ammo and guns aren't everywhere, and morale is actually a mechanic (and yes, your NPCs can be eaten by zombies and be gone forever).
An interesting and, in my opinion, awesome mechanic is its rogue-like feature that will save your game up until you die.  At which point, you must start over.  This only adds to the suspense of the game once you've built and expanded your survivor community.
The game play itself is very well thought out.  The mechanics work upon each other to create a more realistic rendition of survival during a zombie outbreak.  There are a few mechanics that are wonky and can be exploited (about to die?  Exit the game to be teleported alive back to base).  But all in all, well balanced.  The only serious gripe with this game is the outdated graphics.  I've seen better graphics from games put out in the early 2000s.  If the developers would put a little time into developing HDR textures, the game would look as good as it plays.  I would definitely recommend this to any gamer who wants a zombie survival game.

Dark Souls is, perhaps, one of the best games I've ever played.
It is one of those rare games which manages to pull off nearly everything right: the combat, the aesthetics, the atmosphere, the characters, the bosses, the music, the difficulty, everything; a masterpiece which has remained unaccessable to mainstream gamers, due to its difficulty, but still punishes the player fairly for making mistakes, while also rewarding the player sufficiently for learning the game's mechanics and enemies.
The game's universe—known as the kingdom of Lordran—is a world filled with gods, giants, dragons, monsters, demons, and men, who all are suffering a curse under the threat of the coming of the Age of Dark, which shall begin upon the death of the First Flame. It is the job of the player—the Chosen Undead, if you will—to re-kindle this fire and bring light and life to everyone else. The story presented in the game is minimalistic and stays out of the player's way, but the background lore is extensive, continuous, and occasionally obscure, as most of this information is provided through the descriptions of items that the player will find scattered throughout the game.
The combat of the game is done extraordinarily well, with a focus on attack timing, telegraphed attacks, stamina management, healing, dodging, and blocking, which makes for a deep, complex, yet fair system of battle. There are several classes of swords, a few ranged bows, and three different spell systems: Sorceries, Pyromancies, and Miracles, each with a different focus in terms of fighting.
The bosses are difficult, but for the most part, they are fair and well-deisgned; the Capra Demon and the Bed of Chaos come to mind when discussing poorly-designed and frustrating bosses, though these are in the minority. There are a total of 26 bosses in the game, of which 12 are required to progress to the end of the game.
The levels flow into each other seamlessly, with multiple shortcuts that cause them to lead back into each other from different areas, allowing for faster travel through the first half of the game, before the player receives the ability to warp between certain checkpoints. Enemy and trap placement is intelligent, as corners around hallways will hide enemies; this forces the player to proceed slowly through the area and be constantly aware of his surroundings.
The music is orchestrated, and fits the game very well; a good portion of it is worth listening to outside of the game.
There are, inevitably, some problems with the game. These include:
However, the game still retains difficulty with fairness, genius level design in many areas, and some of the most memorable bosses in any video game. If I had to assign a rating to this game, I would give it a 9/10.

Identifying subject...
Subject identified as "Starbound"...
Commencing review of subject.
Starbound is a side-scrolling exploration and building game with a linear story-line. Observation from early release state the game did not have a linear story-line of now, but instead possessed potential for a separate story for each races. Since then, the plan has been scrapped and lack of consistent observation renders the progression tracking impossible for me.
Multiplayer has gone smoother than earlier iteration, as one does not require setting up dedicated server to begin playing with friends or strangers, although playing with friends is recommended course of action to prevent mindless vandalism committed under anonymity. However, setting up a server is still a viable option as it will allow playing and advancing at all times without having one friend becoming the host and being disconnected from the game upon the host leaving.
Game contents have shifted from more free-form exploration to following a story to progress through, which will guide the player towards more contents within the universe that had been generated. Once the first few hurdles are taken care of however, the player is free to progress as they choose with or without following the story.
Modders community will also greatly enhance or diminish one's experience in this space-faring adventure, as some are enriching to what already exists, or will take down the difficulty and attempt to provide everything. I leave it up to individual player to decide what kind of mods they choose, or if they even choose to mod at all. Playing with mods will add extra challenges to hosting one's own dedicated server if that is in the player's mind.
In comparison to Terraria, art style can be preferred as it is larger, and multitude of blocks as well as the option to simply right click and placing objects in the background provides great ease to construction, as well as not having to create "wall" blocks may be pleasant to some builders. However, this does pose challenge as to have a beautiful and natural-looking project, one must utilize more than a single kind of blocks and have more options in construction, but such difficulty is shared among Terraria, Minecraft and Starbound. However, Starbound lacks the options in Terraria where the natural foilage grows back on its own, or the ability to hit a block with hammer to create angles. The latter problem can be off-set by increasing the thickness of the floors and walls to simulate smoother diagonal lines with more blocks, but those wishing a waterfall creation will still find the options lacking.
For those who care about combat, combat system is simple in that the monsters will have a pattern of attack they follow, but the procedural generation of monster can provide entertainment as one may never know just what a monster is capable of doing, with exception of unique monsters.

I have played and followed this game for a long time, but I cannot recommend it for several reasons. First of all, the PC version is unplayable at current. This is not a single-player game. Unless you want to do the trials (which I spent most of my time doing), you won't have fun offline. To really experience this game, you need to play against human opponents. The online on PC is extremely laggy and inconsistent and slow in terms of the matchmaking process. But the other reasons I wouldn't recommend it are as follows:
Too dependent on match-up knowledge. You can't counter-pick, which forces you to learn ONE character and learn them well. Unfortunately, this is easier said than done. After having cleared all trials and experimenting with every character I still haven't found one that works for me. Whether I win or lose seems to be decided mostly at the character select screen. My performance is not representative of my skill level due to the character I have chosen vs the character my opponent has chosen.
No opportunity to use combos. This might sound like a noob thing to say but despite having excellent execution when in training mode I can never combo anything online not because I can't make the links, but because the opportunity to use it is rarely there. The risk vs reward makes it difficult to justify at times. This combined with the non-existent juggling mechanics mean you have to rely on bread-and-butter combos. This makes the game far too "flow-charty".
Too much poking. Everything in this game feels safe and hard to punish.
And finally, the most important one: NO TUTORIAL. This game is about as accessible as twister is for wheelchair users. There's nothing in the game to help you. Altthough the strategy and fundamentals might be intuitive, the controls and mechanics take a lot of practice and aren't actually all that satisfying. The game requires frame-perfect timing and is infuriating if you don't have the patience.
Don't get me wrong, this is by far my most played game and I've had some great moments on it, but to me it's more fun to watch others play it (e.g. Excellent Adventures). As a spectator game, it's often more exciting. But to play? It's more furstrating than rewarding.

Rank: 7.5/10
Recommendation(s): Be a hardcore Counter-Strike fan, understand the old 1.6 mechanics, and play a little bit of Half-Life.
Major Theme: Hidden treasure for CS players.
Bought at Price: $100 (for Valve Complete Pack)
Single player Counter-Strike was always an interesting concept to throw around. So much in fact, a small studio completed it.
A quick reminder, this game was designed around Half Life. Linear gameplay in a compact space should be expected. This doesn't mean its bad - plenty of single player games are linear - it just takes time to understand if you haven't played Half Life. Level layouts and item interaction are not going to be what you are used to. Is the game perfect? No, and no game is. Due to the for mentioned old game design theories, certain pathways and mechanics will seem odd. Getting players to do a 180, and come back the way they came can be confusing.
I've always been a Counter-Strike fan. There's no denying that. If you are well, you will have a blast with this title (and the Deleted Scenes). This title brings you back to the roots of CS, which allows for a neat experience. Would you play it again and again because of that? Probably not, because I completed the game in 4 hours and that felt like it was enough. I can only really see someone playing this if they are using an old machine with poor internet connection.
Being an old engine, AI isn't very good either. The way around that is to place environmental hazards everywhere such as trip mines. Because of this, it feels more like Half Life then Counter-Strike.
To wrap this up, if you are a CS player, you are missing something by not playing this. If you aren't, go on in life, there's nothing demanding here for you to play.

There are things to like about this game, but for me this would be a neutral review if it were possible.
Back before the special edition was out I tried to play this game a few times. I’d never get past the first chapter because I didn’t want to have to use a guide. I found the main characters voice pretty annoying and I wasn’t really feeling at all connected with the character I would have to stick with for the entirety of the game. Despite that, the concept of the game sounded interesting and at the time I thought it was a well-loved classic of a game. With a closer look, maybe this wasn’t as popular as I initially thought.
I started up the special edition, determined this time to finish. I have to say, I think this game would be impossible for anyone to finish without a guide. Some of the puzzles are a little nonsensical and it seems quite easy to miss clues as to what you’re supposed to be doing. There is a level of logic to what to do, but it was spread very thinly at times. I found this game a little frustrating regarding the puzzles. Admittedly at times I am pretty horrible at point and clicks, but I don’t think I have ever had such a hard time with one as I had with this one. I love Daedalic’s games and I definitely love their charm and style, but this one is probably the worst of theirs I have played so far (although, it should be taken into consideration that this was one of their first games and it is pretty old).
I noticed in other reviews that people mentioned bugs and crashes. Fortunately for me I had no problems at all with that kind of thing. The game ran perfectly for me, as said above, I just wasn’t very good at it.
It has to be said that the art in this game is absolutely amazing. The background scenery really are works of art and they have created a beautiful world here. It was also quite nice that they have added in an icon in the top left that you can press to hear developer commentary. Although spoken in German, it was nice reading it to see the personalities behind Daedalic a little more. You can definitely see where the humour and style comes from.
The concept of the game and the story was enjoyable. I’m not sure it was great enough to say that it made up for my frustration just trying to get through the game, but it was still enjoyable. I grew to like the main character a little more and his cute little sidekick Spot. The game in general had an old-timey fantasy film feel about it. Like Labyrinth or The Never Ending Story. I quite liked that as you don’t really see much with that same feel to it these days.
All in all it’s an okay game. I found it pretty difficult to get through but I wouldn’t say it was bad. It’s a fairly easy game to 100% as long as you save often to keep checkpoints and if you are a fan of the genre or the developers then you may as well give it a go and see how you get on.
I don’t usually say this but for some reason with this game I am interested to know how other people got on with this game. Would you agree that this was a difficult one to get through without a guide or am I really just that bad at point and clicks?
TL;DR : It’s okay, but that’s as far as I could say. I would rate this neutrally if it were possible. The art is amazing, the main character took some coming around to, the puzzles are a little nonsensical and it definitely wasn’t my favourite point and click, but it ran perfectly for me despite other reviewers saying they had problems with bugs and crashes.

Tumblr, if you're reading this, don't kill this game like you did with Undertale.
SPOILER FREE
NITW is a very different game to your usual text based no-skill-required adventures.
The style is beautiful and the world is well designed, not much else to say. Wasn't outstanding, but it didn't need to be, nor was it subpar in any respects.
As for the story, people are 100% right when they say it starts off slow. It makes a huge mistake by starting off slow, almost to the point of making me want to drop it. I have other things that need doing. I don't always expect a huge hook right at the start to make me want to play on, but 2-3 hours of nonsense talking and character introductions for like 5 main characters is not a good idea.
After the intro point, we then get on to "actual gameplay", which means you get to participate in the game, such as playing in the band Guitar Hero style, and other such simple minigames. These were fun, and I'm fairly certain there are achievements tied to them, so go nuts.
Every now and then you get posed a choice, which as far as I could tell, 90% of them did not matter. While the game never pretended to be choice heavy, going down hard and fast routes based on my selections, I did not appreciate being given a choice of "!!!!" or "!?!?!?!". Like, why? It doesn't affect the dialog or events following on, except for a handful of circumstances. It's not needed. It didn't add to the character I was playing.
As for the main cast of characters, I struggled to like them, really. They were either bland with only a cutscene or two of backstory to flesh them out, or so in your face that I actually began to dislike them. They all felt painted with the same brush, where their mannerisms were all the same, bar one being aloof, another hyper, another a big softie. I felt like one person made them all in one sitting. They felt like different parts of the same person (re: the author)
As for the story, this is a spoiler free review, and I definitely don't want to influence how you reading this may percieve the story before going in. I'd rate the ending to be above average. The build up was too long for what the ending was.
Maybe I missed some key points and thus missed out on some scenes? Maybe if I play again I'll see things in a new light and it'll all click. But I don't feel that the game will give me much more for a second playthrough. Replay value is pretty much nil apart from going back for achievements. There are a few little "fetch quests" that you stumble upon and can complete, but I felt no drive to, personally.
Overall, I juuuuuust about enjoyed this game enough to write a review. It was not worth the €20 I spent on it, it's worth maybe half that. Took about 8 hours to finish, but I honestly feel that it dragged on. Just overall, there was a lot more said than needed to be. It certainly wasn't for lack of content, they just stretched it out for some reason.
Also, this is just my opinion, but the style of writing really grated on me. How characters talk with the same tone and humour made it really feel like this whole thing was written by one person, alone, in one go, with no edits. Just a stream of thought. There are no jokes, just talking and talking and attempts at memes. (read; Eff the Cops, Gregg rules ok, etc)
It read like fanfiction does, where what people say usually don't make sense, and it is a little meandering.
When the game tried to get introspective and discuss deep thoughts and meanings, I just got lost in how much nothing was being said. You'll see if you play it, but it was just a lot of "I feel this way, and that kinda sucks, you know?" Again, a lot being said but nothing being said.
I feel that if you like Tumblr, you won't have any issue with this game. It's like Undertale again, except Undertale was actually good in and of itself.

I'm at a loss for words. Night in the Woods was a game recommended to me by a friend. He told me it was similar to Undertale and that it was going to be the 'next biggest thing'. So I bought the bloody game in full price and went in blind, expecting it to be a game with a twist and excitement. Boy, was I wrong.
Game started really slow. I thought I was never going to reach a proper climax, or if there were any in the first place. But as you dive deeper into the game, you start to see things in a different way.
This is not Undertale. This is not an action-packed game like what I expected. This game is strictly about characters and atmosphere and it does a fine good job delivering it.
Pros:
- Relatable and memorable characters.
- Great art style/graphics.
- Beautiful soundtrack
- Relaxing minigames.
Cons:
- Game progresses really slowly at the start.
- Weird and unnecessary dream sequences every night.
- Hidden achievements. All of them.
This is a really great game for people who loves stories, visual novels and lovable characters. I don't see it as a 'game' anymore, rather an interactive story where you influence the main character with your choices and your actions. Sure, the ending won't change drastically; you just went a different path to reach it. But it was worth the time and effort to do so.
I just hope that it doesn't get known TOO well. We've seen what happened to Undertale. It deserves publicity and attention but I just hope that the community can control themselves from ruining the fanbase.
Night in the Woods is a great game but not a masterpiece. It has its flaws but it has more than enough good to compensate them. So sit back, relax, and enjoy a trip of feels and nostalgia that is Night in the Woods.

While the engine was tailored for Japanese RPGs, you can still make other genres of games like
So you've got some freedom with what you can create.  There's tons of tutorials out there, plus plenty of graphical and musical resources for those who don't know how to sprite or compose.

I bought and played Long Live the Queen before it was released on Steam, but decided to pick it up again for the extra content.
The first and most obvious comparison most make is to Princess Maker, and I think an apt way to describe this game is Princess Maker meets Game of Thrones. However, beyond the art and the stat raising, Long Live the Queen and Princess Maker 2 don't really have that much in common. Both involve some level of strategy, but Long Live the Queen eschews the more exploratory bits for a more visual novel style. This is a game about courtly intrigue and trying to survive, and you will probably die multiple times before finally reaching your coronation day.
I've heard complaints that there's little replay value, and while the game is short, it's impossible to get all the skill checks in one go, and getting certain skill checks can open up whole storylines or reveal bits of the plot that you wouldn't see if you hadn't chosen to raise that stat. If you're the type of person who needs to get everything "perfect" in one go, you will probably hate this game.

A game of astonishing depth, beautifully crafted gameplay that puts powerful challenges over you, but allows you to enact exactly the level of idealism you're capable of maintaining. Your choices lead to consequences, can you handle the consequence?
Despite a lot of death you will face, it's not an evil or a specifically vindictive game. It just puts an adversity in front of you and asks if you're queen enough to overcome it. Are you queen enough to overcome it?

On the surface, Long Live The Queen looks like a sickeningly-pink girly Princess dress-up simulation game you'd expect to be shipped out under a Barbie logo, but what waits for you inside this deceptively-dressed strategic simulation game is a plot filled with deception, magic, warfare, and political intrigue like you might except from a Game of Thrones themed sim. I definitely recommend this to any fans of visual novels or simulation games in general.

TL;DR: Foul-mouthed, buggy tactics game with a slow progression curve, deliberately confusing mechanics and aspirations to be a console port.
It's got potential... But it's crude, in every sense of the word. The dialogue reads like a 14 year old's fanfiction (Which may or may not be caused by the dev having a European language barrier, it's not that clear) and the menus are awkward and seem to be designed exclusively for console controllers... Considering that this is a turn-based RPG, you'll be spending most of your time in these menus too, so it rather quickly moves from a minor annoyance to a major issue.
There is a large variety of tactical options and elements available, but it's often unclear which elements apply to which skillsets. Lightning is attached to Lightning, for instance, which is a mixture of Special and Physical, whereas Wind is attached to Agile, and is primarily Special... It gets confusing quickly, and discovering after generating a fire-mage main character with massive levels of Special that it's best move deals Physical damage is fairly disheartening.
Progression is an issue too. Those of us that play tactical RPGs in this sort of vein tend to enjoy the sense of achievement as units grow from single-ability rookies into perfectly-statted murderhobos... But in Street Posse, units barely grow at all. The first multi-fight dungeon of the game offers 10xp per fight... And fights are a serious time investment. With your units requiring 100xp+ to grow (Or more if you picked the 'slow learner' drawback), things can feel a little slow... And as far as I can tell, there are no random encounters in the early part of the game, if at all.
The final issue I came across was a fairly significant game-breaking bug. One of my units died, and the game hung without presenting a menu. Now yes, this is Early Access, so it's sort of expected... But there's no visible save menu, and when I booted up the game again, I discovered that there's no autosave feature either. By examining the keyboard-layout image presented to the player before the menu, I discovered that the save menu is attached to the ALT key, but by then, I'd sort of had enough.
Now the above may not seem like a huge issue for an early-access game... But the developer released an Alpha version of Street Posse on a website (You can find the link in the Discussion forums at the time of writing) and the exact same bug was present. This is a demo that is over a year old, and is vastly different to the finished product... With the exact same game-breaking bug that I ran up against multiple times in the demo.
I hope I'm wrong, but that's a huge red flag to me, that perhaps the developer isn't all that serious about finishing Street Posse... I'll be back on release to see if things have improved, but right now, Posse isn't worth it's price.

Overall the gameplay / controls / camera controls make this game rather difficult to play. Translations are also pretty rough around the edges, which makes numerous parts of the plot / story difficult to follow. Sort of like jumping into the middle of the Harry Potter book series, but with second language hiccups in grammar.

Devoid of Shadows is mainly a game you would play if you're just a fan of mysterious, old school RPGs that don't hold your hand or if you're just a RPG collector in the first place, and seek a new game to add to your collection. You have three classes: Warrior, Rogue or Magician. There are many weapons, potions and scrolls to craft, and a large amount of armor to follow. The game may seem very linear at first but if you're willing to playthrough the game over one time you'll discover many secret locations, monsters and items which you may not have discovered from the first playthrough. The final verdict for Devoid of Shadows is a 8 out of 10. There could be more but there are a few flaws that could keep someone from playing.

Sadly, what I hoped would be a review of praise, is instead a warning for all buyers interested.  Do not buy this game.  The following list is why:
Long load even with an initial SSD
Terrible English translation
Tutorial:  Doesn't make sense.  You're not sure what to go or click on half the time, and you stumble through it to start the game.
Camera:  A bad design choice for this style of game.  The camera is too low, so the 3D walls get in the way as you turn it.  There is no auto Camera, meaning you must continually manually fix it as you move through a maze of coridoors.
Generic keybinds for this type of game do not function.  I ended up having to click to open my inventory, then click to open my character, then click to equip.  Oh, and discovered I had stat points to raise that the game never told me about.
The Big One:  The gameplay is awful.  Being a diablo-like, you would think, "I can hold down the button to basic attack".  No, you can't.  "Ok, I'll just click then."  Except that the clicks don't always respond.  This right here kills the game, when the core gameplay is a mess.
I will say the music is nice, and the dungeon is decent looking, but it has so much to go before I could call it a finished game, even at its price point.  I feel bad for the devs, but people should not support this as it is.

I felt like the devs made this game for me specifically, which is an amazing feeling.  I really related to Mae, both in a good way and in the bad. I think a lot of people will feel the same way too.
Play the game if:
-you enjoy story centric games
-enjoy reading. Seriously there is a TON of things to look at and read about.
-you're looking for well rounded characters that struggle with realistic issues (mental disorders, relationships, and religion)
-love a chill soundtrack (super unique and well thought out)
-don't mind that it is more of a interactive story than a game (mostly fun mini games and minor platforming)
-enjoy easy platforming that puts huge emphasis on the groovy art style
Don't play the game if:
-you are looking for a horror game (It's very spooky and surreal but never overt horror. Think Lovecraft in regards to the tone as far as the horror element goes.)
-you have difficulty with waiting for a plot to "take off".  The story comes to a climax very very slowly, and it's very enjoyable if you have the patience for it. Totally not everyone's cup of tea, and thats ok.
-you dislike story's that do not have clear cut endings.  There are a lot of things IMPLIED about certian plot details, but the story is not necessarily ressolved, which does fit the narrative and theme of the game.  I'm just warning you incase these kind of open ended finales bother you.
-you have trouble getting into a game when the setting is very seasonal.  This game takes place in late fall into early winter, so I can understand that it might not feel as atmospheric if you're playing it in the spring.
Seriously, I loved this game and it's characters. I cried a lot. I felt like this game made me think a lot about my life and my relationships with people, which is a very cool thing for a game to accomplish. I'm going to replay it a couple times I can already tell. If you're not sure you like this kind of story based game, wait until fall for a sale.  If I had any negative critique about the game, I wish that they released it in October.

Alrighty, so I had recently deleted my previous review of this game as I found it rather pre-mature and now that I have offically finished the game I will now write a very in depth review, mind you I very rarely write reviews, but I feel this game truly deserves it.
TL;DR
Night in the Woods is a story driven game in which we play as a character named Mae. As we play as Mae we are introduced to a cast of many delighful and very charming characters. Every character is very relatable in their own individual sense as well as being very interesting, throughout this game I never felt like, "Ugh this character is only here to advance the plot and serves no actual story to them of interest." Every character we are introduced to is very interesting and this game has to have the best character development I believe I have ever seen in a game to date.
As for the graphics they are very unique in their own right. I'm not really a gamer that cares much for graphics, but this game surely was very refershing as it is very unique in that regard,
Now for the biggest part of this game, the story. As I have already said, the character development is astounding, the devs totally did amazing in that regard. However, the story does have one major flaw and that is its advancement. The story is basically a roller-coaster, the first hour is very great, then the next 2-3.5 hours feels purely pointless aside from some very minor character developments and some exploring, then finally the last 2 hours of this game is AMAZING. Honestly, the last two hours of this game saved it from being a 6/10 game to a 8/10 game, thats how good it was in my opinion.
In conclusion, I really suggest you buy this game, buy it now before the community ruins it just like Undertale.

Tumblr, if you're reading this, don't kill this game like you did with Undertale.
SPOILER FREE
NITW is a very different game to your usual text based no-skill-required adventures.
The style is beautiful and the world is well designed, not much else to say. Wasn't outstanding, but it didn't need to be, nor was it subpar in any respects.
As for the story, people are 100% right when they say it starts off slow. It makes a huge mistake by starting off slow, almost to the point of making me want to drop it. I have other things that need doing. I don't always expect a huge hook right at the start to make me want to play on, but 2-3 hours of nonsense talking and character introductions for like 5 main characters is not a good idea.
After the intro point, we then get on to "actual gameplay", which means you get to participate in the game, such as playing in the band Guitar Hero style, and other such simple minigames. These were fun, and I'm fairly certain there are achievements tied to them, so go nuts.
Every now and then you get posed a choice, which as far as I could tell, 90% of them did not matter. While the game never pretended to be choice heavy, going down hard and fast routes based on my selections, I did not appreciate being given a choice of "!!!!" or "!?!?!?!". Like, why? It doesn't affect the dialog or events following on, except for a handful of circumstances. It's not needed. It didn't add to the character I was playing.
As for the main cast of characters, I struggled to like them, really. They were either bland with only a cutscene or two of backstory to flesh them out, or so in your face that I actually began to dislike them. They all felt painted with the same brush, where their mannerisms were all the same, bar one being aloof, another hyper, another a big softie. I felt like one person made them all in one sitting. They felt like different parts of the same person (re: the author)
As for the story, this is a spoiler free review, and I definitely don't want to influence how you reading this may percieve the story before going in. I'd rate the ending to be above average. The build up was too long for what the ending was.
Maybe I missed some key points and thus missed out on some scenes? Maybe if I play again I'll see things in a new light and it'll all click. But I don't feel that the game will give me much more for a second playthrough. Replay value is pretty much nil apart from going back for achievements. There are a few little "fetch quests" that you stumble upon and can complete, but I felt no drive to, personally.
Overall, I juuuuuust about enjoyed this game enough to write a review. It was not worth the €20 I spent on it, it's worth maybe half that. Took about 8 hours to finish, but I honestly feel that it dragged on. Just overall, there was a lot more said than needed to be. It certainly wasn't for lack of content, they just stretched it out for some reason.
Also, this is just my opinion, but the style of writing really grated on me. How characters talk with the same tone and humour made it really feel like this whole thing was written by one person, alone, in one go, with no edits. Just a stream of thought. There are no jokes, just talking and talking and attempts at memes. (read; Eff the Cops, Gregg rules ok, etc)
It read like fanfiction does, where what people say usually don't make sense, and it is a little meandering.
When the game tried to get introspective and discuss deep thoughts and meanings, I just got lost in how much nothing was being said. You'll see if you play it, but it was just a lot of "I feel this way, and that kinda sucks, you know?" Again, a lot being said but nothing being said.
I feel that if you like Tumblr, you won't have any issue with this game. It's like Undertale again, except Undertale was actually good in and of itself.

I'm at a loss for words. Night in the Woods was a game recommended to me by a friend. He told me it was similar to Undertale and that it was going to be the 'next biggest thing'. Game started really slow. I thought I was never going to reach a proper climax, or if there were any in the first place. But as you dive deeper into the game, you start to see things in a different way.
This is not Undertale. This is not an action-packed game like what I expected. This game is strictly about characters and atmosphere and it does a fine good job delivering it.
Pros:
- Relatable and memorable characters.
- Great art style/graphics.
- Beautiful soundtrack
- Relaxing minigames.
Cons:
- Game progresses really slowly at the start.
- Weird and unnecessary dream sequences every night.
- Hidden achievements. All of them.
This is a really great game for people who loves stories, visual novels and lovable characters. I don't see it as a 'game' anymore, rather an interactive story where you influence the main character with your choices and your actions. Sure, the ending won't change drastically; you just went a different path to reach it. But it was worth the time and effort to do so.
I just hope that it doesn't get known TOO well. We've seen what happened to Undertale. It deserves publicity and attention but I just hope that the community can control themselves from ruining the fanbase.
Night in the Woods is a great game but not a masterpiece. It has its flaws but it has more than enough good to compensate them. So sit back, relax, and enjoy a trip of feels and nostalgia that is Night in the Woods.

You're a 14-years-old, cute, pink-haired princess whose mother mysteriously (and conveniently for the story) passed away recently. You'll be queen in a year, when you come of age, living under your father's regency for the time. What could possibly go wrong?
Better question is, what couldn't? Between political intrigue, war, dangerous criminals, ballroom galas and birthday parties, you're likely to get maimed, impaled, gutted, pincushioned and eaten by monsters. Beneath the cutesy animesque paint job hides a deep and often dark world, and only by dilligently keeping up with the affairs and studying skills to be able to respond to  arising situations are you going to stand a chance to live to see the day of your coronation.

Legend of Zelda with gambling and Satan.
Nothing in the game is predictable. What items and weapons you get, what enemies and bosses show up, what the level maps will be like. Every aspect of the game is a complete gamble.
At first, it feels overwhelming, arbitrary and unfair.
However, as time goes on, you learn to manipulate luck. You get to know what items synergize well and what combinations have the potency to ruin the run, you'll train your gut feeling to find secret rooms with just a couple of bombs, you'll know how much blood you can afford donating without being ripped to shreds in the next room and how much money to spend on the arcades and where.
Some item combinations are extremely weak, some are overpowered, some are just too gimmicky to care about anything else.
The developers managed to catch the very essence of gambling and distilled it into a Zeldaesque top-down roguelike. It infuriates, it teases you with unrealistic hopes for a great streak of luck that never happens, it captivates, and it sucks hours upon hours of time without you even noticing it.
PS
The visuals are gross. They're only funny if you've been lucky or young enough to not have had your loved ones suffer and die from cancer before your eyes. However, the stellar gameplay makes it worth to try and overlook the teen edginess of the designs and the story.
PPS
Once you beat Mom, don't feel too ashamed to look up item descriptions in the wiki. Many of those I would never have figured out myself, and even more I would have kept forgetting every run.

I don't know if this game is Early Access. I don't believe it is, as I did not see anything saying it was. This game is very clunky, the movement, camera control and combat is all very clunky. Many games of this ilk from that era had similar problems, and going forward those games have gotten a lot smoother, and because of that, are a joy to play.
This game has a very big problem with how the game is controlled, and how bad it feels to play. I have nothing to say regarding the story, or graphics, as I am less concerned with those things, than I am with how bad this game feels to play. It is not enjoyable combat, it is not convenient controlling the camera and windows. You cannot open up inventory using I, or your character screen with C like most RPG's. The options were very limited, with nothing regarding controls, so maybe you can open up the windows with keyboard presses, but I would never know.
The tutorial stage is annoying to the point of wanting to gouge out my eyes. Developers really need to learn how to make tutorials, without making them feel so onerous and annoying.
This game has some interesting features, with upgrading of castle features, to make better crafted items and the like, but honestly that is overshadowed by how not fun this game is to play because of the clunkiness. I really need to say clunky one more time so everyone understands how it feels.
TLDR  The game is clunky, and feels bad to play. It is not fluid, and you get stuck inside enemies unable to hit them for no reason. Save your money, do not buy this game unless the dev actually puts effort into making the game feel fluid, and stop wasting time on making an interesting castle crafting system.

- The game has excellent graphics if you crank em up and mess with the .cfg file.
- It's much more detailed and complicated then most games in the category, it's a good thing IMO.
- Base building is really good BUT I don't like how there a blueprints scattered around the world, just give us all the recipes.
- The vehicle system is OK, the parts system works as advertised. The diversity in vehicles is pleasing BUT some vehicles just don't feel right, not very smooth.
- Clips and bullets for guns are a bit confusing at first. The system needs to be simplified and explained clearer for sure.
- The attachments need to be more common. The grinding for a scope on my sniper, which should have one already, is very tedious and I rely on killing others or raiding bases to get attachments anyway.
- The movement system is OK, definately could be smoother. Much smoother.
- Inventory/Crafting menus could REALLY need a cleanup. Doesn't need to be super pretty just more simple and a better way of organizing, eg. alphabetical, bullet type, food, weight, etc.
- The clan system needs to be implemented much better. The only reason I see for it now is for bases but other than that I feel it could really have a bigger role in the game, especially RP servers.
- The hud in the bottom left is good, nice and simple. But tempature, radiation and oxygen need more of an appearance, or an appearance if any.
- Bandages need a buff.
- Certain guns need tweaking, especially the ones that you can switch between full auto and single fire. Some of those guns are much more efficent in certain modes so it's almost useless to include two.
- The menus are OK, 110% can be smoother. I have problems with the 'Servers' tab, when I choose between 'All' or 'Favourites' sometimes it shows wrong information.
- Character models are nice and clean. BUT, WE. WANT. CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATION.
- I find the menu where you change between female/male and choose your ingame name is nice. Especially the name changing for RP servers.
- Personally, the RP/ No KOS servers are the best. There is much more interaction and intensity then just shooting at whoever you see.
- The map could use a few more stops between the bigger towns/cities
- The location you go once exitting a vehicle REALLY needs to be tweaked to be more consistant, a buddy and I hopped out of our sedan once parked in a garage in the residential area of Pinecrest. We both died. No rhyme or reason to it.
- Flames on cars!! Cars need a much much better way of displaying or signaling they're going to blow up. I've died to cars blowing up and me not knowing more times than I can count on my fingers. They need darker flames or more smoke or SOMETHING to signal it's about to blow! The small white smoke puffs and risking entering the car to see the % isn't going to cut it.
- More attachment compatability, not just the sniper scope on the m40 and holo sight on your ak or the mod16. More guns should be compatable with certain attachments. Some guns are compatable but don't even have a texture for it!! I can put the holo sight on my carlington but you never actually see the holo sight on the gun!! Please fix .

Easily worth the price of the Steam Sale.  The expansions are stand-alone scenarios so if you are wary about buying the game then you can just start with the base.

Fps Config For those who need it.
Just incase someone is having trouble with their fps.
Found a decent config on net.
Make autoexec.cfg put it in your Cz folder.
Enjoy.
Adding these to your Cz link or in Steam (my games > right click on CS > Properties)
-console (add console)
-nojoy (remove joystick support, gives more ram)
-noipx (removing LAN options, gives more ram)
-noforcemparms -noforcemaccel -noforcemspd (disable mouse acceleration)
-dev (removing 100fps limit *STEAM ONLY*)
-heapsize (gives Cz memory, set it by kbytes, example; i have 384mb of ram so i used:
-heapsize 300000 (it tells cs to use 300mb of ram as cache for CS) , set it to 60-80% of your total ram, help's alot in 1.6)
Sensitivity:
Cz is not Quake or UT, you dont need high sensitivity, you dont have rockets and plasma rifles, also CS has a great sound engine so you dont need to make some "FAST" moves. Getting used to low sensitivity will improve your aiming, lower your sensitivity by 0.5 every week, and you may see improvements, it also depents on your mouse and options, personally im using 2.5 because i have Microsoft Explorer. Lower sensitivity is better, so get used to it.

disable voicecomm (we got team-speak, ventrilo, why hear these 10 year old kids yelling?)
voice_scale "0"
voice_enable "0"
voice_modenable "0"

This game looks like it's pretty and pastel and of absolutely no consequence whatsoever.
Five or six deaths later, you may begin revising that assessment.
This is a strategy game. This is a game about staying alive in a hostile environment. You will die. Repeatedly. To the same things that you died to before.
You could lose a civil war.
You could lose an uncivil war.
You could annoy someone by killing their family and be run through in a duel.
You could be shot by bandits.
You could be blown up by an enemy mage.
You could eat poisoned chocolate.
That's not even half of all the ways that you can die in the short year before you inherit.
And if you're crowned, that most distant possibility? Well, sure, you might have taken the kingdom. The question is, will that kingdom still be worth ruling?
You won't be done with this game until you've achieved your perfect realm and learnt all the secrets hidden from your blissfully unaware heir.
After all... How did your late mother, the queen, pass away, anyway?

Title: Night in the Woods
Platform: Windows, Mac, Linux, Playstation 4
Rating: T
Developer: Infinite Fall
Publisher: Finji
Price: $20 USD
Release Date: 21st Feb 2017
Night in the Woods is a masterpiece of an indie game. It has a magnificent narrative with heartfelt and relatable characters, accompanied with a spectacular soundtrack, and beautiful art and visuals, this game is a must have to any story aficionados or anyone who wants a passionate indie game. Although you must know that this game will only appeal to gamers who enjoy story driven games as without that, this game is only a light platformer with eye candy and a lot of text to scroll through.
This game is set in a world full of animals with complete human like traits. Other than how they look, all these characters are completely relatable in a world just as relatable. You play as Mae, a very young adult who drops out of college and returns to her hometown of Possum Springs after 2 years. Without spoiling too much, the plot has paranormal elements but this just accompanies the characters. Because it is the characters that make the game so good. You understand them in every way. As Mae your once best friends are adults now, they have full time jobs and responsibilities. And you imagine the awkwardness and interactions that can happen between this huge wall that was 2 years of a very important part of their lives. And I can safely say that all the dialogue and interactions make perfect sense and you can tell that these characters almost relate to the developers on how real and raw they feel. It may be a bit quirky at first, but I promise if you stick with it you’ll completely understand.
These best friends include Gregg, an energetic destructive yellow fox who was Mae’s best friend in high school with them creating mischief and destruction in their town. Angus, Gregg’s timid boyfriend who had a troubled childhood and just wants to make money to get out of Possum Springs and Bea, a blue-green crocodile who’s stressful job adds to her depression.
With these types of characters you can imagine how serious this game can be. Dealing with themes such as depression, fitting in, death and moving on. But this game can also be very humorous and touching. And again it all relates to the dialogues and characters, It really is incredible how well these characters have been made in making you feel everything they feel. You feel like crap when you realise what your actions have caused, you feel joyous everytime Mae wins a small victory in the overarching plot and you feel angry when something goes wrong. Be ready to feel, because I haven’t been so emotional from a game since Telltale’s Walking Dead series.
Enough about the narrative though, let’s talk about the gameplay. Which has light platforming and exploration but it’s simply to show off the beautiful town. The platforming itself isn’t anything special but it doesn’t matter. You’re only using it to get around and getting around is another amazing part of Night in the Woods. Every in game day you have the chance to explore this town and while you can go to your destination straight away, I implore you to look around this town because then you see just how much effort has gone into make this town live. Each person there has their own story and a lot of them are interactive. You’ll learn about them and everyday their story actually changes so it feels like you are revolving around the game instead of the game revolving around you and your actions.
This will probably be the best looking game in terms of artstyle this year. The autumn orange look blossoms with every leaf on the ground and environment to look at. Everything just looks so great and it helps as you are going through same parts of the town over and over again so it’s good being able to get some amazing views while you do it.
Another thing that helps not make the exploring boring is the score. Even though you are going through the town everyday the music is constantly changing to fit in with the season, the weather and how Mae is feeling. It really is astounding music and I am tempted to find the soundtrack. Which would be a first for me. Sound is good too, not as great as there could be some variations with the jumping sound effects and walking on the floor.
But that gripe is really small as the incredible music drowns it out but if I had to give another it would be the loading screens. They aren’t incredibly long but they can take you out of the immersion. But just like the sound it is a nitpick.
In conclusion Night in the Woods is an almost perfect independent game. It’s almost impossible to describe how this game has made me feel for the characters and just in general. It truly is an emotional rollercoaster and the music and art style only elevates that. That’s why I’m giving Night in the Woods a 5/5. Yea it’s not perfect but no game is and then no game would get a 5/5. But the issues are so small that I really recommend this game and I personally won’t forget it.

The most complicated is to make a character/group of characters follow an NPC.
Exemple: In your story, a friendly NPC will be the guide to your hero(es) for some time. This NPC (let's call him A) will thus lead them from a location to another. You have to set up his multiple variables with coordinates and move routes. Once you're done, you repeat the commands process with the character immediately following him, B. Base B's moves on A's (since B follows A), then C's on B's, etc until everyone following A the NPC has received their commands, if that makes sense. Few people master this and tutorials about this method are rare and long to read.
And yes, you can add some moving clouds to your game with "move picture". Just watch some Youtube videos and check out the web to give you an idea of the full potential of RPG Maker 2003.

(I apologize for any spoilers in this review, I'll try to keep them to a minimum).  I remember awaking in a prison in some forgotten asylum in times past, there the torch was passed from one who could not jouney any longer onto me who had just started his, armed with nothing but the rags on my shoulders, the broken stub of a weapon long since rotted to dust and the fire of a task so grand it would surely reduce what little humanity I had within me to ash, if not for my renewed determination to see the task through and to give hope to all others just like hope was given to me.  What can I say that hasn't been said before, this game is flat out amazing, I remeber when I played it the first time on PS2 (no guide, didn't think to check online until well past my 2nd playthrough), and the world was amazing, it was wonderful that at no point did the game take your hand and gently guide it along, instead it cast you out into a raving mob with nothing but your wits and the skin on your back (or the class & gift you picked at the begining), and challenged you to survive when every last little thing was out for your blood (humanity), sure at the begining the going was rough, and at many times I wanted to chuck the controller, with the game, and the PS2 out the window as some enemies/traps cheesed me to death time and time again, but you learn and with that knowledge you become stronger, it's a game about learning at its core, remembering where that stupid crossbow sniper was when you went to engage the hollow spear men, or remembering the reload and flight times of the silver archer knights while you duel one of their sword wielding bretheren on the angled rooftops of probably the grandest cathedral I've ever seen in a game, or the pattern of a bosses attacks so you remember for the 4th or 5th, or 10th time when to dodge (and not dodge into that great ax the size of a F350) and when to press the attack, while you will stumble and fall many, many times, take heart that the knowledge you gleamed from your last encounter will allow you to push just that much farther than before.  I also love how the lore is scattered around the entire world, it's not just placed in one big encyclopedia game menu for you to gloss over, its all featured in the flavor text of items and equipment, the (few) non-hostile npcs found throughout the world with their small tibits of info when pressed for conversation, even the enemies tell their tale though where their placed, the equipment their wearing or how they go about ending your life time and time again, also the world itself tells its own sad tale from greatness to near-annihilation, to a small glimer of hope.  There's a reason why no matter how far I travel, what worlds, universes, and realities I may visit, I will always find myself back at Lordaron.  Also the reason why I nominated it for the "Test of Time" steam award, and Devs if you do read the comments from time to time, I would adore you for all eternity and happily shell out full price for a (good technical) port of the original demons souls that started it all, I don't have the equipment to play it anymore but would love to see the original nightmare come to PC.
