*Review of original initial release only. Does not account for changes via DLC or subsequent patches.*
Pillars of Eternity is a triumph.
You start the game as just another traveller looking for a fresh start in a new land, flavoured by the choices you made during character creation. A LOT of terrible things happen and before long you are caught up in world where souls are endlessly reincarnated and the natural balance has been shattered. Some individuals can even see and manipulate souls. A lot of the strife, mystery and wonder in this game ties directly back to souls in some way, shape, or form.
Your attributes, talents and choices also ripple out into the greater world. It is not possible to be on everyone’s good side. Treat one group well and another group may become hostile to you for helping their enemies. NPC’s and main characters will react to your race, class, nationality and affiliations. Conversations are influenced by a number of factors, providing you with a number of different conversation options. All of which ties to a reputation system. This helps the world feel much more grey, with right and wrong being a matter of perspective.
The visuals are gorgeous if you have an appreciation for the style being used, even if the world could use a bit more colour in places. PoE does not have traditional cinematics. Instead players are given interactive text adventures with illustrations and sound effects that are directly informed by your stats and choices.
The writing is almost always exceptional. Far, far above the usual flavour text that wraps around typical binary conversations in other games. The text based dialogue and the voice acting are really great. You might not hear as much banter as you will in other games but what is there is entertaining and sometimes surprising. The 8 official companions all bring something unique to the table.
Character creation is one of my favourite parts of RPG’s. PoE is a wonderland in this respect. There are a lot of stats and mechanics to wrap your head around. You absolutely can build a viable character just following the on-screen tips and jumping into a game. The thing is, you won’t know WHY you are making those suggested choices. You’ll have descriptions to read sure, but you just won’t have an appreciation for the nuances of PoE‘s rule-set without experimentation. The game is setup in such a way that anyone can make a safe, viable character following the on-screen suggestions. Failure to Min/Max every damn stat won’t cripple you. Which is not to say you could not create a broken character, just that you’d have to travel pretty far off the beaten path to do it. By the same extent it is possible to break out “the maths” and attempt to make the most deadly backstabbing Orlan Rogue this side of Gilded Vale.
You have lots of choices when it comes to creating your character and they all come with some kind of stat. There are 6 races, 15 sub-races and 11 classes. Some of the races are fantasy stalwarts that have been given a PoE spin like Humans, Dwarves and Elves. Others are a bit more unique.
Combat in PoE is almost always a white knuckle affair. Fights happens in real time but you can pause and issue commands. As a bonus, you can also slow down or speed up time at the press of a button, allowing you that extra time to react to subtle changes on the battlefield or cross a big map as quickly as possible. During combat you have to keep in mind both your Endurance and your Health. Endurance represents how much of a beating your character can take before being knocked unconscious. You can replenish Endurance with items, abilities and spells. While most damage affects Endurance you will also lose Health during combat. Lose all your health and you’ll be maimed. Get hit again and you are dead. Companions can die for good. You can’t replenish Health or remove maimed status without resting at either a camp or an inn.
Party composition, formation, location and more all have major effects on combat. You have to play smart, not just bold. Your party is incredibly powerful so long as you make your choices with care. The enemies in PoE are super aggressive, varied and absolutely ruthless when it comes to hammering weakness. One of the ways PoE is different from other RPG’s is that the restrictions on equipment have been relaxed, meaning your casters can wear heavy armour and wield great swords if you want them too. There are considerations when it comes to armour of course, but it is nice that your casters and such don’t have to be so squishy.
PoE is not a game about grinding. Generally when you clear an area or map it stays cleared. Instead the game rewards players for exploration, discovery, completing quests and making choices. Whether you plan on fighting or sneaking your way through you are always going to have to be on your toes. You can’t just roll over anything you encounter. Some enemies will be too tough to beat. Some areas will be inaccessible without the right gear. You’ll have way more active quests and tasks than you can immediately complete. This means you need to make hard choices and return to questlines and areas when you are better equipped to tackle them.
Besides the standard questing and combat (and a million other little things to be honest), PoE has two big features I love. The first of which is your Stronghold Caed Nua. Once you’re done battling through the Stronghold proper it becomes your base of operations. You’ll repair its buildings, shore up its defences, man it with soldiers, send companions out on quests and more from within its walls. You can even manage it while you are away. In some aspects it may seem a bit dry, but there is enough incentive there to keep making progress. Sometimes your Stronghold will come under attack. Other times you’ll take someone captive and hold them in your dungeons until somebody begs for their release. Even though the game has 8 official companions, you can recruit your own custom made adventurers any time you want as long as you have the cash. Since you can only have 5 companions in your party at a time, when your companions are not traveling with you they can be running quests from the Stronghold for a variety of rewards.
The other unique feature I love is The Endless Paths, which is a sprawling mega dungeon underneath your Stronghold. It’s almost like a game within a game. You’ll encounter all sorts of monsters, heroes and quests as you fight your way deeper and deeper. The whole time you are rebuilding the Stronghold in the back of your mind you worry about The Master Below.
Playing on Normal will provide a serious challenge. You WILL die many, many times. Hard mode is just that; HARD. Playing on Path of the Damned difficulty is pure masochism. Players can even take it a step further by turning on Expert Mode which completely removes all hints and suggestions from the game. If you are feeling truly crazy you can even try playing the game with Trials of Iron turned on which gives you just one save and one life. If you die, that’s it.
The game also comes with some more subtle touches that have a big effect on the game. For one, you’ll never run out of storage space when you are out questing. Each of your companions can hold 16 items in their inventory, but everyone always has access to your party Stash, which as far as I can tell is bottomless. The UI is clean, practical and easy to use. The game allows you to control font size and includes a colour-blind mode.
As far as bugs and glitches go I’ve encountered very few. The game never crashed on me once. I had to reload a save once to get a quest to trigger and I encountered text wrapping around improperly during a conversation with a random NPC. That’s it.

Starbound is a game which takes the 2D sanbox genre and puts it in space. While a simple concept, it works and the game is very enjoyable. A heavy focus of this game is on mining and like most other game within the genre, you will be doing a lot of it if you want to progress. The mining is done mostly with the Matter Manipulator, althought there are alternatives. The mining isn't too monotonous and the underground mini-biomes give you a sense of exploration and discovery. That is until you've seen everything. The unfortunate part about this game is that once you've seen one desert planet, you've seen them all. Once you've seen a certain mini biome, you've seen every other of that same mini biome. The only reason I kept exploring and searching was so that I could find certain structures for building. Speaking of which, the building in this game is fun and the amount of blocks and furniture at your disposal allows for the creation of many different types of buildings and settings. Another aspect of building that works well are colonies. Colonies can be created by placing housing permits inside of buildings. These will attract unique tenants based on the type of furniture used in the home. This allows for players to create thriving towns and cities and liven up their builds. This is something starbound does much better than Terraria, as that only has a select few tenants. Another thing that's (as far as I know) unique to Starbound, is its story. Unlike most other games, Starbound has a story which you can choose to ignore or follow exclusively. While the plot isn't the greatest, it certainly isn't bad and provides something for players who want to know about the universe of Starbound. Lastly, combat. The combat in Starbound is unique, and works intuitively. The combination of 1-handed and 2-handed weapons and secondary abilities allows for different combat strategies.
TL;DR, Starbound is an enjoyable game and is certainly worth the price for anyone who is a fan of the 2D sandbox genre.

I'm going to be brutally honest: I WANTED to like this game. It started out really good with an intriguing premise and likable characters and I was interested in seeing where it went! Heck, I was thinking that maybe this would be that one indie game that isn't the usual indie fare on Steam (i.e Questioning life, heavy amounts of drama, dark scenes, etc.) and it would be the indie game that I could honestly play constantly! I was even able to look past the shoddy platforming mechanics to the point where I could enjoy them! Then comes Act 3 and this is where the game went downhill for me. Not only did it introduce a pointless side story about a "ghost"
, but it started doing the exact♥♥♥♥♥♥I hate most if not all Indie games for: It started to ask questions about life, it brought in pointless drama, and it became pretentious with its dialogue. Why can't there be a indie game that DOESN'T follow the pack?! Once that stuff came up in Act 3, I went from wanting to replay the game to just wanting to get the game done and over with to straight up HATING IT! That is, until half-way through Act 3 when something happened that actually made me think it was not going to be a indie cliche and actually got me interested...until Act 3 continued and the cliches came back. The only good things I'll say about the game are that the artstyle is cute and the characters, until Act 3, are enjoyable and cutely designed. The music is something I won't even bash cause it was surprisingly catchy and pleasant, to the point where I wouldn't mind owning a copy of the soundtrack (And this is coming from someone who loves Power Metal). But, those good things are, sadly, out weigh by the stuff I hated and, for all those reasons I listed plus the fact it pulls of a abrupt ending (something I friggin' hate in games), I can not see myself recommending this game to anyone. It's sad, cause I really wanted to like this game cause it started out strong, but once Act 3 rode around, all the good things got blown away like a feather in the wind.

Quick summary: Razzart Visual does a Sakura game.
When this VN showed up on my Steam frontpage, I thought it looked pretty trashy; but when I saw it was from the studio behind the fantastic Starlight Vega and Love Ribbon, I decided to take a chance and see if it was more than met my eyes. Well... not quite.
Most of the art on this game is truly beautiful: backgrounds are gorgeous and detailed, CGs are well done and in a way that flows seamlessly with the general art style of the game... but character sprites do leave a lot to be desired, and the humongous proportions of the entire cast quickly becomes embarrassing rather than titillating. Which is problematic when it's the one part of the graphics you're supposed to focus on.
No voice acting whatsoever, and the music is rather average; not good enough so I'd go and buy the OST, but not bad enough I'd turn it off either, and for the most part it's a good fit.
No way around it: this *is* for the most part the trashy eroge VN it appears to be at first glance, with a plot as ridiculous as your average Sakura game, and not much more developed either. Characters are shallow, situations contrived, fanservice aplenty, and oh dear Lord the snakes, why.
And yet it's kinda fun when all's said and done; it feels less like an amateur making stupid mistakes, and more like a professional writer having one drink too many and deciding he no longer gives a crap. Thus, the game does have brief bursts of brilliance, both within itself as well as in a more meta context--the sheer length they keep the whole snakes subplot going is so audacious you can't help but laugh.
Took me only 2 hours of playtime to 100% the game, and outside of two choices near the end, whatever choice you get affects one or two lines of dialogue at most. So, no.
To anyone in the market for a Sakura game (you know who you are), I'd strongly recommend this: it's got far better backgrounds, no censorship, and is cheaper to boot. To anyone else... see if you're in the mood for playing a game that actively has you laughing at it instead of with it. Still hitting Recommend because, well, I did have fun after all, I just don't think it's for everybody, or even most people.

Quality puzzles: check.
Quality skill and build diversity: check.
Quality trolling potential: oh yes.
There is only one main component for puzzles: a spirit guide you move around by pressing space. This means cooperation is EVERYTHING in multiplayer mode; this may be why you don't see many public games in the co-op lobby. It's just too damn easy to troll because everyone doesn't have their own spirit guide, but then that could make FORCED game-breakingly easy.
Also, you have a lot of interesting options in how you build your character, but the game doesn't save your build which is pretty lame. If you could actually save your build without having to remember your ideal skill setup for each weapon, FORCED would be hands-down one of the best ARPG's in years. That aside, the game still has plenty to offer and is definitely worth your time. Plus it's incredibly fun to play with friends (that actually want to help you win the game, because it is so easy to troll).

The Whispered World is by no means a bad game. In fact it's actually a really good game, with some exceptional faults that destroy the rest of the magic.
The game is a delight to view, the hand rendered backgrounds are exceptional and even the pen and line animations are good, if slightly halting at times. The cutscenes suffer a little as they pull completely from the Disney style animation and lack the richer background texture and colour palette.
The music is also a delight, and fits the fantastic world well, with soft natural tones that play quietly in the background and aren't a distraction at all. As for the voice acting, it was fairly bad. The narrator (Sadwick's voice) is nasal and annoying, to the point of being so annoying that I simply ended up turning the sound off and played by reading the subtitles. That said albeit it being annoying, the catch is the voice is a perfect one to suit the pessimistic, morose main character.
Now coming to the characterisation, Daedalic seem to enjoy taking unlikable unlikely hero's and making them the protagonists (Rufus in Deponia). Sadwick continues this trend, he complains, and generally acts like a complete misanthrope, to the exasperation of not only his circus family, who deny him doing anything as he invariably messes it up  and himself. It's a difficult character to make a protagonist, as games require an active character, willing to undertake quests and action. As an unwilling character Sadwick seems "forced" and it makes him most difficult to identify with, however his lifting mood and transformation after a few success, that makes him more of an optimist alleviate this feeling, so it is worth sticking with. Spot serves as the ability extender in this game, and he is appealing not only for his unwavering dog-like faith and devotion to Sadwick, but also because you can't help wondering what creature he actually is that he can be dissected, set on fire and compressed and yet still survive. Spot is probably the games greatest mystery, and moreover his transitions between forms is amusing to watch.
The rest of the characters are fairly forgettable, with uninteresting dialogue and generic set-ups that don't add anything particularly new or interesting to the game, mainly serving as clue givers to the puzzle-solving scenarios.
The plot itself is short, and self-contained moves along fairly rapidly between puzzles and is otherwise well constructed, except for the dismal plot-twist ending. It is a plot-twist so generic, cliche and overused that it in fact lessens the impact of the game and delimits the otherwise more interesting philosophical underpinning to the game. It is meant to play upon your heart-strings and emotionally manipulate you, and it does achieve this, you will feel emotionally manipulated, butI still found it to be too disappointing,
The gameplay is itself not bad as far as point and click games go. The major hold up is the frustrating menu system, that slows down interactions, requiring you to click the mouse twice to look, speak or touch and a rather clunky inventory system, that doesn't support mouse scrolling. Walking about is simple enough, however every now and then the click to walk would hang and I found myself only able to click on interactive objects, precipitating a need to exit and re-enter the area. A fairly frustrating little bug.
I really would be able to recommend this short adventure game, but there are better titles out there to play. So only pick this up if it's on sale, you're a Daedalic fan and must own all their titles or have played most of the other more highly recommended point n click adventures and are still looking for a fix.

Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor, gameplay wise, is bascically a fusion of the combat mechanics of the arkham series and stealth and parkour mechanics of the assasins creed.
It beautifully incorporates the two mechanics to produce a fluidic combat system which is highly responsive and really quite fun to play. You can also ride beasts like caragaurs and graugs, wreaking havoc among the orcs, and occasionally feasting over them which is very, very cool.
Graphically, the textures are beautifully rendered which ironically makes Mordor look beautiful in its own way. One of the main strengths of this game is its impeccable voice acting which invigorates and gives life to the characters. They've really nailed Gollum too (Voiced by Andrew Sircus here?! Seems so).
Another interesting mechanic in this game is the nemesis forge system which bascically allows you to influence Sauron's army and thereby create you own unique storyline, you can also control the minds of orcs once you've weakened or sneaked up on them and eventually order them to challenge another orc in duel or murder a collegue which makes interesting effects to the nemesis mechanic. (The repeated introductions of the captains and warchiefs, rubbing your previous defeat in your face do become excessively annoying, especially if you shroud yourself all your life under the insecurity of your competence.)
The game's weakness, however, lies in the disconnectedness the otherwise decent storyline has, and this lack of fluidity weakens the game's dark and gruesome setting. I would have loved to see a fluidity in the story progression like The Witcher 3 which would've made this a 9/10 kinda game.
Overall, I would say that this game is worth for those who liked the arkham and assasins creed series and who are fans of the tolkein universe.

Night in the Woods is one of the best examples of a narrative game you're going to find. A great example of a game meant to tell a story, and its status as a video game does not limit its story telling potential, but enhances it.
Truthfuly, this is not the kind of game that requires skill to achieve, or offers challenge. All you really do in the game is jump and walk around, exploring Possum Springs and deciding which of your friends and neighbors to interact with. The closest equivilent to this game is something like unfortunately named 'walking simulators' like Firewatch, but Night in the Woods still offers a lot to do and much more influence on the narrative. There is a great sense of exploration as you jump across the rooftops, stumbling onto side stories and more characters to interact with. The story also twists its focus onto whichever character the player choices the spend the most of their time with. I know many games simulate this, but the story makes this mutable aspect organic, and it is so very rewarding to see my favorite character in this game become as important to the story as the protagonist.
And that narrative is right up there in the top 10 of the many games I've played. Each character is very well fleshed out, with very real feelings and dealing with very real problems. Even the minor characters you briefly talk to in the streets all have personality and are dealing with the same sort of problems a lot of us real life folks are dealing with. Despite the cartoon apperance of the game world and its characters, their problems are so very real. I've had to take a break from playing the game as it managed to hit 'really close to home.'
And a word about Mae, our heroine. Mae is a flawed character. There's a lot to relate about her, and a lot I don't understand about her. Our command over her is not complete, we can only steer her down a few parallel streets. There were times I was yelling at the screen because she would not do want I wanted her to do, or to say what I wanted her to say. But unlike every game hero I've yelled at in similar fasion, I don't hate Mae. For all the mistakes she constantly makes, she truly cares for the same characters I care for, and in as great a degree as I do, if not more. She just goes about helping them the only ways she knows how. And I can respect that.
I was one of the folks who kickstarted the game. This game made me stop and think about my own life. It put a different light on the choices I've made. It made me appreciate what I do have so much more. Any game that can pull that off deserves your time.

*Review of original initial release only. Does not account for changes via DLC or subsequent patches.*
Pillars of Eternity is a triumph.
You start the game as just another traveller looking for a fresh start in a new land, flavoured by the choices you made during character creation. A LOT of terrible things happen and before long you are caught up in world where souls are endlessly reincarnated and the natural balance has been shattered. Some individuals can even see and manipulate souls. A lot of the strife, mystery and wonder in this game ties directly back to souls in some way, shape, or form.
Your attributes, talents and choices also ripple out into the greater world. It is not possible to be on everyone’s good side. Treat one group well and another group may become hostile to you for helping their enemies. NPC’s and main characters will react to your race, class, nationality and affiliations. Conversations are influenced by a number of factors, providing you with a number of different conversation options. All of which ties to a reputation system. This helps the world feel much more grey, with right and wrong being a matter of perspective.
The visuals are gorgeous if you have an appreciation for the style being used, even if the world could use a bit more colour in places. PoE does not have traditional cinematics. Instead players are given interactive text adventures with illustrations and sound effects that are directly informed by your stats and choices.
The writing is almost always exceptional. Far, far above the usual flavour text that wraps around typical binary conversations in other games. The text based dialogue and the voice acting are really great. You might not hear as much banter as you will in other games but what is there is entertaining and sometimes surprising. The 8 official companions all bring something unique to the table.
Character creation is one of my favourite parts of RPG’s. PoE is a wonderland in this respect. There are a lot of stats and mechanics to wrap your head around. You absolutely can build a viable character just following the on-screen tips and jumping into a game. The thing is, you won’t know WHY you are making those suggested choices. You’ll have descriptions to read sure, but you just won’t have an appreciation for the nuances of PoE‘s rule-set without experimentation. The game is setup in such a way that anyone can make a safe, viable character following the on-screen suggestions. Failure to Min/Max every damn stat won’t cripple you. Which is not to say you could not create a broken character, just that you’d have to travel pretty far off the beaten path to do it. By the same extent it is possible to break out “the maths” and attempt to make the most deadly backstabbing Orlan Rogue this side of Gilded Vale.
You have lots of choices when it comes to creating your character and they all come with some kind of stat. There are 6 races, 15 sub-races and 11 classes. Some of the races are fantasy stalwarts that have been given a PoE spin like Humans, Dwarves and Elves. Others are a bit more unique.
Combat in PoE is almost always a white knuckle affair. Fights happens in real time but you can pause and issue commands. As a bonus, you can also slow down or speed up time at the press of a button, allowing you that extra time to react to subtle changes on the battlefield or cross a big map as quickly as possible. During combat you have to keep in mind both your Endurance and your Health. Endurance represents how much of a beating your character can take before being knocked unconscious. You can replenish Endurance with items, abilities and spells. While most damage affects Endurance you will also lose Health during combat. Lose all your health and you’ll be maimed. Get hit again and you are dead. Companions can die for good. You can’t replenish Health or remove maimed status without resting at either a camp or an inn.
Party composition, formation, location and more all have major effects on combat. You have to play smart, not just bold. Your party is incredibly powerful so long as you make your choices with care. The enemies in PoE are super aggressive, varied and absolutely ruthless when it comes to hammering weakness. One of the ways PoE is different from other RPG’s is that the restrictions on equipment have been relaxed, meaning your casters can wear heavy armour and wield great swords if you want them too. There are considerations when it comes to armour of course, but it is nice that your casters and such don’t have to be so squishy.
PoE is not a game about grinding. Generally when you clear an area or map it stays cleared. Instead the game rewards players for exploration, discovery, completing quests and making choices. Whether you plan on fighting or sneaking your way through you are always going to have to be on your toes. You can’t just roll over anything you encounter. Some enemies will be too tough to beat. Some areas will be inaccessible without the right gear. You’ll have way more active quests and tasks than you can immediately complete. This means you need to make hard choices and return to questlines and areas when you are better equipped to tackle them.
Besides the standard questing and combat (and a million other little things to be honest), PoE has two big features I love. The first of which is your Stronghold Caed Nua. Once you’re done battling through the Stronghold proper it becomes your base of operations. You’ll repair its buildings, shore up its defences, man it with soldiers, send companions out on quests and more from within its walls. You can even manage it while you are away. In some aspects it may seem a bit dry, but there is enough incentive there to keep making progress. Sometimes your Stronghold will come under attack. Other times you’ll take someone captive and hold them in your dungeons until somebody begs for their release. Even though the game has 8 official companions, you can recruit your own custom made adventurers any time you want as long as you have the cash. Since you can only have 5 companions in your party at a time, when your companions are not traveling with you they can be running quests from the Stronghold for a variety of rewards.
The other unique feature I love is The Endless Paths, which is a sprawling mega dungeon underneath your Stronghold. It’s almost like a game within a game. You’ll encounter all sorts of monsters, heroes and quests as you fight your way deeper and deeper. The whole time you are rebuilding the Stronghold in the back of your mind you worry about The Master Below.
Playing on Normal will provide a serious challenge. You WILL die many, many times. Hard mode is just that; HARD. Playing on Path of the Damned difficulty is pure masochism. Players can even take it a step further by turning on Expert Mode which completely removes all hints and suggestions from the game. If you are feeling truly crazy you can even try playing the game with Trials of Iron turned on which gives you just one save and one life. If you die, that’s it.
The game also comes with some more subtle touches that have a big effect on the game. For one, you’ll never run out of storage space when you are out questing. Each of your companions can hold 16 items in their inventory, but everyone always has access to your party Stash, which as far as I can tell is bottomless. The UI is clean, practical and easy to use. The game allows you to control font size and includes a colour-blind mode.
As far as bugs and glitches go I’ve encountered very few. The game never crashed on me once. I had to reload a save once to get a quest to trigger and I encountered text wrapping around improperly during a conversation with a random NPC. That’s it.

Long Live the Queen was not quite the game I expected, in spite of the fact that it's everything it promised to be on the cover. In this royalty simulator, you control Elodie, a precocious little pink-haired 14-year-old princess who, upon her mother's death, has been thrust into the role of matriarch. Establishing this game firmly in the G.R.R. Martin school of political thought, your goal is not so much to save the world from evil or to rule as a beloved queen should, but to survive long enough to reach your coronation.
Your country is weak, your neighbors ambitious, and your education incredibly limited; spend your time training up the many, many skills you'll need to be an effective leader, juggling pressing needs for the kingdom with personal desires to help you get what you want. Meanwhile, the constant flood of events around you will send your emotions scattering all over, and since it's hard to study Military Strategy when you're terrified or Court Manners when you're feeling defiant, you must manage your personal time to keep you in the right state of mind. On top of all that, you'll be asked time and again to commit money or military strength to a number of causes; until you've trained up the proper understanding of economics and military theory, you won't even be aware these resources exist, let alone that they're something you should be mindful of. Screw up along the way and you're dead - assassins, poisoned gifts, bandits, monsters... There are plenty of horrible things out to get you. And they will. Repeatedly. It's a surprisingly anxiety-ridden pile of disasters to manage, and while I adore it, your mileage may vary.
On top of that, there's also a decent story set behind everything, though your point of view limits what you can see. The cast of characters is overwhelming at first, but you quickly start to remember which ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s backstabbed you and which actually seem to be decent enough human beings. There are plenty of story paths to follow, plenty of branches that reveal details otherwise hidden, and plenty of endings to grab. Are you a meek and pretty trophy wife? A blood-stained military empress? A strange and terrifying witch-queen? Bear the demands of the throne, squeeze what you want out of the spare time you are given, and you can forge whatever destiny you so choose.

State of Decay is a SINGLEPLAYER zombie survival game set in the Midwest United States. It involves rounding up smaller bands of human survivors and incorporating them into your 'influencial area', AKA your zombie survival society. While this mechanic is thought out in amazing detail, down to emotions and job distribution, a lot is to be desired for the entire game.
The first problem I encountered starting gameplay was the somewhat steep learning curve. As the de facto 'leader' of your party, a massive amount of responsibilites are shoved into your arms. And I appreciate that for its realism, of course as a leader of a surviving band of humans in a zombie apocalypse a lot of responsibilites are going to be picked up by you, but in State of Decay the concept is blown out of proportion. Your fellow survivors are utterly inept at taking care of themselves, falling off roofs and demanding to be rescued. Rather than an NPC taking care of the problem while you're out trying to aquire medical supplies, YOU have to go out of the way to save him or else he'll die and everybody will be angry at YOU for not saving him.
Another concept that was annoying was the fact you were STUCK with a group of man-children for your survival party. In essence, you had no option to go it alone or become a nomadic survivor. How hard is it to ask for a quiet life in the middle of the woods eating peas and corn out of a can while making the occasional excursion into zombie territory? The main reason why much of my map goes unexplored is because I have to deal with party issues that crop up every twenty seconds or so. I don't want to stop my search for fellow survivors because some idiot back at base slipped and dropped his ice cream.
This is another nitpick I had to deal with- the survivor-survivor interaction in the game was DISMAL. While other (NPC) bands of survivors eke a living out in the zombie territory, they never come off as hostile to the point where they start targeting you. While this may seem like a good thing, it's actually an extremely narrow-minded concept. Example: "oh, all survivors are good, let's all be friends." More than likely in a disaster scenario everyone would be thinking for themselves, take Hurricane Katrina for example. Gangs of looters were prevalent in the suburbs, and murder was commonplace before the National Guard locked the place down. While some NPCs may express hatred towards you or your group, they will never take an action against you short of refusing to come on an expedition with you.
Some other parts of the game greatly affected my enjoyment of gameplay, such as the fact that a solid steel crowbar can break if you hit soft flesh enough times. Close-up mechanics are about as robust as Space Station 13. Gunplay is almost depressing, repeated hits to the forehead from a .44 Magnum revolver to an eight-foot tall inbred zombie monstrosity wasn't enough to put it down, let alone shots from a Remington 750. This was during an early mission, and somehow the thing bugs through the window and tears me in half. Driving cars is fun until you run over enough zombies and your car inexplicably EXPLODES, or you hit a pebble in the road and you go flying. Zombies are also able to latch onto your car even as you're driving past them at 50 mph.
However the game still had some redeeming qualities. Guns are correctly named for the most part, only the ones with copyright licenses in place had to be changed and some others were just renamed for easier naming. (But really, 'Monag' is the new Mosin Nagant!? Since when is a 100 year old pre-soviet era rifle licensed?)
Visuals are great, especially when walking down the highway. Just ignore that constantly updating survivor-♥♥♥♥up-o-meter in the top right and relax. Dialogue between survivors is frequent and expressive.
In the end, this game had a lot going for it, and possibly more in the future, although unlikely. The absence of multiplayer makes playing the game almost a sort of chore. Two heads are better than one, they say. And as of now, there's only one head. This game seemed good, but now it just reeks of wasted potential. The large screen at the start that says "BUY DLC HURR HURR" is really a big sign that shows that the developers really don't care about their players. It's quite sad, really.
I rate State of Decay a 4 out of 10, because there were so many things that could have gone so right that in the end went so wrong. I want my five dollars back.

Sheesh. Where did those 9 hours go? I didn't honestly expect the game to last that long. *Nnn-nnh!*
Anna's Quest is a point-and-click adventure of an innocent little girl bestowed with the gift of telekinesis. Hard times force her to go on a journey to make things right, and to encounter the evils of the world within. On her journey, she will meet allies, enemies, and characters of all sorts, but who is truly trying to help her, and who is trying to merely use her? This is the story of Anna's Quest, and in it you will learn that being a little girl in the big bad world means nothing if you're brave enough to carry on with your purpose. Innocence shouldn't be taken lightly, for Anna is full of wit.
In all honesty though, this isn't a point-and-click adventure as they say: It's a click on everything to solve the insolvable puzzle nightmare. I really don't like looking up tutorials on games because I like to finish them myself, but boy did this game test my wit like no other. It's not so much a bad thing on how the game's setup; it's just that not all puzzles have an obvious answer. My advice to you is: Look at every little detail.
I'd like to point out how well-written the characters are. They're not all predictable and one-dimensional as some characters in stories are written. The dialogue is cleverly written with references to real-life situations and sarcastic humor throughout, and each character itself is unique with their own personality, style of acting, and agenda of their role in Anna's Quest. As I said before, some characters do a fantastic job of playing the part of your friend, but betraying you could be their end game.
The difficulty of the game is where it stands apart from other point-and-click adventures. It's not a simple method of clicking on an item, getting a brief description, and triggering a cutscene like most. Ohhh, no! You have to put on your tinkerers cap and start combining various knick knacks to continue your quest, and there is always only one answer to the puzzle, but it's not at all obvious, so I advise searching each scene carefully because it's extremely easy to miss it.
Replayablity: I'd say I'll come back to the game after I've forgotten some of the story in order to get the rest of the achievements, but it's kinda like going to see a movie at the theater. Do you really wanna go back to the theater to watch it again? Granted, I know you can just buy the movie, but I'm using the theater as an example. The experience is great, and I'll gladly recommend the game to anyone that wants their wit tested that enjoys point-and-click adventures, but you pretty much play through it once, and you get your fill of what you want. Not saying that's a bad thing though. 9 hours for the little I spent on it was more than worth it considering I was surprised how long it took me to complete. (I only looked up a couple tutorial videos for when a couple puzzles became impossible to solve, and the solution was deceitfully obvious)
For $20, I can't say if the game is truly worth that much. I mean, I'd rather get 20 hours out of it to pay that much, but I bought the bundle it came in for $28, so I got 14 games for a little over the base price of this game. Give the demo a try, see if you like it. I enjoyed what I played and I'll recommend it to all who I think would also enjoy it.

Right, where do I start?
Firstly I'm going to explain why I'm not recommending this game:
I managed to get hold of this game after having it in my wishlist for a long time, and was pretty happy and had a lot of anticipation to play it. I launched the game and I started my first survival. I was immediately blown away by the incredible immersion that the first 10 minutes offered. I landed myself on a desert island and scavenged some supplies from a nearby wreck. I started to gather resources that I figured out how to harvest and had a stockpile going. I had no idea how to craft anything and spent a good 20 minutes trying to figure out how to build a simple crude axe. Eventually I stumbled upon the ability to pile different materials together to then unlock the item to craft. A decent achievement in my eyes as it simulated my character actually discovering how to make something from scratch... as you'd expect in a real survival situation. I then eventually found out how to make a fire, catch and cook food, purify sea water, build a small shack and another raft and then got onto venturing out for more resources. The atmosphere was so incredibly immersing, I couldn't fault my game time. The graphics were gorgeous and just played so well into the entire feel of the game. It was nothing like I've ever played before. A true, survival, discovery game that you solved things off of your own back, no crafting menu as such to aid you and a nice physics engine. You're probably thinking right now... "so why the negative review?" And I shall tell you why in three simple parts.
Version 0.06 Update.
I had only played the game before the update for 5-6 hours and was stunned by it's ability to draw me in. I was eager to read the upcoming content and two days after purchasing and playing I heard of update v0.06, "fantastic!" I thought. Oh, I couldn't have been more wrong.
I proceeded to the news page of Stranded Deep and began to read the update changes. I was so eager to read the new content: additions to the game... NOT changes to existing game play. I was pleased to read the additions and was intrigued by the updates on crafting, editing and graphics. Now... I'm definitely not one to judge a game by graphics and will certainly not discard a game if they aren't to a 'high spec'. I play games for entertainment and immersion.
So, after launching the game after the update I was met with a new snazzy menu which had more options than the previous version. I was a bit miffed when I couldn't load my previous game but I was wiling to let that slide and start fresh. Aesthetically, the menu seemed based off the similar style of Dead Island and Far Cry 3. I heard of graphical improvements (in my eyes it didn't need it at all) so I ramped the graphics up fully. I launched the game and was instantly met by sickeningly over the top wave physics which were almost unbearable to watch. I later found out that there was no way to tone it down, which almost immediately put me off exploring in my raft. The textures of the islands, water and pretty much everything else but the sun had changed. It instantly didn't feel like the same game... The same theme kept popping into my head: "this looks like they're trying to replicate Far Cry 3's look". Which they really shouldn't have done.
Probably the only thing I actually liked about the updated version was the extended inventory from 8 to 15 slots, that was welcomed greatly.
They added a full crafting menu in the style of a little bit of paper, telling you what you could build and what resources you need (because obviously everyone who gets stranded on a desert island has an instruction manual telling them how to construct wooden shacks and stone tools). Well... that's a waste of money. Completely stripping back the idea of finding things out for yourself to survive, no! We'll just tell you everything so all you need to do is now scavenge all the materials you need for everything which is pretty much all on one island because the resource spawn was obviously coded for 'super-overabundant'. Rendering travelling to any other islands pointless, not that you'd want to because you'd get motion sickness from the raft. By this point I'm giving up all hope on this game. There's no immersion because of the radical graphics change which forces it to feel like another crafting game rather than a survival simulation, the ridiculous wave physics which don't even link with shoreline waters. The stupid idea that steel girders are obviously a common resource on a deserted tropical island and every other resource in the game is in arms reach. The stupid ♥♥♥♥ing crafting menu that totals your game play time, after you've bought this game and realised how much of a train wreck it's turned out to be, to about 2 hours (if you're lucky).
Honestly I got peed off so much with the change... I would've loved to sink my teeth into this game if it had stayed the same. The only way they could save this game is if they retracted v0.06 and just added more content, instead of trying to change the game's feel entirely. That and add multiplayer.
Seriously, save yourself the pain, don't even bother. It would only be worth playing the pre-v0.06 update.

I've got some mixed feelings here. The Whispered World isn't the greatest point-and-click adventure game I've played, but ultimately it's a solid game that handles its story, characters, and themes really well and features acceptable, if challenging, puzzle mechanics.
The best element of the game by far is its character development: specifically, the way the game develops its protagonist, Sadwick. To put it simply, Sadwick is utterly unlikeable when you begin the game. Picture a combination of Jeffery Dallas from the Julian Smith videos and Marvin the Depressed Robot from Hitchhiker's Guide--except that his complaining, self-absorbtion, and misery are all treated unironically, and not as a source of humor. He writes bad poetry about his feelings, sobs over his rotten circumstances, and loses his temper at his lovably senile grandfather. But while the game doesn't treat Sadwick's disposition mockingly, it also doesn't take him too seriously. Sadwick isn't an existential hero fighting helplessly against tragic circumstances. He's just an ornery kid with a lousy life who responds the way any self-interested person might.
As the game goes on, however, Sadwick slowly and subtly transforms to the point that you are genuinely concerned with his wellbeing and with the success of his quest. Where other characters inertly accept the coming end-of-the-world scenario at the center of the game's story, Sadwick steps up and tries to change things, certain as he is at first that his actions will prove pointless. The further into the game you go, the less gloomy and caustic Sadwick becomes. And as he grows in confidence--or at least determination--he becomes a truly sympathetic character. By the game's end, I loved the little guy.
The game's other characters are more of a mixed bag. Some, such as Grandpa, are quite lovable, while others, such as Bobby (the King's messenger) and Loucaux (the main villain) can be rather unlikeable or one-dimensional. The characters from the game's second section are my favorite. The sleep-deprived landowner Ruben and his loud, enthusiastic servant Bando form the perfect odd couple and are also the most objectively interesting characters in the game.
One thing that can be said for the game's characters is that they all embody the story's main themes in unique and fascinating ways. Time and again, characters that occupy "important" roles in the game's world prove powerless in preventing the world's end, while little Sadwick the clown from the traveling circus does all the work. But the characters in positions of authority are always weak because they choose to be--because the game's main theme is the contrast between activity and stagnation. So Bobby is paralyzed by fear and ultimately turns over his all-important mission to Sadwick. Ruben idly obsesses over his 10,000 silver pearls and can't even enjoy the luxurious life he has made for himself. And the King, who is supposed to save the world, lies dying behind locked doors that only he can open.
It's refreshing to see a story that recognizes that perfection is never static. It's not something that is whole and immaculate until it is broken, but rather something that people must actively work to maintain.
The Whispered World's story and gameplay unfold in four large sections, in which Sadwick does everything he possibly can to save the world despite a prophecy (known only to him) that he will ultimately be responsible for destroying it. The episodic structure of the game has some real benefits--and some pitfalls. For one thing, it means that you wind up going to many more locations and environments than you might in the typical point-and-click adventure game. Since there's not but so much backtracking, the game stresses progress and discovery and strikes a nice balance between presenting new areas and fully exploring old ones.
But since the game doesn't feature an overworld-style main area, you never feel especially grounded as you play the game. That factor, combined with the real sense of urgency in the game's plot, could make you impatient to make progress. And impatience in this game is a real killer, since some of the puzzles are dastardly hard to figure out. For the most part, the game isn't totally unintuitive--solutions usually make sense once you figure them out or look them up--but the game often doesn't provide many context clues to point you toward the proper solution to its puzzles, and certain gameplay scenarios would be near-impossible to figure out without help. I found myself checking a walkthrough almost every thirty or forty minutes, and I only rarely regretted giving up on certain puzzles.
The game is darned tricky, in part because there are just so many ways to interact with the game's environments. In addition to trying out items on environmental objects and on other items, as in most point-and-click adventure games, you can also use your pet caterpillar Spot, in any of various forms you discover throughout the game, to interact with things. And some puzzles require you to use the "mouth" icon (which is primarily used for speaking with other characters) on other objects or talk with the same characters on multiple separate occasions to open up new paths.
Apart from the gameplay and the story, The Whispered World features pretty good visuals. The hand-drawn backgrounds to each area are lovely and intricate, although they tend to carry somewhat of a melancholy mood. And the game's spare and lonesome music only adds to that effect. Character animations, on the other hand, tend to look unpolished and inexact, and somehow the cutscenes are even worse. The quality of the voice acting is so-so, with certain characters who are downright unlistenable, and the game ramrods lines of dialogue into each other, clipping off the first syllable of most lines and making the voices harder to listen to. Dialogue is snappy--Sadwick throws a lot of nice barbs at just about everybody he encounters--but occupies too much of the game. Conversations can go on forever, and you have to go through some of them really thoroughly to advance in the game.
I mean it when I say that this game only gets better and better as it goes along. The story is great, and even the requisite big reveals at the end only add to the meaning of the game. The characters are nicely handled, the gameplay is fun when you don't get hung up for too long, and the game ultimately provides a really satisfying experience to anyone enduring enough to soldier through it.

The Whispered World is a beautiful game that stirs deep emotion and brings a good few laughs along with it, cleverly using satire without overdoing it and creating a depressed character that is 100% likable. Sadwick is amusing, adorable, and superbly written, displaying characteristics of those with depression accurately which allows people to relate to him easily. I have seen rather a few complaints about the voice acting, which personally I thought was brilliant. At no point did I cringe or find it unnatural, and I found that the tone to Sadwick's voice was perfect for his role and his personality. He has asthma, vertigo, depression and anxiety which he either comments on or is obvious throughout the game, giving a wide range of mental instabilities that people can relate to. The backgrounds and soundtrack are absolutely gorgeous, and the artwork you gain for finishing the game are a pleasure to look at and feel like a very worthy reward.
The clicking sometimes doesn't respond and you have to double click or place items in a very specific place, but I found myself wanting to continue the game so much that by a few minutes in I really didn't care about the extra clicking sometimes required and even got used to it. The hotspot indicator is VERY useful in the game and you WILL have to use it in almost every screen, but again I just find the feature useful and it didn't bother me at all.
Daedalic are masters at immersive point and click adventures, and this was just the beginning of their incredible games. Their gift for creating magical stories with interesting and likable characters sparkles in this game, and at the reduced price it is now, it's well worth the money.

The only reason I don't recommend this game is if your play style/preference is similar to mine.
- The combat is too messy. My preference is turn-based tactical. POE combat is real-time and poorly suited to anyone who wants proper control over battles. Even when using pause on/off it's too difficult to know what's happening and player chars  are too hard to locate; and it's a nightmare trying to guess which chars are waiting for their next command or still finishing their previous command. There is a wall of stats to sift through to discern what's happening and figure your best moves, but it's too much and too laborious to find the important bits of info. The battles in POE couldn't have been so amazing and epic due to all the various stats, items, and possibilities. I've since learned on forums that most players just use the Ai to resolve battles - this just seems like a terrible waste to me and a missed opportunity.
- So much text. I'm perfectly fine with lots of text (I've been playing RPGs since forever both CRPGs & Pen & Paper). But I really wish there was a TLDR version/option/summary. You see, these days I don't have half as much time to jump on screens, so I'd prefer not to spend it reading, reading, reading. The quest logs summarize what's to be done, but a rolling summary of ech story arc would be great for those of us who'd like to get on with adventuring. When I'm a senior and retired I'll have all the time in the world to read away.
- The statistics & attributes have broken away from the typical D&D system. That's not necessarily a bad thing of course, but it certainly requires a different mindset and was a bit confusing at first. Admittedly I'm old school and I'm not a fan of every stat/ability/skill etc available to all races & classes.
Everything else about the game is perfect. Lot's of exploring and adventuring, characters to meet, variety of monsters, beautiful graphics, and interesting locations.

I don't even know where to start, to be quite honest. I've been waiting for the release of this game for roughly a year before it actually came out, and finally the wait is over.
I guess I'll start off simple. I love this game. I love everything about it. The art is cute and beautiful, and perfectly changes atmosphere to whatever it needs to be. The soundtrack is just as beautiful, and I can't wait until it's released separately so I can buy that, too.
The writing, oh my god, the writing. This has been one of the most immersive, most real, funniest, just generally gripping experiences I've ever had with a game. I found myself going from laughing to being sad, to just being taken aback frequently, and I fell in love with most of the characters for one reason or another. I am also a huge fan of mystery, and this game just encompassed everything I love about the genre.
The ending took me by surprise - and while that would be a bad thing in many other games, I think it worked just right here, and completely reinforced the tone the game had up to that point.
I know it just seems like I'm gushing, but I honestly don't know much bad to say about this game.
I guess you could say that it's somewhat short - but I don't consider that to be a bad thing. Rather, it didn't overstay it's welcome. It lasted just long enough, maybe it could have been SLIGHTLY longer - but I did not feel like I was cheated out of playtime at all.
Another thing you could critisize is that there's no real way too lose. It's not like an action RPG where you die and respawn, or anything like that. This game is a fairly straightforward experience, with a few choices here and there, and it does not pretend to be anything else. Which is exactly why I can't fault it for that, either.
In short, if you like storybased games, beautiful art, clever and immersive writing and a soundtrack that you will lose yourself in, buy this game. It's well worth the 20 bucks, I would pay them again in a heartbeat, and I am so glad I got to experience this game just after the release, before it gets a ton of exposure and I would run the risk of spoilers or killjoy fandoms forming.
Another thing - this game also has a minigame that you could probably sell as a separate, small, arcade style game. It's very fun, surprisingly tough sometimes and a good timekiller.

Starbound is a game which takes the 2D sanbox genre and puts it in space. While a simple concept, it works and the game is very enjoyable. A heavy focus of this game is on mining and like most other game within the genre, you will be doing a lot of it if you want to progress. The mining is done mostly with the Matter Manipulator, althought there are alternatives. The mining isn't too monotonous and the underground mini-biomes give you a sense of exploration and discovery. That is until you've seen everything. The unfortunate part about this game is that once you've seen one desert planet, you've seen them all. Once you've seen a certain mini biome, you've seen every other of that same mini biome. The only reason I kept exploring and searching was so that I could find certain structures for building. Speaking of which, the building in this game is fun and the amount of blocks and furniture at your disposal allows for the creation of many different types of buildings and settings. Another aspect of building that works well are colonies. Colonies can be created by placing housing permits inside of buildings. These will attract unique tenants based on the type of furniture used in the home. This allows for players to create thriving towns and cities and liven up their builds. This is something starbound does much better than Terraria, as that only has a select few tenants. Another thing that's (as far as I know) unique to Starbound, is its story. Unlike most other games, Starbound has a story which you can choose to ignore or follow exclusively. While the plot isn't the greatest, it certainly isn't bad and provides something for players who want to know about the universe of Starbound. Lastly, combat. The combat in Starbound is unique, and works intuitively. The combination of 1-handed and 2-handed weapons and secondary abilities allows for different combat strategies.
TL;DR, Starbound is an enjoyable game and is certainly worth the price for anyone who is a fan of the 2D sandbox genre.

Stranded Deep is awesome and definitly deserves the popularity it has. Thank you to all of the youtubers who helped this game's fanbase grow.

Stranded Deep is what I like to call a hard-core survival game. You will not be building a mega-base. You won't find zombies, dinosaurs or other unrealistic enemies (sharks are another matter). You will not ever construct a submachine gun, a hunting rifle or a laser blaster.
What you will do is spend each day trying to make it to the next day... up to a point. Up to a point. I deliberately emphasise that, because in calling Stranded Deep a hard-core survival game it imposes limitations on the game play that you need to consider carefully before purchasing it.
The game currently has very little content to it, by way of what most survival style games would offer. A (very) basic shelter and your basic tools can all be constructed within the first few hours of play. On any large island, the slowly regenerating supplies of yucca plants (not for eating), potato plants and coconuts along with an abundance of small fish and crabs in or immediately adjacent to the shallow waters around your island, will soon have all your food and water needs taken care of.
Indeed, you could survive almost indefinitely without so much as ever leaving your home island. Eventually you'll run out of wood and stone (neither of which regenerate), but it's a distant prospect to be sure, several weeks away (in game time) at the earliest.
There is a small amount of other "loot" to be found in the shipwrecks and planewrecks around the islands, though depending on your luck the nearest one may be 20 feet off shore, or an island or two away.
The graphical quality of the game, as should be evident from the screenshots is quite impressive, indeed, they add to a really relaxing experience, and you could easily imagine yourself to be Tom Hanks in Cast Away. The water especially, as befits a game with so much of it, is simply unimpeachable, the best I've ever seen.
There are some flaws in the game. You'll notice the occasional graphical glitch, odd moonlight shading, a tree every now and then not quite connected to the ground, but these are, overall, very minor and fleeting flaws.
The game mechanics are as minimalist as the games philosphy, with much crafting conducted by throwing items on the ground, though recent updates have made the process more intuitive and less prone to looking up wiki's. The crafting is definitely not my favourite style, but I can see why the Devs have gone for it.
The biggest consideration though is the first one I've mentioned. In what will seem like a blink of an eye (because its so immersive) you will have reached the "end-game", such as it is, and you'll either hit a rapidly appoaching wall of boredom, or you will find the atmosphere to the game, which is well developed, is enough to keep you going.
Exploration, in anything other than a nomad like existence, is something which definitely needs improvement. Lacking a map, or even a compass (one can eventually be found), leaving your home island for a short "loot run" carries a very real risk of  getting lost, this issue not helped by the fact the other islands appear as generic place markers until you enter the islands zone (meaning yours will look like one of those very same generic markers the moment you leave its zone).
Again, this is a reflection of the minimalist philosphy behind the game, but it's one where I think the cost in longer-term playibility is too high. Likewise, the short duration you can hold your breath underwater (unless you find rare and non-regenrating scuba tanks), means that much of the deeper ocean areas will be frustratingly out of your reach for most of your game time.
In summary, Stranded Deep is a beautfilly rendered, unapoligetically minimalist survival game, that more than any other, will have you hankering (see what I did there?) to sit down and watch Cast Away once more. You can easily lose hours to it, but buyer beware, it's scope is very narrow and will not suit anyone looking for a more "conventional" survival / building / crafting game.

In FORCED, you are.. FORCED to fight for your life alone or with friends, with up to 4 player co-op with 4 different classes.
In this game, you are tying to survive in challenges put on you by gods, made for their own enjoyment. You are helped by this soul to destroy them and free your people once and for all. In ages past, your race is alive only to fight and die for the entertainment of beings much more powerful than you. This will change.
The four classes available are very different in what they do, being very solid to the class they represent.
The first is ranged, using a bow and agility like abilities and based around lightning. Second, a strength based two handed class using fire and heavy but slow attacks. A rogue is the third, using fast attacks with evasion abilities. The last is a frost themed tank with defensive abilities and stuns to reduce the damage everyone in your party takes. You can choose between them whenever you want, in between levels and depending on what is needed.
The game is a mix of a hack and slash with puzzle elements, really focusing on teamwork when played with others. I found the gameplay boring by myself, but when I played with a friend it was much more enjoyable. It can be very difficult at times, requiring a very good amount of game sense to dodge certain abilities and do certain puzzles. The bosses are very well thought out, giving a nice end to each chapter. They are also very unforgiving.
The price is pretty high when not on sale, much too high for a game like this (its pretty short, being completed in around 8 hours) and I would recommend only getting it on sale. Make sure you get a friend who kinda knows what a hack and slash is, because its much more fun with another person, but having an inexperienced player makes it much much much more difficult.
Overall, 8 hours of gameplay, hack and slash gameplay with puzzle elements and four classes. Don't buy on full price, wait for a sale.
Personal Rating: 3/5

I was pretty impressed with this game, of course the best thing about it is the aestethics. It has gorgeous animation and environment which looks like a fully animated feauture. The artistic theme of Fall colors are present from beginning to end and it ties in nicely with the overall tone and story. There are of course a few missteps, for one the main character Sadwick has an english voice that at times can seem a bit hard on the ears not to mention the silliness of it also kind of distracts from the otherwise pretty somber tone. However it's something I quickly got used to. As for the actual gameplay it is pretty standard adventure game fare, if you've played any of the classic Sierra or Lucas Arts point and click adventures from the 90's especially later titles like The Curse Of Monkey Island you know what to expect. For the most part the puzzles are simple enough but then sometimes you run into that one puzzle that just kinda stops you in your steps and you're forced to switch to a strategy of trial and error. Depending on your abilities some puzzles can be pretty hard to figure out. However that aside the soundtrack, artwork and story really is worth the price of admission on their own and this game has ended up being one of my favorite entries in the genre. Even better, with the special edition a lot of the technical game breaking issues have been fixed so if you were put off from buying this game because of the bugs in the original version (which all owners of the original version seem to have received for free since then) rest assured that this game works just fine and makes for an enjoyable experience.

Some quick positives and negatives:
Pros:
+ Stealth
+ Combat is fluid and extremely fun, with lots of options
+ Good graphics
+ Interesting story in the LotR environment
+ Open World
+ Nemesis system is innovative and fun
+ The entire game consists about killing orcs
Cons:
- While the combat is excellent, it gets a little repetitive after a while
- A few side characters could have been fleshed out more
- You cannot replay the main missions
- The entire game consists about killing orcs
That being said, I got the game on a sale and started playing it without any expectations whatsoever . To my surprise I ended up actually trying to finish it.
The game beginning is very engaging, but it slows down soon afterwards especially once you get stuck in the side quests, which are not very fun. The main story though is certainly fun, and towards the end it gets even better. The voice acting is top notch, especially for the Bright Lord. The cinematic are done very well and fit well with the game.
One of the important aspects of the game is the Nemesis system and manipulating the Orc army with the Brand ability. Which you can check via the in-menu diagram showing the strengths and weaknesses of the Captains and Warchiefs of Sauron's army, who are essentially the game's bosses. It also shows you their various rivalries and loyalties.
→If an Orc kills you (IF!) , he can be promoted to captain and gain power, skill, and influence, or if he's already a captain, he'll be given more responsibility. He then becomes your Nemesis and will track you down and try to kill you again. Also, you can play around and influence the evolution of the Orc hierarchy to your advantage, both through the elimination of certain captains and through the use of the Brand ability.
Overall, the loyalty system and the Nemesis system are very cool ideas and an impressive display of AI programming. But here's where the big problem lies → The game never pushes you to really take advantage of the Nemesis system. The development of the Nemesis system relies on you dying a lot, but the basic combat is so easy this doesn't happen. Without a decent number of deaths, the system just doesn't develop the way the game's developers intended it.
→BUT because the combat is easy, you never really need to actually take advantage of the faction warfare to progress through the game. There's no reason (besides the roleplaying aspect) to go out of your way to create a showdown between two captains when it's so easy to kill them on your own.
If only the combat would've been harder (a lot harder?) and with your death you'd influence the world in ways that you'd have to use the nemesis system to take down captains and warchifs that would've made the game a lot more interesting .
If you really want to play the game to it's full potential get yourself a nemesis (die basically) or it will be just another game in a sea of games that will be "meh I used to play that one was good..."

If I had to describe Pillars in one sentence, it would've been this: I haven't felt so immersed into a world since Morrowind. Having recently completed it again with White Marches I also confirmed for myself the game's replay value just for this sense of immersion. I'm sure I'll be returning to it every now and again in the future, it certainly goes to my classics list.
The world the player is thrust into is oozing with almost palpable gloom. A land ravaged by war is now suffering from a terrible affliction - the children are being born soulless. Is it a curse? Is it a disease? Is it divine retribution? No one knows, no one can tell, all they do know is that it's been going on for years and there're no signs of things getting better. But because no one has an explanation, the sense of despair and urgency is more pressing than most Big Bad Ancient Evil villains. Desperate times invite desperate measures. Cults and charlatans are running amok, tensions and scapegoating are reaching fever pitch.
And as far as storytelling goes it only gets better. I don't think any game ever made me consistently squirm so much about 'the right thing to say/do' in various situations. And with it invited a lot of introspection - something very few games ever do. Furthermore, to its credit Pillars doesn't shy away from punishing good intentions. A couple of unexpected outcomes, even while they were comparatively 'bad', impressed me to the point of 'wow, THAT happened...' (In stark contrast to Wasteland 2's Prison debacle that caused only anger at the writers.)
Companions and their quests are something else entirely too in their uniqueness. Almost none of them have true movie style happy endings and they may seem pointless to some, but they all have a couple of themes in common - dealing with uncertainty, handling your past and making sense of your duty.
Dealing with uncertainty is probably the main undercurrent of Pillars. A lot of people seem to think it's too dark and depressing, I would've rather called it subtle and low-key, and the mood it evokes - contemplative. And how many other games inviting their audiences to grapple with such issues are out there? In my opinion it is a rich and mature story, set in interesting and picturesque world, supported by great artwork and well fitting music, and designed from ground up with actual role playing in mind, offering a lot more ways to meaningfully express your character with words and deeds than most (any other?) RPGs of this decade.
It's not all doom and gloom too. A personal pet peeve of mine are all those reviews that decry "boring" companions. And unfortunately Sawyer's conclusion too was introducing more lighthearted sidekicks (as per his 'lessons from Pillars'). Excuse me, MORE lighthearted? Is Hiravias not lighthearted? Is Zahua not lighthearted? Isn't everyone else delighted with Devil's sardonic quips? What about all the moments of levity involving Eder or Aloth? The ever-cheerful Kana Rua is not lighthearted? /eyeroll I can only hope Obsidian won't overreact to this.
Of course, Pillars is not only story. There's combat too, and plenty of it. My opinion on combat is mixed, this micromanagement fest obivously is not going to be everyone's cup of tea. It can be deep and rewarding (there's loads of material here to push minmaxers and theorycrafters to get those ridiculous achievements like Triple Crown Solo), but for me - an average person who just happens to play a lot - it felt lacking in a few areas. For example, in my 300+ hours I never learned to appreciate chanters and priests. And I'm one of those people frustrated by spell / rest mechanics that turns spellcasters into a burden most of the time and makes them shine only during major encounters. That said, I truly enjoyed fighting in WM1 and WM2 on hard difficulty, and the ultimate fights felt truly epic. Fortunately, if you find combat to be an unbearable slog (and I do understand why quite a few people would), there's story time mode that should allow you to focus on the story. It's well worth it.

An incredible game with a fatal flaw. Everyone plays games like this for one reason, but that reason is different for everyone. Some like thebuilding, some like the exploring, some like the combat (though this game's combat is awful)... But I'll cut right to the point. What is the fatal flaw? Player Griefing. You can destroy anything you want, anytime you want. What's worse? Join a party, and you can go to anyones ship in your party and take anything you please, even trash the place.
What's worse? The Fix for this problem ALREADY EXISTS IN THE GAME, but it's unaccessable. Shield generators which protect tiles from destruction exist, so why is it so absurdly difficult for these developers to allow us to use them to protect our hard work? I spent MONTHS building and creating complex and incredible planets and structures... and all I ask for in return is the ability to protect my work from the complete obliteration of a griefer.
Aside from that, this game is wildly expansive and feels like the next generation of terraria. It really is an incredible game and I've loved playing it. I have loved the storyline and single player which other games lack, and dozens of the other features that this game features which really make it feel just simply wonderful. This is a 5 star game all the way.............once that flaw is corrected. Because of this flaw, I cannot enjoy my creations with the public, I have to sit to my own self or my two trusted friends. I'll never be able to share my server until this flaw is fixed, so I sadly must give this rating a Not Recommended until this absurd flaw is corrected. Because I find myself not wanting to ever play it again as long as everything I design and build through endless hours of work can be destroyed in seconds by anyone I want to share it with.
As soon as the developres put in a reasonable solution to anyone with or without modding/programming knowledge, this will switch to yes and become my favorite and most recommended game.

Once upon a time, I found myself in denial of the goodness that is Starbound. Yet, after seeing a friend play this game, after this person continued to rave about how great the game was simply for exploration, I Bought it. So there are some good things for me, and one major bad.  I'll start on the negative. So the deal is that walking feels like you'd be on ice. Everywhere you go is so close to ice physics that moving can quite literally kill you. Other than that, I have only love to give this babe of a game. First, Character creation is very free. I love how you can make a character of whatever race you please and all of the touches that the devs put in to each of the races. From comments, to personal ships and yet still more. Second, Tiers. One of my favorite things to do in most games is work my way all the way to the top of the power scale. This game does it in a somewhat linear fashon, and yet it never feels linear. Just in order to progress your armor, it requires all sorts of non-metal materials. Just to get better weapons, it requires exploration. It forces you to settle down on a planet and still forces you to run amok on planet after planet. Third, Multiplayer. Simply put, "Man, I'm just a humble PC gamer who needs friends to function, It's just my feeling about the game, man. Don't hurt me, man".

There are two kinds of friends you'll be playing with,
a) The ones who stick around, hang out, co-op, beef up and share a base with, take the time to explore and take things with stride, because everyone knows there isn't really anything to really care about once you get to the end game, and no reason to rush towards it.
b) The ones who go "Hey we should totes play", but are admant on building all their junk on their own ship, never share anything, try to skip the entire early game as soon as possible to go planet hopping for quick tech, constantly complain or go deathly silent doing their own thing, and just sort of exist on the same server without no one in the party ever actually seeing one another or playing together.
Good fun though!
