It should be sometime around the summer of 2002 when I discovered the existence and the concept of not any computer RPG - but specifically
, and every classic computer RPG Bioware and Black Isle Studios produced thereafter. I was just old enough to play a story oriented game by the time, and possessed enough language skills to get a liking to story narrative + fantasy literature. So my formidable adventure with CRPG games began, crafting a fascination for me in the manner of roleplaying and story narrative in video games forever.
It's 2016 now, and as I installed
, the tremendous hype of thousands of CRPG lovers who experienced the genre back in the time in its full glory rang in my ears. A grand expectation was at hand, and I was worried that even though it would be a sweet shot at nostalgia, this might not be a genuine deal. Then I started playing this game. 170 hours in, I completed it and I am positive that
holds the promise of being a genuine successor to old CRPGs, deserving every little bit of praise coming to Obsidian Entertainment’s way. It is a glorious experience.
The mysterious world of Eora - a high fantasy setting developed by Obsidian Entertainment, and home to many creatures and concepts of wonder, both new and old for us - holds many secrets, including the secret of the Watcher. As we begin the game, we create our character, attaining him/her both expected race/class combinations and abilities, and a background to establish former personal experience. The character customization options are various, and each new Watcher we would create would most certainly hold a new approach to this mysterious world. It should be useful to note that every background/class/race combination presents a new outlook and new dialogue options for the said character, promising a diverse gaming experience even as we start.
Whomever we decide to play as in this world, starts up in a caravan journey, approaching the hardy region of Dyrwood, for whatever reason that we hold at the time. The rough journey gets rougher as we get sick with high fever and troubling dreams in the middle of the night, and as the caravan takes a pause near some ruins sacred to the local people of Glanfathans. An age old dispute occurs, a slaughter takes place, then... a biawac appears - a dreaded wind storm speculated to rob people of their souls. It rips the region apart, leaving everyone as hollow, lifeless shells and somehow, we become the only survivor. Witnessing the source of the storm and coming alive out of the chilling supernatural experience, tired and frustrated, we manage to arrive the small settlement of Gilded Vale, only to be called as "the Watcher" by the spirit of a dwarven woman...
Now, we are able to perceive spirits and touch souls, reaching for the boundary between the physical and the spiritual. From thereon, we will take on a long journey, trying to learn the nature of our abilities and the cost they attain to our sanity, searching for the mystery of this biawac, an ancient servant of a secret sect and a life long forgotten by even time itself, yet not by the soul. As we journey, we'll gather companions with their own stories and missions, harbor companionship for many, enmity for some and we'll gather a reputation for our deeds throughout the realm. Involuntarily, we'll come to learn an ancient secret and change the face of Eora forever.
Excited? I knew I was when I realized that I had just spent 8 hours nonstop as I just started to play the game. The world is quite rich, characters are realistic with various personalities, outlooks and aspirations of their own, narrative is elaborate both with philosophical, social and political context - and the humor itself is point on based on party interactions and comments! As I finish the game, I find myself already missing fiery demagogies of Durance, hilarious remarks of Hiravais, smart exaggerations of Aloth and comforting anecdotes of Eder... and quite so many other NPCs with colorful personalities that I'll miss.
Independent from NPC personalities, the core story mechanics and interrelation of cause/consequence are surprisingly successful. There are various ways to conclude a quest, and the way to go with any of them would subtly alter the outcome of the main scenario, as well as the tone and interaction of the world to a degree. Your choices would attain your character some characteristic values like "benevolent", "cruel", "stoic", "smart" etc. As you attain those personality values through gameplay, some NPCs start to treat you differently based on your personality consistency and reputation, presenting new outcomes based on your actions.
A minor example from my experience: At some point in the game I was in Defiance Bay - the main city of the scenario, bustling with side quests. A boy approached me and asked whether I'd get a steel dagger for him. When asked what a 10 year old boy would do with such as weapon, he stated that he'd like to become a squire to a knight and he could do anything with such a weapon. Big dreams, huh? I said "why not", completed the mission and carried on. Sometime later I revisited the city, and turned around the corner to shop, and the town crier declared that a boy lost 3 fingers in an accident! Just... wow.
Graphics exemplify the capability of Unity engine in presenting a classic Infinity engine atmosphere, and behold: results are a glamorous beauty. We have the classic isometric mapping with a six people party formation to roam around, yet on close-up we are presented with tiny artworks at every corner from the architectural wonders to the natural beauties of the realm. Every new map that you tread into is a new source of respect for the labor put into the game. The soundtrack, environmental sound effects and voice acting are all top-notch, presenting an immersive environment in an isometric gameplay - which is a hard feat by nature.
Here comes the trickiest part about any RPG - combat mechanics. I won't go so far to declare that they are the best, yet with various customization options similar to D&D 3.5 mechanics, character builds are formidable. Each and every class have their strong suits and flaws, so all combat mechanics - and even some diplomacy encounters - work better in a full party. Usually, having 1-2 tank fighters - Eder is quite appropriate for that - , 2-3 dps characters - both ranged or close quarter - and a healer - Durance all the way! - is a decent party combination that would put you through the game, with some decent challenges on the way. Side note: alongside both expansions, there are a total of 5 Dragons within the realm and dragons are no joke in this game, as it should be so. Prepare yourself heavily for those encounters, they would take careful planning and more than one venture.
The game harbors various achievements. Some half of those are mostly story and exploration based that would come naturally with your progress. The other half though, contain difficulty achievements that would take you to solo the game on various excruciating difficulties. I heard that Barbarian class - or a carefully arranged Chanter with decent summons - would be the way to go for that, yet the game gets patched quite often even today so I have no idea what mechanic has been polished or watered down to arrange a balance. One single achievement is only granted to kickstarter backers though, so if you haven't been a backer it is sadly out of question to %100 the game in terms of achievements.
As the last verdict,
is a game worthy of the experience. It is basicaly a must for any RPG gamer!

A faithful continuation of the storied legacy of Infinity Engine RPGs. Makes smart changes to the gameplay while maintaining the overall feel of the system (with the sole exception of Disengage attacks, which are a bit broken.).
Characters are written pretty well, though you'll quickly learn to avoid headstones and gold-name NPCS, which are written by backers and completely irrelevant to everything. Otherwise, the plot is quite solid-- not the best writing in all video games, but certainly good.
Mechanically, the game stays pretty solid throughout, but there are some nasty difficulty spikes. Some, like secret dragon bosses, are fine-- they're optional, after all. However, I was annoyed by the large jump in difficulty that the final boss presents. I had to lower the difficulty to beat the game after a frustrating hour and a half of failed attempts-- whether that's a testament to my skill or the game's difficulty curve is up to you to decide. It really put a damper on the endgame in my opinion.
I haven't played the DLC, so I can't speak to its quality. Overall, though, I greatly enjoyed my time with the game.

There's very little I dislike about this game, honestly; every choice I made felt like it had *some* sort of impact on the world around me, the story was compelling and offered a fantastic universe, and the combat made each quest even more memorable.
This style of game is not for everyone, but Pillars manages to make the cRPG formula not only bearable, but modernizes it to a point of pristine polish. If you are a fan of RPGs, I wholeheartedly recommend you give Pillars of Eternity a whirl. I really do love this game to bits.
It's replayable, it's accessible without sacrificing depth, and above all, it's a damn good time. I truly hope that this is a new series from Obsidian, as I believe they knocked it out of the park with this game.
I give Pillars of Eternity 95 xaurip paladins out of 100.

It's a visual novel based on stats. It is completely scripted with no randomness at all. The game plays out in turns. Each turn you select two 'skills' for the Queen to learn. Then you select an 'activity' for her to do, which will change her 'mood', which will affect which skills she can better learn. The game will then check to see if your skills match a certain threshhold every few turns, which will affect the plot and what happens to the Queen.
This is not an erotic themed game.
From the description, I thought the game would be humorous. That the plot would involve laughing as the Queen dies in funny ways. Nope, the plot is completely straight. There are funny moments, to be sure, and some of the deaths are pretty stupid. But no, it's a straightforward story.
Actually, as weird a comparison it might be, this game's plot actually reminded me of something you might see in a Crusader Kings 2 game. Pretty much all of the focus of the game is on feudal politics, and the most important skill is arguably "Court Manners." There is some impressive world building here and I couldn't help but get drawn in. The plot is well written. It's detailed enough to capture your interest, but brief enough you don't get bored. There's enough variance in the plot depending on your results that keep it interesting.
My main criticism I think is that the game has a hard scripted event where you have no choice but to fight one guy, and you must have a specific arrangement of skills developed that you won't know about except through trial and error. There is only a set number of turns before he shows up, so your judgment in developing skills and maintaining your mood is critical. I still haven't been able to pass it despite hours of play. (It would be very simple to use a walkthrough and win, but if you did that the game would have no challenge and little replay value.)
Do I recommend Long Live The Queen? It's pretty excellent as far as these types of games go. I'd call it superior to Heileen 3.  If you're into these types of games, go ahead.
This game is awesome.  That's all you need to know.

Don't be fooled by the cutesy cover art. The Kingdom of Nova is a ruthless place, full of assassins, evil magic, and deadly court intrigue, and you, a mere 14 year old girl, must live long enough to take the crown - which is a hell of a lot harder than it sounds. A lot deeper than it seems at first glance.
Honestly, the game structure is a bit obtuse - not Paradox obtuse, but obtuse - and it can be frustrating if you play without much knowledge. That said, game playthroughs are quick, save scumming is essentially encouraged, and there's a lot of variety in events, the kind of variety that can only come with a game mostly played through text.
...could use more graphics, though. I'd honestly love an update with full VN-style portraits of characters, though that'd probably be hugely cost-prohibitive. Maybe, if it's successful on Steam, we can get more updates! Especially as the game was already massively expanded for its Steam release.
If you enjoy a broad variety of endings and a visual novel like gameplay you'll enjoy this game :)

There's something quite special about Night in the Woods.The game really captures the sense of small-town desparation and sets a tense mood of uncertainty.
The interactions between characters feels so genuine and palpable, with slang and in-jokes being tossed into casual conversations. The dialogue in the game is a class act.The visuals are colorful and neon-esque, even in scenes where there is a lot of darkness.
The brilliance in the storytelling is how the middle of the game felt so aimless and confusing. How we feel as a player going about and doing things that don't really advance the game is how Mae feels returning to a dying town where all her friends, her last bastion of familiarity, are all ready to move on.
I can't really describe how the game made me feel, but it *did* make me feel... something. Getting in a fight with your mom felt terrible, like you knew what was coming but you didn't want to believe it. That made me feel bad. But then there's the unbearable lightness of hanging out with Gregg and missing every pierogi or lightbulb that was thrown.
Mae clings onto the childish things in her life that make her feel safe while avoiding the heavy reality of adulthood and responsibility. The game tosses around some really weighty themes ranging from sexuality, dealing with mental illness and depression, death, financial struggles, injustice, and failure. In between are bouts of guitar-shredding, bike-riding and baseball-bat swinging that lighten the mood and keep you engaged. I'm certain there are a ton of secrets to find, and it'd worth it to replay it at least once to play all the different story branches or make different choices.
If you are the kind of person who enjoyed games like Undertale or Dust: an Elysian Tail, you will also enjoy this story-driven adventure game.
My only complaint were the lack of precise controls and sometimes very small interactable hitboxes for dialogue and inspection. The jumping can get awkward, and the game could probably do well to have a sprint or some sort of temporary short distance boost to shorten those long jogs across the town to get things done.
I rate a solid 9/10. Very fun game and worth every penny of the $20 pricetag.

A rogue MI6 agent, without spoiling the plot targets important US assets as an attempt to bargain for the withdrawal of all US troops in international territories. Gameplay is fast paced, or slow as you prefer, and the AI is quite receptive to sounds and things that you do, shooting out a bulb nearby an enemy alerts them for instance.

These are simple puzzles or annoying challenges that you need to find a plan on how to solve. It could be lasers, or bombs or just a simple "kill everything mission". After a mission you are returned to a "world map" inbetween missions. You may change between 4 classes and 2 people can't be the same class. The classes act a little different and are good for different things.
In each mission you can earn 3 crystals, which is basically the leveling up system of the game. Once you reach a certain number of crystals you unlock additional skills you can use instead of the basic ones. How do you earn the crystals? It's a little different depending on the mission but mostly it's about clearing the mission within a certain time frame, not taking damage or doing something fancy.

I've only played for a short while, but I like this game.  It is definitely not the typical "open-world" game in that EVERYTHING persists.  That Twinkie and bottle of aspirin you left in the trunk of that station wagon outside the forest ranger station in the beginning of the game is still there 3 days later.  Jumping into a car and joyriding through the small-town streets, wrecking the car in the process, is not a good idea.  In addition to wrecking the car (which does not magically respawn of course) you will draw a lot of attention to yourself.  Everything wears down or breaks after too much use, including weapons and vehicles.  Combined with the mission system and the interactions with other survivors, this aspect basically rewards the kind of behavior that probably would actually pay off in a real zombie apocalypse:  move quietly, search for supplies and food, try to get along with the few others left alive.
Definitely worth the summer-sale price!

an excellent game to introduce you to the genre, although the absolute best in-game tutorial for fighting games would be in skullgirls. this game does not have an in-game tutorial and many concepts are left for you to figure out on your own. i can't think of anything in the current state of the game that a casual player would immediately be able to identify as cheap or spammable. you must exercise fundamentals to get anywhere in this game and those skills (zoning, footsies, neutral, decision making, positioning, match-up recognition, frame data) can easily translate to other games in the genre, or all games if you're a huge nerd like me! i highly recommend learning the game with a buddy since the online player base is highly experienced and, even though you can learn from losses, you will get much more from playing with someone on a similar skill level.
, youtube tutorials, and watching streams of the game on twitch.tv are good ways to learn, but nothing beats playing a friend.
settings wise, it is a MUST that you turn OFF vsync (having it on will introduce input lag, although i heard it is not bad if you implement it on a driver level) and set frame rate to FIXED (allows the game to always run the game at 60fps, even if that means skipping frames [essential for gameplay since it keeps timings consistent and is as the game was intended to be played]. setting this to variable or smooth will allow the game to run under 60fps and this is bad due to multiple gameplay and netcode reasons.)

The combat: It is amazing, you have high-detail next gen spaceships at your disposal, ready to attack enemy planets. There are so many different colors you can be, every time I am a new color, I feel like I am being born again, there is so much variety in the colors and the way they attack.
Multiplayer: With internet getting about 4kb/s, I feared I wouldn't be able to play online, boy was I wrong. For the first time, I was able to play an online game without lag. I played with my friends and we worked together to conquer the planets. There are so many different gamemodes to pick from, I felt overwhelmed.
Soundtrack: The music in this makes me want to get up and dance in the middle of my game. The song is constantly stuck in my head all day, but I actually like having this song in my head.
Extras:
+While playing the game there are neutral planets, all of these have clever, realistic names to them, adding more atmosphere to the game.
+I just can't stop talking about the graphics, I literally fell backwards when I first opened the game, I felt as if I was actually in space.
+Online, with eight people playing simultaneously, it's hard to even put into words. There's just so much happening at once, so fast, without any lag too.
Galcon 2 might be the craziest, most intense video game experience I've had in years, but it's also amazing. With stunning graphics, beautiful music, intense, fast paced battles, and so much variety, I couldn't think of one way to improve this game.
Final Score: 11/10 - Best game I have ever played in my life. Game of the century. I would be shocked if I managed to find a game better than this.

There's something quite special about Night in the Woods.The game really captures the sense of small-town desparation and sets a tense mood of uncertainty.
The interactions between characters feels so genuine and palpable, with slang and in-jokes being tossed into casual conversations. The dialogue in the game is a class act.The visuals are colorful and neon-esque, even in scenes where there is a lot of darkness.
The brilliance in the storytelling is how the middle of the game felt so aimless and confusing. How we feel as a player going about and doing things that don't really advance the game is how Mae feels returning to a dying town where all her friends, her last bastion of familiarity, are all ready to move on.
I can't really describe how the game made me feel, but it *did* make me feel... something. Getting in a fight with your mom felt terrible, like you knew what was coming but you didn't want to believe it. That made me feel bad. But then there's the unbearable lightness of hanging out with Gregg and missing every pierogi or lightbulb that was thrown.
Mae clings onto the childish things in her life that make her feel safe while avoiding the heavy reality of adulthood and responsibility. The game tosses around some really weighty themes ranging from sexuality, dealing with mental illness and depression, death, financial struggles, injustice, and failure. In between are bouts of guitar-shredding, bike-riding and baseball-bat swinging that lighten the mood and keep you engaged. I'm certain there are a ton of secrets to find, and it'd worth it to replay it at least once to play all the different story branches or make different choices.
If you are the kind of person who enjoyed games like Undertale or Dust: an Elysian Tail, you will also enjoy this story-driven adventure game.
My only complaint were the lack of precise controls and sometimes very small interactable hitboxes for dialogue and inspection. The jumping can get awkward, and the game could probably do well to have a sprint or some sort of temporary short distance boost to shorten those long jogs across the town to get things done.
I rate a solid 9/10. Very fun game and worth every penny of the $20 pricetag.

Splinter Cell: Blacklist is a stealth third-person shooter developed by Ubisoft Toronto and published by Ubisoft. It was released in August 2013. Blacklist is a very good game that excels in freedom of approach in mission in which complements the excellent story. The main protagonist is Sam Fisher and Fisher is one of the main operatives part of the new Fourth Echelon. Blacklist incorporates a new story while expanding and not forgetting events that occurred in the previous game Conviction. This review will discuss the campaign in relation to missions and story, the gameplay and the Paladin, the multiplayer, and the graphics and performance. I did not play the DLC.
Blacklist features a very intense campaign that shifts the dynamic from typical FPS shooters. The Fourth Echelon's motive is to combat The Engineers, who are perpetrators of the Blacklist and these are a bunch of attacks aimed at America with a countdown on each event. Your team lives on a Paladin and uses a Strategic Mission Interface (SMI) and this replaces the traditional menu screen in other FPS games. It features a world map and allows you to coordinate your plans. For instance, you can play campaign missions, side missions, and the multiplayer portion. The SMI is very unique and frankly I love it because it fit right into the context of the story and setting. In saying that, it was frustrating to launch the game to play multiplayer with friends only to be inserted right into the campaign because I was unaware that the SMI was a thing and was the main UI of the game. Upon beginning the game there was already tension attached to the story and a sense of urgency. This is where Blacklist excels at, making sure the prologue kick-starts the story and each mission and the overall story are progressed while never ceasing intensity. Furthermore, Blacklist improves on the storytelling aspect of making Sam's personality shine through his drive on stopping The Engineer and not doing it sorely for his daughter Sarah Fisher because in Conviction all his motives were for her, so it provides a nice change.
I highly praise the dialogue because the profound amount of it complements the story. For instance, it's refreshing that after every campaign mission there is new dialogue for all team members, Sam and other personnel. I think the dialogue adds to the characterisation of all characters within the game by creating diversities between each while not forgetting past issues. The game features sixteen refreshing side missions. I love it because there is a total of sixteen missions from four different team members and all have unique objectives, gameplay approaches and add to the overall story. They have good length and while they are not long as the main campaign, they are not short which means they feel significant and not unnecessary. Lastly, the various missions are set in different locations in the world so the feature does not ever feel stale. The campaign overall was excellent but I felt it really missed the jackpot. It's difficult to explain without spoilers but I felt that the game could have had some more time to breathe because the motives of The Engineers were major and certain sequences in the campaign were significant so I think more explanation and more storytelling would have added a ton to the quality of the overall game and story. But, for what was presented, it still was great.
The game's core component is the Paladin. The Paladin is a plane that is the home of Fourth Echelon and that is where you conduct all briefings for missions and communication with team members. It is very unique because the Paladin is the operations area for the campaign, it includes the SMI, which as stated replaces the traditional menu, and it is involved in a major way that I will not spoil. Furthermore, you can upgrade it using in-game currency that you earn through completing missions and challenges. For instance, you can upgrade the medical bay on the plane to improve your health during missions. In other words, I commend Ubisoft for creating something new to use and I think it worked for them.
Blacklist features standard FPS gameplay but moreover expands on the gameplay and combat known to the Splinter Cell series.  It emphasises experiment on how you approach your missions as the majority of missions you can approach with gun-fire and action or proceed with stealth, so it expands on the Splinter Cell concept in being secretive in your movements and actions but has enough leeway that certain missions do not penalise you for shooting people without stealth. I believe the overall gameplay quality feels more fresh and fluid and is a clear upgrade from Conviction.
I enjoyed the classic multiplayer mode of Spies vs. Mercs. It features 4v4 games with different maps. Each map had varied objectives as one map would have the attacking team find positions and plant bombs while the defenders had to defuse them or, the attacking team would have to hack certain positions and get data while the defenders had to stop them. So this mode is fun as there were diverse objectives on varied maps and the servers do have a niche fan base. I found the matches to be rewarding by the end but at the same time, frustrating if on the losing end.
With positives comes its negatives and the multiplayer had some serious and unfixed issues. For one, you cannot leave a multiplayer match, enough said. Secondly, I hated the spawn positioning because there was frequent spawn killing and frequent enemy players spawning right next to some of the objectives. Lastly, online players have very high sensitivity, particularly among walls, because I found a lot of the time I was sprinting I would latch onto walls instead of sprinting and potentially killing an enemy.  So, I found the gameplay portion of online to be sloppy.
I played the game on high settings with v-sync off. I obtained mostly a 50-60 FPS window making for mostly smooth gameplay. With these settings, the graphics were good and there were some nice textures and colours, but for the most part they feel dated. My screenshot showcase has some screenshots of within the game and its settings.
I was extremely annoyed at the game starting in windowed mode on every launch and also the game reverting to windowed mode whenever I alt-tabbed. I also encountered some bugs in the campaign and multiplayer but the main source of in-game issues was with the coop/side missions component which in some missions was mostly unstable and buggy. Other than these negatives, the other negatives I encountered were mentioned above.
Splinter Cell: Blacklist is a very strong game that is a true sequel to Conviction. It triumphs in a well-thought out and intense story. It incorporates side missions that add to the game rather than negate from the overall experience. It has compelling characters that are likeable and does not omit their past issues. And, I praise Ubisoft for creativity in regards to the Paladin and the SMI being the main interface. I played 26 hours of Blacklist and the majority was spent in single player, which exceeded my expectations, but the multiplayer hurt my overall score of the game. Regardless, I loved this so I highly recommend this game.
Ratings are calculated by adding up each discussed component and averaging them. Then, I take out or add points to the overall score depending on the severity of issues or negatives with the game.
Campaign: 9.5/10
Gameplay: 9.5/10
Multiplayer: 7/10
Performance/Graphics: 8.5/10
Overall: 8.75/10

Nice. Very Nice. But sometimes you miss missions, because you´re to occupied with killing zeds.

+ Randomised, persistent sandbox. Big, no invisible walls (except from bad models). Suits zombie apocalypse very well (scouting, hunting & gathering, back to basics). Lots to do.
+ Playthroughs vary by PCs and equipment found.
- Repetitive basic tasks. It suits the theme (survival is basic work), but can be a nuisance, especially since you can't directly control NPCs in your group or initiate the tasks yourself. See Responsibility/Power Mismatch.
+ Good humanity simulation. Things like stamina, illness, persistent injuries and limited carrying capacity are not used often enough - your limitations are what make survival a horrifying uphill battle, not imaginary hit points and an ammo counter.
- Writing is really basic with no dialogue outside of plot and side missions. Everything is a binary choice. All PCs have the same lines, so there's no character depth.
+ Vehicles. Another thing that should be a staple of these games, but often isn't. Risk vs Reward at its best.
- Moon physics. ♥♥♥♥ sliding off surfaces and cars flipping from hitting a soup tin.
- Bad collision detection. The parkour is just good enough, but don't expect Assassin's Creed. Animations go through surfaces in fights, models hover on elevated surfaces etc. Some teleporting due to code freaking out. Cars hit invisible objects (most likely collide with world, see Moon Physics).
+ Atmosphere. Even if the writing is basic and vanilla, the game is very atmospheric until the very end. The map is detailed, the world alive. Radio contact suits the mood of remote isolation well.
+ Gore. Things blow up, things burn, things get torn apart. Very nice. Gunshots leave visible wounds and melee cakes people in guts.
- Writing pulls punches. Without spoiling anything, there really are few if any haunting scenes and events. They obviously know of TWD (Kirkman references), so why not incorporate next-level events - or maybe Microsoft stopped them.
- Responsibility/power mismatch. You are instantly in charge of your group (huh?!) and directly responsible for everything and everyone, but you can't directly tell anyone - or the group - what to do. This gets really tiring as people are constantly wandering off and getting in trouble, and you can't stop or help them (except by going there yourself)! The game is forgiving about solo survival, as long as you keep Outposts up.
--- You can't choose your final mission group. What the♥♥♥♥♥♥ devs!? Good luck getting the right gear on.
- Consolitis. Clumsy micromanagement UI with too much info (yet not enough, somehow) crammed like an Excel sheet into too small a space for low-res and controller support, does not like mouse. The engine responds poorly to mouse+kb overall: UI misses clicks due to bad focus coding, kb controls have delay (activation delay coded in because kb is not analog) etc. Canned animations have no cancel and allow little freeform, resulting in lots of involuntary or needlessly imprecise actions. No vertical hit detection (or mouse aiming in melee).
+ Enjoyable melee, gunplay. I did not find fighting tiresome at all. Gunplay is another good Risk/Reward mechanic. The engine has some hiccups in fights and hit detection is dodgy for zombies in animations (hitboxes sit wrong on the model). Using damage-dealing effectively is difficult though (again, bad aiming indication).
- Mediocre AI. Whereas the AI melees reasonably well, it does not use guns or items, does not sneak, does not react to the environment (only to zombies, and only when following you), paths poorly and gets confused in groups. The pathing is really sad when your favourite survivor gets rescued and then beelines into a freak and gets torn apart. Literally.
- Unfinished assets, even after 2 DLCs. Many houses and models have gaps so you can see through the environment - or human torsos. Most of the game is fine though, it's just a really immersion breaking moment when you do notice these things.
I wish the game featured stronger writing and RPG, and had a proper engine under the hood instead of a port, but as it is, it's a fun and highly addictive sandbox tweaking game. I actually enjoyed the main plot and characters once I got the game proper going, and vanilla isn't bad - it's just the lack of variety and polish that bothers me.
Definitely recommend getting on sale if you like zombie games and don't mind sandboxing and ports.

The game has a easy but good and somewhat thrilling story. The graphics and music are great and proper. The riddles and combinations of different items is often intuitiv and clearly logical. That's something what differs this game to other games like e.g Deponia and that's what this makes the game really fun to play. I played the game with english voice and german subtitles. The voice actors did a great job and the translation was really good. Good work Deadalic!
The game shouldn't take to long to finish. Depends on how fit you are on riddles but you should need about 6-10h. The only "sad" thing is that there are no auto safe points and you will definetely miss some achievments and therefore you need a second playthrough to get a complete game.
I definetely recommend this game even if you don't play all day long Point and Click adventures.

Often in adventure games, the protagnist is called upon to bend the rules: stealing, tricking, and exploiting their way to victory,  and this is usually hand-waved as a case of the ends justifying the means for the sake of gameplay. Anna's Quest is the first adventure game I've played which explores this concept as a core theme of the narrative in a very clever way, making full use of the adventure genre as one of the best for ludonarrative harmony.
Anna's quest asks the question: "if those who fight monsters must take care not to themselves become a monster, HOW careful must they be?" but it does so in a way that doesn't come across as preachy. The game begins with a seemingly fairly simple story and then adds world building at a well paced disgestable rate. The world itself is a fun mixture between a classic fairytale setting, with the occasional addition of contempory technology, in the style of the Monkey Island series, of which it's clear the game has taken inspiration from.
The puzzles are mainly based around interacting with inventory items, which is a style I personally enjoy. Some items make themselves useful a number of times, which I like firstly, because it keeps you guessing, and secondly, because it helps with the illusion that the items don't simply exist to solve puzzles, although most inventory items are expended by the time each act is over - it would have been nice to hold on to a few items for longer and have to remember them at some crucial time much later, or have an item be useful many times throughout the entire span of the game.
Still, the puzzles that the game has are all pretty creative. There wasn't much that I felt was contrived, and for the majority of the time, I felt like I was being given enough hints for a fair challenge, without having my hand held. Most sections of the game have multiple tasks for the player to accomplish, allowing challenges to be approached non-linearly, again, in the style of the Monkey Island series. For pepole who haven't played many point and clicks before: that's good, because means if you get stuck on one puzzle, you can switch your attention to another puzzle for a while.
Although the puzzles aren't all inventory based: there are a few skippable mini-games which provide some variety, but not so many that it makes the game feel as though it's apologizing for being in the adventure genre. There's also a smart puzzle that all takes place during some dialogue, though saying much more would give it away.
The art style has a nice whimisical look to it, the most notible ones being the shopkeeper, who you can tell is going to be a grouch from the moment you see him, the town guard, and the Swan Prince, whose cocky expressions made me laugh out loud at some points, probably making him my pick for funniest character of the game. Although I'd probably say my least favorite character design is probably Anna herself. I think it would have been better if she'd been more expressive.
With all that said, I was sad to see this game end, not only because (without revealing too much) of the bittersweet finale, but because I really enjoyed it and was left wanting more. I'd be very excited for an Anna's Quest 2.

This game looks, feels, plays just like a Baldur's Gate series game, but with all the modern game mechanics. As a fan of Baldur's Gate II, this is an awesome "remake" of a old classic. Here we have all good aspects of a classic game: the isometric perspective, six-member party (everyone with their own story and issues), large selection of classes, items, and abilities to choose from, very detailed world, full of quests and factions, epic story. And it introduces (upgrades) many aspects of the genre: enchanting weapons and armor, owning, upgrading, and defending your own keep, have unique playable characters join your party or hire/create your own characters how you want them, and an optional, challenging 15-level Diablo-type dungeon.
It also very impressive how well balanced the classes, skills, and weapons are: you can wear heavy armor, and suffer an attack speed penalty, or use a shield, and suffer accuracy loss, or use a single one-handed weapon, and get huge accuracy bonus, or dual-wield hatchets and get good bonus to deflection. Classes work well with one another: paladin can boost attack and defense of the warriors who can knock down enemies of their feet, and let the rogue mess them up while they are defenseless. Additionally, this game cleans up all the annoying aspects of the old games: slow travelling, tidious inventory management, random stats, negative effects that linger after the battle
If you liked any of Baldur's Gate/Icewind Dale games, you will love this one.

It's difficulty comes in form of inexpierence, the game itself isn't broken and you can never complain something is too hard without getting seemingly stupid advice of "get gud." until you realise people run the entire game and beat every boss, optional bosses as well, with literally nothing; the bare fist no armor challenge runs. The game challenges you to constantly try and to do better than your last death, I can not find another game that so uses death as a game mechanic rather than a punishment.
And I imagine only heroin comes close to the elation of beating a boss that has killed you over and over again. Dark Souls creates amazing memories within people that are so incredibly relatable. Everyone rememvers "that boss" that they fnially killed and they literally jumped out of their seat screaming in joy. And so few games accomplish this, which makes Dark Souls a very rare game that can truly be praised to be more of form of art. It tells a story and it makes you feel, Play this game.

I've been looking for a while for an  open-world, permanent death zombie thriller. State of Decay just barely makes the cut.
Don't get me wrong, it's a good game, but I imagine it was a much better game for the consoles than for the PC. It just didn't quite make the perfect transition to keyboard and mouse. That said, it's definitely something you get used to and can look past.
For me the coolest part about this game is the idea that your character can die permanently, and, depending on their death, can turn into a zombie themselves. You would then have to play as another character and go to their place of death in order to recover their inventory, and possibly kill their reanimated corpse. The realism of the lack of bullets and makeshif weapons is fairly decent as well.
I do have one more problem with this game, and that is the zombies themselves. It's sort of like Left 4 Dead, where you have specialized and common zombies, but here the common zombies can walk, crawl, jog, or run, and they're hard to kill without a headshot. You will get bitten often, and to combat this, that is not how the disease spreads; you must die in order to turn into a zombie. I don't prefer this system, I would rather they all be common and walk aimlessly around, like in the Walking Dead, but hey, they're still o.k.
All in all, it's a good experience. However, if you're eyeing a game you know is good and this one, go with the former. This game is more or less a good experiment rather than an investment.

From start to finish, this is one of the most charming point-and-click games I've ever played, and while the story itself is rather run-of-the-mill (Defeat the witch to break a curse), the experience is anything but.
You play as Anna, a young girl who sets out to find a cure for her grandfather's sudden onset illness, only to find herself captured by an evil witch. Very early on in the game, Anna discovers that she is gifted with telekenesis (the ability to move and manipulate objects with her mind), which is used frequently (and often with very creative outcomes) throughout the game.
The game itself is presented in a charming 2D style, composed primarily of flat, but vibrant colors, which present an almost illustrated feel to the game. The animated cutscenes can be compared in style to other Daedalic titles such as the Deponia series.
The voice acting is top-notch, and though it's clear that some of the accents are a little bit forced, it's a good effort on Daedalic's (a German developer) part for not being native English speakers.
As I said before, the story is very standard stuff, but there's a bit of mystery surrounding a torn family portrait found in the first area which will continually come up throughout the game, keeping you interested, and never telling you more than you need to know.
The puzzles are challenging, but fair, and there's not a whole lot of lunar logic with pervades so many of the games in this genre. Once you get momentum on solving a problem, the feeling of accomplishment is tangible. There were a handful of parts where I felt really stumped, but figuring out the common sense answers really made me feel like I had accomplished something. There was only one part
where I was forced to refer to a walkthrough.
All in all, this is a solid 8-hour game, and the ending gives a lot of closure and leaves you feeling satisfied that your money was well spent on this charming little game.

Dangerous forests, evil witches, psychic powers and bears!  Oh my!  And that's just the first half hour of this delightfully colorful adventure game.  Lead Anna on a point and click adventure to save her grandfather while at the same time discovering secrets about the world and herself.

Based on this games lovely artwork, enjoyable interactions, and amazing ending, I would recommend this game. The only thing that I absolutely hated in this game was Anna herself. Playing such a sickeningly sweet girl made her one-dimensional. She was downright stupid in how "good" she was. I realize what they were going for, a bigger metaphor of sorts, but I found myself clicking through her dialogues just to not here that squeaky voice. I give Anna's Quest a thumbs up, I give Anna herself a thumbs down.
If you have 7-10 hours to kill,. this is a great game. It is not however, the best adventure game out there or even in my top 10.

What can I say about Dark Souls? Well, for one it is an absolutely fantastic game that does not hold your hand unlike a majority of games nowadays. Some may try it for the first time only to get to the first or second boss fight and completely give up on the game and series after that. I know I did when I first started playing originally on the Xbox. But there was just something about this game that intrigued me so much. For one, the combat system is very good and not to mention the difficulty skill curve that must be overcome. After abandoning this game for a week, I came back because I wanted to master this game and actually explore what the game had to offer.
Starting off I died A LOT. As will most people who play the Souls series. Eventually I learned new skills such as the godly rolling ability, which saved my a$$ many times over. I carefully observed the movesets of the bosses and enemies in order to defeat them with ease. I eventually ended up beating the final boss and conquering the game. That feeling of sucess never felt better in a game. Not to mention the storyline either. This game has by far one of the most intriguing storylines in the series. This is the game that I can come back to play over and over again and never get tired of. Even after putting hundreds of hours on the Xbox 360 version, I still felt this game was worth a purchase on the PC.

Condition Zero was the last GoldSource game published by Valve. The development of CZ began in 2001 by Rogue Entertainment and was passed to Gearbox Software (Half-Life: Opposing Force), then Ritual Entertainment (SiN), and finally Turtle Rock Studios (L4D/L4D2).
While Turtle Rock Studios' later collaborations with Valve, the two Left 4 Dead games, were a big success CZ didn't turn out so well. This hyped singleplayer Counter-Strike title gave us nothing more than a mappack, most of which were just remasterings of 1.6 maps, which had to be completed with the aid of friendly A.I. You have to assemble your team of counter terrorists in CZ, the better bots being more expensive in in-game currency than the weaker ones. Once your squad is all set you're off to beat terrorists X amount of times on a certain map to continue to the next map to do the same exact thing. The main flaw with this campaign is that in order to progress the player must often partake in counter-intuitive challenges, such as killing three enemies with the auto shotgun while surviving the round. It takes what could have been a nice simple campaign and making it very tedious and overly long. Hey, if Turtle Rock wanted a longer game, they easily could have whipped up more maps. Most of the maps in this game are slight redisgns of Condition Zero Deleted Scenes. Oh, speaking of which:
Condition Zero Deleted Scenes is an unfinished but functional version of Ritual's CZ. It's a mission pack of 18 levels and 99% of its assets are recycled in Turtle Rock's CZ. Deleted Scenes is a great campaign with mod support.
In conclusion, Condition Zero isn't that good but it's a worthy buy for Deleted Scenes. Valve must have known CZ wasn't as good as its Deleted Scenes since most of the advertisements show Deleted Scenes levels.

This game offers a burst of life to the dying sidescrolling survival genre. Upon release I was worried that it was going to be another Terraria clone, but boy was I pleasantly surprised. This game is a breath of fresh air, with crafting, great upgrade mechanics, interstellar travel, and now with the addition of scripted events it feels more solid then ever before. The feeling of maneuvering my ship through the uncharted galaxy made this 65 year old squeal. That's not to say that there aren't a few gripes I have with the game. The major one being the replay value, I find myself only coming back to the game after there has been an update, and after completing the new content I have no intention to start again.  This cycle of riding the new releases is annoying, although it is a early access game still so you have to give the developers time. Other then that there are a few things that make this game a spectacular buy. Like the looting system, allowing you to customize your star adventurer with thousands of rare pieces of armor throughout the game.  or the dungeons, scripted missions that are a blast to play with friends. To sum it all up, this game is a masterpiece in its own right. When you compare it to minecraft, some contention arises. Minecraft has done everything that this game has done but BETTER. I played minecraft after having played 60 hours of starbound and the adrenaline rush I got from the vastly superior gameplay that Minecraft offers made me repeatedly slam my head into the dry wall until the pain  from my bludgeoned skull was only matched from the agony I was feeling on behalf of my throbbing manhood.
Minecraft: 10/10

So before reading this I'm going to state that I play this on a whitelisted PvE server simply because I prefer surviving against what the game has to offer rather than other players;
So in short this game does what it does better than most games in it's category. DayZ, H1Z1 and all the rest don't really come close to this game.
I play purely PvE and I'm loving it. While  a simple mutant or 2 is generally pretty easy to deal with, there are much scarier things in this game. Brutes. Holy crap do they hurt.
The survival aspects are fairly basic at the moment [it's in alpha so I feel like being forgiving].
Get some food, get some water and keep on top of your health. What I love though is the genuine sense of challenge. Going into a town full of mutants is genuinely tricky. Sure you can shoot them but that attracts more and if you aggro a brute then you're in trouble. The stealth system seems to work reasonably well.
The crafting system is fairly basic at the moment but I'm liking it. Building structures, weapon attachments, medical items and things like that is very straightforward so there's no learning curve in that respect.
The game runs extremely well and this is important to me as I've suffered with the horrible optimisation seen in DayZ and H1Z1. Impressive that it runs this well in an alpha whilst using the CryEngine too.
The weather effects are absolutely incredible. Being stuck in a storm, surrounded by Silent Hill-esque fog or seeing a tornado adds a hell of a lot to the atmosphere and while they don't effect gameplay at the moment, I know that they will in the future when the temperature system gets implemented.
The only downsides at the moment is that the map is fairly small, there's not a lot in terms of character customisation as there aren't a whole lot of clothing options. While the selection of weapons is good I'd definitely like to see more.
All in all I'm absolutely loving this game. It might not be unique but it does what it does better than most games in it's category and it's only in alpha so I have no problem recommending this.

Absolutely gorgeous game. Haven't seen this nice graphics in an open world game in a while. There's a lot of weapons and vehicles and the game runs smoothly on high settings. I like how the character inventory works,looks nice too. But crafting is annoying. You have to be in your inventory while crafting,and sometimes it just stops for no reason. Also the fact that crafted stuff weighs more then its components i don't get.
That being said let me paint you a scenario. Im a begginer,trying to start a base. I cant craft ANYTHING because my inventory is full. I manage to throw some stuff out of it, to craft a plot sign. So after some effort i manage to put it down and now its time to craft a storage box. I manage to do that too and put some stuff into it so i can continue making walls. But the weight limit is exceeded and my small storage box is full. I throw some more stuff on the ground. So while im building walls for a 4x4 small cube(without a roof becase there are NO DEFAULT ROOFS...) my stuff despawns and im left without food. So annoyingly enough i have to go get food so i can keep building. But i have nowhere to put it. And its going down fast. So i keep running out of food and i cant manage to build for hours. I put a campfire down it despawns on me after 10 minutes of me not being there with my meat in it. Walls do not fit into eachother. Buildings have holes. At some point i manage to get 2 cars to help me with my storage problem. And a player shoots at my cars through a tiny hole in the wall and all my cars explode.After managing to park a few cars in my compound and managing to somehow close the door behind the last car, I get stuck between the door and the car and closing the door kills me (?!).
So base building is truly horrible. Needs more components,more content,more storage. I have two teammates and all 3 of us are allowed to have 2 storage boxes in total if we want to stay in the same base. Thats ridicolously small. Walls do not click into eachother and they create holes that other players can shoot through.
Everything else is very smooth. I like the mutants and how they behave, the only thing i dont like is that when u try to melee them they move kinda weird. Its hard to hit them. But maybe its suppose to be like that.
I really like the map,I love the cities,the buildings are gorgeous. I know this game has come a long way and that the developers are still working on it. So far so good id say. Ultimately it comes to this: ,,Did I have fun in this game?" Yes,I really did. I had a lot of fun. But with friends of course. And that's how id recommend it. :]

Conviction was fun but not very Splinter Cell like, so I wasn't really expecting anything great here. However, they seem to have got the best parts of conviction and mixed it with the best parts of the old games, and I'm loving it so far.
I've chosen to go down the non lethal stealth route, but if you fancied going guns blazing for example, you'd get rated on a different set of rules and still earn a nice sum of money.
The money system is extremely similar to Payday 2 (down to ShadowNet as the mission selection as opposed to CrimeNet, I'm not sure which came first), and it seems to work really well. It gives you something to work towards without witholding anything important (like having no goggles for most of conviction), even if it's just for the stats since everything pretty much looks the same.
So far I've not had a chance to try coop (we're doing the campaign to get kitted out in better stuff first), but in Conviction I had more fun in coop than I did with the campaign, so hopefully it'll be the same here. One downside is that the new look and voice actor for Sam Fisher just makes it feel like you're playing a generic spy, but he's still pretty badass at least.

It's a great game. I am so glad to see that they tried to go back to the roots of SC series.
It's still more action oriented game than the first games of the series, but at least you have a choice to play (well, most of the time) without killing the enemies. But hey! The gun-play of this game is very well done, so why not shoot at the bad guys? Silently. Most of the time (If you have the patience).
I really liked the story, the characters and the bad guys. The side missions are very bland. All of them have very simple objectives and most of the time you don't have a room to do things your way. And every story mission had the same "mission checklists", I guess the developers were a bit lazy in that aspect.
There are a lot of gadgets to choose from to help you in the field. There are a lot of weapons to suit your killing style. Armor pieces - too. I really like that stuff in games. And yeah, you can even upgrade some of it too. So. Lots of options for the players.
At certain moments of the game I felt like I was playing Assassin's Creed or Mass Efffect, or even Batman: Arkham Knight. This game has a handful of good little pieces from those games in a good way.
Even tho this game feels quite open-worldly, but at the same time it's pretty linear. There are not much room for creativity. But it didn't bother me. actually.
Oh! And Sam Fisher has a new voice. The very first second I thought that he is Arnold Schwarzenegger (ahaha), but after a few missions it grew on me and everything was fine.

Overall I would rate this game a 8.5/10. Good graphics and sound to be sure, good realism. The controls get a bit clunky at times when dodge from cover to cover but it still works well. The AI in the game is pretty good. The voice acting is decent as is the story line. I got a good 20 hrs gametime out of it completing the campaign. I did a few of the extra missions given out by the other members of the team, but overall those missions were diifficult and annoying. Many of the missions really force you to use stealth because if you do not then you get ganged up on by another 15 enemies and little remote control car bombs rush at you from every direction. Some of these missions actually abort if you are discovered. I gave up on completing many of those becaue I would get to the end and not be able to finish.

Beautiful to watch and play, and listen to the story.  Anna was an awesome hero.

Anna's Quest is a colourful and pleasant point and click adventure game.
The artwork and visuals are presented by a cartoon style that looks beautiful.
The voice acting is also really good and captures the characters perfectly.
The puzzles all make sense and a hotspot button makes the game easy to play so you dont ever have to pixel hunt.
Another thing that impressed me was the attention to detail in the dialogue branches and how Anna responds to different actions you may ask of her.
The game is not without faults however.
The game is really short and the ending to the game is very abrupt. It feels like the game was rushed near the end game and completion of the game seems to lack any great detail in what happens in the ending. This underwhelming ending to an otherwise brilliant adventure game stops it getting a 9/10 review from me.
Some people may not like how the game almost feels like its aimed at kids and that the main character, Anna, is a child with an innocent outlook on everything as expected of a young girl. This can make it feel a bit kiddy and girly but the puzzles have enough depth and satisfaction that a child would not be able to complete this game but adults would still like it.
Enchanting but short - 8/10.

This is a heck of an adventure game. Don't be put off by the cutesy graphics and fairytale setup - the story is well-told and has the characters grow and show surprising depth. This is one of the very few games i've played that features a child protagonist who is not only not annoying, but actually sympathetic. A young and innocent Anna takes off on a quest to save her grandfather and gets caught up in a wonderful fantasy world that blends German fairytale classics with some very light science fiction and solid heroic melodrama. This is a top-notch Daedelic title - great voice acting, beautiful cartoon art, tons of dialog, intuitive puzzles and super slick interface. The only thing i was a little surprised about was that there is no German voice dub, but the English is just fine here. If you're into Daedelic games or modern adventures in general it's a must-buy.

Options include Subtitles, Hotspot Indicator, Achievements notice, Minigame Skip Button, and Open Inventory by Clicking, all of which are selected by default except the inventory one.  Separate sliders for Music, Voices, Effects, Cinematic Volume, and Global Volume, plus Fullscreen, Resolution from 640x480 to 1920x1080, Additional Animations, HD Cutscenes, and a slider for Brightness.  There are also six languages to choose from.
I did the game entirely as point-and-click, but there are keyboard shortcuts if you prefer.  Left-click to interact, right-click to examine, press down on scroll button (or the space bar) to indicate hotspots. Double-click on an exit to immediately leave the scene.
The game offers a tutorial, which will guide you through the basics of gameplay, including how to combine items, interact with the environment, and use your powers.  Be aware that you MUST right-click (examine) some items in order for the game to progress, so remember to look closely at your environment and inventory items!
The game never tells you that there are 12 candy pieces scattered through the game.  Nothing happens when you click on them, save that they disappear.  Finding all 12, though, will net you an achievement.  You can find the Steam

, and it includes all of the candy locations.
Gameplay is mostly logical, though there are a few odd tasks and solutions.  Overall, I'd say that it's one of the easier point-and-clicks out there.  Anna gives you the occasional gratuitous hint, and she won't let you do anything that would be game ending (like jumping off a cliff ;p )  Do REMEMBER TO SAVE, though!  There is an auto-save function, but it's not set up by default.
I found the game to be delightful.  There are many references to fairy tales scattered throughout the game, not to mention hidden references to other Daedalic games.  The story is very dark if you stop to think about the full implications of what's going on around you, but the way it's presented takes away the horror edge completely... Well, *almost* completely. ;)  The beings we meet can be weird, amusing, colorful, wicked, mysterious, sweet, and more, making for a cast full of interesting characters.
There is a deeper message to
; one that is not immediately evident.  I will not ruin it for you by explaining further, but I will say that it had an unexpected impact on me.  Overall, I have to say that I thoroughly enjoyed the game, and recommend it to those who enjoy the genre.

All the positive reviews here are completely true, but here's why I have to take mine back:
The developers have a lot of individual talent, but not enough collective direction, and this is most obvious when you compare the beta with the finished product.  The things I loved most about this game were actually removed from the final build, for seemingly no reason other than to railroad the player.
Before, you could land on a start on a range of planets, now you're locked to the same one until you go through a series of forced quests.
The game Hub was a nice thing to discover when you were about 10 or so hours in, now its been moved to early-game, since accessing it is the only way to visit other planets.
I was hoping tech progression would be fixed in the final build too, but it looks like the developers decided to give up and simply award the player the various techs as soon as they beat the first quest.
Gameplay in these types of games is not meant to be curated, but it was decided that there was one 'true' way to play the game, and all other ways should be disabled to ensure everybody has the same experience.
So yeah, tl;dr the unfinished game was actually better.

Please Read this and other negative reviews before buying. The story is amazing, but the actual combat gameplay has some SERIOUS errors.
I really didn't think I would be giving this game a thumbs down, but here I am. This game isn't bad, but I wouldn't recommend it to anyone.
Before I say anythign else, I do want to say that the majority of the story is fantastic. If it werent' for the story, I would have put this down and never picked it back up. SO if you only care about the game having a good story, ignore this. Just flip the game to storymode and go through.
The basic tl;dr:
What really held this game back was it's balance. It felt like the game was made by a bunch of amazing writers who have no clue about mechanics and balance. Every fight was either too easy or too hard, there was no middle ground. Fights where the enemy had 2 or more healers felt almost impossible. I'm going to break this down into what I think caused the balance to fall through.
Companions:
The companions are very well written. I can nitpick ehre and there about certain personalities, but that's preference. The writing and creativity behind them, brilliant. However, it's embarassing how poorly created they are. the cipher hero come sin with some medium armor and dual weilding, for example. I tried to make that work, but no. It doesn't work. Don't do it. Every companion could have been made better by anyone who understood the mechanics. I'm sat here looking at the barbarian companion wondering why she has 4 ranks in stealth Or why the ranger is using a fox. The fox isn't even a major part of her story. There's no reason that pet couldn't have been more useful, like a bear or wolf.
This is negated by the fact that you can create your own companions and roll with them, but you miss out on the story behidn the companions, AKA one of the big reasons you're playing this game.
Class Balance:
The creators missed the mark big time on this. They did a great job on the wizard, fighter, Cipher, and priest. Everythign else has some glaring issues. The druid has an awesome spirit shfit mechanic that they can focus on, but putting them in melee range is suicide. The barbarian, rogue, monk,a nd any class that isn't the fighter or pally trying to be a melee DPS can't do that. You're either in full plate and specc'd to tank, or you die too quick. Medium armor is not viable. This is because the game punishes you for not specializing. Every person in the group needs to be extremely one way or don't bother using it. Then there's the palladin. The palladin is jsut broken. It's a tank, it's a DPS, and a healer all in one. a team of all palladins could trivialize this game. No joke. The hardest enemies in the game were AI palladins.
Basic mechanics:
They tried too hard to not be DnD. The stats all were way too complicated. Nothign was every just "this increases your damage" Every stat governed an X, Y, and Z and come complete with a wall of text to explain it. In the end, the system encouraged you to be a generalist, but the combat punished you for it. This was a giant issue. What ended up happenign is you chose between defenses, damage, and being able to hit. They only pushed this further by shields and armor. the heavier the armor, the slower you moved and attacked. Then the shield, the better the shield the more accuracy it sucked from you. So a tank had low accuracy to begin with, too another accuracy hit for the shield, then moves and attack at 50% if using full plate.
Lastly every character can engage a max of one person. You can spec this to go up to 3. So unless you chokepoint a lot of fights, you will have enemies on your backline.
Spells:
With a handful of exceptions, spells are either useless, can only be used in specific circumstances, or can hurt your allies. This is one of the biggest factors in my opinion. If there wasn't any friendly fire, this game would be a lot more doable with spell casters. However, because there is friendly fire I couldn't really use my best spells. I could use targeted AoEs on backlines in big fights, but that's about it. I had to just sit on some of the highest damage spells because they fired in a straight line, did their damage in an AoE around the caster, or if I did use it I'd hurt my front line really bad and prepare myself to lose. SIngle target dps spells are not common in this game.
If they released a patch tomorrow that fixed all the broken balance issues, I'd change this review so fast it'd make my head spin, let alone yours. As it stands, the actual video game side of this video game really dropped the ball for them. As of writing this I'm still working on the White Marches, and the only thing keeping me in the game is a desire to know more about the story, the world, and the companions. If it wasn't obsidian tier writing, I would have tossed the game out a long time ago and not even thought about it twice.

I backed this game on Kickstarter, despite never having played Baldur's Gate or any of the other predecessors this draws on. I thought the concept was interesting and I knew I liked Obsidian's work in the past, so I took a chance on it, and it paid off!
First the niggles, because this game still suffers from a lot of the same problems most other RPGs do. You inevitably accumulate piles and piles of garbage loot for no apparent purpose other than to sell it, which requires you to individually select every item you want to sell. You get quests like "Find a druid who knows about this thing" but you can't actually ask anybody "Hey, any idea where I might find a druid who knows about this thing?" so you have to ask every single person you meet until you find the right one. And... well, really, those are the only complaints I have - ridiculous loot bloat, and quests that rely on brute-forcing through dialog options to find what you're looking for (which may tempt you to just check out the wiki). These are pretty common RPG problems, though, nothing Pillars is any more guilty of than its competitors.
What Pillars of Eternity does have is really interesting worldbuilding, for one. The way souls are woven into the fabric of the world's magic and science is really interesting, and presents a lot of unexpected parallels to real life. The game's take on gods and religion is interesting too, and there's a great sense of local history and politics in the story. The only shame is that despite presenting the player with a wide-ranging, complicated controversy around the subject of animancy, that controversy ends up fading into a secondary plotline. Really, the world is crying out for a sequel that especially delves deeper into the politics and culture of animancy. The rest of the writing is also great, though the voice acting can sometimes sound like the actors thought what they were saying was kind of ridiculous (which it sometimes is).
The gameplay is also pretty fun, with a fairly broad variety of spells and abilities, and so many class/race/weapon/skill/talent combos that I frankly got a little overwhelmed at all the possible ways I could develop my character. But hey, as far as I'm concerned character development is a key part of RPGs, so the more choice, the better. I played on an easier setting, because I have a job and a life and don't have time to bang my head against a wall, and while the easy settings felt perfectly fun and balanced during the first half of the game, I eventually over-levelled compared to the enemies to the point where I wiped the floor with them on autofight, and made the mistake of choosing to stay at the easy difficult when prompted (you get prompts when you start The White March, Act III, and Act IV if you're too high level, and can choose to scale up the difficulty for sport). This is really just my bad, though; if you are playing on Story or Easy, I recommend increasing the difficulty when you're given the option to do so later on in the campaign.
I played with The White March, which is also excellent, but a word or warning - I think that the best narrative effect comes form playing Part I of the White March and then running around in the main game again for a bit before returning to Part II. I'm not sure if this is possible if you have both of them installed, but the way the White March II starts makes the most sense emotionally and narratively if you've been away from Part I for a bit.
Overall, this was a really fun RPG with very interesting lore and characters and fun gameplay, even if it doesn't dodge some of my personal RPG pet peeves. Give it a shot!

Let me begin by saying that Splinter Cell Blacklist plays very smoothly, and at times, can be very intense. The AI is smart. The motions of Sam as he vaults, shoots, executes, stabs, snaps necks, climbs, or whatever are very impressive. It never got old watching Sam execute enemies in a variety of ways using the classic Karambit.
This is a kind of game where you sneak into battle knowing that your armor can hardly stand intense punishment, and you may use your wallhack goggles immensely to make sure you don't get snuck up on by a stray patrol. You listen intently for the pants of dogs or time when the camera moves so you can pass through certain corridors. Depending on your playstyle (Panther, Ghost, or Combat) the outcome of battles vary. Sometimes, you can avoid a gunfight entirely.
However, there is little variation in the actual outcome of the story (except a line of dialogue) when you are faced with actual decisions. Your actions are literally meaningless, regardless of whether or not you spare this guy or that guy or sneak through a map or go through the map guns blazing. Replayability is difficult since the patrols are all the same. Enemies telegraph their movements too easily by shouting out their positions (if you haven't spotted them via wallhacks), or how snipers have stupid red lasers that mark exactly where they are looking.
Some missions in the single player story force you to follow conditions, such as not killing/disturbing anyone or only using non-lethal weapons. Failing these conditions will instantly fail the mission. At first this was fun since it mixed up gameplay, but scenarios like these just BEG for multiple endings or branching missions. After two times I was sick of having conditions applied to my game.
tl;dr version:
++Looks visually stunning both graphically and in the animation
++AI is impressive at hunting you down (sometimes too impressive...)
+Can get intense as you sneak through open rooms or during CQC/CQB
---SUPER linear story
---Lack of replayability (thanks to linear story)
---Too easy (Even on Hardest difficulty)
---Air Support sections straight out of Call Of Duty
---No meaning to any decisions

Anna's Quest is a light hearted point-click adventure for kids or adults that are young in heart .This is a kid friendly story but there are some slightly dark jokes and mature references .Similar to Brothers Grimm stories it is a fairy-tale with a sinister undertone . Artstyle reminds me AdventureTime which is good but overall this game is not very relevant to adults when it comes to humor .
My initial impression of this game was negative because it felt generic . I played many point-click games that start you inside locked room so it was very overused concept. However I think this game gets more interesting toward the second half . There are some creative puzzles,characters and enviroments that eventually won me over . Overall this is a solid puzzle game with fluid controls and interesting artstyle .
Puzzles themselves were just hard enough to make you think but not burn your brain . I have encounterd only 2 that had wird solutions which is actually good compared to some other games I played . You can also hold a button to see the items that you can interact with which makes it a lot easier . Text in game was well designed to give hints for solutions that are not self-explanatory ( short,fun and to the point)
It should take you around 10 hours to beat it at casual rate . For a point-click game it is a good length . I got it on sale and was very pleased with the ammount of content .
Voice acting was very top quality which I assume is a common thing with this developer (very consistent and not over the top ) Just the fact that there are so many characters and each had uniqe personality makes it awesome . Also I found myself laughing a lot because of inside jokes targeting people who play point-click games. Developer of this game clearly knows the audience .
Anna's Quest is by the book point&click adventure so it plays exactly like a game in this genre should . I think most people like myself will dislike the kid friendly tone of the game but it actually gets really dark by the end . While the game in general offers little in terms of originality it works well as a casual entry-level puzzle game .

I absolutely LOVED this game, but really disliked the stats and their associated gameplay mechanics, even before the expansions. It is a complete departure from AD&D, which I was acustomed to from similar titles from years ago. Then, the first expansion came and it basically ruined the game for me. The changes made to the "tank mode" of the Fighter and Paladin were a significant nerf, as well as the change to perception in which it no longer adds to Deflection, basically completely ruined my previous builds and game saves. When you build characters a certain way, and then there is a change to what stats give which bonuses or how much those bonuses are, it breaks the builds you've used. I found that very disheartening and it ruined the game for me.
The story was engrossing, the voice-acting was outstanding, and the overall appearance of the game was great. The menus and character creation screens are well-done. The large number of race and class choices are great. If you enjoyed the gameplay of Baldur's Gate or Icewind Dale, the feel of this game is very similar, but with much better graphics and a completely different set of game system mechanics. Overall, it was rewarding to master the mechanics and see the resolution of the original story line, but the stats and the choices you have to make with them force this into a bad Min/Max character game that I imagine would be difficult for the average player to navigate.
Pre-expansion, I would have recommended this game, but with the time you have to invest in developing a character, this is not for most people. (Especially if they change the stats again!)
