According to Splinter Cell's timeline, Sam Fisher is 56 years old in this game. Now, Tom Clancy games require a severe suspension of disbelief, but it's still a little tough to imagine a 56-year-old globetrotting master spy flying around in a mobile Pentagon. And then it's even tougher to believe this is the same Sam Fisher we saw in previous games because they went with a voice actor who is younger than Fisher by
. And you can hear the difference in every line of dialog.
Ubisoft's explanation for dropping Michael Ironside (seven years older than Fisher) for a younger actor was that they wanted the same actor who performed Fisher's motion capture to read his dialog. I'm not exactly sure, however, why that was important. Fisher pretty much only talks in closeups. It seems to me there are a myriad ways to incorporate both Ironside and Eric Johnson (
).
For many who followed the
franchise since its inception, Ironside's departure is clear and jarring. Ironside gave Fisher his personality, which was both charming and gruff. Fisher never really was a hard♥♥♥♥♥ He cracked wise, made ironic remarks (even about his relatively old age), and was a generally likeable character.
Eric Johnson's portrayal, however, had none of that. His delivery was flat and unconvincing, and the youth apparent in his voice made it really difficult to believe that he had a daughter in her twenties.
Why am I talking so much about the actors? Because
is nothing without Fisher, and Fisher is nothing without Michael Ironside. Sure, it's still a third person stealth shooter that has all the hallmarks of the titles preceding it. The plot is even somewhat interesting for a military shooter. It even manages to be personal on a lot of levels like the previous games were. The gameplay itself was a healthy mix between everything through
and the more action-packed
. It's a really fun game, honestly, and the extra game modes are refreshing and offer replayability to the game.
But immersion is sucked right out of Fisher's flying fortress as though from explosive decompression when you hear Sam speak. He sounds 33. In
, when he was 53, he sounded 53. In

As Anna you've spent all life with your dad in a farm far away but, when he suddendly falls ill, you decide to travel to the nearby city to find some medicine: this simple journey soon becomes a grandiose story with witches, dragons and talking animals where Anna will not only find out about her telekinesis powers but also grow as a girl.
Anna's Quest is a point and click adventure game set in an exquisitely crafted fantasy world and with an engaging and lengthy narrative, it easily comes out as one of the strongest entries in Daedalic's already good catalogue.
-good art style, it looks like a succesful cross between a storybook illustration, children's drawings and a cartoon
-great soundtrack and voice acting
-excellent story is engaging, features some emotional moments and a good amount of unexpected twists
-Anna is a fine, albeit quite archetypal, heroine with believable reactions and an appropriately childlike optimism: the other characters have a decent depth to them and even the antagoinist comes out as a sympathetic character
-draws deep from fairy tales and folklore when it comes to characters and game areas, creating a rich and interesting world
-most puzzles are decent
-good length, expect around 10 hours, there's also a bonus Prologue to flesh out the story
-some puzzles can get a tad obscure and/or annoying (e.g. finding the right lever combination or requiring you to select dialogue choices in the right order): the fact you can't interact with some items or pick them up until certain requirements are met can also make things confusing
-can get a bit too verbose during exposition-laden moments
Anna's Quest might look simple and somewhat childish at first, Anna is a young girl after all, but as the plot unfolds situations do take a more mature and at times tragic tone: Anna'll experience some darker events, doing her best to fix what she can, and come out a stronger, wiser person in turn. The lengthy story manages to stay engaging thanks to the plethora of different areas you'll explore and the varied cast of characters you'll end up interacting with: the fact many of them come from well-known stories or legends is also interesting, and Daedalic adds enough originality to the mix to spice things up.
I found puzzles a bit of a mixed bag though and, as detailed above, the fact you can only pick up/ interact with/ combine certain items only when "the time is right" can lead to some truly head-scratching moments where you wonder what you are supposed to do: logic puzzles with levers and such are also not my cup of tea but they at least make sense for the area they're in.
Despite a few gripes with the puzzle design I can easily recommend Anna's Quest though: it's a very nice game and Anna's journey is one to see for yourself.

What an absolutely adorable game. A delightful throwback that captures the spirit of more traditional point and click games, but with modern controls and graphics, and far less frustration.

+ Decent story. Nothing particularly original, but a well told mash up of fairy tales with a telekenesis spin. The writing and art style gel together superbly.
+ Voice acting is decent enough (not stellar but does the job!)
+ Great length which makes it pretty good value for money (I left my game running when I wasn't playing it so ignore the run time, but I'm guessing at least 15 of those were active play)
+ Good mix of exactly the kind of puzzles you'd expect for a point and click - nothing that'll have you tearing your hair out, either
+ Very satisfying ending. Nothing surprising, but it wrapped up all the loose ends and felt fitting with the story.
+ Slick controls/UI. No complaints there at all, and I'm usually pretty fussy about these things.
Very little I can think of to be honest. The main character does some pretty dumb things at times but that's completely congruous with her trusting character (and she is a child, after all).

Anna's Quest is best described as what would have happened if the King's Quest series had been produced by Nicelodeon:
...That having been said, what you're buying is a classic style, point & click adventure game, at least as far as the game mechanics are concerned, so the format should be very familiar to many. The developers weren't exactly breaking new ground.
Rather than having magical talent, the main character has a Telekinesis ability that is used to help solve puzzles in the game almost as frequently as her inability to properly pronounce the word. The one thing that will immediately strike most is that the game is geared for a very young audience, and at best could be rated PG for the occasional harsh language. It is the sort of game a parent could be comfortable letting their kids play through.
The story itself is classic Germanic Grimm's fairy tales, and it is very well told, but again, no major suprises. If you're used to watching kids shows ala Dora the Explored etc. etc... you can see that the dialogue is pretty straight forward and is pretty bland.
One of my sticking points is that the voice-acting is pretty sub-par, and I found Anna's shrill, monotone, I'm-an-innocent-little-girl voice to be pretty grating. Sadly, there are a few instances where some of the other, younger female characters voice acting is so much better, I was left wishing that they had been chosen for the main protagonist instead.
Overall, the game is really good, and the puzzles in the later part of the game really require a lot of thinking and are not blatantly obvious to solve, and if you'r a fan of this style of style of game, you'll not be disappointed.

Anna's Quest is by far my favourite point and click game! It's about a little girl with telekensis who sets out on an adventure to find a cure for her sick grandpa. Her level of innocence, empathy, and resourcefulness makes Anna a great character to play as.
Much to her detriment, though, she is very naive and trusts everyone too easily. And I guess that has been the best part of her character arc having reached Chapter VI so far. Learning who to trust and not to trust has become a fundamental aspect to the story, and it's great to see her keep pressing onward despite of the betrayals and disappointments she's confronted with.
The puzzles in this game are very logical, fun, and very rewarding to figure out. Point and click games are known to have some cryptic puzzles that you'd either need a guide for or several hours staring blankly at the screen, frustrated and scratching your head.
You won't have that problem with Anna's Quest, as the puzzles are easy enough to respect your lateral thinking, but not so hard that you sigh or groan is resignation from trying. There were only a couple of times where I needed a guide, but I know that if I spent a little more time to think or exhaust one more possibility, I would've figured them out on my own.
My gripe with this game along with anything by Daedalic, though, is the lip sync. Like, is it really that hard to program the lip sync to go with the vast amount of dialogue in this game? What I would also like to see from this company is some close up shots on the characters while they talk, kinda like in Broken Age, and maybe more physical gestures from the characters as they speak.
There's also the problem of dialogue strings starting off as if the first syllable or so gets cut off and it's a bit jarring when you're so invested in the dialogue exchange.
Lastly, what I do love about this game is the amount of maps there are in it to traverse through per chapter. The point and click games I've played so far have had the tendancy to recycle maybe the same 5 or so locations for most of the game, and that gets a bit boring.
Also:
All in all, Anna's Quest is a solid game. I got it full price and don't regret it, but if you ever see it on sale, do not hesitate to get it! If you get it for even 50% off, it will out live its value.

You will die, a lot. You will die on the end of a sword, on the edge of an axe, crushed by a boulder, impaled on fangs; you will be poisoned, eaten, stabbed, assassinated and pushed off cliffs. Death is everything in Dark Souls. It's education, it's progress, it's the recurring stylistic and thematic motif that runs through all of its spectacularly varied, decaying and depraved environments. The first thing that you have to understand about this game is that survival is in itself a tremendous accomplishment. It can be punishing, cruel, sadistic and uncompromising. It can also be the purest, most thrilling adrenaline rush in gaming – it can take over your life and reward you like nothing else can. Exactly because your chances of success are so slim, each victory feels monumental.

I really wanted to like this game, sadly it has too many issues.
The game presents itself with a really good dark theme and with the complicity of the visuals and musics it really delivers a great atmosphere. Sadly the first think you discover has many problems is the combat: it has the typical crpg style of combat but there's no mana only a limited amount of usages for any spell, the interface doesn't let you properly understand enemies hp/weakness or your chars positions and there's a really weird gear system: the better the armor the slower you attack (yes, for real), so the optimal way to play at higher difficulties is to have a big tank in the front and all the other characters naked in the back casting spells or throwing arrows ...
The leveling system disencourages combats and exploration, everything is quest related, after you killed a certain type of enemies a couple of times you won't get any more exp from killing them, it's a really weird system that seems stupid and dumb to implement in a high-fantasy "classic" crpg, maybe it will work better on their next game "Tyranny" but in this game is a disaster. So I've played Baulder's Gate 1 before. I'm a pretty big fan of oldschool RPG's and, although a recent release, this game really lives up to that classic feeling. I'm finding it to be pretty flawless.
The story/lore is some of the best I have ever experienced in any game. I am completely immersed in the goings on, right down to reading the descriptions of every single item. The voice acting is fantastic, and the script is well written. The dialogue options really allow me to roleplay my character, as well as my other party members.
The music of Pillars is mind blowing. Sometimes RPG soundtracks can get a little old - but not this one! It does what an OST should do - it works to really draw you into the game. The last time that I encountered a soundtrack that did it this well was Skyrim and the Witcher 1.
Combat is fun and varied. All of the classes have well defined differences - and boy, there are a lot of classes! I really enjoy the mage's spell system, and being able to learn spells from other (dead) mages. Exploration is awesome, and finding hidden loot is even more awesome - especially since upgrades actually feel like upgrades in this game.
Having a stronghold is SO COOL. It's like Path of Exile's hideouts on steroids... plus it's really nice to see old party members being stationed there, ready for your beck and call.
Finally, you really get what you pay for. I'm 26 hours in and only just now beat act 1. It's been a great time so far, and it only gets better the more I play.
I'd really suggest picking this game up if you're a fan of oldschool RPG's, D&D, or really any pausable combat system RPG. It's been totally worth the time I've invested in it, and I cherish sitting down to this game every night.

Took me a while to properly get into since I hadn't played a proper traditional CRPG for almost a decade. But once it grabbed me, it became one of my favourite recent RPGs.
Pros:
- The combat system, once you get into it, is unbelievably addictive.
- Huge amount of variety in skills, perks, spells etc.
- The aesthetic is beautiful. It's not the most advanced game or anything, but some of the handdrawn backgrounds are gorgeous
- The sheer amount of content is pretty amazing. I've put a good 70 hours into it and I'm nowhere close to finished
- The difficulty, although it has a couple of strange spikes is pretty well tuned. It remains challenging for the most part.
Cons:
- For people new to the genre, or getting back into it after a while, like me, it's almost impenetrable early on. In my opinion, the game does a poor job of explaining several mechanics. Stealth, for example is barely touhed upon, despite it being extremely useful, and on higher difficulties, absolutely vital. Crafting isn't explained at all too.
- The load times are infuriatingly long and far too frequent. A loading screen every time you enter and leave a building? Jesus.
- Party AI and pathfinding is really poor. This becomes a huge issue in some of the cramped spaces the game throws at you, and with a party of 6+ NPCs, they constantly get stuck behind doors and in narrow corridors.
- Disappointing lack of variety in loot.
- The main plot is pretty weak
Overall: Flawed, yes, but it's a real gem. Highly recommended for anyone who loved Baldur's Gate/Planescape Torment/Icewind Dale

After the utter disapointment that were PC Double Agent and Conviction, needless to say I approached blacklist with a great dose of apprehension. In Splinter Cell terms, that means crouched and in the darkness. Be advised though, if you see pets crouched and in the darkness, usually it's a sign they are about to deliver a smelly present in your living space. But that's not the point.
So, it was a good thing that I was actually pleasantly surprised by Blacklist. Blacklist have a more open approach to missions which is akin to what Phantom Pain did, namely giving you a hub/nexus from where you decide which mission to tackle next, and which you can upgrade as well as upgrade and purchase gear using money you gain by completing said missions.
I kinda like that, and it helped the game controls were refined and actually more instinctive than in previous games. They aren't perfect, and prompts are still wonky, but it's getting there. Instead of forcing us into a more actionny gameplay that was in Conviction, Blacklist come back to the fundamentals of stealth, albeit with a more simple system than in Chaos Theory. It also leave room for people who want to play a more action type of gameplay, though it's not avaible for all missions, some having stealth requirements for scenario reason, and for people who don't want to go non lethal and avoid ennemies, but want to sneak around and cut throats and shoot people in the head. Each mission has you rated in thoses 3 categories(Ghost, Panther and Assault), and add replayability if you want to get the best score possible for each.
Side missions are gimmick missions with special conditions, which offers challenges and story in equal measure, and can, best all, be played in coop, which is a pretty good thing. Coop is actually pretty fun and usually enjoyable, albeit it suffers from a chatting system not working for a lot of people. The problem is, your partners aren't always playing with a style similar to your, so trying to get ghost mastery when you have a guy near you who is going loud and lobbing incendiary grenades everywhere can be quite a nuisance.
The single player campaign is mostly well done and enjoyable(though it has a few missions that are pretty annoying and meaningless and which could have been served better with a very long cutscene instead). Characters are surprisingly pretty well done, and we get to see how Sam has changed due to the events he had to go through. It hits a more grey moral zone. The story still has big chunks of Tom Clancy in it, and you will find again the cliché of having antagonists who are pretty much against the US dominion and must try very hard to not say "capitalist pigs" every 5 seconds. The problem I have with that is it doesn't convey the real problems some of the third world countries, or war torn countries can have, or what their opinion really is. Honestly the US dominion did nothing in comparaison to the british colonialism in term of dammage, and the US have considerably reduced their involment in foreign affairs thoses last years, so the whole thing kinda falls flat. So for me, the motivation of the antagonists is misguided and overplayed with very little true motivation, which is a shame, because they could have done something better with their villain. Also it's difficult to not think of Kane from Command&Conquer every time you see the guy.
The missions are pretty well designed, offering multiple avenues of approach, and usually giving you tools to deal with what you have between you and your objective.
Weapons are a bit disappointing in the sense most of them are pretty useless if you don't go loud, and among the others, some are simply way better than all the rest. Some balencing would have helped here. Especially because if you go ghost, you won't be using any or so little, because you will need non-lethal stuff.
The soundtrack though is extremely dispointing, often on the border of electronic stuff which is more of a pain than anything. The pause menu soundtract being the main offender.
Be also aware that the game is buggy, especially in some places where you climb/chimey, and where you can get stuck if you try to do something like shooting or opening a window. This happens way more than it should, and it's a complete soft lock forcing you to restart at the last checkpoint. The game will also get into windowed mode for no reasons at time when you launch it, and all the times you alt-tab.
Overall this is a pretty enjoyable experience, at least worth 20 euros to me, but which you will probably be able to get for less(you can get it for 5 during a sale, which is a pretty good deal). People are still playing the game at the moment of this review so finding a coop partner is easy, which is appreciable.
Also, if you are still crouched in the dark, at least I hope you dug a hole and plan to cover it before you leave...

TL;DR - Quests, Economy, Planets
Let me start with this: ignore any negative reviews saying "This game is so different!"
Those reviewers are people who sat through this game when it was still undergoing major changes in Beta, with new systems revamped and changed every time.
Now, however, it's a full game. This game is unbelievably fun if you're a fan of space exploration or adventure/survival games. If you like Terraria, you're almost guaranteed to love Starbound. This is a game with a great story and good gameplay mechanics, and it'll take me too long to put the full list of good reasons for buying this game here. Let me point out some of the slightly more annoying points though:
The quest system in Starbound is, simply put, very limited as of 6/1/2017. There are only a few quests (excluding the main story and any quests received by people befriended at the Ark) and I can list them here:
-Impression Quests-
These are quests that require you to do things leading up to apparently one NPC befriending another. The two types of this quest (to my knowledge) go like so:
1. Gathering Quests
These are simple quests. You're asked to take some plant seeds, let them grow, and then return the product to the person who asked you for them.
2. "Note" Quests
These quests go like so: You're given a note and asked to take it to someone else, who will give you a note back to give to the recipient. Then you are asked to get the person to make something, which you then give to the person who asked for it. Finishing it, you simply give this item to someone else.
-Seek and Destroy Quests-
1. Bounty Quests
These quests are simple. You're asked to find someone (usually a rogue or a criminal/outlaw) and kill them, then return to the person. You will always be assigned 1-2 guards during these quests to help you.
-Escort Quests-
1. Rescue Quests
The name says it all. A person will say that their friend was supposed to do
with them, but didn't appear and got lost at
to the
of your current location. You simply have to go and fetch the person, kill anyone that might be guarding them, and then bring them back to the person.
2. Trader Quests
-to be added
This is the next thing in the game that I want to drag out of the game and crush. When you hover over an item in your inventory, it'll show the base value. However, with
every item in the game, if you take this item to a shop or trader, you can only sell it for 1/5th of the base value. Take for example, a hammer said to be worth 5000 Pixels (the game's currency). If you take it to a shop,
This doesn't apply to all items, as some may be worth slightly more than 1/5th or even slightly less.
Finally, planet design. Now, planets themselves are extremely well designed and have little flaws. However, the extreme designs are the problem here. Having extremely detailed designed planets means extremely hard work, and that's why for each type a planet can be based on its danger, there are only 3 sprites. For example, Dangerous (radioactive star) planets always have only 3 designs, Extreme (frozen star) planets have 3 designs, and Inconceivable (fiery star) planets only have 3 designs. Which the designs are quite nice, it becomes boring to see the same kind of planet designs over and over, and having a higher count of slightly less detailed planets would be nice (or better yet, more planet designs of the same quality, but I won't push you devs! it's up to you!)
That wraps up my review. Another thing bugging me is that I cannot get high FPS at all, but that may be just due to my computer. Thanks for reading.

Dark Souls - hard, unforgiving, but fair. Dark, disgusting, but beautifull. Basic concept of this game is just attack, dodge and repeat. If you fail, and I prosim you that you will fail and die a lot, learn from it and continue - easy to say but hard to do.
Story is really interesting, but hidden in small pieces of conversation with NPCs, in item descriptions and even in details of beautifull world. So, if you want a story, you can look for it, have it and even add some of you own fan-fiction to it, but if you are not interested, it wont bother you during your playthrough. Lore of this game is rich and thrilling, at least in my opinion, so do not close your eyes in front of it.
Gameplay is quite simple on a paper, but hard in practice. If you are not used to this style of games, it will take time to learn and adjust to it. It will take time to get used to this unforgiving playstyle, but after 20 failled attemps on boss and 1 final victory, you will achieve an amazing feeling.
On the other hand, Dark Souls has some flaws. Biggest ones are FPS drops in certain areas, problems with connection to other players and of course, you will need a controller. This game was originally made for consoles so this version for PC is not best or flawless.
In the end I definitely recommend this game to everyone. You can wait for sales and get it for around 5 Euros, but you will need a controler too. Yes, it is unforgiving and hard, yes you will die and get really angry, but after some time you will love it!

You will die, a lot. You will die on the end of a sword, on the edge of an axe, crushed by a boulder, impaled on fangs; you will be poisoned, eaten, stabbed, assassinated and pushed off cliffs. Death is everything in Dark Souls. It's education, it's progress, it's the recurring stylistic and thematic motif that runs through all of its spectacularly varied, decaying and depraved environments. The first thing that you have to understand about this game is that survival is in itself a tremendous accomplishment. It can be punishing, cruel, sadistic and uncompromising. It can also be the purest, most thrilling adrenaline rush in gaming – it can take over your life and reward you like nothing else can. Exactly because your chances of success are so slim, each victory feels monumental.

Anna's Quest is by far my favourite point and click game! It's about a little girl with telekensis who sets out on an adventure to find a cure for her sick grandpa. Her level of innocence, empathy, and resourcefulness makes Anna a great character to play as.
Much to her detriment, though, she is very naive and trusts everyone too easily. And I guess that has been the best part of her character arc having reached Chapter VI so far. Learning who to trust and not to trust has become a fundamental aspect to the story, and it's great to see her keep pressing onward despite of the betrayals and disappointments she's confronted with.
The puzzles in this game are very logical, fun, and very rewarding to figure out. Point and click games are known to have some cryptic puzzles that you'd either need a guide for or several hours staring blankly at the screen, frustrated and scratching your head.
You won't have that problem with Anna's Quest, as the puzzles are easy enough to respect your lateral thinking, but not so hard that you sigh or groan is resignation from trying. There were only a couple of times where I needed a guide, but I know that if I spent a little more time to think or exhaust one more possibility, I would've figured them out on my own.
My gripe with this game along with anything by Daedalic, though, is the lip sync. Like, is it really that hard to program the lip sync to go with the vast amount of dialogue in this game? What I would also like to see from this company is some close up shots on the characters while they talk, kinda like in Broken Age, and maybe more physical gestures from the characters as they speak.
There's also the problem of dialogue strings starting off as if the first syllable or so gets cut off and it's a bit jarring when you're so invested in the dialogue exchange.
Lastly, what I do love about this game is the amount of maps there are in it to traverse through per chapter. The point and click games I've played so far have had the tendancy to recycle maybe the same 5 or so locations for most of the game, and that gets a bit boring.
Also:
All in all, Anna's Quest is a solid game. I got it full price and don't regret it, but if you ever see it on sale, do not hesitate to get it! If you get it for even 50% off, it will out live its value.

I went into NitW knowing literally nothing about it, other than what the initial trailer showed us. Having just beaten it, I can say that I was blown away by it!
The story is intriguing, hilarious, and at times even somewhat scary (but that could be just me), and all of this is reinforced by the game's atmosphere,  rich color palete, and fantastic character design. There's an underlying air of mystery to the whole thing, that deepens as the game goes on. While not leaving us with an outright cliff-hanger, I feel that there are more stories that can be told with these characters and their world. I do hope this game sells well enough to warrent a sequal!
The main four characters are all fantastic (Gregg being the stand-out hit, with his goofy arm flailing winning me over immediatly), and even the random schmucks you meet on the street have their own unique personality quirks, and many of them can be influenced by whether or not you decide to talk to them at all.
The soundtrack to the game is beautiful, even more so during the dream sequences, where the music changes dynamically as you progress.
Finally, I believe that the game has a fair bit of replay value: There is some stuff that you will not see during your first playthrough, some things are well hidden, and certain events and characters that only pop up during certain portions of the game.
Overall, the game was a joy to play, and I enjoyed every minute of it. My only real complaints are that the game's sense of humor (dry and sarcastic) may be grating to some, and that there are still some things in the plot that aren't resolved when the game ends; I myself have quite a few questions about the implications of the game's final sequence! Despite that, I'd give this game two crisp thumbs up!
(Seriously please make a sequal, I love the game and want more of it)

PROS:
Gintama is a very special Taiwanese Finger-puppet Show (known in the west as simply
). To be upfront: it is the best anime. While many shows only take a surface-level look at the dynamics and complexities of their settings, scenarios, and character matrices, Gintama instead takes a deep dive into all of the above while also providing a powerful and damning critique of the medium and industry itself. No one is free from the genius gorilla's scathing and illuminating gaze, be it producers, politicians (both US and Taiwanese), or gangsters. The man has never shown his face in public because of this - Gintama is the tapestry through which he takes on all of society and it has earned him many enemies. Rumors whispered in dark and seedy red light districts suggest that he was born in the gorilla mask -- molded by it. But I digress.
So, what is the essence of Gintama? It is the quintessential drama with a great deal of perfectly executed comedy and deeper, woeful tragedy. The exact ratio is the same as the renowned Fresh Prince Ratio: 4.6:1 comedy to tragedy. Ancient Mayan texts reference this ratio quite a bit and it is apparent that both Will Smith and the Gorilla came to the same conclusion on separate (or the same? wait a minute... could Will Smith be...?) archaeological expeditions. The story focuses on an adult man who simply tries to get by day-to-day performing odd jobs. I want to highlight the fact that this is an adult man - despite his laziness our lead is mature and you won't see him fall prey to the typical growing pains characteristic of the many younger leads in the finger-puppet industry. Gintoki has dealt with the hardship and cruelty that befell him during his formative youth, and now as an older man in his late 20s he has
. In a refreshing way Gintoki takes on the traits of what I think an older, more mature Fresh Prince would look like - a man who still loves fun and is in ways lazy, but who now knows and acts on what has to be done to help others. All the while he passes on the lessons of Uncle Phil in his own way. Through the course of the show, Gintoki has helped countless individuals and groups in complex scenarios sort themselves out - in a way he helped them
, the rooms of their souls cluttered with the empty snack wrappers of fear and self-loathing.
The show is a collection of amazing character studies involving a profound cast framed against the backdrop of a decade-old struggle to build a wall. A big beautiful space wall. There is really no preaching about whether or not the wall should be built, and the arguments of both sides are covered fairly. I just think its unreasonable to expect Planet Hamek to pay for it.
There are fights in this show. Not many, but they are there. This show doesn't devolve into any power-level BS either. All fights are very well choreographed and 99.999% don't involve dumb energy blasts. I would rate the action scenes 9/5.
I could write about this show for 5.2 years but this is enough for now. Watch it.
CONS:
Not enough JoJo references.

I absolutely cannot reccomend this game enough. For everything it does wrong, it does two more right. It's an imperfect game (with a terrible ending) but the fun is in the journey, and what a journey it is.
State of Decay is a 3rd Person Open World Zombie Apocalypse Simulator, complete with everything that brings. You want guns? There's a ton of 'em. You want melee weapons? There's a whole world full of 'em. You want do drive (or walk) from one end of the (admittedly small) world to the other? Pick a car off the street and go. You want to rescue survivors, scavenge for resources, and build up your settlement? Oh boy, you can do that to your heart's content.
Even at full-price, this game is a STEAL if you enjoy survival games. Now, I don't mean a survival game like Rust, Minecraft, or Don't Starve. I mean a survival game like small-town GTA had all it's inhabitants turn into shambling corpses. The default story mode has you moving from place to place, trying to work your way out of the valley the military has you trapped in. Don't worry, you won't be shooting other survivors, army included. You're all trying to make it out alive, and you're trying to bring everyone you can with you. The story ends pretty abruptly and reaches a terribly unsatisfying conclusion, but the gameplay is so engrossing all it'll make you do is want to play MORE.
The gameplay focuses around looting damn near every building in the valley. Almost every single house, store, and warehouse can be entered and looted, which is pretty impressive when you look at other open world games and realize that most of those don't let you go inside most of the buildings. On occasion, you'll find other survivors trying to make it on their own and you can do some missions for them to raise their trust in you and ultimately have them join your own group.
The survivors you'll find aren't perfect, however. Some are alcoholics, others are asthmatic, and still more are just lazy. Most survivors you find are just average people. The awesome thing about State of Decay is that you can switch to playing most of these characters, so you can increase their skills so they aren't completely useless. On occasion you'll find survivors that have special skills that are needed to keep some parts of your settlement running. Mechanics, gardeners, and librarians are just some of the people you'll need to fully upgrade your settlements.
The real kicker is that once a character dies, they stay that way. If a survivor dies, you switch to another character and the overall moreale of your settlement goes down a bit. You can thankfully recover all their gear should this happen. You can also loot houses and other structures for weapons, medicine, food, ammo, and building materials. All of these are needed to perform various actions at your settlement, from cooking big meals, to repairing vehicles, to building and upgrading new workshops, medical labs, storage facilities, and more. You can also set up outposts to provide a small safe area away from your main settlement. Outposts provide you with access to your settlement's inventory and also set traps to kill meandering zombie hordes.
So all that's nice, but how does it control? Well, if you've got a gamepad laying around I'd suggest you use it. The game can be played with a keyboard and mouse just fine, but it wasn't made for it. Each character has a variety of different attacks and moves they can perform, and the vehicles drive adequately enough, though sometimes the vehicle physics will cause cars to flip over, rendering them useless.
There's DLC for the game, Breakdown and Lifeline. Breakdown is an endless survival mode that, in my opinion, is better than the base game. Lifeline is a seperate story set in a smaller map where you play as a military squad tasked with escorting survivors out of the city. It's a fun time, but is exceptionally more difficult than the base game or Breakdown. Both are worth the money if you enjoy the base game.
The graphics in the game can be a bit frustrating. Lighting is a bit harsh with regards to just how dark shadows can be, even to the point where you need a flashlight to search houses during the day. Luckily, there's mods to fix such things. Overall, the game isn't terrible looking, but it won't be winning any beatuy awards. Generally, the graphics get the job done, and the game performs well enough on PC. Framerate isn't limited as far as I know, and the game runs at 1080p just fine for me.
Seriously, I've played this game more than any other (besides maybe Minecraft) in the last year or two. Everyone owes it to themselves to try this game out.

Above average in many ways, but lacks consistent uptime on the servers. Multiplayer only with no local host options make this game dependent on other people to ensure the host servers are up to date to allow you to continue playing on a server.
Most players I’ve encountered are all kill on site making them generally the only threat in the game. This creates an entertaining and suspense filled environment.
Graphics: 8/10 – Developed on the Cryengine, Miscreated already takes a step in the right direction. The dirt, grime and litter are expertly presented making this truly feel like a post-apocalyptic survival game. I won’t mark this too harshly as the game is still in early development (at time of writing) so the small issues I have such as the copy and paste house and shop layouts/designs shouldn’t be taken too seriously.
The game loses a few points because there are a few things that just really stick out, such as the trash in the boots and bonnets of the cars that aren’t manipulable looks like it’s from a 90’s fps. Outside of that the game is exquisite.

Content: 6/10 – The enemy AI doesn’t vary a great deal and the major threat to the player is other players and bleeding. The crafting recipes aren’t abundant and you can’t craft your own bandages, which I personally think is ridiculous.
The crafting guides that you require to have larger amounts of storage in your base (if you ever get the opportunity to build one) are quite rare and in my time playing thus far have only ever found 2, both reasonably useless for my needs.
The updates don’t come regularly and seems to have been reasonably stagnant for some time. If more work gets put into this game, I can see it becoming a staple in the multiplayer survival genre.

Sound/Music: 6/10 – Tracking the enemies (sometimes the only way is by sound) is quite difficult as even with a 7.1ch headset they are difficult to gauge the direction of. In saying that, when you’re plopping along minding your own business at midnight, surrounded by fog and mutant zombie things and you hear the growl of a brute (big bad guys) that itself is enough to require you to change pants.

Replayability: 6/10 – I found the game quite a grind. I had managed to get all of the essential items and build a base in a new server within the first half hour or so multiple times. There isn’t much to do beyond this point outside of raiding other players as the AI isn’t much of a threat once you have a decent stash of bandages.

Overall: 6/10 – I think I’m going to give this a 6/10 as an overall. I would suggest looking at a handful of youtube videos before investing. This is a multiplayer only game with servers only hosted through one company (that are extremely expensive) which reduces the ability to play with just your friends in an attempt to survive against the elements and environment.

I must admit, I was more excited about writing this review than I am about picking the game up and playing it again. The quality and potential is there, but it’s simply not in a state that I can recommend purchasing the game. If the developers allowed for local hosted multiplayer at the very least, then I could definitely recommend this and could see myself spending far too much time on, but as it stands and with the slow release of updates, my recommendation is to hold on to your pennies and look into other games in the same genre for now.

Anna's Quest is a very good Point&Click Adventure made by Daedalic Entertainment. It took me about 11 hours to complete the story and another 2 hour to complete the rest of the achievements.
You are following Anna who lives with her Grandpa. But sadly he got sick and you must find a cure. On your journey you will have to solve riddles and puzzles to achieve your goal.
The story is very good and has some interesting twists. I wished there would be multiple endings. With only one ending I had not much interest in replaying it a second time.
There are many side references to other Daedalic-Games and fairytales from the Brothers Grimm.
I liked the art. Very well drawn and there are fun and interesting details you can spot in every scenes. Only weird thing is the missing eyeballs of Anna. It was kind of creepy at the beginning but I got used to it after minutes.
Sadly this game comes only with english audio but with several subtitles. Although I am not a native speaker I enjoy all my game in english. But if the developer is a german company I always switch to german audio because that is the language it has developed with. Nonetheless the english audio is very very good. The speaker made a great job. As a german speaker you may have some funny moments, when it comes to the pronounciation of some german words like "weisse frauen, hans, wunderhorn, etc."
Main inputdevice is the mouse. Well that's why it is called "Point&Click". Some elements can be controlled by your keyboard, like opening the inventory or showing interactive elements. But you don't have to use the keyboard at all. I played it completely with my mouse only.
Interactions are devided into use, look, open inventory, dialogs and special power.
For replay aspects you can skip every dialog by clicking with your mouse to skip the current sentence or hit escape on your keyboard to skip the conversation topic.
This game is very easy to 100%. There are several story based achievements you will unlock during your normal playthrough. After finishing this you can replay every chapter to get the funny "side objectives". If you explore everything you may get some of them in your first playthrough.

I wasn’t expecting the payoff to be so impressive. Because initially, Anna’s Quest felt like a kid’s game. It has all the trappings of a fairy tale – an evil witch, a little girl in distress, a quest she must undertake. Even the puzzles were fairly simplistic, very rarely posing a challenge in the game’s first act, so I wasn’t expecting to be taken by surprise.
But Anna’s Quest has a little twist at the end of every chapter, each getting slowly bigger – one or two of which might be predictable – and an excellent ending that tugs at all of the right heartstrings.
Anna's Quest is only brought down by the second-last chapter. And even that section has a twist or two. Overall, a sweet story, beautifully told, with a satisfying ending. As far as fairytales in games go, I don't think I'd ask for much else.

In short, Night in the Woods is a great game, but mileage will vary. If assurance that the game is good is all you're looking for, just go play it now.
I'm somewhat sad that I've finished the game, that my time with the characters I've met and developed relationships is over. I almost want this game to keep going, just feed me the same mundane stuff for hours on end until I'm bored with it. When I say "mundane", I certainly don't mean this in a derogatory sense. Rather, I feel the world the developers created and the characters that populate it revel in the mundane. Possum Springs feels like a real world, with real people and real problems. Where many games champion escapism as experiencing extraordinary events vicariously, Night in the Woods stays grounded in reality....for the most part. (I'll get to that)
The characters in this game are just so darn likable and relatable. It certainly helps that the writing is (probably, I'm no expert) good, especially when compared to most games. Each main character, and many of the lesser characters, have distinct personalities, quirks, and routines. The player character is, unlike many games, also bursting with personality and charm. Most of these characters are also realistically portrayed (besides being a bunch of animals) and they are developed well over time. They talk like real normal or offbeat people. You aren't without influence over the world. You have a little, but it's enough that it feels like your choices make some difference. Many conversations don't even happen if you aren't in the right spot on a given day and you have some dialogue options that allow you to sometimes express yourself or shape conversations. There's a good mix of agency and inevitability.
There's a significant presence of routine. The game is divided into several days and takes place in and around a small midwest-ish town. You spend most of your time bumbling around talking to people, who are generally doing some of the same things each day, mostly working. You can choose to engage with different characters each day and this affects their attitude towards you and what they say. Night in the Woods puts you in a routine and you can get very comfortable in doing just that. It helps that there are so many little touches throughout the world, stuff you might not notice or pick up on the first time through an area. The game also uses this structure to call attention to surprises or changes in the world.
It's also worth mentioning that there's a neat little dungeon crawler included within the game, one that's surprisingly fleshed out for what could have been a simple minigame. It's almost entirely separate from the rest of the game.
There are some other things I could talk  about, but they're best left unmentioned in a spoiler-free review. I could go on about this game, but I really just want other people to experience it...and I want to play the spin-off games.

A suprisingly good game. The game looks extremely dated, and looks like its not worth it, but the game is actually very fun. The game is basically counter-strike, execpt with a single player "Tour of Duty", or actual somewhat campaign in deleted scenes' case. Cause the review is taking me to Condition Zero, the regular version, even though I wanted to just talk about the Deleted Scenes, I will talk about both. So yeah, the big thing about this game is that you have a single player mode. The version in the regular version is a "Tour of Duty", which is just doing the bomb or hostage games with bots on both sides, with a few missions you have to complete before the game ends. While this just sounds like something that should have been a update for regular Couter-Strike, it actually throws in some great ideas. Like being able to select who you want to be on your team. Each character takes up a certain amount of points, meaning you cant select them all willy nilly, and they come with individual stats and weapons. These stats include, bravery (how willing they are to fight), skill (how well they are at aiming), and coop (the chance that they will listen to your commands). Thats another cool mechanic, you can talk to your teammates with the voice command buttons, and they will listen...sometimes. They also have free will so that they can ethier say "No" because they can't, or because they don't want to, making sure that you choose your teammates wisely. In Deleted Scenes, instead of "Tour of Duty", you instead have various situations that have cutscenes, listed objectives that change as you go, and only certain weapons for each situations. This adds alot more variety to the game, and makes playing each individual missions worth it. And thats really it for the games. I can't review the multiplayer since I can't find a server. I say that if ya have some left over money and need something to do, buy these games, if ya can only buy one, get Deleted scenes.

This is the first game that I wish had a "maybe" to answer the question, "Would you recommend this game."
State of Decay has many of the things that I have long looked for in a Zombie Survival horror type game. But before I get ahead of myself lets break it down.
Graphics are fairly good in my opinion. The specular maps aren't really anything to write home about and the texture resolution will not light the world on fire but for the price and from a small developer they did alright.
The sound if pretty satisfying. Different guns and bomb have a variety of splody sounds and I'm not really one to care too much about bass or presence...my gaming rig doesn't even have a sound card O_o
Storyline is fairly simple. In the campaign you are a survivor with a friend camping in the mountains when you realize the world has gone to♥♥♥♥♥♥ You meet up with other survivors, find shelter and have quest missions while you try and figure out how to get out of town for good...blah blah blah. To be honest I found the storyline campaign long, and annoying. Far too linear and the fetch quests became really annoying after a while. The rest of this review deals solely with Break Down.
Breakdown is the sandbox version of the story campaign with ALL of the storyline elements and quests removed. It lets you set up a base, and "outposts" around the town that provide a "safe area" where zombies can't spawn into. These outposts can be set up around, food, medical, ammo, or building supplies which can give a bonus to your total supply cache.
Scavenging is the major function of this game. Search houses, find anything helpful and take it back to the group. The player is rewarded with "influence" points that allow them to set up more outposts, relocate the base, or perform special actions from special characters within their group. A military character will have an "artillery strike" option. A priest has "words of encouragement" that can remove negative fatigue status from a character. Influence is also needed to remove any supplies a player might take on a scavenging run, guns, ammo, melee weapons, medical supplies or food.
Break down's goal is to survive until the "escape RV" is located, fixed and supplied. The player then chooses a small group of characters to get on the RV and leave the town. You are then randomly spawned back into the same town and the difficulty increases. More zombies, fewer supplies, harder special zombies.
There are a LOT of zombies as well as special zombies. Combat becomes a balance of choosing the right weapon for the right characters. (ie: matching the proper weapons with a characters stats.) Using the right moves in combat that will maximize damage output while minimizing the use of stamina. You will meet randomly generated NPC characters that can join your group. The player is capable of switching between characters and infact HAS to in order for previous characters to rest, or heal from wounds.
This is where the tedium comes in. State of Decay is full of crap, awful characters. You will find drunks, slobs, jerks, sleazeballs and s luts. None of whom will aid you in your survival. You have a maximum number of characters that your base can support and the game quickly turns into a macabre "culling" of the "dead weight" from your group. You can and will take characters out on supply runs and make sure they your ally never returns. Or you may just take direct control of a character and throw them off a cliff to break a leg and be eaten by zombies. You won't do this once, or twice. You will do this as many time as it takes, until the game spawns good characters. The problem is that you don't know the stats of survivors you invite to join you...until they have joined you.
This can become mind numbingly boring. The environments are HUGE and mostly empty. You will drive for miles into the country, past farms and fields. There are only two towns in the game. Missions and friendly "enclaves" spawn randomly so if you are in the southern most town you can receive a quest on the other end of the freaking map...hope you like driving.
Another issue is that the game had "Early Access" and I believe it also had a beta and there are still tons of glitches and flaws in this game. There is an active game forum on their website. You can report glitches and the staff is usually quick to respond but I hate small developers turning paying customers into their own game testers. I've been a game tester before and if I'm reproducing a bug for a developer...I'm getting paid for it.
State of Decay Vanilla had tons of bugs, many that crashed the game. Before those were fixed, Break Down DLC came out. The bugs still haven't been fixed and they are releasing their second DLC.
Inconclusion, I guess I can't recommend State of Decay. If you can get it bundled 75% off or more on a steam sale or humble indie bundle, go for it. But full price...noooooo.

By the end I was completely hooked and simply had to find out the truth. Highly recommended if you liked Firewatch or similar games, or if you simply enjoy a good mystery and thinking for yourself.
The game doesn't hold your hand (similar to The Vanishing of Ethan Carter), so it can feel quite difficult at times. But when stuck (which will happen) there is usually something you forgot about. If you did a good job of photographing important clues, or if you revisit your collected documents, you can ususally figure out how to progress. However, if you completely missed an important clue, you don't really have a choice, other than to backtrack and retrace your steps through multiple locations, which can be a bit tedious (but it's realistic for detective work though).
I really enjoyed the game and finished it in about 10 hrs in just two sittings.
Positives:
The clues are often subtle and feel quite realistic in the way they add to the narrative. Most clues are referenced in writing in either a journal or scattered notes, so, while often difficult, it's usually possible to progress the story by revisiting your notes, journals or photographs. This forces you to think for yourself, making you feel like a real investigator.
Story is very exciting, with several potential motives and a lot of "small town secrets". Almost every piece of writing found adds materially to the backstory and contributes to the solution of the murders, keeping you interested throughout.
For a free-form open world game where you decide the order of the investigation, the pacing and storytelling is fantastic.
The town, building interiors and important objects of the game are all beautifully designed and most locations feel like real places formerly inhabited by real people.
If you are really thorough, it is possible to definitively solve the crimes by finding hard evidence. If you are less throrough, you must base your conclusion on the clues you've gathered. I was happy with this, as I sort of anticipated an open ending where you had to deduce who the killer(s) is/are based on open-ended or contradictory clues (as has been the case with similar games, e.g. LA Noire).
Negatives:
The graphics are mediocre, but do the job well enough. This is a reasonably priced indie title after all.
Some lazy typos in newspaper articles and other documents (I can forgive typos in the journals as these could be seen as part of the characters who wrote them).
The town is supposed to be set in the US, but has a more medieval, rustic European feel to it. I just imagined it was in England to counteract this :)
It's easy to get stuck if you miss an important clue and backtracking multiple locations can be tedious. If you check the forums, look out for spoilers as they might ruin the game or certain suprises for you. The devs are active in the forums and helpful with clues when stuck.

(Spoiler free)
Fantastic. Absolutely fantastic. Categories get a base score, followed by pros and cons.
Visuals: starting at +10
================
+ Graphics overall look great. Lots of polished handiwork. Lots of small details that really bring the world to life.
- Some minor clipping/seaming issues and graphical modeling nuances (e.g. a key only modeled on one side). Some objects you can walk right through, albeit they are few and far between. -1
Final score: 9/10
Sound/Music
=========

- Music is heavily repeated. I will say the tracks used are pretty good, but you hear them so much you get sick of them. -2
- Sound effects are implemented, but are very weak and lack any weight to them. This is not a huge issue but it does get minus points. -2
Final score: 6/10
Performance
=========
+ Runs extremely well once it loads in
+ Never crashed once
- Once the game loaded, it never crashed, but a couple times on startup, it failed to "start up" -1
- Minor graphical lag spikes, even on top tier machines. Some optimization problems. Nothing huge though. -1
Final score: 8/10
Story
====
You are a reporter. A case was left unsolved in the town of Painscreek. Time to go investigate and figure out what happened.
+ Overall story is absolutely fantastic.
+ Great cast of characters, fleshed out with exceptional detail to the diaries you find throughout the world. There is no voice acting whatsoever, and this is a game where that works extremely well with the given narrative, at least it did for me. If you love to read books, this is a game that you will most likely adore.
+ Story really takes off with the help of Steve Moss. Awesome.
Final score: 10/10
Gameplay
=======
Walking simulator. As someone who mostly doesn't like walking simulators, I chose to look at this game as a detective game. You have all you need in front of you, now you just have to piece everything together.
+ You can pick up objects to investigate them. You'll find keys, items, and various puzzles.
+ This game will NOT hold your hand. You will have to use your own wits in order to solve the mysteries. I consider this a good thing, as some games make it too damn easy telling you where to go next.
+ For those that understand this reference...Goldeneye running implemented.
+/- This game can and will frustrate you just slightly with the amount of backtracking you'll be doing. It's not a good thing or a bad thing, just a slightly annoying aspect of the game that cannot be avoided.
Don't read the following until you beat the game. This last part is more of a personal critique.
Final score: 8/10
Overall: 8.2/10 (41/50 = 0.82)
=====================
I thoroughly enjoyed it. After getting off work each day, I was excited to come home and continue the mystery solving experience. Highly recommended for those that love a good story, consider themselves detectives, and a don't mind a decent amount of reading. Great job to the developers!

The Painscreek Killings is an outstanding game that is worthy of your time. It does a better job than perhaps any title I can remember of truly making me feel like a detective. You play a reporter who comes to an abandoned town to investigate an unsolved death from a few years ago.
There's one serious fault I need to discuss: game performance. The game is poorly optimized and has long loading times. I'm running on a GTX 970, and I still saw bad performance. It's also not alt+tab friendly. Sometimes after playing my whole computer would still be running incredibly slowly and I'd have to restart. I'd wasn't enough to deter me, but it was bad enough that I have to mention it. Now on to the meat of the review.
Let's be clear: this is no walking simulator. You need to explore, thoroughly, to uncover dozens of secrets of the people who inhabited this town. There are plenty of puzzles along the way, and there is no handholding at all: you need to take your own notes and can't rely on any quest markers.
Amazingly, the puzzles are incredibly fair. While you need to look inside every drawer and cabinet you find, there's never any obtuse leaps of logic to be made or pixel-hunting for some tiny switch. While there are, indeed, tiny switches and the like, all such puzzles have the solutions communicated to you in some document that you need to find. If you ever come across such a puzzle, it's a sign that you should explore elsewhere.
The game's puzzle approach is refreshingly nonlinear, and you can start your investigation from any place, too, and generally find enough clues to proceed. You can even get in your car and leave the town at any time, if you think you have enough information to complete your report. Though, to be clear, the game does have a clear ending, but giving you the freedom to have another ending at any time is another sign of the game's unique design philosophy.
There's an incredible story hidden behind all of the locked rooms, waiting to be discovered.

Ooh Stranded Deep, how you made me happy, then sad, then happy again.
Stranded deep is an interesting survival game where your air plane suddenly drops out of the sky and you have to use your life raft to get to the nearest island before the sharks decide that you're the next lunch (DAMN YOU BRUCE!!!). You usually start of with the normal things in a survival game, such as a knife, lighter and a bottle of water. Everything else, you have to collect for yourself from the islands around you or the shipwrecks under the water. Just keep an eye out for the bubbles that hint to their location.
This game did give me a thrill from trying to survive while navigating those shark infested waters just so I can collect the items needed to survive.
But after a while though, the bugs and glitches, the lack of content, and the islands that all look almost exactly the same started to get to me and I started to feel like quitting. Those negative comments on this game that tell the story of the developers who seem to have abandoned this game made me second think about buying it.
Then I discover that little option inside the games properties window that allow you to try the experimental releases of the game.
Ooh you sexy thing you. The lush new graphics, new oceans, new islands, new content and entertaining new bugs. Thankfully, some bugs were fixed. And the best thing about this is that the developers seem to release experimental updates every few months.
I wish it was monthly updates, but this is understandable because making a big game is a lot like trying to complete a dungeon raid on nightmare difficulty. You need the right tools and equipment (which isn't cheap), it takes lots of time, planning and experience, and it helps to have a large group of people (which these developers do not).
With my joy renewed, I'm happily exploring these new vast waters while trying to get over my Thalassophobia (fear of the sea).
To sum up however, the pros and cons are:
+ Pretty graphics
+ Variety of islands and locations to explore
+ Building and crafting
+ Lots of sea life
+ Interesting survival mechanics
+/- Entertaining bugs and glitches
- Lots of bugs and glitches
- Game does become repetitive after a while
- Development team is a bit slow updating the game
To conclude, this is an amazing game that is already enjoyable to play and will become even more amazing over time (especially if you use the experimental releases). It does have it's fair share of problems and the development team seem to be more focused on updating the art and content than fixing these problems. But these things will be resolved in future updates. Minecraft was the exact same 5-6 years ago.
I would happily recommend this game to others. For those who want something closer to perfect and bug free, wait till it's closer to full release.

There is still a lot of work to be done as this game is very much in development.  And given the magnitude of some of the changes, one should expect that updates are going to be sporadic.
Should you buy it?  It depends.  The older stable branch contains a lot of the earlier designs and is reasonably enjoyable.  I was able to get 10 hours of gametime out of it which I consider money well spent.  The newer experimental branch is a glimmer of things to come, but is still incomplete and needs polishing to be properly playable.  It does give a promising glimpse of this game's future and the future looks good.

The gameplay is solid and being able to level up characters the way you want is great, as you can make sure every survivor has a designated role to play.
My only real complaint is that the base building feels a bit lacking, and I wish that you could choose any building as your base instead of preset locations. Things can get a bit repetitive too when survivors continuously decide to give you missions while you're trying to advance the main story, but dont want negative concequences to happen from ignoring it.

I really owe this game a review.  I've had more fun with this playing with friends than any other game.  No other game has permitted me to talk at such loud levels to the people sitting next to me.
It's a lot like gauntlent but a greater challenge in my opinion.  Where as gauntlent is more geared toward grinding mobs down, this is more for how well can you work together on a particular goal.  I haven't encountered many games that make you have to be this tightly coordinated.  Weak links will become apparent and quick.  Each level brings a new way of having to making a plan.  Each monster has to be learned how to be dealt with.  Kiting isn't an option.  Understanding how each fighter operates is vital.
My warnings:  This is meant for co-op.  You can play single player, but you aren't going to have as much fun.  More importantly, you will want to find a consistant person or so to play with, which I know isn't always easy.  Pugging this game usually ends in a bad result, and there aren't enough people in the lobby to make games happen when you have time to play.  Also, I would not say this is for a casual gamer.  If you haven't built up a reasonable degree of twitch, I feel you are just going to get frustrated.  I'm not saying people can't learn, but I've seen people that don't play a lot of games say this is not for them.
Games are fun, but to me this one was an experience.  One I could share with some good friends.

The Painscreek Killings is probably the best detective game I have ever played. I wanted something similar to The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, and while this game isn’t as polished visually or performance-wise I got a lot more than I expected! And I don’t say that lightly because I really enjoyed TVoEC, but this game has much more to offer the player.
+ Gameplay is sublime (although ultimately a walking sim)
+ No hints, quest markers, hand-holding etc.
+ Story unfolds at an excellent pace and is very powerful
+ Clues/puzzles are intuitive and realistic
+ Promotes using a notepad irl for documenting
+ Nice music
+ Active developer
+ Reasonably and honestly priced
+ Forces you to pay attention to details. Solutions are subtle, but ultimately in plain sight
+ The level design is great
/ Decent graphics overall, not gorgeous, not bad
/ OK performance, 50-80fps maxed at 1440p - GTX1080, i7-6700k, 16GB DDR4
- Can become tedious if you miss a fundamental key, note or item. The village/area(s) are rather large, if/when there is no more ‘thread to pull’ you can become stuck in an overwhelmingly large area without a hint system (although adding one would destroy the game, so catch 22, and an unavoidable mechanic). Luckily if you get stuck the community and devs are helpful!
- I subjectively wasn’t fond of the style of buildings in the village. It has a bit of a Cotswolds vibe but is supposed to be set in the USA. I just thought it clashed a bit
- A few typos (I'm really struggling to come up with negatives)

Ever wanted to play a detective without an AI holding your hand too much? This story-rich and atmospheric game keeps the player on the edge as they delve in the mysteries of the abandoned village and solve the murders that happened there. The player will be in charge of how much they find out about the previous residents and their secrets with multiple endings depending on their actions.

This game is one of the best murder mystery games I've played. I love that there isn't any hand holding and that you really have to investigate everything in order to figure out what happened. One of my biggest problems with the game though is the random glitches; at one point, I walked through the stairs into pitch black, couldn't back out, and due to force of habit I saved and quit which the game warns not to do in the start. Due to this, I had to restart all over again -_-. The game froze up a few times to, but as long as you just exit without saving, you will start off at the last save point. The game is good at saving when you enter a new location. Other than these problems, it's a great mystery and it's atmosphere is fantastic! I love that the town is completely void of life and you really feel all alone but at the same time, watched by someone you can't quite see. I hope to see another game like this in the future, minus the bugs of course. Great job guys!

I really liked this one.  You can forgive the grammatical errors and typos because the attention to detail in the rest of the production is good; sometimes astoundingly good. The objects you need to examine and the many cupboards and drawers you need to open are high quality and very realistic looking.  The atmosphere is convincing. The story is well paced, realistic and (mostly) believable.  The music is composed of repetitive short scores and is initially effective but soon wears thin and becomes annoying and I found myself muting the sound - but then I do that in quite a few games. I was perplexed by a couple of small details (e.g. dates not matching between medical records and gravestones), but after an update I noticed they had been corrected.  There's still one big error though - an old letter dated 1972 is written on stationery that mentions a website in the heading. I thought this was a clue at first, but now I think it's an oversight. Nevertheless,  I had fun playing detective and  I would recommend this game and, if they make another, I would buy that too.

I recommend the game for anyone that likes detective games. It is basically a walking simulator where you explore a town to uncover the truth behind a murder. The town is abandoned so it's a solitary experience for the most part. You will slowly fill in the story by reading diaries, newspapers, and letters around the town. You will have to revist places many times as you slowly get keys and codes needed to unlock new areas.
There are some downsides. The game has occasional frame rate problems even on solid hardware. I spent about ten hours solving the story and only found 95% of the clues. That is a large amount of back tracking to the various locations. Some of the puzzles make no sense at all. I had to get past a couple through trial and error as the clues did not help. The current version has no controller support, but I had no issues playing through with a Steam controller and maping the keyboard to the buttons.
The last thing I will discuss is the ending. Without giving anything away the ending makes no sense in the context of the game. This has nothing to do with solving the mystery. I enjoyed that. The events that happen at the end of the game have no place in this type of game and are a jarring experience. I had no interest in going back to try and get a good ending as this ending sequence made no sense and I had no interest in revisiting it. This is a minor gripe and others may enjoy the sequence.
I personally enjoyed the mystery and feel it overrides any other downsides of the game. There are not a lot of games that have this level of detective work and for that alone it is recommended.

Okay yes, the game runs badly. Yes the game is not optimized very well. But despite all that, The Painscreek Killings is a great game that has a charm other games lack. The story is intriguing and the game does not hold your hand, but lets you uncover its plot in whatever direction you see fit. The game treats you like a smart adult, so you have to put the clues together and work out where to go. I loved the whole experience. 8/10.

There are basically two types of games out there:
The ones that don't really have an ending like endless runners or MMOs. There you wish you had the final highscore or the most best ever epic gear there is, until the next expansion shatters your little dream.
...
And there are adventure games like Anna's Quest that have a definite ending to their story.
The big difference between them is that in this game you don't want it to end with all the memorable characters, the cute yet simple graphics, the great voice over and the quirky twisting and highly unexpected storytelling. Well you can guess what's happening but the authors of this game have a very special ride in it for you!
Help the female protagonist(s) to overcome the hurdles in front of them and discover the truth hidden throughout the game. Get support from bearded suspicious men and murdered children to bring elderly women behind bars, fake documents and ruin a wedding. Few times before psychic powers, black magic and technology have been brought so close together with easter eggs everywhere and a intuitive story.
This game can walk upright alongside other titles like "Edna escapes" or "The Book of unwritten Tales".
If you like adventure games with good storytelling, brilliant dialogues and an unexpected ending then this game is a must-have!
The only point that could have been a bit more userfriendly is a hints-button that would point out on some screens where the riddles are not so quite clear. But as you can Shift + Tab to Steam and search the community discussion boards help is quickly found. So no point reduction there.

TL;DR Galcon 2 is a high quality, fast paced, indie RTS and it's totally free. No matter if you're looking for something to play for a couple minutes to pass the time, or you want an RTS that you can really dig into and master Galcon 2 is for you.
Actual review: Alright, I may as well throw a review out there for Galcon 2. Long story short I've been playing different versions of Galcon since mid 2008. I've always loved real-time strategy games, and Galcon (being the very core of what makes them great) hooked me instantly. Galcon takes the idea of an RTS and condenses it into it's purist form. No spending the first 5-10 minutes building up your base, scouting the enemy, making sure you build the right units to counter your opponent. You have planets that generate ships, those ships can be sent to attack other planets to generate more ships or left to defend your planets. Now add 8 or so other people and you get an action packed fast paced arcade style RTS.
The game is super easy to learn, there's a tutorial, single-player bots with a wide range of difficulty levels, and even a co-op mode to play with your friends against bots. Once you've got the hang of it, multiplayer is a whole new world. Galcon 2 is the very definition of easy to learn, hard to master.
To top it all off, this version is totally free. The only micro-transactions are cosmetic, running a tournament, or running your own server which you really only need if you want to run mods (did I mention the game is modable?). You don't need to pay a penny to get the full experience, plus you can earn the in-game currency over time (but I'm not going to dive into that system here).
The community around this game is also dedicated and nice, there's always someone willing to help teach you if you'd like to learn more, just visit the forums and ask.
Anyway, I'm absolutely biased, like I said I've been playing versions of this game for 5 or 6 years now. I also currently help moderate the forums, and have admined past versions of the game. But I've only stuck around this long because I really do love the game and it's community.
If you've ever got any questions about the game, want help getting better, or just a friendly face to play some rounds with, feel free to message me (Chi-Ro) on the website and I'll be happy to help!

I don't normally care to review games, but I wanted to post some kind words for this one.
I bought this on a whim due to it's aesthetically pleasing art style and didn't really know what I'd be getting into. I thought it was going to be a cute light hearted game, but that mindset quickly changed as I began playing through it.
Mae, is both outrageous and relatable. I found myself crying from laughter and sadness because of her dialogue. I won't spoil her story, but I feel anyone who has ever felt lost in the world, or experienced a fear of transitioning into adulthood, will be able to connect with this character.
All of the characters in this game are endearing in their own way. You may find yourself being more invested in certain characters and progressing through their own personal stories as you play. You may even develop genuine affection for some of them. They are that adorable. In the weirdest way, it really feels like you're growing a proper connection with the townfolk as you play through the game.
I don't want to make this review too long, so just a quick round up of my opinions,
-The music is awesome. At certain parts, it slows down and becomes increasingly intense to fit the mood.
-The characters are amazing and adorably written, relatable, etc.
-The story may not be for everyone, but I think everyone will find some sort of wisdom to take away from it.
-The art is beautiful, unique, very easy on the eyes.
-It's hilarious. I was often laughing my butt off through out the game.
I highly recommend this game for anyone going through that weird phase in their life where they are transitioning into being an adult, and are having a difficult time adjusting to that.
