I found The Painscreek Killings to be significantly enjoyable for a few reasons, but most relate back to classic adventure gaming tropes being married with excellent storytelling and appropriate graphics, creating a wunderkind lovechild that is wholly unique and fun.
The Pros are numerous. The puzzles are difficult, but not stupid. There is zero handholding; you are a journalist responsible for discovering what happened on a fateful day in 1995. You enter the abandoned town, and go to work. On your way, you will pick the narrative out of an avalanche of information, all of which must be read and re-read in order to continue forward.
You will uncover conspiracies and heartbreaks, secret plots and rooms and red herrings and all the things that make up an excellent mystery.
You will do this investigating without any timing pressure, or threat of violence. This is probably my favorite feature in the game, because I have two toddlers running around and frequently need to jump out of my gaming fantasy. It's also great because the game builds enormous tension using its excellent music, mood lighting and writing to put the goosebumps on you. It really works.
To say one more thing about the writing: these are characters you never meet, but yet they come alive in their absence, through their written words and their belongings and their photos. It's a powerful achievement. As you learn about these folks (likely in your own organic way, as the game is almost entirely non-linear), they come alive in your heart.
Some typos and syntax errors and very brief recorded dialogue detract the tiniest iota from the immersion, but that is truly my only complaint about the game.
The Painscreek Killings was a one of a kind experience for me; a deft blend of mystery novel and adventure game that left me pining for more.
I hope that another mystery awaits us from these developers.

I should have expected this to be terribly optimized when, upon launching the game, I was immediately greeted with an introduction screen that warned me about what to do if the game started crashing or freezing.
I can play pretty much any current game on my computer but I can barely walk three steps in any direction in this game without debilating framerate issues. I tried turning down all the settings in the game graphically on the off chance that it'd help; it somehow made it worse???
I am typing this review as I'm reloading the game for a FIFTH time after wandering around a town filled with buildings that are identical replicas of one another for several hours with a map that barely functions as such and a vague objective about solving some random af murders. So far, there are 10+ characters that I can't keep straight (and who all seem to have the same issues with spelling/grammar), and entirely too many locked doors.
One small perk: This probably isn't a positive since it was technically a graphical issue with the in-game textures, but at one point all the doors and leaves on the trees turned into Matrix-like rainbow blocks. It was pretty rad. If the game is going to be poorly optimized, can it at least have more of that?
As a last note, I get that this game's intent isn't to hold your hand like some others tend to do, but the point is taken a bit too far here. Some of the "hints" the game gives you are literally just descriptions of where you are (I picked up a key in a locker to find that its 'hint' was 'key found in Mansion locker"...) which isn't helpful at all. Keep your 'hints' and save my time, I've got more identical buildings with locked doors to investigate ffs!
*Edit after completing the game with 100%*: The story is actually really good, and the idea behind the game (exploring without clues) is unique and quite challenging -- if the technical issues could be fixed (as well as the issues w/ achievements unlocking), I'd recommend it. (That said, during the final scene, I fell through a floor I'd walked on 20 times before and continued to fall forever until I restarted the game, having to redo about half an hour of puzzles/exploring/unlocking things -- I reeeeally want to stress that I would NOT recommend this game in its current state as of 11/29 unless you want to experience an intense amount of frustration).
UPDATE ON 12/22:
A new update to the game was made and per the dev's recommendations, I just reinstalled for the achievements; they did work, however, I had to restart the entire game to get the "You're Fired" achievement despite trying to leave before getting the actual real answers. I'm not sure if this is intentional; possibly because I had nearly all the evidence and letters/documents/etc already by that time (save for 1 thing inside the church).
Unfortunately, while the Achievement issue seems to have been fixed, the game didn't appear to run any more smoothly than it did a month ago. :( The first time I launched after this update, it  caused my entire computer to freeze up during the very first loading screen and I had to restart my whole system. Upon trying to relaunch, the familiar wait was back at it again from these intensely long loading screens (damn, Daniel!).
The framerate issues persist through the areas with lots of foliage and the start of the Mansion area, the sound gets louder/quieter at odd moments (I take 4 steps in one direction and it goes from absolute silence to screaming birds?? More terrifying than anything else in the game tbh, those birds are very loud).
While I'd be happy to recommend the game for its story and unique mechanics of solving the crime/using obtained clues, I can't at all recommend it for its actual playability until these issues are fixed completely.
That said, thank you to the devs for the update and for the hard work! I've completed it with 100% now in both game content and Steam Achievements and appreciate the effort that's gone into it.

What a fantastic game! It is lengthy but never feels tedious, because you are constantly uncovering new information and new places to explore.
Pros
- Stunning visuals and a highly detailed village
- Gorgeous music that sets a perfectly creepy tone

- Very well-developed characters
- No glitches or frame rate issues (others have mentioned these but I experienced none)
- Perfect balance between having a good idea of what to do but not being spoon-fed information
- Long enough to justify the price tag (don't be afraid to purchase at full price, it's worth every cent!)
Cons (very minor)
- Lots of grammar errors in the various diaries/notes
- I had to keep reminding myself that we were in the USA, because the village feels incredibly English (it even has a red phone booth!)
- This game has set the standard for murder mysteries so high that it'll be difficult to enjoy others lol
If you enjoyed games like Firewatch, Everybody's gone to the rapture, and What remains of Edith Finch then you'll love this game too.

I absolutely recommend this game.
I will say, that it can be overwhelming in the beginning: Upon starting, you have a huge town to wander in and about 10,000 locked doors, but one by one you start to find a puzzle piece or clue to follow up on, until all of a sudden you have so much to follow up on you're not sure where to start.
10/10 STORY is very well developped. You are a journalist coming to an abandoned town to solve an old string of murders. There are probably about 10 fully fleshed out characters and stories as well as some side characters. It is not an obvious solution: I wasn't sure of whodunnit until far into the game
9/10 GAMEPLAY is totally based on finding keys, entering codes, finding old documents and opening diaries, BUT IT DOES THIS VERY WELL. Notes and journals are placed logically in locked desks. Keys are found in places that make sense and string together IE you get the key john's house and in john's house is a box with the key to the hospital cause he works there and in the hospital is the key to jane's house cause she works as a nurse etc etc. FOR THE STYLE OF GAME THAT THIS IS, it is very enjoyable. There is little to no direction. I only needed help on one puzzle (SPOILER: the chess piece order is written on the lock)
7/10 MUSIC is a little repetative but you forget about it after a while. There were a few themes I enjoyed, but some seemed oddly inappropriately creepy, or repeating to the point of distraction.
HORROR This game is about murders yes, but there aren't any jumpscares and almost no human interaction (MINOR SPOILER you do escape the killer at the end, in a quite sudden change of gameplay style, but its brief and makes sense). It is quite atmospheric though.
9/10 VISUAL The game is really beautifully laid out, and absolutely huge. The mansions, streets, church are all great fun to explore with only a few repeating assets. Some assets are a little polygonal, but its not distracting.
PROS
Story
Gameplay (if you like being completely on your own to solve a mystery with no direction)
CONS
Faint sense of frustration in the beginning before you know your way around and have started to figure things out.

Urbex, Urbexers, Urbexing - the exploration of urban areas that have long been abandoned. So many people across the world now hold a great deal of fascination for this subject and so many books containing the most beautiful photographs of dust and cobweb covered interiors shrouded in damp and decay have now been published. It is indeed a subject that also fascinates me but unfortunately it isn't something that I am physically involved in myself.
Painscreek...... a beautifully rendered designer village with natural stone dwellings and cobbled streets has it's secrets. Jealousy, deceit, revenge and murder are rife in this American village. The story is set in the years of the 1970's through to the 1990's and the decor in the houses indicate just that. The graphics are beautifully rendered with enough settings options for you to tailor the look of the game to your taste.
There is some beautiful in-game mood music and sound which changes as you enter each different village location. The village streets, the hospital, the mansion and the church as well as various houses all have music that indicate whether something good, bad or sad had happened there. Diaries, diaries and more diaries - every character has one or more and as in real life they indicate the type of personality of the character as well as the secrets they hold and the information for you to move on further with the game.
Keys, keys and more keys are needed and there are a plethora of them as well as all shapes and sizes. Some doors are locked and some not. There are rooms that you can see that you really want to get into but cannot. Patience is a much welcome ally as there are times when you can't think what to do next and nothing seems obvious.
I myself bought The Painscreek Killings a week ago and I have played it slowly for four hours a night. These games are very few and far between so I like to make them last. Yes there are similar games where you shoot or have to run for your life and I've played a fair few of them, but games like Gone Home, INFRA and Painscreek  are so good because of their atmosphere's ability to make you feel that you are being watched or followed and in Painscreek that feeling is quite exceptional. The graveyard is typical of this - surrounded by trees rustling loudly in the strong wind as you stand among the graves, you really cannot help but keep looking round behind you.
There is much more I could write but I'll leave it to you to find out for yourselves. Painscreek is atmospheric, sad, easy and enjoyable to play. There are plenty of help and hints online - don't use them, solve it yourself - it's not impossible!
I can sense now that I am nearing the end of the game, so much is now revealed and I am dreading that moment when it is finished and I have to wait for someone else to offer something in this genre - I hope I don't have to wait too long!
Michael

I really like this game which might be visible based on the hours I've played it. I have written an extensive review at
but here is a quick overview of the pros and cons:
Pros:
- captivating story with a lot of well-designed and believable characters
- intensive atmosphere (if you are the type of gamer who is able to dive deep into such games)
- deep story with many characters with different motivations
- feels as if you are there in person investigating - no unnatural or illogical actions to be taken
- a lot of secrets
- beautiful weather, you hear birds, the wind in the trees
- semi non-linear gameplay
Cons:
- most of the time you really walk around from place to place (but it's not as annoying as it sounds)
- there is only one music per scene/room/building
- no controller support (though I initially wanted to use XPadder I got used to the keyboard controls quickly)
- low framerate in certain situations (when there is a huge complex to be rendered like at the entrance to the mansion)
- extremely slow load times in several places - it takes sometimes minutes switching between the different areas - but it should be a lot faster using an SSD (which I didn't try)
- no translations into other languages (yet)
I like it more than Everyone's Gone To The Rapture and FireWatch (though the latter was as captivating to me as this game). If you like narrative exploration games you should give it a try.
Anyway, I really enjoyed the game and if there will be another game from EQ studios I'll buy it blindly.

This game doesn't have a hell zone, it doesn't have many objectives, and it doesn't have any pvp. It also doesn't have a single reason for me to complain about it. Hell is not at the center of our planet, should it exist, the less objectives there are, the more freedom you have to do whatever you want, and the fact that there isn't any pvp keeps negative-competitive attitudes out of the game.
There are many sandbox games out there, many much more famous or cheaper than Starbound; Minecraft, Terraria, Castleminer Z, etc. Those games give you a wide open world to do as you please (Terraria only has a chunk of one though). Starbound has a small planet, but its greater than any other sandbox game in that it gives you an ENTIRE UNIVERSE to play in. There are several races to chose from, and some are unique to this game (my personal favorite: the Novakid), they all have special distinctions, enough that you'd never confuse two species. There are proper weather conditions based on numerous things in each system. You roam the universe, go to any system, and watch as the stars determine the planets, which then determine the creatures living there.
The game is so vast that I have to bookmark every planet i visit just to see how little of the game i've truly seen. And i'll never forget my starting planet: my home of Sabik Nest 2. I'll never forget the first enemy I saw, the Popatop, as I admired its beautiful humming, nor the first time I made a house for a guest and found him giving me gifts every couple of days.
Everything is so detailed, not in fancy graphics, but in simple pixels and data to make things realistic. Theres just enough of a picture to make your brain fill in the rest of the details using your imagination. It really makes me think about other life in the stars...
May this game have many updates, and many more sequels with the same quality and care that went into this game that I now hold as one of my most favorite games of all time.
Godspeed ladies and gentleman,

A point and click adventure game with heart, Anna's Quest does something that I haven't seen the genre do for a while: tug directly on the heartstrings in terms of empathy. While it's gameplay is what you'd want out of the genre and does a great job in really being in that sweet spot of not being too easy, but not being too painfully frustrating, it's the story telling and characters that carry it in a way that hasn't been done in the genre for a while. There's not a lot of humor and the visuals lack compared to some of their prior work in Deponia, but its clear that they wanted to make a heart-warming story more then anything else, and great voice acting and writing makes you want to see what happens next. It's a game that I'll be completing for the story alone, and that's what you need out of a game in this genre. Definitely worth a pick up for narrative focused fans or Point and Click lovers.

Counter-Strike is a first-person shooter in which players join either the terrorist team, the counter-terrorist team, or become spectators. Each team attempts to complete their mission objective and/or eliminate the opposing team. Each round starts with the two teams spawning simultaneously.
A player can choose to play as one of eight different default character models (four for each side, although Counter-Strike: Condition Zero added two extra models, bringing the total to ten). Players are generally given a few seconds before the round begins (known as "freeze time") to prepare and buy equipment, during which they cannot attack or move (one notable exception is that a player may receive damage during freeze time. This happens when a map is changed to spawn players at a certain height above the ground, thus causing fall damage to the player. This is a method map designers use to alter the starting "HP" of players on a map). They can return to the buy area within a set amount of time to buy more equipment (some custom maps included neutral "buy zones" that could be used by both teams). Once the round has ended, surviving players retain their equipment for use in the next round; players who were killed begin the next round with the basic default starting equipment.

TL;DR: Night in the Woods is a wonderful (if a little depressing) narrative wrapped in an atmospheric platformer that is definitely more than worth its price and the time you'll put into it.
It's very rare that a game leaves me with impression strong enough to actually feel driven to take time out of my day to give it a solid recommendation. (That's honestly why I never felt motivated to finish giving Life is Strange a good word past its later episodes.)
Whether it's the time in my life in which Night in the Woods arrived, or the fact that the writing may actually just be near perfect, this game left me with a feeling beyond description. What made the writing stand out to me was how much both the major and even the minor characters actually felt like living beings within their setting as opposed to being stand-ins or objects for the sake of progression. Each character is at a different stage in their life and views the world with their own perspective that is sometimes comical, sometimes tragic, and often in at a strange ground in between. If you've been through a bad job, the loss of someone close to you, or are simply frustrated with the place you're at in your life right now, you'll probably find yourself empathizing with them more often than most characters from other games of recent or distant memory. More over their interactions more often than not feel meaningful. For the player who enjoys a narrative, the writing alone can carry this game, but that's far from it's only strength.
One design principal that Infinite Falls made very obvious through their work on this game is that they wanted the art, music, and gameplay of Night in the Woods to be tailored to the story and not the other way around. The result of this is an atmosphere that always feels perfect to the narrative it accompanies. Despite its simplicity, the art if this game through its style, color, and chemistry with the music will often lead you to pause simply for the sake of taking it all in. True talent went into the music as well as it doesn't try and force you into feeling one way or another, but instead reacts to how a given moment leaves you feeling. While sometimes repetitive, the platforming in this game always feels smooth and fitting to (the protagonist) Mae's character. One off minigames and occasional rythm sequences (there are only three) add some variety to the game and often have you looking forward to taking part in the strange things that Mei and her friends get up to.
All of that being said, I highly recommend giving Night in the Woods a couple of playthroughs, given the choices and secrets that it holds. It is more than well worth the time.

There are times when you don't realize how much you wanted something until you've gone through. NitW is one of those things.
All right, let's cut to the chase: do you like melancholic, slice of life character driven drama and narrative with cute animals? Then this is right up your goddamn alley. Because it's all of that. This is a game which feeds the niche craving of "I want to see characters just going through the struggle of life." How is that a game? It kind of is, and it kind of isn't.
I have a bias. Serious drama with furries might as well be my thing. I don't see enough material like it. Two examples I could think of are Fantastic Mr. Fox and Bojack Horseman, and neither of those are inherently "furry." They're just real stories with real characters told with cute animals.
Back on track, as for the game, like I said - and many others say - it's story and character central. There are platforming elements and minor puzzles to solve, but they're kind of like the glue to everything. Aside from ONE PARTICULAR JUMP (you know the one) none of it will challenge you in the sense that "video games" do. They're merely another vehicle to other plot points and exploration elements. For those who take their time, they'll see lots of character interactions and dialogues, giving everything a greater sense of a lived in world.
If I had one criticism it's that I can't hang out with all of Mae's friends. And you know why that's a criticism? Because it HURTS. Bae, for instance, is my favorite. I can honestly say I've experienced some of the exact things she's gone through in her written life and as such, I feel a deep connection with her. So, every chance I got, I hung out with her. But by doing so I "ended" the day, leaving Gregg or Angus out of the loop. That sucks. I just want Mae to hang out with her friends!
Anyway, with a lovely, appealing graphical style, appropriately written character dialogue (some like, some don't), and a plot that works on both the "mundanity of life" and "creepy cosmic horror mystery," it hits all the good points. And now I desperately want more of this kind of stuff, of which sadly, there really isn't any.

Walking simulator that quickly evolves from liesurely exploration of an abandoned gated community into a full-blown murder mystery adventure game.

Every place has its secrets.  Every suspect is hiding something.  Look through drawers, cupboards, the homes and belongings of the persons you are investigating to lead you closer to truth.
You play as an investigative reporter with one simple objective: Solve a cold case file by determining who killed wealthy socialite philanthropist Vivian Roberts and provide a front page photo.  Can you find the murder weapon?  Can you learn the whole truth about what happened in the now vacant Painscreek?

You'll need patience and a sharp mind to get the most from this experience.  There are no artificial guide posts to your objective, just a trusty digital camera to record important clues or environmental details and lots of reading.  You'll need to enjoy reading as the many scattered diaries, documents and letters left behind paint a much bigger picture of the events and point to other mysteries.  This deducing on your own the events that resulted in bloody murder is very satisfying.
The game allows you to end your investigation at any time by leaving Painscreek, but compels you to stay with these deep story threads.
Technical stuff and Cons:
Looks great even on my mid-range pc, but requires a powerful computer for the smoothest gameplay and has some long, dark loading screens in transition areas.  Uses several intensive post-processing effects (but which can be toggled from the menu.)  Chromatic aberration, Vignetting, Depth of Field, and Bloom.  Otherwise standard Unity based configurations.
Audio is Master volume only.  Music and effects would be preferable to a single slider. Subtitle option does not always remain enabled.
The game relies on a single autosave during transitions, which could pose inconvenient problems if play is interrupted. [I reloaded the game at one point to continue, but did not remember to pick up an important item again when the game reset me to the doorway where I first entered, for example.  It was hours later when I realized the item wasn't in my inventory...and on the other side of town through multiple loading screens.]
Numerous typos and some awkward translations in the text, although it is well written and uses readable handwriting fonts.
Notable Pro features:
Readable handwriting fonts.
Flashlights have realistic brightness and never run out of batteries. In the fifteen or so hours I used it, I never had to scrounge for batteries.
The digital camera has a seemingly realistic capacity to take as many photos as you please, which became a great mechanic for "note taking" and getting the clues you need to progress.  It was also fun to capture what I chose as the required cover photo for the newspaper.
The ending is fantastic, surprising, and totally worth your efforts.  This mystery (depending on how you get there, results may vary) turned into an exciting, but totally unexpected thriller for me.
The developers are active in the forums and have been steadily addressing issues and bugs since release.
Overall:  Excellent indie interactive mystery story with a few minor technical flaws, but great for any fan of adventure games with a steep mental challenge and plenty of rewards for exploration and puzzle solving.

quick review: rest in pieces, very tepid recommendation for american made SF game
What made SF3 so great was all completely removed for SF4, and in lieu of parry, parry, punish we then had jab jab focus backdash. I know I'm oversimplifying things here, but I always felt SF3 (and eventually my all time love, 3S) moved passed the clunky controls of SF2 and Hyper fighting and all that towards something that was more active, more offensive, more about feeling that zing you get from being aggressive and being rewarded for it. Parry made everything safe, yet not. A mechanic that gave even the ♥♥♥♥♥iest characters a fighting chance but not one that could be over abused (the basic rock x paper x scissors mindset was still the real meta) — grabbing now leading to more offensive ideas instead of outright wrecking your opponent (SF2). SF4 did nothing to tell the player how to establish advantages with safe-jumps, how mechanics like option-selects work, or anything -- the gameplay was dumbed down but somehow the mechanics were re-mystifyed to like an Alpha 2 level (where the OG in the arcade would woop you with X-ism combos) and everything else was like one of those big grids with conditional statements caught between arrows, all of them in this game pointing toward BACKDASH, or if you had meter, reversal, focus cancel THEN back dash. Ugh. I guess that's all right but now that we're into Ultra territory (with all most 50 characters in a game who at Capcops is even THINKING "balance" anymore?) and G4WL now replaced with laggy steamworks, I'll play something else. What I'm wishing for Ultra (I've yet to play it) is that they buff things quite a bit and then ease them back down with small patches. SFxT (a *far* superior game to any SF4 incarnation) did this beautifully but was sadly canned by the FGC because of Capcops decision to release a tamer product and then re-release the game with what should've been the standard all along --- guess right twice (or thrice), have perfect execution, and end a round. Roshambo'ing on the playground never  needed a patch to its rules. Seems Capcom lost sight of their own directive long ago. We'll see.

10/10 This is by far one of the best games like this that I have played (I believe they are called CRPGs, idk). Where to begin... From the good ol' days of Baldur's Gate, Planescape: Torment and Icewind Dale; this masterfully crafted games stands side by side with the classics! Outstanding writing and plot, plus amazing characters (and character development). The setting is truly unique, and I feel right at home in this original world. The game is as challenging as it is rewarding, at times I had to do other quests and level up to progress past certain points. It was not annoyingly challenging, just enough to make it feel great when you finally down that tough boss.
This game is full of intrigue, diplomacy and other non-combat interactions you would expect from something like D&D. The music is always fitting for the moment, and I thoroughly enjoy all of the music and sounds. The voice acting is great, but be ready for lots of reading (as expected with a game like this). There is so much that I love about this game, and I am unable to describe it all. What I know is that this is an instant classic, and it deserves all the praise that it has received. I am so pleased that this game exists, and I shall continue to support it through the great DLC that they continue to release! Wish you all the best of luck out there, have a blast with this masterwork! A TRUE 10/10!

Imagine if Stephen King wrote a coming-of-age story set in a failing Animal Crossing village. Then it got adapted into a platforming game with Guitar Hero interludes.
That sounds like an utter mess, doesn't it?
Night in the Woods manages to hit all those notes and somehow make it work.
+ Found myself genuinely caring about even minor characters, from the random homeless guy up behind the church to the fisherman-poet down in the subway.
~ The game has a decent resolution, but the ending feels hurried somehow. (Going straight from
back to the usual daily cycle was pretty bizarre.) On the other hand, I'd much prefer to be left wanting a bit more than bored and overwhelmed.
~ Illusion of choice - a lot of the choices you're presented only affect the next few lines of dialogue, and while there are a few choices that somewhat change the story, there is little indication if they are a point-of-no-return or a short interlude.
- If you hate clicking through text or mildly-tricky platforming puzzles, you
hate this game. An auto-click option would help a lot for the one, and helping the other would be an overhaul of the entire game.
Good story, great characters, not sure why they made it a platformer rather than point-and-click or straight up visual novel.

Take the character design of Animal Crossing, the writing style of good young adult literature and the art style of an internet web comic and you have Night in the Woods.
It's a coming of age tale with many a twist.
Let me tell you about this game. Spoiler free.
If there's anything that NEEDS to be stressed about this game, it's the writing and character building.
The writing is as natural as anyone speaks to one another, it's real as ♥♥♥♥.
The characters are very well fleshed out, Undertale's characters ain't got♥♥♥♥♥♥on the citizens of Possum Springs. Yes I went there. Undertale's characters are well written but they're also fictional caricatures of fantastical things. There's parallels to reality of course but come on, it can be argued that some of those characters are a stretch too far into fiction.
But with the characters in Night in the Woods, I can say I have EASILY met and spent time with people like any one of these characters in real life. These characters of Night in the Woods may look like caricatures out of a web comic, but MANNNN do they have real life issues and depth.
This game literally makes me feel as if I'm hanging with real friends every night I play it. (Yes, play it at night, in the dark.) I always look forward to the laughter, the tears and the fears of Mae Borowski and her gang.
This game has moments that are genuinely hilarious, sad, scary and hey, without spoilers I will even say... Mind blowing.
This game touches on a lot of mature themes despite its gentle exterior, again without spoilers it touches on the following topics...
- Love
- Death
- Change
- Crisis Existentialism
- Religion
- Peer pressure
- Jealousy
- Suggested hallucinogenic mental disorders
- all the drama that follows the years AFTER adolescence.
And that's about all I can say without blowing the lid off.
The gameplay? It's more than just walking around. There are light minigames throughout the story and without spoilers... There's a FULL META GAME built into the game that some people spend more time on than the main game. And it's actually a game that could have released independently. Seriously.
The game itself is linear in the fashion that it tells it's story, if you go to bed at night, there's no way to go back to any of the events of that day you missed, and thus, this game requires multiple playthroughs. I'm on my second one now. :)
Anyways, I just had to get that off my chest. There are folks saying this will be the next "Undertale" craze so... Get into it before it's supposedly "uncool" and "cool to hate"
So yeah.

Lately I became a happy owner of 3 wireless game controllers.
Naturally I started collecting (more like "hoarding") locally cooperative games. FORCED is one of the first i bought.
It was on sale, and had excellent reviews, so being always on a lookout for some local mp games I thought I'll give it a try.
It was an excellent purchase.
My buddy and I have sat through it's levels on numerous nights, from dusk till dawn, and couldn't get enough.
Surprisingly though game is easy at first but very challenging in longer run. First few levels are kinda slow-paced and trivial, You get to know your characters and their capabilities, and you don't really care for speedrunning, nor challenges, But what's brilliant about this game, is that it makes you go back and revisit levels and play them through perfectly, for sake of progressing through other hard levels.
FORCED is a story of skill on a very interesting level. Game such as this- easy to play, hard to master- is not a very common thing these days, so I would recommend it to anyone. Playing with a buddy is greatly rewarding experience, so I'd recommend playing it in coop.

This game is pretty awesome. In the main game there are only a handful of buildings you can't go into. The freedom alone is worth buying this. My first play through I looted nearly every building and ended up having to end that playthrough simply because I had run out of resources to find and pick up. Seriously, this game is great!
The freedom of the game is what I love the most. The characters you interact with are different each time (mostly) and you have the freedom to choose how to play each one. You can choose to help neighbors, or just let them face the horde themselves. You can help out a friend, or take him on a trip and feed him to an infestation. The plot of the main game is... well it's stupid. There's no way around that, but really you'll be playing the game for reasons other than the plot. The Breakdown DLC is essentially just that. State of Decay without the plot. It was probably my favorite version of the game. More challenging and I didn't need to suffer through the zombie tropes. Lifeline is a great DLC too. There's a plot there, not sure what it is, but I liked it. Of the three I actually liked Lifeline the most. At that point the game devs seem to have figured out how to properly set this game up.
This game is no where near perfect though. At this point one of the zombie horde's listed powers should be the power to glitch. They will glitch through walls, ceilings, floors, cars, and anything else. Heck I saw thim glitch onto rooftops. That's kind of funny for regular zombies, but the super ones will do that too (I'm looking at you teleporting Juggernaut that nom nommed Sasquath's face off). In long stretches of play it beceoms really clear just how many awful glitch zombies there are. It can give the game charm for the most part, but when the glitch kills a mission character good luck finding the bright side.
The real problem I had with the game though wasn't with the glitches. Like I said, I enjoyed a sizeable part of those. The real problem is that this game doesn't respect the gamer's time at all. Unlocking the Breakdown heros takes an insane amount of time. And they pretty much universally suck. Buildings take forever to build, and that's if they don't get delayed for arbitrary reasons (like needing tape). There were so many times where I ended up just leaving the game running and walking away so that I could complete something. Or some challenges are just difficult to the point where I was crying. 25 headshot streaks. That sucked. No two ways about it. Seeing Sasquatch get killed time and time again. That sucked. Those kinds of things nearly killed this game for me. I did manage to get every trophy, but I really wonder if it was worth my time.
This is a really fun game that I would recommend to friends just to play. If you're thinking about getting all the achievements get prepared for a load of frustration. Just playing for playing's sake this is top notch, will do it many more times, but playing to complete it is nothing more than a frustrating slog. After about 70 hours with the game I finally caved and modded the game so that I could get through the final bit. And let me tell you, the mods on Nexus for this game are pretty fun. Just saying, there's lots of ways to just play and enjoy this game.

This game doesn't have a hell zone, it doesn't have many objectives, and it doesn't have any pvp. It also doesn't have a single reason for me to complain about it. Hell is not at the center of our planet, should it exist, the less objectives there are, the more freedom you have to do whatever you want, and the fact that there isn't any pvp keeps negative-competitive attitudes out of the game.
There are many sandbox games out there, many much more famous or cheaper than Starbound; Minecraft, Terraria, Castleminer Z, etc. Those games give you a wide open world to do as you please (Terraria only has a chunk of one though). Starbound has a small planet, but its greater than any other sandbox game in that it gives you an ENTIRE UNIVERSE to play in. There are several races to chose from, and some are unique to this game (my personal favorite: the Novakid), they all have special distinctions, enough that you'd never confuse two species. There are proper weather conditions based on numerous things in each system. You roam the universe, go to any system, and watch as the stars determine the planets, which then determine the creatures living there.
The game is so vast that I have to bookmark every planet i visit just to see how little of the game i've truly seen. And i'll never forget my starting planet: my home of Sabik Nest 2. I'll never forget the first enemy I saw, the Popatop, as I admired its beautiful humming, nor the first time I made a house for a guest and found him giving me gifts every couple of days.
Everything is so detailed, not in fancy graphics, but in simple pixels and data to make things realistic. Theres just enough of a picture to make your brain fill in the rest of the details using your imagination. It really makes me think about other life in the stars...
May this game have many updates, and many more sequels with the same quality and care that went into this game that I now hold as one of my most favorite games of all time.
Godspeed ladies and gentleman,
.................................~A Protector

Okay, so I was sent Painscreek and I was curious and REALLY interested. As someone who streams games like this and really enjoys pulling apart mysteries with my buddies in the audience -- this seemed like my kind of thing. The story is fascinating and you'll be taking notes almost immediately. It holds you accountable for what you learn and there's not a single bit of guidance. It essentially sets you on your way from the start.
I will say that optimization should be looked into. I run a very high-end gaming PC and it was struggling with frame rate when we'd go into new areas. The loading times are a bit intense and you'll find yourself wondering if the game froze. The game will also, well, freeze. There were moments I couldn't move, I'd get stuck trying to unlock a door and have to restart the game from the title screen.
Visually, it's actually quite impressive. Perhaps too ambitious, if I'm being honest. It seems like the heft of that framerate issue could've been helped by maybe not having a ton of useless exterior buildings. What do I know though? I just write about games -- I don't make them. The music is good at building the drama and I will say, I did NOT expect some of the things that occurred. I liked that. The game does keep you on your toes despite being touted as a walking simulator mystery experience.
I would like to see the bugs and things hammered out a bit more in an upcoming update so that I can feel better about cracking this game open on stream again. At its current state, I spent most of my time stuck in frame-rate drops and chugging, loading screens and just an overwhelming sense of feeling like I was on my own to figure out what I could do to reduce those things.
The developers are onto something though and I will say that the story DOES make up for those situations. I had questions, I had notes and I was really interested in finding out who killed Vivian. I also really dug the fact you can end the game as SOON as you think you figured out who did it and you even have to include a good picture for the expose you're writing.
Fix the bugs and you've got a fan for life, folks.

Counter-Strike: Condition Zero is the singleplayer addition to the timeless classic: Counter-Strike. The game adds a singleplayer campaign, bots, and graphical polish. While the game itself is very similar to the original Counter-Strike it adds many needed features that the first game lacked.
For starters the new graphical polish that the developers added (I think there were something like 4 total devs) makes the game much more believeable and more fun to play. I felt the the developers really took the time to make sure the weapons were as close to real as possible. Because of this the game feels much more tactical than the first. In my personal opinion, this is the most tactical CS game you will find (when I say that I am excluding CS:GO).
As for the bots they could've used a bit more work. From todays standards the bots are everything but smart. They often have trouble deciding whether they want to climb a ladder or not and frequentely stare at the wall hoping something exciting will happen. While these bugs are excusable for the age of the title, they do detract from the game. The singleplayer campaign is good and fun to play at times. If you are confused as to what to expect on the singleplayer campaign picture Half-Life but in the Counter-Strike world. Basically if Valve wanted to make CS a singleplayer game they probably would have done it similarly to how it was done in this campaign. It can be fun and actually quite exciting but anything far from challenging. The most challenge you will get out of the campaign is a big enemy with lots of armor and a machine gun.
If you are a beginner looking for a introduction to the world of Counter-Strike, this is the way to go. The bots are a perfect difficulty for any new player and the game maintains the feel of the original Counter Strike.
Overall Rating: 8/10

TL;DR: Night in the Woods is a wonderful (if a little depressing) narrative wrapped in an atmospheric platformer that is definitely more than worth its price and the time you'll put into it.
It's very rare that a game leaves me with impression strong enough to actually feel driven to take time out of my day to give it a solid recommendation. (That's honestly why I never felt motivated to finish giving Life is Strange a good word past its later episodes.)
Whether it's the time in my life in which Night in the Woods arrived, or the fact that the writing may actually just be near perfect, this game left me with a feeling beyond description. What made the writing stand out to me was how much both the major and even the minor characters actually felt like living beings within their setting as opposed to being stand-ins or objects for the sake of progression. Each character is at a different stage in their life and views the world with their own perspective that is sometimes comical, sometimes tragic, and often in at a strange ground in between. If you've been through a bad job, the loss of someone close to you, or are simply frustrated with the place you're at in your life right now, you'll probably find yourself empathizing with them more often than most characters from other games of recent or distant memory. More over their interactions more often than not feel meaningful. For the player who enjoys a narrative, the writing alone can carry this game, but that's far from it's only strength.
One design principal that Infinite Falls made very obvious through their work on this game is that they wanted the art, music, and gameplay of Night in the Woods to be tailored to the story and not the other way around. The result of this is an atmosphere that always feels perfect to the narrative it accompanies. Despite its simplicity, the art if this game through its style, color, and chemistry with the music will often lead you to pause simply for the sake of taking it all in. True talent went into the music as well as it doesn't try and force you into feeling one way or another, but instead reacts to how a given moment leaves you feeling. While sometimes repetitive, the platforming in this game always feels smooth and fitting to (the protagonist) Mae's character. One off minigames and occasional rythm sequences (there are only three) add some variety to the game and often have you looking forward to taking part in the strange things that Mei and her friends get up to.
All of that being said, I highly recommend giving Night in the Woods a couple of playthroughs, given the choices and secrets that it holds. It is more than well worth the time.

There are times when you don't realize how much you wanted something until you've gone through. NitW is one of those things.
All right, let's cut to the chase: do you like melancholic, slice of life character driven drama and narrative with cute animals? Then this is right up your goddamn alley. Because it's all of that. This is a game which feeds the niche craving of "I want to see characters just going through the struggle of life." How is that a game? It kind of is, and it kind of isn't.
I have a bias. Serious drama with furries might as well be my thing. I don't see enough material like it. Two examples I could think of are Fantastic Mr. Fox and Bojack Horseman, and neither of those are inherently "furry." They're just real stories with real characters told with cute animals.
Back on track, as for the game, like I said - and many others say - it's story and character central. There are platforming elements and minor puzzles to solve, but they're kind of like the glue to everything. Aside from ONE PARTICULAR JUMP (you know the one) none of it will challenge you in the sense that "video games" do. They're merely another vehicle to other plot points and exploration elements. For those who take their time, they'll see lots of character interactions and dialogues, giving everything a greater sense of a lived in world.
If I had one criticism it's that I can't hang out with all of Mae's friends. And you know why that's a criticism? Because it HURTS. Bae, for instance, is my favorite. I can honestly say I've experienced some of the exact things she's gone through in her written life and as such, I feel a deep connection with her. So, every chance I got, I hung out with her. But by doing so I "ended" the day, leaving Gregg or Angus out of the loop. That sucks. I just want Mae to hang out with her friends!
Anyway, with a lovely, appealing graphical style, appropriately written character dialogue (some like, some don't), and a plot that works on both the "mundanity of life" and "creepy cosmic horror mystery," it hits all the good points. And now I desperately want more of this kind of stuff, of which sadly, there really isn't any.

As much as I love this game, I acknowledge that it certainly isn't for everyone; however, if you're even slightly interested in an interactive story-oriented game with a fantastic soundtrack, a simple but beautiful art style, largely realistic writing, that really gets you invested with the (oftentimes relatable) characters, I strongly suggest you give Night in the Woods a try. I won't call it flawless, but it does everything it offers very well and hits close to home.

This game doesn't have a hell zone, it doesn't have many objectives, and it doesn't have any pvp. It also doesn't have a single reason for me to complain about it. Hell is not at the center of our planet, should it exist, the less objectives there are, the more freedom you have to do whatever you want, and the fact that there isn't any pvp keeps negative-competitive attitudes out of the game.
There are many sandbox games out there, many much more famous or cheaper than Starbound; Minecraft, Terraria, Castleminer Z, etc. Those games give you a wide open world to do as you please (Terraria only has a chunk of one though). Starbound has a small planet, but its greater than any other sandbox game in that it gives you an ENTIRE UNIVERSE to play in. There are several races to chose from, and some are unique to this game (my personal favorite: the Novakid), they all have special distinctions, enough that you'd never confuse two species. There are proper weather conditions based on numerous things in each system. You roam the universe, go to any system, and watch as the stars determine the planets, which then determine the creatures living there.
The game is so vast that I have to bookmark every planet i visit just to see how little of the game i've truly seen. And i'll never forget my starting planet: my home of Sabik Nest 2. I'll never forget the first enemy I saw, the Popatop, as I admired its beautiful humming, nor the first time I made a house for a guest and found him giving me gifts every couple of days.
Everything is so detailed, not in fancy graphics, but in simple pixels and data to make things realistic. Theres just enough of a picture to make your brain fill in the rest of the details using your imagination. It really makes me think about other life in the stars...
May this game have many updates, and many more sequels with the same quality and care that went into this game that I now hold as one of my most favorite games of all time.
Godspeed ladies and gentleman,

Cooperative Action Puzzle RPG. You collect crystals throughout levels by beating them, and optionally, completing challenges. These crystals unlock active abilities, passive abilities, and slots for both active and passive abilities (up to 3 each). There are 4 varying classes you can choose from any time while in the hub. You can't have more than 1 class chosen at a time. My favorite class is Frozen Captain America.
It's got simple combat where you can dodge most enemy attacks with good timing, and puzzles involving an ethereal sphere dude you call to your position, that you can also carry with you. It's used by guiding it through shrines, which can have a healing, explosive, speed boost, etc, effect. You can also guide it to a block, which can be pushed and pulled to your location by calling it. You can also activate other things, like torches, as well as purify things and destroy enemy spawners.
The game has about 20+ something stages, and a challenging boss and new environments after every several stages.
It's a pretty difficult game, and I suggest you try it with at least one other person, or you'll probably go mad in solo.

I had fun playing this game. Having first played through the first few levels with some friends until we stopped for a while, I had decided to pick it back up on my own after a few years. Yeesh... this game is tough on your own!
I found that many challenges took a lot of observation and some trial-and-error until I found the right setup of skills and passives to complete them. I never felt cheated or that it was impossible to do on my own, there was always a combination (along with some patience) that worked.
You are given the choice to play as one of four gladiators, each with their own weapon type: archer, shield, hammer (AoE style), and dual blades (fast single-targeting). I played as the shield for most of the challenges, as he has the ability to heal himself while moving faster, reflect enemy attacks for a duration, make himself immune to damage (and immobile) for a while, and dash through enemies. Almost every level had me rearranging my abilities to complete them, and that's what kept me going; I never felt that I was doing the same thing every level.
I'd highly recommend giving this game a shot. If you have some buddies to play it with, you'll have a blast. If you don't, this game is still a lot of fun on your own and is a good challenge.

You are mostly gathering resources, growing your settlement, expanding your territory, and fulfilling various scenario tasks, all within a usually very creative map that includes valleys, river crossing, mountain passes, and other fun strategic stuff. Maybe half of the scenarios end with you destroying another faction, but this is definitely not a military-focused game.
The good:
-Very solid game engine: never a bug or crash after 5 months of playing on Windows Vista 64-bit with a GeForce 9800GTX and graphics settings maxed-out
-Immersive period graphics and another solid ambient period music score by Dynamedion (Best German Soundtrack 2007)
-Creative maps/scenarios that are generally not too difficult and typically take around 3 hours each
-Vegetarian rating allows you to replay old maps using a different strategy
-Active user community creating custom maps for you
Cons:

Amazing game with amazing gameplay. You can choose to be stealthy if you want to or you can run in slashing and slicing left and right. Even if you don't understand the story, it's still super fun to run around killing orcs.
But the best part in my opinion would be the Nemesis System. As you play the game the Nemesis System keeps track of the orcs you fight. It keeps track of when you kill orcs, when orcs run away from you, when you run away from orcs, and, of course, when you get killed by an orc. The more you interact with any one orc, the more likely they'll become your nemesis. Once your nemesis reaches a certain "nemesis level" they'll start to appear more often and will reappear even if you kill them creating your own personal story between you and your nemesis that no one other than you experiences. Everyone's nemesis is different and how that nemesis interacts with you depends on how you've interacted with them previously.
tldr: The Nemesis System is the greatest thing about this game on top of the already great gameplay. Highly recommend it.

Middle Earth Shadow of Mordor is a third person fighter, and it's an absolutely fabulous game, one of my new favourites. I am a pretty huge LOTR fan, and as such this game is a godsend. I have written marathon reviews in the past, however I'm going to try and be conicse here.
Gripping, emotional, riveting, awe inspiring and just plain brilliant. While it conflicts with some of the previously established elements of Tolkien's works, I myself theorise this game franchise may take place in it's own universe, and as such this gives the Devs more freedom to do as they wish with the story. No spoilers, it's amazing.
The gameplay, the most important element of a game in my eyes, shines truly here. It's very rare that I can put 30+ hours in to a game without ever getting bored once. Seriously. And I'm not just saying that. The amount to do is phenomenal, and in a good way. The base gameplay is based upon the Arkham system, with of course it's own flairs and unique elements, with counters and combos being a primary factor in combat. You can build up your combos to perform brutally beautiful executions, Wraith moves such as flash, blast, and more, and other such moves. Furthermore, gameplay also prevents boredom in any way with a large number of awesome upgrades and unlockable abilites; by the time you reach the more endgame abilities you willl feel truly powerful.
I feel now is a good time to talk about the Captain mechanic, and the revelutionarily brilliant Nemesis system. If an Uruk, (your main enemies are Uruk Hai) manages to kill you, their power increases and they become a captain. The 'Sauron's Army' screen shows the captains you have and haven't identified, and their respective Warchiefs, the highest ranking Uruks in the game. You can target Captains and take them out, or if you take a particular liking for one, or they are particularly powerful, you can do what is knwon as Branding.
Branding is a fantastic mechanic which adds new levels oif depth and replayability to the game. Unlocked by progressing far enough through the main story, Branding allows you to take over the mind of an Uruk, be they regular, Captain or Warchief, and make him your ally; If it's a Captain or Warchief, then their followers (if they have any) become yours also. You can then cause wars and riots by setting them upon each other, and also get Captains you like to Warchief, efectively allowing you to customise the Uruk ranks.

Bought this for $4 during the Summer Sale. I've bought a lot of $4 games during the sale, from ones that were originally like $8 to begin with to AAA titles that were originally $6t0+ like this game. Even counting what I get "for the money," this has to be the worst purchase I've made during the sale, possibly on Steam ever. I do concede that the game looks good, but I have three main gripes that just ruined Shadow of Mordor for me.
1. Controls are extremely clunky: Designing a control scheme around controllers doesn't mean you can't include a good keyboard+mouse control scheme...
Biggest problem is that there is no toggle option for stealth and sprint. "Regular" movement is a super slow walk that's slower than stealth, so I either have to hold shift or space, or both to move at any appreciable speed. I understand that a lot of people play PC games on controllers nowadays and this control scheme might be okay for controllers (I'm assuming stealth/sprint are done by holding trigger buttons), but making a control scheme well-suited to controllers does not mean you have to absolutely butcher the keyboard+mouse control. Yes, you can remap the stealth/sprint keys to slightly more ergonomic locations, but it's a never-ending inconvenience that hits you at the worst times and you never fully adapt to it.
Also, who thought it'd be a good idea to make picking up items share a button with grabbing enemies, especially in a game where combat is basically never-ending? If I killed a boss, I want to pick up my rune and see what it is. I shouldn't be denied my loot for another 15 minutes because I keep grabbing into thin air because my auto-targeting thinks I'm trying to grab an uruk.
Interaction with walls is also atrocious. As another reviewer said, I can pretty much climb any wall, which looks ridiculous in its own right. The control problem is that this climbing feels very clunky, where sometimes I'll climb immediately, and sometimes there's a noticeable delay or it simply doesn't register because I somehow didn't click into the location I have to be at in order to climb it. Comeon, this game was released in 2014. I don't think characters sliding into an invisible slot on a wall is expected in an AAA title.
2. Combat system is atrocious: Sure, it looks really cool and "challenging" for the first couple fights, but is it really "good" if it gets old that quickly?
Whatever good ideas like nemesis system, uruks fighting among themselves, abilities, etc. are rendered completely irrelevant by the mindless combat that seemingly lasts forever. It'd be fine if the combat was fun, but it's really not because I never felt like I had control over my actions other than mashing left clicks, mixing in occasional right clicks, and F every 8 attacks. The game targets enemies for me, so I constantly end up killing intel sources I wanted to keep alive, or not be able to use my finishing moves on intended targets. Sure, the combat is cinematic and looks like you're doing a lot of cool stuff from a spectator's point of view, but as a player, after maybe 10 minutes of seeing the same cinematic kills that you barely have any control of over and over again, those slo-mo killcams are just another way to make the game feel drawn out. Also, can't forget to mention practical invincibility because of how broken it is to just mash space bar for dodge actions.
I wish the enemies had higher attack damage across the board for more challenge. I wish there was actual element of timing with combat, where I have to commit to an attack/counter/dodge and have to carefully plan what I'm going to do next. On top of that, enemies should have either been lower HP and keep this swarmy-feeling, or much more challenging individuals coming in small numbers. In fact, those two could have been both included in the game to control the tempo and keep battles varied but lasting for a reasonable duration instead of two uruks joining the fight every time you kill one, making a single instance of frontal assault last 10 minutes when you've already been bored with it after the first 45 seconds.
3. Open world?: A large pit where the only thing you can do is fight "freely" is not an open world.
Sure, you get to fight whoever you want (kind of, unless the inevitable "5 uruk captains just joined the fight" happens) and can do trivial side-quests that really have no impact on the world, but is that really open world? Yes, the uruk captains change based on your killing them/getting killed by them and "impact" the world, but it's just another randomly generated uruk filling in for anaother randomly generated uruk with no real influence over the world.
Maybe I'm just picky, but open world means something like the Elder Scrolls series, where I can actually do things other than combat to a meaningful degree. For example, if I decide to roleplay as a warrior who pulverizes anyone in his path, I definitely can. I can also decide to roleplay as a petty thief who is afraid of killing people so he just pickpockets and steals things, sneaking around and avoiding combat. I can roleplay as a merchant, alchemist, hunter, ordinary citizen. There's none of that in Shadow of Mordor, where the only thing you can do is fight, fight, and fight, and the only freedom you have in the world is you get to half-choose if you want to fight someone now or later. I saw the "open world" tag and was excited to explore Middle Earth with actual interaction with the world, but climbing literally every wall is the only real interaction with the environment. On that note, being able to climb every wall doesn't reinforce players with "wow I can go anywhere; this is a truly open world!" kind of feeling, but just takes away from the challenge and creativity.
This is the first review I've ever written for a game, which says a lot about how disappointed I am with Shadow of Mordor.
Bottom line: I wouldn't buy it if it was being sold for $0.99. If it's free, sure, knock yourself out for an hour or two. However, if you go by "it's a decent deal if you've paid $1 per hour of playtime" idea like I do, this is not a good deal.

Having thrown myself against this game twice now I think it's safe to say it is not my cup of tea and while it is incredibly gauche to make comparisons, the most glaring flaw is that Pillars of Eternity isn't Baldur's Gate. Or even Neverwinter Nights for that matter.
The "D&D but not" RPG system just feels so incredibly awkward in every single facet: the attributes are all jumbled up and different, there are a plethora of status effects that overlap but are often ineffectual and the spells/abilities are familiar but slightly shifted in some manner. The endurance/health system is garbage and seems to exist solely to justify enemies doing absurd damage because technically you have health that you can heal into. Just let them have 400 health and having healing act normally, there's nothing unique or useful about the endurance system.
It's unfortunate that the gameplay and combat are so god awful because the worldbuilding and side characters are at least intriguing. The story isn't anything new but it's serviceable and works for the intention of establishing a new IP.
If they didn't try so hard to make an alternate gaming system this could have been a decent game.

Dark Souls is an RPG with a different approach compared to others in the genre, the action is more about player skill and strategy than levels and equipment, the story is hidden for the player to find rather than forcefed. The difficulty, while not as extreme as a lot of people make it out to be, is still harder than most modern games, it is just hard enough to be really satisfying when you succeed without becoming overly frustrating when you fail.
Pros:
- Level design
- Interesting locations with great atmosphere
- Great combat system
- Interesting and mysterious story
- Hard but fair
- Cool boss fights
- Unique multiplayer systems
- Build/equipment/covenant diversity, hidden areas/quests and a new game+ system makes multiple playthroughs still fun to play
Cons:
- A couple of unfair moments
- While this is by design, the game can sometimes go a little too far when hiding things from the player. (Special mention: on how to access the DLC area).
- Bad PC port (get DSFix for general fixes and 60fps, DSCM for the multiplayer and DSMousefix if you want to make kb/mouse playable, otherwise go with a controller)
With how unique and different the game is, it might not be to every RPG fan's taste, but that is also the reason why everyone should at least try it.

Take the character design of Animal Crossing, the writing style of good young adult literature and the art style of an internet web comic and you have Night in the Woods.
It's a coming of age tale with many a twist.
Let me tell you about this game. Spoiler free.
If there's anything that NEEDS to be stressed about this game, it's the writing and character building.
The writing is as natural as anyone speaks to one another, it's real as ♥♥♥♥.
The characters are very well fleshed out, Undertale's characters ain't got♥♥♥♥♥♥on the citizens of Possum Springs. Yes I went there. Undertale's characters are well written but they're also fictional caricatures of fantastical things. There's parallels to reality of course but come on, it can be argued that some of those characters are a stretch too far into fiction.
But with the characters in Night in the Woods, I can say I have EASILY met and spent time with people like any one of these characters in real life. These characters of Night in the Woods may look like caricatures out of a web comic, but MANNNN do they have real life issues and depth.
This game literally makes me feel as if I'm hanging with real friends every night I play it. (Yes, play it at night, in the dark.) I always look forward to the laughter, the tears and the fears of Mae Borowski and her gang.
This game has moments that are genuinely hilarious, sad, scary and hey, without spoilers I will even say... Mind blowing.
This game touches on a lot of mature themes despite its gentle exterior, again without spoilers it touches on the following topics...
- Love
- Death
- Change
- Crisis Existentialism
- Religion
- Peer pressure
- Jealousy
- Suggested hallucinogenic mental disorders
- all the drama that follows the years AFTER adolescence.
And that's about all I can say without blowing the lid off.
The gameplay? It's more than just walking around. There are light minigames throughout the story and without spoilers... There's a FULL META GAME built into the game that some people spend more time on than the main game. And it's actually a game that could have released independently. Seriously.
The game itself is linear in the fashion that it tells it's story, if you go to bed at night, there's no way to go back to any of the events of that day you missed, and thus, this game requires multiple playthroughs. I'm on my second one now. :)
Anyways, I just had to get that off my chest. There are folks saying this will be the next "Undertale" craze so... Get into it before it's supposedly "uncool" and "cool to hate"
So yeah.

Finally played this game that I've wanted to try for a very long time. Blacklist came out 2013, and I have to say that it still looks brilliant. It was a blast to play since the game is very nice optimized. SLI supported so I played it on ultra at 1440p, 144 fps. This most have been one of the best looking games of 2013, because it's still impressive.
Personally I would really like to play this in first person. There's 2 missions where you can play first person, but the rest is in third person. I looked around for a camera option, but I found that there is none. It's only in the missions that they selected. Too bad about that, because I though that was a lot more fun.
The strong part of this game is in my opinion the story. A terror group called the engineers is threatening USA with attacks if they don't pull back their troups out of other countries. Sam Fisher and his team is trying to find the people behind it, and the cutscenes add a lot to the story. Voice-acting and lip-sync is good and help the story out. What kept me playing to the end was absolutely to see how the story ended, and I liked it.
There's a pretty cool upgrade system. You get points based on what you playstyle is. Combat, panther or ghost. Now I tried to sneak a little, but most of the time I went for combat. Since I chose the combat/panther path I upgraded my gear for that. More powerful weapons, and gear with better armor. If you wanna sneak better you can upgrade to more sneaky gear and gadgets. I really like that I got the choice and wasn't forced to play in any perticular way. Some missions are unfortunately sneak only, but it's limited. Those missions frustrated me a little, but I can look past it.
I didn't feel like the guns had that powerful feeling and the gunplay was a little dull in my opinion. Melee takedowns was cool though. I though the gunplay was much better in the few first person missions. I just wish I could choose to play that way in every mission. But that's really the only downside that I personally felt.
All in all, this is a good AAA-game that you can play in your own way. Blacklist has a nice story, that is pretty lenghty and definitely replayable, with maps that have multiple paths and bonus objectives. I rushed through it and it still took me about 10 hours, but if you want you can spend a lot more time then that. I'm personally done with blacklist after one  playthrough and have no desire to go back, but im still glad I played it. I simply have a lot of other games I wanna play too, but if you are that person that like to play a game many times over, this is probably a game for you.
There is a lack of stealth games on the market, and this is one of the better ones. It runs super well, sounds good and the gameplay is fun. Sure I have some criticism on it, but it's minor things that most people won't care about. I would recommend it to everyone that like sneak games, third person shooters and games with a good story. I'm happy I played it, even though it wasn't what I expected before going in. I think people should give it a shot, on sale or even at full price. Gunplay was no more then decent in my opinion, but story, stealth, graphics and optimization made up for it.
Gameplay all good. But the worst thing is that me and my friend bought this to play coop, and it doens't even work, so we can't play together, which is a waste of money.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

I received this game as part of a bundle purchase and paid it no mind for a long time. I was craving something different recently and decided to give it a shot. To start, let me say that I have a bad habit of abandoning games that don't pique my interest quickly enough. When the game launched and I discovered that it was a point-and-click experience with pixelated graphics (not traditionally my cup of tea), I was sorely tempted to quit and uninstall. Experience has taught me, though, that sticking with a book or movie or, in this case, a game that doesn't immediately grab you can--and often does--result in a pleasant surprise.
I've always been more interested in character-driven stories than plot-driven fare, and that's exactly where this game shines. All of the main characters are relatable, unique, and well-written. Even better, the voice acting for most characters is outstanding and is probably what kept me from leaving the game initially. Turing, your companion throughout the game, is voiced so well that I sometimes found it difficult to ascertain the character's gender, which turns out to be a central theme of the story (more on that in a moment). Turing's excellent voice acting, along with the character's relatable plight to find a place in a culture eager to reject those whom are different, allowed me to develop an emotional attachment and investment in the story. This is a tremendous achievement.
As for the game's story, I have to commend its attempt to tackle themes that our society is still (sadly) trying to figure out. Gender identity, sexual orientation, loneliness, and alienation are central to the story, and you get to experience all of this vicariously through Turing (and others). The conflicts feel somewhat contrived at times, but they're important to discuss nonetheless and it's unusual to see such polarizing issues explored in games.
Ultimately, I'm glad I stuck with this game. There are a few faults and gameplay elements that I found aggravating, but these amount mostly to nitpicks. Viewed in its entirety, it's a fantastic game for what it is and demonstrates a lot of confidence in its story and its characters. I recommend checking it out.

Harder than Minesweeper

If I had to describe this game, I'd say it's a novel take on minesweeper. You are given a pattern with numbers, and you click to recreate that pattern, each click starting a counter of it's own, and incrementing the counters around it. This sounds nothing like minesweeper, but it uses a lot of the same kind of logic and reasoning.
The game is short. It's roughly an hours worth of puzzles, maybe two at most.
And would really benefit from a random mode. Perhaps where the levels are still symmetric in some way, but randomized. It would also benefit from having a windowed mode, so you could play it like one would with minecraft - while you're waiting on something else.
The music is a single soundtrack, with no option to disable it. So while it's enjoyable at first, it eventually becomes quite repetitive. The only audio feedback is in the form of beeps when you click, so you can just turn down the volume on your computer and you aren't missing anything.
Lastly, the game isn't without bugs. For example, it doesn't always wait for you to finish solving the puzzle once you've got it figured out. It robs you of that sense of satisfaction you get when solving the puzzle. It only seems to happen some of the time, but doesn't seem to be checking for all the simple "1" clicks you'd have to do to complete the puzzle. There's also a bug that resets your progress if you select the first level from the "Select Level" menu.
All in all, it's a gratifying but short game. It's just
that I have a hard time justifying the price of $2. It feels a bit skimpy compared to other games you can get for the same cost. I still recommend the game, but suggest only picking it up if you can find it in a bundle or on a really good sale.
