I really, really want to like this game, a lot, but the execution is so poor that it feels insulting sometimes.
I should say for the record, I bought this game because I loved VA-11 Hall-A. I'd had it on my radar for a while before, but after playing the sequel I couldn't help but want more. The writing in that game was so real; the game was so instantly immersive and consistently gripping throughout, and the writing struck a perfect balance between touching, deep, and hilarious. VA-11 Hall-A introduces a rich, diverse world full of unique characters with different worldviews and struggles, and within minutes it makes you deeply invested in those characters -- the entire experience was gripping, and I felt moved afterwards. 2064: Read Only Memories is none of that.
With VA-11 Hall-A, it was always clear what the developers were trying to show, from an outside perspective. It's a game with a viewpoint, and if you think about the content of the game, that viewpoint becomes clear. But that doesn't matter; what matters is that the game expresses its viewpoint well, and the message is convincing precisely because the world and characters feel like real people, who talk like real people and have personalities and emotions to match. 2064, on the other hand, is a game where the message feels sloppily patched in last minute. The viewpoint is the same, but instead of expressing it through a rich world and three-dimensional characters, it's shown through stilted stereotypes and their immersion-breaking asides.
Oftentimes playing this game I find myself thinking, "gosh, I'd probably agree with whatever the author is trying to say, but I really wish they wouldn't have taken me out of the game to tell me it." And this feeling of dissonance is made stronger by the fact that, every time the writer inserts their social message into the dialogue or narration, they choose to express it in a way that feels extremely dated. Good sci-fi has an air of timelessness to it; 2064 regular finds itself using buzzwords and talking points that I'm pretty sure everyone gave up on in 2011, which is all the more baffling because the game came out in 2015. The result is an uncomfortable mess, and it breaks that spell that only good writing can put one under.
In a good work of sci-fi, the author might use the world they've built and the characters they've created to show the reader the merits of their viewpoint, through the actions and feelings of the characters that you've come to like or dislike as a reader. But 2064 is not good sci-fi. Instead, 2064 has moments where a character yells at you, the player, for picking dialogue options you were forced to. 2064 has moments where it interrupts the flow of conversation to navigate a clunky dialogue tree, all in the name of inclusivity, and then immediately makes fun of itself, as the game, too, realizes that it could have picked a much less intrusive way to accomodate to everyone. What 2064 does not have, in the amount that I could stand to play it, is a single moment where any character felt like a real person, good or bad or complicated. For a visual novel, that is a death sentence.

There are multiple ways you can approach each scenario, so I'm sure this will be one I'm going to need to go back and play over again a few times. I appreciate that you can skip whole swaths of dialogue if you're playing through a scene again. The puzzles were fun and not too terribly challenging, though I did completely bomb one of them.
My only complaint is a lack of auto-save, meaning you have to remember to go in and manually save frequently to prevent losing any progress. This has its advantages, though, as with some forethought you can save at strategic points to test out how different actions turn out. Two save slots help with this, too, and I imagine I'll be even more thankful for this when I'm trying to max out achievements on future playthroughs.
The storyline is one I found myself thinking about when I wasn't playing, and I am not ashamed to admit that I cried a little bit at the end. Definitely well worth the purchase!

When I first saw this game, I instantly knew I would want to play it. I was searching for a fun and interactive cyberpunk game to play, and this game was exactly what I was looking for. However, it gave me ALOT more than I thought it would. I also want to preface this game by saying that is does an excellent job of including LGBT+ content, both in the min character and in others.
The first time I started this game, I didn't do it justice. I played for maybe 2 hours and then stopped for a few months. When I came back, the game had had an update, and it was entirely voiced. This really helped me play through the game, and kept me interested.
Now, the story for this game is its ultimate strong suit. The more and more I played, the better the plot and its progression got. The OST helped a lot with this, as moments where nothing serious happening had more lighthearted music, and serious moments had more intense and emotionally appropriate music. The game never felt tale with the story it was giving me. For a game that can take maybe a good 10 hours if you're really getting into it, nothing that I experienced felt unnecessary. All the little dialogue felt needed and very much welcome. With this game being a visual novel, this was a key part to get right.
A part along side the story that was done just right were the characters. The cast is very unique, and all the characters have enough story tied to them to where they are all important. Albeit some have more than others, all the characters have development, and watching them adapt while bouncing of of each other was so much fun. Watching their personalities clash and work along side each other felt so fluid and natural.
The best part is that with multiple endings, there is still so much I've yet to experience, granted, it will take some time to get too, but I know it will be worth it. This game has left a strong impact on me, and I won't soon forget it. Games recently have had a harder time leaving me with an emotional impact, but this game did so in a magnificent way.
I would recommend this game to anyone who wants a good visual novel to play, and especially if you want a good cyberpunk one at that.

I’m torn on this one. I really want to like the game for a number of reasons, but there are so many flaws present here that I really can’t recommend the title.
I like the central idea of the narrative to a certain extent. The artwork and the music are – for the most part – also enjoyable, though there are a few rough spots on both accounts. And I like a lot of the characters and their writing definitely reflects their unique personalities and I respect that the developers tried to be inclusive by also giving room to homosexual and transgender people.
But that last bit already spells out a major crux of the game where I really started having problems. Of the cast of characters, a majority belongs to what in the real world would be considered a minority. That’s not really a big deal, but the game itself makes a big deal out of it by needlessly dwelling upon it with numerous characters. This is already pretty apparent when you can choose your preferred pronouns at the start of the game and aren’t just limited to the biologically accurate representations of sexual dimorphism but also all that nonsense in between and that’s where my personal acceptance of this whole thing stops.
Without wanting to go too deep into gender politics, the rest of the game falls flat for a host of different reasons outside of that. For one, the point-and-click aspect isn’t all that interesting. At the start of the game, I tried to click on every interactable thing and get to know this world, but the game treats this as an opportunity for either an exposition dump or a tired reference to our current time, given that it’s set in the year 2064. So you’ll either get to read a wall of text about something entirely inconsequential – plants tend to come up at an alarming frequency –  similar to how games like Snatcher and Policenauts did it, or they’ll throw in a quip about retro gaming and even reference a few other indie games like Duck Game or CrossCode, which really breaks my immersion. It’s like the game is nudging you with its elbow and winking at you, trying to say “see how cool my devs are, how much they’re into retro-inspired stuff like you are for playing this game?” and that’s an attitude I can’t stomach. I already don’t see eye-to-eye with a lot of people who are enthusiastic about the same things I like exactly because of this type of self-congratulatory behavior, I don’t need it out of my entertainment as well.
This all comes at the expense of actual puzzles you get to solve. In all reality, it’s more of a visual novel than a point-and-click and I would’ve preferred if the game could make a definite choice on that matter, because the hybrid solution they went with isn’t satisfactory. I have too little experience with visual novels to give a definite recommendation based on that fact, but I can say that I found that the game was way too wordy for my taste. This is only really a problem because you’re forced to click every single time you want to progress a line in the script. I can understand that for a game that only features written text – as this game originally also did – but they patched in voice-acting after the fact, so just read off the entire conversation without having me wear out my mouse button just to get through your wall of text. It just breaks the flow of the conversation if it constantly pauses even just for a split-second. Especially since the game has a tendency of not reacting to input even though the arrow indicating that you’re permitted to continue has already flashed on the screen.
The voice-acting overall is ok, given that most of what you’ll get to hear comes from Melissa Hutchinson, who also did Clementine in the Walking Dead. But there’s also some voice-acting in there that’s not so spotless and can come off as annoying at times. As much as I like Jim Sterling, developers should just avoid putting him in games. He’s not a voice actor, and it shows. It rips me out of the experience, since he’s not acting and he also just uses his natural voice, so the game just sounds like a Jimquisition episode for a few minutes.
The game also claims to be a cyberpunk adventure but I honestly don’t feel it. It always claims that life in this world is s
hit for so many people but we never actually get to see it. There’s just not a lot of personality in the setting of this game. The game for instance claims that the genetically engineered furries in this game along with other augmented people get treated like sh
it, but we never see it and even a protest outside of a gene clinic, mirroring real protests outside of abortion clinics, is given way more nuance to the point where a lot of this supposed conflict that the narrative pushes never ends up on screen. What I’m saying is that for a dystopic cyberpunk future where private corporations rule everything, way too much of this world is too clean and the people are too happy. And when they’re not happy, they’re pis
sed off for no real reason at all.
The main conceit of the game that it deals with the technological singularity and tries to also draw parallels to other things. How we should treat sapient machines and what this potential future conflict can do to inform our current treatment of LGBT people. You know, it’s funny. When Deus Ex: Mankind Divided coined the term “mechanical apartheid”, people got up in arms, bit
ching about how you can’t use that term to highlight the divide between people who want humanity to stay pure and those who embrace augmentation, but when a game specifically made by people involved in the LGBT community us the exact same reasoning as a source of conflict – in this case augmentation as well as gene-splicing – it’s totally ok. Not to mention that the pro-humanity group in this game is literally called the Human Revolution as a not so subtle wink towards that game.
A lot of the nomenclature in this game tends to fall short of achieving a more fleshed out world than there is. For one, a ton of cities just have the prefix “neo” tacked on. The game takes place in Neo San Francisco, but Neo Tokyo and Neo Chicago also get namedropped. That they didn’t include a Neo New York borders on a miracle. Similarly, they chose to use tons of modified names of real-world objects for copyright reasons, so you’ll get a ton of spoonerisms in there as well and it all really just doesn’t want to gel with me. Just call it an NES, Nintendo ain’t gonna sue you. You don’t have to call it a Familink. And yeah, I’ve seen the Polybius arcade cabinet at the bar, you’re so clever.
As you can see, a lot of what bothers me about this game outside of the lackluster gameplay experience has to do with the typical too cool for school retro gamer attitude, which I really can’t stand. If you can stomach it and the heavy-handed inclusion of gender politics, maybe you’ll enjoy the game more than I did, but I got bored a couple of hours in and couldn’t wait for the game to end. Especially because it has a tendency of throwing in another layer of fetch-quest just as the main trail starts picking up, so you’ll end up doing something unrelated for a bit before you’re allowed to finally continue.

First off, this game shows a -lot- of heart and love put into it. It just oozes as a labor of love in almost every aspect. The dedication to the cyberpunk setting, the LGBT cast, the world building, the character development, the retro graphics and interface shows a lot of effort and a lot of thought. The voice acting is pretty good and really helps you get a feel for the characters. The cast is diverse and full of great designs, which is really important for an adventure game. If you like retro adventure games, this is a definite buy.
It does have some flaws though. Characters can come on a little grating, particularly Turing (though part of that is due to points where you may end up having them repeat lines over and over because you're not sure what to do or they just give the same stock answer for a lot of items to check/do) and some characters like Lexi feel underused so you wind up not caring about them much or they're just minor bumps, while some get a lot of exposure.
The plot also tries to go bigger than I think they set up for it. I don't want to go into spoilers but as the story progresses the initial mystery is kind of dropped and it feels like the cast makes a -lot- of assumptions and leaps in logic that could have been clarified or just don't seem reasonable actions. It tries to weave together a few different threads but I just don't feel like it succeeded as well as it thought it did and the eventual antagonist is a great reference but not a great antagonist/character on its own. The finale is interesting but doesn't really come off as satisfying and I think goes too big. You can see where the writers were coming from with the themes they were developing but given the story they wrote, the ending doesn't grok as well as it could have without having developed the themes further.
Puzzles are a little too simple. I would have liked to see some things that involve items and/or characters across different locations or more alternate solutions but for the most part, every puzzle can be solved in the same screen/location. Some also devolve into 'use everything in your inventory and see what works' rather than feeling intuitive. Plus, I have to give credit for being able to use the milk in the end, that was grade A+ hilarious.
The controls can be a little wonky at times, particularly when it comes to the mini games you're forced into. This is made especially grating because you're not given much heads up or much opportunity to save beforehand so it feels particularly frustrating to lose when you don't feel prepared and lost because of a misclick or non-responsive click.
I know there's achievements for replaying it and treating characters differently, but I don't feel like there's as much replay value to warrant them, at least not doing it in rapid succession, I beat the game and didn't have much incentive to dive back in to check out doing things like a jerk. I will go back and replay it eventually but it'll be a little while.
Lastly, the bar with 3 drinks per page and having to sit and listen to all their descriptions hunting for the 'right' drinks was just agonizing. No excuse for this sort of tedium, even given the retro feel.
In general though, it's a great little adventure, it's a treat checking out new locations and meeting all the different characters that populate this world and seeing where the story goes while seeing all the different references and homages built into the setting. I would love to see MidBoss do more installments in this series or just more games in general with an eye toward inclusion and representation.
Overall, I'd say like a B/B+ grade, it shows the craftsmanship and dedication that went into it and while it doesn't make the landing as well as it could have, it's great for retro adventure game lovers.

I gotta admit that I've been skeptical at first about what is gonna happen with the Splinter Cell franchise after I've played SC:Conviction, however I was pleasantly surprised with SC:Blacklist.
SC:Blacklist still has its flaws but if I had to describe it in one sentence then I'd say: It took over most of the featuers we loved about SC:CT (the variety of gadgets for instance) while giving us more ways to customize our gear (the options are by no means limitless but it's a great addition regardless) as well as allowing us to play the game the way we want to (SC:Conviction style included) which adds a lot of replay value.
My main complaint about SC:Blacklist is that it's way too easy for my taste, mainly because of balance issues. Mark and Execute has made its return and while I can see why people like this feature, I personally don't but luckily you can disable it by choosing the highest difficulty available (big plus for me). Now the difficulty would have been fine if the game was better balanced (although it would still be too easy considering it's the highest difficulty one can choose from).
The crossbow in the singleplayer of this game is completely overpowered as it only costs you one gadget slot while easily being worth +12 gadget slots. My reasoning behind this? It offers a bolt for most of the gadgets you'd normally use while having them in much larger amounts, on top of that you don't even have to choose and get all of the different bolts for one gadget slot. Oh and yeah all of those bolts also have a much greater range than it's normal gadget counterparts (as those are thrown by hand).
To make it short: Don't use the crossbow if you want the game to be sort of challenging at least. I've cleared every level on highest difficulty with the best rating in ghost playstyle and it was really fun, even if I'd wish it to be harder. If I however had used the crossbow (as it's meant to be played) it would have been a piece of cake and I'd get bored before being halfway through the game.
There are a lot of missions one can play in coop (there will be a handful of missions that suits your playstyle at the very least) as well as a purely coop dedicated campaign. I've enjoyed all of them except of the ones where you had to defend yourself against waves of enemies, I thought those were kind of misplaced in a stealth game.
Spies vs. Mercs also has made its return but to be honest I've been fairly disappointed with it. It seemed rather dead to me while SC:CT multiplayer on the other hand was quite active even years after (I know cause I've played it like crazy back in the days). The multiplayer is a little hacker infested just as the multiplayer in Chaos Theory and Pandora Tomorrow was which is unfortunate, but the thing that bugs me about it the most is that spies are able to kill mercs now. By that I don't mean just grab them from behind as it used to be, but literally just shoot them with your firearms and one-hit-kill them with a melee weapon, even if they are facing you during the process.
Overall I've enjoyed the game a lot and would recommend it to people who have enjoyed SC:Conviction as well as to fans of the older Splinter Cell games.

I first knew about this game when its Kickstarter campaign launched and ever since I’ve been kind of enamored. It’s been three years since then, three years dreaming of its release date and nightmareing with the possibility of it not matching my expectations. But as I was playing it, it struck me how much a person can change in three years.
Night in the Woods speaks a lot to 2014 me. Its aesthetic, its focus on narrative, its self-consciousness, its anthropomorphic animal people… It’s almost a formula to make me liking it. But it shouts at 2017 me in a way that got me to tears several times through my (slow) playthrough.
Its narrative is thematically so well structured that no dialogue seems superficial, no quest feels unnecessary and the cliché plot devices can be easily ignored. No joke made me laugh out loud, but every single one made me smile or giggle. Its length and replayability are surprisingly rich.
I’ll always recommend this game. It’s one of those soulful gems only our medium can produce.

This game is highly adivitive and extrodinarily fun. The gameplay mechanics are a rather good turn for the zombie apoc survival genre. I found the lack of a main character(s) that never dies to be well executed and potentially a game changer for future survival games. Combat can be both exciting, easy, hard, fun, and unfortunantly buggy on occasion. The zombies will force their way through walls or climb over obsticles heading in the opposite direction of you. Cars can be over powered at time since they can kill any zombie horde standing in it's way (the only zombie that poses as a threat to cars is the juggernaught). Cars do have a few issues, items getting stuck under a truck and wont go away resulting in an annoying grinding sound and reduced speed, they flip rather easily, and they engine starts puffing out white smoke after hitting only a few zombies but wont progress further for quite some time. Yes the car has issues with balancing and handling but it is useful although do not drive close to npcs they might freak out and cause a loss of trust.
The other factions in the games such as the named ones and enclaves do have a few issues with being rather repetitive and difficult to interact with outside of missions. However they add a different dianamic because interactions with them are based more on decisions rather then gun/melee skills witch define many games. The factions can not go to war with each other witch seems odd because there is some rivalries between everyone and the Wilkersons...... Dont trust that group...... Overall the factions can be good at times and then simply placeholders at other times. The main missions help progress story but a few side stories that are longer then one mission would be rather nice.
One feature I really enjoyed witch surprised me because I was weary of it while purchasing is the influence and locker mechanic. Don't freat over being able to purchase items from footlockers because while you are able to purchase them most of them are earned first and then put in the locker by yourself or (ammo) is resupplied via turning in ammo loot rucksacks. Enclave and named factions will have items based on how well off they are and how much they trust you to their stuff so there is much progression and looting to be had to even use the footlocker effectively. I did find influence rather easy to gain when you have a truck, house, and plenty of supplies.
I enjoyed the base mechanics of the game. Morale missions need some variety (both reasons for the mission and the activities of the mission) but were a good idea. Trading missions were nice however I never figured out how to set up a trade myself if it is even possible. At first there seems to be a good amount of bases to be located in but you quickly find that all the locations excect a few are for lower populations, one thing I wish there was with base was more building options perhaps being able to build a wall out a little further in some of the farm homes to allow for more spaces would be nice and more complex of a facility mechanic, the mechanic right now is limited to, bunkhouse, kitchen, dinning room (useless), training room, medical room, warehouse, workshop, and library. While this seems to be a decent amount there is only a hand full of options to do with each and most are only upgradeable once with the exception of a few. Also prebuilt facilities in the homes can't be upgraded? What crap is that? Maybe make a bunkhouse be upgradeable to a baracks witch has more beds and isnt made out of a tent or a kitchen is upgrade able to resturant. The home system can be better but even with these few flaws it is still enjoyable, although i will say characters should be able stay with you when you start a mission. Won't people be moving around in more then groups of two in a real apoc?

So, first of all, let's get one thing out of the way :
If I don't recommand this game, it is not because I don't think it's good or interesting, I even could recommend it to you if I knew you enough to guess if you would like it or not. But it is because I want to balance the evaluations ratio,
Done. now let me explain.
There are over 95% of the evaluations that recommend this game. Not that this game doesn't deserve them, but this extremely good ratio might trick you to buy a game you don't actually like.
Let me add some details here. I think that the main reason why there are so many people here who recommend this game is the game's appearence and how it teases, what audience it targets. This game doesn't have more than what it shows, but even if its variety or originality is restricted, it is very, very deep. You might not get what I am trying to say, but it basically means that if you stumbled across this game, it is probably because you have an interest towards :
- Anime, manga
- Touching stories
- Visual novels
...Or at least two of them. If you don't, you probably won't bother to hesitate upon buying it or not. But if you are reading this, it surely means you DO. And if you do, chances are that you will LOVE this game.
There are exceptions, I should know it, I am one. This game supposes that if you have an interest in whatever I listed above and that you spend enough time on your computer to be luring around steam searching for visual novels, you would relate to the hero. And you might, like the hundred thousand people who recommend it.
But it happens that you don't. I think you could relate to this game if your parents don't get drunk every night and beat each other, If you are not TOO interested in philosophy, if you don't enjoy life too much like by just going out for pleasure, just to walk, just to breathe but also if you're not depressed (those are opposite equivalents), if you're not cold blooded enough to analyze your situation before acting on impulse and, finally, if you don't have a partner (at least one that doesn't also have the same interests for everything as you do, but that's scarce anyway, and also kinda bad for you and your own palette of enjoyments (...yeah, sorry)). However, if you don't check multiple of these points, I can nearly ensure you that you won't resonate with this game the way the game wanted you to, so it may lead to an empty gaming experience. Still...
I hope you enjoy the game. Have fun !

It would seem (to me) that most of the negative views have come from players who've spent very little time playing this at all. I got this game on sale (£0.29 no less!!) and was amazed at the value for the game.
Now if you played games like Hotel Tycoon 2 I would say this game is rather similar, it gives you freedom to buy plots of land to build everything in (giving you option to spend less but have less room to build untill you buy another plot) and most of the buildings are simple 'plop and leave' giving you more time to spend on the only buildings that truely need managing and the main point of the game, casinos!
Casino building is where things get complicated, as you get to layout the entire innards of the casino you have placed, from adding in different heights, slot machines and gaming tables to placing your mechanics, security and hosts, and that can be kind of bewildering on your first visit to a large one (like seriously, how DO you fill those things haha). My advice for that though would be to layout your casino with different levels first, as this is actually free to do, and not only helps with organising the casino (and you only need to fill 1 section at a time if your lacking money), it looks pretty awesome to boot.
Other than that, the game is pretty simple once you familiarise yourself with everything, which is pretty much fully explained through the first 2 campain levels, which I would highly recommend doing, as you cant simply "own" without learning the game (in fact the same with most games) which could explain some of the 10 min played negative reviews.
As for the cons to this game, I would say theres not enough content in the game, it may seem dwarfing at first, but after a while I've found myself using the same few gaming tables and such, and the buildings outside, for me atleast, are more asthetic and just ways to get more people into my hotels and casinos.
In short, I would recommend this game as it has its quirks but is pretty fun once you learn the game. Would I recommend it at full price (£2.99) possibly. Would I recomend it on sale, yes. Would I recommend it at just 29 pence? You'd be crazy to miss that one lol.

This was very much a game of two halves as far as I was concerned.
The first chapters seemed very exposition-heavy (more like story-telling than a game); the quests all seemed trivial; and progress was slow to the point of boredom.
But in the second half, the pace picked up, the story ramped up, something important seemed to be going on, and I found myself thinking it was a good game as the credits rolled.  I'll play the game again some time, but it's not one of those games where you want to dive back into it immediately you finish.
It's nice to have a game where LGBTQ+ folk are treated as ordinary characters, rather than letting their queerness define them.  And I have to say it rather expanded my horizons (despite being gay myself): when I met a bearded character later in the game who used female pronouns, I didn't even blink.  I thought
were very sweet.
The game mechanics can be frustrating at times.  Most of the time all you can do is press the spacebar or click the mouse (on a PC); and sometimes these keystrokes and clicks don't register, which is annoying.  Saving the game is a real palaver; at very least, a "quick save" option would help.
I'd suggest getting this game when it's on sale (as I did); the asking price seems a little steep to me otherwise.

I gotta admit that I've been skeptical at first about what is gonna happen with the Splinter Cell franchise after I've played SC:Conviction, however I was pleasantly surprised with SC:Blacklist.
SC:Blacklist still has its flaws but if I had to describe it in one sentence then I'd say: It took over most of the featuers we loved about SC:CT (the variety of gadgets for instance) while giving us more ways to customize our gear (the options are by no means limitless but it's a great addition regardless) as well as allowing us to play the game the way we want to (SC:Conviction style included) which adds a lot of replay value.
My main complaint about SC:Blacklist is that it's way too easy for my taste, mainly because of balance issues. Mark and Execute has made its return and while I can see why people like this feature, I personally don't but luckily you can disable it by choosing the highest difficulty available (big plus for me). Now the difficulty would have been fine if the game was better balanced (although it would still be too easy considering it's the highest difficulty one can choose from).
The crossbow in the singleplayer of this game is completely overpowered as it only costs you one gadget slot while easily being worth +12 gadget slots. My reasoning behind this? It offers a bolt for most of the gadgets you'd normally use while having them in much larger amounts, on top of that you don't even have to choose and get all of the different bolts for one gadget slot. Oh and yeah all of those bolts also have a much greater range than it's normal gadget counterparts (as those are thrown by hand).
To make it short: Don't use the crossbow if you want the game to be sort of challenging at least. I've cleared every level on highest difficulty with the best rating in ghost playstyle and it was really fun, even if I'd wish it to be harder. If I however had used the crossbow (as it's meant to be played) it would have been a piece of cake and I'd get bored before being halfway through the game.
There are a lot of missions one can play in coop (there will be a handful of missions that suits your playstyle at the very least) as well as a purely coop dedicated campaign. I've enjoyed all of them except of the ones where you had to defend yourself against waves of enemies, I thought those were kind of misplaced in a stealth game.
Spies vs. Mercs also has made its return but to be honest I've been fairly disappointed with it. It seemed rather dead to me while SC:CT multiplayer on the other hand was quite active even years after (I know cause I've played it like crazy back in the days). The multiplayer is a little hacker infested just as the multiplayer in Chaos Theory and Pandora Tomorrow was which is unfortunate, but the thing that bugs me about it the most is that spies are able to kill mercs now. By that I don't mean just grab them from behind as it used to be, but literally just shoot them with your firearms and one-hit-kill them with a melee weapon, even if they are facing you during the process.
Overall I've enjoyed the game a lot and would recommend it to people who have enjoyed SC:Conviction as well as to fans of the older Splinter Cell games.

Through the use of a variety of weapons - ranging from assault rifles to sniper rifles to an electrifying bolts shooting crossbow -  you usually have to infiltrate a building, capture a target, or kill one. When playing on the hardest difficulty it really is a challenge to remain undected, as shooting your way through the game will become very, very difficult. Like a large variety of modable weapons, there is also a large numbers of gadgets to aid you, for example a recon drone, sleeping gas, or - if you're more of an assault style player - proximity mines and breaching charges. Next to the singleplayer campaign there are also some co-op missions (2 players max.). Some of these can be played singleplayer as well - making them more difficult, of course. I really enjoyed the game, and I recommend it, but be aware of one thing: the singleplayer campaign is short, so you will have finished the game in approximately 15 hours. The storyline is not extremely good, but still okay; the gameplay is great, and that's what I value most. There is also multiplayer, but, unfortunately, there are no people who play that anymore. Finally, the graphics are pretty good, and the game does not require a very strong pc to run it.

Old school RPG for the modern times.
You will feel right at home if you ever enjoyed games like Baldur's Gate, Planescape: Torment, Icewind Dale and the original Fallout. If you never played such games, here's what you need to know:
As such, it could be overwhelming to those new to the genre, however the developers have managed to make it accessible to everyone with a wide selection of difficulty options that range from "almost godmode" to "dark souls on cocaine". PROs
+ Amazing pre-rendered 2D backgrounds packed with details
+ Music fits perfectly with the high fantasy genre
+ Loads of details in the lore and narrative
+ Lots of hours of gameplay, especially with the expansion
+ Works great on older systems
CONs
- The lore is dumped on you quite abruptley and can cause confusion in the beginning (it gets clarified later on)
- Central plot could've been more interesting
- Minor inaccuracies in the in-game descriptions of items and spells
- Steep learning curve on account of the lackluster tutorials

Probably the best RPG experiences I've had to date. My first playthrough was on Hard difficulty, and I'm working on a PoTD playthrough.
Pros:
-character building is impactful, unique (the interaction between stats happens in a way I haven't seen before), and fair. There are a lot of viable ways to build your party. The key is balance and having ways to solve certain types of puzzles.
-Story is pretty good. and the choices your pc makes affect what happens in the world pretty significantly. I really enjoyed the ending :)
-Fights are (in my opinion) quite fun in a technical way. Some of the basic mobs have really "interesting" traits that force you to think a bit. It's hard to cheese unless you build your party specifically for hit and run strats. Additionally, the game does a good job of mixing the mob types and environments to present some surprising challenges. Particularly in the expansions.
-No experience for killing people, avoiding the common rpg pitfall of "complete the quest then kill everyone" with a gating mechanic.
-Lots of well written and interesting side quests
-Dev commentary is cool!
-Puzzles that you can actually solve without a wiki ::glares at divinity::
Cons:
-NPC attributes are locked in. This feels bad, since the NPCs are so much more interesting than custom characters.
-Last area feels like it's not fully fleshed out.
-DLC content throws off the scaling of the game. You can adjust to improve enemy strength, but either way a well built party will make the game trivial later on (besides bosses, which always require planning + attention). I felt that the balance of the game was spot on before doing WM.
-Lack of good attribute choices at the highest character levels. In a lot of cases you'll end up just taking stuff you ignored for better things at previous levels.
Definitely recommend for anyone who likes a mental challenge and doesn't mind a lot of reading.

Where to start with Pillars of Eternity.
Like most of us here on steam, we have that infamous library of shame, and for the longest time, this hidden gem was one of them. I can't even remember how I came to acquire this game in all honesty, but however I did, I am beyond grateful for the purchase/acquisition.
If you like RPG games with a rich story, true player choices that affect the game in subtle, but dramatic ways, than Pillars of Eternity is for you. It is a party based game where you can either use the companions the game provides, or spend some in game gold and hire your own adventurers, which are customized from the ground up if you purchase them after level 1. So the amount of player options is truly amazing for this style of game, and the story... I could write a ten page review as to why this is one of the best stories in a game like this. But I will let you experience it for yourself. No spoilers.. Yay!
It takes a bit of a different approach to the party based mechanics, where you are allowed to pause the game to issue commands to each person. Though this might break immersion a tinsy bit, since some of the combat is very faced pace and you might not have enough time to dictate your actions, you can find your healer or archer dead before you can even blink.  Or worse yet, have your strongest person be temporarily mind controlled against you! I can't attest to how many times that ability made me grumble and want to smash my keyboard.  There is also the wonderful thing of trial and error, there are some combat set ups that simply can't be done with some party builds, or at least ,not without being a massive pain in your♥♥♥♥♥♥ The game does not hurt you for this, and gives you ample opportunity to find just the right set up to get whatever your mission is done.
With that said, below is my summary for the game. Keep in mind this is my opinion, and you should take it with a grain of salt. After all, this type of game is not for everyone.
In short, if you love RPG games that have in depth story, sophisticated combat, and interesting side quests, this is a game for you! I will leave it at that however, and let you decide for yourself if this is a worthy game for your money.

Pillars of Eternity is a reminder of a different time and not only because it tries to recreate the atmosphere of the immortal classics, but because it treats the player the same way the games a decade ago did. It doesn’t straightly assume that the players are clueless (can be read as stupid) and doesn’t hold their hands in everything they do, instead it gives the players the opportunity to learn through trial and error and discover the game by themselves. Difficulty and logic are notions almost lost to this new generation of games and with some producers saying that their games are more difficult than they should be (when it is quite the opposite), the future doesn’t look so bright. Games like this one come to stand against the current trend and their success show that there is still hope.
Pillars of Eternity is not a flawless game and knowing Obsidian’s work, that was never going to happen, as the people working there have a huge history with bugs dating before the existence of this studio. The game makes an appeal to nostalgia for a time that is never coming back, but it stands on its own and shines like a diamond, a little rough on the edges, in a sea of carbon yet failing to be the masterpiece of this age.
This title also stands as proof that Kickstarter crowdfunding is not a way of just cashing on the hopes the fans, redeeming this concept from the latest mishaps.
If I can let my suppressed subjective side speak freely for a short passage during this review, I want to say that I enjoyed this game immensely, more than most of the games in the last couple of years. It was a heart breaking moment for me when I heard that Obsidian Entertainment was so close to bankruptcy and I’m glad that the fans of this genre and of this studio made their continued existence possible. By the time I write this review, Pillars of Eternity is a known success, it has an expansion in works (already announced during Kickstarter) and this can only make me happier.
Obsidian Entertainment (inXile and some other smaller studios), don’t ever leave us, because without you and your games, the PC gaming industry and the RPG genre will be much bleaker.
As an ending note I would like to say this: The Witcher 3, Shadowrun: Hong Kong and Torment: Tides of Numenera, come and challenge Pillars of Eternity if you can, because this RPG is high up there!

The game is quite different from what I expected when I was buying it. It's not that much about puzzles or real combat skills (I imagined something like dodging at the right time, using different attacks per enemy weaknesses, combo-ing, etc). No, it's more about great cooperation between players (voice chat is an absolute must), selecting correct skills from the skill tree for that particular level, and, unfortunately, also about grinding. The game is quite hard, don't expect a casual multiplayer co-op game. You'll need to repeat every level many times to at least finish it. And then, you'll need to repeat it many times more in order to fulfill the challenge or time criteria. If you don't do it, you'll be very much underpowered in the later levels and the difficulty will go from high to insane.
So, the principle of the game is not to enjoy many different levels. The number or levels is quite low (25). The principle of the game is to rinse and repeat until you finish them
. It's not what I expected and it's not what I enjoy, but tastes differ, I'm sure many people will like it. That's not why I'm giving it a thumbs down.
The thumbs down goes for technical execution. From technical level, this game is horrible. Network issues are extremely common - the game splits and people see different things on their screens, someone can't move at all, someone dies but gets stuck in the dying animation and glitches the level, unable to complete it, and the list goes on. But, that's not the worst thing. The worst thing is the
. It deserves a paragraph on its own.
The camera. The devs had an idea that you need to see all characters at the same time, all the time. So if you go into different directions, the camera zooms out to make sure you see all characters. Questionably a good idea, with the worst implementation ever. First, this camera mode is mandatory, you can't switch between "focused camera" (seeing just yourself in the center of the screen) and "overview camera" (seeing everyone). No, it's just the overview camera. So, if you go far apart (necessary in some levels), you're zoomed out immensely, and your characters (and enemies) are very small. Try to use your skills effectively then! You're also in a corner or near the edge of the screen, so you have no idea what's near you in certain directions. The camera constantly shifts (as others move around), which throws your aim out of balance (especially frustration when playing the archer character). And to top all of that, the devs even botched it so much, that very often the camera actually crops your character and you're behind the edge or the corner of the screen! So, you don't actually see yourself, or the enemies around you, and you're expected to fight them and survive. Please don't forget this game is extremely punishing for even the smallest errors. You'll cry, you'll shout, you'll tear things apart. That's how bad the camera is.
One final note, this game has to be played with a stable group of friends. No one might be missing any time. The reason is that every time you start a game, you'll only receive those gems, which have been completed by *all* members of the party. So if one of your friends was not available last time, you'll need to repeat all levels with him/her again, and complete all of it again. This was not the best design choice, and again, you have no option to configure this, you need to live with it. Consider it, if you don't have a stable group of friends to play and finish this game with.
So, to sum it up, the game mechanics are not necessarily bad, they can be even enjoyable. But the technical execution is definitely a reason to avoid this game. And that's 18 months after release, so there's no hope of having it improved, ever.

This is actually quite a decent game though flaws with the AI hamper it from reaching its full potential.  The biggest upsides are the number of options and how much you can customize the interiors of casinos to your wishes.  You can make your casino as lush or barren as you want, make it a blackjack/craps paradise or only focus on slots.  With the largest casino, you can do both, but not every customer will like or appreciate all the gambling options.  Craps creates noise (ever been near one in Vegas?) while high rollers won't care for your low-limit slots.
The negative/positive benefit system is actually quite rewarding and nice.  The trick is that negatives can be offset by positives, once you learn that, you won't be bothered by people complaining about smell or noise, just add fountains or something else that creates positive calm or beauty.  Those positive objects though, come at a price, including maintenance, electricity and water if appropriate, but realy once you learn how to play the game, money isn't much of an issue anymore, which is something that could be improved.
Learning not to build everything is another lesson that takes time.  Your property and casino can't be everything to everyone.  High rollers want luxury and high stakes games, while degenerate gamblers want drinks and your typical family want entertainment and lower stakes.  Unfortunately, the best way to make money is to cater to the high rollers, but then that might be realistic since I haven't seen a new casino in Vegas built for penny slot players either.
The flaws of the game are in the AI and will require micromanagement to solve.  Maintenance workers won't fix buildings or objects until they break, meaning that you will have to manually direct them to actually maintain buildings and objects before that happens.  The worst part though is with the janitors who will just stand around and have to be told to specifically go to an area in order to clean the trash.  This becomes tedious and no matter what, you'll have to live with some litter on your properties and inside that lush casino you built.
In all, this game is fun and addictive, but is too easy once you figure it all out.  Plus the AI issues make it annoying at times.  Still it's easily worth $5, you'll get many hours of fun playing and building your dream casino.

State of Decay starts off as a fun game. You're traveling with some companions, you're scavenging, getting things done. Then you run into your first village with said companions. Suddenly you need to use a resource system to hire those companions to travel with you. Cause, you know, them being an extra body to ensure survival costs them back at base, who were fine before we came along.
So you decide to use that resource and hire them. You're out adventuring along and you get into a hard fight. You're getting mauled and chewed one while they just stand there watching. When the character you're playing dies, they then decide to come and aid you.
My god is the path for AI companions in this game horrendous. This isn't a once in a while thing, it's an all the time thing.
I could overlook this if everything else was above average. Other survival games just do this better. My big issue is that they go for some measure of realism while at the same time spawning zombies right in front of you. I have been walking places and suddenly there's a zombie that pops up right in front of me. I also don't buy that suddenly more and more zombie hordes just automagically appear as I've already cleared the town, ya know? You can't go for survival, have an autosave only system, and try to be realistic. Maybe a little control over the saves would have better? Quick saves and save slots do not have to be a thing of the past.
I'm also annoyed by the system of a lot of quests with hidden timers for you to start them. One can't possibly do them all and there's a penalty for not doing them. In most cases you're better off not doing them unless you need something from it.
Really, there's nothing special about this game. A multiplayer version of what they have with minimal PVP interaction would be more fun. As the game stands, it's kind of a stinker.

Buried beneath the successes of Valve's blockbuster titles, Condition Zero is a hidden gem that boasts both singleplayer and multiplayer entertainment. The main reason you should consider this is for the Deleted Scenes section, which contains a variety of content not used by the base game. From a legitimate story mode (with rather cinematic and interesting moments) to fun new weapons (M60's and blowtorches, to name a few), it pretty much is worth the price of admission. The base game is decent as well, but it can be easily replicated by playing CS:S or Global Offensive with bots. Deleted Scenes features a story mode with, well, a story. 18 unconnected stories, sure, but the variety of locations ingame makes up for the lack of consistency.
Overall, it's a fun diversion when you're yearning for another story-based game from Valve. At a price of 5-10 dollars, you're basically getting two high-quality games for the price of one. I would recommend it to Counter-Strike and Half-Life fans alike.

This was the first in the series that eventually saw the release of two more episodes. By genre Drizzlepath is a short, atmospheric walking simulator that can easily be completed in a couple of hours. The idea of such games is immersion; the beautiful landscape and the folk music both help us achieve that. This is a namesake brand; subsequent episodes bear the same name but are slightly different.
If my memory still functions properly this was the first (and perhaps only) attempt to use the CryEngine for creating such a wonderful landscape by Tonguç Bodur. This has its price: there are frequent FPS drops as we go high up the hill along the beaten track until which reach our destination atop the mountain. Halfway on our journey the scenery changes and the sunlit green foliage is replaced by cold, dark mountains with snowy tops.
As mentioned above while the game looks stunningly beautiful there are performance issues here and there. Unfortunately, in terms of graphics options Drizzlepath only allows preset values to choose from. I could not figure out what the difference was between "medium" and "very high", though. Toning down the graphics did not result in any FPS gains nor did I notice any changes in the scenery.
Minimalistic, as it is common for such walking sims. Still, later games released by Mr Bodur put way more emphasis on the understanding aspect of it. Here, it is difficult to hear the narrator (who regularly speaks once a new checkpoint is reached) who clearly speaks with a heavy accent. In later games subtitles were included in the options menu (available in several languages).
I have grown fond of Bodur's walking sims but only the ones that were released later. Drizzlepath is rough around the edges. I recommend it as I appreciate the work invested into it but perhaps it is only worth a playthrough if you have a particularly powerful PC setup. Its sequels and other products such as Nephise or Bottle all seemed more streamlined.

When a game needs to tell me that it's "a cyberpunk adventure" on its splash screen, I already get very suspicious. Why the need to say it unless you're a wolf in sheep's clothing?
Indeed 2064 ROM is very far away from the gloomy, burly, rough on the edge image that you normally associate with cyberpunk. That would be totally fine as long as it offers a realistic anticipation SF insight. Unfortunately that's not the case as the writing is so childishly naive it's sickening.
2064 ROM happens in a future which is much more tolerant. Racism and homophobia have completely dissapeared and nobody even alludes to those. This a refreshing (albeit optimistic) perspective. The new hate is now cyborgphobia, as people with implants are being ostracized. Think deus ex.
That was a promising setting but it's not executed in a clever way. Despite attempting to be very liberal, the game reeks of conservative morals all over. Everybody is super very nice, good manners prevail, and there is not a single human character which cannot be trusted. Even the bad guys and the haters are just super very nice guys who are misguided.
This goes in complete contradiction with the "evil corporations plot to control the earth" background of the story and renders the plot unconvincing and ridiculous as a result.
There's even a free DLC about the joys of being nice to others during Christmas time.... nice Cyberpunk lore there...
Homosexuality is an important theme in 2064 ROM, with almost every single main character being gay. Being gay is an awesome thing - no contest. Unfortunately, like with most themes, the game just tries so hard to spread positive vibes that it becomes obvious, forceful and irritating. If you want a gay SciFi story Va11 Hall-A does it with more finesse.
2064 ROM is a very linear point and click. Each scene has a couple of screens on average and branching is limited.
The point and click sections are rather straightforward. No challenge too obscure, which is a plus. Certain items offer silly interraction choices on the side of the story which is a nice touch.
And then there are the minigames...
...urgh...
The minigames are just awful. No other word. Example: you're stuck in a 90s like 3d dungeon without a map and need to find the exit... fun it is not.
None of them are. The rules are obtuse and poorly explained. They add nothing to the game.
The final boss minigame is so frustrating and obscure that it had me give up and switch off for a day.
 
The music is excellent. Really keeps you in the game when the story falters. OST is worth listening to on its own; for sure the best side of 2064 ROM.
The 8-bit art style has been praised but personally I can't find a liking. The characters look like simplistic children cartoons. They lack age, expression, and a sense of life. The best looking character is a robot - basically a blue circle with a smiley face. This speaks volumes.
The backdrops are nothing special and the city looks a bit too neat/clean for the world the story tries to depict.
All in all I have to give the thumbs down, for the lackluster gameplay, and the naive writing which tries so hard to make me feel good that it achieves the opposite result.
If you are a less cynical person than me in search of some feelgood time, can overlook the poor minigames, and like the art style, you might still find it worth your time.

Probably the best RPG experiences I've had to date. My first playthrough was on Hard difficulty, and I'm working on a PoTD playthrough.
Pros:
-character building is impactful, unique (the interaction between stats happens in a way I haven't seen before), and fair. There are a lot of viable ways to build your party. The key is balance and having ways to solve certain types of puzzles.
-Story is pretty good. and the choices your pc makes affect what happens in the world pretty significantly. I really enjoyed the ending :)
-Fights are (in my opinion) quite fun in a technical way. Some of the basic mobs have really "interesting" traits that force you to think a bit. It's hard to cheese unless you build your party specifically for hit and run strats. Additionally, the game does a good job of mixing the mob types and environments to present some surprising challenges. Particularly in the expansions.
-No experience for killing people, avoiding the common rpg pitfall of "complete the quest then kill everyone" with a gating mechanic.
-Lots of well written and interesting side quests
-Dev commentary is cool!
-Puzzles that you can actually solve without a wiki ::glares at divinity::
Cons:
-NPC attributes are locked in. This feels bad, since the NPCs are so much more interesting than custom characters.
-Last area feels like it's not fully fleshed out.
-DLC content throws off the scaling of the game. You can adjust to improve enemy strength, but either way a well built party will make the game trivial later on (besides bosses, which always require planning + attention). I felt that the balance of the game was spot on before doing WM.
-Lack of good attribute choices at the highest character levels. In a lot of cases you'll end up just taking stuff you ignored for better things at previous levels.
Definitely recommend for anyone who likes a mental challenge and doesn't mind a lot of reading.

Where to start with Pillars of Eternity.
Like most of us here on steam, we have that infamous library of shame, and for the longest time, this hidden gem was one of them. I can't even remember how I came to acquire this game in all honesty, but however I did, I am beyond grateful for the purchase/acquisition.
If you like RPG games with a rich story, true player choices that affect the game in subtle, but dramatic ways, than Pillars of Eternity is for you. It is a party based game where you can either use the companions the game provides, or spend some in game gold and hire your own adventurers, which are customized from the ground up if you purchase them after level 1. So the amount of player options is truly amazing for this style of game, and the story... I could write a ten page review as to why this is one of the best stories in a game like this. But I will let you experience it for yourself. No spoilers.. Yay!
It takes a bit of a different approach to the party based mechanics, where you are allowed to pause the game to issue commands to each person. Though this might break immersion a tinsy bit, since some of the combat is very faced pace and you might not have enough time to dictate your actions, you can find your healer or archer dead before you can even blink.  Or worse yet, have your strongest person be temporarily mind controlled against you! I can't attest to how many times that ability made me grumble and want to smash my keyboard.  There is also the wonderful thing of trial and error, there are some combat set ups that simply can't be done with some party builds, or at least ,not without being a massive pain in your♥♥♥♥♥♥ The game does not hurt you for this, and gives you ample opportunity to find just the right set up to get whatever your mission is done.
With that said, below is my summary for the game. Keep in mind this is my opinion, and you should take it with a grain of salt. After all, this type of game is not for everyone.
In short, if you love RPG games that have in depth story, sophisticated combat, and interesting side quests, this is a game for you! I will leave it at that however, and let you decide for yourself if this is a worthy game for your money.

Pillars of Eternity is a reminder of a different time and not only because it tries to recreate the atmosphere of the immortal classics, but because it treats the player the same way the games a decade ago did. It doesn’t straightly assume that the players are clueless (can be read as stupid) and doesn’t hold their hands in everything they do, instead it gives the players the opportunity to learn through trial and error and discover the game by themselves. Difficulty and logic are notions almost lost to this new generation of games and with some producers saying that their games are more difficult than they should be (when it is quite the opposite), the future doesn’t look so bright. Games like this one come to stand against the current trend and their success show that there is still hope.
Pillars of Eternity is not a flawless game and knowing Obsidian’s work, that was never going to happen, as the people working there have a huge history with bugs dating before the existence of this studio. The game makes an appeal to nostalgia for a time that is never coming back, but it stands on its own and shines like a diamond, a little rough on the edges, in a sea of carbon yet failing to be the masterpiece of this age.
This title also stands as proof that Kickstarter crowdfunding is not a way of just cashing on the hopes the fans, redeeming this concept from the latest mishaps.
If I can let my suppressed subjective side speak freely for a short passage during this review, I want to say that I enjoyed this game immensely, more than most of the games in the last couple of years. It was a heart breaking moment for me when I heard that Obsidian Entertainment was so close to bankruptcy and I’m glad that the fans of this genre and of this studio made their continued existence possible. By the time I write this review, Pillars of Eternity is a known success, it has an expansion in works (already announced during Kickstarter) and this can only make me happier.
Obsidian Entertainment (inXile and some other smaller studios), don’t ever leave us, because without you and your games, the PC gaming industry and the RPG genre will be much bleaker.
As an ending note I would like to say this: The Witcher 3, Shadowrun: Hong Kong and Torment: Tides of Numenera, come and challenge Pillars of Eternity if you can, because this RPG is high up there!

There's a simple litmus test for Pillars of Eternity: did you like any of BioWare's RPGs up to and including Knights of the Old Republic? If the answer is yes, buy this game immediately. If the answer is no, buy one of those games first, fall in love, *then* come back and buy this one.
No, the game is not perfect. Combat can easily devolve into an opaque cluster of swords and sorcery. It's an Obsidian game, so there are bound to be bugs somewhere (althought I haven't found any 20+ hours in), but the story is compelling, the world is beautifully drawn and the writing is top-notch. It doesn't hold your hand, but it also doesn't have absurd expectations of the player, with lots of "there if you want it" lore content to provide context to the story. And, despite what I said earlier, the combat and character-building systems have been streamlined effectively; players have all the options laid out for them with a clear understanding of what everything will do, so they can make informed decisions and build combat strategies to suit their preferences. That's important, because combat can be hard. If you rush into a fight without knowing what you're doing, your whole party will be down in a matter of seconds. I had to lower the difficulty twice just to get past some of the game's more challenging fights, but clearing those challenges, even after lowering the difficulty, was a highly satisfying experience.
I only have two complaints, one of which stems from the combat system: enemies seem to have a longer line of sight than the party does, so a fight will frequently lure in additional hostiles as it progresses, which I don't think was intentional and led to balancing issues more than once. Also, there are no rogue-class companions in the base game, which makes lockpicking and trap detection a real chore until the later stages if the player isn't a rogue. They fixed rectified this with the first expansion, but players shouldn't have to pay extra to add a key utility character to the party.
Overall, though, it's a beautiful love letter to a bygone era of video games. It's noteworthyfor that reason alone, and a must-have for RPG fans because it stands on its own as a wonderful game.

This game has so many negative reviews and I've played enough hours now that I feel I should write my own review: a positive one.
Although the visuals are not as fancy and modern as other city-builders, I found this game was far more complex and detailed than Sim City Societies while having the same kind of fun aspect.
You have different screens to monitor things like income, reputation, which demographic of people a certain building or lot appeals to, the state of repairs of buildings and gambling machines. You can click on some staff buildings and see the employee's skills, speed, attention and charisma and how much their wage are, you can hire more employees and fire them. You can upgrade certain buildings so that they more attract the people you wish them to (e.g. you can add a bell boy to the hotel so that the VIPs are happier to stay there) . You can click on each individual visitors and see their line of thought, this will let you know of things like if your restrooms are too hard to find, if the place is dirty, if your guests would like to do some drinking while they are gambling etc. Clicking on the visitors also allows you to see what they prefer (gambling, activity, rest er whatever) and what demographic they belong to (family, tourist, high roller or else) and you can build your lot to target certain people specifically because you can't please every one (people who are looking to relax will not like a lot that has many loud buildings such as casinos and circus' that appeal to people looking for activities).
The game has the option of sandbox or campaign. You set the difficulty in the sandbox to be as you are comfortable with and it is useful for practicing in preparation for the campaign which gets pretty challenging. The campaign includes the tutorial which is a bit annoying to go through. Also, the game doesn't save automatically and you can't save before finishing each campaign chapter it seems, bit annoying. The second campaign is not a tutorial at all and has events that require actions that were not covered in the tutorial, a bit of digging and trying things out is required to win. The third campaign chapter is more challenging even and I haven't been able to win it but as I'm learning it's getting closer and closer to beating my competitor neighbour.
A few things I dislike about the game: there is no undo button, when you accidentally place a staircase a square away from connected to the upper-level floor, for example, your only options to correct the mistake is to sell the staircase for regain of a percentage of what it cost to place or to leave the staircase there. This makes it so you have to be very careful where you put down things and it's kind of hard to gauge where they'll go because there is no truly visible grid inside the casino.
Also this game seems to require a lot of management: Buildings will get in very poor state of repairs if you don't tell the mechanics to go visit them, slot machines will get nonfunctional because the cashier hasn't gone to empty them and this is on top of you having to monitor each building's reputation, income generation (which you can control by choosing within a range of fees charged and, on casino games, house advantage among other things).
Overall, I like the game. Quite a lot actually. It's definitely not a game everyone would like though but if you like city-builders and management-heavy games that have only okay graphics I would recommend this game.

Played with a full 4 players, and while it was fun at first, the puzzle elements quickly became too fiddly and the overall level of difficulty too great.
The main puzzle mechanic is that there is a companion character who is basically a glowing ball, which you move around only by calling it to where you are currently standing with a button press; in this way it will only move point to point in straight lines.  Moving the ball over various level objects actives them; you flip switches, move crates, and activate temporary buffs for your character this way.  However the problem is that you have to be quite precise with these movements; the ball is often quite small in relation to the screen and must move exactly over the thing you want to active.  This demands far too much precision in a game where you're often trying to focus on combat at the same time, and dealing with an isometric camera that is frequently zooming out to fit all characters on screen.  If the ball had a larger radius of activation, it would go a long way to making the game more entertaining than frustrating.
The level of precision required is the main source of the game's excessive difficulty.  The combat by itself is reasonable, but almost everything after the first set of levels requires managing the ball to solve puzzles while fighting at the same time and the game isn't rewarding enough to make investing the effort feel worth it.

Night in the Woods is a wonderful adventure game that kept me hooked from start to finish. At its core, the story is about a young woman returning home from college to her old hometown. She works hard to re-connect with her old friends, even as she struggles to understand how much their lives have continued and changed them in her absence. Ultimately they have to work together and be there for each other as a series of increasingly strange events in their town seem to haunt them at every turn.
This is a really solid and fun adventure game with unique expressive visuals and a really great soundtrack, but what really sets it above the crowd is the writing, the characters, and their development. All of the main characters (and many of the side characters) are endearing and have you invested in them almost immediately. The writing is phenomenal and does an excellent job of feeling real. Not like, semi-fake-sounding tryhard real like some similar games pull, but really, really solid real. Conversations just feel organic and development feels natural.
Overall, the game is excellent quality for storytelling and characters, it's a really good length (meatier than i expected, but did not overstay its welcome), and given that you can't see all of the side stories for each character on a single playthrough, it definitely warrants at least one replay. So yeah, great game, great characters, great content, gregg rulz. ok.

Drizzlepath is a casual, environmental, walking simulator. It's one of those games where gamers tend to get into a debate whether these games should even be considered a game in the first place. Personally, I don't mind them being labeled as such as long as there's some kind of interactivity within the game.
Unfortunately, Drizzlepath doesn't meet that one requirement.
The soundtrack isn't consistent in the game. Very disappointing, because it really is beautifully done and nice to listen to. Instead, it comes up at checkpoints--they've basically used the music to provide you with motivation to move forward in the game. Because when there's no music, you've got silence, and (almost) nobody likes that.
Along with the soundtrack of the checkpoints, there's also a female narrator. She has a unique and lovely voice, but due to her thick accent, it's difficult to understand everything she says. Another problem is the lack of subtitles that could've helped us to understand. And one last problem is not everything she says makes sense. It's more like a freestyle of speech that's overloaded with too many similes and metaphors.
The graphics are the best parts of the game, which they should be in a walking simulator. There are a lot of locations for some beautiful screenshots, and not everything looks reused over and over again.
What gameplay? You can walk, you can jump, you can crouch.
You. You and the disembodied female narrator and
. We don't know anything about ourselves, only that we're headed to the top of the Mountain of Fire. We don't know the female narrator. An ex of some kind? A significant other? A victim? Dunno.
I didn't have any technical issues with that game that deterred me from finishing. I know some people can get stuck at some places, which is why there are checkpoints. One of the minor turn-offs was the environmental rendering of rocks and the snowy path. They're...warped.
I hesitate to rate this as a thumbs-down, but even as I'm doing so, I think anyone who enjoys walking simulators should give this one a go. It's a beautiful game, it's just...lacking.

This is a really solid and fun adventure game with unique expressive visuals and a really great soundtrack, but what really sets it above the crowd is the writing, the characters, and their development. All of the main characters (and many of the side characters) are endearing and have you invested in them almost immediately. The writing is phenomenal and does an excellent job of feeling real. Not like, semi-fake-sounding tryhard real like some similar games pull, but really, really solid real. Conversations just feel organic and development feels natural.
Overall, the game is excellent quality for storytelling and characters, it's a really good length (meatier than i expected, but did not overstay its welcome), and given that you can't see all of the side stories for each character on a single playthrough, it definitely warrants at least one replay. So yeah, great game, great characters, great content, gregg rulz. ok.

A beautifully dark world with good RPG mechanics but marred by an unplayable combat system.
The game can't decide if it wants to be turn-based or real-time, and it fails miserably at both. If this game had been turn-based, it would have been an easy recommend. Unfortunately, given the current system, its almost impossible to tell what is  happening.
PROS:
-Wonderful animation
-Good voice acting
-Good character building (can hire new chars from the Inn to build as you please)
-Wide variety of abilities (not sure on how viable they all are)
CONS:
-REALLY bad combat. Major lack of UI information. A giant confused mess.
The game cannot decide if it wants to be real-time or turn-based. Combat is "real-time" but you constantly need to pause the game to issue orders (which have varying cast times). You then unpause the game to watch the action unfold. Unfortunately, this system requires you to pause incessantly. Combined with horrible UI and a major lack of information, it is extremely hard to tell when different spells/abilities cast by different party members end exactly (which results in you just rapidly pausing the game).
In short, combat gameplay consists of you CONSTANTLY pausing the game every 2 or so seconds, sometimes more often. You can set a number of "auto pause" settings (so the game automatically pauses when certain actions happen). The existence of these options, although helpful to gameplay, further go to show just how much you will be pausing.
Now combine this incessant pause mechanic with an awkward combat system and a UI that gives you very little information. You will watch your guys constantly attack against opponents, but good luck if you can tell just how much damage (if any) your various characters are doing on each attack.
In fact, good luck being able to tell what exactly any of your abilities are doing WHEN you actually use them (not the tooltip info, which is plentiful).
I really *REALLY* wanted to like this game, but the combat is AWFUL. I tried to force myself into it for 5 hours hoping it would improve but its one of the worst combat systems I have ever played.
It is a solid crpg with better combat than most RTwP systems as seen in the IE games, Kotor, etc.
