For people who follow my reviews, I want to start by saying that this is a re-review of the finished Starbound product as my previous review was for the Early Access game. Since the game has launched I felt it was worth a second look at the title.
Have you ever been to a theme park for the first time after wanting to go for almost as long as you can remember? That expectation before you arrive and that initial thrill as you walk through the entrance? But then, after spending a few hours at the park you realize that there is perhaps only half a dozen rides and the majority of the park is filled with shops and places to eat. Welcome... to Starbound Land.
Just like a theme park, Starbound has a handful of features which are initially amazing. That moment when you get your stardrive back online and start traveling the galaxy. The bosses which don't even fit completely on the screen and that first time when you stumble across a ruined castle or hi-tech alien laboratory and promptly clear the place of dangers before making it your own personal home. These are the moments that make Starbound great. Unfortunately, when it does these great things over and over and over, you start to wonder what else there is to do. This is where Starbound falls flat on its face just like those theme parks.
There is a ton of craftables... but you loot stuff so frequently which is better than anything you could craft that you generally don't bother crafting anything except for the stations needed to get better armor. Once you have the tier-6 armors you pretty much stop crafting entirely. But between the start and tier-6 armor there is plenty of materials you need to track down to get there. So if you like exploration, that is catered to nicely at first. There is also the massive menu of food to make... but you soon discover that the more complicated recipes are unnessersary since basic meals are perfectly fine since the advanced food buffs are very short duration anyway and the food requires a wide variety of materials to make. Causing them to be impractical.
Next you have the 'pets' and crew members. Who are so inept that you find that they barely qualify as useful for anything except cannon fodder. So exploring the galaxy for crew and monsters becomes pointless since they don't add anything significant and worse still is that the quality of the NPCs and pets you can get will improve depending upon how advanced the world they came from is. Much like how you discard low level gear, you have little choice but to discard crew and pets too.
Starbound actually runs into this issue of making its own content redundent far more than it needs to. It happens with almost all of its content. For example, planets are tiered much like the armor. A planet orbiting a gentle (low level) star has Copper, Iron, Silver and Gold. But a magma ocean planet (end game) planet has those ores but also gives you all the other materials. Furthermore asteroid fields have so much Copper, Silver and Gold that it isn't even funny. So despite being open world, you end up with no reason to explore worlds once you update your environment suit to allow exploration of end game worlds. Everything you find on those worlds from drops, crew, monsters and materials is better than everywhere else. So despite being a game about an endless universe of discovery. the poor design choices made here actually kill the point of playing. Why bother making all this proceedual stuff when the content is disposed of faster than a baby's filthy nappy? I know that many RPGs do this progression method, but in a game that the developers have worked hard to make appealing for exploration it just doesn't work since you've now coaxed the player into a linear path through the game and little point to turn around.
So, can I recommend Starbound? Is it entertaining. Is it value for money? Well, yes. For a time it is entertaining and you'll get many hours of enjoyment from it before you hit that 'wall' where you notice that you've been on all the rides at least 5 times already. As for replay value, that rests not with the game itself but with the modding community. Much like how Minecraft was made successful not on its own merits but on the effort put forth by the community - so the same applies to Starbound. But, with the core design flaw created by the way content becomes redundent its going to take a really incredible mod to overhaul the game to make it worth exploring once you reach the end of the armor tree. Looking for legendary loot is not enticement to keep playing more after tier-6 when you're already overpowering mobs without it but that is yet another issue with the games design that I won't get into.

I decided to try this out after seeing the ratings on it and I have not been disappointed.
I'm a fan of single player fantasy RPG games but tend to favour the 3rd person style games over the isometric ones, that said, this has been a brilliant game so far.
I'm enjoying the story and the play mechanics, the classes and their abilities have a familiarity that reminds me of a D&D based game and the story telling has that intriguing quality that I've come to expect from Obsidian Entertainment (who made Dungeon Siege 3, Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic 2 & the Neverwinter Nights 2 series which are some of my favourites)
I quite enjoy that classes aren't restricted in their weapon use, allowing my wizard to run around with a wand & grimoire and switch over to a flail & sword when someone gets close. The skill system is nice and easy to use as well, again this isn't class restrictive allowing any character with the right points to sneak around, disable traps or gain bonuses from camping.
Inventory management is a pleasure, there isn't much of a restriction as there is a Stash option for the party that is accessible from the inventory itself, and all items take up a single block so no messing around with trying to fit items into a confined space: loot hoarder approved!
The game features real-time combat with a pause function, allowing for micromanagement of your party and their actions. There's an AI option as well but I haven't tested this out as I prefer to manually direct my party members.

Hello fellow gamers!
I'm a gamer myself, since 1997. I've started playing Knights Online back in 2004 and I've been through a lot of servers.

Last, but not least, the staff of the game. They are laughable, at best. They won't ever be there if you have any problems, unless the problem you are facing is a problem on a payment method, then all of a sudden they will be there for you.

Overall I enjoyed my time playing the game. However as a Splinter Cell fan since day one I felt let down. The voice actor change probably left the biggest dissapointment for me, especially knowing Michael Ironside supposedly coached the new actor. Somehow every game as Sam gets older, he gets buffer and more agile. I wished at this point they did a batman beyond thing and just had a new splinter cell be the main character, like briggs. As with conviction, parts of the story are impossible to do 100% stealth although I tried very much on perfectionist to hand to hand kill only without getting detected. The story itself isn't bad but doesn't leave a sense of urgency for what's actually happening. Most of that is done through calling your daughter which feels weird considering both actors sound to be the same age. They nicely took from Conviction though and improved upon its faults gameplay wise and took on a more Double Agent (next gen version) style of knowing if you are hidden or not, basically no more color desaturation.
Co-op itself was very fun for the most part. The briggs missions started and ended fun but some missions seemed near impossible to stealth or literally were impossible to stealth, especially with the highly annoying re-addition of dogs since I believe Pandorra Tomorrow. The briggs missions also were the only story based co-op missions. The 3 others were very much like deniable ops from conviction. Charlie missions are wave based and after doing one for the full 20 rounds with loud weapons, my friend and me decided we did not enjoy them whatsoever. Kobin missions did give the more classic splinter cell vibe and can be compared to hunter missions in conviction. Grimm missions were also quite fun as they were similar to infiltration from conviction with a mix of added objectives.
Multiplayer is back in its true form. I've not actaully touched on mutiplayer in the PC version too much but I did play it considerably on console. At this point if you are just getting into the game, you may want to play with only friends or else you will find yourself unable to do much as the learning curve has always been high with SvM. I found that the new SvM blacklist mode to be the best of them all giving you 4 mercs vs 4 spys and having to try and hack 3 terminals. Unlike Double Agent, you dont actually need to maintain presence at the terminal, just in the region. There is a throwback mode to Chaos Theory/Pandora Tomorrow which is 2v2 Classic. I didn't actually enjoy it too much considering how much I played Chaos Thoery SvM. There's nothing wrong with it, it plays quite well but I found myself liking the 4v4 mode with new stuff more. There are also other modes which combine spies and mercs on one team however they just don't feel that much fun to play even though I liked the old gen SvS in Double Agent. The addition of loadouts added a much new feel to SvM. I personally liked it because it gives you more ways to counter the opposition. If you dont like that though, the Classic mode will be perfect as it limits loadouts.
Overall I do recommend this game because it is fun and well put together, but at this point its only worth getting if you desperately want the story or have a friend to play co-op with. If you've never played a Splinter Cell game before, then I think it is a great game to get into as there isn't really any expectations. Getting it for multiplayer is questionable as the community is small and learning curve high with most people playing max level now.

I am giving this game a thumbs up not because it is a good game, which I've yet to determine, but because of the hidden DLC that comes with it.  Oh, I'm not talking about UPlay, no no, I'm talking about the hidden 'Gypsy Curse' DLC it comes packaged with.  This special DLC really brought the excitement to life.
Think I'm making things up?  Ha, I wish.
After running the gauntlet that was UPlay to get it installed and play it, I thought my trials were done, that I'd survived the worst the game had to offer.  What more could it do? I sat back and enjoyed being a badass black ops♥♥♥♥♥kicker.  Life was good.
Then my computer started making a weird noise.  Well, these things happen, everything seemed to be working fine.  I loaded into a mission, a pretty tough mission, and I put in the work to succeed.  Just as I'm about to exfiltrate and claim my reward, the Curse strikes.  My computer powers off suddenly.  What?  What could have happened?  Just a power surge, just gotta turn it back on and pick up where I left off.
No, wait, the power supply completely blew.  Burnt right out.  Dead.  Kaput.  Executed, if you will.  For the first time in my computer owning life, a part of my computer actually kicked the bucket.
Now I have to go out in the middle of the Chinese New Year and try to find a PSU.  Yeah, right.  Well, somehow I manage it, so the next day I'm out a hundred bucks and a day of holiday, but I can get back to playing. Alright!
I load back into that mission, and ghost it like a boss.  I turn to head for exfiltration, and the game closes suddenly.  Is it the power supply again?  No, it's the Curse.  This time in the form of a forced Windows update.  No warning, no option to delay, just bam, restart.
What could have been so important?  A security update for a version of Word I don't even use.
Do I dare boot the game a third time?  Do I risk suffering the curse?  Can I afford to?  What might happen next?
...literally as I was writing that last sentence my virus checker asked if it could restart the computer.
Play the game if you must, dear reader, but beware always...the Gypsy Curse! Also UPlay, which really sucks and added several hours to the set up of the game.

When I was little, I used to play game called Pocket Tanks with my friends a lot, this game brought back those nice memories.
The game has incredible amount of features. There are hundreds of weapons, different tank parts, upgrades, maps. And a huge number of things that gets unlocked as you continue to play and level up.
There are a lot of different game modes, from classic deathmatch to soccer game, point game, accuracy based mode. You can modify those modes to your liking very easily. You can set wind speed, whether you shoot in turns or at the same time, amount of HP, number of turns, and much much more.
However it also has quite a bit of flaws:
- You start with small number of available weapons and unlock them as you level up. In my opinion the weapons get unlocked very slowly and sometimes you might find that you are encouraged to grind to unlock them. Some weapons have some ridiculous requirements to unlock such as: "GOD RAYS - Defeat the game developer".
And so the only thing that I find missing from this game is some kind of mode where there would be random weapons and each player would choose what weapons to pick in turns and then start with those weapons, akin to Pocket Tanks. This would make game so much more fun. Or some random mode with all the weapons in the game available.
I also noticed a bug that when you start a server and want to invite a friend after clicking on "friends only" random people can still join the game for some time and I have to kick them for a minute or so before my friend can join. I hope this get fixed to respond quicker to the privacy change.
The fact that you have tank upgrades also make it so that lvl 99 is almost unbeatable to lvl 1, which shouldn't be. I think that the game should only have weapons and maps unlock, without those upgrades as it makes it quite a bit unfair and discouraging to the new players as they see how much they have to grind to get to the same lvl.
Overall thought I'm having so much fun playing with my friends and I think that this game is wonderful and the graphics and weapon effects are very beautiful and unique. I will keep playing this game for a long time, though it could be a bit less of a grind.
Overall: Very good game, with lots of incredibly fun weapons.
Score: 9/10

Gdy byłem młodszy grałem dużo z kumplami w Pocket Tanks, ta gra przywołała te dobre wspomnienia.
Gra ma niesamowitą ilośc zawartości. Setki broni, mapy, części do czołgów i wiele innych. Większość rzeczy odblokowywuje się wraz z wbijaniem coraz wyższych poziomów.
Gra posiada bardzo dużo trybów gry. Od klasycznego deathmatchu, do gry w piłkę, na punkty i wiele innych. Można modyfikować te tryby wedle uznania. Ustalać siłę wiatru, ilość tur, HP, czy strzelacie w jednej turze czy osobno. Bardzo prosto można więc stworzyć taką grę, jaką chcecie.
Jednak gra posiada trochę wad:
- Zaczynacie z bardzo małą ilością dostępnych broni a resztę zdobywacie poprzez lvlowanie, niestety im wyższy lvl tym trwa to dłużej i staje się bardzo żmudne i gra wydaje się zachęcać do gridnowania. Niektóre bronie mają tak trudne wymagania do odblokowania, że aż śmieszne. Np. "GOD RAYS - pokonaj developera gry". Powoduje to, iż możecie zapomnieć o posiadaniu wszystkich broni, no chyba że zamierzacie spędzić setki godzin w grze.
Biorąc to pod uwagę jedyna rzecz której brakuje mi w tej grze to jakiś tryb gry w którym gracze dostawali by bronie z całej gry randomowo i mogli wybierać na zmianę z którą chcą zacząć, coś jak w Pocket Tanks. Dzięki temu gra byłaby duzo fajniejsza. Albo przynajmniej tryb w którym dostępne są wszystkie bronie i można je przetestować.
Zauważyłem także błąd przy tworzeniu nowej gry. W momencie kliknięcia "tylko znajomi" przypadkowi ludzie dalej mogą wejśc do gry, przez co trzeba ich wyrzucać przez jakiś czas dopóki znajomemu nie uda się dołączyć. Mam nadzieję, żę zostanie to naprawione.
Fakt, że czołg można ulepszać powoduje też, że lvl 99 jest nie do pokonania dla lvl 1 w deathmatchu , a tak nie powinno być. I enjoyed it.
I didn't fall in love with the game and it did not blow my mind with some over-achieving thematic quality. Yet what should we really expect from a bit-game short story? With a play time of about 8-10 hours and a semi-endearing robot companion, your goal is to solve the murder of your newfound friend's creator. The game cycles through dozens of predictable tropes and has relatively lackluster character development. The story itself is somewhat predictable, but still fun enough to maintain minor interest. I would not recommend this game to people who are trying to redifine their understanding of video games and I would not even go so far as to say it is even a great story game. It reminds me of a television show that you watch to have the proverbial watercooler discussion. A conversation for which the duration would most likely not exceed 5 minutes; which is appropriate for the watercooler because a break for water doesnt even require that kind of time.
So whats good about this game? Well, ultimately the main character, Turing, is...adorable. "They" are awkward, aloof, and innocent. You are inexplicably inclined to help them. Of course, you have no reason to, and there is no real motivation to want to leave your in game apartment; aside from the desire to see what this little blue robot will do around the NPCs in the world of the future. At the end of the day though, you are the one playing video games late into the night. So... who are you to judge when it comes to the topic of motivation? (Not criticizing, as I am also playing games late into the night.) Other than that however, the well is pretty dry here. It is much easier to critique the faults of this game but that is really not worth the time and also not really fair to the developers. As with many of these indie story games, it is possible that the writer's excessive use of tropes was nothing more than a sarcasm to the very notion of the use of tropes. A subtle irony maybe. It could even be said, that mentioning them is nothing more than me playing into the trap they have set to castrate reviews such as this. I highly doubt, however, that they are reading the pitiful scrabblings of a lowly evening gamer such as myself. Which furthers my belief that sarcasm was the ultimate goal. And in that notion, I find something simple but elegant about this game. It plays on my preconcieved notions about what a story game should be. I found myself constantly questioning "should I read into that line?", "should I predict where this chapter is heading?" Ultimately it doesn't matter. I finished the game and I moderately enjoyed myself. Maybe that is good enough. I think with this game its best not to over analyze it, just play it a bit and have some bagel bites while doing so. Enough said.

Shadow of Mordor is a very enjoyable game. The gameplay begins as some sort of violent and slightly harder Assassin's Creed, then moves on to some crazy combat due to the various Wraith perks. There are 2 zones and 20 main missions, so the story is a little short, but it's very interesting if you are into Tolkien's Lore. The ending is a little weird though.
The game runs well, the characters are interesting, and most of all, the game KEEPS GETTING MORE INTERESTING as you unlock new abilities, even after 5 hours.
There are Sword, Dagger and Bow challenges everywhere, as well as other types of missions. So if you are a completionnist, the game is potentially quite long. However, these types of missions, while the vary, are always based on the same basic principles, and can get repetitive.
The main cons are :
- The Nemesis system is an interesting concept, but you quickly realize that it's a bit pointless to kill off the weaker generals
- The game is a little too easy, even though you CAN die if you never retreat
- The top bosses are really disappointing. The are hyped to death, and end up being weaker than most Warchiefs
8/10, very nice surprise. If you see this game under 10€, buy it right away.

A soft yes.
Pillars of Eternity marks a return to what might best be described as roleplaying museum. You walk slowly from interactive painting to interactive painting, running a D&D system and reading a long description in place of the action.
Let's begin with the paintings - they are a bit drab. The visual style is not distinct, trending European early Renaissance bland with a few flashes of color. Given the setting, perhaps an Indian-influenced architecture would have helped make the artistic vision more exotic.
The D&D system was the highlight. Lots of choice, lots of creativity, and plenty of options to change your mind. Because you can only see the same things on replaying, and this is a very long game, it's a welcome option to reroll within the same save.
Then there's the writing. The vision trades heavyhandedly on the theme of the early-Renaissance setting in making a trite series of theological points. This lends itself in game to a series of sub-plots, including your own, built mostly on broken visions and failed dreams. It would be oppressive to play if not for the fact that games struggle to convey a narrative. There's so much clicking on monsters between plot points that no one's story, including your own, grants much meaning. The lack of cut-scenes, the jangling mish-mash of spoken and written dialogue, the somewhat dull setting; all of it creates an experience that's not particularly immersive but neither is it wholly without merit.
So a soft yes. If you like this sort of game, you'll like this game. If you were hoping for Planescape: Torment, as I was, you'll be mildly disappointed. But you'll still have fun.

I usually don't like single-player games that make me micro-manage multiple characters; it tends to make me focus on inventory and number-crunching more-so than the story and the adventure.  With that said, I bought Pillars of Eternity because I was looking for an adventure akin to table-top RPGs and also out of support for the cRPG genre.
Unlike its predecessors, Pillars of Eternity shaves off a lot of the busywork of babbysitting companions. Stuff like streamlined inventory management, leveling and other features such as the combat AI, the game was a lot easier to get into.
Speaking of "easy", I think my main gripe with the game was in its difficulty.  While not a complete stranger to strategy games and RPGs, I found myself struggling in "easy" mode yet, at the same time, was not getting a satisfactory victory in "story time" mode (as things died WAY too easily for my tastes).  After completing the game after only 9 hours, I suspect that my issues were due to me not exploring enough and/or not participating in enough side-quests; leaving my group under-leveled for the content.  Still, I find it odd that, even in "easy" mode, some group of monsters were able to completely crowd-control and annihilate my entire party; regardless of how often I'd reload the game and tried different tactics.  So, for anyone who's looking into getting this game, I'd watch out for that.
I'm definitely going back in with a new character, exploring more content (including the game's DLCs) and hopefully try to play through it in "normal" difficulty.
- The various vistas are great to look at; lots of details without confusing the eyes and without taxing the computer.
- The (usually rare) voice-overs performances are serviceable and soothing.
- The music is enchanting (I especially enjoy the light-hearted tone from the combat track ~ which is rare these days).
- The story, while confusing and slow, is still pretty good.
I was pleasantly surprised.  An RPG that encouraged me to role-play; it's been a long time since.

EDIT: I have since played Pillars to completion multiple times, and can now offer a more satisfactory review. STILL, I'll leave the old review down here for future reference.
>>OLD REVIEW<<<
This is a great game that combines many of the aspects we enjoyed from old-school CRPGs like Baldur's Gate and Neverwinter Nights...
...except, I found myself that I am too old and lacking in time to enjoy games such as these anymore. And it is a crying shame, because from what I've played, Pillars of Eternity gets the formula just right, as expected of Obsidian. As such I must warn you that I barely even scratched this game's surface, but from what I've played, it's stupendous.
>>NEW, UPDATED REVIEW<<
It's great.
I just didn't enjoy it.
It's the mechanics, mostly. They just didn't click with me. It's to be expected. I unfortunately completely missed the Infinity Engine games when I was young, and so didn't develop an early taste for the classics, such as Baldur's Gate, Planescape Torment and all that.
So - yes. The moment-to-moment gameplay felt like a chore to me. This is a COMPLETELY SUBJECTIVE NOTION and shouldn't be taken as an absolute. That's the reason I'm still giving this a positive review, and with a wide berth at that.
Yet - I -had- to play it. I loved Tyranny to bits. It felt like Pillars-lite to me, and the mechanics clicked nicely with my preferences, even though they're not THAT different from it's spiritual predecessor. However, I realized that that game would probably never get a sequel, right around the time that Pillars 2's crowdfunding campaign came out. When I learned that it would import saves and decisions directly from the first game, I just had to buckle up and play it - four times, to be precise.
It is with no shame at all that I'll say that I cheated all the way through. That's why I have no achievements, even though I spent quite a bit of time playing it. I had no love for the mechanics - I was just there because I'm a huge sucker for Obsidian's storytelling. In that, I can confidently say that Pillars did not disappoint. Not even a bit.
My main, not-so-subjective criticism: Pillars isn't your babies' first medieval fantasy. There's a lot of very interesting lore all over the place. The problem being, that the game's first act is painfully, grindingly slow, and takes a while to hook you in. That's what turned me off in the beginning. Once I got past that, I was in the clear, and every morsel of lore felt like a reward.
That's it, really. I won't spoil anything, so I'll just go ahead and say that the journey was long and at times painful - but definetly worth it if you're a fan of Obsidian's stuff. The story is compelling, the characters are universally fun and well-crafted (Well. Some more than others - looking at you, two characters written by Chris Avellone that are really hard to NOT keep in my party), and if you're a fan of the Infinity Engine cRPG formula, you're in for a blast.

I feel the urge to write this review, because there are so many positive ones and they are so much in contrast with what I felt...
I guess, my major problem is that at the time of Baldur's Gate and other masterpieces of the genre I was no more than a toddler, so this game brings no nostalgia to me at all. And the second mistake I made was playing this after playing Witcher 3, which is just what I think a perfect game should look like...
Anyway, I want this review to be helpful, so I aim at organizing it.
What is definitely good about the game? Well, the style is really cool. Every building, piece of land etc. is thought trough and designed perfectly. And it totally feels like Neverwinter or Planescape Torment, brings back 1997, so to say. And if one listened to the devs comments on the matter of design, the amount of work they did becomes even more impressive. There are also no texture glitches or anything like this, which a common flaw for rpgs.
Gameplay is nice too. I like that it's not turn-based, like in Divinity Original Sin, because it makes the game much more dynamic. And the way D&D system which is not really D&D is applied is well-balanced too. Battles are actually fun, even though the mobs are kinda boring. Though the classes are a bit unbalanced, say, if playing on easy level, the chanter can’t even finish chanting and cast any spells before the battle ends…
So basically for those of you who play games for battles, mashing and enjoying the scenery, that’s a very good game.
However I play mostly for the plot, for the involvement with the world and the characters and that’s where Pillars of Eternity fail tremendously. The story is slow and consists of so much text it gets boring. The authors failed to make the problems of the world feasible, interesting and touching altogether. There are children dying in this world, and I wasn’t able to feel anything about it at all.
The characters are all so flat it makes one sad. I felt more involved with the fates of my companions in Diablo 3, which says a lot. And the fact that they rarely play a role in dialogs or express their opinions only makes it worse. Plus, as was already mentioned by others, the companions have no alignment which is just ridiculous for the genre. I want my companions to be alive, have opinions and talk to my character, but in Pillars “talking” companions are no different from mercenaries for hire.
The same flatness can be attributed to the world too. There is no feedback from the world. And I don’t only mean that NPCs have no idea that you slayed Roderick or did any other quest-related things, that’s common for games like this. For me the major problem is that the world does not react to my actions and neither do companions. You decided to play a godlike, who are supposed to be feared? Whatever, no one notices, in fact you can meet your kind all over the place. You slaughtered and innocent family? Ok. That’s just not how it should work.
Then there comes the problem of voiceovers, or, to be more precise, the almost total lack of those. I mean, we’re in the 21st century here, even the cheapest games have voiceovers at least for main quests. And in Pillars there is the void where some talking should happen. I don’t mind reading, but if I wanted to read that much, I would have read a book rather that play.
I almost forgot the Kickstarter element. I understand that people, who backed the game, want something in return. But that doesn’t mean that the whole map should be swarming with sponsored NPCs with strange stories, who just annoy the player and make it harder to find necessary characters. I played other backed games, and none of them screamed “I am backed on kickstarter people” this much…
Last but not least, the localization. I don’t know who localized this game for Russia, but that’s possibly the worst game translation I’ve ever seen.  Even overlooking grammar mistakes, the writing is horrible, translation sometimes omits the whole sentences and in very many cases doesn’t make any sense. I am fortunate to speak English, so I just switched, but that’s really an act of disrespect towards Russian-speaking players.
Summing up, this is a good game to play for fighting, mechanics and design, but not so much if you’re interested in the plot.

Pillars of Eternity is a great game, that is, until you get to the beginning of Act 3 when all of the drama of the first 2 acts completely fizzles. It's a bit of a let down. The quests during Act 3 become tedious and uninteresting, and even unnecessary. If you've done all the other quests in Acts 1 & 2, you can beat the game by doing just the main quests in Act 3 (you should be around level 12+).
Many reviews say that this game harkens back to the old Baldur's Gate games, which in my opinion were amazing. Unfortunately, it seems like those reviews were written by people who only played the game to get a "feel" for it, and not those who played it all the way through.
The gameplay is pretty good though, and while I like receiving xp from quests, it seems like the game punishes those players who just want kill things. A mix of xp from monsters and quests would be better in my opinion.
Another weird thing is the voiceovers. While the actors do a good job of conveying the text, it's strange and a bit jarring when a block of text comes up that explains how a character feels, and you're trying to read that as the VA speaks what comes after the text. For example, you might see "Aloth slumps in a chair while quickly scanning the room." He says, "I don't understand." but when the block of text appears, the voiceover is already saying, "I don't understand" while you're reading "Aloth slumps..." It's very strange and removes the intended effect of the story.
Overall, POE is just ok. I can't recommend it because of the 3rd Act, but if you're looking for a game to tide you over for the summer that tries to mimic the old Infinity-based cRPGs, then this game might be for you.

I played this game from 2004 till 2011 on its own platform, and decided to stop playing for the amount of cheaters in game. Then when they announced their debut on Steam in January 2016, I wanted to give it a shot again. I am not gonna include anything from my past experiences on this game, and this review will be solely based on my experiences playing Knight Online on Steam.
So if you don't know anything about this game, it's an mmorpg game with heavy grinding required to level up and get strong items in game. Having said that, let me start by going with pros and cons on this game;
- Its PvP is probably the best, I've played a lot of mmorpg games including the World of Warcraft, and Knight Online's PvP system is by far the best one.
- Knight Online's upgrade system is pretty good and addicting, especially after a certain point, items start glowing and at +9, they glow like a light bulb and people always try to upgrade +9 items, and it's fun trying to upgrade items, of course if you fail, it destroys your items.
- Securitywise it is much better on Steam. Although it is usually too late, GMs usually ban cheaters.
- When GMs ban the cheaters, it is usually too late, because they sell the illegal items and in game coins to websites before the GMs ban them, so it doesn't really matter after they get their profit. They can open up a new character and quickly level it up by using the 3rd party software again. This affects the overall economy of the game, and cheaters create monopolies on items that are really hard to get.
- Selling in game items and coins for real money is illegal per their policy, however one of the websites of the NTTGame, publisher of Steam Knight Online, have a lists of resellers of their game codes which they clearly advertise, however most of these websites are selling gold bars(in game coins), and in game items as well, which are hard to get if you play legally. This is completely absurd because these websites are doing the exact opposite thing of what Knight Online's policy suggests, yet they are still being advertised on their websites. If this is a mistake, and they are not aware of this, it needs to be fixed ASAP.
- Your computer needs to be on for you to buy and sell items, they do not have an auction house system where you can set your items for sale and then you can turn off your computer. This is not the case in Knight Online, as my hrs on record suggests. And as I mentioned cheaters are getting banned but it affects the overall game economy, which ruins the lives of legal players. For example, while a legal player merchants day and night to make some in game profit, personally as my hrs on record proves, someone can go onto a website and buy a gold bar(100m in game coins) in like 5 minutes. This is not fair, and is the reason I uninstalled this game from my computer after playing for 1,385.2 hrs.
- Forums are a mess in my opinion, especially the Turkish side of the forum. Especially the Turkish GMs are in power trips in my opinion, and forums(mostly the Turkish side) are ran like a dictatorship.
- This is probably the worst game management I've ever seen. The population dropped from 20k+ players to less than 10k players in 6 months, but they are still doing the same mistakes.

Got this game when it was on sale a little while back. Had a lot of fun playing it and meeting the different types of people that roam around in the world of Miscreated.
(Keep in mind that this is my first review ever)
First off. It looks amazing. The world that these guys build is absolutely beautifull. You can really feel that they put a lot of time in perfecting the atmosphere. Because of this the world is not crazy big and when you die you tend to always spawn around the same areas. This of course lets you figure out the map quite fast, but can also make you feel like you've seen everything that the world of Miscreated has to offer you in the first couple of hours. Don't let that spoil your fun though because I recommend checking the internet or talking to Miscreated players about finding some interesting hidden spots on the map.
Sadly this is only a short term solution for the boredom that COULD come and haunt you down the line. Sometimes this game can make you feel like the only thing you're doing is running around and looking for loot. Once you're satisfied with that loot your stuck at the beginning.
Building
Well let's start a base then wouldnt you say? Wrong! Base building is not something that this game does very well. For me this is not a big problem because I never felt it necessary until.. you're at that point that you've picked up so much loot that you have no choice but to store it somewhere. This is normally where you're storage crates come in. Sadly this is one of the, in my opinion, more annoying bugs. Crates despawn. Well Dave, what about picking up a tent? Despawns!
I could talk forever about these little but very annoying bugs. But you gotta keep in mind that we are still talking about an Early Acces game. And sure it was first released in 2014, the year that Zack Brown raised $55,000 on Kickstarter to make potato salad. But it is still an Early Acces game. And there are still updates coming out every few months.
PVP/PVE
I'm not sure what to say about the PVP aspect of this game. The lack of ammo on some servers can really put a strain on having a fun gunfight. Servers invested with clans are also an uprising problem (in my opinion) and really makes finding good loot difficult.
Recently they've added more Muntant (PVE) to the game. This also puts a strain on your gaming experience, coming back at not being able to find, carry or store loot. The best thing you can do when you're being chased down by 4 mutants, of which you have no idea how they've found you, is to run into a building or jump over stuff until they get stuck somewhere. Overall I'm not a huge fan of PVE in this game. Running into a Mutant can make you're frames drop and really kill the immersion.
Survival
There's not much to say about the survival aspect of this game. Surviving in Miscreated consists of finding food and water. That is it! (atm)
So.. can I recommend this game to other people? I think I can. But only to the people that have patient. The people that understand that this game, although beautifull, still needs work.
For the price that it is at right now, I highly recommend picking it up. It is definitely worth a try compared to other similar games out there.

TL;DR - Miscreated is doing a lot better than it used to. I would really love to see further improvements, some of which I outlined, and look forward to playing it more in the future and keeping an eye on it. The performance is acceptable provided you're on relatively recent hardware, and it's a damn sight better than DayZ Standalone.
I've owned and watched Miscreated since it's unveiling in 2014. My play since then has been sporadic, giving it roughly four to six months before I jump in to see how the performance and content looks.
With what I've seen as of this Febuary (2017), I'm pleased that I bought it when I did. While it doesn't look quite as smooth as the trailers would have you think, the team at Entrada are making solid progress towards a finished product.
The map is growing. I've visited all of the towns and the big city, the majority of the tiny neighborhoods, and peeked my nose into most ever house I've seen. The world is mostly well crafted, though there are some things that could use polish here and there (See untextured bus interiors, odd light reflections, etc).
The vehicle system is satisfying, and overall more functional than any other survival game that I've taken part in - It doesn't feel tacked on; it's much more of an achievement than it is in H1Z1, and it isn't quite so aggrivating as it was in the first iteration of DayZ, though some of the animations with it could use work.
Weapons, and their accompanying modifications, are good. Incoming shots sound nice on the ricochet, though they're a little lacking in overall impact and oomph. The occasional glitch with attachments not wanting to hold hands with guns can be encountered, but that's something easily fixed in time I'm sure. The ammo system is very DayZ, Escape from Tarkov, et cetera - Load bullets into magazine, magazine into gun, reload, point and shoot. I did notice that the guns seemed to have a bit of fluctuating effacacy. One moment my shotgun would feel good, would drop what I wanted it to drop without a problem, and on other occasions it would feel like a BB gun, which was both confusing and frustrating.
The crafting is a little odd. I'm not sure how I feel about it after coming from games like Rust, ARK, Conan, Hurtworld, et-cetera where people more or less innately know how to build a load bearing structure. They're taking a chance with that, and I think that it does have the ability to pay off provided people have the patience and the knowhow to take time with construction.
The zombies and mutants are genuinely a threat. The smaller variety with needles-for-arms don't seem to be particularly smart, but their slightly more naked relative will hound you for a fair amount of time and neither are afraid to stick you in a corner. The neighborhoods largest rippling muscle friend doesn't take no for an answer and has no qualms with setting you back to square one. I recommend not shooting them with a .22.
I was relatively pleased with performance overall. At 1080, and with settings as high as I could take them, I averaged out at 50 FPS. Occasional frame drops into the teens were uncommon but did exist, which would be a problem should those hiccups occur during PvP.
The clan system is .. There. It ties in with the building system, and grants access to doors, editing abilities, et cetera - ARMA 3 Group system it is not, and it doesnt' disable friendly fire, but this is post-apocalyptic and to my knowledge the player characters don't have cyber implants to see where their clan-mates are. An item, or a set of items, that eventually do that would be nice however.
Graphically, the game is usually aesthetically pleasing, though some problems should be expected. Animations are a bit buggy sometimes, in a quirky early access kind of way. Water will flicker in and out of shiny-ness, wrists will randomly break while moving and aiming down sights. Sitting in a car and driving will often make your characters have seizures in their seats, which is only slightly alarming.
I did see room for improvement, most certainly - Primary weapons (and smaller backpacks) being placed in large backpacks and storage containers would be *fantastic*. You could tell me that I can't fit an AR-15 in a backpack, but you're wrong and I've tried it to make sure. This would allow for bases being more  than just a place to store food, ammo, and more base building supplies - It would add a profitable reason for raids to exist, which would certainly be an improvement. A colorblind mode would be nice as well, but who really wants to be able to see things?
Over all, Miscreated has made phenomenal progress. I recommend checking it out, at least, and keeping an eye on it. While it might not be suitable for lower end computers, it can be a lot of fun with a group and it certainly has enough to keep people enjoying it for some time regardless of storage woes.

I actually played Blacklist back when I was primarily using my PS3 (hence the low play time on Steam). I must have sunk a good 100 hours into it - not a ridiculous amount of time but enough to consider myself a big fan of it. Like Hitman: Absolution, it gets a lot of stick from longtime fans for not staying true to the original formula and, as a longtime fan of both myself, I was afraid I wasn't going to like them.
Thankfully (and surprisingly), I was mistaken in both instances. However, on further reflection, I began to think that perhaps change wasn't necessarily a bad thing in this case. It's not like the Splinter Cell formula was infallible after all - there were some definite issues present in the other games. It wasn't like Blacklist came along and tried to screw with perfection; it came along and tried to do things a little differently in a series that probably could have done with a little revitalisation anyway. To that end, I think it did a bang-up job of refreshing the series.
There are a lot of great features in this game. The fact that it rewards you for approaching each mission differently is a nice touch. For once, I didn't feel like a stealth game was guilt tripping me for going the "Screw stealth - let's go nuts" approach. Going in guns blazing is now a viable option  - even if it's not what Sam Fisher would conventionally do. Actually, plenty of the equipment on offer is directed at precisely the type of people who prefer that distinct lack of subtlety. The little mini-missions given out by your team members are also a good way of breaking up the main missions. They also help you to unlock better equipment for Sam to use in the main missions, so they're well worth doing.
Long story short - it's not a conventional Splinter Cell game, but don't let that put you off. Convention is overrated anyway. There's plenty of things to like in Blacklist as long as you don't get hung up on how different it plays to previous games. Enjoy it for what it is and you'll walk away happy with your purchase.

I barely knew crap about this game before picking it up. Saw a youtuber playing it and it really peaked my interest. So I bought myself a copy of it and played it myself all the way to the end. And oh my god.
What an adventure.
First off, the art and visuals are amazing. Timeless. All the animal characters gave it a cute, fun vibe to the game. Making all the characters more alive and memorable. You can easily write this off for a "child's game" but I am telling you the looks are deceiving as hell. It is a very well mature, deep, and dark game that connects with you. Hell there's even pets like cats and yet you play as a cat! Does that make it under the bar slavery? It doesn't bother me. Bothers me a bit.
And the writing is amazing! The story, the lore, and the characterizations! All these cute characters have surprisingly deep backgrounds that isn't just like dumped on you like how other games have done. You get to understand their personality, their feelings, and connect with them. You can easily see the humanity reflecting from their lives which creates a beautiful contrast that just effing works. I honestly never had as much fun exploring every nook and cranny just for dialogues and fun bits before.
And the main story itself is just something you have to experience for yourself. If you are like me who is curious about this game by watching some guy on youtube playing it and is interested. Whatever you do STOP watching and buy this game when you can for yourself! It is worth the $20. Even with my 9 hour experience there was still things I have not explored like alternative dialogue options and paths. Which is a great reason for me to be able to replay it to see all the things I miss.
So get it already so I can stop fighting the urge to slip even ONE spoil story bit. You. Need. To. Experience it.

Drizzlepath is a flawed game that can still be enjoyed. It’s a walking simulator and the first iteration in a series of Steam projects created by the talented Tonguç Bodur. Yes, a one-man team developing indie games with CryEngine assets. Not an easy task and from what I’ve read in the many negative reviews this game has been receiving, it’s not that rewarding either to have your hard work constantly criticized or mocked by individuals who never created a single thing (digital or not) in their entire lives.
It’s important to see this title as the raw, initial attempt that kickstarted the entire series from which it is an integral part. I admit that I didn’t know the meaning of the word “drizzle” before playing this game, since it’s rarely used outside of the meteorological jargon. It’s a type of precipitation and it fits the story like a glove, since rain shall be your constant companion during the hour-long journey from a lake and all the way to a mountain peak. An abstract experience which I perfectly understood from the start, that it’s not something everyone would enjoy. Some players may find it either pretentious or outright tedious. Be warned that there’s no action in Drizzlepath. Nothing to kill, nothing to gain. Or is it?
Even if I wanted to spoil its plotline, I’d have to acknowledge the existence of one, first. It baffled me for its first half of the gameplay duration, but then I realized that Drizzlepath wants players to feel confused and out of place in the increasingly strange world they keep exploring. You are not being given an objective or any suggestions. You just follow the dirt road in front of you and even if you stray from it, there’s no mortal danger awaiting your unsuspecting pass-through. It would have been simple and to the point, if only the road ahead wasn’t littered with symbols of various shapes and sizes. You need to discover them by yourself.
Judging by its licensing information on Drizzlepath’s credits screen, the game is powered by CryEngine 3. Crytek has every reason to be proud that its technical legacy lives on, at least in some of the indie games found on the Steam Store. More precisely, the ones which make good use of its assets and convey a story along with them. I found this title to look stunning at times. Was it enough? Well, eye candy is a nice bonus to any video game but I’m always going to care more for the overall performance, in terms of both stability and a certain threshold as far as the frame rate is concerned. Drizzlepath walks a very thin line from a technical perspective. Frames were all over the place, no matter if I switched between 2K and 4K resolution. I still went with the latter, simply because the screenshots would look better and no ugly jagged edges would appear.
No antialiasing option in the settings so it’s not like you have a lot of room to maneuver. Running Drizzlepath maxed out and on 4K res, I’d get close to 40 frames, with the occasional dip to 37 or sudden increase to 45. These aren’t exactly minor stability issues but at least I experienced no crashes to desktop or freezes, like some folks rightfully complained about. Inverted mouse controls couldn’t be changed, no matter how many times I went back to the Main Menu and attempted to switch them off. Also be warned that despite the game’s relative short duration, manual saves aren’t an option and the automatic checkpoints only work for as long as you didn’t exit the game. In other words, if you wish to finish the game without any subsequent frustration that your progress wasn’t saved, simply complete the journey in one sitting if possible.
I liked the guitar riffs playing in the background, or the piano which made its presence felt near the end of the journey but I didn’t quite understood what the female narrator was aiming for. She seemed to read poetry of some kind, though the verses were unfamiliar and nearly as abstract as the rest of title. She wasn’t annoying and even without subititles she was eloquent enough but I always like reading subtitles in my games, despite not having to rely on them. It’s an old habit and I’m thankful that Romania doesn’t use dubs in either cinema or TV films and series. Subtitles are important to maintaining the intended language and experience intact and for improved coherence in Drizzlepath’s case.
Not much more can be said about the gameplay. You walk at a fortunately faster pace than most walking simulators on Steam and you just have to reach the mountain top, by sticking to the dirt path that isn’t that hard to notice. You can stop along the way, whenever you wish and just take in the sights. That’s what I did, and took nearly 30 screenshots within Drizzlepath. I’d like to think that the journey is somehow a metaphor relating to life’s constraints as we get older. Allow me to explain. At the beginning of your adventure, you rise from a lake and all around you, there are hills which you may explore by your heart’s desires.
As you progress down the dirt path, symbols start emerging and by the time you’ve reached the mountain and your final destination, you cannot explore or even move a lot, since the road has become very narrow. Night sets in, rain becomes snow. The end is near and even if you may still return and leave the mountain, curiosity forces you to press forward. Sure, real life never gives you the chance of turning back from all the decisions and consequences you’ve had to accept, but the inevitability of death is food for thought regardless. I don’t really believe in destiny and I’m firmly convinced that I’m making or at least influencing my own future in real time and constantly. Consider Drizzlepath as you will, but don’t judge it harshly for its ambiguity. It’s a game design choice, not a mistake.
Another aspect to consider is the game’s price tag. Drizzlepath is not overpriced but if you still regard it so, because of either short duration or performance issues, buy it when it’s bundled or during a Steam Sale. Problem solved. Just make sure you like abstract walking simulators, or at least be willing to give it a chance and find out. I could have rated it below 60 and thus stop recommending it, but Drizzlepath is crucial to the entire series and also represents a clear comparison to its sequels and the improvements they have implemented.

Game Review: ★★ (2/5 Stars)
Drizzlepath is a relaxing walking simulator that places you in the position of a man who is alone on a journey up a mountain in a beautiful landscape. As with the other games from this developer, the game convinced with gorgeous graphics and an atmospherical beauty that so many games are missing.
The story was very difficult to follow - despite there being an attempt of a storyline created by regular voice acting sequences playing in the background, it was impossible to understand what that voice actor said due to a strong accent and a lack of subtitles, making it impossible to understand what the game was all about.
While the graphics as well as the animations are gorgeous, any changes on the resolution or graphic files would cause the game to crash sooner or later before completion, and with the standards being reset after a restart, it was therefore not possible to discover the game's full graphical potential.
A distinct lack of music was present throughout the game - music only appeared shortly before, during and after a moment of voice acting but despite - admittedly well done - ambient sounds, the rest of the game felt fairly empty. I have a feeling that this could be intended to add to the feeling of natural isolation you find yourself in, but even a quiet or occasional background track would have improved the game experience a ton.
Gameplay wise, I was positively surprised to find myself able to swim! I hadn't been expecting that and it was a great feeling to jump into the sea and dive and swim away from my troubles. The running speed, while not adjustable between walking and running, was well balanced and didn't feel too fast or slow, making the walking simulator fairly enjoyable. Jumping also worked well and almost made me jealous of this person's ability to jump quite far.
In conclusion, the game itself was very relaxing and enjoyable, however with the lack of music and ability to understand the story (due to the lack of subtitles), I found myself a little bored after a while just aimlessly following a path. The beautiful environment still made the game a very nice experience, but in my eyes some small adjustments could improve the quality of that experience by far.

Quite a few people complained, and perhaps rightly so, that Dear Esther didn't have a "run" button. I'm inclined to make a similar complaint about Drizzlepath's lack of a "walk" button.
While it only takes a little time to get used to the fact that your avatar is a fitness fanatic, who likes to jog and jump like a pentathlete training for the Olympics, it doesn't exactly help to immerse one in the atmosphere of what is, ultimately, an atmospheric and reflective stroll through some stunning scenery. A walk button would have been a great way to encourage the player to stop and sniff the flowers a bit more often, as opposed to persistently prodding the player through the game's meagre thirty minute running time in order to reach a frankly underwhelming conclusion.
What about the positives? Well, there's no denying that, apart from the occasional jagged edge on a body of water and whatnot, the graphics are gorgeous in the extreme. The music is also quite lovely, if a bit start-stoppy, again preventing a very-nearly immersive experience from becoming overwhelmingly so. On both a technical and superficially aesthetic level, there's no denying this game is quite the triumph for what would appear to be the developer's first effort. Dig a little deeper, though, and there doesn't seem to be an awful lot here to gush about.
The "story" went straight over my head (poetry is often wasted on me, triply so when it's spoken in pidgin English), and the gameplay is essentially non-existent. There's literally one point in proceedings when the game tells you to hit the jump button to traverse a potentially fatal gap. So who's this game for, then?
Well, screenshot aficionados will have a field day. And anyone looking for a fairly casual, "relaxing" game (though again, that missing walk button would have worked miracles in this department). I certainly wouldn't recommend it to anyone who HASN'T already played the similar yet notably superior Dear Esther, a game every bit as beautiful, but with a few more secrets and a tad more story up its sleeve.
Look, let's be fair. There's far, far more insulting things for sale on Steam, and three dollars certainly isn't an unreasonable ask for the quality on offer. Just don't expect a whole lotta depth or bang for your buck. Drizzlepath is basically the video game equivalent of marrying a supermodel: admire the exterior all you want, but you'd be a fool to think she's gonna make for intelligent conversation once the honeymoon is over.
Verdict: 7/10.

The game is primarily an active clicker with a nice feature that you can simply hold your mouse button to have it auto-click for you. (Saves your mouse and finger) It also has an idle feature using your town’s folks to build, gather, sail, etc… at a cost of gold per/second. The game is free and I recommend giving it a shot if you enjoy clickers and building/management games.  Nothing to lose except a few hours.
Update:
After about 25 hours of gameplay I was able to reach New Game+. The progression to New Game+ was pretty smooth progression wise and overall enjoyable.
I would recommend the game for up to New Game+
After New Game+ is where I would recommend stopping the game till the Dev's add Progression Reset at New Game+. (The ability to start over with all bonuses saved. So your click, xp, building, etc... bonuses are saved and allow you to progress faster in the next run of the game.)
The problem is the game does not allow you to progression reset till after you beat New Game+ The main issue here is the curve of required materials for buildings suddenly spikes to 1000's of times more and gets to the point that it takes days to farm enough matreials for a single building.
The smooth progression that you experience up to this point is gone and now the game turns into a job and is no longer fun.
I would still recommend playing the game till you reach New Game+ if you enjoy clickers.

It's like the developers took everything that fans loved about old school RPG like Balder's Gate and Icewind Dale and actually made it BETTER!  The combat system is much more intuitive than the old silly 2nd edition rules that those older games used.  They slimmed down and trimmed the fat off the skill system.  Added many cool feats and abilities, some you can use every fight (encounter) and some every day (rest).  This is nice as some spellcasters don't necessarily become useless the second they run out of spells.  Everything is so similar to D&D, yet tweaked and renamed to make it something original.  Deflection instead of Armor Class.  Accuracy instead of Attack, etc.  There are some cool new classes like Chanter and Chiper that play different than any other class you've seen.  Then there are genius additions to the game like you can create your own hirelings for your party if you aren't satisfied with the companion characters.  And building your own stronghold is fun.  I've been playing on average difficulty and while few of the fights are too easy, the boss fight are just the right perfect challenge.. you have to use a full party's potential to win,as it should be.  I literally have nothing negative to say about this game 40hrs in.  Perfect.  10/10

Whatever you might believe, Dark Souls is not a game about dying over and over again (though you will, so if that's your thing this game has got you covered), but a game about not giving up. The story is that you are undead, and strictly speaking you can not really die unless you give up. This game can really cost you some time, depending on how you play it. You might find yourself saying
or
or maybe even just
It can be really addictive.
It is important to note that this game doesn't really tell you what to do. It gives you hints, yes, but I have yet to find out how to even get to my second target. Personally this game turned into chaos for me after I completed my first quest. I have no idea where to go or what I am doing, going places I am not even supposed to be yet, but it's so fun!
So what about the combat and the bosses?
As far as I have gotten in the game and depending on the things I have seen/fought it feels like the enemies you encounter on your way to them are harder than the bosses themselves. It might just be an illusion, given that most enemies respawn whenever you rest at a bonfire, but the bosses don't. Maybe it's because they are faster, smaller, or more to fight at once. Maybe I just fought the wrong bosses. The AI itself is definitely not the best though. Sometimes I felt like I cheated, even though what I did might have been a legit strategy. Falling off a bridge and a boss jumping after you is probably not a very legit strategy though. I don't know, my usual approach is to hit things until they die. (Hint : This might not be a very good idea in this game.) The great thing about the combat is that you actually CAN'T do that! I mean, you CAN, but you will most likely die. You need to ration your energy. You need to dodge. Or block. Or both at the same time! Even if the AI sometimes screws itself over, these guys are still capabale of landing painful hits. You can also kick enemies off of a cliff, which definitely deserves some recognition, because I played enough games where they can do this to YOU but YOU can't do it to THEM.
What I also like about this game is the atmosphere. I haven't seen anything like this before. This game is mostly singleplayer, which gives you a feeling of isolation in a world that tries everything to kill you. Nice. Totally my thing.
What makes it better though, are actually the multiplayer aspects of this game.
You can communicate cryptically with and even summon other players. Sometimes you might see a phantom/imprint from other players. You can even invade other players and kill them. Yes, even YOU can ruin someones day! You can also touch someone elses blood to get an idea about how they died.
My favorite part about this are, however, the player messages. Most of the time I have seen them they are actually helpful and give you hints. Sometimes they are used for trolling. Wheter or not you believe what is written depends on you. My favorite message was near the edge of a cliff where someone wrote "Try : jumping" and that definitely made my day! I also like how you can't just write whatever and you get lists to choose from.
I really recommend this game, just for its amazing atmosphere.
And if you can get behind the fact that the AI might screw up. Usually itself. You can use it against itself. Strategy!

Dark Souls is is a game that is both immersive and satisfying if you get the hang of it. Its combat mechanics are satisfying and are easy to learn, but can take a while to master. The world and enemy design is brilliant and one of the best parts of the game, sometimes gorgeous, sometimes disturbing. The storytelling in the game is subtle and you really have to pay attention to know what is going on in the game.
Dark Souls does have flaws though: It can be difficult to get into since the early parts of the game are a bit confusing and  some mechanics are not outright explained to you.
Overall I would recommend Dark Souls and encourage anyone to buy it.
Note: I very highly recommend installing the DSFix mod, it will make your life MUCH easier since it can help configure the game to match your computer better (If you are planning to play with mouse and key board I would also recommend the DSMousefix mod).

Dark Souls, and its two sequels, are the only games in my steam list that stay installed and are the first to be re-installed after system upgrades. No other game (or series) has managed to capture my attention in this manner. While the first is arguable the best of the lot, the sequels are fun in their own right. The first is also the game I first owned on the XBox 360 and then immediately purchased for PC once it was available on Steam with the additional content. I still remember the first time I tried to cross the bridge only to have a giant dragon fly overhead, spewing flames down the length of the bridge, and finally taking perch atop the surround at the opposite end. I have a lot of nostalgia for the game (despite it being relatively new), but also a lot of respect because its dying is learning mentality harkens back to the golden age of PC gaming when developers didn't need to hold your hand through how to play a game, much less how to overcome its challenges. Many games today tout that they are "rogue-like", but none capture the magic that is Dark Souls: A simultaneously beautifully rendered and tough as nails while remaining fun and engaging. Now to go find where the controller landed...

+ Great concept of a fast action hack'n'slash with added "puzzles" which are not actually puzzles, more like triggers needed to complete each level
+ Nice looking graphics reminiscent of Torchlight, Deathspank and others
+ 4 Unique classes with interesting skills
+ Unique skill gem system that encourages level replayability, but can be frustrating at times (see below)
+ Developers involved in the community and responding extremely fast to any reported issues
+ Great sounding music and almost perfect voice acting with a few minor hiccups here and there
- No difficulty setting (overall game difficulty is Medium-Hard with a few Hardcore levels)
- Frustratingly difficult levels mixed with stupidly easy ones.
- Luck can make or break a game, skill rarely comes into effect
- Unbalanced classes, found myself playing the shield wielder more than any other class
- Mostly impossible to complete level challenges for casual players, some levels require as much as 50 runs to get all the gems, the timed ones are really a pain to complete, better stick a fork in your eye than attempt them
- Broken co-op multiplayer, connection to other player's "servers" works 2/10, there is no option to configure the server at all. There isn't even an explanation about it, I still don't know if the gem numbers on servers represent the required number to join or just an indication to the host's "level"
It's hard to give this game a note because there isn't something to compare it too. I think it can be polished some more and it sure needs the difficulty to be decreased for more casual players. Right now it feels like you are taking part in a championship or tournament that has no prize at the end making all the frustrating experience to go through all of it pointless.
Maybe some extra levels at the end or a fifth class to be unlocked could have made it more interesting, especially to encourage co-op replayability.
I will give it a 7/10 though especially for the idea, effort and team commitment.

There is also this orb that you can control and is the main aspect of pretty much all puzzles, and even some combat.

My advice: DO NOT buy this game. The description is misleading: there is no RPG element to this game. Nor is singleplayer actually possible, despite it being an option: you simply cannot complete many of the challenges. All it is a coop puzzle arena, and even that I would not mind if the coop worked. It does not. Well, it does for a while, but if you get more than, say, 20 enemies onscreen at one time, something breaks in the game's netcode and everyone who is not hosting suddenly gets massive lag. Looks like GPU lag almost. So we tried different host. Same thing, the host always seeing the game fine, the guests getting 1-5 FPS during intense fights.
TL:DR This is a multiplayer only game that does not support multiplayer, avoid at all cost.

The problem here is that these puzzles are all really uninventive and quite frankly boring, and using the orb for all puzzles doesn't make for a rewarding and interesting experience.
The level design reminds me of iOS games because of its infatuation of having really short, play-while-you're-on-the-toilet missions which give you a ranking between 1 and 3 depending on how well you did. One for completing the level, one for doing some special thing, and one for doing it quickly. I really think this is a
practice for PC games and I was hoping for some Diablo-style adventuring which would fit the game a lot better than how it is now.
These problems combined with the shoddy netcode (this was playing with 3 others with pings varying between 10-30ms) lead to a really unresponsive and disapointingly mediocre experience.

If you like walking around, looking at scenery, and occasionally listening to narration, go play the sequel Drizzlepath: Genie. This game has several problems which made it hard for me to really immerse myself.
First, there were technical problems: At first it kept freezing at the start of the game. Later I got it to play, but after a half hour it randomly went to white screen for some narration (possibly it was supposed to, for emphasis, though it hadn't for earlier narrations), then froze and I actually had to restart my computer to get out of the game.
Second, there is no sound balance, and there is no setting you can change. The music is interesting but covers up most of the narration, and they always play together. There isn't even a subtitles option. The sound of your footsteps is too loud, in my opinion, which gets annoying. The narrator has a strong accent, which makes decipering what she is saying difficult even without the music covering half of it - altogether I usually understood one word out of five. Since the narration is half the game, this really put me off.
There also seems to be nothing tying all these musings together, and from what I *could* understand even the sentences didn't always seem coherent in themselves. Nothing, even at the very start of the game, gives you any indication that you need to start walking, keep walking, and stay on the path to reach checkpoints/narration points. Drizzlepath: Genie at least gave you a reason to walk and had clear narration.
The visuals are okay, though a bit dated compared to today's graphics. Nothing so beautiful or interesting I had to leave the path and go exploring, which was half the charm of its sequel. Lots of glare off the wet ground, which sometimes made lighting a bit odd with heavy light/dark contrast and lense glare in some areas. The rain would bead on the screen as if you were looking arond through a camera instead of actually being there.
Frankly, between lack of understandable narration and boring visuals, nothing really drew me into this game. For anyone who loves this sort of game, I suggest skipping Drizzlepath and playing its sequel, Drizzlepath: Genie instead.

This game is a walking simulator. You walk. On a path. And it drizzles, whence the name Drizzlepath. The good things:
- it's not so expensive
- it's relaxing, easy and there's no combat
- it uses the Cryengine so the visuals are nice
- sombody put effort into it
The not so good things:
- it lacks everything a game is supposed to have. This is the minimal effort one has to make to end up with something that can be asked money for.
- there are many texture glitches
- a girl's voice reads poetry at each checkpoint. The poetry sounds like it's procedurally generated and makes no sense at all, is hard to understand (she is not a native English speaker) and adds nothing to the story, if there was one to begin with. It sounds as if it was written by someone who believes that making something unintelligible makes it art. But sentences like "drops of water precipitating upwards into finite infinity"?

When I was little, I used to play game called Pocket Tanks with my friends a lot, this game brought back those nice memories.
The game has incredible amount of features. There are hundreds of weapons, different tank parts, upgrades, maps. And a huge number of things that gets unlocked as you continue to play and level up.
There are a lot of different game modes, from classic deathmatch to soccer game, point game, accuracy based mode. You can modify those modes to your liking very easily. You can set wind speed, whether you shoot in turns or at the same time, amount of HP, number of turns, and much much more.
However it also has quite a bit of flaws:
- You start with small number of available weapons and unlock them as you level up. In my opinion the weapons get unlocked very slowly and sometimes you might find that you are encouraged to grind to unlock them. Some weapons have some ridiculous requirements to unlock such as: "GOD RAYS - Defeat the game developer".
And so the only thing that I find missing from this game is some kind of mode where there would be random weapons and each player would choose what weapons to pick in turns and then start with those weapons, akin to Pocket Tanks. This would make game so much more fun. Or some random mode with all the weapons in the game available.
I also noticed a bug that when you start a server and want to invite a friend after clicking on "friends only" random people can still join the game for some time and I have to kick them for a minute or so before my friend can join. I hope this get fixed to respond quicker to the privacy change.
The fact that you have tank upgrades also make it so that lvl 99 is almost unbeatable to lvl 1, which shouldn't be. I think that the game should only have weapons and maps unlock, without those upgrades as it makes it quite a bit unfair and discouraging to the new players as they see how much they have to grind to get to the same lvl.
Overall thought I'm having so much fun playing with my friends and I think that this game is wonderful and the graphics and weapon effects are very beautiful and unique. I will keep playing this game for a long time, though it could be a bit less of a grind.
Overall: Very good game, with lots of incredibly fun weapons.
Score: 9/10

Gdy byłem młodszy grałem dużo z kumplami w Pocket Tanks, ta gra przywołała te dobre wspomnienia.
Gra ma niesamowitą ilośc zawartości. Setki broni, mapy, części do czołgów i wiele innych. Większość rzeczy odblokowywuje się wraz z wbijaniem coraz wyższych poziomów.
Gra posiada bardzo dużo trybów gry. Od klasycznego deathmatchu, do gry w piłkę, na punkty i wiele innych. Można modyfikować te tryby wedle uznania. Ustalać siłę wiatru, ilość tur, HP, czy strzelacie w jednej turze czy osobno. Bardzo prosto można więc stworzyć taką grę, jaką chcecie.
Jednak gra posiada trochę wad:
- Zaczynacie z bardzo małą ilością dostępnych broni a resztę zdobywacie poprzez lvlowanie, niestety im wyższy lvl tym trwa to dłużej i staje się bardzo żmudne i gra wydaje się zachęcać do gridnowania. Niektóre bronie mają tak trudne wymagania do odblokowania, że aż śmieszne. Np. "GOD RAYS - pokonaj developera gry". Powoduje to, iż możecie zapomnieć o posiadaniu wszystkich broni, no chyba że zamierzacie spędzić setki godzin w grze.
Biorąc to pod uwagę jedyna rzecz której brakuje mi w tej grze to jakiś tryb gry w którym gracze dostawali by bronie z całej gry randomowo i mogli wybierać na zmianę z którą chcą zacząć, coś jak w Pocket Tanks. Dzięki temu gra byłaby duzo fajniejsza. Albo przynajmniej tryb w którym dostępne są wszystkie bronie i można je przetestować.
Zauważyłem także błąd przy tworzeniu nowej gry. W momencie kliknięcia "tylko znajomi" przypadkowi ludzie dalej mogą wejśc do gry, przez co trzeba ich wyrzucać przez jakiś czas dopóki znajomemu nie uda się dołączyć. Mam nadzieję, żę zostanie to naprawione.
Fakt, że czołg można ulepszać powoduje też, że lvl 99 jest nie do pokonania dla lvl 1 w deathmatchu , a tak nie powinno być. Wydaje mi się, że gra nie powinna posiadać tych ulepszeń, ponieważ nowi gracze kupując grę mogą czuć jest trochę roczarowani widząc jaki grind przed nimi żeby wbić ten sam lvl.
Mimo wszystko, mam bardzo dużo frajdy grając w tą grę z przyjaciółmi. Grafika i efekty broni są przepiękne i każda broń jest unikatowa. Z pewnością będę jeszcze długo w to grał, aczkolwiek grind jest jednak zbyt duży.
Podsumowanie: bardzo dobra gra, z mnóstwem niesamowicie fajnych broni.
Ocena: 9/10
Update: Wraz z oficjalnym polskim językiem i bardzo częstymi aktualizacjami gra jest jak najbardziej warta polecenia.
