There are a lot of negative reviews that criticise the games political views and characters personalities. I'm leaving a positive review to outline the strengths and weaknesses of 2064:ROM that hopefully shouldn't come across as too emotional or dogmatic.
The setting is fairly unique, and features a detailed depiction of a futuristic San Francisco (Neo San-Francisco), working within a 2D pixel-art style. I wasn't sure what to make of 2064:ROM at first, however I enjoyed the story buildup and progression of the characters. Turing is an endearing robot that informs about important events in the story, beginning with its creators kidnapping, and the robots relative naivete towards human interaction is amusing. Lexi is a well-meaning police detective run down by the corporate system that dogs her, and while the interactions between her and characters like Turing could have been explored further, she is likable all the same.
You play a role of a journalist within the game, which is not explored to huge depths, but it sets the scene for a riveting tale of betrayal and redemption.  Your assistant TOMCAT, a hacker with connections to Hayden, desires to uncover the kidnapping of Turings creator along with Turing, and through uncovering the depths of Turings intelligence and longing, there is a motive to help the sapient Turing undercover the reasons behind the kidnapping. Also, the motives of both The Human Revolution, a fairly radical group against recreational human engineering, and the "hybrids", part-people, part-animals are discussed starkly, and in depth. It draws parallels to contemporary genetic engineering of 2017, and interested me through thought-provoking spiels and empathetic analysis.
Story-wise, there are a few twists and turns which I won't spoil, however they are mostly unpredictable and feature swathes of narrative and exposition, dialogue-heavy sections which may put off more action-oriented gamers. The puzzles for the most part are not challenging with a few exceptions. Most the challenge lied in the more dynamic puzzles which took quick thinking and a bit of luck to solve. Some of the puzzle mechanics were a bit unclear, and there should have been more explanation on what was happening during the games more action-oriented puzzles (at least in terms of the plot). The point and click puzzles were easy, even for a casual gamer like myself, and I was barely challenged by them at all. While I appreciated how logical most of the puzzles were, they could be a bit too obvious, and the hand-holding I would have preferred to have not been there in the first place (option to turn hints off maybe?)
Jess, an attorney who appears later in the game, has attracted some negativity due to discussion of gender and humanity issues. I feel the issues were handled well within the game, and her bad attitude is understandable due to hardships she faced within her job and as a "hybrid".
Musically, the game was great, and featured a bunch of catchy chiptune music, that I didn't mute once. The graphical style is nostalgic and aesthetically pleasing as well, with a variety of colourful interactive locations. I never felt like I was going through the motions, and I always looked forward to the next chapter, or scene. The dialogue is witty and intelligent for the most part, with topics such as love, friendship, gender, genetic modification, work, philosophy, robotics, corruption and emotions covered. The topics are all covered with reasonable tact, and allowed players to select from a variation of responses to said topics.
The save system was fine, and even though my game crashed several times, because I saved often, I recovered progress quickly. The game is more like a visual novel than a point and click adventure game. You can get into trouble, or fail to progress, but you can't get stuck or die easily. Again, it's quite casual, and the puzzles are simplistic to the point of non-interactivity. It's quite on-rails, and while the dialogue can change the story, there are few items to combine or logical leaps to make, since most of what you need to progress is spelled out for you. There's even a limit to what you can interact with, which narrows down possibilities almost too quickly. Interaction with the environment can sometimes be quelled by urgency of the story, instead of letting the player slow down, and explore some of the surreal environments. I managed to get the best ending on my first try without meaning to, so take that as you will.
Despite these issues, I would wholeheartedly recommend this game at the current price. I got this game off of Humble Bundle, and I felt like I got a great deal. As long as you don't expect an ultra-long puzzle fest of an adventure, it should be an amusing and an interesting time.

I have noticed that many of you found my little rant helpful, which is nice I guess. However, I also know that my little rant is far from being an accurate review of this game as I believe I owe you that much.
Beyond specifics, this game has a long history. It has undergone various changes that have brought both terrible things and potentially entertaining features. I will try to provide you with my experience on STKO so far, for which I will be using the list on my little rant.
Community
You all know the basics, I presume. The game is swarmed by a Turkish majority. In fact, it is basically a Turkish game now. Do not expect them to speak English; it is a four-leaf-clover. I do not really want to criticize Turkish people through a game majorly filled with uneducated children; however, even though I am Turkish myself, I find it quite hard to communicate with the player base of this game. The only thing that keeps me here is my clan, a group of select few. It is sometimes beyond me how people do not even know how to be a decent human-being, but I guess it is a universal issue. Whatever. TL;DR Deduction: You need a group of good friends to achieve anything.
Customer Service
I do not even know what to say about this. I lost a good amount of points (National Points earned by killing the enemies in PvP zones) due to a bug while I was basically donating them to my clan (guild) so that the clan would get better (noob friendly explanation ftw). It has been almost 2 months, nothing fixed even though I sent various tickets. They simply cannot do anything. The publisher and the developer are different companies, which slows down the process of getting the game better, simply put. TL; DR: Nothing comes to my mind other than "Terrible".
Content
You have a low level (35 {or something} - 59) PvP zone and a high level (70-83) PvP zone. Some farming maps (Krowaz, Juraid Mountain, Lost Temple, etc.), some events requiring you to sign up for a queue, some other stuff that are not even worth mentioning... There is nothing else, no stories to make anything interesting, no lore whatsoever. It is just a PvP game with good combat mechanics. Speaking of PvP: So many people use various external devices to boost their DPS as those devices help them hit as fast as possible. They actually pay for those USB connecting devices. Check out "kopedal", it is mind-numbing. Let's talk about language? Better not as some of the mobs' names are written wrongly (Shaman > Shamna). Various in-game explanations of the quests are probably translated by a primary school student who constantly gets F on English.
Premium Services
Extremely expensive, nothing else should be said. In PvP, you need special buff scrolls which boost your character's health, defence, attack, etc. You absolutely need those for PvP as there are skills which remove those buffs for a time or until either a priest or rogue cures them. The in-game skills which actually do the same buffing effect are removed once the debuffs are cured, and then you need to receive them again from various classes. The ones you buy from the store are constanly on you for 30 minutes (are not removed if you are debuffed, comes back once you are cured). Without those scrolls, it is basically impossible to PvP. A normal player who likes PvP must pay more than $100 a month (which is quite a low estimation by the way). A premium service that gives you certain benefits for 720 hours (a month), for example the War Premium (gives more points for PvP kills basically), is 3500 cash = $35... LoL! How much was WoW again?
So guys, you might say why the hell are you still playing the game... Well, I still am stupid, but I have close friends who make me forget those negatives. The PvP is still far more thrilling than many of the MMOs I have played so far, which is the only reason the game is still alive, against all odds.
Do I recommend the game? Well... NO!
You really do not need this game in your life. I will probably leave it all together soon as well.
You want to know more about the game? Let me know. I can explain things as best as I can.

Whatever you might believe, Dark Souls is not a game about dying over and over again (though you will, so if that's your thing this game has got you covered), but a game about not giving up. The story is that you are undead, and strictly speaking you can not really die unless you give up. This game can really cost you some time, depending on how you play it. You might find yourself saying
or
or maybe even just
It can be really addictive.
It is important to note that this game doesn't really tell you what to do. It gives you hints, yes, but I have yet to find out how to even get to my second target. Personally this game turned into chaos for me after I completed my first quest. I have no idea where to go or what I am doing, going places I am not even supposed to be yet, but it's so fun!
So what about the combat and the bosses?
As far as I have gotten in the game and depending on the things I have seen/fought it feels like the enemies you encounter on your way to them are harder than the bosses themselves. It might just be an illusion, given that most enemies respawn whenever you rest at a bonfire, but the bosses don't. Maybe it's because they are faster, smaller, or more to fight at once. Maybe I just fought the wrong bosses. The AI itself is definitely not the best though. Sometimes I felt like I cheated, even though what I did might have been a legit strategy. Falling off a bridge and a boss jumping after you is probably not a very legit strategy though. I don't know, my usual approach is to hit things until they die. (Hint : This might not be a very good idea in this game.) The great thing about the combat is that you actually CAN'T do that! I mean, you CAN, but you will most likely die. You need to ration your energy. You need to dodge. Or block. Or both at the same time! Even if the AI sometimes screws itself over, these guys are still capabale of landing painful hits. You can also kick enemies off of a cliff, which definitely deserves some recognition, because I played enough games where they can do this to YOU but YOU can't do it to THEM.
What I also like about this game is the atmosphere. I haven't seen anything like this before. This game is mostly singleplayer, which gives you a feeling of isolation in a world that tries everything to kill you. Nice. Totally my thing.
What makes it better though, are actually the multiplayer aspects of this game.
You can communicate cryptically with and even summon other players. Sometimes you might see a phantom/imprint from other players. You can even invade other players and kill them. Yes, even YOU can ruin someones day! You can also touch someone elses blood to get an idea about how they died.
My favorite part about this are, however, the player messages. Most of the time I have seen them they are actually helpful and give you hints. Sometimes they are used for trolling. Wheter or not you believe what is written depends on you. My favorite message was near the edge of a cliff where someone wrote "Try : jumping" and that definitely made my day! I also like how you can't just write whatever and you get lists to choose from.
I really recommend this game, just for its amazing atmosphere.
And if you can get behind the fact that the AI might screw up. Usually itself. You can use it against itself. Strategy!

Dark Souls is is a game that is both immersive and satisfying if you get the hang of it. Its combat mechanics are satisfying and are easy to learn, but can take a while to master. The world and enemy design is brilliant and one of the best parts of the game, sometimes gorgeous, sometimes disturbing. The storytelling in the game is subtle and you really have to pay attention to know what is going on in the game.
Dark Souls does have flaws though: It can be difficult to get into since the early parts of the game are a bit confusing and  some mechanics are not outright explained to you.
Overall I would recommend Dark Souls and encourage anyone to buy it.
Note: I very highly recommend installing the DSFix mod, it will make your life MUCH easier since it can help configure the game to match your computer better (If you are planning to play with mouse and key board I would also recommend the DSMousefix mod).

I've barely made a ripple in the vast pool that is Pillars of Eternity as I write this, and I'm already stuck in.
The spirit of the great top-down RPGs have been captured extremely well in this game. The interface is polished, and while some clunky elements remain (if you want to sell 150 items, you have to click 150 times), it just seems to add to the feeling that you're playing one of the classics like Planescape Torment or Baldur's Gate.
And truly, I have to tip my hat to the devs. I can play for hours at a time and not get bored. On the other hand, I can as easily forget about it for days, and come back and still be as immersed as I was when I left it. Few games I've played can ever have this quality, and it really must be commended for this.
It's a testament to how good the game is that I'm regretting spending time away from it writing this review.

Amazing game. In addition to what everyone else has said...
Disclaimer:
I haven't finished the game yet but the game says I'm about 88% through it.
Pros:
- Game runs very well with no frame dropping at high settings, capped at 60 FPS with vsync on (I have a GeForce 770 GTX)
- No bugs that I've noticed other than some model clipping...only a visual detail though
- New mechanics get introduced throughout the entire game which keeps gameplay fresh. I didn't find any of these mechanics useless...they're all the right tool for some situation
- I love the collectibles! It's not so many that it'll take all day to get, and they're all marked on your map, but still gives some satisfaction of exploring the map and finding things
Cons (only minor):
- Horizontal lines occasionally appear. I thought vsync was supposed to fix this. It seemed to help but not eliminate the problem. This is at 60 FPS (capped) with vsync on.
- For some people (like me), ergonomics matter. This game abuses your right hand if you use a controller. You'll be holding the right trigger down for a good portion of the game which did end up stressing my wrist a bit. This might be customizable...it wasn't enough of an issue until the endgame so I didn't bother looking into it
Other thoughts:
The difficulty curve is really odd. In my experience, the first few hours of the game were hardest. I died a few times when I found out some captains hit really hard. Others don't. There is no obvious correlation to me on how "hard" a captain (boss) is to beat even with their strengths and power level known. Some are hard, others (even at the top) are super easy. The side missions related to your weapons can also be quite challenging toward the end, mostly because when you fail them, the game keeps you where you are and you have to flee and run back to the starting point. For main missions, it'll restart just that last checkpoint which is much better. In general, the bosses and main missions seemed to get easier throughout the game whereas the side missions got harder.

Night in the Woods is a story about a young woman who returns to her small town and and learns something about the most difficult thing there is, loss.
While that opening sentence came off pretty pretentious, I stand by it, and by the story it tells.
Most of your time in Night in the Woods will be spent running here and there talking to the wonderfully colorful cast of character that live in Possum Springs, and while it was a joy, it does note a problem. There isn't a whole lot of gameplay here, besides some light platforming and dialouge choices, but that isn't a bad thing. Just something that might turn some people away.
Choosing who you're going to go hang out with and when can shape our main character's, Mae's, story, and reveal things she never knew about her friends, her town, or even herself now and then.
The story was excellent, deep in places, hilarious at others, and had me wanting to skip work just to see how it ended. I didn't, but I wanted to really badly. With all the friends you can go do things with, there is a bit of replayability as well, though I expect that may get a little repetitive. I know I'm going to go back in just to see what misadventures I may have missed.
It's not for everyone, with so little gameplay and lot of running around the same place some people may find it boring or rote. However, for those captivated by stories of loss, fun, nihilism, and some young adult angst, I can say that despite all it's characters being animals, the story itself turned out to be very human.

I must say this indie title is astonishing. It is one of the most mature games I've ever played and definitely the most soulful and empathetic with amazingly written and believable characters (even with their cartoon-animal appearance).
Despite its core story is focused on "semi-paranormal" events It's a game about friendship, about rebuilding broken bonds with friends, parents and maybe at first glance its not noticable it is saturated with moralistic vibe. It tells you that you are not alone even when you feel cut off from the rest of the world and nobody has the power to help you better other than your close ones. And that's what makes it so great and unique -
.
I'm aware not everyone may like this game because to "unlock its full potential" you have to get emotionally affected by its story or/and identify with at least one of its characters.
If you won't you will only scratch the surface. Sure you will get a beautiful 2D pseudo-platformer and visual novel/adventure game hybrid with some great mini games (there are even phenomenal yet very difficult to perfect music rhythm sections based on Guitar Hero and a fully-fledged isometric rougelike !). However you probably won't have much fun of this game with this attitude anyway because over 80% of its playtime is based on holding talks and without the emotional allegiance mentioned above you will most likely either mindlessly scroll dialogue lines (sadly there is no voice acting here) or just get bored while reading them. Hovewer hopefully you are not that person.
The only thing I really dislike in this nearly perfect game is an illusion of choice. Despite it is so heavy dialogue based the choices NITW offers are mostly residual, meaningless and only a very few have a major impact on the story and protagonist development. But to me it's all negative I can say.

In some ways Miscreated greatly improves upon other games of its type; the developers made a reasonable choice of game engine and they have created a world with a truly eerie, lived-in aesthetic. Vehicles and base building are there, so it's already miles ahead of its direct competition. In other ways this game is another poster child for avoiding Early Access.
I can respect the developers for pushing out regular updates but unfortunately this game suffers from many of the same core flaws that define the open world survival genre right now, namely that the performance leaves a lot to be desired and many basic elements of the game are janky or outright broken. Its fans will no doubt raise the point that it's in alpha, and rightfully so, but after waiting more than two years to give this game time to mature I expected far better and the progress so far does not fill me with optimism. I can't see a point one, three, or even five years from now that this game looks and plays like a polished labour of love, I just can't.
While I am not going to recommend this game I don't want this review to be taken as a totally negative one, if the option were available I would give it a neutral rating or mark it as "one to watch". Unlike a lot of these early access titles, I can potentially see myself coming back at some point in the future.

I gave up after 8 minutes. This game chugs along at 25fps on a 980Ti, and the supposedly "beautiful" graphics you see in the screenshots and in the other reviews are just a sham. The path you're supposed to walk looks okay, even if it's all just pretty standard CryEngine stuff, but the moment you look to the side the game looks horrible. No draw distance and the distant scenery is just blobs. On top of that, the geometry and textures warp around you as you move, further pulling the aesthetic experience down.
And there's also the fact that you don't actually do anything. You walk along a samey-looking path in total silence until you hit a checkpoint, at which time you will either get about 10 seconds of acoustic guitar music, or a random length of music and a woman with a heavy accent reading some mindnumbingly pretentious poetry that's impossible to follow because of her heavy accent and strange inflections. I think the last line she said before I noped out was "I am the rust and rot in your brain", which doesn't mean anything to anyone except moody teenagers who think they're geniuses because they've heard of Nietzsche once or twice.

I've enjoyed the Worms series in the past, so when I saw this one being played on YouTube, it held my interest.  Since I've played it for the last few weeks, I haven't been disappointed.  The graphics are simple but bright and eyecatching, the physics are well-done, the weapons are fun and funny, and the upgrade system is interesting and encourages you to use as many types as possible rather than just stick with a favorite few.  Tanks are also upgradable with armor, movement, damage, and luck, and can make for some interesting builds.
Along with all that, there's extras like shields, teleports, and jet packs, an in-game currency won during matches to buy goodies like bonus weapons, battlefield customizers, and victory music.  And if you don't feel like fighting against real people, there a challenging (and occasionally frustrating) single mission mode to help introduce you to the game, various weapons, and concepts like bumpers and portals.  It's also hard to believe this game is early access; it shows much more polish than some more expensive and bigger name games I've played in the last few years.
My one complaint with the game is one that usually befalls multiplayer games; there are the odd occasions where you have rude, stupid, or rage-quit players.  This is pretty much expected, though, and to be honest I've encountered far more nice players than trolls.
Overall, its a fun game with a surprising amount of complexity for a simple concept.  Definitely recommended.

State of Decay is in my personal top 3 zombie games of all time with the very first Dead Rising and  Walking Dead Season 1.

It's actually differed from the "other" zombie games. That is , because there's a character progression. You character evolves, will level his fighting if you fight alot of zombies or other traits... Also, there's a community which is actually where the whole game is based.
For example, when you're searching for supplies in a house , you can choose to radio home for them back at camp to come there and take the items you selected IF you don't have room for more into your inventory. Also, When you find survivors and save them , they join your camp and grow stronger as a defense to the zombie apocalypse.
In the beggining of the game , you're given a piece of wood and your kicking as your sole defense. Although it's enough for you to not die. You can choose to go out with 1 other person to help you.
The noise mechanics are adequate. I would not expect anything less-more since it's good. Using cars is not safe because if you rev high, the zombies ( Zeds as they are called in SoD ) will hear it and come after you.
Cars have a storage. You can store up to 5 or 6 items into it's trunk which is really useful.Also, you can hit zeds with your door.
There can be different types of zeds except your normal-like zombies.

♥♥♥♥. Yes.
With accurate retro visuals and a color pallette resembling late 80's/early 90's cyber, this little marvel will hit all your nostalgic buttons. Paired with those throwback graphics is a wonderful soundtrack and an amazing cast of voice actors that soothe your ears.
The gameplay is simple, yet surprisingly immersive! The puzzles are fun and make you feel accomplished. Even though this is a point-and-click, don't expect to be able to take all the time you need on all challenges though! The pressure of time can and will get to you in some of the minigames and even in the later puzzles!
Now, the big whooper. The story.
It's just a few days before Christmas, and you're just writing yet another boring product review. Suddenly, this little robot who claims to be sentient breaks in and demands you help them. Their creator has gone missing! After literally dragging you into it, you begin suspecting things... The Human Revolution, a protest group vouching for the purity of humanity, apparently has something to do with this all. Hybrids, humans who have undergone gene therapy, get involved too. You suddenly find yourself torn between three factions: humans, hybrids and ROMs. On top of it all, you need to find out what happened to this robot's creator! What will you do? Can you bring the three factions together, or do you choose one over the rest? What has a network company to do with this all? Guess you'll have to play the game to find out!
Like playing DnD except my whole party is voiced by Matt Mercer. 10/10

It's a neat game, a good game even but it rides the coat tails of Baldur's Gate and other Infinity Engine games before it and when viewed in that light it is shown to be a rather pale imitation of what has come before.
A few points...
The game is needlessly taxing on the computer. Sure it runs easily enough on any modern PC but it requires so much more than the games that inspired it and offers almost nothing in return. It would be great if it ran better on old PCs and mediocre laptops, I could recommend it to far more people and I wouldn't have to play on my desktop or listen to my laptops fans spin.
It's not D&D/Forgotten Realms, it's an imitation. Aumaua? Godlike? Orlan? What? No thanks. The classes are a little more classicly inspired but things like mediocre rangers and their mediocre and required pets really put me off. Charcter attributes/stats are also classicly inspired but with needless changes that only seem to make the game 'different' but not more coherent or fun.
The playerbase also seems needlessly focused on the numbers behind it all. Searching for questions you might have in regards to character creation and weapons leads to so many posts on math and numbers and the "right" attributes and skills that I wonder if people even bother exploring the game world and rules behind it and if not, why even play? In short it feels like a large portion of the playerbase are min-maxers and that the game was built with them in mind.
A good game but if you're here because of Baldur's Gate then go play that. Perhaps with a new class?
If you like pixel art, good voice acting, and fun characters, then this is for you!

I was ready to love this game. Good characters, interesting world, fun adventure game writing.
Two issues stymied me.
First, the save system. I don't know if it's a bug or not, but on my computer it was a crapshoot whether saves actually worked or not. Sometimes they reverted back to the beginning of the chapter, other times they simply didn't work. Either way, given that there's no way to quickly skip through dialogue/scenes, it made me very insecure about quitting mid-game.
Second, the final boss. Maybe I'm just dumb, but I simply could not deal with this boss, a more complex version of an puzzle that I had no issue with from earlier in the game. Character A told me the rules to this fight and then five seconds later the boss broke them. It was frustrating and obnoxious. After several tedious replays (remember, there's no way to skip dialogue, and the game restarts ahead of a several pages of dialogue that you must tediously click through) I just decided to watch the endings on YouTube. I'm disappointed I couldn't play through myself, but I'm also not going to bother fighting through a game that doesn't respect my time.

Read Only Memories is an adventure-esque visual novel about the first sentient true AI. So far so good.
The art design is retro and the story itself isn't that bad at all, if it wasn't for some particular parts and content I personally hadn't any issues with but which I believe to possibly have a negative impact on most players.
While being an open-minded indiviual having no gripe with pretty much anything the art and indie industry could throw at me, I need to point out that there is a massive amount of 'new-age-genderism' within the game. Out of the roughly dozen of characters from the main cast, half of them is gay (no big deal) and / or transgender (for example a bearded man named Sympathy, consistently refered to as 'she'). There's also genetically engineered furries (I kid you not) and the ability for the main character to pick his/her/its/their/xes/zis personal denominator (or a custom one, you can literally make up yourself) that the game will continue using consistently. And while I am totally open-minded about all of the above, I think it was deliberately put in there not because of necessity, but because some of the developers are super deep into that kind of scene (had to chuckle when I read that Zoe Quinn also worked on this in the credits), which makes the whole setting come over a lot more weird than it would have been necessary story-wise.
The main companion, sentient AI Turing, is also abysmally annoying and childlike, with a very strong emotional moral compass, which isn't exactly what I personally would consider a realistic take on a newly formed sentient mechanical conscience and the game does miss a lot of opportunities to get philosophical within the boundaries of its main theme. It also tries to pitch in as many tropes at any given time as possible, which might be your cup of tea, but started to personally annoy me after the dozenth pop-reference within five sentences.
What it yet does depict is a world completely different from hours, set about 40 years into the future. And while in some regards being quite over the top in a way that Gamergate was 'mildly' over the top, I'm even willing to believe that the world could be and look like that in a couple of decades, even although it definitely wouldn't be my personal favourite of possible outcomes.
So in regard to a recommendation: While being an interesting little game with five branching story paths, your tolerance level for homosexuality, transgenderism, transhumanism, and whatever you would scientifically call genetically altered humans to become true furries should be exceptionally high, otherwise you probably will get mad quite often throughout the game. And even if you can easily be okay with all of that, the remaining game is a very simple and dialogue heavy visual novel with average writing and average written characters, railroading you towars plot twists that aren't twists at all and fulminating in some of the most unspectacular endings I have ever seen within visual novels.
All in all I didn't regret playing this, but I don't believe I can recommend it to anyone, let alone the general public.

Amazing game. In addition to what everyone else has said...
Disclaimer:
I haven't finished the game yet but the game says I'm about 88% through it.
Pros:
- Game runs very well with no frame dropping at high settings, capped at 60 FPS with vsync on (I have a GeForce 770 GTX)
- No bugs that I've noticed other than some model clipping...only a visual detail though
- New mechanics get introduced throughout the entire game which keeps gameplay fresh. I didn't find any of these mechanics useless...they're all the right tool for some situation
- I love the collectibles! It's not so many that it'll take all day to get, and they're all marked on your map, but still gives some satisfaction of exploring the map and finding things
Cons (only minor):
- Horizontal lines occasionally appear. I thought vsync was supposed to fix this. It seemed to help but not eliminate the problem. This is at 60 FPS (capped) with vsync on.
- For some people (like me), ergonomics matter. This game abuses your right hand if you use a controller. You'll be holding the right trigger down for a good portion of the game which did end up stressing my wrist a bit. This might be customizable...it wasn't enough of an issue until the endgame so I didn't bother looking into it
Other thoughts:
The difficulty curve is really odd. In my experience, the first few hours of the game were hardest. I died a few times when I found out some captains hit really hard. Others don't. There is no obvious correlation to me on how "hard" a captain (boss) is to beat even with their strengths and power level known. Some are hard, others (even at the top) are super easy. The side missions related to your weapons can also be quite challenging toward the end, mostly because when you fail them, the game keeps you where you are and you have to flee and run back to the starting point. For main missions, it'll restart just that last checkpoint which is much better. In general, the bosses and main missions seemed to get easier throughout the game whereas the side missions got harder.

*SPOILER FREE REVIEW*
My favourite visual novels tend to be pretty big name ones, but this is definitely one of those instances where an indie company comes out of nowhere and makes something really worth paying for.  I believe this game was born from a Kickstarter project that proved so promising that it doubled its goal, and after playing it, I can understand why.
Lucy explores one of Japan's all-time favourite themes; can robots and humans live in harmony?  Since there are so many well done, higher-end games and anime that present that situation, I was expecting a slightly lukewarm experience, but I was really pleasantly surprised by Lucy for several reasons.
On surface level, the CGs and soundtrack were really nice, decently atmospheric and definitely enhanced the experience of the game.  They felt very professional and effortless for an indie production.  Story and gameplay wise, the plot unfolded at a good pace that felt natural and realistic.  The humour sprinkled into it was genuinely funny and always happened at the right moments.  I also found the characters to be written very well, particularly the protagonist's father; people were genuine in their emotional reactions to things, often becoming unreasonable and cruel due to their fear or selfishness; it was sadly very real when you consider how people can gain negative perspectives on things when they're experiencing an emotional turmoil that they don't want to address, or are stuck in their misguided beliefs.  That's one of the reasons I really enjoyed Lucy - the characters were very realistic, and the situations became appropriately difficult to deal with and therefore provoked a bigger emotional reaction from me as I played.  I really admire this writing.
I also enjoyed the different routes you can go down as you get towards the game's finale.  There were big revelations, emotional moments, and different possibilities for the end scenario depending on how you chose to deal with situations that I honestly thought were all emotional and good in their own rights.  I found myself getting very invested in the characters and desperate to bring them a happy ending through my choices.  And yes, if you're like me, you're going to cry!
Overall, I'd say Lucy is definitely worth the money you pay for it.  I was really pleasantly surprised by this novel that made me feel so much and get so invested.  Please give it a go, as it's one of the best visual novel experiences you'll find on Steam!

The full release will definitely wash the taste of the time it took to get here. This game is pretty much what No Man's Sky aspired to be. Exploration and adventuring make your story. The main questline is simply a skeleton for you to grow the meat on, if that makes any sense. How you get there, what you do on the way, the things you come across, that's the real fun. Finding a guitar and playing Fur Elise while your friend decides to be a jerk and plays Canon D with a harmonica over you? Struggling to get your stuff back because you picked mediumcore and softcore is for wimps? Starbound is pretty damn cool.

For people who follow my reviews, I want to start by saying that this is a re-review of the finished Starbound product as my previous review was for the Early Access game. Since the game has launched I felt it was worth a second look at the title.
Have you ever been to a theme park for the first time after wanting to go for almost as long as you can remember? That expectation before you arrive and that initial thrill as you walk through the entrance? But then, after spending a few hours at the park you realize that there is perhaps only half a dozen rides and the majority of the park is filled with shops and places to eat. Welcome... to Starbound Land.
Just like a theme park, Starbound has a handful of features which are initially amazing. That moment when you get your stardrive back online and start traveling the galaxy. The bosses which don't even fit completely on the screen and that first time when you stumble across a ruined castle or hi-tech alien laboratory and promptly clear the place of dangers before making it your own personal home. These are the moments that make Starbound great. Unfortunately, when it does these great things over and over and over, you start to wonder what else there is to do. This is where Starbound falls flat on its face just like those theme parks.
There is a ton of craftables... but you loot stuff so frequently which is better than anything you could craft that you generally don't bother crafting anything except for the stations needed to get better armor. Once you have the tier-6 armors you pretty much stop crafting entirely. But between the start and tier-6 armor there is plenty of materials you need to track down to get there. So if you like exploration, that is catered to nicely at first. There is also the massive menu of food to make... but you soon discover that the more complicated recipes are unnessersary since basic meals are perfectly fine since the advanced food buffs are very short duration anyway and the food requires a wide variety of materials to make. Causing them to be impractical.
Next you have the 'pets' and crew members. Who are so inept that you find that they barely qualify as useful for anything except cannon fodder. So exploring the galaxy for crew and monsters becomes pointless since they don't add anything significant and worse still is that the quality of the NPCs and pets you can get will improve depending upon how advanced the world they came from is. Much like how you discard low level gear, you have little choice but to discard crew and pets too.
Starbound actually runs into this issue of making its own content redundent far more than it needs to. It happens with almost all of its content. For example, planets are tiered much like the armor. A planet orbiting a gentle (low level) star has Copper, Iron, Silver and Gold. But a magma ocean planet (end game) planet has those ores but also gives you all the other materials. Furthermore asteroid fields have so much Copper, Silver and Gold that it isn't even funny. So despite being open world, you end up with no reason to explore worlds once you update your environment suit to allow exploration of end game worlds. Everything you find on those worlds from drops, crew, monsters and materials is better than everywhere else. So despite being a game about an endless universe of discovery. the poor design choices made here actually kill the point of playing. Why bother making all this proceedual stuff when the content is disposed of faster than a baby's filthy nappy? I know that many RPGs do this progression method, but in a game that the developers have worked hard to make appealing for exploration it just doesn't work since you've now coaxed the player into a linear path through the game and little point to turn around.
So, can I recommend Starbound? Is it entertaining. Is it value for money? Well, yes. For a time it is entertaining and you'll get many hours of enjoyment from it before you hit that 'wall' where you notice that you've been on all the rides at least 5 times already. As for replay value, that rests not with the game itself but with the modding community. Much like how Minecraft was made successful not on its own merits but on the effort put forth by the community - so the same applies to Starbound. But, with the core design flaw created by the way content becomes redundent its going to take a really incredible mod to overhaul the game to make it worth exploring once you reach the end of the armor tree. Looking for legendary loot is not enticement to keep playing more after tier-6 when you're already overpowering mobs without it but that is yet another issue with the games design that I won't get into.

State of Decay: One of the greatest - if not THE greatest - single player zombie survival games.
Here's a short summary:
-Several NPCs, who you can eventually play as
-Various characters
-Short and sweet backstories
-Zombie killing by hand, by gun, or by car. Blood everywhere.
-While driving, you can open your door as a 'door attack'. Hilarity and bloodsplatters.
-Stealth kills and sneaking away from hoardes: intense
-Loot all the things!
-An abundance of missions in a fairly expansive world
-Build-A-Base mechanic makes your survival a changeable experience
-Don't die! Hardcore lives. You die, you can't come back. Only play as another character. The autosave feature enhances this, as you can't just go and select a save file. Be safe out there.
The game, in my opinion, is fantastic. I've had so much fun in the short time I've played it, and it looks like I have a way to go.
There are a few problems, though, but not any that ruin anything.
-Small glitches in fighting, grounded zombie can suddenly stand up and attack you from behind
-Some repitition (though wouldn't surviving like this be repetitive?)
-Dialog repeating (can get annoying)
-Very easy sometimes. The difficulty should be toggleable, as right now some 'hard'-type missions can be done easily.
If you're on edge about getting this game, I nudge you towards buying it. This game is full of moments, which is something I look for. Sometimes you'll be barely sneaking back to your base through zombies, other times you'll be driving down the road in a rusted up pickup truck, opening your doors to whack a couple of hitchiking zombies. Absolutely marvelous as far as zombie games go.

This game has a LOT OF TEXT to read. Let's just get that out of the way, right now. Many NPCs, especially party members, have much of their dialogue recorded as voiceovers, but even significant amounts of that is only available as text.
Now then:
Pillars of Eternity is the spiritual successor to games like Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Planescape: Torment, and such.
It is a top-down, pauseable, party-based tactical fantasy RPG with heavy influences from Dungeons and Dragons; however, unlike its inspirations it doesn't actually utilize a modified DnD system.
This game does have its quirks and quibbles, and it isn't perfect, but as an avid fan of Baldur's Gate 1 and 2, this game is right up my alley.
NPCs have a LOT to say, but much of that is completely optional, and text you aren't interested in or have seen before can be easily skipped with the spacebar. The storytelling in general is pretty interesting, and there is lots of secondary lore you can find in the form of books and papers as well as just delving deep into conversation options and the game's built in "Cyclopedia".
Combat is HIGHLY dependent on positioning, tactics, and at least a moderate amount of planning, even on the 2nd-easiest difficulty. Which itself is still quite challenging for some encounters, although there's plenty of more difficult options for masochists.
Fights are typically over fairly quickly if you make a critical error or are simply outgunned, but retrying it with proper tactics can make a world of difference.
You will have to "micromanage" your party in combat, although there is a rudimentary and fairly simple "AI" feature you can utilize if you want. But given the immense importance of positioning and tactics in this game, directing one's party in combat doesn't feel like a chore or micromanagement, really. You will have plenty to do and your decisions are very important.
Overall, I am enjoying it greatly on the "Normal" difficulty so far. I haven't yet run into a fight I couldn't win through subtlety, planning, and shifting my tactics, but most "boss" type encounters will test your knowledge and abilities to the point that you may need to restart a time or two. Save your game often!
This game is excellent and definitely recaptures that "oldschool computer RPG" feel, while bringing some more modern features to the table. The in-game encyclopedia in particular, as well as the extensive in-game tooltips--complete with "wiki" style internal links, can shed a great deal of light on otherwise obscure mechanics.
Obsidian (who were also the brains behind Fallout: New Vegas by the way) did an excellent job.

An enjoyable experience that feels like an Assasin's Creed game with a better combat system. Once again, there are high towers that you need to climb in order to enable quick travel and light up the map. This then reveals a plethora of busy work for you to work on: flowers to pick, secrets to find and slaves to set free. This will completionists occupied for hours on end.
In addition to the fantastic soundtrack, the combat feels smooth and enjoyable. At least for the majority of the time. Imagine the following situation:
> You and your army of branded Uruks have waged war for what feels like ages
> Only you and one loyal ally survive
> More enemies start to close in
> You charge forward valiantly with your partner running right behind you
> Your combo is charged and sword flaming
> Press execute
> Turn 180 degrees
> Decapitate your only living ally
Events like this happen from time to time and can be infuriating. Especially if you end up taking out a friendly captain or warchief who you've pushed to the top of the food chain.
Despite my grievances with parts of the game, it is overall a very enjoyable hack and slash title. The graphics are fantastic, the soundtrack solid and controls responsive. Especially with how heavily the game is discounted nowadays it is well worth your time and money.

This game my friends
is not what it says on the tin.
It's a virtual experience, relaxing, soothing.
Do I recommend this game?
If you've got some bucks and an hour or two to slay, totally! Don't buy it to slander it. It's like a good massage, sure, some points can be uncomfortable, like some graphical glitches, missing vegetation if you stray from the path, and the narrators accent (the narrative consists mostly of poetry), which is thick as oil, but this can also be very soothing. But you'll see the world through a different lense afterwards, maybe it even motivates you to go out and look at the world around you. Sit back and let it have it's effect on you.
The best thing about this game?
The soundtrack, which is included in the game as a free download and available in your steam library and on your computer. The original artist did a very good job with that. It adds up to the whole experience.
Story?
As previously mentioned, the narrators accent is thick. Indian, if I'd have to take a guess. The basic premise is, you walk along a path to the top of the peak of the mountain of fire, traversing beaches, bushes, cliffs, snow and just nature in general.
From what I scraped together from the narrative, it seems to me that the main character found a girlfriend, broke her heart, she turned out to be a witch who cursed him to have to go up the drizzlepath every four years(?) I think, maybe. And as soon as he arrives on the peak, its a new beginning for him.
(Just wanted to leave my understanding of it here in case someone might have been in the unclear about it). Also, no magic in the actual game, it's "only" walking and enjoying the view and nature.
Again, don't see this as a game, look at it as a unique experience.

Here are some things I like and dislike about Drizzlepath:
+ Do you love foliage? Well then step right up because Drizzlepath has got you covered. Personally I love it: beautiful plants and trees, rich textures, warm lighting and a soothing yet quite persistent drizzle of rain accompany you as you walk along the unwinding storyline. There are houses as well, but don't expect any human life forms on this Island (the chickens won't talk to you either). Oh and don't get to close to the waterfalls. Those are kinda ugly, sorry.
+- I like the fact that you can walk away from the linear path if you wan't to. Unfortunately if you don't like chasing frogs it's not very rewarding. You'll just discover dead ends and a need to travel back to the path in order to hear the story being told. So in the end there's not a lot to do in this walking simulator.
+ The story told is not all that coherent, but I think it's allright. I don't mind the voice either, although sometimes the lady can be hard to understand because the music is too loud. Which brings us to the next point.
- The (lack of) options menu: To get to the options menu you must quit the game you're playing and start the game over again. Why the hell is that?
- Not that there is a real reason to go there since here are no options to adjust music or voice volume, nor are there subtitles available. To me this is an almost gamebreakingly bad omission in any game (when omitted of course).
- When you quit the game you have to start over again. I'm sure this is just a short experience meant to be completed in one sitting, but it's a rather unfriendly thing to do anyway.
- Why am I a generic douchey bald guy in generic white trash clothing?
All in all I like Drizzlepath. It's a little underdeveloped, short but pretty and offered with discount on a regular basis. So get it when it's on sale and enjoy a short hour of leafs and sunshine.

Shellshock live is a fantastic value. A simple game that has a lot of content to unlock in terms of new weapons, upgraded weapons, new maps, improvements to your tank such as better tracks, more armor and more critical hits. I have played the game for more than 200 hours and I am still playing. The only negative I can say about the game is that it can become fustrating at higher levels. Even though the game is fairly simple (just move your tank, aim and shoot) some players don't realize what they need to do to help their team at higher levels. At the begining of the game the area effect weapons are not very powerful. It doesn't matter if your teammates are close together. But at higher levels, as the area effect weapons become more powerful, it can really hurt your team if they bunch up. It can be very fustrating if another teammate moves close to your tank because the enemy will target you with their large blast radius weapons, knowing that they can hit two tanks with one weapon.
Overall I highly recommend this game, it is a great value for the price and alot of fun. Just be prepared for some fustration at higher levels if you don't have good teammates on your side.

It's a decent game, but I'm still giving this one as well as the Breakdown DLC a thumbs down.
The game starts out quite promising, but turns out to be repetitive and boring as soon as you've established a decent home base. The zombie sandbox seems vast at first, but excitement fades when you realize that the houses are pretty much the same everywhere. There aren't that many interesting items or people to find. And even though Breakdown seemingly adds more challenge to the game, things get pretty easy as soon as you've established a home base and started upgrading your characters.
Your neighbors are super needy, you constantly need new equipment for your home base and there's always some shmuck that has to be saved or a zombie horde that has to be mowed down. In the end you just drive repetitively from one waypoint to another until you've helped everyone with their needy needs and the game is over.
At worst the zombies are mildly annoying. The fight system doesn't offer much immersion. You just keep clicking and "smash spacebar not to die". The game would have benefited from a more hands on fight system like they had in Condemned.
State of Decay had some redeeming qualities, mainly the way you're able to earn people's trust and create a community of survivors. The scripted events breathe life into the characters who are actually able to do some useful stuff on their own while you're completing missions. And if they die you can't bring them back. The graphics are pretty okay and there's a satisfying POK sound when your baseball bat hits an armored zombie's helmet.
The game is very ambitious, and while it doesn't suck horribly, I still feel it falls short.

I purchased this for the xbox however since then have all but abandoned it entirely in favour of PC gaming. For this and because I was hoping it would run alot better in general on PC I recently bought it when it was on sale.
The good thing is its definately superior to the xbox version, which quite frankly felt like it was struggling to truly run it properly - things rendering slowly, objects poping out of nowhere while moving round... Well my experience so far (i3 2100, 8gb ram, Raedon HD 7750) is its a smoother experience by miles so far. I can't seem to get better with 50fps (while running fraps though) and min was around 26-27, but stable 30-40s when not on the higher graphic settings (which tbh wasn't significant enough for me to care). I was however disapointed not to be able to hit 60+ fps and while I know I haven't got a high end rig its not bad at all and runs much more graphically intensive games nicer. It seems strange to me it has the same issues of objects popping in on screen and such that the xbox has, it seems practically like this was how it was programmed so that it could originally run on the xbox to me. Either way my rig loads up these missing objects and such a great deal faster than the xbox, which is a small positive to take from that.
Settings wise its a bit of a disapointment if you want to be able to fully customise them, just a simple slider with presets. Mouse and keyboard, despite me hearing it being awful on release with my experience in game so far works great. Had to change a few keybindings for my preference but other than that works fantastically, and I highly recommend it as aiming with the controller (asif you need telling) is terrible!
Gameplay for anyone who hasn't played it certainly won't disapoint. You lead a group of survivers trying to stay alive. You need to build up your settlement, find and rescue other survivers, find supplies to keep alive, look after your group, and so on and so on... If you like RPGs this game is great. If you like zombie games you'll love this. Combat (except lifeline perhaps) encourages you to avoid engaging zombies, or to use guns (if you've even found any and enough ammo for them!) as a last resort. Meleeing will be your main approach in a combat situation with one of many weapons such as baseball bats, crowbars, frying pans...! And this aspect of the game is absolutely solid. Gunplay is equally fun but I highly recommend using keyboard and mouse over the controller or precise aiming may be tricky. And its important since you can only kill zombies with headshots, likewise you can only actually kill zombies in melee by decapitating them, which usually involves knocking them around till you can knock them down or stun them, then going for the finishing blow.
Overall I'd say this is definately a port and it shows to me, however this is a fun game which you could (especially with the dlc, which I haven't even covered) be spending many fun hours playing if this so far sounds like something you'd like. I definately recommend it, but if you have it on xbox then unless you want to play with mods or keyboard and mouse you might want to consider it more carefully before buying it on here, because it definately performs better, just not necessarily as well as you'd think.

This caught me out.
I struggled through quite a majority of this Visual Novel. My comments to friends regarding how I felt about it were fairly negative, I complained incessantly; the tiny voice in my mind was constantly criticising, and I originally planned to write a very half-hearted review highlighting all of the flaws and simply leaving it at that.
However, the old saying; 'Don't judge a book by its cover' should be referenced heavily here. It is not about the style of the text nor about the illustrations, but primarily how the story is interpreted and how it makes us think and feel.
Ultimately, I was wrong, I was the sceptic reader, and  I...was the one who burst into tears at 11:30 pm on a Wednesday night over some watermelon. It felt like I'd been slammed sideways by a train, actually. Which I'm still fairly surprised about considering it was only until the
that I understood what was happening, and my cynicism was instantly humbled.
I do hold overall high praise for 'Lucy: The Eternity She Wished For,' but I can not dismiss that it is not without flaws.

There are a few, particularly in the direction of the script. Where was the proof reading? I tend to allow a little space for translated texts, but the sheer number of spelling errors, translation malapropisms, and punctuation flaws – spending a little extra time with a critical eye would have been incredibly beneficial here.
The translation itself felt very...robotic! Stilted language has a habit of slowing down the natural flow and pace of a story, which is very important to fully immerse a reader in the world you are creating. (I am certainly not the greatest writer, but it did feel like trying to drag a particularly large and heavy table around with me at all times. Yes, a table, why not a table.)
I do wish there had been more animation, that more varying slides of art had been used, and that the translation was clearer.
- The extra content included I would deem as essential to experiencing the full story. Please don't forget those.
- I believe that the steam store page provides enough basic information on the plot for me not to reference it any further here. I would avoid checking out video reviews if you can to avoid spoilers.
I have to recommend this, as it is only one of two games that have made me cry, and anything that can drag that much emotion out of me, is definitely worth recommending. However, if script errors irritate you, even in the smallest doses, I would advise thinking carefully before investing money.

Miscreated, that one survival game people got attracted by its flashy trailer.
However, Miscreated is actually a good game, most of the negative reviews are people who didn't take their time to learn this game and instead went crying on the reviews. It's insanely easy to find your friends once you learn the map, it's easy to find a gun with bullets, even in a 40 pop server, it's easy to find action in a >30 pop server, so please stop crying about those things.
The reason I'm actually not recommending this game is thanks to its development.
A while ago, there were big patches, so much new content added every month, now what? Even doe it seems the development team has got bigger, it seems like they took 3 steps back with the new content. Just go ahead and read the patch notes, every single thing seems something worked on about 1 hour just to increase the patch notes lenght and keep the fanbois happy. They say they listen too much the community, in reality it's bs. They don't listen to the community for that particular reason. BASE BUILDING. Yeah base building, the cancer of this game. It's been out for 2.5 years, and they yet have to fix floating bases, they yet have to make it entertaining, something like base raiding closer to rust, with explosives and stuff like that, but no, you just have to grab some food, some hatchets, find a base that is not floating (good luck) and keep spamming mouse1 at the door, then the next door and repeat this process for an hour.
Also the game says "Survive even Mother Nature itself" hahaha. Enter a house, and you will 100% find food and water.
What about vehicles? Oh well, it seems like fewer and fewer spawn because people just store them in their floating bases and use them as a storage and there's literally a Cap for cars to spawn. What about PvP? It's the only fun of this game, but as you may have guessed, many people tend to just be taken away by bases. Even doe PvP gets your heart racing and stuff like that, don't waste your time in this forever-early access survival bs.
TL;Dr
Pros
- Good PVP
- Good Graphics
- "Fun" to explore the map
Cons
- Bs development
- Floating Bases
- Base Building based on grinding
- Car hoarding
- Literally no survival aspect
Oh and if you complain that people always go KOS, please uninstall or go in a RP server.

Holy smokes this game makes me sweat! Bought it about two months ago and have been totally hooked.
Pros:
-The game is frickin gorgeous! Even on my mid-range rig I often find myself stopping to simply admire the scenery. The weather effects are super immersive.
-Loot is not easy to find at first, but it spawns in logical places and after a few hours I had a grasp of how to get geared up pretty quick.
-Mutants (zombies) are not really a huge threat in small numbers, but if you get complacent (too loud, not paying attention) they will humble you really quick.
-Interaction with other players is an absolute adrenaline rush. Whether you are stalking a geared up team, or putting yourself out there to help a fresh spawn you could be killed at any time...or meet your new best friend.
-The development team has been super consistent with monthly updates. They add content, and then they hotfix any resulting bugs over the next few weeks instead of letting them fester until the next scheduled update.
-You can catch mofos on fire with a crossbow!
Cons:
-The bugs are there. The cursor bug, phantom gunshots, invisible items in storage, spawning in the middle of the ocean, vehicles clipping through the world floor, etc. Most of these bugs can be worked around, but this review would not be honest without mentioning that there will be some frustrating moments. #earlyaccess
-Floating bases still exist. People will secure their posessions in the best way they are able to, so we get these eyesores. This will eventually be fixed.
-Server hosting is a bit tedious. There is only one option for renting a server (i3d) and admin powers are fairly limited right now. (Choose restart times, set day/night pattern, initiate weather effects, ban players.) For the record I don't think admins should ever be able to spawn or despawn items.
Overall this game is extremely enjoyable. The paranoia and danger of interacting with other players, combined with losing all your stuff if you die creates a real sense of desperation and a fear of loss. You will be shaking the first time you get in a gunfight and make it out alive.
Oh and come on out to our server called GASTOWN.

This review is for the BREAKDOWN DLC, because there appears to be no way to review the DLC on its own page
First, I will say this: I think State of Decay is possibly the best zombie game I've ever played.  A perfect middle-ground between tense, thoughtful, strategic survival sim and arcadey zombie-killing fun.  It's clearly a labor of love, and I commend Undead Labs for what they've achieved.
That said, the Breakdown DLC: a DLC that, in essence, adds an 'endless' mode to the base game by changing the scripts around, recycling the base map, and gradually ramping up the difficulty.  A good addition, in theory, albeit a bit expensive for what it does.  My big problem is that, for whatever reason, the breakdown DLC actually ADDS BUGS to the game.  Within an hour of playing, I noticed two problems that weren't present throughout my first playthrough of vanilla SoD: first, the on-screen button prompts flicker between keyboard and gamepad input; a problem that isn't necessarily debilitating if you've played it through already using one input or another, but it definitely wasn't present before the DLC.  Second, and considerably more game-affecting: while driving, if you pull up the in-game map and then close it, your character leaps out of the vehicle they're driving.  WHAT?  This was NEVER a problem, and this is SERIOUSLY debilitating if you want to be able to drive and know where you're going.  The fact that I've noticed these two bugs in less than half an hour of play is telling.
I loved vanilla SoD, and I stand by it as an excellent zombie survival sim.  That said, I cannot recommend the Breakdown DLC in its current state, no matter how much I love it in theory.  Caveat emptor.

.EXE is a Rouge-Lite Platformer game about an emoticon trying to escape deletion. In this game, you will jump and shoot through several randomly picked levels, collect items and powerups, and fight enemies until you reach the exit.
I was pretty on the fence about whether I should reccomend this game or not. Personally, though I do have a lot of problems with the game, a decent amount are personal, and should be taken with a grain of salt. I do find the game fun when I'm not having to play through a low power level, and when you get a run that only gives you good power-ups, then it's a great time. The music in this game is also really great to listen to. I would say that you should check this game out if you are really interested in it. You may see something in it that I did not.

Quite a fun platformer that has high replay-ability! The art style is by far one of the simplest but most elegant styles ever implemented into a platformer/rouge-lite game. The feel of this game captures some of the best elements from the Binding of Isaac series as well as Super Meat Boy. It is a difficult but rewarding game! I am most looking forward to the level editor which will further this games potential! At its current price-point, this game is by far a good one to pick-up (even before the release of the level editor).
Ultimately this game takes me back to my SNES/SEGA days as a gamer. Unlike the vast majority of games now-a-days, this game is actually difficult and at time unforgiving but completion is very much rewarding. Just like many of the platformers from SEGA, SNES, NES, etc. Its retro style stirs memories from the past while the new-age elements bring this game full circle.
Fun and easy to pick up.

The Binding of Isaac, what started out as a flash game put onto Steam eventually became overhauled and put in the spotlight, allowing it to go from just a Steam-exclusive game to fulfilling McMillin's dream of having one of his games on an official Nintendo console. Now, as much as I love the mods to death here, I'll try to stay within the Vanilla package.
Story: Isaac and his mother lives in a small house on a hill. "God" comes in and demands his mom to 'cleanse' him of his sins, which includes taking away his possessions and locking him away in his room. Without anymore things to 'clean' off Isaac, He commands his mom to sacrifice him to prove that she loves Him above all else. It's relatively typical, though also pretty fantastical in the extremes Isaac's Mom goes to "clean" him for God. 8.5/10
Graphics: The style here is pixel-art, and I must say that it's some of the best work done yet. Out with the butt-ugly drawn butt-ugly enemies and bosses and in comes the pixelated and well-drawn butt-ugly enemies and bosses. Each stage has its own unique theme and each variant has their unique touches to make the game seem so large. Ingenius, though the only one that doesn't have its own unique stage creation is The Void, though it does have its own theme. 9.5/10
Sound and Music: While Danny B. is not involved in Rebirth, he's replaced by Ridiculon, who does a great job interpreting their music into the game and have it incorporated into the actions of Isaac. While a lot of sounds have been replaced, some are reused from Edmund's sound library, but they do lend themselves fantastically to the killing of localized eldrich abominations. Overall: 10/10
Controls: Controls are tight, using WASD to control Isaac in this labyrinth of rooms and floors. In contrast with a lot of games, which either uses just the arrow keys or WASD, they also incorporate the arrow keys to direct Isaac's tears towards where ever you shoot, which is pretty amazing in itself. E for bombing and R for resetting, whether scumbaggy or not, is pretty good in their right. Finally, CTRL for dropping potentially unwanted trinkets and/or pills makes it much easier to control what build you want to create. 9/10
Overall and other mentions: This game is really a masterpiece of the Steam Indie Games. Where as a reboot or a remake usually fails on key components, primarily due to age difference or different engines, this game takes the original game, puts it on steroids, and have it beat the living Hell out of the original. The absolutely best part is the mods available to you for any owners of Afterbirth+. This game really is something fantastic, so it gets a 9.5/10 because it's as close to perfect without actually being perfect.

If you're here for a review, well too bad!
Instead, I'm gonna teach you how to make some good ol' meatballs!
So, Lets get started:
Meatballs are easy to make, versatile and a great all-round crowd-pleaser. Here, we show you how to make them.
They’re perfect in homemade tomato sauce, served with spaghetti, rice, mashed potatoes, polenta or a nice chunk of crusty bread. They’re easy to freeze, too – why not whip up a double batch and pop the leftovers in the freezer, ready to add straight to the pan for a quick weeknight dinner?
Meatballs are at their best when you use a mixture of meat, such as beef or veal and pork, to really maximise the flavour and texture. Combine with breadcrumbs, egg yolk and your preferred herbs and spices and you’ll have the makings of a nutritious, firm family favourite.
These meatballs with a sweet, chilli-spiked tomato sauce serve four people. Get your shopping list here, then follow the simple steps below. A little tip to make your life much easier; wet your hands before you start rolling your meatballs to stop the meat sticking to them.
HOW TO MAKE MEGA MEATBALLS EVERY TIME
To make the tomato sauce, peel and finely chop 1 small onion. Place in a pan over a low heat with a splash of olive oil, cover and cook until really soft. Increase the heat, bash and add 1 small fresh chilli, then pour in 1 x 400g tin of plum tomatoes and 1 wineglass of water
Season lightly and cook gently for 30 minutes, then break up the tomatoes
Whiz 2 stale slices of bread (crusts removed) in a food processor. Place in a large bowl with 250g each of quality minced beef or veal and higher-welfare minced pork. Separate and add 1 egg yolk
Finely chop and add the leaves from 1 sprig of fresh rosemary and a few fresh sage leaves. Finely grate in the lemon zest and ½ teaspoon of fresh nutmeg, then scrunch and mix with wet hands
Season and shape into little balls – roughly the size of gobstoppers
Add 3 to 4 tablespoons of olive oil to a hot pan. Brown the meatballs all over, but be careful not to break them up
Add them to the pan with the tomato sauce, stir carefully, cover, and braise gently for 45 minutes or until cooked
Serve each portion with rice or crusty bread, scattered with a few raw peas, pecorino shavings and fresh marjoram leaves, if you like.
Follow this basic principle and you’ll be whipping up meatballs in no time at all. When you get the hang of it, tweak the flavours to what you like best – try adding parsley, garlic and even grated Parmesan for an indulgent twist or swap out the meat altogether and use fish instead. Enjoy!

Visual novels are one of my favorite forms of storytelling, and after finding this game through
, I was excited to play it, expecting similar but still different themes as they are set in the same universe.
I was very wrong, and that's probably for the better.
2064 is definitely a better GAME. While Va-11 Hall-a was a better story, but that doesn't mean 2064 was bad in anyway. It was just different on several different levels. Let me explain.
While Va-11 Hall-a follows one character (ie. Jill), while 2064 follows the duo of Turing and it's Protagonist (ie. YOU). This creates more of a social feel to 2064, kind of like that you're never alone, but also completely rules out the use of internal monologue. By far the main difference in between the two, is while Va-11 Hall-a has a very melancholy tone, where the sadness is more than present, you always feel like it will be okay in the end throughout the entire novel, but that feeling is very much absent in 2064, the entire game is just simply far darker and there are many moments where you feel like everything is gonna be f*cked and there's nothing you can do about it, which, after the ending, makes it a very round and good experience
Now lets compare one last thing between the two games: Waifus
An all important topic to cover at any stage of review for any game, the quality of Waifu in a game much uphold to the style and setting of the game as well, if that made sense.
Va-11 Hall-a is called WaifuBartending for a reason, Jill is actually a very lovable protagonist and you always feel as though you want the best for her, while in 2064, YOU are the progagonist, and you may or may not be a massive d*ckhead, quite probably the former.
Supporting cast wise, both are evenly matched, both have a quirky robot,
, both have adorable hackers,
, both have a dynamic duo
, and both have an all important badass
. So supporting cast wise the game are quite similar, with a few small changes.
Overall the game was a pleasent experience, I finished it in the span of a day and while it was enjoyable I don't intend on replaying it anytime soon.
