I learned about this game way back when SuperGreatFriend was sampling different demos for the Ouya. The old skool point and click style mechanics and cyberpunk aesthetics really hit something positive with me, and I waited patiently for it to grace Steam with it's presence.
I've played and beaten the game twice, before and after getting the major patch release, and overall this game certainly packs a lot of nostalgic cyberpunk charm.
Mechanics are simple enough; it emulates just like a classic point and click adventure game that you would run across old PC-98 titles, or those such as "Snatcher". Speaking of the later, if you're an avid fan of that game, you'll find quite a few visual tributes scattered in ROM. The Arcade mini-game is a HUGE nod to it.  Only minor issue is sometimes I have to click a few times in the menu to get to a new screen. I use a track pad so I don't think this is a big deal.
There's a huge diverse cast of characters, with very realistic personalities and goals.  The voice talents did a fabulous job maintaining that with their respective characters as well. (4Moolah and Charlie being some of my top favorites.)
In the updated version, it opened up more character backstories with Jess and Leon, which I really appreciated.
I very much enjoy the animation and art style, hands down. My growing up with 90's anime may or may not have anything to do with this.
My only critique is that I feel sometimes it's better to show than tell a situation. I would get easily lost in some of the techno-speak, and moments regarding Hayden himself doesn't feel as impactful if it's just being discussed. For moments like reviewing the data cache and disks, I would rather see it than just be told what's going on.
Other than that, this is a fun and engaging game. It's got a bit of replay-ability depending on what dialogues you choose. (and if you♥♥♥♥♥♥off certain characters too many times.) Also pay close attention to the posters at the bar if you want to unlock a new area.
I will gladly continue supporting MidBoss as they develop new and engaging titles.

I originally heard of this game through a friend of mine as a cyberpunk point and click adventure game that has a cute AI sidekick. As someone who grew up on point and click adventure games, I was intrigued by the premise and eventually got the game through Humble Bundle when it was on sale. I played through the original Read Only Memories, then the 2064 updated release. I got every achievement, saw every ending, and even after 70+ hours of gameplay, I'm still finding new things in the game.
Overall, it's a great game and I really enjoy playing it. The 2064 update improved on several points of the base game, making it an even better experience. If you are interested in a brighter variety of cyberpunk (though it's got plenty of dark as well) exploring the age old question of what it means to be human with a heavy social commentary on the side, then this game might interest you.
The graphics are inspired by Japanese adventure games like SNATCHER, and there's a charm to the artstyle. The character portraits and animations are fluid and really help conveying the emotion in the dialogue. As far as scenes go, the game is fairly static using fade-ins/outs to convey events happening on the screen. There are a few dynamic scenes in the more important parts of the game, such as characters running towards a taxi.
The music is done by 2 Mello, which is really catchy and fits the game's mood and atmosphere.
I found the sound effects to be charming, such as the jingles when you find a solution. The characters also have "voice blips" whenever they talk without voice acting, with different characters having different pitches.
The voice acting is also excellent and really helps deliver the game's story. The voices fit their characters well. There are some quality issues, such as some of the minor characters' voices sounding like they come from a headset, but that didn't detract from the overall experience.
Another note is that the voice acting is unfortunately inconsistent, as there are parts of the game where voice acting isn't available. This mostly applies to flavor texts, but there are a few mandatory parts of the game where I feel should have been voice acting. However, it's been explained by the developers that initially they only wanted to cover major scenes of the game, then branched it out only later on, so not every line made it into the cut.
The game is advertised as a point and click adventure, and it does contain elements of that. You can navigate your way in the game world and LOOK, USE, TALK to your surroundings where it applies, or have the option to use your inventory items on objects/people. There's a lot of flavor text to explore this way, adding to the world building and are often humorous as well, making it worthwhile to observe everything.
The game's puzzles are fairly simple and straightforward, which I didn't mind too much because of how counter-intuitive adventure game puzzles can be at times, but at the same time it can feel lacking in this department. What I liked however, is that there are multiple solutions to a given situation and each result in different dialogue. For example, you can pick up a brick at one point, which can be used for 3 puzzles during the game, or keep it in your inventory through the whole ordeal. Failing puzzles aren't punishing either, and in fact serve as alternate routes, adding to the replay value. For example, failing to catch two people lets you request help from two different options, each with unique dialogue later on.
However, the game definitely leans more on dialogue and storytelling than puzzles. Your dialogue choices shape your relationship with the characters, which feels quite organic and your treatment of others does have consequences.
It's important to note that the game lacks auto-saving, and currently there's no way to speed up/skip dialogue, but both issues have been noted by the developers.
Lastly, the game allows you to choose from nonbinary pronouns or even pick custom ones, which is a really nice touch for those who need it.
The plot takes place in the world of Neo-San Francisco, 2064 AD. You are a bumbling journalist trying to make ends meet by writing reviews about free headphones, when Turing, the first sapient machine, breaks into your house and kicks off the plot. Turing asks for your help to find Hayden Webber, their creator, who has gone missing.
As you delve deeper into the mystery, you meet a variety of people along the way, such as a hotheaded punk with a geeky companion, a budding musician or an old lady with a bear butler. Despite being an optimistic and more colorful cyberpunk story, there's plenty of dark beneath the surface that will pull its punches on you. The issues brought up within the game also eerily parallel real life problems, pretty bluntly in fact, which isn't necessarily a bad thing as I found it quite thought provoking and actually changed my view on a few matters. Even though your mission is grim and the secrets aren't all that pretty, there's still plenty of lighter moments and humor which didn't feel jarring and still made me chuckle.
The game's endgame is very emotional and intense, Chapter 6 is easily my favorite all the way through and the highest point in the story.
After that, everything's wrapped up in a light hearted post-game chapter, Endless Christmas, but not without leaving you thoughts to consider and wonder about for the events to come in the game's world.
As noted, there's the player character, you as a journalist in a nutshell. You are pretty much a blank slot with loose ties to some of the characters (like Hayden being a close friend of yours, Lexi being your long-time friend) which helps you immerse yourself in the game's world and story, I found myself wondering what was my past with them. It may have helped to have a more defined protagonist, but I enjoyed my role in the story regardless.
Turing is pretty much the main character of the story. Turing does the exposition and often does the talking for you. I felt like there were responses that could have been done by the player instead of just Turing to make scenes feel less one-sided.
But that aside, Turing as a sapient machine and a very new being, thus is like a child. They'll be often rather bratty and have a tendency to talk down, but they need help to go on as well. Depending on how you treat Turing, they develop and grow accordingly. I felt your relationship with Turing was handled very organically, and seeing how Turing grew as a character and how our adventure together affected them was great to see all the way through. Turing is ultimately very much lovable and cute. Well, they know they are cute, though.
The rest of the cast is very much diverse. You meet people of varying sexuality, gender and race, but nobody felt like a walking stereotype or hamfisted. Also, none of the characters are who they seem at first. You get a better grasp of some of them during the course of the story, others take reflection to wonder about their true personalities and motivations. Overall, the cast is quite likable and intriguing.
Despite the issues and imperfections the game has, it left a great impact on me and I'm really glad I got to experience it all. It's a memorable game I'm going to cherish for a long time, I can only recommend it.

I don't have an excessive time in it, but my experience with what I have done with the game so far was so bad that I refunded it.
Let's give some context here, Here is a game that is no longer in early access and with system requirements that my computer easily exceeds. So why is it that whenever the game decides it's going to rain my FPS has to completely drop to 30 or lower? Why is this a normal occurance that this community just accepts? Performance is all over, it's overall playable I guess, but if what I hear is true, once you get to populated planets or a hub the framerate is terrible too. This rediculous, and these positive reviews were not covering this as if it didn't matter??
But I'm Me, I played on an Intel HD 1000 for a long time in the past, low fps is something I can handle. But the UI, ohhhh my goodddddddddd. The UI is awful, I mean this is not a subjective thing, it IS DREADFUL to use, it is so jarring to play games like Terraria, Minecraft or most any PC game and then go to this game. You find it's clunky, difficult to find anything, difficult to navigate and so on. It's digusting how bad a PC games interace is. And it does get in the way, you WILL fight with it. Why can't I just right click crafting stations, storage, doors etc like every other PC game of this genre? You instead have to hover over it and press E. Because of course, the slower route is basically the only route right now.
Add onto this, crafting is annoying, it takes time to craft things, and you need to keep the crafting window open which can be annoying to watch, but I guess this is a survival game technically. By like the furthest definition of it. Which brings me to the food meter, that doesn't get explained to you in the tutorial until your close to starving, I seriously didn't even know it was there, it's just a bar sitting up in the corner, it doesn't have a food icon or anything. It feels like such a tacked on feature that doesn't have to exist, and wouldn't lose anything by getting rid of it.
Finally the games melee combat is terrible, especially against multiple enemies, the sword doesn't just swing like it should, it does a little combo animation thing over and over, which looks nice but doesn't keep enemies back even if you are backpeddling away from them. It also doesn't strike smaller units that manage to be under the sword when you are striking and it feels very unfun to use. Terraria did this much better by having swords arch down more.
I know my hours don't show much, but this was enough to make me refund the game, it feels very unprofessional and I have no idea what is in store after I leave the beginning planet, and quite frankly I don't care anymore.
If these seem minor to you then pick it up if the other reviews convince you, if these could bother you, then maybe check into workarounds or wait to see if they get fixed.

Pillars of Eternity has vastly improved since it was released. Back then, I loved everything about it except the gameplay- it was just too f*cking hard and there was NO difficulty settings! So, I was unable to enjoy the rich storyline. Luckily, the devs listened and created a fully fleshed out Difficulty System as would be expected in any other game. I recommend that you swallow your pride on this one and play on either Story mode or Easy mode, because anything higher is brutal on a level I haven't seen since Dark Souls.
★STORY★
The story is absolutely well done. In a time when a unique story is hard to come by, Pillars provides with gusto. There's lore a plenty and volumes of text to read about everything within the world you'd want to know. The quests range from casual to brutal and are interesting through and through.
★GAMEPLAY★
Instead of the HP system that we've all come to love and accept, Pillars said, "Naw, let's do endurance instead!" And there's the main problem. Yes, there's a priest class, but they can't heal HP. In fact, NOTHING can heal HP in Pillars of Eternity except resting. Yep, so that means tough fights just got a whole lot tougher for no reason. So, I'm taking a star off for that one.
★SOUND & MUSIC★
I paid extra just to have the soundtrack to Pillars of Eternity, that's how good it is. When I'm playing other games, I'm listening to their soundtrack instead. The voice acting is also top notch, very well done with unique voices added to the mix. This is one area where the game excels.
★BUGS & BOTHERS★
Most of my complaints have been fixed so kudos to you, Pillars!

One of the two games that came out in the rash of Kickstarted CRPG's alongside Wasteland II and Divinity:Original Sin.  Obsidian tried to recapture the feel of Infinity Engine Games in this release and did a good bit of work in making it feel familiar to Baldur's Gate.
The game follows the story of a migrant who travels to a cursed land and survives an accident with an eventually fatal and debilitating injury to his soul.  You journey around the land to find out what happened to you, find a conspiracy which created the curse in the land, work to remove it and learn a little about the metaphysics of the world you belong to.
Such follows the story in a nutshell.  The only problem I had was how it felt rushed in some places.  While the game is not rushed, (there are a lot of side quests small stories set as an aside, with plenty to do to keep you occupied) the main story is in some places.  In many cases it feels that as you are exposed to the antagonists you feel a rush to resolve things quickly at a fast pace and it feels that the main story is just a side quest with more meat to it in an open game.
The encounters are carefully crafted and will require you to understand your characters, their classes, and how they function.  Improper gear and tactics will cause you to suffer even at the lower difficulty levels.  Furthermore, difficulty only changes the number of enemies you face and not the difficulty of them - save for Path of the Damned difficulty which gives the enemies a large boost to their stats.  Character growth is kept carefully controlled, you should only be able to finish some encounters instead of others and there is a cap to the amount of xp you can receive from enemies so the game is very aware of your strength and how much it can challange you.
The first thing which I had to beat in my head while I was playing this game, was despite its similarities, it is not an Infinity Engine Game and the classes and attributes are not D&D.  You need to understand what your attributes are and how they affect your build, I would very much suggest reading guides on this to understand what they do before you jump into it.  Classes also behave similarly - even though they have D&D parallels, they function nothing like they do in D&D so have a look at how they work.
The next thing to notice is that once you understand this is that the story companions are somewhat underpowered with poor attributes or attributes that slot them into only one role which you may not desire.  This isn't necessarilly bad, the game does teach you that min-maxing is unnecessary but desirable.  It doesn't matter since you can hire characters you stat and create at any inn.  However, the story companions are so well written and have nice enough ambient dialogue, you feel like you're missing out if you don't take them.  Even if you have problems later in the game you can respec and change the abilities of any of your characters at any point in the game to match an encounter or group of enemies (Provided you have White March Installed).
You will find more than enough money to make it through the game and be able to frivolosly spend it as you need on weapon enchantments, character respecs, new characters, and whatever to kit yourself out for a dungeon or floor.  However, the early game will always have issues in money aquisition.
You will also get a stronghold where you can do a lot of merchant work, play around in inns get quests and enter a large dungeon.  It is also depressingly empty.  I remember the podcast where obsidian showed it off to a reviewer and the first question he asked was "Where are the NPCs?" and the obsidian rep looked as though it was the first time he noticed it.
The UI and menus are easy to work with aside from some uncomfortable shifting with windows to manage storage and character inventory.  It's easy to work with, intuitive, and is a better example of UI polish than what Beamdog did with the Enhanced Editions of Bauldur's Gate.
I won't address the expansions in this review beyond saying they expand gameplay a lot and, if you have them installed, you should enter them as soon as possible in the story for the prospect of new things to do - the White March integrates itself into the midgame seemlessly without you having to wait until the endgame.
In all, I'd say it's a well polished game with a few problems from bits of story that feel cut short.  I'd recommend it to any fan of CRPG's and this is a must buy for any fan of Infinity Engine Games.

For lack of a more concise description, this is basically a fully 3D Diablo 2 with a much more diverse class system.
Theres 6 different classes, each with 3 masteries or - if you prefer - you can make a hybrid which takes any 2 masteries and smashes them together into a single class for you. Skills arent presented in trees and instead allow freeform purchasing: they just cost extra SP the higher a skill they are and you can "buy back" used skill points to re-apply them to higher skills later on.
Theres no inventory tetris and instead you just have a fixed number of bag slots which can be increased by finding other bags of holding. There is, however, an equipment slot for every damn body part to think of.
Its not a terribly pretty game, but its all randomly generated. You start in a town which has residents, vendors et al which can starve,  catch diseases and may also come under attack. Its up to you to babysit them while dungeoneering.
Lot of play for that price.

I've been a huge Splinter Cell fan since the first part and so played every single one of the franchise.
So I felt like Chaos Theory was the last )
(and best!) Splinter Cell in terms of gameplay and stealthiness. The 2 following games,
and
felt quite disappointing and not like good 'ol Splinter Cell to me.
That being said, I was unsure if I really should give
a chance, as I also was warned that it might disappoint me aswell.
When the game was offered for around 10 bucks, I decided to give it a try.
And honestly I was quite surprised!
+ the game offers you to choose your own playstyle. You're able to choose between 3 different approaches each mission: Ghost (remain unseen and no kills!), Panther (no alarms and stealthy kills) and Assault (just shoot at everything in your sight). If you want to have that original Splinter Cell feel, you definitely should go for Ghost, as it is the most fun (Panther too, but it feels too easy) and I think also most rewarding gamestyle.
+ you can do a lot of sidemissions and you're still able to do a lot of stuff after the quite short main campaign (around 8-10 hours, depending on how your playstyle is)
+ a lot of different weapons and gadgets.
+ the story is quite alright, although nothing really extraordinary. But it does keep up the tension (although you might already know how it ends anyway)
+ the maps/levels are quite cool, also because not everything is during night.
~ it has a coop mode! (Note: I didn't really play it, so I won't judge it as positive or negative. But there are still people who play it, so go ahead!)
~ Uplay. While I'm actually not bothered by it, some people may see this as  negative. I just wanted to mention it, but it doesn't really bother me. A negative point would be that your achievments can only be seen in Uplay, but that's it for me.
~ The soundtrack is alright, but nothing outstanding. Does fit to the game.
~ Graphics are decent, too. The game is around 2-3 years old, so it should run on most computers. Nothing special, though.
- I'll start with the biggest one: the last bossfight.
Oh god, it's so awful. I don't what their aim was for that one, but it is boring, annoying and you don't really know what to do. I think I needed to do it 5-6 times, not because it was difficult but because it's so confusing. As it is the only boss fight, it's forgiveable, but it will be my alltime favorite for worst boss fight of all time. ( I don't want to spoil your *fun*, so that's everything I'll say about it)
- cheesy characters and dialogues.
The hacker dude really has some cringe-worthy moments and lines (tells a bad joke, nobody laughs, he says "What?". Oh god.)  and is such a stereotypical character. Also some dialogues are just too action cliché like. It isn't that bad, but I can't just overlook it .
- The main story is quite short, but I think the additional side missions somehow make up for it.

I wouldn't say that it is a must have because of some minor to major flaws but if you're a fan of the Splinter Cell series and a fan of stealth games, I definitely would say that you should pick it up! Also because it isn't that expensive right now and most importantly it's fun!

I've always liked stories and games involving androids, particulary humanoid ones.  I find the philosophy and ethics surrounding them to be nothing short of fascinating.  So, after being introduced to, and enjoying Emily is Away, I decided to see what Steam had for visual novels.  After some searching, Lucy went on my wishlist and I eventually purchased it when it went on sale, where it sat in my library for several months.  Over the past couple of days, I went through Lucy's storyline and I could point out where I believe it has flaws, because it has a few here and there, but I'm not going to.  That's because everything else about the experience completely overshadowed any negatives I could nitpick at.  It's a touching story with both humor, sadness, and happiness that makes you think.  In addition, being a visual novel, the artwork and soundtrack only enhance the experience.  In particular, the soundtrack is absolutely beautiful.  The only thing to reinforce to anyone curious about this game is that it really isn't a game, per se.  It's a book enhanced with audio and visuals and an admittedly uncommon dialogue choice peppered about for some interactivity.  So, if you're curious about trying out a visual novel for yourself, look no further, because Lucy was truly a rewarding experience.
RATING:  A

TL;DR - Very little content, and multiplayer is too hard. Avoid, unless you like salty Spam n' cheese.
(Updated for Ultra)
1) GFWL
- Support for online play through Games for Windows Live expired July 2014?
Update: Online play has been transfered over to Steamworks. Capcom made statements implying that AE (Steam) players would be able to play against Ultra players. However, I have been unable to confirm this. Servers for GfWL are supposedly still active. So, if you did not transfer your game to Steam, have recently purchased AE via Amazon, or still have your old "CD key"... you can still play on GfWL... supposedly. I have not been able to confirm this either.
2) Trial / Challenge Mode
- A number of factors make this mode impossibly difficult. This mode asks you to perform a specific set of moves/attacks in a sequence. However, there is no explanation and no demonstration. Believe me, it sounds easy to do these sequences, but they are anything but that. The game will ask you to hit your opponent with say, 2 light kicks in a row. You won't be able to do it! It makes no logical sense whatsoever!
- I'm told these are "links". I'm told that with patience and experimentation, you can eventually learn them. I found that you must have perfect timing, spacing and execution. A fraction of a second off, and you fail. The average player will NEVER clear all trials for one(any) character. (Even if you use a guide!) The worst part is that the "dummy" character will block semi-randomly. This means that even if you are good at performing the links, you still risk failure.
3) Online Play
- The game's matchmaking system is just horrible. It's gotten even worse since the beta patch. The game ranks you in a number of different ways. The game is supposed to use this to find similar opponents. I, for example, have roughly 500 Player Points(PP). When I attempt to find opponents using the "same skill" setting, it gives me players with 3000+ PP. It isn't even remotely close to fair. This, and other factors, make online play is exceedingly difficult.
4) It Doesn't Matter How Much Time You Play
- The level of competition in this game is too high. My win percentage, after nearly TWO YEARS of serious effort, is around 35%. I've put over 700 hours into this game. (More than shown here, I know. I played on a friend's Xbox before I owned this version. Also, Steam didn't record hours played in offline mode.) I've spent nearly as much time researching in an effort to get better. Nothing has worked-out. Ultimately, I gave up on being good. Improving in the game feels more like work than entertainment.
- The sad part is that I'm actually pretty good at the game. It just doesn't matter because my average opponent is still x10 better. I've wasted a lot of time on this game. Don't make the same mistake! Abandon all hope if you play USF4 online.
5) Online PLAYERS
- The vast majority of people you'll run into online are jerks. There is a lot of trash talk. There is a lot of rage. (Not surprising really.) It is so bad, I had to mute voice chat. The better players will stomp you, and then play around. They won't even fight you. They'll just run away as long as they have the advantage. If you try to give up, most players won't accept it. They'll hit you a few times, and then taunt until time runs out. Alternately, they send a trollish message like, "whats wrong ;D".
- The kind of person that plays this game... you don't want to know that kind of person. Here's a quote from "The Fighting Game Primer" which can be found at the popular shoryuken website: "Your job is to take the tools the designers have given you - characters with moves - and turn the game into a sheer mess of broken parts that no one ever wants to play again." This ideal has been widely adopted by online players. It is a very good reason to avoid this game. Being locked into place, unable to move because your opponent's attacks never end? That's not fun.
- The Fighting Game Community(FGC) are made up of the most elitist people you will ever encounter. They like to say, "nothing is cheap". Yet these same people complain when someone is "random" or "lame" or "spammy". Their gameplay is highly respectable, yours is lame. See?
6) Arcade Mode
- The best part of this mode is the arcade experience. By that, I refer to the "Battle Request" feature. This allows online players to challenge you whilst you play Arcade Mode. (Just like at a real arcade!) Aside from that, it's bad news. Even on "medium" CPU opponents can be unbelievably difficult. (Blocking everything and countering/punishing with ultra/super!)
- A.I. has improved considerably in Ultra. It now fights much like a typical online warrior. Which means it will cheese you to death. It will find a move you have trouble dealing with, and it will spam it. If you have trouble teching throws, it'll throw you at every opportunity. If there's a specific special move that keeps hitting you, it'll use that move frequently. This is both good AND bad. For one thing, it's really annoying. (It's nice to just fight a dumb A.I. sometimes.) On the other hand, it better prepares players for online play. Anything that can do *that*, is a BIG plus. The A.I. will also block/avoid/punish a lot of things that previously, it would ignore. (Like Ultras. Instead of just eating them. Although it still does that occassionally.)
- Seth still too strong. It must be hard to balance a character with all the greatest moves the game has to offer! Still... more than a little ridiculous that everything he does is un-punishable.
7) Ultra Combos
- Ultra combos are like super moves, only more potent. Ultras are represented by a meter separate from your super meter. The ultra meter is charged as you take damage. The idea is that this gives you a big attack with which to make a comeback. Unfortunately, most characters make it VERY obvious that they are going to utilize their Ultra. As a result, most Ultras are very easy to block or evade entirely. Even worse, your character will just stand there helplessly for several seconds afterward. So, performing your Ultra could lose you the match.
- It is possible to make your Ultra part of a bigger combo. However, this almost always requires a difficult timing that demands precise execution. (Which can be ruined by marginal lag.) It's just another tool for the good players to beat you. So much for a comeback!
8) Old-School Experts
- Many of Street Fighter's biggest fans (and pros) have joined Capcom over the years. As a result, SF4 is "By pros, for pros." If EVO is any indication, they like SF just the way it is. Many pros acknowledge the game is quite difficult to get into, but they have no idea. If you developed your skills back during the days of S-Turbo, then you don't know what it is like to start these days. A lot of what you have learned has become something you just assume, or take for granted. I'm being asked to learn, before I can EVER hope to win, TWENTY-FIVE YEARS worth of tactics and strategies.
I gave up on this one. I only play to remind myself why I quit! I can't recommend it to anyone. Even if you have LOADS of free time to sink into the game. After two years of effort, I'm ready to say it's just not possible to get into this genre. You have to have natural talent. You simply CANNOT train to be good at this game.
Don't believe me? Have fun losing. Because, if you are not god-like-perfect at fighting games, losing is the only possibility when you play Street Fighter IV online. If you hear that this game is great for casual play, please know this is a lie. This is not a game for casual or even average players. This game is for fighting game PROS ONLY. Anyone else will waste their money and time. (Like me.)

Drizzlepath is a pure walking simulator with great atmosphere and changing environment as you progress farther. It’s a very short experience accompanied by nice sounds and narration. There is nothing to discover / explore, just the beautiful landscape.

This is an interesting experience and its worth your time.
It is a one man project and the first one of that Developer.
Yes, you walk along a path and get narration and music along it, it is a "Walking Simulator", and not a game in the usual sense. It does have fall damage, so you can die, but thats about the only thing that will prevent you from finishing Drizzlepath.
You will find beautiful sights along your way, and you can explore almost anywhere you wish to, but for the most part its pretty linear. The details get less when you decide to walk off the path, as its designed to look great along it. The main path will take you maybe about 30 to 60 minutes to reach the end, depending on how fast you take it, it is not a very long experience. But is an idyllic one for sure. The music highlights certain parts of the way, and there could have been more of it.
There are also things that could be improved, Subtitles for example would have helped me greatly to understand the voice of the female narrator, which has a Spanish accent that made me sadly unable to follow much of what she said. I didnt think the narration held any deeper significance and served more as a tool to accompany the character on his way.
Also there where graphical oddities when i wandered off the path, and the waterfalls didn't look right for me, but that might be an issue with my hardware. The game dosent offer much in terms of options for graphics or other settings, but it did run well for me. All in all Drizzlepath looked stunning while following the main path, I think it is a great use of the CryEngine.
You most likely will get value out of this experience, its relaxing, even if it doesn't offer much in replayability. Especially with the very reasonable price point this is offered. Just don't expect something that will keep you busy for a long time, its about taking a short walk along a beautiful path, and thats probably something we all don't do enough =)

This is an older game, but excellent.  You choose to play as a count, duke, or king in Europe and the surrounding era during the Great Crusades, and rule over your family for the next several hundred years.  It has a lot in common with other Paradox Grand Strategy games, however I found this one more engaging and easier to jump into.  It's less about war and more about building a dynasty to last while protecting the faith in missions from the church.
It's absorbing in the way only strategy games can be, but a little buggy and crash-worthy, and a few mods come in handy for fixing the questionable interface graphics, particularly the minimap.  Already becoming one of my favorites games.

Crusader Kings in many ways is a biographer's wet dream. It has mechanics of Europa Universalis 2, the warfare, the economics, the diplomacy but unlike that grand strategy epic, this grand strategy epic portrays you not as some nameless entity ruling your nation through the ages but as the head of a noble medieval family, your faith not tied into the success of the nation you rule but the rulers themselves.
You start the game by picking which family to control, you can start off as a great King yes but you can also choose to play as a powerful Duke or even an impoverished Count. You then set about forging alliances, mostly through marriage, produce offspring that can one day take over the mantle of leadership and assert your claim to various noble titles. As you grow in power and influence new challenges will arise. Conquer too quickly and others will see you as a warmonger, your vassals may grow too powerful and seek to claim your titles for themselves and should you have too many children they may differ over who should rule when you are dead.
Each character has a set of characteristics and traits that wouldn't feel out of place in an RPG. Some traits are purely positive while others make you an inept ruler. Each trait also has an opposite, brave to cowardly and so forth and characters with opposing traits will often dislike each other and this all works together to create a great web of intrigue that makes holding together a great Kingdom a real challenge.
This great seat of intrigue and dynasty building is not without it's flaws however, the lack of any sort of proper tutorial and the rather extreme wealth of information you get showered with from the moment you start up the game makes it near impossible for newcomers to get into the game and even veterans of Europa Universalis 2 will find themselves struggling to keep up with the flow of information.
All in all Crusader Kings is an extremely complex dynasty building game that more often than not throws you into the deep end and see if you can figure out the diplomacy of marriage politics before you die without an heir or have to resort to incest. It is a fun game, once you learn it but unfortunately most people will quit long before that.

This is probably THE reference for all medieval grand strategy fans out there. You can spend hours managing your dynasty's spread across Europe, or keeping in check its many rivals. For a more recent game, check out the sequel : Crusader Kings II.
This game has one of the steepest learning curves ever. If you can figure it out, the gameplay is very satisfying and rewarding.

Read Only Memories is an excellent point and click adventure game. The setting of Neo-San Francisco is well put together, and the world they've built is a very interesting one. You have a lot of control over your actions, and a lot of freedom to solve puzzles in a variety of different ways, not all of which are obvious. However, there are always backup options if you fail one approach, and the game never devolves into pixel-hunting. The game's storyline is also very well put together; it asks questions about what it means to be human without getting overly philosophical, and it's comedic and dramatic without causing mood whiplash. The puzzles serve the story rather than the other way around, so there aren't any points where you feel like you have to look up a strategy guide in order to figure out what happens next. Your choices matter, too, and not just in the "did you get the good ending or the bad ending" way that a lot of games do. All in all, a truly amazing game. Remember to save manually, though!

The story and universe are tightly linked together and fascinating, the best part of the worldbuilding being the intricate world itself. While a few of the level's placement doesn't quite make topological sense, from the player's perspective it's not noticeable.
Dark Souls is a great game to recommend to anyone who has the time to get invested in its world regardless of their ages or skill as long as you have an appreciation for dark fantasy worlds.

I have been a huge fan of RPG's for most of my game-playing life, but few games have been able to recreate the sense of wonder I felt during the Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale times. This game is very different, but it has - at least for me - created a similar sense of immersion and wonder. I've come to care a great deal about my party, the world, and the story even as I see the limitations and shortcomings. The battle system often requires micromanagement, but I find it to be rewarding, engaging, and deep. Many design decisions, such as "per battle" spells, are welcome additions that help stem the monotony of lesser battles. I have my complaints though; the world is smaller than I would have liked and the music isn't as varied as one would expect. However, the moment to moment interaction with the world and overall experience is deep and decision rich.

I've been a huge Splinter Cell fan since the first part and so played every single one of the franchise.
So I felt like Chaos Theory was the last )
(and best!) Splinter Cell in terms of gameplay and stealthiness. The 2 following games,
and
felt quite disappointing and not like good 'ol Splinter Cell to me.
That being said, I was unsure if I really should give
a chance, as I also was warned that it might disappoint me aswell.
When the game was offered for around 10 bucks, I decided to give it a try.
And honestly I was quite surprised!
+ the game offers you to choose your own playstyle. You're able to choose between 3 different approaches each mission: Ghost (remain unseen and no kills!), Panther (no alarms and stealthy kills) and Assault (just shoot at everything in your sight). If you want to have that original Splinter Cell feel, you definitely should go for Ghost, as it is the most fun (Panther too, but it feels too easy) and I think also most rewarding gamestyle.
+ you can do a lot of sidemissions and you're still able to do a lot of stuff after the quite short main campaign (around 8-10 hours, depending on how your playstyle is)
+ a lot of different weapons and gadgets.
+ the story is quite alright, although nothing really extraordinary. But it does keep up the tension (although you might already know how it ends anyway)
+ the maps/levels are quite cool, also because not everything is during night.
~ it has a coop mode! (Note: I didn't really play it, so I won't judge it as positive or negative. But there are still people who play it, so go ahead!)
~ Uplay. While I'm actually not bothered by it, some people may see this as  negative. I just wanted to mention it, but it doesn't really bother me. A negative point would be that your achievments can only be seen in Uplay, but that's it for me.
~ The soundtrack is alright, but nothing outstanding. Does fit to the game.
~ Graphics are decent, too. The game is around 2-3 years old, so it should run on most computers. Nothing special, though.
- I'll start with the biggest one: the last bossfight.
Oh god, it's so awful. I don't what their aim was for that one, but it is boring, annoying and you don't really know what to do. I think I needed to do it 5-6 times, not because it was difficult but because it's so confusing. As it is the only boss fight, it's forgiveable, but it will be my alltime favorite for worst boss fight of all time. ( I don't want to spoil your *fun*, so that's everything I'll say about it)
- cheesy characters and dialogues.
The hacker dude really has some cringe-worthy moments and lines (tells a bad joke, nobody laughs, he says "What?". Oh god.)  and is such a stereotypical character. Also some dialogues are just too action cliché like. It isn't that bad, but I can't just overlook it .
- The main story is quite short, but I think the additional side missions somehow make up for it.
:
I generally recommend this game, as it feels like old splinter cell again (if you're choosing to play ghost!).
I wouldn't say that it is a must have because of some minor to major flaws but if you're a fan of the Splinter Cell series and a fan of stealth games, I definitely would say that you should pick it up! Also because it isn't that expensive right now and most importantly it's fun!

This visual novel by Modern Visual Arts Laboratory feature three different unnamed male protagonists in a futuristic Korean setting, the first of which is a male student simply referred to as You who happened to come across an inactive female android about to be destroyed at a K Robotics junkyard while returning home from school one day. Feeling sorry for the android, You decided to bring the android home, recharge and activate the android which is a PIM-001 android with the name of Lucy Valentine. As You gets acquainted with Lucy in his daily routine amidst the backdrop of a general dislike of androids and robots by the local human population, the visual novel will alternate between You with Lucy and earlier memories of Lucy with her creator also simply referred to as Doctor Ryu.
Although there are no Steam achievements to obtain in this game, the game has an in-game achievement page that will track and show all unlocked in-game achievements that are awarded while playing through the game, making certain gameplay and dialogue choices and reaching a golden ending where additional extra content in the form of additional plot twists, main menu theme background, music and title changes and developer comments will be awarded upon obtaining all in-game achievements and viewing all extra content. There are published community guides to help players get all in-game achievements and extra unlockable content in the game.
The game has more than 2200 positive reviews at the time of this review, great artwork, soundtracks and overall presentation. It would be nice to have a music gallery in the game. Overall, highly recommended when game with ending theme OST are at discount or in a good bundle offer.

This game is extremely cute and extremely familiar for those who grew up in the rustbelt of America (Go Smelters!). An adventure game, where the story and character exploration is the point. Multiple replays are possible and you won't be able to cover everything with one play through, since time is limited and you can only spend so many days out with your buds.
There are also lots of little nooks and crannies, side-quests if you will, if you're willing to explore and look around on a day by day basis as the story progresses.
The end story might seem sudden and fantastical, but it's all easily explained if you carefully put together the pieces (Hint; read the microfilm stories in the library).
The general issues this game deals with are; Growing up, being a weird outsider in a small town, mental illness, poverty and deindustrialization, capitalism, death, family bonds, abuse, relationships, god, and existentialism.
Overall, a great little game. Fantastic aesthetic sense in the art direction, it flows very nicely. Good music, good scenes, great characters with familiar and natural staccato dialogue, great dreamscapes. Expect to spend at least 8 hours on a single playthrough, with multiples possible.

A visually arresting game with a fantastic soundtrack, suprising narrative depth, and a deeply engaging cast of characters. The gameplay itself turns between introspective exploration, light-hearted fun, and often psychologically-difficult minigames, conversations and dream sequences. The amount of agency that the player (as Mae) can exert to make better or worse decisions can sometimes seem frustrating at first, but there's a kind of catharsis that comes from inhabiting her troubled existence that makes even the cringe-iest of moments feel genuine and resonant after they pass. Life can be hard and complicated, and the game confronts you with that directly in both narrative and practical terms.
Night In The Woods really exemplifies the potential of games to be refined, heart-wrenching, interactive art. A definite must buy Indie title.

Another commenter described this game as "Life is Strange: Actually Good Furry Edition," and I'm going to straight up borrow that right here because that is what this game is.
This is a game about life, the good, the bad, the big, the small, and it nails it. Characters, situations, setting, everything is just spot on. I've had games play to my emotions before, but I don't think I've ever legitimately felt for characters as deeply as I have for the cast of this game.
And best of all, when it does mix in fantastical elements, they're done correctly. Whoever made this game understood what the basis of cosmic horror was and how it should be woven into a story. There's a banality, almost a petty smallness, to even them that makes them fit in the story and the world, that makes them feel like they belong there.
TLDR; only game I've played that so efforlessly made the mundane feel magical, and the magical feel suitably mundane. Top marks.

Although I like the concept of a game exploring some of the rewards of hiking and climbing mountains, this ended up being way too pretentious and even less enjoyable than Dear Esther (one of the few games similar to this one); though I might be biased because I've never liked poetry, so I might not be the target audience.
The environmental and visual aesthetics are very good in many respects, but not as diverse and awe-inspiring as Dear Esther in my opinion. Although this is very linear like Dear Esther, Drizzlepath has much more of an open-world feel with less invisible walls. The atmospheric sound-effects were too few and far between for the first half of the game, which drew too much attention to the monotonous footsteps in the midst of near-silence; whereas Dear Esther is chock full of immersive environmental sound-effects every step of the way.
The musical interludes were for the most part too short, too similar and too infrequent to be enjoyable/rewarding for passing through checkpoints; longer songs would've slightly improved the game imo. Given that both Dear Esther and Drizzlepath are very similar types of games, and both have roughly equivalent pretentious elements, I'd recommend getting Dear Esther instead for the extra immersiveness, or Drizzlepath for the extra open-world feel; or both if you want any game that's more interactive poetic film than game.
Please, if any game-devs are reading this, improve on this genre by making similar games that actually reward exploration, while offering thought-provoking philosophical dialogue rather than (imo) inconsequentially poetic nonsense; a pretentious example being "void of finite infinity."

I like walking simulators, they tend to be relaxing, beautiful & a way to express a variety of stories that can run the range from bizarre & non-sensical (The Void, Cylne) to humourous (The Stanley Parable) to mysterious/twisty with some light heartbreak  (The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, Among The Sleep) to uplifting coming of age/teen drama (Gone Home/Life Is Strange) to long descenting rants into rash decisions (The Old City: Leviathan, Dear Esther).
This is probably more in line with Dear Esther, but they allowed a lot more straying from the path because of allowing swimming long distances & climbing slopes; I would have thought this would mean there was either more to the game or at least they expected this to happen, but most of the areas outisde of the intended path show how much they didn't expect players to explore.
I fell through the ground a number of times into underground lakes of not fully rendered water with tree textures criss crossing the top, groups of trees floating feet from the ground, forests of trees that looked great from a distance but up close would make Duke 3D blush; even areas players not intending to test the limits of the game might explore come off badly like some of the really large rock formations which would be cool to take screenshots of & from atop of, are poorly textured up close.
The story was preety good, if this was out before Dear Esther, I wouldn't have a comparison point & this would fare better.
If you want the most enjoyment out of it, don't explore any, let the story happen & you'll probably be okay with spending the $4.

Only have about 9 hours into it so I'm just barely scratching the surface.
But from what I've seen so far this is a pretty amazing survival game.
PROS:
AMAZING WORLD AND GRAPHICS.  This is hands down the most lovingly hand crafted world I've explored in the whole survival sim craze.  The overgrown feel is great and the every building bush and tree looks amazing.
SOUND:  Pretty good so far.  From the soft russel of bushes as you creep through them to the thud of your shoes as you  explore a building is great.
COMBAT:  From what little I've had it's been satisfying.  The Zeds drop with a well placed headshot which feels great.
INVENTORY:  Pretty straightforward and not clunky at all.
SURVIVAL GAMEPLAY:  Food and water are abundant enough where it's not a nusance to survive.  From the lowliest trailer park to the biggest house I haven't had trouble finding what I need to keep myself fed and hydrated.  Everything else as far as guns, ammo, craftables and such seem to be well balanced and sparse so far.  The overall feel to surviving is rewarding thanks to well designed sound ques.  Such as hearing the howling of a pack of wolves while trecking through the wild letting you know to keep quite and head the other way.  The sound of the Zeds inform you of their wereabouts.  Been able to avoid most combat by crouching, watching, listening, and being stealthy.
PROGRESSION:  Though I've only barely begun to dabble in base building it's been pretty clunky but passable.  But what I do really like is finding new "plans" that let you learn new base building parts.  This is great because it adds to your sense of progression when you find one.  It's nice to unlock that new piece to liven up your base and watch it grow from a humble hideaway to a proper fort.
CONS:
Not many so far but here's a few (some of which just come down to personal preference)
Zeds getting stuck on scenery.  Seen this mostly in the bigger towns.
When holding a gun it lowers itself after only a few seconds.  Wow this one really gets me.  If I find a shotgun and I'm exploring a particularly hostile location I'd REALLY like it if my gun didn't lower itself all the time.  It's maddening to have to click a key or press my left mouse button to bring it back up to a ready position.  If  you run smack dab into another player who's stalking you that split second it takes to hit a key to bring it back up could cost you your life.
Inventory glitching out.  Seems like when I've logged in the next day some of my stuff has dissapeared.  Might be just me but I swear I had an axe in my inventory and a smaller backpack when I logged off last night.
Map size is smallish.  This one is completely personal preference.  Like most of us I got into the whole zombie thing by exploring Chenaris which is huge.  BUT...... I have to say what is here is COMPLETELY top notch and lovingly crafted.  So it's just me wishing there was alot more of it  ;)
CONCLUSION:
Probably the most fun I've had in a long time in the zombie survival catergory.  The cons are small and non of them gamebreaking.  Looking forward to what will be added next to the game as it is still in early access.
To the DEVS:  CHEERS AND KEEP UP THE GOOD WORK!!!!

This game almost never failed to bore me. I enjoyed countless hours playing this game, and everyone who had gotten it that I recommended it to didn't regret their decision to buy the game. I highly recommend it to anyone who considers buying it.
And to those comparing Starbound to Terraria, well, here's some differences:
Pros
-Starbound is space-based, meaning there's not just one world, or two, or three. There's way more than you can imagine.
-Starbound has 7 races to choose from, all with their own technological advancements and cultures.
-Starbound has a storyline.
-Starbound includes crewmembers that actually fight with you, unlike Terraria's NPCs that just sit in a house.
-Starbound includes challenge rooms, which are similar to obstacle courses, rewarding you if you succeed, and punishing you for failing.
-Starbound doesn't require you to keep crafting more pickaxes, rather, it requires you to upgrade your Manipulator Module.
-Starbound is much easier to mod.
-Starbound includes quests.
-Starbound includes vehicles.
-Starbound includes pets.
-There's less debuffs in Starbound.
-You can feed your ship pet.
-Starbound doesn't include invasion or events like in Terraria, which some find annoying, but some find fun.
-Starbound has better music, I know this is preference but come on, let's face the facts here.
-You can see your underwear in Starbound <3
-Starbound's armor doesn't include set bonuses, which can be a good thing, as if you find a new, better piece of armor than what you currently have, there's no reason not to equip it right away, whereas in Terraria, you might wanna hold off equipping it because you may want to keep your weaker armor's set bonus.
-Starbound gives you a ship, which is basically an upgradable home already built for you.
-Starbound has 2-handed weapons which generally have a special ability when right-clicked, as well as 1-handed weapons, such as dual-wielding pistols
-Shields actually work as shields in Starbound, they don't just give knockback immunity like in Terraria
-Starbound includes terraforming AND microforming.
-Starbound has much more biomes and mini-biomes.
-Starbound has post-endgame vaults, Terraria has nothing endgame.
-Starbound has procedurally generated weapons, meaning there's more than 1,000,000 weapons. That doesn't include all the other items in-game.
-For Starbound's defense, what you see is what you get in terms of damage reduction. In Terraria, damage reduction is based on half of your total defense in normal, and 3/4ths of it in expert mode.
-After you finish the game, Chucklefish Games gives you a thank-you card (via Esther),which really warmed my heart,aswell as the ending credits.
-Last but not least, THE most game changing feature, is that you can crouch in Starbound. :0
Cons
-Terraria has mounts
-Terraria has accessories instead of techs
-Terraria has equippable grapple hooks; you have to hold them in Starbound.
-Terraria includes fishing quests.
-Terraria has more bosses and side bosses.
-Terraria has expert mode, so rarer drops are easier to obtain, while the monsters are harder to beat.
-The minimal damage you take in Terraria is 1, as opposed to Starbound's 2.
-Terraria has more achievements.
-Terraria has a summoner class, which Starbound doesn't really have much of besides pets and crewmembers.
I could go on and on about the differences between these two games,but there's just something about Starbound that Terraria doesn't have, and I think it's that once you've completed the game, you can look back at all the places you've been and the things you have done. It really is a great game.

When I first got the game, the starting intro was intriguing enough, but I started to get very frustrated a few hours in, so I will start with the negatives since thats what most people will experience and notice first.  In the end, I came back to it a year later, got the expansion season pass and enjoyed it, but to do so, I had to forget my hopes and expectations and approach it as a new game again.  It was easier to do this when I knew the things I hated about it and could make adjustments (not playing as a wizard for my main character, and focusing on the story vs the combat)
Even though the game captures the look and feel of an infinity engine game, they chose to create a new game system instead of liscensing the D&D or some other popular system, and this was the primary source of my frustration.  In particular, the new system is very limited in the spell selection of both wis and int casters compared to the baldur's gate games.
The other thing I dislike about the new system is that rogue backstabing is nearly impossible to pull off, and even when you do, the results are underwhelming for the effort.  Part of it is that even with stealth maxed for your level, it is nearly impossible to sneak close enough to anything to do a backstab, and when you do, the multiplier is only something like 1.5 or 2x, and it is never enough to outright kill anything that is not incredibly weak compared to you.
The stronghold was also a disapointment.  Obsidian did a pretty good job with the stronghold in NWN2, so I had high hopes for the implimentation in this, and they did have some interesting ideas, but they just felt rushed or unfinihsed.  Its not so much that the stronghold is bad, its just not as good as it could have been, and not as good as what they did with NWN2.
Now for the good points.
The story is different and interesting with a lot of twists I did not see coming.  The first part of the game is pretty slow going as you are getting acquinted with the world it is set in, but things really start to pick up once you get to the main city.  I don't want to spoil anything, so I'll just say that the story was good enough to me that it was worth getting past the negatives I listed to enjoy it. The story and quests in the expansion (Whitmarch) are also very well done, and the expansion is well worth getting if you decide to get the game.
I'm gonna give it a positive rating, but for anyone who has not played the Baldur's Gate or Neverwiner Nights series, I would highly recomend any of those over this, and I would also recomend Dragon Age: Origins and Awakening over this (but skip Dragon Age 2, that game is a steaming pile of rubbish).
TLDR: Great story, disapointing game mechanisms.

I was a kick-starter backer for this game and am very happy with the end-result. Being a big fan of story-driven RPGs with nice gameplay elements this game fulfills both niches. A throwback to the 2d isometric hand drawn environments for those of us who are fans of nice illustrations.
This is not the typical RPG we may be used to where we "kill ever bad guy or enemy" we come across. My only complains is that there's a bit too much side-content that draws me away from the main story for too long. A great retro-style, isometric view RPG, probably the best of its kind since Dragon Age: Origins. Though the writing quality is uneven, with some names feeling as though they came out of a fantasy name generator and some plotlines being disappointingly anticlimactic, the narrative as a whole and most of the major side quests are extraordinarily well designed. This, paired with the game's beuatiful, painterly art style and the amount of freedom granted to the player in terms of narrative choices are what makes the game worth playing.
The game is not without its faults: the level of cap of 12 is too low for a game with so much to do, and if you're the sort of player who likes to complete all side quests, you'll find yourself reaching it long before the final dungeon. The megadungeon which forms a major side quest in the game is irritatingly grindy, with interesting points popping up so rarely in between frequently redundant battles as to make the trek through the entirety of it rather infuriating. Finally, and perhaps most problematically, the game's mechanics are a mess: skills, attributes, the array of 8 different damages, and a confused jumble of traits intertwined together just feel incongruous and make no intuitive sense.
Despite all of that, however, the excellent storytelling and fascinating lore of the world are what make this game shine. All in all: a fantastic throwback.

Night in the Woods.  Wow...  This is quite an experience in an indie game.
Mae has just dropped out of college, and she returns home to Possum Springs, an old mining town that has fallen on hard times.
Unlike most adventure games, Mae--the player--doesn't have amnesia.  She knows everyone in town, and she wants to reconnect with them.  She's only been away 2 years, but she discovers everything is different.
Nothing is quite as she remembers.  The people are depressed, and everyone walks around with a chip on their shoulder because Possum Springs is drying up.  Jobs are fleeing, people are out of work, and those who have a job can't make a decent living.
All Mae's old school friends are working crap jobs, and they seem to have grown up, and bitter.  Everyone has matured except Mae.  She is trapped between childhood and adulthood, and she doesn't know how to cross from one to the other.
Something strange is going on in Possum Springs.  Something strange is happening to Mae...
The game is incredibly well-written.  You get to know these people and their extensive histories so well you really do care about them.  Even when they're doing mundane things, somehow they're interesting.  Everyone has a defined personality, and their dialogue reads so fluid and natural.
Night in the Woods is pretty much an interactive cutscene. Think "To The Moon."  Very little gaming to do, but the story it tells is so interesting, and the characters are so much fun to get to know, that I didn't care.
(There's always Demon Tower to satisfy the bloodlust after reading all that dialogue.)
The story thoroughly engrossed me, and I did not expect it to.  It's engaging, funny, and more mature than I expected.  Two of Mae's friends are openly gay!  Mae was apparently a little criminal as a kid, and slipping into that role now was a strange experience.  There are even political undertones in the story.
It's easy to get lost in this town for hours at a time.  Not because the town is massive and interesting to explore.  (It's actually quite small, and while there are some things to do apart from the current "mission," I wouldn't call it open-world.  These side-tasks do affect the narrative in subtle ways though.)  Rather, Mae's childhood friends are so much fun!  I wanted to spend time with all of them!  I even felt bad when I went with one and not the others because I wanted to get to know all of them!
My only complaints are... sprite slowdown?!  Really?!  More than a dozen polygons on screen at once, and the game slows down?!  No excuse for that.  And... loading screens...  Lots of them...  And some events are quicktime, but the buttons on screen do not match my controller.  It told me to press button 8, or 9, or 6, but my gamepad is labeled A, B, X, Y.  Never did fully memorize which was which.  These are hardly game-breaking issues though.
It tells the story of this generation.  Kids who aren't allowed to grow up as their parents did, and they don't know how.  An economy that no longer seems to be working for anyone has made socialists out of an entire generation of young people, and even some of the older fellows.  Surprising to see this in a game story, and it very clearly captures the times.
This is quite a story.  Smart, nuanced, and even profound.  It pulled me in and never let me go.  If you can enjoy a novel disguised as a game, this is a must-play.

Noct has a lot of potential and can become something amazing.
The foreboding atmosphere, the bleak setting and backstory and gameplay fits together very well. I really like the visual presentation of this. It makes me very curious about what happened to the world, who is watching the player from this satellite, and what these creatures are.
The gameplay and music are so good in creating tension in exploration. When you see the 'uh oh' above your little guy's head, turning a corner too fast, or going into a dark house blind could mean death. The sparse ammo makes salvaging bullets a must and you must choose your battles. I really like the sort of 'flashlight' effect on your line of sight. It's cool to be able to see clearly what you're aiming at and really helpful when you're looking out for a creature.
I'm torn between making it a recommended game right now though. As an early access, I can't fairly judge it especially since its very void of content now.
There's nothing to find except roaming creepy crawlers and empty buildings that have weapons and ammo laying around.
In the short time I played it, I got bored quickly since there was nothing to do but rip and tear monsters and find guns. A level system would add a lot to longevity, but it would ruin a rogue-like which I'm guessing this game is supposed to be.
There was barely any water to find which you need to run, and you'll be doing that a lot.

The best game from the Splinter Cell series in my opinion.
A lot of reviews and discussions from the community has said that this game is more action-oriented, weaker than Chaos Theory and Uplay is terrible. I'll try to dismiss some of these claims.
1. First off, this game does have some action sequence (like every Splinter Cell games, duh) that forces you to engage enemies but they are not as many as you might have read or heard. In the main missions, there are some part where you have to take down enemies but you can still do it non-lethally and remain undetected. That's why every mission has the undetected achievement.
You don't have to use guns like how you would in an FPS game. You can use gadgets or hand-to-hand takedown. Probably what most people claim when this is sort of like Call of Duty is because of the improved shooting mechanics compared to previous games. Is that really a bad thing? I don't think so and you're not forced to shoot enemies if you don't want to.
2. Some argue that the game lacks stealth elements such as the meters compared to previous games. Older Splinter Cell games have the Stealth Meter (or Visibility Meter) and Chaos Theory also added the sound meter while this game does not. I think this is a design choice by Ubisoft to remove these as HUDs like they did with Conviction. They are not however, entirely gone. Instead of a meter, Sam's visibility is dictated by the suit, difficulty, cover spots and distance to enemies. If you are in the shadows, Sam's suit will light up to show that you are in the most stealthy position. Enemies that are close to you can still see you so you're not magically invisible.
As for sound, depending on the boots you wear, crouch and moving speed, you can reduce moving noise. In crouch position, Sam has 3 speed: crouch slow, crouch fast and crouch sprint. Caps Lock toggles between crouching fast or slow.  Press Caps Lock once (or push the analog stick softly) to move slowly without any noise. This way, you can move behind enemies and they won't hear a thing. Press Caps Lock again (or fully push the analog stick) to crouch faster but if you move closely behind enemies, they will hear and turn around. Hold down Space (or A button) to sprint and move faster but enemies can hear you from a longer distance.
These are all very similar to previous game so Blacklist still has the stealth elements of previous game, just executed in a slightly different way.
3. I honestly can't say anything bad much about Uplay because it never gets in the way of single player at least for me. I had some minor issues when attempting to play co-op and Spy vs. Merc but a couple of tries afterwards and it usually works. I can't guarantee everyone will have the same experience but I think if all you're doing is playing the single-player part, Uplay probably won't be much of a bother. If you don't want it to bother you even more, just play it offline.
Now the game is fun and all but there are some things I wish they would improve or add into this game or future Splinter Cell.
1. Night vision is almost entirely useless because it took quite some time to see and even then, it's not that clear. I've never worn night vision goggles so I don't know if this is how they are supposed to work but I think Ubisoft can do better. This is still a game not real life.
2. Some stuff should make a come back like, interrogation (plus sarcastic remarks), lock picking and entering key codes (also in point 3).
3. Secondary objectives should play a much bigger role in the game. For example, using thermal imaging to detect fingerprints or accessing certain computers should open more ways or create a distraction or taking down certain enemies can change how the rest of the level plays.
4. In Perfectionist, hand to hand take downs from the front during combat should still be made possible but maybe not by one button but through a combination of buttons and keys. It's hard to imagine Sam, an elite operative, being pushed by enemies just because it's from the front.
5. The sniper laser sight visibility should be reduced. As it is right now, Snipers hardly pose any difficulties.
Overall, Blacklist has some flaws that could be improved upon or in future Splinter Cell game, but even as it is right now, it's still a great game and emphasizes more on stealth than what most people claimed.

The overwhelmingly positive reviews should say enough about the quality of this VN. Here are some obvservations from my play through that other reviews don't necessarily touch on:
For me, a very quick reader, it took approximately 5 to 6 hours to finish.
The choices you make do seem to matter, although this isn't strictly a choice-based game. There are a few different endings.
There were no translation issues that I noticed. All the dialogue was complete without any syntax or grammatical problems.
I am not a fan of comedy and it is extremely difficult for a game or movie to make me laugh; that being said, there were a couple times in this VN where the humor made me genuinely laugh. This is NOT a comedy novel by any stretch, but there is some witty humor in a couple places.
Although this VN addresses some long-held questions about the nature of life, the soul, and artificial intelligence, the story is not cliche by any means. I wouldn't call the story philosophic either, but it does provide enough immersion to make you ponder these things.
While there is a little of [what I like to call] "protagonist frustration" it is most certainly not enough to negatively affect my opinion at all. ("Protagonist frustration" is what I call the common trope in VNs where the protagonist, often labelled as "you", acts or speaks in such a way that annoys the reader, especially because the protagonist is labelled as "you". The protagonist is occasionally rude or uncompassionate, but its not nearly enough to sour the reader of the VN. It's also a common feature of VNs, so I am not too put off by it.)
The plot and artwork of the VN are fantastic and truly top-notch. The music is also good. The characters aren't necessarily deep but they do the job they have to in order to flesh out the plot. The voice acting for Lucy is also good.
Overall, I'd recommend that, if you have any interest in VNs, to stop reading these reviews and to go ahead and buy it. It's seriously that good.

Ever since I completed this visual novel, I struggled for weeks to come up with something significant to say about it. You know, something a little more powerful than "I give this game feels out of 10". As a critic, I don't get many opportunities to actually think about a videogame, especially one that I already finished. Usually I'm too concerned with the next game, and trying desperately to stay on schedule. For
to rattle around in the nether reaches of my brain for so long, perhaps it's something truly special.
Lucy Valentine is an android, an artificial being programmed to mimic the behavior and feelings of a human. Her emotions aren't truly legitimate...are they? This question sparks what could be considered a journey towards validation. She's trying to find her purpose, and prove to those around her that she's more than just a tool. How exactly does one do that? After all, she is an android. Whatever she does or says will be immediately countered with "...but you're a robot. This is all part of your programming."
She isn't real. Well, that goes without saying, considering she's a videogame character and all. The thing is, we as a society carry feelings for numerous persons or objects that aren't "real". Perhaps there is a TV or movie character whose death we lament, a piece of music that stirs emotion, an object of sentimental value, or even just words on a page that make us cry. For us to show feelings for anything that is not flesh and blood, but deny Lucy her emotions, it just seems selfish and wrong.
What makes validation such an interesting concept is that it's what we're always in pursuit of. We spend the bulk of our lives trying to find our place in the sun. Sometimes we never actually get there. We become lost in the fog, not knowing who or what to reach for. After spending enough time in the fog, people lose sight of everything. Take this game's protagonist for example, he has never known what it's like for somebody to take care of him, while he's sick. What we (likely) took for granted when were children, is an absolutely incredible event for him. An android is showing him more care and affection than his human parents ever did. It's the simple times like these that cause the boy to question his anti-robot beliefs.
Lucy is more than just "well-built". She has many wonderful qualities. Every moment spent with her, no matter how inane, is just perfect. Granted, there are times in the story that practically force the player to feel sympathy. The protagonist tends to be a miserable jerk to Lucy, which is frustrating to watch. In all honesty, I'm a bit strange. When it comes to visual novels that involve relationships and/or romance, I tend to get more attached to male characters. In other words, even though I'm a straight guy, I'm totally in love with Kent from
. Maybe this says more about the VNs that I've played, but I don't know. Lucy is quirky, but not annoying. She's naive, but in a way that's charming and not revolting. She has more depth and agency than her programming lets on.
Some would argue that this visual novel is predictable and manipulative. The story isn't exactly unfamiliar to science-fiction enthusiasts, and certain events are expertly composed for maximum effect. Even with that in mind, I was still completely overwhelmed. For me, this was probably the most emotionally impactful media I've experienced since the movie
. This game does so much with a relatively short period of time.

If you're the kind of person who gets upset by overly politically correct things, you should probably steer clear of Read Only Memories. The game introduces your character by allowing you to pick any pronoun from "him" to "xir" or even insert custom ones, and the game has a bit of a problem of being unrealistically diverse, to the point that the first characters you meet are a lesbian, a gay pakistani immigrant, and a catgirl who literally embodies the "die cis scum" meme except replacing "cisgender" with "genotypical". For the most part the characters end up being more than just stereotypes and I don't explicitly have a problem with diversity, but when almost every character in the game feels like they were created with a sort of rule that every one of them had to either be gay or some other underprivileged individual it starts to feel forced instead of progressive.
With that out of the way, outside of that, the game is pretty good. The story starts out a little slow in the first chapter but once it picks up it starts getting good really quickly, and the soundtrack is the kind that you'll want to get to listen to after you've finished the game. I think $20 is a bit much for it, but it's a good for-sale game if you're into point-and-clicks in the vein of Snatcher.

I'm more of a solo player bun I have to say, you need to play Forced in Co-op.
