Night in the Woods.  Wow...  This is quite an experience in an indie game.
Mae has just dropped out of college, and she returns home to Possum Springs, an old mining town that has fallen on hard times.
Unlike most adventure games, Mae--the player--doesn't have amnesia.  She knows everyone in town, and she wants to reconnect with them.  She's only been away 2 years, but she discovers everything is different.
Nothing is quite as she remembers.  The people are depressed, and everyone walks around with a chip on their shoulder because Possum Springs is drying up.  Jobs are fleeing, people are out of work, and those who have a job can't make a decent living.
All Mae's old school friends are working crap jobs, and they seem to have grown up, and bitter.  Everyone has matured except Mae.  She is trapped between childhood and adulthood, and she doesn't know how to cross from one to the other.
Something strange is going on in Possum Springs.  Something strange is happening to Mae...
The game is incredibly well-written.  You get to know these people and their extensive histories so well you really do care about them.  Even when they're doing mundane things, somehow they're interesting.  Everyone has a defined personality, and their dialogue reads so fluid and natural.
Night in the Woods is pretty much an interactive cutscene. Think "To The Moon."  Very little gaming to do, but the story it tells is so interesting, and the characters are so much fun to get to know, that I didn't care.
(There's always Demon Tower to satisfy the bloodlust after reading all that dialogue.)
The story thoroughly engrossed me, and I did not expect it to.  It's engaging, funny, and more mature than I expected.  Two of Mae's friends are openly gay!  Mae was apparently a little criminal as a kid, and slipping into that role now was a strange experience.  There are even political undertones in the story.
It's easy to get lost in this town for hours at a time.  Not because the town is massive and interesting to explore.  (It's actually quite small, and while there are some things to do apart from the current "mission," I wouldn't call it open-world.  These side-tasks do affect the narrative in subtle ways though.)  Rather, Mae's childhood friends are so much fun!  I wanted to spend time with all of them!  I even felt bad when I went with one and not the others because I wanted to get to know all of them!
My only complaints are... sprite slowdown?!  Really?!  More than a dozen polygons on screen at once, and the game slows down?!  No excuse for that.  And... loading screens...  Lots of them...  And some events are quicktime, but the buttons on screen do not match my controller.  It told me to press button 8, or 9, or 6, but my gamepad is labeled A, B, X, Y.  Never did fully memorize which was which.  These are hardly game-breaking issues though.
It tells the story of this generation.  Kids who aren't allowed to grow up as their parents did, and they don't know how.  An economy that no longer seems to be working for anyone has made socialists out of an entire generation of young people, and even some of the older fellows.  Surprising to see this in a game story, and it very clearly captures the times.
This is quite a story.  Smart, nuanced, and even profound.  It pulled me in and never let me go.  If you can enjoy a novel disguised as a game, this is a must-play.

Okay, before I start, I put in around 10 hours into the beta of the game. I didn't enjoy it then, and I still don't enjoy the full release. Wanna know why? Let me tell you.
Starbound ISN'T a "true" sandbox game in my opinion. It has way to much story and quests that influence your choices and decisions. Because of this, I was suckered into thinking this was a completely free sandbox world such as the likes of Terraria or Minecraft. But "Yes!" I exclaimed to myself while reading the store page of Starbound, "Just what I always wanted, an interstellar sandbox game where I can choose my role in the universe, and have no objective!" - This is what the store page lead me to believe this game was. False Advertisment.
First off, The story. Dear lord...
You are a galactic person in a galactic university when a galactic hentai monster attacks earth and you steal a ship and it breaks... Wow.
With such a shallow plot, why did they even include it in the first place? The story is so forgettable and just serves as an anchor for your slow crawl of progression early on in the game. It would have been better just to drop you into a randomized world with no backstory, no lore, but just to scatter parts of information around the galaxy, Which encourages exploration and progression.
The first mission has you sent for 20 core things to fuel your ship. This mission is unskippable. Which makes replayability a ♥♥♥♥ing boring chore. This mission drags on to the point where I wanted to hang myself when I got to 19 cores, and couldn't find the last one.
Also, the combat is utter crap. You cannot aim a weapon in any other direction other than left and right. This makes traveling through caves and tight enclosures really difficult when you have to fight a bat on the ceiling.
Overall, I really dislike this game. The story has about as much depth as a pancake and the almost linear, unskippable tutorial missions drag on way longer than it needs too. I know this game probably has more, but I'm not invested, nor intrerested in the full release.
Luckily, I stopped playing at 1 hour, so I can get a refund.

This game.
I started playing this game because a friend wanted to engage in some Jolly Co-Operation.
I detested it. I loathed it. I hated it with every fiber of my being.
There was no fun to be had, enemies were hiding around every corner, every encounter a trap.
However, for reasons unknown, I stuck with it.
And so I began to learn.
The first few hours of my gameplay was filled with much caution, experimentation, and death.
Typically my own.
I started to understand the benefits each weapon brought to the table.
I started to figure out the intricacies of combat.
Most importantly I started to come to terms with the fact that Dark Souls doesn't care.
And so I began to grow.
Finally, I was comfortable fighting more than one enemy at a time.
I was content facing down champions and demons alike.
Gone were the days of cowering before every new creature.
I was now a force to be reckoned with.
Ambushes kept me on my toes.
Traps made sure I was alert.
I had everything to gain and little to fear.
I had risen to the challenge.
At some point I fell in love with this game.
From the diverse set of characters to the bleak atmosphere.
I found myself delving in to the lore at every opportunity.
I could speak for hours about Dark Souls if I wanted to.
Some of the experiences I've had will likely stick with me for many years.
I don't know if I could recommend a game more than I could this one.
Whether you're in for the challenge or the story, Dark Souls will not be found wanting.
However, if you are planning to play this game, be warned:
Learning to play this game for the first time is not what I would call fun.

As an avid fan of Baldur's Gat I & II as well as Planescape Torment, it was an easy decision to back Pillars of Eternity on Kickstarter. When the final product came out with glowing reviews, my anticipation was high. Luckily I can say POE lives up to the promises of the Kickstarter; albeit with its own caveats.
What's amazing about POE is that it's easily the most accessible for newcomers and veterans alike. You can simply toggle on or off tutorial menus and the like whenever you want. There are new additions to the gameplay and interface that made me admire the attention to detail. Don't be scared off if you've never played this type of game.
On the whole Pillars of Eternity feels like it needs just a bit more creative time in the oven. The core story is a bit lackluster. I never cared for the world or truly understood what the threat was. The writing quality and quantity is still very high, but the stakes never seem worth it. It's like I was back home but all the people and furnishing were different. And when compared to other games in their library, this appears even paler in comparison. The characters also aren't as interesting or memorable for the exception of a couple. There's still a TON of story in this game. You can always find a new tome or book on a shelf ready to be read. Yet I always sold these books at markets instead of reading them. I just kinda wanted the main adventure to be over with.
Side quests are plentiful although a tad redundant. Most missions are kill or retrieve. The consequences of your actions doesn't feel as dramatic as Baldur's Gate II. Plus your options in the dialog tree, while there, don't feel like they're as deep.
Dungeoning is still fun. The action is as intense as before. Spell casting doesn't seem to be as fun. It didn't quite feel like I was on a huge adventure for some reason. Like the confines of the maps were smaller than before. This game is definitely challenging especially if you're not ready for it. It's good to see that the pause mechanic and planning out your attacks is still in good form. I love playing as the ranger class but I was sad to see that there are no arrow/projectile types that you can manage and buy. If you have a bow, crossbow, or sling you have an infinite amount of ammo as your disposal. I guess they came to the conclusion that this got in the way of the fun factor.
What I loved about the original Baldur's Gate games was the sense of an inhabited world. Random events, character interactions, and grand adventures seemed to spring out of nowhere at any time. All distinct and unique from each other. Pillars of Eternity feels like it's cut short in most categories; although, it's still quite up there in terms of quality.
For the year this came out in, it's easily one of the best games of the year. In terms of the Baldur's Gate and Planescape Torment games, it's in the back of the pack but a welcome addition. A sequel is warranted.

OK, I got the game for 3.99 on sale. I 100% the base game and the DLC in 3 days.
STORY
You are a ranger named Talion and you want revenge. The story is really simple.
WORLD
The game features 2 maps in which you can freeroam and do missions.
GAMEPLAY
Throughout most of the game you will be running, fighting or sneaking.
Running in the world feels really smooth and satisfying, but there is also fast travel if you really value your time.The combat REALLY resembles the Batman Arkham series with counters, hit streaks and special moves. But I has the one thing that the Batman games were missing - killing.
In this game you stab, cut throats, chop of heads even blow them up!
The sneaking is really easy even if there are a lot of enemies in the area, thats good.
MISSIONS AND COLLECTIBLES
The game features 20 main missions. There are a lot of side missions which require you to do a lot of the same things like "kill 7 uruks with headshots", "kill 5 uruks while mounting a caragos". They sound boring, but somehow I really wanted to do them to get that sweet EXP.
DLC
You get 2 story DLC - Lord of the hunt and The Bright Lord.
Lord of the Hunt adds 2 new monster types with new abilites which are basically reskins of 2 other monsters from the base game. Main story is about killing Beast masters, so the thing you did in the base game, kill things.
The Bright Lord features controlling uruks and you main enemy is Sauron himself. You get access to the ring to help you kill things. For me it was the hardest dlc because the amount of enemies in some areas.
FINAL THOUGHTS
I woud not buy the game for full price. But I really enjoyed what i got for my 3.99 so I recommend you also get it for a lower price.

I enjoyed being scared out of my pants with monsters that literally pop out of nowhere. Aside from that, the the strategy necessary to survive is simpleton and bland. The playing field is closed-ended, and there is really nowhere to go. There's no direction or real goal other than hoarding resources (they regenerate randomly in the buildings after a few minutes, and monsters don't go in buildings), shooting down or avoiding monsters, or walking around the same-'ol island you cannot get off. There are usually no servers to play with others when I'm on, but even when there are others to play with, where do I go?
Oh yeah, med-kits are basically worthless because all the monsters appear to kill you instantly.
A few suggestions:
*Stop all the one-hit kills. Add a health counter that affects the survivor negatively the lower the health is. This also makes med-kits useful.
*Add a leveling system, a profession system, or a skill tree that allows you customize your character and play. I appreciate the rogue-like aspect of starting from scratch, and skills could be randomized and only under control of the player after spawning, not before, to force players to adapt.
*Scavenging. This is a SURVIVAL-horror game, and many times the resource regeneration does not give you food or water that you need to run. This is not "Do Not Starve", but the only "surviving" is hiding in buildings and running away.
*Balance the monster encounters and resources so that there is more action. Yes, suspense is best served when there is time between encounters, but too much time between encounters means it is boring. Why aren't there monsters in the forests, only in cities?
*Add AI survivors or NPCs where you can trade inventory for items you need.
*Give me more information about what I am holding. How many grenades do I really have? How many bullets can my mag hold? How many mags do I have? How long can I run? How much water do I have? How thirsty am I? How do I know one rifle is better than another? These do not have to be your standard dials, but give me more than "OK" or "LOW'.
*Finally, a journal, scraps of paper, or some other way to gather information on monsters, locations, equipment, skills, story line, history of the ancient evil, etc.
Sorry, I cannot recommend this quite yet. I will probably put it on the shelf and pick it back up when there is another update, or until the final release comes out.

A nice and enjoyable little game.
I liked:
------
-- No random battles - a must for me nowadays. The days of random battles are long past.
-- Quick normal battles - The normal battles do not take long, especially if you know what you are doing. Having just one character to control definitely helps.
-- Good quality overall - Good writing, very good music, good level designs.
-- Some strategy required - Bosses have strategies, too bad the game gets too easy middle-way (see below).
-- Interesting equipments - not just upgrades over your old gear, you have to think before you equip.
-- And last (but not least): The game was ENJOYABLE. Not once during my playthrough did I get bored. And that is the most important thing in a game in my book; Being fun.
I disliked
---------
--The difficulty. Halfway through the game becomes very very easy. At least that happened to me, and I know I did not overfarm enemies. If you don't skip enemies, and search the areas for loot and buffs, you will breeze though the game no problem. At least till you reach the final boss, that will send you packing if you are not truly prepared.
--A little rushed - While the game is quite polished, it shows that it could have been given a little more time from the creator. The last dungeons are quite barren dialogue-wise and event-wise, and there are places where your character can walk up walls etc.
Summary:
I definitely recommend this game for anyone that wants a quick rpg fix during a break from more demanding games. This is not a game you will remember for the rest of your life, but it's a good worth for its money.

Night in the Woods, despite its quirky humor and cartoony design hides a rich, deep, sometimes tragic, and complex world. Or in this case, town.
From the protagonist Mae, to her troop of misfit friends, to the secondary characters all are written with enough wit, depth, and personality that it is difficult not to care for them, and want to engage them in conversation every chance possible.
Gameplay: The world of Night in the Woods is broken between an exploration world, the town itself, that relies on progressive repetition. Every day you (Mae) will wake up and explore the town, with new portions of it opening at a somewhat steady pace as the story progresses. In order to keep it from being tedious, the world is constantly changing. New characters appear, conversations change, tertiary NPC's engage in different conversation that shine a gleam of what has occurred with Possum Springs. In addition, Mae can engage with either Bea or Gregg in different activities. However choosing one will permanently remove the other as an option.
The other segment of the game, is a series of mini games that vary in difficulty, theme, and are again, available depending on which friendship you choose to foster. Oddly enough certain mini games, such as the Band Practice (a guitar hero style game) offers a single try regardless of your performance (which band ever practices just once) and then it's done removing the potential fun on trying to beat your previous performance.
Visuals and Sound: There is no audible dialogue in the game outside of sound queues to signal which character is speaking. The music in the game ranges from light hearthed tunes for daily exploration to, hearth felt pensive for the more thoughtful moments; darker and ominous for some of the dream sequences.
Visually speaking, animations are fluid, expressions are simple, yet spot on with the proper situation. The dialogue is presented in speech bubbles, however, in numerous situations it is the speech itself that is animated with icons, and in some cases with vicious shaking to denote utter and excrutiating agony. But in order to offset the simplicity of the graphics, the game is lush with numerous small details, from leafs that react to movement, to myriad of critters and vermin running around, to weather changes, to beautiful sunsets, and the starry mystical quality of the dream sequences.
Plot: As already stated, the game explores the return of Mae Borowski to her hometown of Possum Springs and her dealings with former friendships, old stigmas, strained family relationships, and the uncertainty of the future as a growing adult.
Here is where the game truly shines. Along with the aforementioned aspects, the game balances the tedium of day to day lives with whimsy and humor, and and incredible amount of wit. All the while, maturely touching of delicate subjects, such as mental illness, child abuse, faith, and violence prone dysfunctional relationships.
All this is told in tandem with both a supernatural mystery, in which Mae must solve strange sightings occurring around town. In addition, the dream sequences further the mystery. In the dream sequences, Mae must traverse a starry landscape, from forests, to oddly angled buildings in order to trigger an event.
As far as pacing, Night in the Woods plays like many of Stephen King's novels. Carrie, Bag of Bones, and Pet Sematary come to mind.
*The following segment contains light spoilers.*
Just as with the mentioned novels, Night in the Woods puts a lot of effort in its storytelling. And just as the novels, it focuses greatly in the daily lives of the characters, setting the story, relationships and all that. And the supernatural part takes too much of a backburner plot, which is contrary to the main reason of why the game exists.
As the pace progresses, the focus remains too much of the daily lives, and suddenly, in the end chapter, the revelations come at a neckbreaking pace, causing more questions than answers, and then the game ends. By no means, does it feel rushed. Night in the Woods dictates the pace deliberately and masterfully, I just wish that the focus had shifted more on the supernatural part, so it didn't feel so "rushed" sort to speak.
Regardless, the game is a true indie gem, and worth a playthrough at the very least.

Short version: Made a depressed cat twerk, poked a severed arm with a stick, cried while talking with a pastor about an uncaring god. 10/10
Long version:
For this kind of genre, good games have engaging stories, fun gameplay, nice music and graphics, relatable characters, and well written dialogue. Great games have all that plus a strong and consistent tone. They set out from the very start to show the player something. This is a great game.
Fair warning: This game is not a fast paced one. If you speed through content and don't like exploring and talking to everyone you can, you'll feel like it's short and shallow. You get out what you put in. If on the other hand you take the time to explore, to chew it over, to talk to everyone, you'll love it. If you play games exclusively to feel good and escape boredom, maybe this isn't for you. But if you play games to get something out of a story, to learn a little about yourself, or generally to experience something, it'll feel very rewarding.
I'm gonna break this down into a full scale review because it deserves more than just a blurb about how good it is.
Pros: Excellent story, characters and theme. Great music. Personal and honest dialogue that will more than likely hurt and empower you personally, and make you feel complex, good, and bad emotions.
Cons: Sometimes the swears are a little lacking and out of character, no easy save/reload feature (your choices and mistakes count), and the occasional difficulty in platforming in dim lighting.
Story
This game's magic is in its story and the well written characters. This is a deeply relatable, emotional, honest game. The scenes have a certain real-ness to them more than most games can ever hope for, mostly helped by the converastional language of the characters. It doesn't feel scripted it just feels organic. The only negative on that front is that to maintain a teen rating, the game had to limit its swears, so there's a lot of "effin" and mild swears like damn and a couple ♥♥♥♥♥. So that kinda felt a little out of character now and then, but otherwise, it was tone aware. Everyone is a deeply fleshed-out character with their own interests. As the main character, you won't win all the time. As a matter of fact you'll find yourself in situations where you can't make the best of a bad situation at all. But that's good, because this story isn't just about you. It's about a community.
This game sets out with a theme, and does it well. The short version is that it's a critique of modern society. In that, it tackles issues of capitalism, social isolation, religion, mental health, poverty, friendship, sexuality, anarchy, environmentalism, war, and defiant hope. Themes that video games, and stories in general really don't often approach well, if at all. Pretty much every scene in the game somehow contributes to this, but does so without coming off forced at all. it's all integrated into the larger whole of the game. Since the theme is pretty broad and far-reaching, you get a lot of different ways of looking at the situation, from the perspectives of all the characters. It's a poignant story that hits close to home no matter who you are.
Gameplay
It's a solid platformer. It controls a lot like limbo or other side scrolling adventure games. There's no real major obstacles or deathtraps, but there are some kinda tricky jumps you might need to do a few times to get right. The platformer thing isn't really the game itself to be honest, it's more the way you get from point A to point B. It could just as easily have been a visual novel or a grid based rpg, but it would have lost some of its charm of exploring the town.
There's a lot of minigames, ranging from guitar hero esque, to a stationary worms tank minigame, to a fully built souls-series-hyper-light-drifter thing that easily could have been a standalone game on its own. All the minigames control well, but they're pretty tough and there's no easy reload button besides force-quitting. None of them are exactly mandatory though so don't feel pressured unless you want all the achievements.
Graphics
it's layers of pretty stylized shapes and incredibly well animated characters. Subtleties in movement and expression help the dialogue too. The lighting and palette are beautiful, and the mood is carried by the graphics well. I can't say too much about the graphics except that they're pretty and fit the theme and mood. My only criticism of the game is in the graphics though, that the lighting in a few of the scenes was a tad dark for my monitor to differ between ground and background so I found myself guessing at where platforms were every now and then, but it was never enough to inconvenience me, and I could have adjusted my monitor for the effort of it.
Sound
I need the soundtrack. It's moody, atmospheric, happy, unnerving, rocking, and fun. It covers a ton of ground with the soundtrack to fit the many moods and emotions. Looking forward to the OST.
Time:
11 hours to play through the first time. To get to some of the stuff you'll have to do multiple playthroughs. There's no proper save and reload function. Your choices stick and that's for the best imo. Unfortunately that means getting some achievements would take a disproportionate time investment, but so does dark souls, so whatever.
Overall: If you like games that make you feel things, if you like stories relevant to the present, if you don't want to feel like a badass, but just want to feel... ironically human, this is for you.

After a seemingly endless wait, and delay after delay, my #1 wishlisted game is finally out. It's pretty much as good as I expected it to be.
At its core, it's more or less an interactive story with branching paths, dealing with the daily life of young adults in some backwater town in a semi-comical, semi-serious way. It presents itself as a 2D platformer, but the platforming is pretty much only there as a way to go from somewhere to elsewhere, never being particularly challenging. What makes this game good is not its gameplay (though it features a minigame, Demontower, which is pretty good in that regard), but its characters and its setting.
The characters are well-written and easy to relate to; I've had my share of "yup, been there too" moments. Even minor characters were interesting, leading me to hilarity, sadness, or just leaving me thinking. The setting and the plot managed to convey that "things are no longer the same and will never be the same again" feeling pretty well. Multiple playthroughs are probably needed to get the whole picture, and that's excluding symbols and stuff that's open to a lot of interpretation. Oh, and there's also Mae's journal to look at, which gets updated now and then with hilarious depictions of her life events.
Most of the time will be spent talking to other characters or jumping all over to reach them (and dealing with Mae's weird habit of walking on powerlines to explore town), but there are a few minigames thrown in there. One of them, Demontower, is some kind of Isaac clone with mechanics inspired by Hyper Light Drifter, and is so well done it could very well have been released independently from Night in the Woods.
+ Well-written characters
+ Branching storyline
+ Mae's journal
+ Excellent music (release the soundtrack pls)
+ Demontower minigame
- Lots of loadings
- Pretty linear and repetitive, world is a bit small
- Platforming sections don't add much to the experience
9/10 I probably overrate it, like many videogames I love. The characters are great. Particularly the minor roles. People should stop making games with good characters or I'll go bankrupt buying them.

Ok, here is a review which shouldn't be written by me as I don't have the play time to make a fair judgement, but it seems no-one else has discussed this.
5 words? FORCED. Seems good, no weight.
Okay, now for the lengthy bit....
What do you mean by 'no weight'? well, that's pretty straight forward really, every strike, stab, stomp and shot you perform has no impression of impact in the sound or visual effects, it doesn't feel like you are striking down someone to the pits of the earth, it feels like you are pushing them over so they gentle fall onto a bed.
Now, while this may make sense for the assassin-type character, this should not be the case with the warrior wielding a freaking HUGE FLAMING AXE.
Don't get me wrong, the art-style is nice, the puzzles are cool, the soundtrack would be nice if you didn't have to choose between silence or being deafened and perhaps that's also the reason the fighting sucks, you have to turn the game sounds so far down in order to be able to hear your friends that you miss out on any subtle sounds such as impacts and also miss out on the soundtrack. The guide however? Oh, he'll violate your ear-drums silly if you don't shut him up quickly.
Overall, FORCED probably isn't that bad, but it just wasn't mine or my friends' cup of tea. It was just boring, and trust me, I really wanted to enjoy it.

This is quite possibly, in my opinion of course, the greatest game I have ever played.  It has four very different and very fun classes, which you can switch between any time you want.  You can play it solo, or you can go co-op and play with both friends and strangers.  The game used to be almost entirely unplayable, as there were so many connection issues that it was impossible to play with others and this is an extremely co-op oriented game.  However, since then the devs have pretty much completely rewritten all network related code and spent a huge amount of time bug hunting, which shows a tremendous amount of dedication as this is the first and only game created by a new and very small company.  However, it did take a while for them to update it considering how much they had to fix, so many people who initially played the game have since forgotten it and not updated the reviews they left half a year ago, so the game's Steam rating is fairly inaccurate.
If you like challenging, co-op based games that involve both problem solving and skill on an intense yet doable difficulty curve, I highly recommend this game.  However while you can play it casually, you will not get much out of it nor will you get very far, so if that's what you're looking for do NOT buy it.

Where do I even start with my complaints?
From painfully low quality sound samples that were obviously taken from their office with the lowest quality recording equipment that make the sounds almost comical, to the abrupt ending with some extras to duct tape a story that's already in bits and pieces..
Unbearable amounts of repetition, truly showcasing the peak of redundancy.
Extreme inconsistencies in the art department, especially obvious when characters A (Relevant character) and B (Insignificant character) stand next to each other. The overall positive reviews are quite deceiving to say the least from what I can tell, but I suspect it comes from people who just wanted a cheap tearjerker to pass their time, although I wouldn't even consider this one, as I was disappointed from start till finish.
I was left feeling betrayed for even attempting to have trust in this game, because it was shattered promptly.

What can I say about Starbound. For one, It's an adventure that will take you beyond the screen. You will feel the full range of emotions. From sheer joy after obtaining that Legendary sword you'd worked so hard to obtain, and you will feel utter rage when your ganked by mobs in the depths of some foreign planet. This is a game that will make memories and keep you coming back for more. I hope that you will like it just as much as I do. :)

Okay, before I start, I put in around 10 hours into the beta of the game. I didn't enjoy it then, and I still don't enjoy the full release. Wanna know why? Let me tell you.
Starbound ISN'T a "true" sandbox game in my opinion. It has way to much story and quests that influence your choices and decisions. Because of this, I was suckered into thinking this was a completely free sandbox world such as the likes of Terraria or Minecraft. But "Yes!" I exclaimed to myself while reading the store page of Starbound, "Just what I always wanted, an interstellar sandbox game where I can choose my role in the universe, and have no objective!" - This is what the store page lead me to believe this game was. False Advertisment.
First off, The story. Dear lord...
You are a galactic person in a galactic university when a galactic hentai monster attacks earth and you steal a ship and it breaks... Wow.
With such a shallow plot, why did they even include it in the first place? The story is so forgettable and just serves as an anchor for your slow crawl of progression early on in the game. It would have been better just to drop you into a randomized world with no backstory, no lore, but just to scatter parts of information around the galaxy, Which encourages exploration and progression.
The first mission has you sent for 20 core things to fuel your ship. This mission is unskippable. Which makes replayability a ♥♥♥♥ing boring chore. This mission drags on to the point where I wanted to hang myself when I got to 19 cores, and couldn't find the last one.
Also, the combat is utter crap. You cannot aim a weapon in any other direction other than left and right. This makes traveling through caves and tight enclosures really difficult when you have to fight a bat on the ceiling.
Overall, I really dislike this game. The story has about as much depth as a pancake and the almost linear, unskippable tutorial missions drag on way longer than it needs too. I know this game probably has more, but I'm not invested, nor intrerested in the full release.
Luckily, I stopped playing at 1 hour, so I can get a refund.

Alright, time to put in my two cents.
I enjoyed this game, I really did. The voice acting (save for a few minor characters) was great, the soundtrack was really good, and I enjoyed the characters.There was one part in particular which made me absolutely entranced in that particular moment that very few games have ever done. Now, as you may see from the reviews, the devs lashed out at supporters of Donald Trump. Although I do not agree with lashing out at the fans, I believe the hate stems from the recent green-card banning that occured where people who had every right and ability to live in America (including doctors that were stationed in another country elsewhere, and many stories of families split due to this.) were denied entrance.
Now, the devs are friends with the devs of VA-11 HALL-A, another indie game that got very popular, are from Venezuela. If you have been following the news, then you may know that Venezuela is in a seriously poor condition, with very high inflation and many riots occuring, which is communicated in their game. Putting two and two together, you may see why the devs are angry. Like I said, it wasn't really a good idea to project their anger and hatred to this man at his voters and I do wish they apologize for it, I can very much see why.
So, Trump voter or not, I absolutely recommend this game for how good it is. The devs aren't evil at all and the fact that they made a huge patch in which they paid very talented and very famous voice actors and celebrities (like the voice of Peacock from Skullgirls, the voice of Clementine from the Walking Dead, wrestler Xavier Woods, Jim Sterling, the voice actor of the Woodsman and Bigby from the Wolf Among Us, etc.) to voice characters in the game, polish the graphics of the game itself, fix some the bugs, and even rework voice lines from the game. Thank you for reading this review and I hope it makes up your mind on your decision, even if this really wasn't even much of a review of the game itself.

This game is beautifully done, with a great atmosphere and spooky gameplay, but it still isn't finished so I'm going to use this review to tell people what it could improve on.
Sometimes while adventuring around the map, if I exit a house the outside will still be dark, so I can't see until I get out of the "dark area" centered around that house. I nearly died like this to a monster I couldn't see, so the house mechanics still need to be worked on.
The ammunition system is a little ambiguous, only saying "Ok", Low" or "Out", but I reckon it could do with a "Med" setting, used when you aren't at full ammo, but aren't two or three clips away.
There's very limited structures around the map, and not much to do with them so if there were barricaded doors or something, then you'd have to whack them open, alerting monsters and players in the area. Maybe windows could be a good idea, who knows?
For a multiplayer game, there aren't a lot of aspects that distinguish it from single player, so maybe you could drop ammo or rations for other players it's make sticking together much more worthwhile.
And finally, the monsters. I think instead of having all monsters behaving the same way, you could have some chase relentlessly or hide behind walls to make monsters a bit more diverse, even going as far to have them interact with each other, would make it a lot more immersive.
Nonetheless, this game is a beautiful concept and will be very interesting when more players join. Thanks for reading, and have a nice day.

I finished State of Decay, I enjoyed it, and I would recommend it--but with some hesitations. The more I played the game, the more it felt sort of rote and a little tiring. It feels like the developers built a great core gameplay loop, but didn't do much to add to that.
The way the game works is thus: You have a base stocked with survivors. As time passes, the base uses up resources. So you go around a few towns and surrounding countrysides, break into houses and warehouses and the like, and steal stuff. You'll find both items that your character can use, and resources that your base can use. You carry regular items in a backpack, which has both a slot and weight limit after which you get encumbered and tired more easily. Base resources are loaded into a large rucksack, which further encumbers you. If you can't carry everything at an area, you can send for someone from your base to run to where you are, pick up the remainder, and bring it back to the base. NPCs can get caught by zombies while they're making their way out to the looting point or while they're making their way back.
You can designate certain buildings to be "outputs". The game doesn't explain at all why you would do this, but the internet explains: the most important reason to do it is that an area designated a outpost spawns no zombies and is booby-trapped so that if external zombies move through, they get killed. You'll want to put at least a few outposts near your base to sort of create a zombie-free buffer. The second reason, which is not made clear in the game at all, is that if you leave base resources in an outpost, you will have a permanent daily allowance of that resource, which lowers your need for scavenging. By the end of the game I had a daily surplus of food and medication and broke even on fuel, so I only needed ammo and construction materials.
After a while your character will get tired. Fatigue lowers your maximum stamina. You can keep playing, but it'll keep getting worse. So you're advised to go back to home base and switch to another character. Likewise, serious injury lowers your maximum health. This is the game's way of forcing you to use multiple characters. This can be frustrating if you only have a few with good skills. Skills include cardio, wits (ability to search through things quietly), melee combat, shooting, and reflexes (appears to relate to combat) and they are leveled up by using them; someone who shoots all the time will quickly get a high level of shooting skill. At a certain point, once you've leveled skills, you can also select "specializations" for your characters. The game does not explain this, so it was about 2/3rds of the way through the game before I discovered this was a thing.
While you're out and about, you'll be asked to do missions. Missions could involve helping out neighboring groups of survivors, going to save one of your runners who has been caught in a zombie-infested area, helping to board up a building, climbing tall buildings to locate new sources of resources.
You can also find new areas to move to, as each base has different built-in facilities and different numbers of expansion slots. I only moved my base once, from the default church into a spacious and facility-rich warehouse. You can use materials to build different areas in your base; a guard tower, a garden, a medical tent, a research library, a cooking area, a gym/training area, etc. Some require particular survivors with particular skills to staff them, but most just give you a sort of passive boost. You can upgrade most building facilities. Ultimately other than areas that help survivors recover from fatigue or injury, I didn't really notice much of an impact from base facilities at all. It felt like another mechanic that was sort of neat but ultimately hollow.
There is a plot, but not much of one. At random, you'll get radio missions to go deal with various groups of people. There are military personnel who are here for an unknown reason, local small criminals and drug/weapons dealers, a group of friendly survivors, a courthouse serving as some kind of post-collapse civilian government, and a few one-offs. The actual plot missions themselves differ very little from the random missions you get. For example, taking the sheriff on a ride-along to clear out zombie infestations and save a trapped civilian is exactly like clearing out zombie infestations and saving trapped civilians.
Your player characters are basically randoms. You start as a camping dude named Marcus who has great default skillset. He's accompanied by a perpetual whiner who is useless named Ed. You meet up with an ex-military woman named Maya. Pretty much everyone else after these three are total blind randoms. There are five or six NPC voices that voice everyone; there's a wide wide wide variety of dialogue but little in the way of characterization. They do this because anyone can permanently die. During my first run-through, I lost both Marcus and Maya due to bad planning about 10 minutes apart 4 hours in. I was so gutted that I restarted the game. In my second and final playthrough, I was about 7 hours in when I lost Marcus on a routine errand. I considered restarting again. So they've done a good job of making the loss of a high level character pretty tragic. Marcus was my only loss that wasn't ordained by plot reasons on my second playthrough.
I guess I would describe my experience as sort of hollow. I loved the melee combat, which is quite complex and very tense (although poorly explained). I loved driving around in my car and opening my door to whack a passing zombie, or doing a donut and whipping a zombie hanging off the back into a telephone pole. But... I guess I never really felt like anything matters. I'd just wander around and scavenge (unnecessarily, my resources were never low) until I'd get a mission, missions were basically no different than wandering around in general, I'd play side missions until I got a plot mission, which were no different really. Occasionally I'd have to go back to my base to check on construction or switch characters. I was never scarce on weapons or ammo or meds at my base. I always had more than enough influence, the game's currency.
So in conclusion, I'd say that this is definitely a game that's worth trying, but that if you're like me, you might get tired of part-way through because there's not a lot of variation and much of the game seems a little like busy-work.

I have a very love hate relationship with this game. I unfortunately have only had the chance to play through the single player campaign, so I am not sure how much differs between it and multiplayer. In other words, what I say about it may not apply to the entire game, just the part I have played. Now this game is obviously geared towards multiplayer, which isn't bad but for those of us who prefer single player or can only do single player, it seems a bit unfair. Even in some of the dialogue it assumes there are multiple gladiators, rarely using singular terms when refering to them. But while it is probably more difficult to do this alone, it isn't impossible. Infuriating at times, yes, but possible. For those who have not played the game i'll try to sum up the gameplay real fast.
There are four 'classes' you can chooe from, and unlike what you may be used to, you do not select it at the beginning, at least not permanently. You can switch between them before each trial. Of the four I have only used 3, but i've glanced over them all. There is the DPS dagger like gloves, with quick attacks. That one I never really used. There is the heavy hitter hammer which I ended up using a lot simply because of that. The shield I only used once for a challenge but he seems to be a tank like character, meant to avoid a lot of damage. Then there is the bow, the ranged attacker which I used almost as much as the hammer. Each trial may require you to use a different set of weapons, you can't just stick with one. And I mean that, I don't mean it'll just be more difficult, some areas I cannot see you doing without a certain character.
An interesting mechanic the game brings into play is your spirit mentor, Balfus, a floating orb of light that acts as your guide and support. You can summon him to different locations, which you'll to do a lot as to activate altars you have to make him pass through them. These altars can do any number of things, some are required to be activated to continue the level, some give Balfus a healing aura, while another will actually push enemies away and much more. I really liked this mechanic as at times it required you to do some thinking, which is a nice break from the usual hack and slash. I just wish there were more puzzles that required extra thought beyond the second area. Balfus will also give you advice and tell you about new additions to the trials as they appear. However. One of my biggest gripes is that there are times where his advice and warnings come after the fact. For example, there is a part in the second boss in the very beginning where something is happening to Balfus but he says nothing. And if you stay close to him, you end up caught in a shockwave that damages you. No warning, nothing. Not until LATER does he warn you of the dark pulsing. And then there are times where he doesn't say anything at all and you have to figure things out on your own, like in the third boss with the eggs.
You do not level up like you would in a normal game, instead you unlock new skills and skill slots by completing challenges and gathering crystals from them. There are three crystals in each trial, one for beating the trial, another for completing that trial's challenge, and the last one is for the time trials. I'm not sure if there are different challenges in multiplayer, nor do I know how the time trials scale with more characters, but at least in singleplayer they do not waste time in making them difficult to complete, and expect to experiment with different characters to be able to complete them. And some of these challenges are quite infuriating. And don't expect to be able to get by with just completing the levels because the final trial has a requirement of, at least in singleplayer, 40 crystals. These can be difficult to get and require a lot of patience(or sheer stubborness).
Now there are some things I had a problem with regarding the classes. Each one has the same amount of health, armor and speed. The dagger and archer should be much faster then the shield or hammer in movement speed, it only makes sense and you are punished for using the archer because many enemies are much faster then you, even if you are running full speed(which requires you to move your mouse in the direction your gladiator is facing btw). What makes this more annoying is that while the weakest enemies don't do a ton of damage, each hit slows you down even further. So good luck on those time trials where you have to try and avoid enemies, you'll be doing them a lot. I also have yet to see any other character besides archer being able to safetly despose of those exploding enemies without the use of a skill, which while those skills help they don't do much in situations where there are lot of them and you can't just run away till the cooldown is finished because, that's right, they're faster and will catch up with you. This is where I started to feel like the scaling for single player wasn't quite right.
What caused me the most grief, however, were the challenges. By the end of it all I was ready to slam my laptop against the wall. These trials require absolute perfection at times, sometimes being borderline impossible. And since it requires you to get an extra 15 crystals to get to the final boss you have no choice but doing some of the most difficult ones. I'd suggest not doing what I did by finishing this game in one seven hour sitting, and instead do these challenges in spurts, for the sake of your sanity.
Speaking of the final boss, and i'm not going to spoil anything, I have to say it was my favorite part of the whole game. The game's music is great, but the music for the final boss really got me into the mood, it made me feel like I was in the middle of a legendary struggle, so much that even after all the frustration that had been built up prior to it, I didn't rage once at a death no matter how close I came to defeating him that run. Unfortunately it is where I encountered the only bug I found in the entire game, and made the last half of the fight childs play(he got stuck running in place in the middle of the room). However I still left that boss fight feeling accomplished, which is what really matters in the end.
Now my favorite aspect of the game was not the gameplay, but rather the voice acting and story. Yes, the story isn't the main focus of the game, just a given reason to explain why you are doing all this, but I really enjoyed the bits of it you got after every trial. And the voice acting was just wonderful. Balfus was masterfuly done in my opinion, which is good considering he's with you the entirety of the game. However, while I do enjoy the story, it never felt complete. Slight spoilers in this next bit, i'll mark it for those who want to avoid it.
For all my gripes and frustration with this game, it is actually quite good and i'd recommend it to play with friends, but only do challenge if you have extreme patience or like that kind of challenge. It's a challenge experience but one that draws you in and makes you want to complete it and it never feels old, you are always coming across something new and fresh in each trial. So if you are a very casual gamer, i'd stay away, but if you are one who likes being challenged, go for it.

However, it does come with a big downside when the dialog gets a little heavy and the characters are stuck with a neutral expression. This seems to be an intentional choice, but it doesn’t always work for me.
The audio is good and used well to set the mood, but rarely stood out to me as great. I wish that the game had used varying text typing audio to convey emotion in the dialog that the faces weren’t capable of doing. Again, this may be intentional choice, but seems like a missed opportunity.
The story mostly hangs on the characters, each with a unique voice and motivation. They treat the characters as very real with their own tastes, fears, shames, and ideas. Conflicts are misunderstandings and growth happens when they learn more about each other. The plot itself is very simple for most of the game, a series of parties and events. Then there’s a big unveiling of narrative near the end that drags out a little too long and still leaves many questions unanswered.
I enjoyed spending time with these characters and seeing them at their best and worst. The town feels like a real place to visit. I’m a little too old to relate directly with the young adult angst, but it’s interesting seeing those familiar feeling from a distance.

This isn't very much a game. Definitely visual novel territory.

Audio: The voice acting quality is really hit or miss. Minor parts like the Bouncer and Froyo guy have such poor audio quality. The Froyo guy also has 3 different voices. It's all over the place. There's not much audio besides the voice acting in the game.
Graphics: Well done. I really feel like the graphics work for the game are in a good place. My only complaints would be that the pixels are far too zoomed in. Something akin to the resolution of the PC-88 could have really improved the way the game looks and the details the artist could have included. The other complain, the fonts. Again, I feel that not having the pixels so large would have accommodated a much easier to read font. These are minor grievances overall. I did like the graphics.
Characters: They're all jerks. They really are. Turing is constantly talking down to you, being a smug little jerk. He's SO superior. You and your house are just insignificant to him... BUT he NEEDS your help, he can't do this on his own! You have to help him! ... BUT you don't actually help him at all. Your character doesn't interact with the world, at all. All the dialog options could have just been covered by Turing. Turing does all the talking. Turing does all the desicion making in the game. Turing does EVERYTHING. You're just there on a leash to press the Space bar every so often to advance dialog.
TOMCAT talks down to you, calling you rude, if you don't understand all the mumbo-jumbo they and Turing are conversing about. My character is SUPPOSED to be a freelance reviewer. I shouldn't know all these terms. Talking to me like I'm some kind of ingrate for not understanding really rubbed me the wrong way.
Jess is just a total sourpuss. Literally. She pretty much screams at you, calls you a bigot and a racist just for DARING to speak to her and ask her if she knows TOMCAT.
I met Dr. Fairlight briefly, and he talked down to me too, thankfully. Good thing the story is predictable enough that I know he's the main villain, so the talking down was acceptable in this instance. Why was he in my room just hanging out? "Oh the admins told you to?" Admins wouldn't ask you to wait in a random hospital room with sick patients just to wait for an appointment.
Other: The text moves at an incredibly slow pace, way slower than the voice actors. I'd often have to press Space to have the text fill in, just to keep up with the voice acting.
The game hassles you to "save frequently" because it doesn't auto-save, but then goes on 40 minute tirades of dialog and doesn't give you a chance to save. Also, it's not like you can die, or that there's any actual puzzles to solve for saving to even matter. Saving just prevents you from having to go through 40 minutes of button mashing to get through dialog.
The name, pronouns and diet options seemed entirely unnecessary and just a way to cater to people. I don't even remember the game USING the pronouns. None of the characters even seem to address the main character and only address Turing anyways, so it all seems for not.

PROS:
-Wonderful encouters with a wide range of people.

-Weapons have impactful sounds. First time playing, I was wondering for like 40 minutes and suddenly a shotgun pops off nearby and my heart starts racing.

I tried to love this game, but the spark was missing. I wish I had dreamt about the world, obsessed over the story and clicked "New game" again as sooned as the credits rolled out.
There were moments of brilliance in the companions' storylines (Grieving Mother and especially Durance. Not Kreia's level of awesomeness, but Avellone did a damn fine job on that priest), gorgeous writing, a few great twists on the classical D&D setting, a vivid world full of lore and gods, but ultimately, the storytelling fell flat.
Playing this game felt like watching the landscape through a train's window: the scenery was beautiful but the emotional engagement was nonexistent. I never cared about the characters I met. I felt like a stranger in a strange land, and though the plot was increasingly unsatisfying, I powered through, hoping for a wonderful resolution which never came.
Since the dev dream team had complete creative freedom and a great starting concept, it's a shame to accept that this ambitious game ended up being "just a solid 7/10 if you're a fan of the genre".
This game is fan service for veterans of Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale and Planescape: Torment. If you know all these games inside out and are a completionist, you will enjoy Pillars of Eternity.
If you discovered Obsidian through newer games such as NWN 2, KotoR 2, or Fallout New Vegas or got used to fast-paced RPGs such as Dragon Age Origins, The Witcher, The Elder Scrolls or the Mass Effect series, don't be surprised if Pillars of Eternity leans heavily towards the old school:
- there are a few huge difficulty spikes coming out of the blue,
- you will spend a lot of time running back and forth between areas,
- you will spend a lot of time reading the quest journal and bestiary to figure things out,
- you will spend a lot of time reading dialogues (the prose is magnificent, but you'll stop reading the golden characters backstories soon enough),
- you will spend a lot of time getting your guys unstuck from the terrain,
- you will spend a lot of time staring at loading screens (about ~3 hours out of my 50 hours playtime).

The only problem I have with it is there's no romance system and far less interparty banter than I expected. I've heard the excuses, Obsidian, and I consider them just that.
On the other hand, this is the best isometric party rpg since Baldur's Gate 2... that I can think of immediately off the top of my head, at least. You should buy it. Play it. Play it again. Keep playing.

I am giving Stranded Deep a tentatively positive review. While the core of the game, expolration, resource gathering, and general surviving is very good in a design frame work there is still a lot that needs to be done. However, these major aspects are quite compelling.
While I am aware that this is an early access game, it is just that, still a game in development.
With the many aspects of the game that are appealing to me, there does lack a sense of finality or of something more than some self motivated, "I know what ill do...." sorts of things. Again, this goes back to the unfinished nature of the game.
At this point I will say that there is active development, which is a good thing, yet it seems to be focused on conquering technical challenges and a gradual building of features.
As a fan of the gaming industry and game development, I do support this title and everything that it becomes, yet I feel that this game is taking a "Minecraft" style approach with a big focus on player freedom, but not as much on player purpose. Please, don't get me wrong, I highly enjoy these kinds of explorative games. I know things will change, i hope that many of the lack-luster aspects will fall away with time, but as it stands right now, its slow going.
One final note, is that there is not a clear guide, in-game, to the crafting system. Many of the more advanced crafting items made me look to a guide to discover just how to go about constructing them.

I do recommend this game but, there are a lot of things wrong! I don't hate this game for what it is, I hate it for what it isn't!
List of things that I think are great about this game:
1. Open world zombie game.
2. Survival elements.
3. Drivable cars.
4. Great melee and shooting mechanics.
5. Multiple home bases to choose from.
6. Resource and community management.
There are probably many more, just can't think of it right now.
List of things I feel are wrong with this game:
1. The character generator really sucks!  With all of the possible variations you could have, it still generates the same dozen people and it drives me crazy! Example: I find these 2 guys that are just friends (not even related) and they are the same guy: same face, hair, clothes and voice! Just different names. I have 6 people in my camp that look exactly the same!
2. Way too many of the same cars around. Could really use more variety. Even with the selection the game has, they aren't spread out well enough.
3. Though the shooting is good, aiming with the mouse still doesn't feel quite right. Its very obvious that it's a console port. Makes for bad aiming sometimes, especially when trying to get head shots!
4. Too many, very obvious immersion breaking continuity errors. They would take forever to list.
5. Bad design of home base building areas. There are areas in the base that you could obviously build there, but the game won't let you. I'm not really sure why they designed it that way.
6. No CO-OP! You can tell that this game was designed to be an MMO. But still doesn't have a multiplayer feature at all, and that really sucks!
7. There are some really bad graphical problems with this game. Frame rate issues even on a monster rig. Lag issues. Way too many graphical glitches!
With all that said, I still recommend the game to zombie and survival game enthusiasts. If you can look past all those problems, this game is fun as hell and I can't think of any other game like it!!

Which one is better, Terraria or Starbound..? It's hard to say as both play out very different from one another. Where Terraria's main focus is on combat, Starbound is mostly about exploring and building. So just because you liked the former, doesn't mean you like the latter and vice versa. In the end it comes down to your personal preference and what you expect from them.
So what sets Starbound aside and makes it unique.. For starters it offers a huge galaxy with thousands of planets. Each one with its own different themes and the possibility of a wide variety of cities and dungeons. This can be everything from underwater metropolises to small farming villages, ruins of forgotten civilizations, creepy dungeons and hightec research labs. Even beneth a planets surface there's strange settlements and secrets to uncover as well.
These places will be populated with different races and animals. There are seven playable main races who all got their own lore and backstories. This is mostly presented in the form of different codices you can gather and read (some of which are pretty hilarious). Besides that there are numerous sub-races and factions running their own agenda. Some peaceful, others not so much. It's even possible to have some of them move in and offer unique supplies or serve as guards.
This combined with some beautifully hand crafted metroidvania like missions where you undertake puzzles, dodge traps and fight bosses helps make Starbound a really interesting world to explore. All in all its a very colourful and diverse univers.
Starbound also allows for very different playstyles and almost everything is optional in order to progress. You can build villages or huge farms for profit, explore for resources or mine them, become self sufficient or survive by trade, do quests and gather a crew or roll as a lone wolf.. All valid options in order to survive. This also means your expected to find your own path and as such, there's very limited handholding. Which might throw some people off as there won't be a clear indicator on what to do next besides the overall objective. It's sorta like a "create your own adventure" story wherein the missions only serve as stretch goals.
Now combat ain't as streamlined as in most games of this genre. It's more a part of a whole, rather than the main focus. Building, farming crops, questing and exploring is as much a part of Starbound as combat is. So if your looking for a hack'n'slash combat focused experience, then you'll be disappointed and proberly find the game lacking as it can seem a little simplistic.
Don't get me wrong, combat in Starbound ain't bad. It's just different. For example there's no ammunition to speak of, instead every weapon draws from a commen energy pool. Also most weapons come with a special attack and the ability to dual wield them in almost any way you see fit. There's a wide variety of awesome and crazy weapons to help make it interesting like swords, spears, hammers, pistols, shotguns, sniper rifles, 'nade launches, flamethrowes, rocket launchers etc etc..
Starbound is a game suited for people that like to build, explore and create their own little adventures. If you take the time to enjoy its univers and all the different concepts it has to offer, then you'll get a plesant and enjoyable experience.
Closing argument and metaphor..
If Terraria is like a lego technic set, where you have to follow a specific schematic in order to achieve your goal. Then Starbound is a huge box of lego blocks that requires your imagination to reach it instead. It really only comes down to what you prefer.
